# Sūrah al-Naḥl (Chapter 16) — Expanded Verse-by-Verse Commentary

## Introduction to the Sūrah

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Chapter of the Bee and the Chapter of Blessings**

Sūrah al-Naḥl, "The Bee," is the sixteenth chapter of the Qur'an and contains 128 verses. It takes its name from a single passage near its center — verses 68 and 69 — where God is described as "revealing" to the bee its way of life, and where the honey that comes forth from its belly is called "a healing for mankind." That so large and varied a sūrah should be named after so small a creature is itself a lesson. The Qur'an repeatedly directs the human gaze downward and outward toward what is ordinarily overlooked — the drop of fluid, the seed, the ant, the gnat, the bee — and asks the observer to find in these the fingerprints of the Creator. A civilization that learned to see God's wisdom in a bee's flight would be far less likely to be dazzled into idolatry by the size and power of stone statues or human tyrants.

The classical commentators recorded a second name for the sūrah. Al-Qurṭubī notes that some of the early scholars called it Sūrat al-Niʿam, "the Chapter of Blessings," because no other chapter enumerates the favors of God upon humankind so systematically, so patiently, and so concretely. Cattle, horses, rain, crops, olives, dates, grapes, night and day, sun and moon, the sea and its fish and pearls, ships, mountains, rivers, roads, landmarks, stars, milk, honey, spouses, children, houses, tents, wool, shade, caves, garments, armor — the sūrah is almost an inventory of ordinary life, and its central claim in verse 18 is that this inventory can never be finished: *"And were you to count the blessings of God, you could not number them."*

**When and Where It Was Revealed**

The sūrah is Makkan by the near-unanimous judgment of the scholars, revealed in the late Makkan period not long before the Emigration (Hijrah) to Madinah. Several of its passages presuppose the intense persecution of the final Makkan years: the reference to those who "emigrate for the sake of God, after having been wronged" (v. 41), usually connected with the earlier emigration to Abyssinia; the verse on those coerced into words of disbelief while their hearts are at peace in faith (v. 106), connected with the torture of ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir; and the closing verses on restraint and patience under provocation (vv. 126–128).

Because of this, a number of early authorities held that certain verses were Madinan. The last three verses (126–128) are said by many, including Ibn Kathīr and al-Ṭabarī in reporting the opinions before them, to have been revealed after the Battle of Uḥud in the third year after the Hijrah, when the Prophet ﷺ saw the mutilated body of his uncle Ḥamzah and the Muslims vowed to retaliate in kind. Verse 110, which promises mercy to "those who emigrated after being oppressed, then strove and were patient," is also sometimes assigned to Madinah. Other verses proposed as Madinan by one authority or another include 41, 95–97, and 112. Al-Rāzī noted that a Madinan dating for the final verses is not certain, since the sūrah reads as a unity and the closing counsel of patience fits perfectly the situation of a persecuted Makkan community. Whatever the exact chronology, the working assumption of this commentary is that the sūrah addresses, first and foremost, a community under pressure, being taught to look at the world as a field of God's gifts rather than as a battlefield of human power.

**The Argument of the Sūrah as a Whole**

Al-Naḥl is not a random collection of themes. It moves with an inner logic that the reader should keep in mind while studying each verse.

It opens with a solemn warning: "The Command of God is coming; so seek not to hasten it" (v. 1). The Makkans had mocked the promised Judgment because it did not arrive on their schedule. The sūrah's answer is not, at first, to argue about the Hereafter directly. Instead, it turns to the present world and asks the doubters to look at it honestly. Who sends down the rain? Who created the cattle? Who set the mountains and the stars? The first forty verses build a case from the visible to the invisible: the One who alone creates, sustains, and knows is the only One entitled to worship, and the only One capable of resurrecting.

The middle of the sūrah exposes the incoherence of the idolaters. They dedicate a share of God's provision to idols that "know not" (v. 56). They attribute daughters to God while burying their own daughters alive (vv. 57–59). They excuse themselves by saying "Had God willed, we would not have worshipped aught apart from Him" (v. 35) — using the doctrine of divine will to escape moral responsibility. The sūrah answers each of these with reasoning, parable, and, above all, with a renewed catalogue of blessings that leaves the ungrateful with no excuse.

Then comes the passage that many consider the ethical heart of the whole Qur'an: verse 90, "Truly God commands justice, virtue, and giving to kinsfolk, and He forbids indecency, wrong, and rebelliousness." The Umayyad caliph ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz (d. 101/720) ordered that this verse be recited at the end of every Friday sermon in place of the political cursing that had crept into the pulpit — a practice that continues in mosques around the world to this day. Around it cluster the verses on oaths and covenants (91–96), the promise of "a good life" to every believing man and woman who works righteousness (97), and the instruction to seek refuge from Satan before reciting the Qur'an (98).

The final movement returns to the opponents' accusations — that the Prophet ﷺ fabricates the revelation, that a foreign man is teaching him — and answers them. It presents the parable of the secure and prosperous town that became ungrateful and was clothed in "the garment of hunger and fear" (v. 112), an unmistakable mirror held up to Makkah. It clarifies the dietary law and forbids inventing prohibitions in God's name (vv. 114–119). It presents Abraham as "a community" unto himself, a grateful monotheist whom the Prophet ﷺ is commanded to follow (vv. 120–123). And it closes with the method of calling to God — "with wisdom and goodly exhortation" (v. 125) — and with the discipline of the wronged: retaliate only in like measure, and better still, be patient, "for God is with those who are reverent and those who are virtuous" (v. 128).

**Why Gratitude Is the Key to the Whole Sūrah**

If one word unlocks al-Naḥl, it is *shukr*, gratitude, and its opposite, *kufr*, which means both "disbelief" and "ingratitude." The Arabic root *k-f-r* originally means to cover something over, as a farmer covers seed with soil; a *kāfir* is one who covers the truth or covers a favor as though it had never been given. The sūrah's method is therefore psychological before it is theological. It does not begin by demanding assent to abstract doctrines. It begins by making the reader notice — really notice — the milk in the cup, the shade over the head, the wool on the back, the child in the arms. Once a person has truly noticed a gift, the question "From whom?" arises naturally, and the further question "What does the Giver ask of me?" follows on its heels.

This is why the sūrah alternates blessings with warnings. Gratitude is not merely a pleasant feeling; it is the correct response to reality. Ingratitude is not merely rudeness; it is a falsification of reality, a lie told with one's whole life. The Qur'an treats the ungrateful person the way a wise physician treats a patient who insists he is healthy while his body fails: not with flattery, but with clear description and honest warning.

**How This Commentary Proceeds**

What follows is a verse-by-verse expanded commentary on all 128 verses. Each verse is treated as an independent, complete discussion, even where the source text grouped several verses together. For each verse the commentary draws on the Arabic vocabulary and grammar of the text explained in plain language, on cross-references to other passages of the Qur'an cited in their actual wording, on authenticated sayings of the Prophet ﷺ with their collections identified, on the views of the classical commentators — al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Qurṭubī, al-Rāzī, al-Zamakhsharī, Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Taymiyyah, and others — and on the living reasoning that connects a seventh-century Arabian text to the moral and psychological life of a human being today.

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:1

> **The Command of God is coming; so seek not to hasten it. Glory be to Him and exalted is He above the partners they ascribe.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Chapter That Opens With an Arrival**

Most sūrahs that speak of blessings begin gently. Al-Naḥl does not. Its first words are a verdict already in motion: *atā amru Allāh* — "the Command of God has come." The verb *atā* is in the past tense, though the event it describes — the Judgment, or the punishment that precedes it — still lies in the future. Arabic, like the language of the prophets generally, uses the past tense for a future event when that event is so certain that it may be spoken of as already accomplished. The classical grammarians call this usage *taḥqīq al-wuqūʿ*, "confirming the occurrence." One finds the same device in 54:1, *"The Hour has drawn nigh, and the moon has split,"* and in 39:68–69, which describe the Resurrection in the past tense as though the reader were standing in the middle of it. The listener is meant to feel that the thing is already on its way, that its arrival is not a question of whether but only of when.

Al-Ṭabarī explains the choice of tense plainly: the Command has "come" in the sense that its coming is near and inevitable, and God speaks of what He has decreed as though it were already present, since nothing can prevent it. Al-Zamakhsharī adds a psychological note: the past tense is used to make the arrogant deniers feel the nearness of what they scoff at, so that they may stop treating it as a distant rumor.

**What Is "the Command of God"?**

The word *amr* carries two senses in Arabic, and both are present in the Qur'an. It can mean a "command" in the sense of an order — as when God says *"His Command, when He desires a thing, is only to say to it 'Be!' and it is"* (36:82) — and it can mean an "affair" or "matter," an event that God has decreed. Here the commentators offer two main identifications, and they are not in conflict.

The first is that "the Command of God" refers to the Hour, the Day of Resurrection and Judgment. This reading is supported by the structure of the sūrah, which repeatedly returns to the reality of resurrection (vv. 21, 25, 27, 38–39, 77, 84–89, 111), and by parallel verses in which the arrival of God's "Command" clearly means the end of the world, such as 40:78: *"So when the Command of God comes, judgment is passed in truth, and the falsifiers are lost there."*

The second is that it refers to the punishment threatened against the Makkans in this world — the defeat, humiliation, and loss that would in fact overtake the leaders of Quraysh at Badr some years later. In the Qur'an, the "coming of God's Command" is used in this sense too, as when Noah is told that the Flood would begin *"when Our Command comes and the oven gushes forth"* (11:40; cf. 23:27).

Ibn Kathīr harmonizes the two: the Command that is coming is the Hour, and the punishments that fall on stubborn nations in this world are its forerunners and previews. Whether the reader has in mind the death that will end his own life, the collapse that ends a tyrannical society, or the trumpet that ends the world, the principle is one: God's decree is not slowed by human mockery.

**The Occasion: A Threat Mocked**

The commentators, including al-Zamakhsharī and al-Qurṭubī, connect this verse with the Makkans' reaction to earlier warnings. When the verse *"The Hour has drawn nigh"* (54:1) was revealed, the disbelievers of Quraysh reportedly stopped in their tracks and waited, half-alarmed, to see what would happen. When days passed and nothing happened, they turned the warning into a joke, saying in effect, "We see nothing of what you promised — bring it, then, if you are truthful." The Qur'an records this very taunt in several places:

> *"They say, 'When will this promise be fulfilled, if you are truthful?'"* (Qur'an 10:48; 21:38; 27:71; 34:29; 36:48)

and even the more defiant

> *"O God, if this is the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky, or bring us a painful punishment."* (Qur'an 8:32)

Verse 16:1 is the answer. God does not respond to a demand for haste by hastening; He responds by affirming that the matter is already decided and by forbidding the demand itself: *fa-lā tastaʿjilūhu* — "so seek not to hasten it."

**Why Human Beings Demand Haste — and Why It Is Foolish**

The verb *istaʿjala* is on the tenth verbal form, which typically expresses seeking or demanding something. *ʿAjal* is haste, and *istiʿjāl* is the seeking of haste — wanting a thing before its time. The Qur'an makes this a signature weakness of human nature:

> *"Man was created of haste. Soon shall I show you My signs; so seek not to hasten Me."* (Qur'an 21:37)

> *"And man prays for evil as he prays for good, and man is ever hasty."* (Qur'an 17:11)

Three kinds of people ask God to hurry. The scoffer demands haste because he does not believe the threat is real; his demand is a form of argument, as if to say that a punishment that has not yet come will never come. The Qur'an exposes the logical error in this: delay is not disproof. A creditor who gives a debtor time has not cancelled the debt. The impatient believer, by contrast, may ask God to hasten judgment because he is suffering and wants relief; the Qur'an gently corrects this as well, teaching that God's timing contains wisdom that the sufferer cannot see. And the third kind, the merely curious, want to see wonders. To all three the reply is the same: the matter is coming; your job is not to schedule it but to prepare for it.

There is a mercy hidden in this prohibition. Al-Rāzī observes that if God responded to demands for haste, the very people making the demands would be the first to perish, with no opportunity to repent. Delay is respite, and respite is grace. The Qur'an says elsewhere:

> *"And were God to hasten evil for people as they would hasten good, their term would already have been decreed for them."* (Qur'an 10:11)

Every day the Hour does not come is a day in which a heart may turn. The scoffer who says "bring it on" is, in reality, asking God to close the door of repentance in his own face.

**"Glory Be to Him" — The Verse Turns From Threat to Praise**

The second half of the verse shifts register entirely. *Subḥānahu wa-taʿālā ʿammā yushrikūn* — "Glory be to Him, and exalted is He above the partners they ascribe." The word *subḥān* comes from a root meaning to swim or glide swiftly through water or air; in the religious vocabulary it came to mean declaring God free and far removed from every deficiency, as though the mind moved rapidly away from any unworthy thought about Him. To say *subḥān Allāh* is to affirm that God is beyond weakness, beyond need, beyond partner, beyond every likeness to created things.

*Taʿālā* is from the root of height and exaltation; the form implies rising far above. Together the two words declare that the God who is coming in judgment is not a rival to the idols, competing for space with them; He is on another plane entirely.

Why does a verse about the coming Judgment end with a declaration of God's transcendence over "the partners they ascribe"? The commentators suggest a precise logic. The Makkans' demand for haste rested on a false picture of God — a picture in which He was one power among many, whose threats could be tested, whose deadlines could be mocked, and whose worship could be shared with statues. To deny the Hour was itself a form of *shirk*, association, because it implied that the idols they trusted could shield them from consequences. The verse strips away the picture. The One whose Command is coming is glorified above everything they set beside Him; therefore nothing they set beside Him can delay, prevent, or soften what is coming.

The phrase *ʿammā yushrikūn* is grammatically capable of two readings, and both are intended. It may mean "above that which they associate" (the idols themselves) or "above their act of associating" (the sin of *shirk*). God is exalted above the idols, which are lifeless things He created, and He is exalted above being affected by the idolaters' associations, which harm only those who commit them. The same closing phrase occurs in 16:3, 10:18, 23:92, 27:63, 28:68, 30:40, and 39:67, always with this double sense.

**The Theology of the Opening in Simple Terms**

Put plainly, the verse teaches four things. First, judgment is certain — so certain that God speaks of it as already arrived. Second, its timing belongs to God alone, and demanding it be hurried is both irrational and self-destructive. Third, God is free of every defect and every partner; He is not a power to be bargained with or tested. Fourth, and by implication, the correct response to the coming Command is not to ask "When?" but "Am I ready?"

The Prophet ﷺ expressed this reorientation in a well-known exchange. A man came to him and asked, "When is the Hour?" The Prophet replied:

> *"And what have you prepared for it?"* (al-Bukhārī 6171; Muslim 2639)

The man answered that he had prepared no great quantity of prayer or fasting, but that he loved God and His Messenger. The Prophet said: *"You will be with those whom you love."* The question of timing was set aside; the question of readiness and love was placed at the center. That is exactly the movement of 16:1.

**A Living Application**

Every human being has a private version of "the Command of God" approaching: death, which the Prophet ﷺ called the individual's own "Hour." Most of us treat it exactly as the Makkans treated the promised Judgment — as a rumor to be dismissed because it has not yet arrived. We scoff at it not with words but with habits: procrastinated repentance, unrepaired relationships, unpaid debts to God and to people. The verse asks for a different posture, one that neither panics nor demands, neither morbidly wishes for the end nor pretends it will not come. It is the posture of a traveler who knows that the train departs at a fixed hour he cannot see on any board, and who therefore keeps his bag packed and his affairs in order — living fully in the present while never forgetting the destination.

And it asks for one more thing: that even the thought of judgment should lead to praise. The verse does not end in dread; it ends in *subḥānahu wa-taʿālā*. The believer who contemplates the coming Command is meant to arrive, by the end of the thought, at glorification — because the One who judges is also the One who is free of injustice, free of caprice, free of every partner who might corrupt His verdict. A judgment by such a Judge is not something a sincere heart needs to fear so much as something it can trust.

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:2

> **He sends down angels with the Spirit from His Command to whomsoever He will among His servants, "Give warning that there is no god but I, so reverence Me!"**

**Expanded Commentary**

**From the Coming Command to the Sent-Down Command**

The first verse spoke of God's Command *coming* toward humanity in judgment. The second verse speaks of God's Command *descending* to humanity in revelation. The contrast is deliberate and merciful. Before the Command arrives as verdict, it is sent as warning. The same word, *amr*, appears in both verses: in verse 1 as the decree that will end the matter, in verse 2 as the source from which the Spirit of guidance is sent. A just Judge does not spring His law upon people without notice; He publishes it first through messengers. Verse 2 is thus the foundation of every claim the sūrah will later make about human accountability. People can be held responsible for the coming Command because the sent-down Command reached them beforehand.

**The Vocabulary of Descent: *Yunazzilu***

The verb *yunazzilu* is the second verbal form of *n-z-l*, "to come down." The second form typically indicates gradualness and repetition — sending down piece by piece, again and again. The Qur'an uses this form for its own revelation, which came down over twenty-three years in response to events, and it uses the fourth form *anzala* (a single, complete act of sending) for its descent as a whole on the Night of Power (97:1). Here the gradual form fits the content: God sends the angels with the Spirit continually, to messenger after messenger across history, and to the final Prophet ﷺ verse after verse. Revelation is not a one-time thunderclap but a sustained conversation between heaven and earth.

**Who Are the Angels, and What Is "the Spirit"?**

The angels sent down are, in the first instance, Gabriel (Jibrīl), the angel charged with revelation, as al-Jalālayn and most commentators specify; the plural "angels" honors his rank and may include the angels who accompany him, as the ḥadīth literature describes at the descent of certain great sūrahs. Ibn Kathīr notes that the plural may also be understood in light of the angels' role as a general category: the entire angelic realm serves God's Command, and Gabriel is its chief in the matter of revelation.

The word *rūḥ*, "spirit," is one of the richest in the Qur'an, and the commentators have discussed its meaning here at length. The soundest view, held by al-Qurṭubī, al-Ṭabarī, and others, is that "the Spirit" in this verse means revelation itself — the Qur'an and, more broadly, the divine message given to every prophet. Several verses support this identification directly:

> *"And thus have We revealed to you a Spirit from Our Command. You knew not what the Book was, nor faith, but We made it a light by which We guide whomsoever We will of Our servants."* (Qur'an 42:52)

> *"He casts the Spirit from His Command upon whomsoever He will of His servants, that he may warn of the Day of Meeting."* (Qur'an 40:15)

The second of these verses is nearly a twin of 16:2 — the same Spirit, the same "from His Command," the same "whomsoever He will of His servants," and the same purpose of warning. Together they establish that in the Qur'an's own vocabulary, revelation is "a Spirit from God's Command."

Why is revelation called a Spirit? Al-Qurṭubī gives the classical answer: as the spirit gives life to the body, revelation gives life to the heart. A body without spirit is a corpse, however handsome; a heart without revelation is dead, however clever. The Qur'an makes this analogy explicit:

> *"Is he who was dead, and We gave him life and made for him a light by which he walks among people, like one whose likeness is in darkness from which he never emerges?"* (Qur'an 6:122)

Ibn Kathīr, commenting on that verse, identifies the "life" as faith and the "light" as the Qur'an. Verse 16:2 tells us where that life comes from: it descends from God's Command, carried by angels, to His chosen servants.

A second, related meaning is that "the Spirit" is the angel Gabriel himself, who is called *al-Rūḥ al-Amīn*, "the Trustworthy Spirit" (26:193), and *Rūḥ al-Qudus*, "the Holy Spirit" (16:102; 2:87). On this reading, the verse means God sends the angels with Gabriel at their head. The two readings are not opposed: Gabriel is the bearer, and revelation is what he bears; both are "spirit" in that both bring life from God.

**"From His Command" — The World of the Spirit**

The phrase *min amrihi*, "from His Command," ties the Spirit to God's creative and legislative authority. The Qur'an elsewhere places the Spirit within the domain of the divine Command in a way that is deliberately reticent:

> *"They ask you about the Spirit. Say, 'The Spirit is from the Command of my Lord, and you have not been given knowledge save a little.'"* (Qur'an 17:85)

Classical Muslim thought developed from verses like these the distinction between *ʿālam al-khalq*, "the world of creation" — the visible, measurable world of bodies — and *ʿālam al-amr*, "the world of the Command" — the realm of spirit, angels, and revelation, which comes into being directly by God's word "Be!" without material process. Whatever one makes of this technical vocabulary, the plain teaching of 16:2 is that revelation is not a product of human culture, psychology, or literary genius. It comes from above the world, from the same Command that brought the world into existence.

**"To Whomsoever He Will Among His Servants"**

This clause answers an objection the Makkans raised repeatedly: Why him? Why should a man from among us, an orphan, neither the wealthiest nor the most powerful, receive revelation? The Qur'an records their complaint:

> *"And they said, 'Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a great man from one of the two towns?'"* (Qur'an 43:31)

The answer given in 43:32 is decisive: *"Is it they who apportion the mercy of your Lord?"* Verse 16:2 says the same thing in advance. The choice of a messenger rests with God alone — *ʿalā man yashāʾu*, "upon whomsoever He wills." Al-Ṭabarī explains that this refers to God's selection of prophets and messengers, and that no one earns prophethood by wealth, lineage, or effort; it is pure divine appointment. The Qur'an states the principle in 6:124: *"God knows best where to place His message."*

Yet the phrase also contains a quiet dignity: *min ʿibādihi*, "among His servants." The prophets are not demigods. They are servants — the highest title the Qur'an gives to any human being. Muhammad ﷺ is called "His servant" precisely at the moments of his greatest honor: the Night Journey (17:1) and the descent of the Qur'an (18:1; 25:1). Revelation is given to a servant so that servanthood, not lordship, becomes the model for those who follow him.

**The Content of All Revelation in Seven Words**

Now the verse gives the message itself, and it is startling in its brevity: *an andhirū annahu lā ilāha illā anā fa-ttaqūn* — "Give warning that there is no god but I, so reverence Me." Everything else in scripture — law, story, promise, threat — unfolds from this kernel.

Notice first the command *andhirū*, "warn." The root *n-dh-r* means to warn of an approaching danger. The prophets are called *mundhirūn*, warners, before they are called anything else, because their first duty is to alert people to a reality they are ignoring. A warner is not a salesman; he does not flatter. He is more like the man who sees a fire starting behind a crowd and shouts. Whether the crowd thanks him is not his concern; his concern is that they hear.

Notice second that the warning is not "there will be punishment" but "there is no god but I." The greatest danger facing a human being is not any particular sin; it is the misdirection of the whole self toward what is not God. From that root every other evil grows. Correct the direction, and the branches begin to heal on their own.

The Qur'an confirms that this was the message of every prophet without exception:

> *"And We sent no messenger before you but that We revealed to him, 'There is no god but I, so worship Me.'"* (Qur'an 21:25)

The parallel between 21:25 and 16:2 is exact except for one word: 21:25 says "so worship Me" (*fa-ʿbudūn*) and 16:2 says "so reverence Me" or "so be mindful of Me" (*fa-ttaqūn*). The two are inseparable: worship is the act, and *taqwā* is the inner state that keeps the act sincere.

**Why *Taqwā* Follows Necessarily From *Tawḥīd***

The little word *fa-*, "so," in *fa-ttaqūn* carries a logical weight. It means "therefore." If there is no god but God, then it follows that He alone is to be feared, hoped in, and obeyed. Fear of any other power becomes irrational, because no other power is ultimate. Hope in any other patron becomes irrational, because no other patron holds the outcomes. The verse thus presents *taqwā* not as an arbitrary demand but as the only coherent response to the truth of *tawḥīd*.

*Taqwā* itself, from the root *w-q-y*, "to shield or protect," means placing a protective barrier between oneself and what harms — ultimately, between oneself and God's displeasure. A useful picture is a person walking a narrow mountain road at night with a lamp: he is not paralyzed with terror, but he is alert, watching every step, because he knows the drop is real. That alertness is *taqwā*. The prophets are sent to give people the lamp and to tell them the drop is real.

**Why the Message Comes Through Angels and Men, Not Directly**

A thoughtful reader might ask why God, who is nearer to a person than his jugular vein (50:16), sends His message through a chain — Command, Spirit, angel, prophet — rather than speaking directly to each human heart. The Qur'an answers that direct speech is not the ordinary human capacity:

> *"It is not for any human being that God should speak to him except by revelation, or from behind a veil, or by sending a messenger to reveal, by His leave, what He wills."* (Qur'an 42:51)

The chain is a mercy suited to human weakness. It also serves a moral purpose: it creates the conditions for a free response. Guidance delivered through a fellow human, with signs sufficient for the sincere but not overwhelming for the stubborn, leaves room for choice, and choice is what makes reward and accountability meaningful. Had God shown each person the unseen directly, faith would collapse into mere sight, and the test of this world would be over before it began.

**A Ḥadīth on the Spirit's Descent**

The believers were given a glimpse of what this descent looks like in the ḥadīth of ʿĀʾishah recorded by al-Bukhārī and Muslim, in which al-Ḥārith ibn Hishām asked the Prophet ﷺ how revelation came to him. He replied:

> *"Sometimes it comes to me like the ringing of a bell, and that is the hardest on me; then it leaves me, and I have retained what he said. And sometimes the angel appears to me as a man and speaks to me, and I retain what he says."* ʿĀʾishah added: *"I saw him receiving revelation on an intensely cold day, and when it left him his forehead was streaming with sweat."* (al-Bukhārī 2; Muslim 2333)

This report grounds the abstract language of 16:2 in physical reality. The descent of the Spirit was not a poetic metaphor for inspiration; it was an event with weight, witnessed by others, leaving marks on the body of the one who received it.

**Practical Meaning for the Reader Today**

Three lessons follow. First, the message that reaches us through the Qur'an is not a human product to be revised by fashion; it comes from the world of God's Command, and it deserves to be received with the seriousness one gives to news from the only source that truly knows. Second, the whole of religion can be carried in the heart in seven words — *lā ilāha illā anā fa-ttaqūn* — and a person overwhelmed by the complexity of religious duties can always return to this center and rebuild outward from it. Third, since the Spirit gives life to hearts as the soul gives life to bodies, a heart that feels dead — cold in prayer, unmoved by wrong, indifferent to the poor — should not be treated as a mystery. It is a heart cut off from the source of its life. The remedy is the same as it was for the first Makkans: return to the Spirit that was sent down, listen to its warning, and let *taqwā* grow from *tawḥīd* again.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:3

> **He created the heavens and the earth in truth. Exalted is He above the partners they ascribe.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The First Sign After the Message**

Having declared in verse 2 that God sends down revelation with the message "there is no god but I," the sūrah immediately begins to prove that claim from the created world. Verse 3 is the opening of the great catalogue of signs that runs through verse 18. The order is instructive. The sūrah starts with the largest possible sign — the heavens and the earth in their entirety — and then descends step by step to the smaller: man from a drop (v. 4), cattle (vv. 5–7), riding animals (v. 8), rain and crops (vv. 10–11), sun and moon (v. 12), the sea (v. 14), mountains and rivers (v. 15), landmarks and stars (v. 16). It is as if the reader were first shown the whole canvas and then led close to examine its brushstrokes.

**"In Truth" — The Two Meanings of *Bi'l-Ḥaqq***

The heart of this verse is the phrase *khalaqa al-samāwāti wa'l-arḍa bi'l-ḥaqq*, "He created the heavens and the earth in truth." The preposition *bi-* with *al-ḥaqq* admits of two closely related meanings, and the commentators generally affirm both.

The first meaning is that creation was accomplished *by means of* truth — that is, by God's true word, His command "Be!" which is never false and never fails. On this reading, the truth is the instrument of creation. The verse that follows shortly, 16:40, states this instrument explicitly: *"Our Word unto a thing, when We desire it, is only to say to it, 'Be!' and it is."*

The second meaning, more commonly emphasized, is that creation was accomplished *with* truth — with purpose, justice, and wisdom, and not in vain, not as sport, not by accident. Al-Ṭabarī explains that God created the heavens and the earth "for a true purpose, and did not create them in play or idleness." The Qur'an itself states this opposition repeatedly:

> *"And We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in play. Had We wished to take up a diversion, We would have taken it from Ourself, if We were to do so."* (Qur'an 21:16–17)

> *"And We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in vain. That is the supposition of those who disbelieve; so woe to those who disbelieve from the Fire!"* (Qur'an 38:27)

> *"Did you think that We created you in vain, and that you would not be returned to Us?"* (Qur'an 23:115)

The last of these verses reveals why the point matters so much in a sūrah about judgment. If the world was created in truth — with purpose — then it must have an outcome in which that purpose is fulfilled. A purposeful creation without a reckoning would be like a trial without a verdict or a story without an ending. Al-Rāzī draws out this argument: the Makkans denied the Resurrection, yet the very structure of existence proclaimed it. To create in truth is to create for a reason, and reason demands that the righteous and the wicked not end up identical in the grave. The Qur'an makes exactly this inference in 45:22: *"And God created the heavens and the earth in truth, and so that every soul may be recompensed for what it has earned, and they will not be wronged."*

**Truth as the Fabric of the World, Not Just Its Origin**

There is a further dimension. To say that the world was created "in truth" means that reality itself is trustworthy. The laws that govern water, fire, growth, and decay are consistent because they come from a Creator who is *al-Ḥaqq*, the Truth, one of His most beautiful Names (22:6, 62; 24:25). This is why the Qur'an so confidently invites investigation of the natural world: it expects that honest study will reveal order, not chaos, because the maker of the world does not deceive. The scientist who trusts that tomorrow's experiment will follow the same laws as today's is, whether he knows it or not, relying on the principle of 16:3.

It also means that falsehood, wherever it appears, is a foreign intrusion into a true world. Lies, idols, injustice, and oppression have no root in the structure of reality; they are parasites on it. This is the ground of the Qur'an's optimism that truth will ultimately prevail: *"Nay, We hurl the truth against falsehood, and it crushes it, and behold, it vanishes"* (21:18).

**The Argument Against Idolatry Contained in the Verse**

The verse ends with the same refrain as verse 1: *taʿālā ʿammā yushrikūn*, "Exalted is He above the partners they ascribe." The repetition is not idle. In verse 1 the phrase followed the mention of God's coming Command; here it follows the mention of His creation. The logic is: the One who created the entire cosmos is obviously beyond comparison with the idols, which did not create a single thing (as verse 20 will state) and were themselves made by human hands. Al-Zamakhsharī notes that the mere mention of the creation of heavens and earth is itself an argument for *tawḥīd*, since even the Makkans admitted that God alone was the Creator:

> *"And if you ask them who created the heavens and the earth, they will surely say, 'God.'"* (Qur'an 31:25; 39:38; 43:9)

The Qur'an's method is to take this admission and press it to its conclusion. If God alone creates, then God alone deserves worship; a being that cannot create cannot be a god. The whole passage from verse 3 to verse 21 is an extended application of this single principle.

**Why "Heavens" Is Plural and "Earth" Is Singular**

The Arabic reads *al-samāwāt*, "the heavens," in the plural, and *al-arḍ*, "the earth," in the singular — a pattern maintained throughout the Qur'an, which speaks of "seven heavens" (2:29; 65:12) but never of "earths" in the plural, though 65:12 says God created "of the earth the like of them." Al-Qurṭubī and others note that the plural "heavens" impresses upon the listener the vastness of what lies above, layer upon layer, while the singular "earth" reminds the human being of how small his own home is within that vastness. The humble creature on this one small earth is being asked to consider the scale of what was made "in truth" and to draw the right conclusion about the size of the One who made it.

**The Contrast With Human Making**

Human beings also "make" things, and we naturally judge a maker by what he makes. Yet everything a human makes is assembled from pre-existing material, according to pre-existing laws, using pre-existing faculties — none of which the maker himself created. God's creation is of a different order: it brings into being the material, the laws, and the makers alike. The commentators frequently point out that the verb *khalaqa* in its full sense — to bring into existence from nothing according to a determined measure — is properly attributed only to God, and that when the Qur'an uses it of Jesus forming a bird from clay (3:49; 5:110), it does so "by God's leave" and in the derivative sense of shaping. Verse 16:17 will make the contrast explicit: *"Is He Who creates like one who creates not?"*

**The Emotional and Psychological Bearing of the Verse**

A person who believes that the universe is an accident will, if consistent, come to believe that his own life is an accident, and from this flows a quiet despair that modern societies know well. Verse 16:3 offers a different foundation. If the heavens and the earth were created in truth — with purpose, by a wise Creator who does not act in vain — then the individual human life set within them also has purpose. Nothing is wasted; no suffering is meaningless; no act of goodness disappears into the void. The verse does not simply inform the mind; it steadies the heart. A child who knows that his home was built with care by someone who loves him walks through it differently from a child who thinks he is squatting in an abandoned building.

**A Practical Discipline of Reflection**

The Qur'an praises those who *"reflect upon the creation of the heavens and the earth"* and conclude *"Our Lord, You did not create this in vain; glory be to You"* (3:191). Notice that their reflection ends in exactly the two phrases of 16:3: the affirmation of purpose ("not in vain") and the glorification of God ("glory be to You"). The Prophet ﷺ himself modeled this. ʿĀʾishah reported that he wept one night reciting these very verses of Āl ʿImrān, and when asked why, he said:

> *"Woe to the one who recites them and does not reflect upon them."* (Ibn Ḥibbān 620; a similar report is in Ibn Abī Ḥātim's Tafsīr)

The believer today can practice this discipline deliberately: at night under the sky, at the sea, on a mountain, or simply looking at the intricacy of a leaf, pausing to say inwardly what the verse says — that this was made in truth, by One exalted above every partner. Such moments are not sentimentality. They are the reactivation of the very faculty of recognition that the sūrah is about to name repeatedly: reflection (v. 11), understanding (v. 12), remembrance (v. 13), and gratitude (v. 14).

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:4

> **He created man from a drop, and behold, he is a manifest adversary.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**From the Cosmos to the Drop**

Verse 3 placed the heavens and the earth before the reader; verse 4 turns abruptly to a single drop of fluid. The shift in scale is a rhetorical masterstroke. The same Creator who set the galaxies in motion also shaped the human being from something so small and unimpressive that people ordinarily wash it away without a thought. The verse forces two realizations at once: how great the Creator is, and how humble the origin of the creature who now presumes to argue with Him.

**The Word *Nuṭfah***

The Arabic *nuṭfah* denotes a small quantity of liquid — a drop, or what remains in the bottom of a vessel after it has been emptied. The root *n-ṭ-f* means to drip or trickle. In the Qur'an the word designates the reproductive fluid from which human life begins, and it appears in more than a dozen passages that trace the stages of human development:

> *"Then We made him a drop in a secure resting place; then We made the drop a clinging clot; then We made the clot a lump of flesh; then We made the lump bones; then We clothed the bones with flesh; then We brought him forth as another creation. So blessed is God, the best of creators."* (Qur'an 23:13–14)

> *"Was he not a drop of fluid emitted? Then he was a clinging clot, and He created and proportioned."* (Qur'an 75:37–38)

> *"Indeed We created man from a mingled drop, to test him; so We made him hearing and seeing."* (Qur'an 76:2)

The word choice is precise. The Qur'an does not say "God created man from a mighty seed" or "from a noble essence." It chooses the humblest possible description. Ibn Kathīr comments that the mention of the drop is intended to remind man of his weakness and lowliness of origin, so that he may not be arrogant. There is a well-known saying attributed to the early scholars, cited by al-Qurṭubī and others, that man should reflect on three moments: what he was made from, what he now carries within him, and what he will become — a drop of fluid, then a vessel of impurities, then a corpse — and ask what in this sequence justifies pride.

**"And Behold, He Is a Manifest Adversary" — The Surprise in the Verse**

The second half of the verse opens with *fa-idhā*, a particle of sudden surprise — "and lo!" or "and behold!" It signals something unexpected. What is unexpected? That the creature made from a mere drop should turn out to be *khaṣīmun mubīn*, "a manifest adversary" — an open, articulate disputant against his own Maker.

The word *khaṣīm* comes from the root *kh-ṣ-m*, "to dispute, to contend, to litigate." A *khaṣm* is one's opponent in a legal case; *khaṣīm* is the intensive form, one who is skilled and persistent in argument. *Mubīn* means clear, open, evident. Together they describe a person who does not merely doubt in private but argues publicly, with eloquence and confidence, against God.

The commentators offer two ways of understanding this description, and both are valid.

The first, adopted by Ibn Kathīr and al-Zamakhsharī, takes it as a rebuke: man was created to be a servant (*"I created jinn and mankind only to worship Me,"* 51:56), yet he has made himself into an opponent. He denies God's power, disputes His revelation, and — the specific target in this sūrah — argues that resurrection is impossible. The verse expresses astonishment at the ingratitude of it: a being who owes his very existence to God, who was nothing but a drop, now stands up in the assembly of Quraysh and lectures the Creator about what He can and cannot do.

The second, noted by al-Rāzī and others, takes it as a description of human capacity rather than only of human sin: from a drop, God brought forth a being capable of reason, speech, and argument — a being who can dispute clearly. On this reading, the verse is itself a proof of divine power. That a mute drop should become a creature who can construct a syllogism is one of the great marvels of creation. The sin is not in having the faculty of argument but in turning it against the One who gave it.

The two readings converge. The more capable the creature, the more shocking its rebellion. Al-Ṭabarī summarizes the sense: God created man from something insignificant, and then man became one who argues against his Lord with the very intelligence his Lord gave him.

**The Occasion: Ubayy ibn Khalaf and the Bone**

Al-Wāḥidī and other collectors of the occasions of revelation report that this verse — and its close parallel in Sūrah Yā Sīn — was revealed in connection with Ubayy ibn Khalaf, one of the fiercest enemies of the Prophet ﷺ in Makkah. He is said to have come to the Prophet holding a decayed bone, which he crumbled in his hand and blew into the air, saying, "O Muhammad, do you claim that God will bring this back to life after it has decayed?" The Prophet replied: "Yes — God will resurrect it, and He will cause you to die, then bring you back to life, then enter you into the Fire." The passage in Sūrah Yā Sīn is nearly identical in wording to 16:4 and gives God's answer to the challenge:

> *"Has not man seen that We created him from a drop, and behold, he is a manifest adversary? And he sets forth for Us a parable and forgets his own creation. He says, 'Who will give life to bones when they are decayed?' Say, 'He will give them life Who brought them into being the first time, and He is Knowing of every creation.'"* (Qur'an 36:77–79)

This parallel unlocks the logic of 16:4. The "manifest adversary" is the one who argues against resurrection. And the answer to his argument is contained in the first half of the very verse that describes him: he was created from a drop. If God could produce a thinking, speaking human from a drop of fluid, the reconstitution of that human from dust is not more difficult but, by any rational measure, easier — as the Qur'an says in 30:27, *"It is He Who originates creation, then repeats it, and that is easier for Him."*

**The Logical Structure of the Refutation**

It is worth laying out the argument plainly, because it is one of the Qur'an's most frequently repeated proofs and one of its most accessible.

Premise one: You, the objector, agree that you now exist as a living, thinking person. Premise two: You agree that you did not always exist; you began as a drop of fluid. Premise three: The transition from a drop to a person is a greater transformation than the transition from dust to a person, since dust already was a person, whereas a drop never was. Conclusion: Whoever accomplished the greater transformation is certainly capable of the lesser.

The adversary's mistake, as 36:78 diagnoses it, is that he "forgets his own creation." He treats his present existence as a given, a starting point that requires no explanation, and then asks how a second existence could be possible. The Qur'an's remedy is memory: remember what you were. Al-Rāzī observes that the whole force of the argument depends on the humble origin; had man been created from something grand and durable, the inference would be weaker. It is precisely because the origin is a drop that the objector has no ground to stand on.

**Weakness as the Ground of Humility**

Beyond its role in the debate about resurrection, the verse teaches a permanent lesson about the human condition. The Qur'an says elsewhere: *"God is He Who created you from weakness"* (30:54) and *"Man was created weak"* (4:28). The mention of the drop is a reminder of this weakness at the root. Every human achievement — every empire, every fortune, every reputation — traces back to a beginning that no one would boast of. The Prophet ﷺ pressed this point in a ḥadīth recorded by al-Tirmidhī and Abū Dāwūd:

> *"God has removed from you the pride of the Age of Ignorance and its boasting about ancestors. One is either a God-fearing believer or a wretched sinner. People are the children of Adam, and Adam was from dust."* (Abū Dāwūd 5116; al-Tirmidhī 3955)

The arrogance the verse rebukes is not only theological arrogance against God. It is also the social arrogance of one person over another, which the Qur'an traces to the same forgetfulness of origin. A man who remembers that he and the poorest laborer began identically, as a drop, finds it harder to look down on him.

**The Psychology of the Argumentative Self**

The verse also describes something every human being can recognize in himself: the tendency to argue. The Prophet ﷺ said:

> *"Man is, more than anything, given to disputation."* (al-Bukhārī 7347; Muslim 775 — reported in the context of the Prophet's night visit to ʿAlī and Fāṭimah, when ʿAlī answered his encouragement to pray by citing God's decree, and the Prophet turned away reciting 18:54)

The verse he recited on that occasion is 18:54: *"And man is, more than anything, given to disputation."* The faculty of argument is a gift; it is what allows the human being to seek truth, to defend the wronged, to refute error. But left undisciplined, it becomes a tool for evading truth rather than finding it. The "manifest adversary" of 16:4 is a person who has become clever in his own defense against God — who can always find another objection, another demand for proof, another "but why?" The tradition's counsel is that argument must be subordinated to sincerity. The Prophet ﷺ promised:

> *"I guarantee a house in the outskirts of Paradise for one who gives up argument even when he is in the right."* (Abū Dāwūd 4800; graded ḥasan)

This does not forbid the search for truth through debate; the sūrah itself will command that disputation be conducted "in the most virtuous manner" (16:125). It forbids the pride that argues in order to win rather than in order to know.

**A Modern Application**

Contemporary culture prizes the articulate skeptic. The person who can raise objections fluently is admired as intelligent, while the one who submits is suspected of naivety. Verse 16:4 offers a different measure. It asks: What is the relationship between your cleverness and your origin? The one who gave you the tongue with which you argue is the one you are arguing against. This is not an argument against thinking; the Qur'an demands thinking at every turn. It is an argument against a particular kind of thinking that has forgotten its own source — the intellect that dismisses its Creator with the very faculties its Creator installed. The remedy is not to think less but to remember more: to include in one's reasoning the fact of one's own creation, which changes every conclusion.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:5

> **And cattle has He created for you, in which there is warmth and [other] uses, and whereof you eat.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Turn From Man to What Serves Man**

The sūrah has spoken of the creation of the heavens and the earth (v. 3) and the creation of man (v. 4). It now turns to what God created *for* man, and it begins with cattle. The choice reflects the world of the first listeners — the pastoral and trading society of Arabia, in which a family's security, mobility, food, clothing, and shelter all depended on its animals. But the lesson is universal: the first blessings the sūrah names are not luxuries but necessities, and they are named in the order in which a human being in a harsh climate would feel their absence — warmth first, then use, then food.

**The Meaning and Scope of *Anʿām***

The word *anʿām* is the plural of *naʿam*, and in Arabic usage it designates the grazing livestock: camels, cattle, sheep, and goats. The Qur'an itself defines the category in 6:143–144 as "eight pairs" — two of sheep, two of goats, two of camels, and two of oxen. The word is related to the root *n-ʿ-m*, which also gives *niʿmah*, "blessing," and *naʿīm*, "bliss." The classical lexicographers noted this connection: livestock were called *anʿām* because they were, for the Arabs, the most visible form of God's *niʿmah*. To hear the word was to hear "blessing" inside it. In a sūrah that al-Qurṭubī reports was also called "the Chapter of Blessings," this etymological resonance is fitting.

**The Grammar of Priority: "For You"**

The Arabic reads *wa'l-anʿāma khalaqahā lakum*, with the object *al-anʿām* placed before the verb. This fronting draws attention to the cattle themselves, as if to say: "As for the cattle — He created them for you." The little phrase *lakum*, "for you," is theologically weighty. The sūrah will repeat it constantly (vv. 5, 10, 12, 14, 15, 72, 80, 81). It affirms that the natural world is not indifferent to human beings; it was arranged with them in view. This does not license abuse — the same Qur'an forbids waste and cruelty — but it does establish that using the world's resources with gratitude is not a crime against nature. It is the intended relationship.

**Warmth: *Difʾ***

The first benefit named is *difʾ*, "warmth." The word refers both to warmth itself and, by extension, to whatever produces it — garments, blankets, tents made from wool, hair, and hides. Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to have explained *difʾ* as "clothing," and al-Ṭabarī adds the broader sense of everything derived from the animals' coats and skins that protects against cold. Verse 80 will return to this theme and specify "furnishings and enjoyment" from wool, fur, and hair.

That warmth is mentioned before food is psychologically astute. A person exposed to a desert night without covering is in more immediate danger than a person who has missed a meal. The verse names what one would reach for first. Al-Rāzī also notes the elegance of listing a benefit that does not require killing the animal: the wool and hair are shorn while the animal lives and grows back. God's provision through cattle is renewable before it is consumptive.

**"And Other Uses": *Manāfiʿ***

The word *manāfiʿ*, plural of *manfaʿah*, means benefits or uses in general. The commentators enumerate them: riding, carrying burdens, ploughing, milk, offspring that multiply wealth, hides for water-skins and leather, bones and horns for tools, and even dung for fuel and fertilizer. Al-Qurṭubī observes that the Qur'an leaves the term general precisely because the uses are too many to list, and because new uses continue to be discovered. Elsewhere the Qur'an itself expands the catalogue:

> *"And truly in the cattle there is a lesson for you. We give you to drink of what is in their bellies, and you have in them many uses, and of them you eat. And upon them and upon ships you are carried."* (Qur'an 23:21–22)

> *"Have they not seen that We created for them, of what Our hands have made, cattle, so that they are their owners? And We subdued them to them, so some of them they ride and some of them they eat. And in them are uses and drinks; will they not then be thankful?"* (Qur'an 36:71–73)

The last passage ends with exactly the question that al-Naḥl is designed to raise: *afalā yashkurūn*, "will they not then be thankful?"

**"And Whereof You Eat": Food Named Last**

The Arabic *wa-minhā taʾkulūn*, "and of them you eat," uses the partitive *min* — "of them," not "them." Ibn Kathīr and al-Zamakhsharī draw attention to this: one eats *some* of the cattle — their meat, their milk, their fat — while the rest of the animal continues to serve in other ways. The same partitive appears in 36:72: "and some of them they eat." The wording thus quietly resists the idea that animals exist only to be slaughtered. Their edible portion is one benefit among many.

It is also notable that food comes last in the list, after warmth and general benefit. Al-Rāzī suggests that this order reflects both urgency and value: warmth is needed before food in the harshest conditions, and the ongoing uses of a living animal exceed the single use of its flesh. There is a lesson in this for a consumer society that thinks of animals primarily as meat. The Qur'an thinks of them first as companions in survival.

**Why Livestock Is a "Sign" and Not Just a Resource**

The sūrah does not merely list cattle as useful; it lists them as *created* — *khalaqahā*. The point is that the animal's usefulness is not an accident of evolution that humans happened to exploit, but a designed fit. Consider the sheep: it grows a fiber that insulates precisely in the range of temperatures humans inhabit, converts grass that humans cannot digest into milk and meat that they can, and is docile enough to be herded by a child. Consider the camel: it stores fat for weeks without food, closes its nostrils against sand, kneels to be loaded, and gives milk richer than a cow's in a land where cows cannot survive. Al-Rāzī, contemplating verses like this one, argued that the correspondence between animal capacities and human needs is too precise to be unintended. The verse invites the reader to see a Provider behind the provision.

**The Ethics That Follow From Seeing Animals as Gifts**

If cattle are God's creation given in trust, then how one treats them is a matter of religion. The Prophet ﷺ made this explicit in numerous reports. He said:

> *"God has prescribed excellence in all things. So when you kill, kill well; and when you slaughter, slaughter well. Let each of you sharpen his blade and spare the animal he slaughters suffering."* (Muslim 1955)

He forbade branding animals on the face, using living creatures as targets, overburdening them, and withholding their food. He told of a woman punished in Hell for imprisoning a cat until it died, and of a man forgiven for giving water to a thirsty dog (al-Bukhārī 3318, 2363). He said of riding animals:

> *"Fear God concerning these beasts that cannot speak. Ride them when they are fit, and leave them when they are fit."* (Abū Dāwūd 2548)

The believer who reads 16:5 correctly does not conclude "animals exist for me, therefore I may do as I please." He concludes "animals were given to me by God, therefore I will answer to Him for how I used them." The phrase "for you" creates a debt, not a license.

**Gratitude in Practice**

The classical scholars understood that the primary purpose of listing blessings is to awaken *shukr*, gratitude, which they defined as recognizing the blessing as coming from God, expressing that recognition with the tongue, and using the blessing in obedience to Him. Applied to this verse, gratitude for cattle means: acknowledging that the wool coat, the leather shoes, the glass of milk, and the meal of meat came ultimately from God's creative choice; saying "praise be to God" over them; and not using them in disobedience — not being wasteful, not being cruel, not being stingy with the poor, and not, as the pagans did, dedicating them to idols (which verse 56 will condemn).

The Prophet ﷺ gave a form of words for the last of these moments, the meal, which encapsulates the whole attitude of the verse:

> *"Praise be to God Who has fed me this and provided it for me without any strength or power on my part."* (Abū Dāwūd 4023; al-Tirmidhī 3458)

"Without any strength or power on my part" — that is precisely the recognition 16:5 demands. The human being did not create the animal, did not design the wool, did not invent the chemistry of milk. He received. The only fitting response to receiving is thanks.

**A Wider Reflection**

The modern reader may live far from herds and rarely think about where wool or leather or milk originates. But the verse's principle scales to every technology of comfort: the heating system, the winter coat, the supermarket shelf. Behind each stands a chain of natural provisions — fibers, fuels, animals, plants — that no human being invented. The sūrah asks the reader to trace the chain back to its Origin and to let that tracing become a habit of the mind. This is what the Qur'an means when it later calls such things "signs for a people who reflect." The sign is only a sign to one who follows it to what it points at.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:6

> **And in them there is beauty for you, when you bring them home, and when you take them out to pasture.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Verse About Beauty in a List of Necessities**

Among all the passages in the Qur'an that mention livestock, this is the only one that names their *jamāl*, their beauty, as a benefit. The verse before it listed warmth, uses, and food — the practical necessities. This verse pauses to affirm something that a purely utilitarian account would omit: that the sight of one's flocks and herds moving out to graze in the morning light and returning at dusk is beautiful, and that this beauty is itself a gift from God, deliberately granted.

The commentators did not miss the significance. Al-Rāzī builds on this verse a whole hierarchy of creation according to benefit — from animals essential to survival, to those that provide adornment and beauty, to those of no evident benefit, to those unknown to human beings altogether (v. 8) — and observes that the Qur'an here honors beauty as a real good, not a frivolous one. God did not have to make the world beautiful in order to make it functional. That He did so is a mark of generosity beyond necessity.

**The Meaning of *Jamāl***

The word *jamāl* comes from a root that carries ideas of beauty, grace, and comeliness in both physical and moral senses; the adjective *jamīl* describes a handsome face and also a gracious act (as in *ṣabr jamīl*, "beautiful patience," 12:18). The Prophet ﷺ used the word in one of the most cited ḥadīths on the subject:

> *"God is beautiful and loves beauty."* (Muslim 91)

He said this in response to a man who asked whether it was pride to want one's clothing and sandals to look fine; the Prophet distinguished between beauty, which God loves, and pride, which is "rejecting the truth and looking down on people." The distinction illuminates 16:6. Taking pleasure in the beauty of one's herds is not vanity; it becomes vanity only when it produces contempt for others or forgetfulness of the Giver.

**Why Beauty Is Tied to Two Moments**

The verse specifies the beauty of the cattle at two times: *ḥīna turīḥūn*, "when you bring them home" in the evening, and *ḥīna tasraḥūn*, "when you take them out to pasture" in the morning. The two verbs are precise. *Arāḥa* means to bring animals back to their resting place (*murāḥ*) at nightfall; *saraḥa* means to send them out to graze at dawn. The commentators — al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Zamakhsharī — all note that these are the two moments when the herd is seen as a whole and its owner's heart is gladdened.

Why does the verse mention the evening return first, when chronologically the morning departure comes first? Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Rāzī answer that the beauty is greater at the return. In the evening the animals come back full-bellied, udders heavy with milk, walking together, kicking up dust in the reddening light, and the owner watches them file into the enclosure with a satisfaction that combines security, prosperity, and the sheer pleasure of the sight. In the morning they are lean and hungry, and the beauty is more that of promise than of fulfillment. The Qur'an names the more beautiful moment first.

There is also a social observation embedded here. In a village or encampment, the size and health of a family's returning herd was visible to all, and it conferred honor and standing. Al-Qurṭubī notes that the beauty is not only aesthetic but also a matter of dignity among people. The verse recognizes the human desire for this kind of respect without condemning it, while implicitly reminding the owner that the source of his standing is God's creation, not his own genius.

**The Lesson: God Provides for the Heart, Not Only the Body**

The most profound teaching of the verse is that God's provision addresses the whole human being. The body needs warmth and food; verse 5 supplies them. The heart needs beauty, satisfaction, and a sense of dignity; verse 6 supplies them. A religion that spoke only of survival would treat human beings as animals. The Qur'an treats them as beings who can be moved by a sunset over a returning herd.

This has consequences for how one views the world. The Qur'an repeatedly draws attention to beauty as a sign:

> *"And the earth We have spread out, and cast therein firm mountains, and caused to grow therein every beautiful kind."* (Qur'an 50:7)

> *"Have they not looked at the sky above them — how We built it and adorned it, and it has no rifts?"* (Qur'an 50:6)

> *"Truly We have made whatever is on the earth an adornment for it, that We may test them as to which of them is best in deed."* (Qur'an 18:7)

The last verse is instructive. Beauty is described as a test. The question is not whether one enjoys it — one is meant to — but whether one traces it to its source and responds with gratitude and good deeds, or whether one is captured by it and forgets the Giver. The herd is beautiful; the question is what the sight of it does to the heart.

**The Discipline of Enjoying Beauty Correctly**

The Islamic tradition developed a nuanced attitude toward worldly beauty, and 16:6 is one of its anchors. On one side, the tradition rejects the ascetic extremism that sees all pleasure as suspect. The Qur'an asks pointedly:

> *"Say: Who has forbidden the adornment of God which He has brought forth for His servants, and the good things of provision?"* (Qur'an 7:32)

On the other side, it rejects the materialism that makes beauty an end in itself and accumulates possessions for display. The Prophet ﷺ warned against the man whose concern is wealth alone, and the Qur'an describes the man in Sūrah al-Kahf who walked into his beautiful garden saying "I do not think this will ever perish" (18:35) — and lost it all. The balance is captured in the phrase *lakum fīhā jamāl*, "there is beauty in them *for you*." The beauty is a gift addressed to you; a gift is enjoyed most fully when one remembers the giver.

**The Verse as a Window Into the Prophet's World**

For the first audience, this verse described a scene they had watched every day of their lives. The Prophet ﷺ himself had been a shepherd in his youth, as he told his Companions: *"There is no prophet but that he herded sheep"* (al-Bukhārī 2262). He would have known intimately the sight the verse describes and the feeling it names. Something of that intimacy survives in the verse's economy: it does not explain the beauty; it simply names the two moments and trusts the listener to see them.

**A Modern Reading**

Most readers today do not own herds. But the principle extends. The pleasure a person takes in a well-kept home, a garden, a view from a window, a child's face, the sea at dusk — all of these are instances of *jamāl* that God has placed in creation "for you." The verse permits and even sanctifies such pleasure, on one condition: that it be recognized as a gift. There is a difference between a person who looks at a beautiful scene and feels only ownership or envy, and a person who looks at it and feels gratitude. The second person has understood 16:6. And there is a further step. The believer who has been given beauty is asked to be beautiful in return — in conduct, in speech, in generosity — because, as the ḥadīth says, God loves beauty. The sūrah will later command *iḥsān*, the doing of what is beautiful (16:90), and will end by placing God's companionship with *al-muḥsinīn*, those who do beautiful deeds (16:128). The beauty received in verse 6 is meant to become the beauty given in verse 90.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:7

> **And they bear your burdens to a land you would never reach, save with great hardship to yourselves. Truly your Lord is Kind, Merciful.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Third Gift of the Cattle: Movement Across Distance**

Verses 5 and 6 spoke of what livestock give while standing still — warmth, food, beauty. Verse 7 speaks of what they give in motion: they carry. *Wa-taḥmilu athqālakum*, "and they bear your burdens." The word *athqāl*, plural of *thiql*, means heavy loads — the goods, provisions, tents, and merchandise that a caravan transports. The reference is primarily to camels, the beasts of burden of Arabia, though oxen, mules, and donkeys serve the same function elsewhere, and verse 8 will extend the theme to riding animals.

The Qur'an dwells on the reality behind the verse: *ilā baladin lam takūnū bālighīhi illā bi-shiqqi al-anfus*, "to a land you would never reach except with great hardship to yourselves." The phrase *shiqq al-anfus* is vivid. *Shiqq* means splitting or cleaving; *bi-shiqqi al-anfus* means "with the splitting of souls" — that is, with an exertion so severe that it seems to tear the self in half. Al-Ṭabarī explains it as "with the exhaustion and hardship of your bodies," and al-Zamakhsharī notes that the expression conveys an effort that consumes half of a person's strength or endurance. Without the animal, the journey to Syria or Yemen — the two poles of the Makkan trade described in Sūrah Quraysh (106:2) — would have been not merely difficult but nearly impossible.

**What This Meant for the Makkans in Particular**

The first listeners were merchants. Makkah produced almost nothing; it lived on trade. The caravans that left for Syria in summer and Yemen in winter were the city's lifeblood, and every one of them depended on camels. The verse thus touches the most sensitive nerve of Makkan prosperity. The very wealth that made Quraysh arrogant rested on an animal they had not created and could not have designed. Al-Rāzī observes that the verse turns the source of their pride into an argument against their pride: every dirham they earned had been carried to them on the back of a creature made by the God they refused to worship alone.

The Qur'an makes this point about the caravans explicitly elsewhere:

> *"For the security of Quraysh — their security in the journey of winter and of summer — let them worship the Lord of this House, Who has fed them against hunger and secured them against fear."* (Qur'an 106:1–4)

**The Wider Human Truth: Civilization Is Built on Borrowed Strength**

Beyond Makkah, the verse states a principle about the human condition. Human beings are physically weak relative to the tasks they undertake. A person can carry perhaps a third of his weight over a short distance; a camel carries several times as much for days. Every great human achievement in transport, trade, and travel before the modern era was accomplished with borrowed muscle — the strength of animals that God made willing to serve. Even in the modern age, the fuel that drives a truck or aircraft is drawn from the earth, not manufactured by human ingenuity from nothing. The principle stands: human beings move through the world on power they did not make.

The verse's phrase "a land you would never reach" also acknowledges human aspiration. People have always wanted to go where they are not — to trade, to learn, to pilgrimage, to escape. God did not merely permit this desire; He provided for it. In the same way that He created cattle "for you," He created the means for you to fulfill purposes that your own bodies could not achieve. This is what the Qur'an calls *taskhīr*, the subjection of creation to human use, a theme that verse 12 and verse 14 will develop.

**"Truly Your Lord Is Kind, Merciful": Why These Two Names Here**

The verse ends with two Divine Names: *inna rabbakum la-raʾūfun raḥīm*, "Truly your Lord is Kind, Merciful." The choice of these Names in this place has occupied the commentators, and their observations are illuminating.

*Raʾūf* is derived from *raʾfah*, which the lexicographers define as the most intense and tender form of mercy — mercy that cannot bear to see the object of its care suffer. *Raḥīm*, from *raḥmah*, is mercy in general, encompassing and continuous. The two together describe a Lord who not only provides but provides with tenderness, anticipating the hardship His creatures would face and sparing them from it before they even ask.

Al-Rāzī suggests that the mention of "great hardship to yourselves" is what calls forth these Names. God saw the hardship you would suffer, and out of tenderness He created the animal that spares you from it. The camel is not a random feature of the landscape; it is an expression of *raʾfah*. In the same way, a mother who packs warm clothing for her child before a journey is not merely being practical; she is being tender. The verse asks the traveler to feel, in the animal that carries his load, the tenderness of his Lord.

Al-Qurṭubī draws attention to the word *rabbakum*, "your Lord," rather than simply "God." *Rabb* is the One who nurtures, sustains, and brings a thing to its completion. The Lord who provides the means of travel is acting precisely as *Rabb* — as the Caretaker who looks after the needs of those in His charge.

**The Emotional Structure of the Verse**

There is a movement in this verse from hardship to mercy that mirrors a movement the Qur'an wishes to create in the heart. First the listener is made to imagine the alternative: the journey on foot, the load on one's own back, the splitting exhaustion. Then he is made to see what he actually has: the beast that carries it for him. Then he is told the name of the One who arranged this: the Kind, the Merciful. The sequence is a training in gratitude. One does not feel grateful for what one takes for granted; one feels grateful when one sees what one would have suffered without the gift. The Qur'an deliberately walks the listener through the deprivation in order to make the provision visible.

This is a general principle of spiritual psychology in the Islamic tradition. The Prophet ﷺ advised:

> *"Look at those who are below you, and do not look at those who are above you, for that is more likely to keep you from belittling God's blessing upon you."* (Muslim 2963)

To imagine oneself without the camel — or, in a modern setting, without the car, the road, the train — is to "look below" in exactly this sense, and the result is the same: one stops belittling what one has.

**The Prophet's Own Gratitude on a Mount**

The Sunnah preserves the concrete expression of the gratitude 16:7 calls for. Whenever the Prophet ﷺ mounted his camel to set out on a journey, he would say "God is greatest" three times and then recite:

> *"Glory be to Him Who has subjected this to us, and we could not have subdued it ourselves. And truly unto our Lord we are returning."* (Qur'an 43:13–14; the practice is recorded in Muslim 1342 and Abū Dāwūd 2599)

The words "we could not have subdued it ourselves" are the exact spirit of 16:7. The rider acknowledges that the animal's willingness to be ridden, its strength, its endurance, and its very existence were not his doing. And the closing phrase — "unto our Lord we are returning" — reminds him that every journey across land is a rehearsal for the final journey. The Companions who traveled with the Prophet learned, from these few words, to turn a commercial trip into an act of remembrance.

**A Practical and Modern Reflection**

The distances the verse describes — Makkah to Damascus, roughly a month by camel — are now crossed in two hours by air. It might seem that technology has made the verse obsolete. The opposite is true. Every element of modern travel rests on gifts no human designed: the physical laws that allow flight, the fossil fuels formed over millions of years, the metals in the earth, the intelligence in the human mind that discovered how to combine them. The traveler who boards an aircraft and does not feel that he is being carried "to a land he would never reach save with great hardship" has simply lost the imaginative capacity that the Qur'an is trying to restore. The verse invites him to recover it — to feel the miracle in the ordinary and to say, as the Prophet did on his camel, "Glory be to Him Who has subjected this to us."

And it invites one more thing: to carry the burdens of others as the animal carries ours. The believer who has been carried by God's kindness across every distance of his life is asked to become, in turn, a bearer of other people's loads — a principle the Prophet ﷺ expressed by saying that God helps His servant so long as the servant is helping his brother (Muslim 2699). The kindness received in 16:7 is meant to propagate outward.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:8

> **And [He has created] horses, mules, and asses, that you may ride them, and as adornment, and He creates that which you know not.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Second Category of Animals**

Verses 5 through 7 dealt with *anʿām* — camels, cattle, sheep, and goats, the animals that give food, warmth, milk, and transport of goods. Verse 8 introduces a distinct group: *al-khayl wa'l-bighāl wa'l-ḥamīr*, horses, mules, and donkeys. The Qur'an treats them separately for a reason that the commentators draw out: these animals serve primarily for riding and display rather than for food. The verse says they were created *li-tarkabūhā*, "that you may ride them," and *zīnatan*, "as adornment." It does not say "and of them you eat," as verse 5 said of the cattle.

Each of the three animals had a specific role in the ancient world. The horse was the animal of speed, war, and prestige — the possession of the noble and the warrior. The mule, a hybrid of horse and donkey, was prized for its strength, endurance, and sure-footedness in mountainous terrain; it was the animal of long-distance travelers and of officials. The donkey was the humble mount of the ordinary person, the farmer, and the trader, cheap to keep and patient under load. Together they span the social range from king to peasant, and the verse counts all three as gifts.

**The Legal Discussion: May These Animals Be Eaten?**

Because the verse mentions riding and adornment but not eating, the jurists debated whether the meat of these animals is lawful, and their discussion is preserved by al-Qurṭubī, Ibn Kathīr, and others.

Regarding domestic donkeys, the matter was settled by the Prophet ﷺ at Khaybar in the seventh year after the Hijrah, when the Muslims had begun cooking donkey meat and he ordered the pots overturned. Anas ibn Mālik reported that a crier announced:

> *"God and His Messenger forbid you the flesh of domestic donkeys, for they are impure."* (al-Bukhārī 4199; Muslim 1940)

Mules, as the offspring of horses and donkeys, are treated by most schools as following the prohibited parent and are therefore also forbidden.

Regarding horses, the schools differ. The Shāfiʿī, Ḥanbalī, and one view within the Mālikī school hold that horse meat is lawful, on the basis of the ḥadīth of Jābir:

> *"On the day of Khaybar the Messenger of God forbade the flesh of domestic donkeys and permitted the flesh of horses."* (al-Bukhārī 4219; Muslim 1941)

Asmāʾ bint Abī Bakr also reported: *"We slaughtered a horse in the time of the Messenger of God and ate it"* (al-Bukhārī 5510). Abū Ḥanīfah, however, held horse meat to be disliked (*makrūh*), citing this very verse, 16:8, as one of his proofs: if horses had been created for eating, God would have mentioned eating as He did with the cattle in verse 5; instead He mentioned only riding and adornment. His companions Abū Yūsuf and Muḥammad al-Shaybānī disagreed with him and followed the ḥadīth of Jābir. The Mālikī school largely regarded it as disliked as well, partly because the horse is too valuable as a mount and a means of *jihād* to be consumed.
