Ibn Kathīr and al-Qurṭubī both report the debate and both incline to permissibility on the strength of the explicit ḥadīths, noting that the verse's silence about eating is not a prohibition but merely a statement of the animals' principal benefit.

The debate is a useful example of how scholars reason from the Qur'an: they attend closely to what a verse says and does not say, but they do not treat silence as a legal ruling when clearer texts exist.

**Riding as a Gift**

The first purpose named is riding. It is easy to underestimate the transformation that a riding animal brings to a human life. A person on foot covers perhaps thirty kilometers in a hard day; on horseback he can cover twice that with far less exhaustion, carry weapons or goods, and see over obstacles. To ride is to be lifted above one's natural limitations — a small foretaste of what verse 12 will describe as the subjection of the cosmos to human use. The Qur'an counts this elevation as a divine gift and, in another passage, teaches the rider to remember its source:

> *"...that you may sit firmly upon their backs, then remember the blessing of your Lord when you are seated upon them, and say, 'Glory be to Him Who has subjected this to us, and we could not have subdued it ourselves.'"* (Qur'an 43:13)

**Adornment: *Zīnah***

The second purpose is *zīnah*, adornment or beauty of display. The horse in particular was — and remains — an animal of great visual splendor, and to be mounted on a fine horse conferred dignity and presence. Verse 6 spoke of the *jamāl* of the returning herd; verse 8 speaks of the *zīnah* of the mount. The Qur'an recognizes that human beings are moved by appearance and standing, and instead of denying this it channels it, affirming that adornment is a legitimate good so long as it does not become pride.

The Prophet ﷺ loved horses and spoke of them with unusual warmth:

> *"Goodness is tied to the forelocks of horses until the Day of Resurrection: reward and spoils."* (al-Bukhārī 2852; Muslim 1873)

He also distinguished three kinds of horse owners, in a ḥadīth recorded by al-Bukhārī (2371) and Muslim (987): the man who keeps horses for the way of God, for whom they are a source of reward; the man who keeps them for self-sufficiency and dignity without forgetting God's rights in them, for whom they are a covering; and the man who keeps them for pride, show, and hostility toward people, for whom they are a burden of sin. The same animal can be reward, neutral covering, or sin, depending on the heart behind its use. The verse's mention of *zīnah* should be read in this light: adornment is a gift that becomes a test.

**"And He Creates That Which You Know Not"**

The verse closes with a clause that opens onto infinity: *wa-yakhluqu mā lā taʿlamūn*, "and He creates that which you know not." Having named a few specific creatures, God reminds the listener that the list is a sample, not an inventory. There are creatures the Makkans had never seen, creatures no one had yet discovered, creatures in the depths of the sea and in distant lands and in the unseen realms, and — the commentators add — creatures God will bring into being in the future.

Al-Zamakhsharī explains that the clause expresses the immensity of divine power, which exceeds human knowledge in every direction. Al-Qurṭubī and Ibn Kathīr note several dimensions of the phrase: creatures on earth unknown to the audience, the wonders of Paradise and Hell that no eye has seen, and the creatures of the heavens. Some of the early commentators applied it to the vermin and insects that human beings notice only when they cause harm, others to the animals of remote regions. The Qur'an elsewhere confirms the breadth of the hidden creation:

> *"And among His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth, and whatever creatures He has scattered throughout them."* (Qur'an 42:29)

> *"Glory be to Him Who created all the pairs — of what the earth grows, and of themselves, and of that which they know not."* (Qur'an 36:36)

The phrase in 36:36 — "and of that which they know not" — is the exact companion of 16:8. The Qur'an twice declares that the catalogue of creation extends beyond human knowledge.

**The Humility and the Openness the Clause Produces**

Two attitudes follow from taking this clause seriously. The first is intellectual humility. Every age imagines that it has surveyed the world. The Arabs of the seventh century knew camels and horses; they did not know of the kangaroo, the giant squid, or the bacterium. The scientists of the nineteenth century believed the fundamental picture was nearly complete; the twentieth century revealed galaxies beyond galaxies and a subatomic world of bewildering strangeness. The Qur'an's phrase anticipates this pattern and warns against the arrogance that mistakes the edge of one's knowledge for the edge of reality.

The second attitude is openness to discovery as an act of worship. If God creates what we do not know, then learning what He has created is a way of deepening awe. The Muslim naturalists and physicians of the classical period — al-Jāḥiẓ writing his *Book of Animals*, al-Damīrī compiling his zoological encyclopedia — worked in the spirit of this verse. Each new creature identified was another item in the inventory that verse 18 will declare impossible to complete.

Some commentators, including al-Qurṭubī, also read the clause as applying to modes of transport that had not yet been invented — since the verse's immediate context is riding. Whether or not this was the primary intent, the modern reader cannot help noticing that the horse, the mule, and the donkey have been joined by vehicles the first listeners could not have imagined, all made from materials God placed in the earth and by intelligence God placed in the human mind. The clause remains as open today as it was then. Whatever the future produces, it will be produced from what He creates.

**Drawing the Threads Together**

The verse teaches that God's provision for human beings includes not only survival (verses 5 and 7) and beauty (verse 6), but also mobility and dignity (verse 8), and that behind all named gifts lies an unnamed abundance beyond human reckoning. The correct response is threefold: to use the gifts for what they were given for, to remember the Giver when using them — as the Prophet did each time he mounted — and to remain humble before the vastness of what one does not know. Arrogance is a form of ignorance that has forgotten it is ignorant. The final clause of the verse is the cure: *He creates that which you know not*.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:9

> **And it is for God to show the way, for some of them lead astray. Had He willed, He would have guided you all together.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**From Physical Roads to the Road of the Soul**

The preceding verses spoke of animals that carry travelers across the land toward distant destinations. It is a natural transition, then, to speak of the road itself and of the One who shows the way. The Arabic *qaṣd al-sabīl*, "the straight way" or "the direction of the road," continues the metaphor of the journey. Just as the traveler across the desert needs a guide to distinguish the road that leads to water from the track that leads to death, the human being traveling through life needs a Guide to distinguish the path that leads to God from the many paths that lead away from Him. Al-Bayḍāwī and al-Zamakhsharī both note that the verse turns the physical guidance of the journey into a parable of spiritual guidance.

**"It Is for God": The Meaning of *ʿalā Allāh***

The verse opens *wa-ʿalā Allāhi qaṣdu al-sabīl*. The preposition *ʿalā* ordinarily indicates obligation or responsibility — "incumbent upon." Read literally, the clause means "it is incumbent upon God to show the straight way." This phrasing raised a theological question that the commentators addressed with care: can anything be "obligatory" upon God?

Al-Zamakhsharī, following the Muʿtazilite school, took the phrase at face value: it is a self-imposed duty of God, arising from His wisdom and justice, to make the path clear, since He would not hold people accountable for a path He had hidden from them. Al-Rāzī and al-Bayḍāwī, from the Ashʿarite side, preferred to say that the guidance is an act of pure bounty and grace which God has promised and taken upon Himself, not an obligation imposed on Him from outside — nothing binds God but His own word. The Qur'an itself uses this kind of language of divine self-commitment: *"He has prescribed mercy upon Himself"* (6:12, 54) and *"Truly upon Us is guidance"* (92:12).

The practical meaning on either view is identical and immensely reassuring: God has undertaken to show the way. The clarity of the path is guaranteed. No one will stand before God on the Day of Judgment able to say honestly, "The road was never shown to me." The Qur'an repeatedly affirms this principle of prior clarification:

> *"And We never punish until We have sent a messenger."* (Qur'an 17:15)

> *"Messengers as bearers of glad tidings and warners, so that mankind might have no argument against God after the messengers."* (Qur'an 4:165)

Verses 2 and 36 of this very sūrah affirm the same: God sends the Spirit with the warning, and He has sent a messenger to every community. Verse 9 states the principle underlying those facts.

**What Is *Qaṣd al-Sabīl*?**

The word *qaṣd* means aim, intention, directness, or moderation. *Qaṣd al-sabīl* is the road that goes straight to its destination — the shortest, most direct, most balanced route. Al-Ṭabarī explains it as "the clarification of the straight path," and Ibn Kathīr identifies it with the religion of Islam, the path of moderation between excess and neglect. The word *qaṣd* also carries the sense of the mean between extremes; the Qur'an praises the *muqtaṣid*, the moderate person (35:32), and the *ummah wasaṭ*, the middle community (2:143). The straight way is thus also the balanced way — neither the road of those who make religion so hard that it breaks people, nor the road of those who abandon it altogether.

**"For Some of Them Lead Astray": The Reality of Wrong Roads**

The second clause, *wa-minhā jāʾir*, "and of them is that which deviates," refers back to *al-sabīl*, understood collectively as "roads." Of the roads, some are *jāʾir* — crooked, veering off, unjust. The root *j-w-r* means to deviate from the right course and, by extension, to act unjustly; a tyrant is *jāʾir* because he has left the path of justice. The verse acknowledges that not every road leads home. The traveler who says "all roads are equally valid" is not being open-minded; he is being reckless, in the way a person lost in the desert would be reckless if he declared that every direction leads to water.

This clause is a quiet correction of a modern assumption as much as an ancient one. The Qur'an does not teach that sincerity alone guarantees arrival regardless of direction. It teaches that there is a way that is straight and ways that are crooked, and that God, in mercy, has distinguished them. The Prophet ﷺ illustrated this with a physical gesture. Ibn Masʿūd reported:

> *The Messenger of God drew a line for us with his hand and said, "This is the path of God, straight." Then he drew lines to its right and its left and said, "These are paths, and upon every one of them is a devil calling to it." Then he recited: "And this is My path, straight, so follow it, and follow not the ways, lest they separate you from His way."* (Aḥmad 4142; al-Nasāʾī in al-Kubrā; the verse is 6:153)

The drawing is a commentary on 16:9. One straight line; many diverging lines; and on each diverging line, someone calling.

**"Had He Willed, He Would Have Guided You All Together"**

The final clause, *wa-law shāʾa la-hadākum ajmaʿīn*, "and had He willed, He would have guided you all together," is one of a family of Qur'anic statements that have generated the deepest theological reflection in Islam on the relation between divine will and human freedom. Similar statements occur in 5:48, 6:35, 6:149, 10:99, 13:31, 32:13, and later in this sūrah at 16:93.

The plain sense is that God has the power to compel universal guidance — to create every human being such that he could not disbelieve — and that He has chosen not to exercise that power. The reason is that compelled belief is not what God wants from human beings. He wants the free response of a creature who could have refused. The Qur'an states this explicitly to the Prophet ﷺ, who longed for his people to believe:

> *"And had your Lord willed, all who are on earth would have believed together. Will you then compel people until they become believers?"* (Qur'an 10:99)

The two great schools of classical theology read the clause differently in emphasis. The Ashʿarites, as al-Rāzī reports, took it as confirmation that God does not will the guidance of everyone — that His creative will encompasses both the guided and the misguided, and that guidance is a gift given to whom He chooses. The Muʿtazilites read it as confirmation of human freedom: God is *able* to compel, but He has instead granted the freedom to choose, so that reward and punishment are just. Al-Rāzī also mentions a second Muʿtazilite reading: God could have guided everyone to Paradise regardless of deeds, but He willed that only those who earn it by their choices enter it.

**Reconciling the Two Halves of the Verse**

A careful reader will notice that the verse holds together two truths that seem to pull apart. The first half says God has undertaken to show the way; the second half says He has not willed that everyone follow it. The tension dissolves once one distinguishes between *showing* and *compelling*. Ibn Taymiyyah and his student Ibn al-Qayyim articulated this distinction with clarity, building on earlier scholars: there is a guidance of *clarification and direction* (*hidāyat al-bayān wa'l-irshād*), which God gives to all through revelation and reason, and there is a guidance of *success and inner enablement* (*hidāyat al-tawfīq*), by which God places faith in the heart of the one who sincerely seeks it. The first is universal; the second is particular. The Qur'an uses the word "guidance" in both senses: of the first, *"And as for Thamūd, We guided them, but they preferred blindness over guidance"* (41:17); of the second, *"You do not guide whom you love, but God guides whom He wills"* (28:56).

Verse 16:9 contains both. "It is for God to show the way" is the universal guidance of clarification. "Had He willed, He would have guided you all" refers to the guidance of enablement, which He grants according to His wisdom and, as many verses indicate, in response to the sincerity or stubbornness of the servant himself: *"And those who strive for Us, We shall surely guide them to Our ways"* (29:69); *"So when they deviated, God caused their hearts to deviate"* (61:5).

**Why God Does Not Compel: The Logic of the Test**

Why should God not simply guide everyone? The Qur'an's answer is that this world is a test — *"to try you as to which of you is best in deed"* (67:2) — and a test in which every answer is filled in beforehand is no test. Love that is programmed is not love; obedience that cannot be refused is not obedience. The dignity of the human being lies precisely in the capacity to choose God when he could have chosen otherwise. Al-Rāzī notes that the angels, who cannot disobey, are honored, but the human being who obeys despite the capacity to disobey attains a rank the angels do not. The freedom that makes misguidance possible is the same freedom that makes true worship possible. One cannot have the second without the first.

**The Emotional Message: Reassurance and Responsibility**

For the believer, the verse gives two gifts at once. The first is reassurance. The path has been made clear; God Himself has taken responsibility for that. One does not need to invent a religion, discover the meaning of life by unaided speculation, or wander through every philosophy before finding the way. The way has been shown. The second gift is responsibility. Since the way has been shown and since God has chosen not to compel, the walking is up to the walker. A person cannot hide behind God's will as an excuse for not moving — a mistake the sūrah will expose sharply in verse 35, where the idolaters say "Had God willed, we would not have worshipped aught apart from Him."

**A Practical Picture**

Consider a person using a navigation application while driving through an unfamiliar city. The application shows the route clearly; that is the guidance of clarification. But the application does not turn the steering wheel. If the driver ignores the voice and turns down side streets, he cannot complain that the route was not shown. And if he follows the route faithfully, he arrives — but he arrives by a way he did not design and could not have found alone. Both the credit for arrival and the blame for straying are distributed exactly as 16:9 distributes them: the way is God's to show, the steps are man's to take, and the arrival is by God's grace. The believer's daily prayer, seventeen times in the Fātiḥah, is precisely the prayer this verse teaches him to make: *"Guide us upon the straight path."*

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:10

> **He it is Who sends down water from the sky, from which you have drink, and from which comes forth vegetation wherewith you pasture your cattle.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Return to the Catalogue: Water First**

After the interlude on guidance in verse 9, the sūrah resumes its inventory of blessings, and it resumes with water. This is no accident of arrangement. Water is the precondition of every other blessing already named: without rain, there is no pasture; without pasture, there are no cattle; without cattle, there is no warmth, food, milk, or transport. The verse goes to the root. It also prepares the cluster of verses that follows (10–11), which the classical commentators treated as a unit on rain and growth, and it links thematically to verse 65, where rain will be invoked again as a sign of resurrection.

**"He It Is Who": The Emphatic Pronoun**

The verse begins *huwa alladhī*, "He is the One Who." This construction, common in the Qur'an, is emphatic and exclusive. It does not simply say "God sends down water"; it says "He — and no other — is the One Who sends down water." In the context of a debate with idolaters, the emphasis is a challenge. Which of your idols sends rain? The Qur'an poses the question elsewhere as a demand:

> *"Say: Who provides for you from the sky and the earth? Or who has power over hearing and sight? And who brings forth the living from the dead and the dead from the living? And who directs all affairs? They will say, 'God.' Then say, 'Will you not then be mindful?'"* (Qur'an 10:31)

The Makkans knew that rain came from God; they prayed to Him for it in drought. The verse takes this admission and places it at the head of the argument.

**The Verb *Anzala* and the Origin of Rain**

The verb *anzala*, "He sent down," is the same root used for the sending down of revelation (v. 2). The Qur'an consistently uses this verb for rain, describing water as something sent from above rather than merely occurring. The physical description is exact: the water that falls as rain has indeed been lifted from the seas and lakes by the sun, carried as vapor, condensed in clouds, and released. The Qur'an describes this cycle in several places:

> *"And We send the winds as fertilizers, and We send down water from the sky and give it to you to drink, and you are not its keepers."* (Qur'an 15:22)

> *"Have you not seen that God drives the clouds, then joins them together, then makes them into a heap, and you see the rain come forth from within them?"* (Qur'an 24:43)

The phrase in 15:22 — "and you are not its keepers" — is worth pausing over. The human being does not store the water of the world; he cannot manufacture it, summon it, or guarantee it. Every civilization has depended on a supply it did not control. The verse reminds the listener of a dependence that agriculture and irrigation may conceal but cannot abolish.

**"From It You Have Drink": The First and Most Direct Benefit**

The phrase *lakum minhu sharāb*, "from it you have drink," names the most immediate use of water and, in a sūrah about gratitude, one of the most humbling. A human being can survive weeks without food but only days without water. The verse names the blessing that stands between every person and death within a matter of days.

Al-Rāzī reflects that the delivery of fresh water is a double marvel. The seas are salty and undrinkable, yet the process of evaporation leaves the salt behind and delivers pure water from the sky. Had God sent rain as salty as the sea from which it rose, all life on land would fail. The Qur'an makes the reader confront this contingency directly:

> *"Have you considered the water that you drink? Is it you who sent it down from the clouds, or are We the sender? If We willed, We could make it bitter; so why are you not grateful?"* (Qur'an 56:68–70)

The final question of that passage — *fa-lawlā tashkurūn*, "so why are you not grateful?" — is the implicit question behind every clause of 16:10.

**"And From It Comes Forth Vegetation Wherewith You Pasture Your Cattle"**

The second benefit is indirect: *wa-minhu shajarun fīhi tusīmūn*, "and from it [comes] vegetation in which you pasture." The word *shajar* usually means "trees," but the classical lexicographers and commentators — al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Zamakhsharī — explain that here it has the broad sense of whatever grows from the earth, including grass and shrubs, because the context is pasture. The verb *tusīmūn* comes from *sāma* (root *s-w-m*), which means to let animals graze freely; *sāʾimah* in Islamic law is the term for livestock that graze on open pasture rather than being fed at home, and such animals are subject to zakāh.

The verse thus draws a chain: water falls, plants grow, animals graze, and human beings benefit from the animals. This chain is what the earlier verses (5–8) assumed. Verse 10 shows what those verses rest upon. It is a small lesson in ecology, taught fourteen centuries before the word existed: the blessing of the herd is really the blessing of the rain, and the one who thanks God for his cattle without thanking Him for the rain has understood only half of his debt.

**The Structure of Dependence**

There is a broader teaching here about how God provides. He does not, as a rule, hand human beings finished goods. He provides the beginning of a chain and lets nature and human effort complete it. Rain does not fall as bread; it falls as water, which becomes grass, which becomes milk, which becomes cheese in a human hand. This structure honors human agency — the farmer, the herder, the cook all have a real role — while making it impossible for the honest person to claim that he is the source. The Qur'an captures this partnership precisely:

> *"Have you considered what you sow? Is it you who make it grow, or are We the grower? If We willed, We could make it chaff, and you would be left wondering."* (Qur'an 56:63–65)

You sow; He grows. Human effort is real but not sufficient; divine provision is decisive but not exclusive of effort. The person who sees only his own effort becomes arrogant; the person who sees only God's provision becomes idle. The verse trains a mind that sees both.

**Rain as a Recurring Sign of Resurrection**

The Qur'an's mention of rain almost always carries a second meaning beneath the first. Water revives dead earth; God revives dead bodies. The sūrah will make this explicit in verse 65: *"God sends down water from the sky, and thereby revives the earth after its death."* Other passages state the analogy openly:

> *"And you see the earth barren, but when We send down water upon it, it stirs and swells and grows every beautiful kind. That is because God is the Truth, and He gives life to the dead, and He is powerful over all things."* (Qur'an 22:5–6)

> *"And God is He Who sends the winds, and they raise clouds, and We drive them to a dead land and revive thereby the earth after its death. Thus will be the Resurrection."* (Qur'an 35:9)

The Makkans who denied that the dead could live again watched every year as the dead land around them turned green after rain. The verse asks them to draw the inference. The one who does this annually before your eyes can do it once at the end of time.

**The Prophet's Practice With Rain**

The Sunnah teaches a specific gratitude for rain. When the Prophet ﷺ saw rain fall, he would say:

> *"O God, make it a beneficial rain."* (al-Bukhārī 1032)

Anas reported that once the Prophet uncovered part of his garment so that the rain would touch him, and when asked why, he said:

> *"Because it has just come from its Lord."* (Muslim 898)

That phrase — "it has just come from its Lord" — is the whole of 16:10 in five words. The Prophet did not see weather; he saw a gift arriving. And he taught the believers to attribute rain to God's mercy and not to the stars, warning against the pagan habit of saying "we were given rain by such-and-such a star." In the ḥadīth qudsī recorded by al-Bukhārī (846) and Muslim (71), God declares that whoever says "we were given rain by God's grace and mercy" is a believer in Him, while whoever attributes it to the stars has disbelieved in Him. The verse's insistence that *He* is the One Who sends down water is thus not an abstract point of theology; it draws the line between gratitude and ingratitude in something as ordinary as a comment about the weather.

**The Modern Reader and the Tap**

For someone who obtains water by turning a tap, the verse may seem distant. But the tap does not create water; it delivers what the rain provided. Reservoirs fill from rivers, rivers from rain, rain from the sea, the sea from the great cycle that God set in motion and that no human agency sustains. Cities that have suffered drought understand this instantly; cities that have not may need the verse to remind them. The believer who drinks a glass of water and says *al-ḥamdu li'Llāh* is not performing an empty ritual. He is correctly identifying the source of the thing that is keeping him alive, and correcting, for one moment, the illusion that his survival is his own achievement.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:11

> **Therewith He causes the crops to grow for you, and olives, and date palms, and grapevines, and every kind of fruit. Truly in that is a sign for a people who reflect.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**From Pasture to Table**

Verse 10 traced the rain to the pasture where cattle graze. Verse 11 traces the same rain to the fields and orchards where human food grows directly. *Yunbitu lakum bihi* — "He causes to grow for you, by it" — the pronoun *bihi* refers to the water of the previous verse. The verb *anbata*, from the root *n-b-t*, means to cause a plant to sprout and grow; the imperfect *yunbitu* indicates a continuous, repeated action, season after season. God does not merely once cause growth; He causes it every year, and the verse invites the reader to notice that repetition rather than being dulled by it.

Once again the phrase *lakum*, "for you," appears. The growth is directed toward human benefit. Al-Rāzī observes that plants grow in a way that serves human needs at every level — for food, for medicine, for shade, for beauty, for building — and that this serviceability is itself evidence of purpose.

**The Five Categories Named**

The verse names five things, and the order is instructive.

First, *al-zarʿ*, "crops" — the grains and cultivated plants that form the staple food of most peoples: wheat, barley, and their kin. The word comes from the verb *zaraʿa*, to sow; it designates what human beings plant deliberately. It is listed first because it is the most basic sustenance; bread is the foundation of the meal.

Second, *al-zaytūn*, the olive. The olive tree was central to the economy and diet of the Mediterranean and the Levant, and its oil served as food, lamp fuel, medicine, and cosmetic. The Qur'an calls it "a blessed tree" (24:35) and swears by it (95:1). The Prophet ﷺ said:

> *"Eat the oil and anoint yourselves with it, for it is from a blessed tree."* (al-Tirmidhī 1851; Ibn Mājah 3319)

Third, *al-nakhīl*, the date palm — the tree of Arabia, whose fruit sustained the peoples of the peninsula, whose fronds roofed their houses and mosques, whose fibers made their ropes, and whose trunk supported the Prophet's own pulpit before a wooden one was built. The Qur'an mentions the date palm more than twenty times, and the Prophet ﷺ compared the believer to it because of its enduring benefit (al-Bukhārī 61).

Fourth, *al-aʿnāb*, grapevines. The plural *aʿnāb* suggests abundance and variety. Grapes provided fresh fruit, raisins for travel and storage, and juice; verse 67 will return to the date palm and the vine together.

Fifth, *min kulli al-thamarāt*, "of every kind of fruit." Having named four specific things, the verse opens onto everything else. As in verse 8 ("He creates that which you know not"), the Qur'an refuses to close the list. The partitive *min*, "of," is significant: God brings forth *some of* every kind of fruit in every land — no land has all of them, but every land has some, so that the earth as a whole is a table spread with variety.

**Why These Four in Particular?**

The commentators asked why the olive, the date, and the grape are named alongside grain. Al-Qurṭubī notes that these were the most valuable and most nourishing of the fruits known to the Arabs, and that each can be eaten fresh, stored dried, and processed into something further — oil, date paste, raisins and juice. Al-Rāzī observes that the four together cover the categories of human nourishment: grain for staple energy, olive for fat, dates for concentrated sugar and nutrition, grapes for fruit and drink. The list is thus not random but representative of a complete diet.

There is also a geographical sweep. The date palm belongs to the hot desert oases; the olive to the temperate hills of Syria and Palestine; grain and grapes to a wide band between. In naming them together, the verse gathers the produce of many climates into one act of divine growing, reminding the listener that the God of Makkah is the God of every land.

**Diversity From a Single Source**

A subtle but powerful point lies in the grammar: one water produces all of this. The same rain, falling on the same soil, nourishes a bitter olive, a sweet date, a tart grape, and a bland grain. The Qur'an draws attention to this phenomenon directly in another place:

> *"And in the earth are neighboring tracts, and gardens of grapevines, and crops, and date palms, growing in clusters and singly, watered by one water — yet We make some of them excel others in taste. Truly in that are signs for a people who understand."* (Qur'an 13:4)

The philosophical weight of this observation was recognized by the classical theologians. If the output differs while the input is identical, the difference cannot be explained by the input. Something other than the water and the soil is determining that this seed becomes a date and that seed becomes a grape. The Qur'an names that something: the creative will of God, Who "causes to grow." The verse thus offers not merely a list of gifts but an argument from design — from the intelligibility and variety of results to the intelligence and intention of the One producing them.

**"Truly in That Is a Sign for a People Who Reflect"**

The verse closes with the first of a series of formulas that mark the signs in this section of the sūrah. Verse 11 ends "for a people who reflect" (*yatafakkarūn*); verse 12 ends "for a people who understand" (*yaʿqilūn*); verse 13 ends "for a people who remember" (*yadhdhakkarūn*); verse 14 ends "that you may give thanks" (*tashkurūn*). The commentators noticed the progression and reflected on it.

*Tafakkur*, reflection, is the act of turning a thing over in the mind, examining its parts, and tracing its implications. It is the appropriate response to the growth of plants because that process invites analysis: a seed is placed in dark soil, water reaches it, and from these unpromising elements emerges a structured, colored, fruitful living thing. The person who *reflects* asks how, and why, and by whom. The person who does not reflect sees a field and thinks only of the price of grain.

The Qur'an insists that the sign is only a sign *for* those who reflect. The evidence is universal; the perception is not. This is a recurring Qur'anic teaching about knowledge: the world is full of signs, but a sign is like a written word — it means nothing to one who refuses to read. Al-Rāzī notes that the Qur'an here calls not for blind acceptance but for the exercise of reason on the data of experience. Islam's confidence is that honest reflection leads to God; what it fears is not thought but thoughtlessness.

**The Ethics of the Harvest**

The verse also has legal and moral consequences that the tradition drew out. Because crops and fruits are God's growing, "for you," they carry an obligation. The Qur'an says of harvests: *"Eat of its fruit when it bears fruit, and give its due on the day of its harvest, and be not wasteful; truly He loves not the wasteful"* (6:141). From this and related texts the jurists derived the zakāh on produce — a tenth of rain-watered crops, a twentieth of irrigated ones, according to the ḥadīth in al-Bukhārī (1483). The gift creates a share for the poor. The verse's *lakum* is a collective "you," not a private one.

The Prophet ﷺ also elevated the act of planting itself into worship:

> *"No Muslim plants a tree or sows a crop, and then a bird or a person or an animal eats from it, but that it is counted as charity for him."* (al-Bukhārī 2320; Muslim 1553)

He said this even of the end of the world: *"If the Hour comes while one of you has a sapling in his hand, and he is able to plant it before it comes, let him plant it"* (Aḥmad 12902). The believer who understands that God is the true Grower participates in that growing with his own hands, expecting reward from the One who makes the seed sprout.

**A Reflection for the Reader**

Every meal is a summary of this verse. The bread is *al-zarʿ*, the oil is *al-zaytūn*, the sweetness is *al-nakhīl* and *al-aʿnāb*, and the salad and the fruit bowl are *min kulli al-thamarāt*. Behind all of it is water that fell from the sky by no human command. The person who pauses before eating, looks at what is on the plate, and traces it — even for a second — back through the field and the rain to the One who "causes to grow," has done what the verse asks. He has become, for that moment, one of "a people who reflect." And the sūrah's promise is that such reflection, repeated, transforms the whole person: it turns consumption into gratitude and gratitude into faith.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:12

> **He has made the night and the day subservient unto you, and the sun, and the moon, and the stars are subservient by His Command. Truly in that are signs for a people who understand.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Lifting the Gaze From the Field to the Sky**

The previous verses looked down: at animals, rain, and crops. This verse looks up. Having shown God's provision on the earth, the sūrah now shows His governance of the heavens, and it uses a single powerful word to describe the relationship between the cosmos and the human being: *sakhkhara*, "He made subservient."

**The Meaning of *Taskhīr***

The verb *sakhkhara* comes from the root *s-kh-r*, which in its basic sense means to compel something to work or to make it serve a purpose — as one might press a laborer or an animal into service. The noun *taskhīr* has become a technical term in Qur'anic vocabulary for the subjection of the natural order to the service of human beings by God's decree. The Qur'an uses it of the sun and moon (7:54; 13:2; 31:29; 35:13; 39:5), the sea (16:14; 45:12), ships (14:32), rivers (14:32), birds (16:79), the mountains and birds that praised with David (21:79; 38:18), and the wind for Solomon (21:81; 38:36).

Al-Rāzī defines *taskhīr* here as God's designing and constraining these phenomena so that they serve human needs in a regular, dependable way. The sun does not decide whether to rise; it is made to rise, and its rising benefits human beings. That reliability is the essence of the subjection. If the sun rose at random intervals or the night sometimes lasted a month, human life would be impossible. The order of the cosmos is not a neutral fact; it is a service rendered.

**Night and Day: The First Pair**

The verse begins with the alternation of night and day, and the Qur'an elsewhere spells out why this alternation is a blessing:

> *"It is He Who made for you the night that you may rest therein, and the day giving sight. Truly in that are signs for a people who hear."* (Qur'an 10:67)

> *"And of His mercy He made for you the night and the day, that you may rest therein and that you may seek of His bounty, and that you may be grateful."* (Qur'an 28:73)

> *"Say: Have you considered, if God made the night perpetual over you until the Day of Resurrection, what god other than God could bring you light? Will you not then hear?"* (Qur'an 28:71)

The last verse is the thought-experiment the Qur'an wants the reader to perform. Imagine perpetual night; then imagine perpetual day. Either would destroy human life — the first through cold, blindness, and the failure of plants; the second through heat, exhaustion, and the impossibility of rest. The alternation is calibrated to the human body, which requires roughly a third of each cycle for sleep. Al-Zamakhsharī notes that night is the time of rest and day the time of seeking God's bounty, and that the human being needs both in proportion.

The verse's *lakum*, "for you," carries the same force it has carried throughout the passage. Night and day were not made for the sun's sake or the earth's sake; they were arranged with the human being in view.

**Sun, Moon, and Stars: "Subservient by His Command"**

The second group — *al-shams wa'l-qamar wa'l-nujūm*, the sun, the moon, and the stars — is described as *musakhkharātun bi-amrihi*, "made subservient by His Command." The addition of "by His Command" is significant. It ties the subjection of the heavenly bodies to the same divine *amr* that verse 1 said was coming and verse 2 said was sent down. The cosmos runs on God's Command in the same way that revelation descends by it. Physical law and moral law have a single source.

The three bodies each serve distinct human purposes. The sun gives light, warmth, and the energy that grows the crops of verse 11. The moon marks the months — *"They ask you about the new moons; say, they are measures of time for people and for the pilgrimage"* (2:189). The stars, as verse 16 will state, guide the traveler by night. The Qur'an gathers these purposes:

> *"It is He Who made the sun a radiance and the moon a light, and determined for it phases, that you might know the number of years and the reckoning."* (Qur'an 10:5)

> *"And it is He Who made the stars for you, that you may be guided by them in the darkness of land and sea."* (Qur'an 6:97)

**The Philosophical Question: Do the Heavens Obey?**

The commentators pondered what it means for a lifeless object to be "made subservient" or to be "commanded." Al-Rāzī presents two views. On the first, the language is figurative: God created the sun and moon with natures that necessarily produce their motions, and calling this "subservience" is a way of expressing that the arrangement was intended for human benefit. On the second, taken more literally, the heavenly bodies genuinely receive and obey a divine command of some kind appropriate to their nature. Al-Rāzī notes that this second reading agrees with the plain sense of many verses:

> *"Then He directed Himself to the heaven while it was smoke, and said to it and to the earth, 'Come, willingly or unwillingly.' They said, 'We come willingly.'"* (Qur'an 41:11)

> *"The sun and the moon [move] by precise calculation, and the stars and the trees prostrate."* (Qur'an 55:5–6)

> *"Have you not seen that unto God prostrates whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth, and the sun and the moon and the stars, and the mountains and the trees and the beasts, and many of mankind?"* (Qur'an 22:18)

The Prophet ﷺ himself spoke of the sun in language of obedience. He asked Abū Dharr where the sun goes when it sets, and said:

> *"It goes and prostrates beneath the Throne, and seeks permission, and permission is given to it. And a time is near when it will seek permission and it will not be granted, and it will be said to it, 'Return whence you came.' And so it will rise from its west."* (al-Bukhārī 3199; Muslim 159)

Whatever the precise metaphysics, the teaching is clear: the cosmos is not autonomous. It is in a state of submission — *islām* in its cosmic sense — to its Creator, and the only beings in the visible world who can withhold submission are human beings and jinn. The sun that never fails to rise is a daily rebuke to the person who fails to prostrate.

**Why "For a People Who Understand"?**

The verse ends with *la-āyātin li-qawmin yaʿqilūn*, "signs for a people who understand" — using the verb *ʿaqala*, whose root sense is to tie or bind (an *ʿiqāl* is the cord that hobbles a camel), and which came to mean the exercise of reason that binds conclusions to their premises. Verse 11 called for *tafakkur*, reflection; verse 12 calls for *ʿaql*, reasoning. The difference is apt. The growth of plants invites open-ended wonder; the motion of the heavens invites calculation. The regularity of the sun, the phases of the moon, the fixed positions of the stars — these are the raw materials of mathematics and astronomy, and the person who applies his intellect to them discovers a precision that demands an explanation.

Ibn Kathīr notes that the signs in this verse are described in the plural, *āyāt*, where verse 11 used the singular, *āyah*. The heavens present not one sign but many: the alternation itself, the exact lengths of day and night in each season, the sun's path, the moon's phases, the stars' order. Each is a distinct proof, and the mind that reasons can multiply them indefinitely.

**Humanity's Place: Vicegerent, Not Owner**

The doctrine of *taskhīr* raises a question about the human role. If the cosmos is subjected to human beings, are they its masters? The Qur'an's answer is that they are its stewards — *khalīfah*, vicegerent (2:30) — trusted with a world they did not make and will answer for. The sun serves human beings; human beings serve God. Al-Rāzī connects the subjection of the world to this vicegerency: God honored the human being by placing creation at his disposal, and this honor is a trust, not a title deed.

This distinction has consequences. The person who thinks he owns the world will exploit it without limit; the person who knows he is trusted with it will use it with care. The Qur'an's warning against *fasād*, corruption on earth, and its praise of balance (*mīzān*, 55:7–9) follow from the fact that *taskhīr* is a service arranged by God, not a conquest achieved by man.

**The Personal Meaning of the Subjected Sun**

Every morning a person wakes to a sun that rose without his permission and will set without his consent. He did not earn the day; it was given. Every night he sleeps under a darkness that was arranged for his rest, beneath a moon that measures his months and stars that could guide him home. The verse asks him to see all this — not as scenery but as service, rendered by a cosmos in obedience to a Command that also asks something of him. The one who understands this cannot easily fall into two opposite errors: the arrogance of thinking himself the center of a universe that serves him by right, and the despair of thinking himself an accident in a universe that does not care. He is neither. He is a servant among servants, singled out by the gift of choice, in a world arranged for his benefit by a Lord who asks only to be recognized.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:13

> **And whatsoever He created for you on the earth of diverse hues — truly in this is a sign for a people who reflect.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Returning From the Sky to the Earth**

Verse 12 lifted the eyes to the heavens; verse 13 brings them back down. Ibn Kathīr observes that the verse marks a return from the celestial signs to the terrestrial ones, and that the transition is itself meaningful. The sky's signs are few and grand — sun, moon, stars. The earth's signs are innumerable and intimate. Having shown the reader the ordered vastness above, the sūrah now says: look around you, at what is within reach of your hands, and notice its variety.

**"Whatsoever He Created for You on the Earth"**

The verse opens with *wa-mā dharaʾa lakum fī al-arḍ*, "and what He has multiplied/created for you in the earth." The verb *dharaʾa* is distinct from the more common *khalaqa*. Its root, *dh-r-ʾ*, carries the sense of creating in abundance, scattering, and multiplying; the Qur'an uses it for the propagation of human beings and animals (42:11; 23:79; 67:24). The word choice emphasizes not merely creation but proliferation — the sheer profusion of things spread across the surface of the earth.

Once again *lakum*, "for you," appears. Everything on the earth is described as created for human beings. The Qur'an's most direct statement of this is 2:29: *"It is He Who created for you all that is on the earth."* The jurists derived from such verses the principle that the default status of earthly things is permissibility (*al-aṣl fī al-ashyāʾ al-ibāḥah*) — that what God created for human beings is available to them unless He has specifically forbidden it. The verse thus carries a legal implication alongside its call to gratitude: the world is not a minefield of prohibitions but a table of gifts, with a few items set aside.

**"Of Diverse Hues": The Meaning of *Mukhtalifan Alwānuhu***

The heart of the verse is the phrase *mukhtalifan alwānuhu*, "differing in its colors." The word *lawn*, plural *alwān*, means color in the first instance, but the commentators — al-Bayḍāwī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Qurṭubī — all note that it extends to differences of kind, shape, quality, and type. In Arabic idiom one speaks of "colors of food" (*alwān al-ṭaʿām*) to mean varieties of dishes. So the verse points to the entire spectrum of diversity on earth: the colors of flowers and fruits, the shapes of leaves and stones, the textures of soils, the kinds of animals, minerals, plants, and the varieties within each kind.

The Qur'an develops this theme most fully in Sūrah Fāṭir:

> *"Have you not seen that God sends down water from the sky, and We bring forth thereby fruits of diverse colors? And in the mountains are streaks white and red, of diverse colors, and others intensely black. And among people and beasts and cattle are those of diverse colors likewise. Only those of His servants who have knowledge fear God."* (Qur'an 35:27–28)

That passage names the same phenomenon — diverse colors — in fruits, in mountains, in human beings, and in animals, and concludes that it is the knowledgeable who are moved by it to awe. Verse 16:13 makes the same connection more briefly: diversity is a sign for those who reflect.

**Why Diversity Is an Argument**

The classical theologians saw in the diversity of created things one of the strongest proofs of a free and intelligent Creator, and the argument deserves to be stated clearly because it is both simple and profound.

If the world were the product of a blind necessity — a single cause acting uniformly — its products would be uniform. A machine that stamps coins produces identical coins. But the earth does not produce identical things. From the same soil, the same water, and the same sunlight come the red rose and the white lily, the sweet fig and the bitter colocynth, the heavy iron and the light pumice. Al-Rāzī, discussing verses of this type, argues that the variety of effects arising from apparently uniform causes points to an agent who chooses — a *fāʿil mukhtār* — rather than a mechanical necessity. Difference where sameness would be expected is the signature of will.

There is a second layer. The diversity is not chaotic; it is patterned. Colors are not randomly splashed; each species has its own, and within the species there is ordered variation. The diversity is a diversity of *kinds*, each internally consistent — which points to a wisdom that both individualizes and orders. This combination of variety and order is exactly what one would expect from an intelligent Creator and exactly what one would not expect from chance.

**The Human Response: Wonder and Its Loss**

The verse asks for *tadhakkur* — "a people who reflect," or more precisely, "who take heed" or "who remember." The verb *yadhdhakkarūn* comes from *dh-k-r*, the root of remembrance, and its form suggests an effort to recall and bring to mind. Al-Ṭabarī explains that the sign is for those who reflect on God's proofs and take a lesson from them. Why remembrance here, where verse 11 asked for reflection and verse 12 for reasoning? Perhaps because the diversity of the earth is something everyone has already seen; what is needed is not new observation but the recovery of a wonder that familiarity has worn away.

Children see the world as the verse describes it: full of astonishing colors and kinds, each demanding attention. Adults typically stop seeing it. The Qur'an's call to remembrance is a call to reverse this dulling — to look at the red of a pomegranate or the striations of a rock face as if for the first time, and to ask who made them so. The verse does not ask for a laboratory; it asks for attention.

**Diversity Among People and the Ethics of Difference**

The passage in Sūrah Fāṭir extended the theme of diverse colors to human beings, and the Qur'an makes human diversity an explicit sign elsewhere:

> *"And among His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the diversity of your tongues and your colors. Truly in that are signs for those who know."* (Qur'an 30:22)

> *"O mankind, We created you from a male and a female and made you peoples and tribes that you may know one another. Truly the most noble of you in the sight of God is the most God-fearing of you."* (Qur'an 49:13)

Though 16:13 speaks primarily of the natural world, the same principle governs the human world. Difference of color, language, and custom is not a problem to be solved but a sign to be read. The Prophet ﷺ made the ethical consequence explicit in his sermon at the Farewell Pilgrimage:

> *"O people, your Lord is one and your father is one. There is no superiority of an Arab over a non-Arab, nor of a non-Arab over an Arab, nor of a red person over a black one, nor of a black person over a red one, except by God-consciousness."* (Aḥmad 23489)

The person who sees the diverse colors of the earth as God's deliberate creation is prepared to see the diverse colors of humanity in the same light — as the work of the same Artist, no shade of which is a mistake.

**The Aesthetic Dimension**

Finally, the verse affirms something about beauty that verse 6 introduced: God did not make the world merely functional. A colorless world would grow crops and support life. God made a world of color. The classical commentators did not develop an aesthetic theory, but they noticed the fact. Al-Rāzī remarks that color is a benefit to human beings both practically — enabling them to distinguish things — and in the pleasure it gives. The Qur'an itself pauses over the beauty of what grows from the earth: *"every beautiful kind"* (50:7), *"a delight for beholders"* (27:60). The diverse hues of the earth are a gift to the eye, and the eye that receives the gift with gratitude has understood the verse.

**A Practical Exercise Drawn From the Verse**

The verse is an invitation to a specific spiritual practice: the deliberate noticing of variety. A walk through a market, a garden, or a forest becomes an act of remembrance if one attends to the differences — this fruit's skin against that one's, this leaf's shape against another's — and traces each difference to the choice of a Creator who could have made them all the same. Such noticing is not sentimental. It is the disciplined use of the senses to arrive at the truth that verse 17 will state as a rhetorical question: *"Is He Who creates like one who creates not?"* No idol ever produced a single color. The One who produced them all deserves the gratitude that the diversity of the earth, rightly seen, awakens.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:14

> **He it is Who made the sea subservient, that you may eat fresh meat therefrom, and extract from it ornaments that you wear. You see the ships plowing through it, and [this is so] that you may seek His Bounty, and that haply you may give thanks.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Sea as the Fourth Realm of Blessing**

The sūrah has now surveyed the animals of the land (vv. 5–8), the rain and the plants (vv. 10–11), the sky (v. 12), and the diverse products of the earth (v. 13). Verse 14 turns to the sea. For the Arabs of Makkah, the sea was the Red Sea to the west, reached by the port of Jeddah, and the wider seas beyond, from which came pearls, coral, and the goods of India and Africa. The sea was both a source of wealth and a source of terror; to speak of it as "subservient" was to make a startling claim.

**"He It Is Who Made the Sea Subservient"**

The verse opens with the same emphatic *huwa alladhī* as verse 10 and the same verb *sakhkhara* as verse 12. The sea is subjected. What does it mean for the sea to be made subservient? Al-Rāzī explains that it means God made it usable — its surface bears ships, its depths yield food and ornament, and its behavior is regular enough that human beings can learn to navigate it. The sea remains dangerous; the Qur'an elsewhere describes the terror of those caught in a storm who cry out to God alone (10:22; 17:67; 31:32). But it is not hostile in its nature; it has been arranged so that human beings can draw from it. Its very dangers are part of the test, driving the human heart back to God when its own resources fail.

**The First Benefit: "Fresh Meat"**

*Li-taʾkulū minhu laḥman ṭariyyan*, "that you may eat fresh meat from it." The word *ṭariyy* means fresh, tender, soft — the opposite of dried or tough. Al-Ṭabarī identifies the meat as fish, and the adjective "fresh" was noted by the commentators for its precision: fish spoils quickly and must be eaten fresh, unlike the meat of land animals which can be dried and stored. Al-Rāzī sees in the word an allusion to the delicacy of God's provision — He does not merely feed but feeds with tenderness, matching the description of Himself as *raʾūf*, tender, in verse 7.

The legal status of sea food is one of the clearest illustrations of the ease of Islamic law. Whereas land animals must be ritually slaughtered, the creatures of the sea are lawful as they are. The Qur'an states:

> *"Lawful to you is the game of the sea and its food, as provision for you and for travelers."* (Qur'an 5:96)

And the Prophet ﷺ, asked about making ablution with seawater, gave an answer that became a foundation of the law:

> *"Its water is pure, and its dead are lawful."* (Abū Dāwūd 83; al-Tirmidhī 69; al-Nasāʾī 59; graded ṣaḥīḥ)

"Its dead are lawful" — fish that die in the sea and are washed up, or are caught already dead, may be eaten. Sea food may also be taken by the pilgrim in the state of *iḥrām*, in which hunting land animals is forbidden (5:95–96). The mention of fresh meat from the sea in 16:14 is therefore not merely a gift but a gift wrapped in ease. God provided a whole realm of food with almost no restrictions attached.

**The Second Benefit: "Ornaments That You Wear"**

*Wa-tastakhrijū minhu ḥilyatan talbasūnahā*, "and that you may extract from it ornaments which you wear." The verb *istakhraja*, on the tenth form, means to draw out with effort — the diver's labor is implied. *Ḥilyah* means adornment or jewelry. Al-Ṭabarī and the majority identify the ornaments as pearls and coral, which the Qur'an names explicitly in another passage on the sea:

> *"He released the two seas, meeting together, between them a barrier they do not transgress... From both of them emerge pearl and coral."* (Qur'an 55:19–22)

The verse is notable for granting adornment the status of a divine gift, exactly as verses 6 and 8 did with the beauty of cattle and the *zīnah* of horses. The Qur'an does not despise ornament. It affirms that God placed beauty within the sea — hidden in the shell of an oyster, buried in a reef — and gave human beings the ingenuity to bring it out. The ornament is described as something "you wear," *talbasūnahā*; the commentators note that though men are forbidden gold and silk, the wearing of pearls by women and their gifting between spouses is a legitimate joy. Al-Qurṭubī cites this verse among the proofs that adornment for women is lawful and even commendable.

**The Third Benefit: "You See the Ships Plowing Through It"**

*Wa-tarā al-fulka mawākhira fīhi*, "and you see the ships cleaving through it." The word *mawākhir* is the plural of *mākhirah*, from the root *m-kh-r*, which describes the sound and motion of a vessel cutting through water, pushing it aside and leaving a wake. Al-Ṭabarī explains it as the ship's splitting of the water, or of the wind, as it moves. The image is vivid: one sees the ship's prow parting the sea.

The Qur'an lists ships among God's signs and blessings again and again (2:164; 14:32; 17:66; 22:65; 30:46; 31:31; 35:12; 42:32–33; 43:12; 45:12), and the reason is clear from the verses themselves. A ship is a human artifact, yet it depends entirely on divine arrangements: the buoyancy of water, the force of wind, the strength of wood, the stars for navigation. The Qur'an makes this dependence explicit:

> *"And among His signs are the ships in the sea like mountains. If He wills, He stills the wind, and they remain motionless on its surface. Truly in that are signs for every patient, grateful one."* (Qur'an 42:32–33)

The human being builds the vessel; God supplies everything that makes the vessel useful. This is the same structure of partnership that verse 10 showed in rain and crops — human effort resting on divine provision.

**"That You May Seek His Bounty": Trade Sanctified**

*Wa-li-tabtaghū min faḍlihi*, "and that you may seek of His bounty." The Qur'an uses this phrase consistently for lawful commerce and the pursuit of livelihood (2:198; 17:12, 66; 28:73; 30:46; 62:10; 73:20). The ships plow the sea so that merchants may trade across it, and the profit they earn is called "God's bounty." The verse thus does something important: it sanctifies honest commerce. The merchant who sails to distant ports and returns with goods is not engaged in a worldly distraction from religion; he is seeking God's *faḍl*. The Prophet ﷺ himself had been a merchant, and he said:

> *"The truthful, trustworthy merchant will be with the prophets, the truthful, and the martyrs."* (al-Tirmidhī 1209)

The word *faḍl*, bounty, deserves attention. It means what is over and above the necessary — grace, surplus, favor. Trade profit is thus framed not as something the merchant wrested from the world by his cleverness but as an overflow from God's generosity that his effort positioned him to receive. This framing has a psychological effect. The merchant who thinks his profit is *his* becomes greedy and anxious; the merchant who thinks his profit is God's bounty becomes generous and calm.

**"And That Haply You May Give Thanks": The Purpose Stated**

The verse ends where the whole passage has been heading: *wa-laʿallakum tashkurūn*, "and that you may be grateful." The signs of verses 11, 12, and 13 were for those who reflect, understand, and remember. Now the sūrah names the goal of all that reflection, understanding, and remembering: gratitude. The word *laʿalla*, "that perhaps," expresses purpose and hope: God arranged all this in order that human beings might respond with thanks, and He leaves open — because He has given them freedom — whether they will.

*Shukr* in the Islamic sciences has three components: recognition in the heart that the blessing is from God, acknowledgment on the tongue, and use of the blessing in obedience. The fisherman who knows his catch is from God, says "praise be to God" over it, and shares it with his neighbor has fulfilled all three. The one who eats without recognition, boasts of his own skill, and hoards has fulfilled none.

**A Reflection on the Sea Today**

The modern world draws more from the sea than the Makkans could have imagined: not only fish and pearls but oil from beneath the seabed, salt, minerals, medicines from marine organisms, and the shipping lanes that carry the overwhelming majority of global trade. Every container ship is a *fulk mākhirah*, cleaving the water so that people may seek God's bounty. The verse remains as literally true as the day it was revealed. What is at risk is not the truth of the verse but the response it asks for. A civilization that takes from the sea without gratitude — and, one might add, without care for a gift that can be spoiled — has read only the first part of the verse and ignored its conclusion. The believer who stands on a shore, sees a ship on the horizon, and remembers Who subjected the sea beneath it has read the whole verse. And if he then says *al-ḥamdu li'Llāh*, he has answered it.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:15

> **And He cast firm mountains in the earth, lest it shake beneath you, and streams, and ways, that haply you may be guided,**

**Expanded Commentary**

**From the Sea to the Solid Earth**

The sea of verse 14 is the realm of instability — moving, heaving, dangerous. Verse 15 turns to its opposite: the firm ground and the mountains that anchor it. The sequence has its own logic. Having spoken of what is unstable yet made usable, the sūrah speaks of what is made stable so that human life can rest upon it. Al-Rāzī observes that the mountains, rivers, and roads named in this verse together describe the conditions of settled life on land, as the ships and fish of the previous verse described the conditions of life drawn from the sea.

**"He Cast Firm Mountains": The Verb *Alqā***

The verse opens *wa-alqā fī al-arḍi rawāsiya*, "and He cast into the earth firm ones." The verb *alqā* means to throw or cast down, and the commentators noted its force: the mountains are described as if placed onto the earth from above, deliberately, like weights set to steady a load. The word *rawāsī* is the plural of *rāsiyah*, from the root *r-s-w*, which means to be firmly fixed, anchored, immovable; a ship at anchor is said to have *rasā*. "Firm mountains" is thus the standard rendering, but the Arabic literally says "anchors" or "fixed ones," with the word "mountains" understood. The image is of the earth as a vessel and the mountains as what holds it steady.

**"Lest It Shake Beneath You": *An Tamīda Bikum***

The purpose clause *an tamīda bikum* has been read by the grammarians as "lest it sway with you" — the Arabic idiom omits the negative, saying literally "that it sway with you," with the sense of "for fear that it should." The verb *māda* describes swaying, tilting, oscillating, like a ship rolling or a person staggering. The verse states that the mountains were placed so that the earth would not do this beneath its inhabitants.

The Qur'an makes this claim in several places, with striking consistency:

> *"And We placed on the earth firm mountains, lest it should shake with them."* (Qur'an 21:31)

> *"He created the heavens without pillars that you see, and cast into the earth firm mountains lest it shake with you."* (Qur'an 31:10)

> *"Have We not made the earth a resting place, and the mountains as stakes?"* (Qur'an 78:6–7)

The last verse's image of the mountains as *awtād*, "stakes" or "pegs," has been much discussed. A tent-peg is driven deep into the ground, with only a small part visible above; its function is to hold the tent firm against the wind. The verse suggests that mountains have roots beneath the surface and a stabilizing role. The classical commentators, including al-Ṭabarī and al-Qurṭubī, understood the mountains simply as weights that keep the earth's surface from lurching and quaking. Readers today often note that the geological picture of mountains as having deep roots extending into the crust, and of their role in the balance of the earth's surface, resonates with this language; one may observe the resonance without insisting that the Qur'an was written as a geology text. Its purpose is to draw the eye from the mountain to the One who set it.

**The Contrast With the Last Day**

The stability the mountains provide is temporary, and the Qur'an is emphatic that on the Day of Resurrection they will be undone:

> *"On the Day the earth and the mountains will shake, and the mountains will become a heap of shifting sand."* (Qur'an 73:14)

> *"And the mountains will be like carded wool."* (Qur'an 101:5)

> *"And they ask you about the mountains; say, My Lord will scatter them as dust, and He will leave them a level plain."* (Qur'an 20:105–106)

The mountains that "shall not shake" in this world are the very things that will be pulverized in the next. The point is sobering: what seems most permanent in human experience — the mountain, the symbol of endurance in every culture — is held in place only by God's decree and will be removed by the same decree. The believer who stands before a mountain range is meant to feel both the security God has granted and the contingency of that security.

**"And Streams": *Anhār***

The verse continues *wa-anhāran*, "and rivers." Al-Rāzī notes that rivers are mentioned immediately after mountains because rivers originate in mountains — snowmelt and highland springs feed the streams that flow to the plains. The pairing is repeated in 13:3 and 27:61. Mountains not only stabilize; they gather water and release it. The Qur'an elsewhere states that God "made rivers subservient to you" (14:32). A river is water made available continuously, without the labor of drawing from a well, and the great civilizations of history — along the Nile, the Tigris and Euphrates, the Indus — rose where rivers made settled agriculture possible.

**"And Ways": *Subul***

*Wa-subulan*, "and roads." The word *subul* is the plural of *sabīl*, the same word used in verse 9 for the "straight way." Here it refers to physical routes: the passes through mountains, the valleys along rivers, the tracks across plains by which people travel from place to place. Al-Ṭabarī explains that God made paths in the earth so that people could reach their destinations. Mountains might seem to block travel; in fact, they contain the passes, and rivers cut the valleys, through which roads run. The Qur'an makes this connection explicit elsewhere:

> *"And We placed therein lofty mountains and gave you to drink sweet water."* (Qur'an 77:27)

> *"And We made therein broad passes as roads, that they might be guided."* (Qur'an 21:31)

**"That Haply You May Be Guided": The Double Meaning**

The verse ends *laʿallakum tahtadūn*, "that you may be guided." In its plain sense, this refers to the roads: God made routes so that travelers might find their way. Al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī, and al-Zamakhsharī all give this as the first meaning. The next verse (16) will develop it: landmarks and stars guide the traveler by day and by night.

But the word *tahtadūn* is the very word used for spiritual guidance throughout the Qur'an, and the commentators did not miss the second meaning. The roads of the earth guide the body to its destination; the signs of the earth — the mountains, the rivers, the very existence of ordered paths — guide the mind to its Creator. Verse 9 said that it is for God to show the way. Verse 15 shows Him doing so literally, in the layout of the land, and suggests that the person who reads the physical guidance rightly will find the spiritual guidance beneath it. The mountains that keep the earth from shaking are also, for the reflective mind, a sign that keeps faith from shaking.

**The Psychology of Stability**

There is a human truth in this verse that reaches beyond geography. Human beings need firmness beneath them in order to function. A person who lives in constant physical instability — an earthquake zone, a war zone, a life of endless displacement — is worn down by it; the mind cannot rest when the ground may move. God provided stability as a gift so that life could be built. And the same is true inwardly. The soul needs anchors — *rawāsī* — fixed truths that do not shift with fashion or mood. The Qur'an calls the believers' relationship to God a firm handhold: *"whoever rejects false gods and believes in God has grasped the firmest handhold, which never breaks"* (2:256). Just as God cast mountains into the earth so it would not sway, He sent down revelation into human life so that it would not sway. The believer who has grasped the firmest handhold has an inward mountain range.

**The Prophet's Regard for Mountains**

The Prophet ﷺ is recorded as looking upon Mount Uḥud and saying:

> *"This is a mountain that loves us and we love it."* (al-Bukhārī 4083; Muslim 1365)

The saying reflects the sensibility the verse cultivates: the mountain is not a dead lump but a part of a creation that praises God (17:44; 34:10) and stands in relationship to the believer. To love a mountain in this way is not idolatry; it is the recognition of a fellow creature, placed by God, serving God's purposes.

**Practical Meaning**

Every person who walks on ground that does not move, drinks from a river he did not dig, and travels a road he did not build is living inside the three gifts of this verse. The verse asks him to notice — to feel the firmness underfoot and attribute it, to see the water flowing and attribute it, to follow the road and attribute it. And it asks him to go one step further: to let the physical guidance the earth provides remind him that guidance itself is God's, and that the same Lord who laid out roads for feet has laid out a road for souls. The traveler who arrives home along a mountain pass and thanks God for the pass has understood the first meaning. The traveler who then asks, "And am I also on the road that leads to Him?" has understood the second.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:16

> **and landmarks, and by the stars they are guided.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Short Verse That Completes a Thought**

Verse 16 is grammatically a continuation of verse 15. The preceding verse ended "...and streams, and ways, that haply you may be guided," and this verse adds: "and landmarks, and by the stars they are guided." The brevity is deceptive. In seven Arabic words the verse describes the two systems by which human beings have found their way across the earth for the entire span of history until the invention of instruments — the signs on the land by day and the signs in the sky by night. Al-Rāzī sums up the completeness: God provided guidance for the traveler in every condition, by day and by night, on land and at sea.

**"Landmarks": The Meaning of *ʿAlāmāt***

The word *ʿalāmāt* is the plural of *ʿalāmah*, a sign, mark, or distinguishing feature. It comes from the root *ʿ-l-m*, the root of knowledge (*ʿilm*) — a *ʿalāmah* is that by which something becomes known. The commentators interpret it here as the visible features of the terrain that travelers use to orient themselves. Al-Ṭabarī and al-Qurṭubī list mountains, hills, and rock formations; al-Zamakhsharī adds springs and watering places along the routes; al-Qurṭubī also mentions the winds, whose direction and character the desert Arabs read with great skill, as a kind of landmark.

The knowledge of landmarks was a matter of life and death in the desert. A caravan that mistook one valley for another could wander for days and die of thirst. The Arabs therefore developed an intricate knowledge of the land — every distinctive peak, every well, every color of soil — and passed it from generation to generation. The verse names this knowledge as a gift. The landmarks did not arrange themselves for human convenience; God placed them, and God gave human beings the capacity to read them.

There is also a broader sense. Everything distinctive in the world is a *ʿalāmah*, a mark by which knowledge is gained. The whole thrust of verses 10 through 16 has been that the natural world is full of signs. Verse 16's "landmarks" are literally the marks that guide the body, but they are also examples of the marks that guide the mind. The same root that gives *ʿalāmāt* gives *ʿālam*, "world" — the world is so called, the classical scholars said, because it is a sign (*ʿalam*) pointing to its Maker.

**"And by the Stars They Are Guided"**

*Wa-bi'l-najmi hum yahtadūn*, "and by the star they are guided." Two features of this clause attracted the commentators' attention.

First, the word *najm* is singular — "the star," not "the stars." Al-Qurṭubī and al-Zamakhsharī offer two explanations. The singular may be used generically, standing for the whole class of stars, as Arabic often does. Or it may refer to a particular star or group of stars used for navigation — the commentators mention the Pleiades (*al-Thurayyā*), the Great and Little Bear, and above all the Pole Star (*al-Jady* or *al-Quṭb*), which alone among the visible stars holds its position through the night and points north. In either case, the meaning is that the stars serve as a fixed reference by which direction is determined.

Second, the pronoun *hum*, "they," is placed before the verb: literally "and by the star, *they* are guided." The commentators noted this shift from the second person ("that *you* may be guided," v. 15) to the third person. Some saw in it a subtle rhetorical turn: the verse now speaks of people in general, or specifically of those who make use of the stars — the travelers and sailors — as a group whose skill is observed. Others suggested that the placement of *hum* is emphatic: it is by the stars, and not by their own unaided power, that they find their way.

**The Qur'an on the Stars as Guides**

The theme recurs throughout the Qur'an:

> *"And it is He Who made for you the stars, that you may be guided by them in the darkness of land and sea. We have detailed the signs for a people who know."* (Qur'an 6:97)

> *"And landmarks; and by the stars they are guided."* (Qur'an 16:16)

> *"And He it is Who has adorned the lowest heaven with lamps, and made them missiles against the devils."* (Qur'an 67:5, paraphrasing the sense of 37:6–10 and 67:5 together)

The verse in Sūrah al-Anʿām names both the land and the sea, and both are relevant here: the caravan across the desert and the ship across the water each depend on the stars when no landmark is visible. Al-Rāzī highlights the sea especially, since at sea there are no landmarks at all, and the night sky is the only map.

**The Makkans' Debt to the Stars**

Al-Zamakhsharī draws out a pointed application. The Quraysh were traders who crossed the desert to Syria and Yemen twice a year. They navigated by the stars. Every fortune in Makkah had been made under a sky that God arranged for guidance. And yet the Quraysh worshipped stones. The verse is thus not only a description but an indictment: you have been guided by God's stars your whole lives, and you refuse to be guided by God's word. The One who lit your way by night is the One you deny by day.

**Why Guidance Comes From Above**

The commentators noticed a symbolic fitness in the stars. The traveler lost in the dark cannot find the way by looking at the ground; he must look up. Al-Rāzī and others read this as a parable: human beings lost in the darkness of ignorance cannot find their way by consulting only the earth — their own desires, customs, and philosophies. They must look up, to what descends from above — revelation. The stars are physical guidance from the heavens; the Qur'an is spiritual guidance from the heavens. Both are fixed; both are visible to all who look; both require only that the traveler consult them honestly.

**The Prophet ﷺ and the Direction of Prayer**

Al-Qurṭubī and al-Rāzī note a specific religious application of this verse: Muslims must face the Kaʿbah in prayer, and in unfamiliar territory, the stars and landmarks are the means of determining that direction. The jurists derived from this verse and from 6:97 the legitimacy — even the obligation — of studying enough astronomy to establish the *qiblah* and the times of prayer. This is a small but telling example of how the Qur'an's celebration of natural signs fed directly into Muslim science: the great Muslim astronomers of Baghdad, Cairo, and Samarqand were, in part, fulfilling the practical demands of this verse.

**A Ḥadīth on the Stars**

The Prophet ﷺ spoke of the stars in a memorable comparison:

> *"The stars are a security for the sky; when the stars go, what was promised for the sky will come. And I am a security for my Companions; when I go, what was promised for my Companions will come. And my Companions are a security for my community; when my Companions go, what was promised for my community will come."* (Muslim 2531)

The stars here symbolize stability and guidance: as long as they remain, the sky is in order. The Prophet and his Companions are the stars of the community — the fixed points by which the later generations find their way. The verse's teaching that human beings are guided by the stars thus extends, in the Prophet's own usage, to the human stars God has placed in history.

**A Practical Reflection**

Modern travelers navigate by satellite, and it might seem that the stars have been retired. But every satellite positioning system depends on the same fixed frame of reference the stars provided — the regularity of celestial motion that God established — and the instruments themselves are made from what God placed in the earth. The verse's teaching is not about technology; it is about dependence. Human beings have always needed something outside themselves and above themselves to find their way. Whoever looks honestly at how he finds his way — across a city, through a career, through the moral decisions of a life — will discover that he is following marks he did not make and lights he did not kindle. The verse asks him to acknowledge this and to ask the further question: if I am so willing to be guided by God's stars, why should I be unwilling to be guided by God's word?

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:17

> **Is He Who creates like one who creates not? Will you not, then, reflect?**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Question That Gathers Everything Before It**

Verses 3 through 16 have been a single sustained demonstration: the heavens and the earth, the human being from a drop, the cattle, the riding animals, the rain, the crops, the sun and moon and stars, the diverse colors of the earth, the sea and its ships, the mountains and rivers and roads and landmarks. Verse 17 stops and asks the only question that all of this was leading to: *a-fa-man yakhluqu ka-man lā yakhluq?* — "Is He Who creates like one who creates not?"

The question is rhetorical, and its answer is so obvious that the verse does not bother to supply it. Al-Rāzī explains the logic: after enumerating the things God has created for human benefit, the Qur'an asks whether the Creator of all this can be placed on the same level as idols that have created nothing.
