The verse is a rebuke to those who called their idols "gods" and gave them the worship due to the Creator alone.

**The Grammar of Contempt**

There is a small grammatical detail that the commentators noted with appreciation. The verse asks whether "He Who creates" is like "*man* lā yakhluq," using the pronoun *man*, "who," which in Arabic is properly used for rational beings. The idols are not rational; strictly one would say *mā*, "that which." Why *man*? Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Rāzī give two answers. First, the Qur'an uses the idolaters' own language: they treated their idols as persons and called them gods, so the verse addresses them on their own terms — "is the Creator like *those* you call gods, who create nothing?" Second, the verse may intend a general comparison covering every kind of false object of worship: idols, angels, jinn, and human beings who were deified, all of whom share the single disqualifying feature that they do not create. The rational pronoun stretches to cover the whole set.

The word *yakhluqu* is in the imperfect tense, indicating ongoing action. God is not merely the One who created once; He is the One Who *creates*, continuously, now — bringing each new child into existence, each new season's crops, each raindrop. The idols, by contrast, *lā yakhluq*, do not create, never have, and never will.

**The Force of "Reflect": *Tadhakkarūn***

The verse ends *a-fa-lā tadhakkarūn*, "will you not then take heed?" or "will you not remember?" The verb is the same as in verse 13. The Qur'an does not say "will you not believe?" It says "will you not reflect, recall, take heed?" The implication is that the truth is already available to the listener; it needs only to be brought to mind. Al-Ṭabarī explains that the question is a reproach: the difference between the Creator and the created is so plain that failure to see it is not a lack of evidence but a refusal of attention.

This is a consistent feature of the Qur'an's method with the idolaters. It rarely argues that God exists; the Makkans did not deny that. It argues that the God they acknowledged as Creator is therefore the only one entitled to worship. The gap it exposes is not between belief and atheism but between what people admit and what they do. They admitted that God alone creates; they worshipped what does not create. The verse simply holds the two facts side by side and asks whether they can be reconciled.

**The Argument Stated Plainly**

The reasoning of the verse can be laid out as a syllogism, and it is one of the simplest and strongest arguments in religious literature.

The one who deserves worship is the one who gives existence, sustenance, and every benefit. God alone gives existence, sustenance, and every benefit (as verses 3–16 have shown, and as the idolaters admit). Therefore God alone deserves worship. The idols give nothing; therefore they deserve nothing.

The Qur'an repeats this argument in many forms. Abraham used it against his people:

> *"He said, 'Do you worship what you carve, while God created you and what you make?'"* (Qur'an 37:95–96)

> *"O my father, why do you worship that which neither hears nor sees nor avails you anything?"* (Qur'an 19:42)

And the Qur'an puts it as a general challenge:

> *"Say: Have you considered your partners whom you call upon apart from God? Show me what they have created of the earth."* (Qur'an 35:40)

> *"Those whom you call upon apart from God will never create a fly, even if they gathered together for it."* (Qur'an 22:73)

The fly is the smallest test, and even that is beyond every false god. Verse 16:17 states the principle; verse 16:20 will apply it directly: *"those whom they call upon apart from God create naught, and are themselves created."*

**The Theological Debate the Verse Occasioned**

The verse's sharp division between the Creator and the non-creator was taken up in a famous debate within Islamic theology, and al-Rāzī reports it in his commentary.

The Ashʿarite theologians adduced this verse as proof that creation belongs exclusively to God. If "the One Who creates" is set apart from everything else by the fact of creating, then nothing else can properly be called a creator — including human beings with respect to their own actions. On this view, God creates human acts, and human beings "acquire" (*kasb*) them; the verse supports the position that no created being is the originator of anything.

The Muʿtazilite theologians responded that the verse does not deny a limited human capacity for "making" or "producing" — the Qur'an itself uses the verb *khalaqa* of human making in 29:17, *"and you create a falsehood,"* and of Jesus forming a bird in 3:49. The verse's point, they argued, is different: human beings, who do possess some capacity to act and produce, should not bow to idols that possess none whatsoever. The idols are below even human beings in capability, let alone below God.

The dispute belongs to the technical science of *kalām*, and this commentary need not adjudicate it. What both sides agreed on is what matters for the ordinary reader: creation in the full sense — bringing into existence from nothing according to a determined measure — is God's alone, and the verse's rhetorical force lies precisely in this. Ibn Taymiyyah, standing somewhat apart from both schools, emphasized that the verse's purpose is *tawḥīd al-ulūhiyyah*, the affirmation of God's exclusive right to worship, built upon *tawḥīd al-rubūbiyyah*, His exclusive lordship over creation, and that this practical conclusion is what the Qur'an insists upon.

**Beyond Stone Idols: The Modern Application**

The Makkans' idols were stone. The verse's principle covers every false object of ultimate devotion. Whatever a person treats as the source of his security, his provision, his worth, or his hope — money, a career, a nation, a leader, a system, his own intellect — the verse asks the same question: does this thing create? Did it bring you into existence? Does it send the rain? Does it hold the sun in its course? If not, then it does not deserve the place you have given it. The Prophet ﷺ described a form of idolatry with no statues at all:

> *"Wretched is the slave of the dinar, and the slave of the dirham, and the slave of the fine cloth."* (al-Bukhārī 2887)

A "slave of the dinar" has taken as his god something that creates nothing. Verse 16:17 is addressed to him as much as to the man kneeling before Hubal.

**Why Reflection Is Required, Not Just Information**

The verse ends by calling for *tadhakkur*, and this choice is instructive. The problem it addresses is not lack of information — everyone knows that stone does not create. The problem is that people do not bring what they know to bear on how they live. They know God creates; they act as though wealth does. They know idols are powerless; they fear them anyway. The Qur'an's remedy is *dhikr*, remembrance — the repeated act of bringing the known truth to the front of the mind until it governs behavior. This is why the sūrah enumerated blessings for fourteen verses before asking the question. Reflection needs material. The person who has just walked through the inventory of rain, crops, sun, sea, and mountains is prepared to feel the force of "Is He Who creates like one who creates not?" in a way that a person confronted with the bare question is not.

**A Closing Thought**

The verse is, finally, a call to consistency. It asks the listener to make his worship match his knowledge. Everyone acts on the basis of what he believes to be the source of his good; the verse asks that this belief be accurate. If the Creator is the source, worship the Creator. If something else were the source, it would deserve worship — but nothing else creates. The logic is inescapable, and the Qur'an trusts it to do its work in any honest mind: *a-fa-lā tadhakkarūn* — will you not, then, reflect?

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:18

> **And were you to count the blessings of God, you could not number them. Truly God is Forgiving, Merciful.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Verse That Names the Chapter's Theme**

If al-Naḥl is also "the Chapter of Blessings," as al-Qurṭubī reports some of the early scholars called it, then verse 18 is its thesis statement. After fifteen verses of enumeration — cattle, horses, rain, crops, sun, moon, stars, sea, mountains, rivers, roads, landmarks — the sūrah admits that the enumeration was never going to be complete: *wa-in taʿuddū niʿmata Allāhi lā tuḥṣūhā*, "and if you were to count the blessing of God, you could not enumerate it." The catalogue was a sample, not an inventory. The whole is beyond counting.

**Two Verbs for Counting**

The verse uses two different verbs, and the difference is precise. *Taʿuddū* comes from *ʿ-d-d*, to count, to number one by one. *Tuḥṣū* comes from *ḥ-ṣ-y*, whose original meaning relates to *ḥaṣā*, pebbles, which the Arabs used for tallying; *aḥṣā* came to mean to count exhaustively, to reach the total, to encompass a number completely. The verse thus says: if you were to try counting God's blessings, you would not reach the end of the count. The attempt is possible; the completion is not.

Al-Rāzī illustrates the impossibility with a single case. Suppose a person tried to enumerate the blessings contained in his own body — the bones and their joints, the muscles and their arrangement, the nerves, the organs, the senses, the faculties of the mind — and the wisdom in the placement and function of each. The intellect would be exhausted long before the survey was done. And this is one body. Extend the count to the blessings outside the body — food, air, water, family, safety, knowledge, faith — and the impossibility becomes absolute. Al-Rāzī concludes that the intellect would be extinguished merely by attempting to comprehend the wisdom of its own creation, let alone all the rest.

**"Blessing" in the Singular**

The Arabic says *niʿmata Allāh*, "the blessing of God," in the singular, not *niʿam*, "blessings." The commentators offer an elegant explanation: the singular is used generically, for the entire category of blessing, and it conveys that even one blessing, examined fully, cannot be enumerated — because each blessing contains within it other blessings, and those contain others, without end. The blessing of sight, for example, contains the blessing of light, the blessing of the eye's structure, the blessing of a functioning nerve, the blessing of a brain that interprets, the blessing of things worth seeing. The single word opens into infinity.

**The Twin Verse in Sūrah Ibrāhīm**

This verse appears once more in the Qur'an, almost word for word, but with a different ending:

> *"And He gave you of all that you asked Him. And if you were to count the blessing of God, you could not enumerate it. Truly man is unjust, ungrateful."* (Qur'an 14:34)

The comparison between the two verses is one of the most instructive exercises in Qur'anic study, and the commentators returned to it repeatedly. In Sūrah Ibrāhīm the verse ends by describing the human being — *ẓalūm kaffār*, "very unjust, very ungrateful." In Sūrah al-Naḥl it ends by describing God — *ghafūr raḥīm*, "Forgiving, Merciful." The same fact — that blessings exceed counting — leads to two conclusions, one about man and one about God.

The two verses are two halves of a single truth. When the human being faces the uncountable blessings and considers his own response, he must confess: I have been unjust and ungrateful, because I cannot possibly have thanked Him for what I cannot even count. When he then turns from himself to God, he finds not condemnation but forgiveness and mercy. Ibn Kathīr notes that God, knowing that His servants can never thank Him adequately, forgives their shortfall. The verse in Ibrāhīm diagnoses; the verse in al-Naḥl heals.

**Why "Forgiving, Merciful" Follows Uncountable Blessings**

The commentators asked why a verse about blessings ends with forgiveness. Their answers converge on a single insight, articulated by al-Rāzī, al-Zamakhsharī, and al-Ṭabrisī.

Gratitude, properly understood, ought to be proportionate to the gift. If the gift is infinite, adequate gratitude is impossible. Every human being therefore stands in perpetual deficit before God. If God dealt with human beings strictly — demanding thanks equal to the blessing — no one could survive the audit. The verse's ending is therefore a mercy tailored to the verse's content: because you cannot count the blessings, you cannot thank for them fully; and because you cannot thank for them fully, God is *Ghafūr*, Forgiving — He overlooks the shortfall — and *Raḥīm*, Merciful — He continues to give despite it.

Al-Zamakhsharī adds a second dimension: God is forgiving of the negligence and ingratitude with which people treat His blessings, and merciful in that He does not cut off the blessings when they are misused. The sun rises on the ungrateful; the rain falls on the one who denies the Rain-giver. This continuity of provision in the face of ingratitude is *raḥmah* in action.

**A Ḥadīth on the Impossibility of Adequate Thanks**

The Prophet ﷺ expressed the same truth in a supplication he taught for the morning:

> *"O God, whatever blessing I or any of Your creation has this morning is from You alone, without partner; so to You is praise and to You is thanks."* (Abū Dāwūd 5073; Ibn Ḥibbān 861)

The supplication does not try to list the blessings; it acknowledges them wholesale and directs all praise to the Source. This is the practical response to the impossibility the verse describes. Since one cannot thank item by item, one thanks in totality and with the recognition that the thanks itself is a further blessing requiring further thanks. There is a saying, often attributed to Dāwūd, that he asked, "Lord, how can I thank You when my thanking You is itself a blessing from You?" and was told, "Now you have thanked Me." The recognition of inadequacy is itself the beginning of adequate gratitude.

**The Prophet's Own Practice**

The most vivid illustration of the verse's spirit is the Prophet's night prayer. ʿĀʾishah reported that he would stand in prayer until his feet swelled, and when she asked him why he did this when God had forgiven him his past and future sins, he replied:

> *"Should I not then be a grateful servant?"* (al-Bukhārī 4837; Muslim 2820)

The reply is a commentary on 16:18. Forgiveness did not diminish his sense of debt; it increased it. Knowing the blessings could not be counted, he did not conclude that thanks was pointless. He concluded that thanks must be unceasing. The inability to reach the end of gratitude is a reason to keep going, not a reason to stop.

**The Psychology of Abundance and the Disease of Complaint**

There is a practical wisdom in this verse for the inner life. The human mind is tuned to notice what is missing rather than what is present. A person with health, food, family, and safety will fix his attention on the one thing he lacks, and this fixation breeds discontent, envy, and complaint. The verse corrects the lens. It asks the person to try, even briefly, to count what he has — and to discover that he cannot. This exercise, sincerely performed, produces a shift in perception that the modern vocabulary calls "gratitude practice" but that the Qur'an prescribed fourteen centuries ago as *shukr*. A person who spends a minute attempting the impossible count of 16:18 finds it very difficult to remain in complaint. The Prophet's counsel to look at those below oneself (Muslim 2963) serves the same purpose.

**Blessing as Test, Not Only as Gift**

A final dimension. The Qur'an treats blessings as trusts that will be questioned:

> *"Then you will surely be asked that Day about the bliss."* (Qur'an 102:8)

The Prophet ﷺ explained that even "cool water" and "the shade of a house" are among the blessings that will be asked about (al-Tirmidhī 3358). If the blessings cannot be counted, neither can the accountability for them be escaped by pleading ignorance. This is where the verse's ending becomes most precious. The believer who realizes that he will be questioned about uncountable blessings, for none of which he has fully thanked, would despair — except that the verse tells him the Questioner is *Ghafūr Raḥīm*. The audit will be conducted by One who forgives the shortfall and shows mercy on the debtor. The proper response is therefore neither complacency nor despair, but humble, continuous effort at gratitude combined with continuous reliance on forgiveness.

**The Verse in a Sentence**

Count what you have been given, and you will fail; recognize your failure, and you will know both your own debt and your Lord's generosity; and knowing both, you will find that the only sane response to a debt you cannot pay to a Creditor who forgives is to love Him and to try.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:19

> **And God knows what you hide and what you disclose.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Turn From Provision to Knowledge**

The passage from verse 3 to verse 18 was about God's *power* and *generosity*: He creates, He provides, He blesses beyond counting. Verse 19 introduces a new attribute — His *knowledge*. The transition has a logic that the commentators draw out. A giver who does not know how his gifts are used could be deceived; a giver who knows everything cannot be. Having established that all blessings come from God, the sūrah now establishes that God sees exactly what each person does with them — including what they do in secret. The verse closes the escape route of hypocrisy.

**The Two Categories: *Mā Tusirrūn wa-Mā Tuʿlinūn***

The verse divides all human activity into two: *mā tusirrūn*, "what you conceal," and *mā tuʿlinūn*, "what you make public." The root *s-r-r* gives *sirr*, a secret — that which is kept within the breast or spoken only in private. The root *ʿ-l-n* gives *ʿalāniyah*, openness — that which is done before witnesses. Between these two categories nothing falls; every human thought, intention, word, and deed is either hidden or shown. The verse thus asserts total knowledge without needing to say "everything." Al-Ṭabarī explains that God knows the inner intentions and beliefs of the heart as well as the outward actions of the body, and that nothing is hidden from Him.

The ordering — secret first, public second — is itself meaningful. One might expect the verse to begin with the obvious (what is public) and proceed to the surprising (what is secret). It does the reverse. Al-Rāzī suggests this is because the secret is what the listener would most want to believe is unknown; by naming it first, the verse forecloses that hope immediately. God's knowledge of what you conceal is stated as primary, and His knowledge of what you show follows as a matter of course.

**The Same Truth Across the Qur'an**

The pairing of the hidden and the disclosed is one of the Qur'an's most frequent formulas, appearing in some form in dozens of verses:

> *"Say: Whether you conceal what is in your breasts or disclose it, God knows it; and He knows what is in the heavens and what is on the earth."* (Qur'an 3:29)

> *"Truly God knows the unseen of the heavens and the earth. Truly He is Knowing of what is in the breasts."* (Qur'an 35:38)

> *"And whether you speak aloud or not — truly He knows the secret and what is yet more hidden."* (Qur'an 20:7)

The last verse extends knowledge beyond the secret to *akhfā*, "that which is more hidden" — which the commentators explained as what a person has not yet thought, what he will think tomorrow, or what is hidden even from himself. God's knowledge reaches not only the secrets one keeps from others but the secrets one keeps from oneself.

**Why the Verse Belongs Here: Three Readings**

The commentators offer three complementary explanations for the verse's placement immediately after the passage on blessings.

The first, from al-Zamakhsharī, is that it is a warning. The idolaters concealed evil intentions — their plots against the Prophet ﷺ, their private mockery, their hidden disbelief beneath a public show of religion at the Kaʿbah. The verse tells them that their concealment is useless. God knows.

The second, from al-Rāzī, is that it refers specifically to the twofold sin of the idolaters: their open polytheism, which all could see, and their hidden schemes to undermine the Prophet's mission, which they thought no one saw. Both are known.

The third, also from al-Rāzī, is that the verse continues the argument against the idols. God knows what you hide and show; the idols know nothing at all — not even, as the next verses will say, when their own worshippers will be raised. The contrast between the all-knowing God and the utterly ignorant idol is another form of the question in verse 17: is the One Who knows like one who knows not?

All three readings hold together. The verse warns the hypocrite, exposes the plotter, and refutes the idolater in a single sentence.

**Knowledge and Accountability**

The verse's theological weight lies in the connection between divine knowledge and human accountability. If God did not know the secret, the secret could not be judged, and the interior life — where most moral struggle actually happens — would be outside the reach of justice. A man who resists the temptation to steal in his heart, though no one sees, and a man who plans a theft in his heart, though he never carries it out, would be indistinguishable to any human court. The verse establishes that they are not indistinguishable to God. The Qur'an makes this explicit:

> *"Whether you disclose what is in yourselves or conceal it, God will call you to account for it."* (Qur'an 2:284)

The Prophet ﷺ clarified the scope of this accounting in a well-known ḥadīth: God forgives his community "what their souls whisper to them, so long as they do not act upon it or speak of it" (al-Bukhārī 5269; Muslim 127). Passing thoughts are not sins; settled intentions and hidden deeds are. The verse's assertion of divine knowledge is thus not a source of terror over every stray thought but a source of seriousness about the heart's real commitments.

**The Effect on the Inner Life: *Murāqabah***

The Islamic tradition developed from verses like this one the spiritual discipline of *murāqabah*, watchfulness — the constant awareness that one is seen. The Prophet ﷺ defined the highest level of religion, *iḥsān*, in exactly these terms:

> *"Iḥsān is that you worship God as though you see Him; for if you do not see Him, truly He sees you."* (al-Bukhārī 50; Muslim 8)

"Truly He sees you" is 16:19 in three words. The person who has internalized this does not need external policing. He behaves the same in the dark as in the light, because for him there is no dark. This is why the Qur'an praises those *"who fear their Lord in the unseen"* (67:12) — in private, when no one is watching. The private self is the true self, and the verse tells us that the true self is fully known.

There is a well-known account of the Caliph ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb overhearing, at night, a girl refusing her mother's instruction to water down the milk they sold. The mother said, "ʿUmar cannot see us." The girl replied, "If ʿUmar does not see us, ʿUmar's Lord sees us." ʿUmar was so moved that he married her to his son; her descendant was the righteous Caliph ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz. Whatever the details of the story, it circulated among Muslims for centuries because it captures precisely the moral effect of 16:19: a person who knows that God sees the hidden does not need a human overseer.

**The Comfort in the Verse**

It would be a mistake to read the verse only as a threat. God's knowledge of the hidden is also a consolation. The believer whose secret good deeds no one notices — the charity given anonymously, the night prayer no one sees, the wrong forgiven silently, the tear shed in private — is assured that all of it is known and recorded. The Prophet ﷺ described among those shaded on the Day of Judgment "a man who gives charity and conceals it, so that his left hand does not know what his right hand spends" (al-Bukhārī 660; Muslim 1031). Such a man has no earthly audience; his audience is the One described in 16:19. And the believer who is wronged in ways that no one else can see — slandered in private, betrayed behind closed doors — is assured that the wrong is known and will be answered. The verse guarantees that nothing good goes unrewarded and nothing evil goes unrecorded, regardless of who else was present.

**A Practical Application**

The verse offers a simple test for daily conduct. Before any action, ask: would I do this if it were public? If the honest answer is no, the verse has already exposed the action, because to God it *is* public. And there is a second, gentler test: what am I doing that no one sees? If the answer includes acts of goodness, the verse promises they are seen by the only One whose seeing ultimately matters. To live under 16:19 is to collapse the distinction between the public and private self — to become, in the Prophet's phrase, a person of *iḥsān*, who worships as though seeing and lives as one who is always seen.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:20

> **And those whom they call upon apart from God create naught, and are themselves created.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Application of the Principle**

Verse 17 asked, "Is He Who creates like one who creates not?" Verse 20 names the one who creates not. *Wa'lladhīna yadʿūna min dūni Allāhi lā yakhluqūna shayʾan wa-hum yukhlaqūn* — "and those they call upon apart from God create nothing, and they are created." The verse moves from the general principle to its specific target: the idols and false deities of the Makkans. It adds a devastating second clause that verse 17 did not contain: not only do the idols not create; they are themselves creatures. They belong to the category of the made, not the Maker.

**"Those Whom They Call Upon": The Nature of the Error**

The verse describes the idolaters' relationship to their idols with the verb *yadʿūna*, "they call upon" or "they invoke." The root *d-ʿ-w* means to call, summon, or supplicate, and *duʿāʾ*, supplication, is what the Prophet ﷺ called "the essence of worship" (al-Tirmidhī 3371). The verse thus names the specific act by which the idolaters honored their idols: they prayed to them. They asked them for rain, children, victory, healing. The absurdity the verse exposes is that they addressed requests to things that cannot hear, cannot answer, and cannot produce anything at all.

The phrase *min dūni Allāh*, "apart from God" or "besides God," is the Qur'an's standard expression for every object of worship other than the One. It covers stone idols, but also angels, jinn, deified human beings, and anything else to which ultimate trust is directed. The Makkans did not generally deny God; they placed intermediaries "beside" Him. The verse's target is exactly that placement.

**"Create Naught": The Absolute Negation**

*Lā yakhluqūna shayʾan*, "they do not create anything." The indefinite *shayʾan*, "a thing," after a negation is the Arabic way of expressing total negation — not one thing, nothing whatsoever. Verse 17 said the idols "create not"; verse 20 makes the negation absolute. There is no partial exception, no small domain of the idol's competence. The Qur'an presses this point elsewhere to its logical extreme:

> *"O mankind, a parable is set forth, so listen to it: those whom you call upon apart from God will never create a fly, even if they gathered together for it. And if the fly should snatch something from them, they could not recover it from it. Weak are the seeker and the sought."* (Qur'an 22:73)

A fly: the smallest, most contemptible creature. All the gods of Arabia together could not make one. And if a fly landed on the offering placed before an idol and carried off a crumb, the idol could not retrieve it. "Weak are the seeker and the sought" — the worshipper who asks and the idol asked of are both powerless. Verse 16:20 states the principle that Sūrah al-Ḥajj illustrates.

**"And Are Themselves Created": The Reversal**

The second clause, *wa-hum yukhlaqūn*, "and they are created," is the verse's decisive stroke. The passive verb is in the imperfect, suggesting ongoing making: the idols are being made, continually, by human hands — carved, cast, painted, replaced when broken. Al-Rāzī notes the irony: the worshipper creates his god. The order of dependence is exactly reversed from what worship requires. The creature should depend on its Creator; here the "god" depends on its worshipper for its very existence.

Abraham's argument with his people turned on exactly this point:

> *"He said, 'Do you worship what you carve, while God created you and what you make?'"* (Qur'an 37:95–96)

Three levels of creation are named in Abraham's question: God created the worshippers; God created the material they carve; and the worshippers carve the idol. At every level, the idol is at the bottom of the chain of making. To worship it is to worship the least of things by the most honored of creatures.

The Qur'an develops the same reversal in the words of the people of Hell, who will say:

> *"By God, we were indeed in manifest error when we made you equal to the Lord of the worlds."* (Qur'an 26:97–98)

The error was one of *equating* — placing the created on the level of the Creator. Verse 16:20 exposes the equation as impossible by simply stating what the two terms are.

**Extending the Verse Beyond Stone**

The commentators recognized that the verse's logic applies not only to carved images but to every created thing that human beings elevate to divine status. Al-Rāzī notes that the phrase covers angels and prophets who were worshipped by some, since they too are created and create nothing. Jesus, whom Christians deified, is described in the Qur'an as one who ate food (5:75) — a mark of created dependence — and who could form a bird from clay only "by God's leave" (3:49). The verse's criterion is universal: whatever is created is not God, however exalted; and whatever creates nothing has no claim on worship, however powerful it seems.

In the modern world, the "gods" people call upon are seldom statues. They are wealth, which cannot create a single day of life; the state, which cannot create a grain of wheat; technology, which is made by human hands from materials God placed in the earth; celebrity, which is manufactured by human attention; and the self, which did not choose its own birth. Each of these is "called upon" in the sense of being trusted as the ultimate source of security or meaning. And each is described by the verse: it creates nothing, and it is itself created. The one who directs his ultimate hope to any of them has, in the Qur'an's terms, taken it "apart from God."

**The Psychological Cost of Worshipping the Created**

There is a practical wisdom in the verse that reaches into ordinary life. To depend on something that cannot create is to depend on something that cannot ultimately deliver. The person who makes wealth his god discovers that wealth cannot create health, love, or peace of mind; the person who makes another human being his god discovers that the human being is as needy and mortal as himself. The idol always fails, because it was never capable of what was asked of it. The Qur'an describes the moment of this discovery at its most terrible — on the Day of Judgment, when the false gods disown their worshippers (16:86; 14:22) — but the same discovery happens in smaller ways throughout life, every time a created thing that was trusted as ultimate proves to be merely created.

The verse therefore does more than refute an ancient error. It offers a diagnosis of a recurring human misery: the misery of asking from what cannot give. And it implies the cure: direct the asking to the One Who creates.

**The Freedom in the Verse**

A final observation. The verse liberates. If everything apart from God is created and creates nothing, then nothing apart from God deserves the fear, the servility, and the anxious hope that people habitually give to created powers. The tyrant is created; the market is created; the opinion of the crowd is created. None of them made the sun rise this morning. The believer who has absorbed 16:20 walks through a world full of impressive powers with a calm that others find difficult to understand, because he knows that all of them belong to the category of *yukhlaqūn*, the made, and only One belongs to the category of *yakhluq*, the Maker. His fear and hope are concentrated where they belong, and the rest of the world loses its power to enslave him. This is what the Qur'an means by *tawḥīd*: not merely a belief about the number of gods, but a reorientation of the whole self toward the only One Who creates.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:21

> **[They are] dead, not living, and they are not aware of when they will be resurrected.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Final Blow Against the Idols**

The sūrah's argument against the idols has proceeded in stages. Verse 17 established the principle: the Creator is not like the non-creator. Verse 19 established God's total knowledge. Verse 20 established that the idols create nothing and are themselves created. Verse 21 delivers the final contrast: the idols are dead and ignorant, while God — as the whole Qur'an proclaims — is the Living and the Knowing. Three attributes distinguish God from His creation in the sharpest possible way: He creates, He lives, He knows. The idols fail on all three.

**"Dead, Not Living": *Amwātun Ghayru Aḥyāʾ***

The verse begins with two words in stark opposition: *amwāt*, "dead," and *ghayru aḥyāʾ*, "not living." The redundancy is deliberate and forceful. To say "dead" is enough; to add "not living" removes any possibility of a hidden life, a latent power, a spirit that might dwell within the stone. The idolaters believed, or half-believed, that their idols housed some presence — that Hubal or al-Lāt could hear and respond. The verse denies it absolutely. They are dead, and — lest anyone suppose a mysterious exception — they are not alive.

Al-Rāzī draws the contrast that the verse invites. God is *al-Ḥayy*, the Living, one of His greatest Names:

> *"God, there is no god but He, the Living, the Self-Subsisting."* (Qur'an 2:255)

> *"And rely upon the Living Who does not die, and glorify Him with His praise."* (Qur'an 25:58)

The idols cannot be relied upon precisely because they are the opposite of the Living Who does not die: they are dead things that never lived. The Qur'an's verse 25:58 gives the practical corollary — trust is properly placed only in what lives and cannot die. Everything else will fail the one who trusts it, if not sooner then at death.

The word *amwāt* also carries a meaning beyond mere lifelessness. In Arabic, *mayyit* can describe inanimate matter — stone, wood, metal — that was never alive in the biological sense. The idols are dead in this sense: not corpses of things that once lived, but material that never had life and never will. Al-Zamakhsharī notes that the description is chosen to contrast with the worshippers themselves, who are living, and who are therefore superior to the things they worship — a superior being bowing to an inferior one.

**"They Are Not Aware of When They Will Be Resurrected"**

The second half of the verse, *wa-mā yashʿurūna ayyāna yubʿathūn*, adds ignorance to lifelessness. The verb *yashʿurūna* comes from the root *sh-ʿ-r*, which means to perceive, to sense, to be aware; *shuʿūr* is consciousness or feeling. The idols have no *shuʿūr* — no perception of anything, and specifically no perception of *ayyāna yubʿathūn*, "when they will be raised."

The pronoun "they" in "when they will be resurrected" has been read in two ways, and both are meaningful.

On the first reading, adopted by al-Rāzī and others, "they" refers to the worshippers: the idols do not know when their own worshippers will be raised for judgment. This is the most complete form of ignorance — the idols were invoked as intercessors and protectors for the Day of Judgment, yet they do not even know when that day is. A protector who does not know when the danger will come is no protector.

On the second reading, noted by Ibn Kathīr and reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, "they" refers to the idols themselves: the idols do not know when *they* will be raised. This reading assumes that the idols will indeed be brought forth on the Day of Judgment — and the Qur'an confirms this. Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to have said that God will give life to the idols on the Day of Resurrection, gather them together with the devils, and command them all into the Fire. The Qur'an supports this:

> *"Truly you and what you worship apart from God are fuel for Hell; you will come to it."* (Qur'an 21:98)

> *"And it will be said to them, 'Where is that which you used to worship apart from God? Can they help you or help themselves?' Then they will be thrown into it, they and the deviators."* (Qur'an 26:92–94)

On this reading, the irony is complete. The idols will indeed be raised — not as gods to judge, but as evidence to condemn, thrown into the Fire alongside those who worshipped them. And they know nothing of this. The stone that the Makkan bowed before will be present at his judgment, not to intercede for him but to be cast in with him.

**The Contrast With God's Knowledge**

Verse 19 said that God knows what is hidden and what is disclosed. Verse 21 says the idols know nothing — not even the timing of the Resurrection. The Qur'an identifies knowledge of the Hour as the exclusive prerogative of God:

> *"They ask you about the Hour — when will it arrive? Say: Its knowledge is only with my Lord; none will reveal its time but He."* (Qur'an 7:187)

> *"Truly God — with Him is knowledge of the Hour."* (Qur'an 31:34)

Even the Prophet ﷺ, when asked about the Hour by Gabriel in the famous ḥadīth, replied: *"The one asked knows no more than the one asking"* (Muslim 8). If the greatest of prophets and the greatest of angels do not know the Hour, the ignorance of the idols is absolute. But the point of the verse is not merely that the idols share the general ignorance of creatures; it is that they have no perception whatsoever. The Prophet did not know the Hour's time but knew that it would come and lived in preparation for it. The idols do not know that anything will come, because they do not know anything.

**Why the Sūrah Ends Its Case Here**

The commentators observed that with this verse the sūrah completes a systematic dismantling of idol worship on three grounds, corresponding to three necessary attributes of a true God.

A god must be a creator — the source of the worshipper's existence and provision. The idols create nothing (v. 20).

A god must be living — capable of hearing, responding, acting. The idols are dead (v. 21).

A god must be knowing — aware of the worshipper's needs and of the future for which help is sought. The idols know nothing (v. 21).

The argument is exhaustive. There is no fourth criterion by which the idols could qualify. And the argument requires no special revelation to grasp; it depends only on facts the idolaters themselves could verify by looking at their idols. This is why the Qur'an so often calls its refutation of idolatry a matter of *ʿaql*, reason, and *tadhakkur*, reflection, rather than of faith in the unseen.

**The Broader Meaning: Dead Ends in Life**

The verse's description — dead, not living, unaware — applies by extension to every false object of ultimate hope. Consider what people substitute for God in the modern age. Wealth is dead: it cannot love, cannot comfort, cannot know. Fame is dead: it is a pattern of attention in other minds, with no life of its own. Ideologies are dead: they are constructions of human thought, with no power to act. None of them has *shuʿūr*; none of them knows when its devotee will die or what will happen to him afterward. The person who serves them is serving what cannot perceive his service. The Qur'an's alternative is not an abstraction; it is *al-Ḥayy*, the Living One, Who hears the whisper, knows the need, and holds the future. The verse's function is to make the choice between the two unmistakably clear.

**A Reflection on Life Itself**

Finally, there is a spiritual lesson in the pairing of "dead, not living" with the mention of resurrection. The idols are dead and will be raised only to be condemned. The believer is alive — and the Qur'an calls faith itself a life, contrasting the believer with one who is "dead" in disbelief (6:122). The one who worships the Living becomes alive; the one who worships the dead becomes, in a sense, dead himself — his heart hardened, his perception dulled, his awareness of the Hour lost. The Prophet ﷺ compared the remembrance of God to life itself:

> *"The likeness of the one who remembers his Lord and the one who does not remember Him is the likeness of the living and the dead."* (al-Bukhārī 6407)

The verse thus asks the reader a personal question beneath the theological one: which category do you belong to? Are you turned toward the Living and therefore alive, or toward the dead and therefore dying? The answer is found not in what one professes but in what one calls upon when the need is real.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:22

> **Your God is one God. And those who believe not in the Hereafter, their hearts deny and they wax arrogant.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Conclusion Stated Positively**

The verses from 17 to 21 refuted the idols negatively — they do not create, they are created, they are dead, they do not know. Verse 22 now states the positive truth that all of that negation was clearing the ground for: *ilāhukum ilāhun wāḥid*, "your God is one God." The formula is among the most concentrated statements of *tawḥīd* in the Qur'an. It appears in this exact wording in 2:163, 22:34, and 41:6, and in a close variant in 16:51, 18:110, and 21:108.

The word *ilāh*, "god," designates whatever is worshipped — the object of ultimate devotion, love, fear, and hope. The word *wāḥid*, "one," negates both plurality and division: there is not more than one God, and God is not composed of parts. The addition of the possessive *ilāhukum*, "your God," makes the statement personal. It does not say merely "God is one" as an abstract proposition; it says "the God *you* must worship is one." The verse addresses the listener's own life and asks for a decision.

**Why Unity Follows From the Preceding Argument**

Al-Rāzī shows how the verse follows logically from what preceded it. If the Creator is unlike the non-creator (v. 17), and everything other than God creates nothing and is itself created (v. 20), and is dead and ignorant (v. 21), then only God possesses the attributes of divinity, and therefore there is only one God. Unity is not asserted arbitrarily; it is derived. The Qur'an elsewhere gives a further argument: if there were two gods, the cosmos would be in disorder, since two independent wills cannot govern one universe without conflict —

> *"Had there been in them gods other than God, they would both have been corrupted."* (Qur'an 21:22)

> *"God has not taken any son, nor is there any god with Him; else each god would have taken away what he created, and some of them would have overcome others."* (Qur'an 23:91)

The order of the world — the very order that verses 3 to 16 displayed — is itself evidence of a single governing will.

**The Diagnosis: Why Do Some Refuse an Obvious Truth?**

Having stated the truth, the verse turns to those who reject it, and it offers a diagnosis rather than merely a condemnation. *Fa'lladhīna lā yuʾminūna bi'l-ākhirati qulūbuhum munkiratun wa-hum mustakbirūn* — "So those who do not believe in the Hereafter, their hearts are denying, and they are arrogant."

The verse identifies three linked conditions. The first is disbelief in the Hereafter. The second is a heart that denies. The third is arrogance. The commentators understood these as causally connected, and the connection illuminates something deep about the psychology of unbelief.

Why does the verse mention the Hereafter specifically, when the topic was the oneness of God? Al-Rāzī and Ibn Kathīr explain: the person who does not believe he will be judged has no motive to accept a truth that would obligate him. If there is no accounting, then acknowledging one God — which entails obeying Him — costs something and yields nothing. Disbelief in the Hereafter is therefore the root that makes rejection of *tawḥīd* attractive. The Makkans' denial of resurrection (v. 38) and their idolatry were not two separate errors but one disease with two symptoms.

**"Their Hearts Deny": The Seat of Rejection**

The verse locates the denial in the *qalb*, the heart, not in the intellect. This is a precise and important claim. The Qur'an does not say "their minds cannot understand." It says "their hearts deny" — *munkirah*, from the root *n-k-r*, which means to reject, to refuse to recognize, to treat as strange or unacceptable. The intellect can follow the argument of verses 17–21; there is nothing difficult in it. What refuses is the heart, the seat of will and desire, which does not want the conclusion.

Al-Qurṭubī explains that their hearts "deny" in the sense of refusing admonition — they do not accept advice or warning, however clear. This distinction between intellectual assent and the heart's acceptance is fundamental to the Qur'an's understanding of faith. Belief is not merely knowing that something is true; it is receiving that truth, welcoming it, submitting to it. A person can know and still refuse:

> *"And they rejected them, though their souls were convinced of them, out of injustice and arrogance."* (Qur'an 27:14)

That verse, describing Pharaoh's court, names exactly the two causes that 16:22 names: injustice (*ẓulm*) and arrogance (*ʿuluww*). The heart that denies does so not for lack of evidence but out of a will that refuses to bend.

**"And They Wax Arrogant": The Root Sin**

The third condition is *istikbār*, arrogance. The verb *istakbara* is on the tenth form and means to consider oneself great — to seek greatness for oneself, to regard oneself as too important to submit. It is the sin the Qur'an attributes to Iblīs when he refused to prostrate to Adam:

> *"He refused and was arrogant, and became one of the disbelievers."* (Qur'an 2:34)

> *"He said, 'I am better than he; You created me from fire and created him from clay.'"* (Qur'an 7:12)

Iblīs did not doubt God's existence or command. He heard the command directly and refused it because obeying it would have placed him below one he considered inferior. This is arrogance in its purest form: the refusal to accept a truth because accepting it would lower one's self-estimate. The Makkan chiefs refused Islam for precisely this reason. To accept the message of an orphan from the clan of Hāshim, and to stand shoulder to shoulder in prayer with slaves like Bilāl, was intolerable to their sense of rank. Al-Bayḍāwī notes that their arrogance prevented them from following the Prophet ﷺ and led them to deny anything they did not already know — the characteristic posture of the proud, who cannot bear to learn from one they look down upon.

**The Prophet's Definition of Arrogance**

The Prophet ﷺ gave arrogance a precise definition that matches the verse exactly:

> *"Arrogance is rejecting the truth and looking down on people."* (Muslim 91)

Two components: *baṭar al-ḥaqq*, rejecting the truth — which is the "heart that denies" — and *ghamṭ al-nās*, despising people — which is the social face of *istikbār*. The same ḥadīth warns: *"No one who has an atom's weight of arrogance in his heart will enter Paradise."* The severity of this warning matches the position arrogance holds in the verse: it is not one sin among others but the disposition that closes the heart against truth itself. Al-Qurṭubī, in his commentary on the next verse, will observe that arrogance is the root of all disobedience, since every sin involves preferring one's own will to God's.

**How Arrogance Blinds**

The verse's psychology can be traced in ordinary experience. A person who has publicly committed to a position, built a reputation on it, and derived status from it finds it extraordinarily difficult to admit he was wrong — not because the evidence is unclear, but because admission would cost him. He develops, over time, a "heart that denies": a settled refusal to look at what would unsettle him. The Qur'an describes this state as a kind of self-inflicted sealing (which verse 108 of this sūrah will mention). The proud man does not see, not because he cannot, but because seeing would require him to bow, and he has decided in advance that he will not bow.

This is why the Qur'an so often pairs the refutation of idolatry with a call to humility. The argument of verses 17–21 will convince anyone whose heart is open. The verse now explains why some hearts are not open: they have been closed by pride. The remedy is not more argument but the softening of the heart — which is why the sūrah began, in verse 2, with the command to *taqwā*, reverent fear, the disposition that bends before God and thereby becomes able to receive the truth.

**The Believer's Contrast**

The verse describes the deniers; the commentators, especially al-Bayḍāwī, draw the implied contrast with the believers. Where the denier's heart refuses, the believer's heart receives; where the denier is arrogant, the believer is humble. The believer contemplates the signs of God — the very signs verses 3–16 enumerated — and benefits from them, because he approaches them with a disposition to accept whatever they show. The difference between the two is not intelligence but posture. The Qur'an says of the believers that when the signs are recited to them, *"their hearts tremble"* (8:2) and *"they fall down in prostration"* (17:107) — the exact opposite of a heart that denies and a self that waxes proud.

**A Practical Examination**

The verse invites a personal audit. It is easy to affirm "your God is one God" with the tongue. The verse asks whether the heart affirms it — whether there is any truth one refuses to accept because accepting it would require humility, any command one resists because obeying it would lower one's standing in one's own eyes or in others', any person from whom one refuses to learn because of who he is. Each such refusal is a trace of the "heart that denies" and the self that "waxes arrogant." The believer who finds such traces in himself has not thereby failed; he has found the work that *tawḥīd* requires of him, which is not merely to count God as one but to bow before Him as one, with a heart that does not resist.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:23

> **There is no doubt that God knows what they hide and what they disclose. Truly He loves not the arrogant.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Repetition With a Purpose**

Verse 19 already stated that God knows what people hide and what they disclose. Verse 23 says it again, four verses later, with a stronger opening: *lā jarama*, "there is no doubt," "without question," "assuredly." Repetition in the Qur'an is never idle. The commentators ask why the truth of God's knowledge is restated here, and the answer lies in what came between: verse 22 identified the deniers by three marks — disbelief in the Hereafter, a denying heart, and arrogance. Two of these three are inward. A "heart that denies" is hidden from human eyes; arrogance may be concealed behind polished manners. Verse 23 answers: hidden or not, God knows.

The phrase *lā jarama* deserves a note. Its literal etymology is disputed among the grammarians — some derive it from *jarama*, "to cut," giving the sense "there is no cutting off of this," that is, no way to escape it; others treat it as a fixed expression of certainty equivalent to "truly" or "inevitably." Al-Ṭabarī takes it in the sense of "truly" and "necessarily." Either way, it adds solemn emphasis: what follows is not merely true but inescapably so.

**What Exactly Is Known Here**

In verse 19, "what you hide and what you disclose" was addressed to the listeners in the second person (*tusirrūn*, *tuʿlinūn*) and functioned as a general statement about all human beings. In verse 23, the pronouns shift to the third person (*yusirrūn*, *yuʿlinūn*): "what *they* hide and what *they* disclose." The subject is now specifically the arrogant deniers of verse 22. Al-Rāzī explains the shift: the verse warns them that their inner rejection, their secret plots against the Prophet ﷺ, and their concealed contempt are as known to God as their public idolatry. The heart that denies cannot hide its denial from the One Who made it.

There is also a consoling dimension for the Prophet ﷺ and the believers. The Makkan leaders sometimes feigned interest, asked questions with hidden mockery, or made private plans while showing public civility. The verse assures the believers that none of this deception succeeded with God, Whose knowledge would be the basis of the coming judgment.

**"He Loves Not the Arrogant": The Heart of the Verse**

The verse's second sentence is its center: *innahu lā yuḥibbu al-mustakbirīn*, "truly He does not love the arrogant." This is one of a family of Qur'anic statements listing those whom God does not love, and reading them together reveals a moral map. God does not love:

the transgressors (2:190; 5:87; 7:55);
the workers of corruption (5:64; 28:77);
the disbelievers (3:32; 30:45);
the wrongdoers (3:57, 140; 42:40);
the vainglorious boaster (4:36; 31:18; 57:23);
the treacherous (4:107; 8:58; 22:38);
the wasteful (6:141; 7:31);
the exultant in worldly goods (28:76);
and, here, the arrogant (16:23).

Against these stand those whom God *does* love: the God-fearing (3:76; 9:4, 7), the doers of good (2:195; 3:134, 148; 5:13, 93), the just (5:42; 49:9; 60:8), the patient (3:146), the repentant and the pure (2:222), those who rely on Him (3:159), and those who fight in His way in ranks (61:4). The sūrah will end by placing God *with* the God-fearing and the doers of good (16:128). The believer who studies these two lists possesses a complete guide to which qualities to cultivate and which to uproot.

**Why Arrogance Specifically?**

The commentators asked why, of all sins, arrogance is singled out here as the object of God's displeasure. Their answers repay attention.

Al-Qurṭubī makes a striking observation that connects the verse's two halves. Arrogance, he says, is the one sin that cannot be hidden. Other sins may be concealed — theft in the night, a lie in private, a secret injustice. But arrogance is by nature visible; it shows in the bearing, the speech, the look, the treatment of others. It is a disposition that manifests. Al-Qurṭubī connects this to the verse's mention of what is hidden and disclosed: the arrogant may hide much, but they cannot hide their arrogance, and God, Who knows both the hidden and the disclosed, sees it from both sides.

Al-Qurṭubī adds that arrogance is the root of all disobedience — *aṣl al-maʿāṣī*. Every sin is, at bottom, a preference of one's own will over God's, and this preference is arrogance in embryo. Iblīs's refusal to prostrate was arrogance; Pharaoh's claim to lordship was arrogance; the Makkans' rejection of a prophet from a humble clan was arrogance. Uproot arrogance and the branches of sin wither; leave it, and no amount of pruning will help.

Al-Rāzī observes that arrogance is uniquely incompatible with the relationship the verse's context demands. The whole passage has been about recognizing blessings and thanking the Giver. The arrogant person cannot do this, because gratitude requires acknowledging dependence, and the arrogant person's entire self-image rests on denying dependence. He must believe that what he has, he earned; that what he knows, he discovered; that what he is, he made. Gratitude threatens this self-image at its foundation. Arrogance is therefore not only a sin among others but the specific disposition that blocks the sūrah's whole purpose.

**The Prophetic Teaching on Arrogance**

The Prophet ﷺ spoke of arrogance with a severity he reserved for few other sins. Beyond the ḥadīth that "no one with an atom's weight of arrogance in his heart will enter Paradise" (Muslim 91), he transmitted a ḥadīth qudsī in which God says:

> *"Pride is My cloak and greatness is My garment; whoever contends with Me over either of them, I will throw him into the Fire."* (Abū Dāwūd 4090; Ibn Mājah 4174)

The image explains why God does not love the arrogant. Greatness belongs to God alone; the arrogant person is wearing a garment that is not his. He is claiming, in effect, a share in divinity — which is why the Qur'an treats *istikbār* as closely allied to *shirk*. The Prophet also described the arrogant person's fate in terms designed to reverse his self-image:

> *"The arrogant will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection like small ants in the form of men, covered by humiliation from every side."* (al-Tirmidhī 2492)

The one who made himself large will be made small; the one who looked down on others will be trodden underfoot. The punishment fits the sin with exact symmetry.

**God's "Love" and "Not Loving"**

A theological note. What does it mean for God to "not love" someone? The scholars of the Sunnī tradition — Ibn Taymiyyah with particular emphasis — affirmed that God's love and displeasure are real attributes, befitting His majesty, not mere metaphors for reward and punishment. God truly loves the God-fearing and truly does not love the arrogant. The practical import is enormous. The human being's deepest need is to be loved by the One Who made him. The arrogant person, by his own disposition, has placed himself outside that love. He has not been arbitrarily excluded; he has excluded himself, because arrogance and the reception of love are incompatible. One cannot be filled while claiming to be already full.

**The Path Out of Arrogance**

If God does not love the arrogant, the believer's task is to become the opposite: *mutawāḍiʿ*, humble. The Prophet ﷺ promised:

> *"No one humbles himself for the sake of God but that God raises him."* (Muslim 2588)

Humility, in the Islamic understanding, is not self-hatred or false modesty; it is accuracy. It is seeing oneself as one actually is — a creature made from a drop (v. 4), sustained by rain one did not send (v. 10), guided by stars one did not light (v. 16), owing everything to a Giver whose gifts cannot be counted (v. 18). The person who sees this cannot be arrogant, because arrogance depends on a false accounting. The sūrah's method of listing blessings is therefore also its method of curing pride: the more clearly one sees what one has been given, the less room remains for the illusion of self-sufficiency.

**A Practical Test**

The verse invites an honest self-examination, guided by the Prophet's definition. Do I reject a truth because of who is telling it? That is arrogance. Do I look down on anyone because of his poverty, his origin, his lack of learning, or his sins? That is arrogance. Do I find it hard to say "I was wrong," "I don't know," "thank you," or "forgive me"? Each of these difficulties marks a place where the self is defending a greatness that belongs only to God. The verse does not merely inform the reader that God does not love the arrogant; it gives him, through this examination, the means of ceasing to be among them — and thereby of entering the company of those whom, as the sūrah's final verse will say, God is *with*.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:24

> **When it is said unto them, "What has your Lord sent down?" they say, "Fables of those of old!"**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Arrogance in Speech**

Verses 22 and 23 described the arrogant in terms of their hearts. Verse 24 lets us hear them speak. When they are asked about the revelation, their answer is a sneer: *asāṭīru al-awwalīn*, "fables of the ancients." The verse thus gives a concrete example of what a denying heart and a proud disposition produce when they open their mouths. The abstract diagnosis of the preceding verses becomes a scene one can picture: a questioner, a question, and a contemptuous dismissal.

**The Setting of the Question**

The verse begins *wa-idhā qīla lahum*, "and when it is said to them." The passive construction leaves the questioner unnamed, and the commentators offer several possibilities that together reconstruct the historical scene. Al-Zamakhsharī and others describe how, during the pilgrimage season, Arabs from outside Makkah would arrive and, having heard rumors of a man claiming prophethood, would ask the Makkan leaders about him and about what he was bringing. The Quraysh, alarmed at the possibility that visitors might be attracted to the Prophet ﷺ, are reported to have stationed men on the roads into the city to intercept travelers and poison their minds against him. When such a traveler asked, "What has your Lord sent down?" — a question that in itself presupposes that something might have been sent down — the answer was prepared: "Fables of the ancients. Nothing new. Old stories."

The question may also have been posed by the believers to the disbelievers, or by the disbelievers to one another in mockery. Whatever the exact scene, the verse captures a standard talking point of the Makkan opposition.

**The Meaning of *Asāṭīr***

The word *asāṭīr* is the plural of *usṭūrah* (or, according to some grammarians, of *isṭār* or *asṭūr*), from the root *s-ṭ-r*, "to write in lines." The root gives *saṭr*, a line of writing, and *masṭūr*, written down. *Asāṭīr al-awwalīn* therefore means, most literally, "the writings of the ancients" — and by extension, the old tales, legends, and myths that had been written down and passed along: stories without truth, entertainment for idle evenings. The word carries the same dismissive tone as "fairy tales" or "old wives' tales" in English.

The charge was a favorite of the Makkan opposition; the Qur'an records it nine times (6:25; 8:31; 16:24; 23:83; 25:5; 27:68; 46:17; 68:15; 83:13). In its fullest form it is given in Sūrah al-Furqān:

> *"And they say, 'Fables of the ancients, which he has had written down, and they are dictated to him morning and evening.'"* (Qur'an 25:5)

The charge, then, was not merely that the Qur'an contained old stories but that the Prophet ﷺ was having them copied from written sources and recited to him. It was a theory of the Qur'an's origin designed to explain it away without engaging its content.

**Why the Charge Was Made — and Why It Failed**

The charge was chosen with some cunning. The Qur'an does contain accounts of earlier peoples — ʿĀd, Thamūd, Noah, Abraham, Moses, Pharaoh — and some of these names were known in Arabia. By labeling the whole revelation as "old tales," the opponents could acknowledge its narrative content while denying its divine origin and, crucially, denying its relevance. Old stories do not demand a change of life.

The charge failed on several counts, which the Qur'an itself and the commentators pointed out.

First, the Prophet ﷺ was known to be unlettered; he neither read nor wrote. The Qur'an makes this a point of evidence:

> *"And you did not recite before it any scripture, nor did you inscribe one with your right hand; otherwise the falsifiers would have had cause to doubt."* (Qur'an 29:48)

Second, the accounts in the Qur'an differed from the versions circulating among the Jews and Christians in ways that could not be explained by copying — correcting, clarifying, and adding details, as with the story of Joseph, of which the Qur'an says, *"You were not with them when they cast their lots"* (3:44), and *"This is from the news of the unseen which We reveal to you; you knew it not, neither you nor your people, before this"* (11:49).

Third, and most fundamentally, the Qur'an is not mostly stories. It is law, argument, exhortation, prophecy, and — as the preceding verses of this very sūrah demonstrate — reasoning from the natural world. The charge of "fables" could only be made by someone who had not listened or who was determined to misrepresent what he heard. Al-Rāzī notes that the accusation reveals the accusers: they described what they had not examined, which is the signature of the arrogant heart of verse 22.

**The Contrast Verse 30 Will Draw**

The verse is constructed to be answered. In verse 30, the same question is asked of the God-fearing — "What has your Lord sent down?" — and their answer is one word: *khayran*, "good." The Qur'an places the two answers six verses apart so that the reader may hold them side by side. The same revelation, the same question, and two utterly opposed responses. The difference is not in the revelation but in the responders. Al-Bayḍāwī and al-Zamakhsharī both draw attention to the contrast: the arrogant call it fables, the reverent call it good, and the difference lies in the disposition of the heart that verses 22–23 described.

**The Psychology of Dismissal**

The verse describes a tactic that has never gone out of use: dismissing a message by labeling it rather than engaging it. The Makkans did not refute the Qur'an's arguments about creation, provision, and resurrection; they attached a label — "fables" — that made refutation seem unnecessary. The label did the work that argument could not. This is a defense mechanism of the proud mind. To engage would risk being persuaded; to be persuaded would require submission; and submission is what the arrogant heart has resolved against. So the mind reaches for a category — "old stories," "primitive superstition," "outdated" — that permits it to turn away without having looked.

The Qur'an's response to this tactic is not to argue about the label but to keep presenting the content. The sūrah goes on, after this verse, to speak of judgment, of previous nations, of the Garden and the Fire, of the messengers sent to every community. It does not defend itself against the charge of "fables"; it continues to do the thing that fables cannot do — reason, warn, promise, and command — and leaves the honest listener to notice the difference.

**"Those of Old" and the Question of Novelty**

There is one more irony in the charge that the commentators noted. The Makkans dismissed the revelation as *asāṭīr al-awwalīn*, the stuff of the ancients — as though age were a defect. Yet the same Makkans justified their idolatry by appeal to antiquity: *"We found our fathers following a way, and we are guided by their footsteps"* (43:22). When the ancient thing was their own custom, age was authority; when the ancient thing was God's message, age was contempt. The inconsistency exposes the real basis of their judgment: not the age of a thing but whether it served their pride.

The Qur'an's own view of the ancients is quite different. The stories of earlier peoples are not "fables" but *ʿibrah*, lessons — *"In their stories there is a lesson for those of understanding"* (12:111). The past is neither to be venerated blindly nor dismissed contemptuously; it is to be learned from. The messengers came to every nation (16:36), and what happened to those who rejected them is a warning that verse 26 will make specific. The person who calls that warning a fable has decided not to learn.

**The Verse's Warning to Every Age**

The believer reading this verse should not think only of seventh-century Makkans. Every age has its version of "fables of the ancients" — its way of dismissing revelation as belonging to a past that has been outgrown. The label changes; the function does not. And the verse's implicit warning is that the person who dismisses without examining bears the consequence of his dismissal, which the very next verse will describe: he carries his own burden and, if he leads others to dismiss as well, a portion of theirs. The tongue that says "fables" is not merely wrong; it is doing something for which it will answer.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:25

> **[This is so], that on the Day of Resurrection they may bear their burdens completely, along with some of the burdens of those whom they lead astray without knowledge. Behold! Evil is that which they bear.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Consequence of the Sneer**

Verse 24 recorded the words of the arrogant: "Fables of the ancients." Verse 25 records their consequence. The particle *li-* at the start of the verse (*li-yaḥmilū*, "that they may bear") is the *lām* of consequence or result: the outcome of their dismissal will be that they carry a double weight on the Day of Resurrection. The verse thus completes the scene. The Makkan chief who intercepted pilgrims on the road and told them the Qur'an was old tales was not merely expressing an opinion; he was loading a burden onto his own back — his own, in full, and a share of every person he turned away.

**The Word *Awzār***

The word *awzār* is the plural of *wizr*, from the root *w-z-r*, which means to carry a heavy load. A *wazīr*, a minister, is so called because he bears the burdens of the ruler. In the Qur'an, *wizr* consistently denotes the burden of sin — the moral weight a person accumulates through wrongdoing and must carry to judgment. The Qur'an speaks of the Prophet's own relief from such a burden: *"And We removed from you your burden, which had weighed upon your back"* (94:2–3). The image is physical: sin as a load strapped to the shoulders, growing heavier with each addition, until the Day when it is weighed.

The verse says the deniers will bear their burdens *kāmilatan*, "completely," "in full." Al-Qurṭubī explains this word with care: nothing of their punishment will be reduced. In particular, whatever misfortunes they suffered in this world as a result of their disbelief — defeat, loss, humiliation — will not count as partial payment. For the believer, worldly suffering expiates sin; the Prophet ﷺ said that no fatigue, illness, or even the prick of a thorn befalls a Muslim but that God expiates some of his sins thereby (al-Bukhārī 5641). The disbeliever who dies in rejection has no such expiation. His burden arrives at judgment *kāmilah*, whole.

**The Second Burden: Leading Others Astray**

The verse then adds a second load: *wa-min awzāri alladhīna yuḍillūnahum bi-ghayri ʿilm*, "and some of the burdens of those whom they lead astray without knowledge." This is the heart of the verse and the source of its enduring moral force. The one who misguides others does not merely commit his own sin; he becomes a participant in every sin that flows from his misguidance.

The Qur'an makes the same point about the leaders of disbelief:

> *"And they will surely bear their own burdens, and burdens along with their burdens, and they will surely be questioned on the Day of Resurrection about what they used to fabricate."* (Qur'an 29:13)

> *"And those who disbelieve say to those who believe, 'Follow our way, and we will bear your sins.' But they will not bear anything of their sins; truly they are liars."* (Qur'an 29:12)

The two verses of Sūrah al-ʿAnkabūt together illuminate 16:25. The misleaders promise to carry their followers' sins — a promise they cannot keep, because each soul answers for itself. Yet the misleaders *will* carry an additional load, not by transfer from the followers but by their own act of misleading, which is itself a sin multiplied by every person it affects.

**The Ḥadīth That Explains the Mechanism**

The Prophet ﷺ stated the principle with a precision that has made it one of the most cited teachings in Islamic ethics:

> *"Whoever calls to guidance will have a reward like the rewards of those who follow him, without that diminishing their rewards in the least. And whoever calls to misguidance will have a sin like the sins of those who follow him, without that diminishing their sins in the least."* (Muslim 2674)

The phrase "without that diminishing their sins in the least" resolves what might seem a contradiction. The Qur'an states firmly, in five places, that *"no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another"* (6:164; 17:15; 35:18; 39:7; 53:38). How can the misleader bear "some of the burdens" of those he misled? Ibn Kathīr and al-Qurṭubī answer using this ḥadīth: the follower's burden is not lifted from him and placed on the leader. The follower bears his own sin in full — he chose to follow. The leader bears a *like* of that sin, a duplicate generated by his own act of leading. Both are fully accountable; neither's burden lightens the other's. The Qur'anic principle of individual responsibility is preserved, and the additional guilt of the misleader is affirmed. The mathematics of sin, in this teaching, is not a zero-sum transfer but a multiplication.

The Prophet ﷺ gave the principle a historical anchor as well. Speaking of the first murder, he said:

> *"No soul is killed unjustly but that a share of its blood is upon the first son of Adam, because he was the first to institute killing."* (al-Bukhārī 3335; Muslim 1677)

Cain bears a share of every murder until the end of time — not because the murderers are relieved of their guilt, but because he opened the door.

**"Without Knowledge": Whose Ignorance?**

The phrase *bi-ghayri ʿilm*, "without knowledge," has been read in two ways, and al-Zamakhsharī and al-Rāzī discuss both.

On the first reading, it describes the misleaders: they lead others astray *without knowledge* — that is, ignorantly, on the basis of conjecture and inherited prejudice, without any real understanding of what they reject. The Makkan who called the Qur'an "fables" had not studied it; he misled on the basis of ignorance dressed as certainty.

On the second reading, it describes the misled: the leaders lead astray people who are *without knowledge* — the simple, the uninformed, the pilgrims from the desert who had no way to evaluate what they were told. This reading highlights the special wickedness of exploiting ignorance. The misleader picks his victims among those least able to resist.

Al-Zamakhsharī then raises the question the second reading provokes: if the followers were ignorant, are they excused? His answer is no. Every human being has been given intellect and the capacity to inquire, and the responsibility to use them. The follower who accepted "fables" from a stranger on the road, without seeking out the Prophet ﷺ and hearing for himself, was culpably negligent. Ignorance that could have been remedied by reasonable effort is not an excuse; it is itself a fault. This is why the verse says the misled bear their own burden even as the misleaders bear an extra share.

**"Evil Is That Which They Bear"**

The verse ends with an exclamation: *alā sāʾa mā yazirūn*, "Behold! Evil is what they bear." The particle *alā* is used to arrest attention — "listen!", "mark this!" — and *sāʾa* is a verb of condemnation, "how evil," "how wretched." The verb *yazirūn* returns to the same root as *awzār*: they are laden, they carry. Al-Ṭabarī explains the sense: how wretched is the load they will bring to the judgment — their own sins, complete, and the multiplied sins of those they led.

**The Two-Sided Lesson: Influence Is Never Neutral**

The verse's principle cuts in both directions, as the ḥadīth of Muslim makes clear. Every human being exercises some influence — as a parent, a teacher, a friend, a writer, a public figure, a person who is watched by others. Nothing that influence produces in others is morally neutral to the one who exercised it. The father whose children learn dishonesty from him carries a share of every lie they tell; the teacher whose students learn contempt for the truth carries a share of every dismissal they make. Conversely, the mother whose children learn prayer from her is rewarded with every prostration they perform; the person who teaches one verse of the Qur'an receives a share of every recitation it inspires.

This is a heavy truth and a liberating one. It is heavy because it forbids the comfortable thought that "my opinions are my own business." Opinions spread; and what spreads from you returns to your account. It is liberating because it means that a single act of guidance — a word of truth spoken to one person — may multiply across generations in a way that the speaker will never see but will certainly receive. The Prophet ﷺ described a person's good works continuing after his death through *"knowledge from which benefit is derived"* (Muslim 1631). The verse's dark side has a bright twin.

**The Modern Amplification**

In the age of the first listeners, a misleader could reach a few pilgrims on a road. Today, a single dismissive comment — "fables," "outdated," "superstition" — can reach millions in an hour. The mechanism described in 16:25 has not changed; its scale has. The person who publicly dismisses revelation without having examined it, and thereby turns others away from examining it, is doing precisely what the Makkan chiefs did, with a reach they could not have imagined. The verse's warning is correspondingly amplified. And so is its promise: the person who uses the same reach to call to guidance, with wisdom and beautiful exhortation (as verse 125 will command), earns a reward multiplied by every person who responds.

**A Closing Reflection**

The verse asks each reader to consider what he is loading onto his own back — not only by his private deeds but by his public words and their effects on others. The Makkan on the road thought he was merely protecting his city's reputation. He was, in reality, filling a sack he would have to carry to God. The believer who understands this becomes careful with his tongue in a specific way: not merely avoiding lies, but avoiding the casual dismissals, the sneers, the lazy labels that turn others from truth. And he becomes eager to speak the truth for the same reason — because every heart that turns toward God through his word lightens his load and adds to his reward, without diminishing theirs in the least.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:26

> **Those before them also plotted. Then God came upon their building from the foundations, and the roof fell down upon them from above, and the punishment came upon them whence they were not aware.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**From Warning to Precedent**

Verses 24 and 25 exposed the Makkans' dismissal of revelation and its consequence in the Hereafter. Verse 26 adds a consequence in this world, and it does so by pointing to history. *Qad makara alladhīna min qablihim*, "those before them plotted." The Makkans were not the first to scheme against God's message; others had done so, and the verse describes what became of them. Al-Ṭabrisī captures the double function: the verse is a consolation to the Prophet ﷺ, who is reminded that plots against messengers are old and always fail, and a warning to Quraysh, who are told that the same failure awaits them.

**The Vocabulary of Plotting: *Makr***

The word *makr*, "plotting" or "scheming," denotes a hidden stratagem — planning harm in secret while presenting a different face. The Qur'an uses it repeatedly for the opposition to prophets and, in a striking usage, for God's response: *"And they plotted, and God plotted; and God is the best of plotters"* (3:54). When applied to God, the word does not imply deceit; it means that God turns the schemers' own plans against them, defeating them by means they did not foresee. The verse under discussion illustrates this exactly: the plotters built, and their building became the instrument of their destruction.
