Other verses that develop the theme of the futility of plotting against God include 6:123, 8:30 (*"And they plotted, and God plotted; and God is the best of plotters"* — of the Makkans' plan to kill the Prophet), 10:21, 13:42, 14:46, 27:50, and 35:43, which states the general law: *"Evil plotting encloses none but its authors."*

**The Building and Its Fall: The Historical Referent**

The verse's central image is a building attacked at its foundations, whose roof then collapses on those inside. *Fa-atā Allāhu bunyānahum min al-qawāʿid*, "so God came upon their building from the foundations." The word *qawāʿid* is the plural of *qāʿidah*, a base or foundation — the same word used for the foundations of the Kaʿbah that Abraham and Ishmael raised (2:127). *Fa-kharra ʿalayhim al-saqfu min fawqihim*, "and the roof fell upon them from above."

The classical commentators, including al-Ṭabarī, al-Thaʿlabī, al-Jalālayn, and al-Ṭabrisī, connect this image with a specific ancient event: the attempt of a tyrant to build a tower reaching to heaven in order to wage war on its inhabitants. Most identify the tyrant as Nimrod (Namrūd), the king who disputed with Abraham about God (2:258), and they describe his tower at Babylon as immense in height. According to these accounts, God sent a wind that toppled the tower from its base, and the roof came down upon the builders. Al-Ṭabarī and al-Zamakhsharī note the resemblance to the story of the Tower of Babel in the scriptures of the Jews and Christians, and some commentators, including Ibn Kathīr, mention Nebuchadnezzar as an alternative identification. These identifications come from the *isrāʾīliyyāt* — reports drawn from earlier scriptural traditions — and the Qur'an itself does not name the builder. What the Qur'an provides is the pattern: a plot conceived in pride, embodied in a construction, and destroyed from the very foundation.

**The Metaphorical Reading: Every Plot Is a Building**

Ibn Kathīr offers a reading that many find more penetrating than the historical identification, and that is fully compatible with it. The "building" may be a metaphor for the entire structure of the disbelievers' schemes — the whole edifice of arguments, alliances, persecutions, and slanders they constructed to defeat the message. God "came upon it from the foundations" means He undid the plot at its root, so that everything built upon it collapsed. On this reading, the verse describes not one tower but every tower: every elaborate scheme against truth is a structure whose foundation is falsehood, and falsehood cannot bear weight indefinitely.

Al-Ṭabrisī adds that the verse may mean that God made the plotters' schemes rebound upon themselves — the harm they intended for others fell on their own heads, as the roof fell on the builders. This matches the general law of 35:43.

Ibn Kathīr also proposes that "the roof fell upon them" may refer to the exposure of a plot that was meant to stay hidden — the collapse of the concealment that a scheme depends on. A conspiracy is like a roof: it shelters the conspirators only as long as it holds. When God exposes it, the shelter becomes the weapon.

**"From the Foundations": Why the Attack Comes From Below**

There is precision in the detail that God struck the building *from the foundations* rather than from the top. A building attacked from above may be repaired; a building whose foundation is removed cannot stand, however sound its upper floors. The image teaches something about how divine judgment operates against falsehood. God does not merely trim the branches of a corrupt system; He removes what it rests on. The plotters' building rested on their confidence that God would not act, on their alliances, on their wealth, on their control of the city. Remove that confidence — as Badr removed it — and the whole structure of Makkan opposition collapsed within a decade.

The image also describes the internal logic of any life or society built on falsehood. Such a structure may rise high and look impressive, but its foundation is unsound, and the Qur'an elsewhere contrasts it with the structure built on *taqwā*:

> *"Is he who founded his building on fear of God and His good pleasure better, or he who founded his building on the edge of a crumbling bank about to collapse, so that it collapsed with him into the Fire of Hell?"* (Qur'an 9:109)

The building on the crumbling bank is the building of 16:26. Its collapse is not an external accident but the natural result of where it was built.

**"Whence They Were Not Aware": The Unseen Direction**

The verse ends: *wa-atāhum al-ʿadhābu min ḥaythu lā yashʿurūn*, "and the punishment came upon them from where they did not perceive." The phrase recurs in the Qur'an (39:25; 16:45) and describes a consistent feature of divine judgment: it arrives from an unexpected direction. The plotters had planned for every contingency except the one that came. Nimrod, in the traditional account, built against the sky and was destroyed by the wind. The Makkans planned against a small band of persecuted believers and were defeated at Badr by that same band, three hundred strong against a thousand.

Al-Rāzī reflects that this feature is inherent in the relationship between human planning and divine knowledge. Human beings can only guard against what they can foresee; God's knowledge encompasses what they cannot. The plotter is therefore always exposed on the side he is not watching. The verb *yashʿurūn* is the same used of the idols in verse 21 — they "do not perceive." There is a bitter symmetry: those who worshipped what does not perceive were themselves struck from a direction they did not perceive.

**Consolation for the Prophet ﷺ**

The verse was revealed at a time when the plots against the Prophet were intensifying: economic boycott, social ostracism, physical abuse of the weak, and eventually a coordinated plan to assassinate him (8:30). To a man watching his followers tortured and his message mocked, the verse said: this has all happened before, and the outcome is already known. The Qur'an offers this consolation repeatedly — *"Messengers before you were denied, and they were patient over being denied and harmed until Our help came to them"* (6:34) — and the Prophet drew strength from it. The pattern of history, rightly read, is a source of steadiness.

**The Believer's Application**

For the reader, the verse teaches three things. First, that opposition to truth is not new and its ultimate failure is not in doubt; the believer who faces hostility for his faith is standing where every believer before him has stood, and the outcome has never changed. Second, that one should examine the foundation of one's own life. What is it built on? If it rests on something other than God — on wealth, status, deception, the approval of others — it is the building of this verse, however tall it has grown, and its collapse is only a matter of time. Third, that no one is secure from the direction he is not watching. The wise person does not trust in the completeness of his own plans; he trusts in God and keeps his foundations sound, knowing that judgment, when it comes, comes from where one did not look.

The Prophet ﷺ taught a supplication that expresses precisely this awareness:

> *"O God, I seek refuge in You from being struck down from beneath me."* (Abū Dāwūd 5074; al-Nasāʾī 5529 — explained by the narrator as referring to the earth swallowing one up)

To pray against being struck from below is to acknowledge the truth of 16:26: the foundation is where the danger lies, and only God can secure it.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:27

> **Then on the Day of Resurrection He will disgrace them and say, "Where are My partners on whose account you were defiant?" Those who were given knowledge will say, "Surely, this day, disgrace and evil are upon the disbelievers"—**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Two Punishments, Two Worlds**

Verse 26 described the destruction of the plotters' building in this world. Verse 27 begins with *thumma*, "then," and moves to the Day of Resurrection. Al-Zamakhsharī states the structure: the collapse of the building was their punishment in this life, and disgrace is their punishment in the next. The Qur'an regularly pairs these two — worldly ruin and otherworldly humiliation — to make clear that escaping the first does not mean escaping the second, and that suffering the first does not exhaust the debt. The Makkan who died before Badr did not thereby avoid what this verse describes.

**"He Will Disgrace Them": The Nature of *Khizy***

The verb *yukhzīhim* comes from the root *kh-z-y*, and *khizy* is one of the Qur'an's most severe words for punishment. It denotes not physical pain primarily but humiliation, shame, exposure, disgrace — the public revelation of a person as contemptible. The Qur'an speaks of *ʿadhāb al-khizy*, "the punishment of disgrace" (10:98; 41:16), and of the believers' prayer to be spared it: *"Our Lord, whomever You admit to the Fire, You have surely disgraced him"* (3:192).

Why is disgrace specifically named as the punishment of the arrogant? The answer lies in the symmetry between sin and recompense. Verses 22 and 23 identified the deniers by their arrogance — *istikbār*, the seeking of greatness. The fitting reversal of self-exaltation is humiliation. The proud person's deepest fear is not pain but exposure; the loss of the image he has constructed of himself is worse to him than any physical suffering. On the Day of Resurrection, that image is stripped away before all creation. Al-Rāzī notes that the disgrace consists in the public exposure of their falsehood: what they insisted upon in this world with such confidence is shown, before every witness, to have been a lie.

**The Question: "Where Are My Partners?"**

God's question to them is *ayna shurakāʾiya alladhīna kuntum tushāqqūna fīhim*, "Where are My partners on whose account you used to be defiant?" The question is not a request for information. Ibn Kathīr and al-Ṭabrisī call it *tawbīkh*, rebuke, and al-Zamakhsharī adds *tahakkum*, mockery — the exposing of an absurdity by asking the absurd party to produce his evidence.

The phrase "My partners" is itself devastating. God says *shurakāʾī*, "My partners," not "your gods." He uses their own language against them — the beings they claimed shared in His divinity — while the possessive makes the claim ring hollow: these were supposed to be partners *of Mine*; produce them. The Qur'an uses this same interrogation in several scenes of judgment:

> *"And the Day He will call to them and say, 'Where are My partners whom you used to claim?'"* (Qur'an 28:62)

> *"Then it will be said to them, 'Where is that which you used to associate apart from God?' They will say, 'They have vanished from us.'"* (Qur'an 40:73–74)

> *"And the Day He will call to them and say, 'Where are My partners?' they will say, 'We declare to You: none of us is a witness.' And what they used to call upon before will vanish from them, and they will know for certain there is no escape for them."* (Qur'an 41:47–48)

The pattern is constant. The question is asked; the partners are absent; the questioned have no answer. The verse in al-Naḥl does not record the disbelievers' reply, and this silence is itself the answer. There is nothing to say.

**"On Whose Account You Were Defiant": The Word *Tushāqqūn***

The verb *tushāqqūn* comes from the root *sh-q-q*, "to split," and the third form *shāqqa* means to oppose, to be at odds, to take the other side of a divide — literally, to stand on the opposite "half" (*shiqq*) from someone. The word appears in the Qur'an for those who oppose God and His Messenger (8:13; 59:4). The verse thus says: you split from Me, you opposed the believers, you tore the community apart — all "on account of" these partners who are now nowhere to be found.

Al-Ṭabrisī and al-Zamakhsharī draw out the double object of this defiance. The idolaters were defiant toward God — refusing His unity — and defiant toward the believers, whom they persecuted for affirming it. The idols were the pretext for both. Every act of hostility the Makkans committed against the Muslims was committed in the name of gods who, on the Day of Judgment, cannot be located. The verse asks them to consider what they fought for.

**"Those Who Were Given Knowledge": The Witnesses Speak**

At this point a new voice enters: *qāla alladhīna ūtū al-ʿilm*, "those who were given knowledge will say." Who are they? The commentators offer several identifications, and all are illuminating.

Al-Zamakhsharī identifies them as the prophets and the learned (*ʿulamāʾ*) who, in the world, called people to faith and warned them — the very people the disbelievers mocked. On the Day of Judgment, those they dismissed as bringers of "fables" pronounce the verdict. Al-Ṭabrisī mentions the believers generally, and also the angels. Ibn Kathīr extends the phrase to all who were noble and truthful in this world and the next.

The description "those who were given knowledge" is significant in itself. The verse does not say "the believers" or "the righteous" but *ūtū al-ʿilm*, "were given knowledge." The Qur'an consistently honors knowledge as the ground of faith and elevates those who possess it:

> *"God will raise those who have believed among you and those who were given knowledge by degrees."* (Qur'an 58:11)

> *"Only those of His servants who have knowledge fear God."* (Qur'an 35:28)

On the Day when the arrogant are disgraced, it is the knowledgeable who speak — because their knowledge is now vindicated. In the world, the disbelievers claimed to know better; they called the message fables and the messengers fools. On this Day, the ones who actually knew declare the truth, and their declaration is part of the disgrace. To be judged wrong by those one despised as ignorant is a humiliation in itself.

**The Verdict: "Disgrace and Evil Are Upon the Disbelievers"**

The words of the knowledgeable are: *inna al-khizya al-yawma wa'l-sūʾa ʿalā al-kāfirīn*, "Truly, this day, disgrace and evil are upon the disbelievers." Two terms: *khizy*, disgrace, and *sūʾ*, evil, harm, ill. The first names the humiliation; the second names the suffering that accompanies it. The word *al-yawma*, "this day," with the definite article, fixes the moment: the Day of Judgment, when what was hidden is manifest and what was denied is present.

The word *al-kāfirīn*, "the disbelievers," reaches back to the whole passage. These are the ones whose hearts denied (v. 22), who called the revelation fables (v. 24), who led others astray (v. 25), who plotted (v. 26). The verdict pronounced by the knowledgeable summarizes the sūrah's case against them.

**Why the Knowledgeable Speak, and Not God Alone**

One might ask why the verse has the verdict pronounced by the knowledgeable rather than by God directly. Al-Rāzī suggests a reason: the involvement of witnesses is part of the justice and the completeness of the judgment. God does not merely punish; He establishes the case publicly, with testimony from those who knew and warned, so that the condemned cannot claim they were judged arbitrarily. Verses 84 and 89 of this sūrah will describe a witness raised from every community. The knowledgeable of verse 27 are among these witnesses. Their speech is the record of the trial.

There is also a reversal at work. In the world, the disbelievers held the podium; they set the terms of public discourse and mocked the believers before the crowds. On the Day of Resurrection, the podium changes hands. Those who were silenced speak; those who spoke are silent. The Qur'an describes this reversal elsewhere: *"So today those who believed are laughing at the disbelievers"* (83:34) — the mirror image of the disbelievers' laughter in this world (83:29).

**The Lesson for the Present**

The verse's teaching for the reader has several layers. First, it affirms that ultimate reputation is decided not in this world but in the next, and that the judgment of the arrogant crowd will be reversed by the judgment of the knowledgeable few. The believer mocked for his faith should hold this scene in mind. Second, it warns against the specific sin of being "defiant on account of partners" — of fighting, dividing, and opposing in the name of something other than God. Every cause that is not God's cause will be absent when its partisans are asked to produce it. Third, it calls the reader to be among "those who were given knowledge" — to seek the knowledge that will be vindicated, rather than the cleverness that will be exposed.

And finally, it teaches the believer how to regard disgrace in this world. To be humiliated for the truth is a small thing, because the Day of real disgrace has not yet come, and on that Day the positions will be exchanged. The believer's prayer, taught in the Qur'an, is the correct response: *"Our Lord, forgive us our sins and remove from us our misdeeds, and cause us to die with the righteous... and do not disgrace us on the Day of Resurrection"* (3:193–194). To be spared *khizy* on that Day is worth any humiliation before it.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:28

> **those whom the angels took while they were wronging themselves. Then they will offer submission, "We were not doing any evil." Nay, but God knows best that which you were doing.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Completing the Sentence of Verse 27**

Verse 27 ended with the knowledgeable declaring: "disgrace and evil are upon the disbelievers—" and the sentence continues here: "—those whom the angels take while they are wronging themselves." The verse thus identifies the disbelievers more precisely by their condition at the moment of death. They are not merely people who disbelieved at some point; they are people whose souls were taken *while they were in the act of wronging themselves*. The moment of death fixed their state. The Qur'an's teaching is that a person is judged by his condition at the end, and the verse describes the end of these.

**"Those Whom the Angels Took": Death as an Encounter**

The verb *tatawaffāhum*, "take them," comes from the root *w-f-y*, which means to fulfill, to complete, to receive in full. *Tawaffā* is the Qur'an's regular term for death, and it is significant that it does not mean "to destroy" or "to end" but "to take in full" — to receive the soul completely, as a creditor receives the whole of a debt. Death in the Qur'anic vocabulary is a collection, not an annihilation. The soul is taken, intact, by the angels appointed for the task:

> *"Say: The Angel of Death, who has been entrusted with you, will take you; then to your Lord you will be returned."* (Qur'an 32:11)

> *"...until, when death comes to one of you, Our messengers take him, and they do not fail."* (Qur'an 6:61)

The mention of "the angels," plural, reflects the Qur'an's picture of the angel of death assisted by other angels — angels of mercy for the believer and angels of punishment for the disbeliever. The verse's specification of the angels as the agents of death is itself a rebuke to the idolaters: not the idols, but God's angels, control the moment they most fear.

**"While They Were Wronging Themselves": The Meaning of *Ẓālimī Anfusihim***

The phrase *ẓālimī anfusihim*, "wronging themselves," is one of the Qur'an's most frequent descriptions of sinners, and its logic deserves attention. The root *ẓ-l-m* means to place a thing where it does not belong — to violate the proper order. The idolater places worship where it does not belong, on created things; this is why the Qur'an calls *shirk* "a tremendous wrong" (31:13). But the verse says they wronged *themselves*. God is not harmed by their idolatry; the harm falls entirely on the one committing it. The idolater's *ẓulm* is against his own soul — its purpose, its dignity, its eternal welfare. Al-Ṭabarī explains that they wronged themselves by persisting in disbelief until death overtook them in that state.

This phrase also appears in 4:97, in a scene the commentators connect with this one: *"Those whom the angels take while they are wronging themselves — [the angels] will say, 'In what condition were you?'"* — a passage revealed about those who remained in Makkah among the idolaters when they could have emigrated. The pattern is the same: death arrives, the angels question, and the answer offered is an excuse.

**"Then They Will Offer Submission": The Word *Al-Salam***

*Fa-alqaw al-salam*, "so they will cast forth submission" — or, on another reading, "offer peace." The word *salam* here is read by the commentators in the sense of *istislām*, surrender, capitulation. Al-Zamakhsharī explains that at the moment of death, or at the judgment, the disbelievers who were arrogant and contentious in life suddenly become submissive and humble. Their defiance evaporates. The word can also be read as an offering of "peace" — a plea for terms, an attempt to conciliate.

The tragedy the verse describes is timing. Al-Ṭabrisī notes that their submission comes only when death has come upon them, and at that point submission no longer avails. The Qur'an states the principle:

> *"But repentance is not [accepted] of those who do evil deeds until, when death comes to one of them, he says, 'Indeed, I have repented now.'"* (Qur'an 4:18)

> *"So when they saw Our punishment, they said, 'We believe in God alone, and we disbelieve in what we used to associate with Him.' But their belief did not benefit them when they saw Our punishment."* (Qur'an 40:84–85)

Pharaoh's cry as he drowned — *"I believe that there is no god but He in Whom the Children of Israel believe"* (10:90) — is the archetype. He was answered: *"Now? When you had disobeyed before?"* (10:91). The door of repentance is open throughout life and closes at the moment described in this verse. The Prophet ﷺ said:

> *"God accepts the repentance of the servant so long as the death rattle has not reached his throat."* (al-Tirmidhī 3537; Ibn Mājah 4253)

The submission in 16:28 comes after that point. It is not repentance; it is the collapse of a resistance that can no longer be maintained.

**The Lie: "We Were Not Doing Any Evil"**

With their submission comes a claim: *mā kunnā naʿmalu min sūʾ*, "we were not doing any evil." This is a remarkable statement, and the commentators examined it with care. Al-Zamakhsharī notes that it is a lie — a final act of the same denial that characterized their lives. The Qur'an records a similar scene in which the idolaters swear before God that they were never idolaters:

> *"Then there will be no excuse for them except that they will say, 'By God, our Lord, we were not idolaters.' See how they lie against themselves, and how what they used to invent has vanished from them."* (Qur'an 6:23–24)

Why would anyone lie to God on the Day of Judgment? The commentators suggest that habitual self-deception does not end at death; a person who has spent a lifetime denying his own wrongdoing arrives at the judgment still denying it, out of reflex, out of terror, or in a desperate hope that the denial might somehow work. It is the last expression of a heart that "denies" (v. 22).

Other verses show the disbelievers admitting their guilt — *"Woe to us! Indeed we were wrongdoers"* (21:46; cf. 23:106; 67:10–11) — and the commentators reconcile the two pictures by noting that the Day of Judgment has stages. At one stage the guilty deny; when their own limbs testify against them (24:24; 41:20–22), denial becomes impossible and they confess. The verse in al-Naḥl captures the moment of denial.

There is also an interpretation, mentioned by some, that "we were not doing any evil" is a claim of *ignorance* rather than innocence — "we did not know that what we were doing was evil." On this reading it is an attempt to plead that they meant no harm. The reply of the verse covers this reading as well.

**The Reply: "Nay, But God Knows Best What You Were Doing"**

*Balā inna Allāha ʿalīmun bimā kuntum taʿmalūn*, "Nay indeed; truly God is Knowing of what you used to do." The particle *balā* is the Arabic word for contradicting a negative — "on the contrary," "yes, you were." Their denial is refuted with a single word and then grounded in an attribute of God: He knows.

This is where verses 19 and 23 pay their dividend. Twice the sūrah has stated that God knows what is hidden and what is disclosed. Now the practical consequence of that knowledge appears. The disbelievers' denial fails not because a witness happens to contradict them but because the Judge Himself knows every deed. There is no possibility of a successful lie before One Who was present at every act.

Who speaks this reply? The commentators — al-Ṭabrisī, al-Zamakhsharī, Ibn Kathīr — mention the knowledgeable of verse 27, the angels, and God Himself as possible speakers. The ambiguity may be intended: the truth is stated, and it does not matter who states it, because it is confirmed by God's own knowledge.

**The Central Lesson: The Moment of Death Is Decisive**

The verse teaches the doctrine that Islamic scholarship summarized in the saying "deeds are judged by their endings" (*al-aʿmāl bi'l-khawātīm*), drawn from the ḥadīth:

> *"Truly a man may do the deeds of the people of Paradise until there is only an arm's length between him and it, and then what was written overtakes him and he does the deeds of the people of the Fire and enters it."* (al-Bukhārī 3208; Muslim 2643)

The disbelievers of 16:28 were taken "while they were wronging themselves" — their ending was in *ẓulm*, and their ending determined their judgment. The verse is thus a summons to urgency. No one knows when the angels will come. The Makkans who planned to consider the Prophet's message "later" died with the consideration unmade. The person who plans to repent "when I am older," "when I have settled my affairs," "after this one more thing," is planning to arrive at the moment of 16:28 unprepared. The believers' prayer is therefore: *"Our Lord, cause us to die as Muslims"* (7:126; cf. 3:193) — a prayer not merely to be Muslims but to be Muslims at the end.

**The Contrast Verse 32 Will Draw**

As with verses 24 and 30, the Qur'an constructs this verse to be paired with another. Verse 32 will describe the believers as "those whom the angels take while they are in a state of goodness," and the angels will greet them with peace. The same event — death, the angels' arrival — takes two utterly different forms depending on the state of the one who dies. The disbeliever is taken in wrongdoing and offers a useless submission; the believer is taken in goodness and receives a real one. The verses are placed apart so that the reader may see the fork in the road and choose.

**A Reflection on Honesty With Oneself**

The verse's deepest warning may be about self-deception. The disbelievers say "we were not doing any evil" not only to the angels but, in some sense, to themselves — it was what they had told themselves for years. The habit of denying one's own wrongdoing is the habit that makes repentance impossible, because one cannot repent of what one refuses to see. The believer's protection against arriving at death with that lie on his lips is the daily practice of *muḥāsabah*, self-accounting — the honest review of one's deeds, the admission of fault, the turning back. ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb is reported to have said: "Take account of yourselves before you are taken to account." The verse shows what happens to those who did not.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:29

> **So enter the gates of Hell, to abide therein. Evil indeed is the abode of the arrogant!**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Sentence Pronounced**

Verses 27 and 28 presented the trial: the question about the absent partners, the testimony of the knowledgeable, the false plea of innocence, and its refutation by God's knowledge. Verse 29 pronounces the sentence: *fa-dkhulū abwāba jahannama khālidīna fīhā*, "so enter the gates of Hell, to abide therein." The particle *fa-*, "so," marks the consequence. Because the trial has established their guilt beyond denial, the verdict follows.

**Who Speaks the Command?**

The commentators discussed who utters "So enter the gates of Hell." Al-Ṭabrisī and al-Zamakhsharī suggest that the words continue the speech of "those who were given knowledge" from verse 27, who thus pronounce the fate they had warned of in the world. Al-Ṭabrisī also mentions the angels — the keepers of Hell, who elsewhere in the Qur'an address the condemned at the gates (39:71). Ibn Kathīr and al-Ṭabrisī also allow that God Himself is the speaker, since the judgment is His. As in verse 28, the ambiguity may be deliberate: the command comes with the full authority of the Judge, whoever voices it.

**"The Gates of Hell": The Plural**

The verse speaks of *abwāb*, "gates," in the plural. The Qur'an states elsewhere:

> *"Truly Hell is the promised place for them all. It has seven gates; for every gate is a portion assigned of them."* (Qur'an 15:43–44)

The commentators understood the seven gates as corresponding to categories of sinners or degrees of punishment, each group entering by the gate appropriate to it. Ibn Kathīr, commenting on 15:44, transmits the view that the gates are levels, one beneath another. The plural here thus suggests an ordered justice: the arrogant do not tumble into an undifferentiated pit but enter through the gate assigned to their particular guilt. The Qur'an describes the scene:

> *"And those who disbelieved will be driven to Hell in groups until, when they reach it, its gates are opened and its keepers will say to them, 'Did there not come to you messengers from among yourselves, reciting to you the verses of your Lord and warning you of the meeting of this Day?' They will say, 'Yes, but the word of punishment has come into effect upon the disbelievers.' It will be said, 'Enter the gates of Hell to abide therein, and wretched is the residence of the arrogant.'"* (Qur'an 39:71–72)

The final sentence of that passage is nearly identical to 16:29, and the exchange that precedes it fills in what al-Naḥl leaves implicit: the keepers ask whether messengers came, and the condemned admit that they did. The verdict is thus preceded by an acknowledgment that they were warned — verse 2 of this sūrah described that warning, and verse 36 will describe its universality.

**"To Abide Therein": *Khālidīn***

The word *khālidīn* means "abiding," "remaining permanently." From the root *kh-l-d*, it denotes lasting duration, and in the Qur'an's usage of the Hereafter it means eternal residence. The sūrah has already used the same root for the Garden (v. 31 will speak of the Gardens of Eden with their reward). The symmetry is deliberate: the abode of the righteous is lasting, and so is the abode of the arrogant. The permanence of the punishment for those who die in disbelief is affirmed throughout the Qur'an (2:39, 81, 162, 217; 3:88; 4:169; and many others), and the classical creeds of Islam — the *ʿAqīdah* of al-Ṭaḥāwī among them — state it as an article of faith.

Why should a finite life of sin earn an eternal punishment? The question has been asked in every age, and the scholars gave several answers. Al-Ghazālī and others observed that the disbeliever's intention was eternal: had he lived forever, he would have disbelieved forever, and God judges by what the heart has resolved. Others noted that the offense is measured not by its duration but by the One offended; a lifetime of denying the infinite God is not a small matter because it was brief. Ibn Taymiyyah and Ibn al-Qayyim emphasized that God's mercy is not thereby limited, since He offered guidance to every soul (v. 9, v. 36), delayed punishment to give time for repentance (v. 61), and forgave every fault but the one that the sinner refused to relinquish until death (v. 28). The eternity of the abode is the consequence of a choice sealed at death, not of an arbitrary decree.

**"Evil Indeed Is the Abode of the Arrogant": Naming the Sin Once More**

The verse ends: *fa-la-biʾsa mathwā al-mutakabbirīn*, "so evil indeed is the abode of the arrogant." The word *mathwā*, from the root *th-w-y*, means a place of long dwelling, a residence one settles into. The intensifying *la-biʾsa*, "how evil indeed," is the Qur'an's formula of strongest condemnation.

The most important word in the clause is the last: *al-mutakabbirīn*, "the arrogant." The passage began, in verse 22, by identifying the deniers as *mustakbirūn*, arrogant; verse 23 declared that God does not love the arrogant; now verse 29 names their abode. The whole passage from 22 to 29 is thus bracketed by arrogance. The Qur'an has traced a line from the disposition of the heart to the gates of Hell and named the disposition at both ends. Al-Qurṭubī's observation on verse 23 — that arrogance is the root of all disobedience — is confirmed by this structure. The sūrah does not say "the abode of the murderers" or "the abode of the thieves"; it says "the abode of the arrogant," because arrogance is what made all the rest possible.

**The Ḥadīth on Arrogance and the Fire**

The Prophet ﷺ made the connection between arrogance and Hell explicit in a ḥadīth in which he described the two abodes disputing:

> *"Paradise and Hell argued. Hell said, 'I have been given the tyrants and the arrogant.' Paradise said, 'I have been given the weak and the lowly among people.'"* (al-Bukhārī 4850; Muslim 2846)

And he described the inhabitants of the Fire in terms that match the verse:

> *"Shall I not tell you about the people of the Fire? Every harsh, greedy, arrogant person."* (al-Bukhārī 4918; Muslim 2853)

The word used in that ḥadīth, *mustakbir*, is the same root as the verse's *mutakabbirīn*. The Prophet's teaching and the Qur'an's are one: the Fire is the destination of pride.

**The Verse's Function: A Warning Delivered in Time**

The Qur'an describes the scene of judgment in the future tense, but it describes it *now*, to the living. This is the mercy hidden inside the warning. The Makkan who heard 16:29 recited in the courtyard of the Kaʿbah was being shown his own future in time to change it. The verse is not a report on the damned; it is an intervention on behalf of those who might yet be saved. The Qur'an says of itself that it was sent *"as a warner to mankind"* (74:36), and a warning that came too late would be no warning at all.

The reader today is in the same position as the first listeners. The verse describes a gate he has not yet reached, an abode he has not yet entered, and a sentence that has not yet been passed. Between him and that scene stands the whole remaining span of his life — a span the next verse will fill with the opposite picture. The choice between the two is what the passage is designed to force.

**The Practical Discipline**

If the abode of the arrogant is evil, the believer's task is clear: to uproot arrogance while there is time. The tradition prescribed concrete means. Sitting with the poor, serving one's own household, accepting correction gracefully, giving the greeting of peace first, walking without swagger, dressing without ostentation, and — above all — remembering one's origin and one's end. The Prophet ﷺ himself, though master of Arabia, mended his own sandals, milked his own goat, and sat wherever there was space in a gathering. When a man trembled before him, he said: *"Be at ease; I am not a king. I am only the son of a woman of Quraysh who ate dried meat"* (Ibn Mājah 3312). The humility of the Prophet is the antidote to the verse's warning. The one who learns it will not hear the command "enter the gates" addressed to himself.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:30

> **And it will be said unto those who are reverent, "What has your Lord sent down?" They will say, "Goodness." For those who are virtuous in this world, there shall be good, and the Abode of the Hereafter is better. Excellent indeed is the abode of the reverent!**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Mirror Verse**

Verse 24 posed a question to the arrogant: "What has your Lord sent down?" and they answered, "Fables of the ancients." Verse 30 poses the identical question to the reverent — *wa-qīla lilladhīna ittaqaw mādhā anzala rabbukum* — and they answer with a single word: *khayran*, "good." The Qur'an constructs the two verses as a deliberate pair, and al-Bayḍāwī and al-Zamakhsharī both draw attention to the contrast. The question is the same, the revelation is the same, and the answers could not be more opposed. The difference lies entirely in the state of the ones answering. The passage from 22 to 29 traced the arrogant from their denying hearts to the gates of Hell; the passage from 30 to 32 traces the reverent from their affirming hearts to the gates of Paradise.

**Who Are "Those Who Are Reverent"?**

The verse describes them as *alladhīna ittaqaw*, "those who were God-fearing," those who practiced *taqwā*. The sūrah's second verse commanded exactly this — *fa-ttaqūn*, "so be mindful of Me" — and here we meet those who obeyed. *Taqwā*, from the root *w-q-y*, "to guard," is the disposition of one who protects himself from God's displeasure by heeding His commands and avoiding His prohibitions — the alert, careful walking of a traveler who knows the road has dangers. Where the arrogant were characterized by a heart that denies, the reverent are characterized by a heart that guards.

**The Answer: "Good" — And Its Grammar**

The reverent answer *khayran*, "good," and the grammarians noticed something in the form of the word that reveals the disposition behind it. In verse 24, the arrogant answered *asāṭīru al-awwalīn*, "fables of the ancients," in the nominative case — as an independent statement, "[It is] fables." Their answer did not grammatically accept the premise of the question that anything had been "sent down"; they substituted their own subject. In verse 30, *khayran* is in the accusative case, which in Arabic makes it the direct object of the verb in the question: "[He sent down] good." Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Bayḍāwī observe that this grammatical difference is the difference between denial and affirmation. The reverent accept that God sent something down and name what it was; the arrogant deny that anything was sent and dismiss what they heard. Even the case endings of the two answers reveal the hearts of the two speakers.

The commentators also note the immediacy of the reverent's response. It is offered without hesitation, without qualification, in one word. Where the arrogant needed a dismissive phrase, the reverent needed only *khayr*. The revelation was, for them, self-evidently good: good in its content, good in its effect, good in its origin. Al-Ṭabarī explains that they answered that God sent down good, blessing, and mercy upon those who followed it.

**The Setting Once More**

As with verse 24, the commentators place this exchange in the context of the pilgrimage season, when visitors to Makkah asked about the Prophet ﷺ. Those who asked the believers received a very different answer from those who asked the Quraysh. The scene is thus historical as well as spiritual. Al-Zamakhsharī notes that some of the Companions were asked this question by travelers and answered as the verse records, and the travelers returned to their tribes with the truth. The verse commemorates these humble acts of witness, which contributed to the spread of Islam beyond Makkah long before the Emigration.

**The Reward in Two Worlds**

The verse then states what awaits those who gave this answer: *lilladhīna aḥsanū fī hādhihi al-dunyā ḥasanah*, "for those who do good in this world there is good." The phrase is compact and admits two structures, and the commentators affirm both.

On the first reading, "in this world" modifies "those who do good": for those who do good in this world, there is good [in the next]. On the second reading, "in this world" modifies "good": for those who do good, there is good in this world — that is, their reward begins here. Al-Qurṭubī reports both. The second reading is supported by verse 41 of this sūrah, which promises the emigrants "a good place in this world," and by verse 97, which promises a "good life" to every righteous believer. The Qur'an teaches that goodness is rewarded in both worlds:

> *"Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while a believer — We will surely give them a good life, and We will surely give them their reward according to the best of what they used to do."* (Qur'an 16:97)

> *"And God gave them the reward of this world and the good reward of the Hereafter."* (Qur'an 3:148)

The verse in al-Naḥl then adds the decisive comparison: *wa-la-dāru al-ākhirati khayr*, "and the Abode of the Hereafter is better." Whatever good the righteous receive in this world — contentment, honor, provision, a peaceful heart — the Hereafter exceeds it. Al-Qurṭubī gives the reason: this world's good is temporary; the Hereafter's is lasting. The Qur'an elsewhere spells out the comparison:

> *"But you prefer the worldly life, while the Hereafter is better and more enduring."* (Qur'an 87:16–17)

> *"And what is with God is better and more lasting for those who believe and rely upon their Lord."* (Qur'an 42:36)

Al-Bayḍāwī and al-Zamakhsharī add a note on proportion: if the good received in this world is measured to the good deeds performed, the good of the Hereafter far exceeds that measure, since God multiplies reward — *"whoever comes with a good deed will have ten times its like"* (6:160).

**The Word *Aḥsanū*: Doing Beautifully**

The verse describes the rewarded as *alladhīna aḥsanū*, "those who did *iḥsān*." The root *ḥ-s-n* means beauty and goodness together; *iḥsān* is doing a thing beautifully, excellently, with more than the minimum. The Prophet ﷺ defined it as worshipping God "as though you see Him" (al-Bukhārī 50; Muslim 8). The verse's sequence is instructive: those who *fear* God (*ittaqaw*) recognize the revelation as *good* (*khayr*), and they *do good* (*aḥsanū*), and they receive *good* (*ḥasanah*). The same root — *ḥ-s-n* — appears in the deed and the reward, matching the Qur'an's principle: *"Is the reward of goodness anything but goodness?"* (55:60). The sūrah will end by placing God with the *muḥsinīn* (16:128).

**"Excellent Indeed Is the Abode of the Reverent"**

The verse closes: *wa-la-niʿma dāru al-muttaqīn*, "and how excellent is the abode of the God-fearing!" The phrase is the exact counterpart of verse 29's *fa-la-biʾsa mathwā al-mutakabbirīn*, "how evil is the abode of the arrogant." *Niʿma* and *biʾsa* are the Arabic verbs of praise and blame respectively, and their pairing across the two verses is the structural hinge of the whole passage. The arrogant have an abode; the reverent have an abode; the first is condemned, the second praised. And the word for "abode" differs subtly: the arrogant have a *mathwā*, a place where one is made to dwell, while the reverent have a *dār*, a home. The Qur'an calls Paradise *Dār al-Salām*, the Home of Peace (6:127; 10:25).

Which abode is meant? Al-Qurṭubī notes that "the abode of the reverent" may refer to the Hereafter, just named as better, or to this world, in which the reverent live well; and some read it as an anticipation of the Gardens described in the next verse. The ambiguity may be intended: the reverent's home is excellent in both worlds.

**Why Recognizing Revelation as "Good" Matters So Much**

The verse makes a single word — *khayr* — the marker of the reverent, and it is worth asking why so much rests on it. The answer lies in what the word reveals. To call the revelation "good" is to have received it — to have understood that its commands are for one's benefit, its prohibitions for one's protection, its warnings a mercy, and its promises true. It is the opposite of the resentful compliance that obeys while suspecting the law is a burden. The Qur'an describes the believers as those who, when the revelation is recited, say *"We hear and we obey"* (2:285) and whose faith *increases* when the signs are recited (8:2). To such people, every verse is *khayr*. And this disposition transforms the experience of religion: the same prayer that is a chore to one heart is a gift to another; the same prohibition that is a restriction to one is a shield to another. The reverent do not merely follow the revelation; they love it, and the love is what the word *khayran* expresses.

**A Practical Question**

The verse invites a personal answer to its question. If someone asked, "What has your Lord sent down?" — what would one's life reply? Not one's tongue, which can say the right word easily, but one's conduct, one's priorities, one's response to a command that costs something. The verse implies that the reverent are recognizable by their unhesitating affirmation that God's word is good — and by the good deeds that follow from that affirmation. The believer can test himself by his reaction to the parts of revelation he finds difficult. Does he receive them as *khayr*, trusting the wisdom he may not yet see, or does something in him reach for a dismissal? The answer places him on one side or the other of the pair of verses, and the passage has already described where each side leads.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:31

> **They shall enter the Gardens of Eden with rivers running below. Therein shall they have whatsoever they will. Thus does God recompense the reverent,**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Naming the Abode**

Verse 30 ended by praising "the abode of the reverent." Verse 31 names it: *jannātu ʿadnin*, "Gardens of Eden," and describes what it contains. The description comes in three parts — the rivers, the fulfillment of every wish, and the statement that this is God's recompense for *taqwā*. Each part answers something in the preceding description of the arrogant. They enter the gates of Hell; the reverent enter Gardens. They abide in a wretched abode; the reverent abide where rivers run. They are disgraced; the reverent are given whatever they desire.

**"Gardens of Eden": *Jannāt ʿAdn***

The word *jannah*, "garden," comes from the root *j-n-n*, whose core meaning is concealment and covering — the same root gives *jinn* (hidden beings), *janīn* (the fetus, hidden in the womb), and *junnah* (a shield that covers). A *jannah* is a garden so thick with trees that its ground is hidden by foliage. The word was chosen for Paradise because it evokes lush, shaded abundance to a people who lived among bare rock and sand.

*ʿAdn* is understood by the classical lexicographers, following al-Ṭabarī and others, to derive from *ʿadana*, "to remain, to settle permanently in a place." *Jannāt ʿadn* thus means "Gardens of permanent residence," "Gardens of everlasting abode." The name is not primarily a place-name but a description of duration. The Qur'an uses it eleven times (9:72; 13:23; 16:31; 18:31; 19:61; 20:76; 35:33; 38:50; 40:8; 61:12; 98:8), always of the Hereafter, and always with the connotation of permanence. Al-Qurṭubī notes that some commentators took ʿAdn to be the name of a specific, central region of Paradise, the highest and most honored — a view supported by the ḥadīth in which the Prophet ﷺ described the highest Paradise, *al-Firdaws*, and the Gardens of Eden within it.

The plural *jannāt*, "Gardens," is significant. Paradise is not one garden but many — levels upon levels, as the Prophet ﷺ described:

> *"In Paradise there are a hundred levels which God has prepared for those who strive in His way; between each two levels is the distance between the heaven and the earth."* (al-Bukhārī 2790)

**"With Rivers Running Below": The Most Repeated Image of Paradise**

*Tajrī min taḥtihā al-anhār*, "beneath which rivers flow," is the Qur'an's most frequent description of Paradise, occurring more than thirty times. To the Arab, water flowing continuously was the very image of life and luxury; a garden with rivers running through it was the opposite of everything the desert threatened. The phrase "from beneath" describes rivers flowing under the trees and pavilions — the whole garden irrigated from below, so that nothing in it can wither.

The Qur'an describes the rivers themselves:

> *"A parable of the Garden promised to the God-fearing: therein are rivers of water unpolluted, rivers of milk whose taste never changes, rivers of wine delicious to those who drink, and rivers of purified honey."* (Qur'an 47:15)

The four rivers of 47:15 — water, milk, wine, and honey — correspond to the four drinks that al-Naḥl itself will name in verses 65 through 69 as gifts of this world. The earthly drinks are the shadows; the rivers of Paradise are the substance.

**"Therein Shall They Have Whatsoever They Will": The Fulfillment of Desire**

*Lahum fīhā mā yashāʾūn*, "for them therein is whatever they wish." This is the verse's most expansive promise. Whatever they wish — without limit, without exception. The Qur'an repeats the promise in several forms:

> *"Therein you will have whatever your souls desire, and therein you will have whatever you ask for."* (Qur'an 41:31)

> *"They will have whatever they wish with their Lord. That is the reward of the doers of good."* (Qur'an 39:34)

> *"They will have therein whatever they wish, and with Us is more."* (Qur'an 50:35)

Al-Bayḍāwī draws from this phrase a philosophical observation: it is only in Paradise that a human being can have all of his desires fulfilled. In this world, desires conflict with one another, exceed one's means, or are frustrated by circumstance; and even when fulfilled, they are followed by new desires or by satiety. The person who has everything he wanted discovers that he wants something else, or that having it was not what he imagined. Paradise is the only condition in which desire and fulfillment coincide without remainder — a condition that requires not only unlimited provision but a transformed self whose desires are all good and all satisfiable.

The last phrase of 50:35 — "and with Us is more" — hints at what the tradition understood to be the highest reward, beyond anything the inhabitants themselves would think to wish for: the vision of God. The Prophet ﷺ said:

> *"When the people of Paradise enter Paradise, God will say, 'Do you want anything more that I may give you?' They will say, 'Have You not brightened our faces? Have You not admitted us to Paradise and saved us from the Fire?' Then He will remove the veil, and they will not have been given anything more beloved to them than looking upon their Lord."* (Muslim 181)

"Whatever they will" thus culminates in what they did not know to will until it was given.

**The Ḥadīth Qudsī on What Awaits**

The Prophet ﷺ transmitted from God a description of Paradise that captures why its contents cannot be adequately imagined:

> *"I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and what has never occurred to a human heart."* Then he recited: *"No soul knows what has been hidden for them of comfort for the eyes as reward for what they used to do."* (al-Bukhārī 3244; Muslim 2824; the verse is 32:17)

The Qur'anic descriptions — gardens, rivers, fruits, spouses, garments — are thus understood by the scholars as true but partial, using the vocabulary of earthly delight to indicate realities that exceed it. Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to have said: "Nothing in Paradise resembles anything in this world except in name." The rivers are real rivers, but not as we know rivers; the fruits are real fruits, but not as we know fruits. The verse's "whatever they will" reaches beyond the named items to the unnamed.

**"Thus Does God Recompense the Reverent": The Principle of Reward**

The verse closes: *kadhālika yajzī Allāhu al-muttaqīn*, "thus does God reward the God-fearing." The word *kadhālika*, "thus," "in this manner," points back to everything just described and presents it as the standard pattern. The verb *yajzī*, "recompenses," comes from the root *j-z-y*, which denotes payment in return for something — a wage, a requital. Paradise is described as a *jazāʾ*, a recompense — not a random gift but a response to something the reverent did.

This raises a question that the scholars addressed carefully. If Paradise is earned, then salvation is by works; but the Prophet ﷺ said:

> *"None of you will enter Paradise by his deeds." They said, "Not even you, O Messenger of God?" He said, "Not even I, unless God envelops me in His mercy."* (al-Bukhārī 5673; Muslim 2816)

The reconciliation, which Ibn Taymiyyah and others articulated, is that deeds are the *cause* God has appointed for entry, but not the *price* that purchases it. No amount of human obedience is equivalent in value to eternal bliss; the disproportion is infinite. God, in His mercy, has nonetheless made obedience the door. The believer works because God commanded it and made it the means, while knowing that the reward vastly exceeds the work. The Qur'an's own phrasing preserves both truths: Paradise is "recompense for what they used to do" (32:17) and also "the bounty of God" (57:21).

**The Verse's Function: Hope as Fuel**

The Qur'an describes Paradise not to satisfy curiosity but to motivate. The human being needs hope as much as fear; the preceding verses supplied the fear, and this verse supplies the hope. Al-Rāzī observes that the Qur'an's method throughout is to pair *targhīb* (inspiring desire) with *tarhīb* (inspiring caution), because the soul is moved by both and neither alone is sufficient. Fear without hope produces despair; hope without fear produces complacency. The passage from verse 22 to verse 32 is a model of the balance.

For the believer, the practical effect of holding this verse in mind is the reordering of desire. The person who genuinely believes that he may have "whatever he wills" in a permanent home finds it easier to forgo what he wills in a temporary one. The Companions, who lived in poverty and were persecuted, endured because this promise was real to them. The verse invites the modern believer to make it equally real — to let the Gardens of Eden, with their rivers, become the horizon against which every earthly loss is measured and found bearable.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:32

> **those whom the angels take while they are in a state of goodness. They will say, "Peace be upon you! Enter the Garden for that which you used to do."**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Counterpart to Verse 28**

Verse 28 described the disbelievers as "those whom the angels take while they are wronging themselves." Verse 32 describes the reverent as "those whom the angels take while they are in a state of goodness" — *alladhīna tatawaffāhum al-malāʾikatu ṭayyibīn*. The parallel is exact and deliberate. The same verb (*tatawaffā*), the same agents (the angels), the same moment (death) — and two completely different conditions. The disbelievers were taken in *ẓulm*; the believers are taken in *ṭīb*. The disbelievers offered a false submission and were refuted; the believers receive a greeting of peace and an invitation. The two verses together teach that death is not one experience but two, and that which one a person undergoes is determined by the state in which he is found.

**"In a State of Goodness": The Meaning of *Ṭayyibīn***

The word *ṭayyibīn* is the plural of *ṭayyib*, from the root *ṭ-y-b*, which denotes what is good, pure, wholesome, pleasant, and agreeable. The Qur'an uses it of lawful and wholesome food (*ḥalālan ṭayyiban*, 2:168), of good speech (14:24), of pure women and men (24:26), and of God Himself, Who is *Ṭayyib*, as the Prophet ﷺ said:

> *"Truly God is good (ṭayyib) and accepts only what is good."* (Muslim 1015)

Applied to those who die, the commentators gave *ṭayyibīn* several complementary senses, all of which al-Bayḍāwī and al-Zamakhsharī record.

The first is moral purity: they die pure of *shirk* and of sin — their beliefs sound, their speech clean, their deeds righteous. This is the primary sense: their souls are in a wholesome state at the moment the angels arrive, in contrast to the *ẓulm* of the disbelievers.

The second is the manner of their death: they are taken gently, with ease, without the violence and terror that the Qur'an describes for the disbelievers — *"If you could see when the angels take the souls of those who disbelieve, striking their faces and their backs"* (8:50). The believer's death is *ṭayyib*, pleasant, because the angels come as bearers of glad tidings.

The third, mentioned by some, is purity from the attachments of the world: their souls leave the body willingly and gladly, because they long for what awaits them. The Prophet ﷺ described this:

> *"Whoever loves to meet God, God loves to meet him."* When ʿĀʾishah objected that everyone dislikes death, he explained: *"When the believer is given glad tidings of God's mercy and pleasure and His Paradise, he loves to meet God, and God loves to meet him."* (al-Bukhārī 6507; Muslim 2683)

The word *ṭayyibīn* thus describes the whole condition of the righteous death: a pure soul, a gentle taking, and a glad departure.

**The Angels' Greeting: "Peace Be Upon You"**

*Yaqūlūna salāmun ʿalaykum*, "they say, 'Peace be upon you.'" The angels' first word to the dying believer is *salām*. Al-Zamakhsharī explains that this greeting conveys God's own greeting and is glad tidings of Paradise. The Qur'an describes the same greeting in several scenes:

> *"Those who say, 'Our Lord is God,' and then remain steadfast — the angels descend upon them: 'Do not fear and do not grieve, but receive glad tidings of the Garden which you were promised.'"* (Qur'an 41:30)

> *"And the angels will enter upon them from every gate: 'Peace be upon you for what you patiently endured; and excellent is the final home.'"* (Qur'an 13:23–24)

> *"Peace!" — a word from a Merciful Lord.* (Qur'an 36:58)

The last passage names the source of the greeting: it is a word from God Himself, carried by the angels. Paradise itself is called *Dār al-Salām*, the Home of Peace (6:127; 10:25), and its inhabitants' speech is *salām* (10:10; 19:62). The greeting the believer hears at death is thus the first word of the language of his new home.

The commentators note that *salām* is also the greeting Muslims give one another in this world — *al-salāmu ʿalaykum*. This is not coincidence. The Prophet ﷺ made the spreading of this greeting a sign of faith and a cause of love among believers (Muslim 54). Every time a believer says it, he is rehearsing the words he hopes to hear from the angels. The greeting of this world and the greeting of the next are one.

**The Ḥadīth of the Believer's Death**

The most detailed account of the scene this verse describes is the long ḥadīth of al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib, recorded by Aḥmad (18534), Abū Dāwūd (4753), and others, and graded authentic. The Prophet ﷺ described the death of the believer:

> *"When the believing servant is about to leave this world and enter the next, angels descend to him from heaven, white-faced as though their faces were the sun, bearing a shroud from Paradise and perfume from Paradise, and they sit at a distance from him as far as the eye can see. Then the Angel of Death comes and sits at his head and says, 'O good soul, come out to forgiveness from God and His pleasure.' And it comes out flowing like a drop from the mouth of a waterskin... and they do not leave it in his hand for the blink of an eye before they take it and place it in that shroud and that perfume, and there comes from it a fragrance like the finest musk on the face of the earth."*

The ḥadīth continues to describe the soul's ascent through the heavens, greeted at each gate, until it stands before God and is told that its record is in the highest register. The phrase "O good soul" — *ayyatuhā al-nafs al-ṭayyibah* — uses the very word of the verse, *ṭayyib*. The Prophet's description and the Qur'an's are the same scene.

**"Enter the Garden for That Which You Used to Do"**

The angels' second statement is an invitation and its ground: *udkhulū al-jannata bimā kuntum taʿmalūn*, "enter the Garden for what you used to do." The preposition *bi-*, "for," "by reason of," connects the entry to the deeds. As with verse 31, this is the language of recompense: the Garden is given in return for a life of righteousness.

The contrast with the disbelievers' scene is again precise. In verse 28, the disbelievers claimed "we were not doing any evil," and were told that God knows what they did. Here the believers are told that what they did is the very reason for their entry. For the disbeliever, "what you used to do" is the evidence against him; for the believer, it is the key to the door.

The commentators observe that this invitation may be given at death, as a promise, or at the Resurrection, as an actual admission — or both, since the believer's soul enjoys a foretaste of Paradise in the grave before entering it fully after the Judgment. The Prophet ﷺ described the grave of the believer as "a garden among the gardens of Paradise" (al-Tirmidhī 2460), and said that the believer in his grave is shown his place in Paradise and told "this is your place until God raises you to it" (al-Bukhārī 1379; Muslim 2866).

**The Doctrine: Death Is the Beginning of Recompense**

The verse establishes a teaching that runs through Islamic eschatology: recompense begins at death, not only at the Resurrection. The moment the angels take the soul, the soul learns its destination. This is the doctrine of the *barzakh*, the intermediate state between death and Resurrection, in which the righteous experience peace and the wicked experience distress. The verse does not delay the angels' greeting to the Day of Judgment; it places it at the moment of taking. Ibn Kathīr, commenting on this verse, cites the ḥadīth of al-Barāʾ as its explanation.

The practical consequence is that death is not something the believer must merely endure until a distant reward; it is itself the threshold of that reward. The Prophet ﷺ said that the believer's soul at death is like a prisoner released — and he called death "the gift of the believer" in the sense that it brings him to what he has hoped for.

**The Meaning of Dying "Good"**

The verse's central lesson is about how to die, and therefore about how to live. To be *ṭayyib* at death is not achieved at death; it is the result of a life spent becoming *ṭayyib*. The Prophet ﷺ said:

> *"Everyone will be raised in the state in which he died."* (Muslim 2878)

And the principle that "a person dies as he lived and is raised as he died" was taught by the scholars as a summary of many texts. The person who wishes to hear "Peace be upon you" from the angels must be, at the moment they come, in a state that warrants it — pure in creed, clean in speech, sound in deeds, and turned toward God. Since no one knows when they will come, the only safe course is to be in that state always. This is what the sūrah's opening command, *fa-ttaqūn*, ultimately means: live in such a way that death, whenever it arrives, finds you *ṭayyib*.

**A Final Reflection**

There is a quiet beauty in the structure of verses 28 and 32 read together. Both begin identically — "those whom the angels take" — and then diverge into two eternities. The divergence turns on a single word: *ẓālimī* or *ṭayyibīn*, wronging or good. Every day of a human life is a day spent moving toward one of these two words. The verses do not merely describe the destinations; they ask the reader which word he is becoming. And they offer, in the angels' greeting, the sound of what awaits the one who chooses rightly: *salāmun ʿalaykum* — peace, at last, without end.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:33

> **Do they await aught but that the angels should come upon them, or that the Command of thy Lord should come? Those before them did likewise. And God wronged them not, but they wronged themselves.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Question of Waiting**

Having shown the two deaths — the disbeliever's in verse 28 and the believer's in verse 32 — the sūrah turns back to the living disbelievers and asks what, exactly, they are waiting for. *Hal yanẓurūna illā an taʾtiyahum al-malāʾikatu aw yaʾtiya amru rabbik*, "Do they await anything except that the angels should come to them, or that the Command of your Lord should come?" The verb *yanẓurūna* means to look toward, to expect, to wait for. The question is rhetorical and its tone is one of sober warning: since they refuse to respond to the message, the only things left for them to wait for are the two events that will make response impossible.

**The Two Events: Angels and the Command**

The verse names two things they might be waiting for, and the commentators — al-Bayḍāwī, al-Zamakhsharī, and others — interpret them on two levels.

On the individual level, "the angels coming" refers to the angels of death, who were described in verses 28 and 32, and "the Command of your Lord" refers to the decree of one's death. On the universal level, "the angels coming" refers to the descent of the angels on the Day of Judgment, and "the Command of your Lord" refers to the coming of the Hour — the very "Command of God" that verse 1 announced as already on its way. The verse thus closes a circle begun at the sūrah's opening: the Command that the Makkans mockingly asked to be hastened is the Command they are now described as waiting for.

The Qur'an poses this same question in several places, and each occurrence illuminates this one:

> *"Are they waiting for anything except that the angels should come to them, or that your Lord should come, or that some of the signs of your Lord should come? The Day some of the signs of your Lord come, no soul will benefit from its faith if it had not believed before."* (Qur'an 6:158)

> *"Do they await anything except that God should come to them in shadows of clouds, and the angels, and the matter is decided?"* (Qur'an 2:210)

The verse in Sūrah al-Anʿām spells out what al-Naḥl leaves implicit: when these events come, faith will no longer benefit. The waiting is therefore self-defeating. The person who says "I will believe when I see the proof" is waiting for a proof that arrives only when belief no longer counts.

**The Folly of Demanding Proof Before Believing**

The verse's rhetorical force lies in exposing a particular error: the demand that God's threat be demonstrated before one takes it seriously. The Makkans said, in effect, "Show us the punishment, then we will believe." The Qur'an's answer is that the punishment, when shown, ends the possibility of belief — as Pharaoh discovered when he believed while drowning (10:90–91).

The logic can be stated simply. Faith, in the Qur'an's understanding, is belief in the unseen (*al-ghayb*, 2:3). Its value lies precisely in that it is offered before the unseen becomes seen. A person who believes only when the angels stand before him has not exercised faith; he has merely reported an observation. The test of this world is a test of whether a person will trust the message before the evidence becomes overwhelming. To wait for overwhelming evidence is to wait for the test to end.

There is an analogy in ordinary life. A physician tells a patient that a certain habit will cause a fatal disease. The patient says, "I will stop when I see the disease." By the time the disease is visible, stopping may no longer help. The physician's warning was the mercy; the visible disease is the consequence. The Qur'an says of the disbelievers that they are like this patient: *"they wait for the punishment"* rather than heeding *"the warning."*

**"Those Before Them Did Likewise": The Precedent**

*Kadhālika faʿala alladhīna min qablihim*, "thus did those before them." The verse invokes the pattern of history for the second time in this passage (the first was verse 26). The earlier nations — ʿĀd, Thamūd, the people of Noah, of Lot, of Shuʿayb — also waited for the punishment instead of heeding the warning, and the punishment came. The Qur'an recounts their taunts:

> *"They said, 'O Hūd, you have not brought us clear evidence, and we are not ones to leave our gods on your say-so, and we are not believers in you.'"* (Qur'an 11:53)

> *"They said, 'Bring us what you threaten us with, if you are of the truthful.'"* (Qur'an 7:70; 46:22)

And it recounts the outcome: the wind, the cry, the flood, the overturning. The Makkans, traveling the routes to Syria, passed the ruins of some of these peoples. The verse asks them to consider that they are behaving exactly as the people whose ruins they walked past.

**"God Wronged Them Not, But They Wronged Themselves": The Principle of Justice**

The verse closes with one of the Qur'an's most repeated and most important theological statements: *wa-mā ẓalamahumu Allāhu wa-lākin kānū anfusahum yaẓlimūn*, "and God did not wrong them, but they used to wrong themselves." The formula occurs, in this or slightly varied wording, in 3:117, 9:70, 10:44, 11:101, 16:118, 29:40, 30:9, and 43:76, among others. Its repetition marks it as a foundational principle.

The teaching has two sides. The negative side — God did not wrong them — affirms divine justice absolutely. The destruction of the earlier nations was not caprice; it was the consequence of their own choices, delivered after warning, after respite, and after the messengers had exhausted every means of persuasion. God's own word is: *"Truly God does not wrong people at all, but people wrong themselves"* (10:44), and *"Your Lord is not unjust to the servants"* (41:46).

The positive side — they wronged themselves — affirms human responsibility. The verse does not say "they wronged God" or "they wronged the prophets"; it says they wronged *themselves*. Al-Zamakhsharī explains that they committed the deeds that necessitated their destruction, and thus the harm they suffered was of their own making. The Qur'an locates the origin of every evil that befalls a person in the person himself: *"Whatever good comes to you is from God, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself"* (4:79).

**The Bearing on Free Will**

The commentators recognized that this verse, with its dozens of parallels, is among the strongest Qur'anic evidence for human moral freedom. If God does not wrong people, and people wrong themselves, then the deeds for which people are punished are genuinely theirs — chosen, not compelled. The repeated Qur'anic assertion that human beings wrong themselves confirms that they are responsible agents. Al-Ṭabrisī, writing from the Muʿtazilite-Shīʿī perspective that emphasizes free will, makes this the verse's central point. The Ashʿarite commentators, who emphasize God's creation of all acts, nonetheless affirmed that the acts are attributed to human beings by acquisition (*kasb*) in such a way that they are justly punished for them. Both schools agreed on the practical conclusion: no one who is punished can say that God wronged him. The Qur'an closes that door.

The verse's logic is also psychologically penetrating. It defines sin as self-harm. The disbeliever who imagines that he is defying God, asserting his independence, or protecting his interests is in fact injuring himself — his soul, his future, his eternal welfare — and no one else. God is not diminished by his disbelief: *"If you disbelieve, you and all who are on earth together, truly God is Free of need, Praiseworthy"* (14:8). The only victim of the sinner's sin is the sinner. This reframing transforms the meaning of obedience. God's commands are not the demands of a needy master; they are the instructions of a Physician who has nothing to gain from the patient's health except the patient's good.

**Practical Meaning: Do Not Wait**

The verse's counsel to the reader is the counsel of urgency that runs through the whole passage. Whatever a person is waiting for before he turns to God — more evidence, more time, a better moment, the resolution of some doubt — the verse asks him to consider that the only things certainly coming are the angels and the Command, and that both come too late for the one who waited. The earlier nations waited and were destroyed; the Makkans were waiting; and the reader, if he is honest, may find that he too is waiting for something. The Prophet ﷺ said:

> *"Hasten to do good deeds before seven things: are you waiting for anything but poverty that makes you forget, or wealth that makes you transgress, or illness that corrupts, or old age that weakens, or sudden death, or the Dajjāl — the worst of absent things awaited — or the Hour? And the Hour is more calamitous and more bitter."* (al-Tirmidhī 2306)

The ḥadīth's opening — "are you waiting for anything but..." — echoes the verse's *hal yanẓurūna illā*. The answer to both is the same: do not wait. The door is open now, and it will not always be.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:34

> **Thus they were stricken by the evil deeds they had done, and were beset by that which they used to mock.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Law of Consequence**

Verse 33 ended by stating that the earlier nations wronged themselves. Verse 34 describes the form their self-inflicted wrong finally took: *fa-aṣābahum sayyiʾātu mā ʿamilū*, "so there struck them the evils of what they did." The Arabic is compressed and precise. What struck them was not something external to their deeds; it was *the evils of their deeds themselves* — the consequences intrinsic to the actions, returning upon the actors. The verse does not say "God struck them with a punishment for their deeds," though that is true; it says the deeds' own evil struck them. Sin, in this picture, is not merely a violation that triggers a separate penalty. It is a seed that grows into its own punishment.

**"Stricken by the Evil Deeds They Had Done"**

The verb *aṣāba* means to hit, to reach, to befall — as an arrow reaches its target. The word *sayyiʾāt*, plural of *sayyiʾah*, means evil deeds, but also, by extension, the evil consequences of deeds. Al-Zamakhsharī explains the phrase as: the recompense of their evil deeds befell them, or the evil deeds themselves, considered in their effects, befell them. Either way, the verse establishes a direct line from action to result. What a person does comes back to him. The Qur'an states this as a universal law:

> *"Whatever good befalls you is from God, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself."* (Qur'an 4:79)

> *"No soul earns evil except against itself."* (Qur'an 6:164)

> *"And the evil plot does not encompass except its own people."* (Qur'an 35:43)

The last verse — that plotting encloses only its plotters — was illustrated in verse 26, where the building fell on those who built it. Verse 34 states the general principle of which that was an instance.

**The Difference Between Punishment and Consequence**

The verse's phrasing invites a reflection on the nature of divine punishment that the scholars developed at length. There are two ways to think about the relationship between sin and suffering. In the first, sin is a violation of a rule, and suffering is a penalty attached to the rule by the rule-giver — as a fine is attached to a traffic offense. In the second, sin is a harmful act, and suffering is the natural outcome of the harm — as illness follows from poison. The Qur'an uses both pictures, and 16:34 leans toward the second. "The evils of what they did struck them" describes poison working, not a fine being levied.

Ibn al-Qayyim developed this insight in his treatise on the harms of sin, arguing that every sin carries its consequence within it: lying corrupts the liar's perception of truth, cruelty hardens the cruel person's heart, arrogance blinds the arrogant to what he needs to see, and denial of God cuts the denier off from the source of his own life. The final punishment of the Hereafter is the full manifestation of what the sin already was in the world. On this understanding, God's justice is not the imposition of arbitrary penalties but the unveiling of what people made of themselves.

This understanding also clarifies verse 33's statement that God did not wrong them. A judge who imposes a penalty might be accused of severity; but no one can accuse the earth of injustice for yielding poison to the one who planted it.

**"And Were Beset by That Which They Used to Mock"**

The verse's second clause is one of the Qur'an's recurring formulas of retribution: *wa-ḥāqa bihim mā kānū bihi yastahziʾūn*, "and there surrounded them what they used to mock." The verb *ḥāqa* means to encompass, to surround, to close in from all sides — it describes a trap closing or water rising. What closed in on them was *mā kānū bihi yastahziʾūn*, "that which they used to mock" — the punishment they had laughed at, the resurrection they had ridiculed, the warnings they had dismissed as fables.

The formula appears in nearly identical words in 6:10, 11:8, 21:41, 39:48, 40:83, 45:33, and 46:26. Its repetition marks a pattern the Qur'an wishes to fix in the mind: mockery of the truth ends with the truth surrounding the mocker. The Qur'an gives the general statement:

> *"Messengers before you were mocked, but those who scoffed at them were surrounded by that which they used to mock."* (Qur'an 6:10; 21:41)

**The Special Wickedness of Mockery**

The verse names mockery (*istihzāʾ*) specifically as what returns upon the wrongdoers, and the commentators reflected on why mockery is singled out. Mockery is the response of a person who has decided not to take something seriously — and taking the warning seriously was the one thing required. Al-Rāzī observes that mockery adds contempt to disbelief. The person who merely disbelieves is wrong; the person who mocks has wrapped his wrongness in scorn, making it harder to abandon, because abandoning it would mean admitting that what he laughed at was true.

There is also a psychological mechanism at work. Mockery is a defense. The person confronted with a warning that frightens him can respond by heeding it or by laughing at it, and laughter is easier because it requires no change. But laughter does not remove the danger; it only removes the perception of danger. The verse describes the moment when the removed perception returns as reality — when what was laughed at stands present and inescapable. The Qur'an's picture of the disbelievers at judgment includes this recognition:

> *"And it will be said, 'This Day We will forget you as you forgot the meeting of this Day of yours...' That is because you took the verses of God in mockery, and the life of this world deluded you."* (Qur'an 45:34–35)

**The Symmetry of Divine Justice**

Both clauses of the verse express a symmetry. The evil deeds return upon the doers; the mocked thing surrounds the mockers. This symmetry — recompense of like for like — is a principle the Qur'an calls *jazāʾan wifāqan*, "a fitting recompense" (78:26). The punishment corresponds to the crime not only in degree but in kind. The arrogant are humiliated (v. 27); the plotters are undone by their own building (v. 26); the mockers are surrounded by what they mocked (v. 34). Al-Rāzī sees in this correspondence a manifestation of wisdom: God's justice is not blunt but precise, answering each sin with the consequence that reveals its nature.

**Consolation and Warning**

The verse, like verse 26, serves two audiences. To the Prophet ﷺ and the believers, who were being mocked daily in Makkah — called poets, madmen, sorcerers, and tellers of fables — it says: this has happened before, and the mockers were surrounded by what they mocked. Do not be shaken by laughter; laughter is not an argument, and its end is known. The Qur'an tells the Prophet explicitly: *"Messengers before you were mocked"* (6:10; 13:32; 21:41), and *"We are sufficient for you against the mockers"* (15:95).
