To the Makkans, and to every reader inclined to treat the warnings of religion as material for jokes, the verse says: what you mock will surround you. Not might — will. The pattern has held in every case the Qur'an records, and there is no reason to expect an exception.

**The Personal Application**

The verse teaches the reader to regard his own deeds with a certain seriousness — not anxiety, but the sober awareness that what he does has consequences that are already in motion. The believer does not need to wait for the Day of Judgment to see the truth of 16:34; he can see it in the way a lie complicates his life, the way a cruelty haunts his conscience, the way neglect of prayer dulls his heart. These are the "evils of what he did" striking him already, in small and reversible form — and they are a mercy, because they warn him before the larger and irreversible form arrives. The Prophet ﷺ described the believer as one who sees his sins as a mountain about to fall on him, while the hypocrite sees his as a fly he waves away (al-Bukhārī 6308). The believer's perception is the accurate one.

And the verse teaches a specific discipline regarding mockery. The believer does not mock the truth, of course; but the verse's principle applies more broadly. Mockery of anything that deserves seriousness — of the poor, of the pious, of the warnings of the wise — participates in the disposition the verse condemns. The Qur'an commands: *"O you who believe, let not a people ridicule another people; perhaps they may be better than them"* (49:11). The one who laughs at what he should have heeded may find, as the earlier nations found, that laughter is the last thing he does before the thing he laughed at arrives.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:35

> **Those who ascribe partners unto God say, "Had God willed, we would not have worshipped aught apart from Him—neither us nor our fathers—nor would we have considered sacred aught apart from Him." Those before them did likewise. Is aught incumbent upon the Messenger save the clear proclamation?**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Excuse That Uses God's Name**

The sūrah now records the idolaters' most sophisticated defense. Having been told that they wrong themselves and will be surrounded by what they mocked, they reach for a theological argument: *law shāʾa Allāhu mā ʿabadnā min dūnihi min shayʾin naḥnu wa-lā ābāʾunā wa-lā ḥarramnā min dūnihi min shayʾ* — "Had God willed, we would not have worshipped anything apart from Him, neither we nor our fathers, nor would we have made anything sacred apart from Him." The argument is this: everything that happens, happens by God's will; our idolatry has happened; therefore God willed it; therefore it must be acceptable to Him, or at least not something for which we can be blamed.

The argument is cunning because it uses a true premise to reach a false conclusion. It is true, in the Qur'an's teaching, that nothing occurs outside God's will. The Qur'an itself says of the idolaters' practices, *"Had God willed, they would not have done it"* (6:137). The error is in the inference. From "God permitted this to happen" they conclude "God approves of this" or "we are not responsible for this." Neither follows.

**The Same Argument in Three Sūrahs**

The Qur'an records this excuse three times, and comparing the passages sharpens the analysis:

> *"Those who associate will say, 'Had God willed, we would not have associated, nor our fathers, nor would we have forbidden anything.' Thus did those before them deny until they tasted Our punishment. Say: Do you have any knowledge that you can produce for us? You follow only conjecture, and you only guess."* (Qur'an 6:148)

> *"And they say, 'Had the Most Merciful willed, we would not have worshipped them.' They have no knowledge of that; they only guess."* (Qur'an 43:20)

Both parallel passages diagnose the argument the same way: it is *ẓann*, conjecture, and *khars*, guessing — not knowledge. The idolaters had no revelation telling them that God approved their idolatry; they inferred it from the mere fact that He allowed it. And the Qur'an's rebuttal is that permission is not approval.

**The Two Wills: The Key Distinction**

The classical scholars, and Ibn Taymiyyah with special clarity, resolved the confusion by distinguishing two senses of "God's will." The first is the *creative will* (*al-irādah al-kawniyyah*), by which God brings things into existence, including things He hates — as He created Iblīs, and permits disbelief, and allows injustice to occur. Nothing escapes this will. The second is the *legislative will* (*al-irādah al-sharʿiyyah*), by which God commands, loves, and approves — expressed in revelation. Faith, justice, and worship of Him alone are what He wills in this second sense.

The idolaters conflated the two. Their idolatry occurred by God's creative will, in the sense that He did not prevent it; it violated His legislative will, in that He forbade it through every messenger. To argue "God willed it, therefore it is right" is to erase the distinction between what God allows and what God commands — and the entire moral order depends on that distinction. Every murder that has ever occurred was "willed" in the first sense; none was willed in the second. If the idolaters' argument were valid, no crime could ever be condemned.

**Why God Allows What He Forbids**

The deeper question — why God's creative will permits what His legislative will forbids — is answered by the reality of human freedom, which the sūrah has already addressed in verse 9. God is capable of preventing all disbelief; He has chosen not to, because compelled belief is worthless and the test of this world requires genuine choice. The Qur'an makes this the direct answer to the idolaters' argument:

> *"And had your Lord willed, all who are on earth would have believed together. Will you then compel people until they become believers?"* (Qur'an 10:99)

God's not compelling them is the very thing that makes them responsible. They took the space of freedom God gave them and used it to argue that they had no freedom. Al-Rāzī notes the self-contradiction: a person who says "I could not have done otherwise" while choosing his words, his gods, and his food taboos is refuting himself with every choice he makes.

**The Ashʿarite and Muʿtazilite Readings**

Al-Rāzī reports that the verse became a battleground between the theological schools. The Muʿtazilites read the idolaters' argument as false through and through — God does not will disbelief in any sense, and the idolaters lied when they attributed it to His will. The Ashʿarites accepted that the idolaters' premise was true in the creative sense — God does will all that occurs — but insisted that the conclusion was false, because God's willing an act to occur does not make it good or excuse its doer. The Qur'an's own language, which affirms both that God "had He willed" could have prevented their idolatry (6:137) and that they are fully culpable for it, supports the second reading. What the Qur'an condemns is not the statement "had God willed we would not have done it" — which is true — but the use of it as an excuse.

**"Nor Would We Have Considered Sacred Aught": The Food Taboos**

The verse includes a second item in the idolaters' excuse: *wa-lā ḥarramnā min dūnihi min shayʾ*, "nor would we have made anything forbidden apart from Him." This refers to the pagan Arabs' invented prohibitions — the camels they declared sacred and forbade to be ridden or eaten, the practices described in 5:103 (*baḥīrah*, *sāʾibah*, *waṣīlah*, *ḥām*) and 6:136–140. Ibn Kathīr and al-Zamakhsharī note that these taboos had no basis in revelation; they were human inventions attributed to religion. The idolaters now claim that even these were God's will. The sūrah will return to this issue in verses 116–117, forbidding anyone to say "this is lawful and this is forbidden" without divine authority.

**"Those Before Them Did Likewise"**

For the third time in this passage (after verses 26 and 33), the verse invokes the precedent of earlier nations: *kadhālika faʿala alladhīna min qablihim*. The excuse from divine will is ancient. Every people confronted by a prophet has reached for it, because it offers the comfort of disbelief without the discomfort of guilt. The parallel in 6:148 adds what happened to those who used it: they persisted "until they tasted Our punishment." The excuse did not save them.

**The Fatalism the Qur'an Rejects**

The source's observation is worth developing: the idolaters' argument is a form of fatalism that the Qur'an consistently rejects, and it appears in other guises. In 36:47, the disbelievers refuse to feed the poor by saying, *"Shall we feed those whom, if God willed, He would have fed?"* The structure is identical: God's creative will is invoked to excuse a moral failure. If God wanted the poor fed, He would feed them; therefore we need not.

This reasoning, if accepted, would abolish all moral effort. Why cure the sick, if God willed their sickness? Why free the oppressed, if God willed their oppression? Why teach the ignorant, if God willed their ignorance? The Qur'an's answer is that God has commanded the feeding of the poor, the curing of the sick, and the teaching of the ignorant, and that these commands express His will in the sense that matters for human action. The believer does not read God's will off the state of the world; he reads it in the Book. The state of the world is the arena in which he is tested; the Book is the standard by which he is judged.

**"Is Aught Incumbent Upon the Messenger Save the Clear Proclamation?"**

The verse closes with a question that shifts the focus from the idolaters to the Prophet ﷺ: *fa-hal ʿalā al-rusuli illā al-balāghu al-mubīn*, "so is anything incumbent upon the messengers except the clear conveyance?" The word *balāgh* means the delivery of a message; *mubīn* means clear, plain, unambiguous. The messenger's duty is to convey the message clearly. He is not responsible for whether it is accepted.

This principle appears throughout the Qur'an (3:20; 5:92, 99; 13:40; 24:54; 29:18; 36:17; 42:48; 64:12) and will recur in this sūrah at verse 82. Its function here is twofold. It consoles the Prophet: the idolaters' sophistries are not his failure; he has delivered the message, and their excuses are between them and God. And it seals the idolaters' accountability: the clear proclamation has been made, so the excuse "we did not know" is closed to them, and the excuse "God willed it" has just been exposed. Al-Zamakhsharī states the sense: having delivered the message, the Prophet is innocent of whatever his people do afterward of their own choice.

Al-Rāzī notes that the Ashʿarites read this clause narrowly: it establishes that the *Messenger* is not responsible for the people's belief, without settling whether the people or God's decree is ultimately determinative. But the whole thrust of the passage — "they wronged themselves" (v. 33), "the evils of what they did struck them" (v. 34), the exposure of their excuse (v. 35) — places the responsibility on the people.

**The Modern Form of the Excuse**

The idolaters' argument has never gone away; it has only changed vocabulary. "I was born this way." "My upbringing made me." "Society determined my choices." "My brain chemistry left me no option." Each of these is a version of "had God willed, we would not have done it" — the appeal to a cause outside oneself in order to escape responsibility for what one did. The Qur'an does not deny that causes exist; it denies that they abolish choice. The person who says "I could not have done otherwise" is asked to notice that he chooses, constantly, in every waking moment, and that he holds others responsible for their choices whenever he is the one wronged. The excuse is one he would never accept from another. The verse asks him to stop accepting it from himself.

**The Believer's Correct Relationship to God's Will**

The verse teaches not that the believer should never speak of God's will, but how to speak of it. The believer says "had God willed" in gratitude and humility about what has happened — "had God not willed, I would not have been guided" — never in excuse for what he has done wrong. He attributes his good to God's grace and his evil to himself, as the Qur'an teaches (4:79). And when he faces the wrongdoing of the world, he does not say "God willed it, so let it be"; he says "God commanded me to oppose it, so I will" — and he leaves the outcome to the will he cannot control while doing the duty he can.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:36

> **We indeed sent a messenger unto every community, "Worship God, and shun false deities!" Then among them were those whom God guided; and among them were those who were deserving of error. So journey upon the earth and behold how the deniers fared in the end!**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Answer to the Excuse**

Verse 35 recorded the idolaters' plea that God's will excused their idolatry, and it ended by asking whether anything is required of messengers except clear proclamation. Verse 36 now demonstrates that the clear proclamation has been made — not once, not to one people, but to every community in human history. *Wa-laqad baʿathnā fī kulli ummatin rasūlan*, "and We certainly sent into every community a messenger." The idolaters cannot claim ignorance, and neither can anyone else. The message has been universal.

The particle *laqad*, "certainly, indeed," with the oath-like *la-*, gives the statement emphatic force. This is not a general observation but a solemn affirmation.

**The Universality of Prophethood**

The verse teaches a doctrine that distinguishes Islam among the world's religions: God has not left any people without a messenger. The Qur'an repeats this in several places:

> *"And for every community there is a messenger. And when their messenger comes, judgment is passed between them in justice, and they are not wronged."* (Qur'an 10:47)

> *"And there is no community but that a warner has passed among it."* (Qur'an 35:24)

> *"And We certainly sent messengers before you; among them are those whose stories We have related to you, and among them are those whose stories We have not related to you."* (Qur'an 40:78)

The last verse is important for understanding the scope of 16:36. The Qur'an names about twenty-five prophets, most of them from the line of Abraham and the lands between Egypt and Arabia. But it explicitly states that there were others it does not name. A ḥadīth recorded by Aḥmad (22288) and Ibn Ḥibbān reports the Prophet ﷺ giving the number of prophets as one hundred and twenty-four thousand, of whom three hundred and fifteen were messengers. Whatever the precise number, the principle is that no community — in China, in India, in Africa, in the Americas, among the peoples of every continent — was left without a warner. The Muslim view of religious history is therefore not that truth appeared in one corner of the world and nowhere else, but that it was sent everywhere, and that its traces survive, in varying degrees of purity, in the traditions of many peoples.

**The Word *Ummah***

The word *ummah*, "community," comes from the root *ʾ-m-m*, which relates to *umm*, "mother," and *imām*, "leader" — the sense being a group united by a common origin or a common direction. Here it means a people, a nation, a generation bound together in time and place. The Qur'an will use the same word in a striking way in verse 120, calling Abraham alone "an *ummah*." Every *ummah* received a messenger; the message did not depend on the size or power of the people.

**The Content of the Message: Two Commands**

The verse states the message every messenger brought in the fewest possible words: *ani ʿbudū Allāha wa-jtanibū al-ṭāghūt*, "Worship God, and avoid *ṭāghūt*." Two commands, one positive and one negative, and together they constitute the whole of the prophetic call.

"Worship God" — *uʿbudū Allāh* — is the command that the Qur'an places on the lips of prophet after prophet: Noah (7:59; 23:23), Hūd (7:65; 11:50), Ṣāliḥ (7:73; 11:61), Shuʿayb (7:85; 11:84), Abraham (29:16), and Jesus (5:72, 117). The uniformity is the point. The religion of all the prophets was one in its essence: the exclusive worship of the One God. The Qur'an says: *"And We sent no messenger before you but that We revealed to him, 'There is no god but I, so worship Me'"* (21:25). Verse 2 of this sūrah stated the same.

"Avoid *ṭāghūt*" is the negative side. The word *ṭāghūt* comes from the root *ṭ-gh-y*, which means to exceed bounds, to overflow, to transgress — as a river overflows its banks (69:11) or a tyrant exceeds his authority. *Ṭāghūt* is an intensive noun meaning anything that has transgressed its proper limit by claiming for itself what belongs to God. The classical definitions gather several senses: idols, Satan, sorcerers, and any being that is worshipped, obeyed, or followed in place of God. ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb is reported to have said that *ṭāghūt* is Satan; Jābir said it is the soothsayers upon whom devils descended. Ibn al-Qayyim gave a comprehensive definition: *ṭāghūt* is everything by which the servant exceeds his limit, whether an object of worship, an object of following, or an object of obedience. The word thus covers false gods, false authorities, and false laws — anything that claims a share of the absolute devotion owed to God.

The two commands are inseparable. One cannot truly worship God while serving *ṭāghūt*, because worship is exclusive by nature. The declaration of faith itself has the same two-part structure: *lā ilāha* (negation — there is no god) *illā Allāh* (affirmation — except God). The Qur'an states the principle in the verse of the firmest handhold:

> *"Whoever rejects ṭāghūt and believes in God has grasped the firmest handhold, which never breaks."* (Qur'an 2:256)

The order in 2:256 is rejection first, then belief. In 16:36 it is worship first, then avoidance. Both orders are true, and together they teach that the two are simultaneous aspects of a single turning: toward God and away from everything that competes with Him.

**Two Responses: Guidance and Deserved Error**

The verse then describes what happened when the message arrived: *fa-minhum man hadā Allāhu wa-minhum man ḥaqqat ʿalayhi al-ḍalālah*, "then among them were those whom God guided, and among them were those upon whom error was deservedly established." The message was the same; the responses divided.

The phrasing is carefully balanced and became a classic text in the debate about divine decree. On the one side, guidance is attributed to God: "whom God guided." On the other, error is described not as something God imposed but as something that *ḥaqqat*, "became due," "was justly established," upon the person. The verb *ḥaqqa* means to become true, right, deserved, obligatory. The error became their due — it was earned.

Al-Rāzī reports the two readings. The Ashʿarites read the verse as affirming that after the message reached all, God guided some and left others to disbelieve, and that both outcomes are within His will. The Muʿtazilites, and al-Bayḍāwī in reporting them, drew the opposite inference from the word *ḥaqqat*: error is something a person *deserves*, which means it is earned by his own choices, not imposed. The Qur'an itself supports the second emphasis in many places, specifying whom God leads astray: *"God leads astray the wrongdoers"* (14:27), *"He leads astray only the iniquitous"* (2:26), and — in the very next verse of this sūrah — *"God guides not those who lead astray"* (16:37). Misguidance is never arbitrary; it is the just consequence of a prior choice to reject.

The balanced formulation of the two traditions is this: God's guidance is grace, offered to all through the messengers and completed in the hearts of those who turn toward it; God's leaving people in error is justice, applied to those who turned away after the message reached them. No one is guided except by God's grace, and no one is left in error except by his own deserving. Both halves of the verse hold.

**"So Journey Upon the Earth": The Empirical Command**

The verse ends with a command: *fa-sīrū fī al-arḍi fa-nẓurū kayfa kāna ʿāqibatu al-mukadhdhibīn*, "so travel through the earth and see how was the end of the deniers." This is a striking turn. Having made a claim about history — that messengers came to every people and that those who denied them met a certain end — the Qur'an tells its listeners to go and check. The evidence is in the ruins.

The command is repeated in 3:137, 6:11, 12:109, 27:69, 30:9, 30:42, and 35:44. It was addressed first to the Arabs, whose trade routes passed through the ruins of Thamūd at al-Ḥijr, and who knew the traditions of ʿĀd, of the people of Lot, and of the cities of the Dead Sea. The Prophet ﷺ himself, passing through al-Ḥijr on the way to Tabūk, told his Companions:

> *"Do not enter upon these punished people unless you are weeping; and if you are not weeping, do not enter upon them, lest there befall you what befell them."* (al-Bukhārī 433; Muslim 2980)

He treated the ruins exactly as the verse instructs: as evidence to be looked at and lessons to be felt.

The command has a broader significance. It establishes that the Qur'an's claims about the moral structure of history are open to verification. Travel, observe, study the remains of civilizations, and you will find the pattern: peoples who rejected the call to justice and to God did not endure. This is an invitation to history, archaeology, and reflection as religious activities. The Qur'an does not fear the evidence; it directs the reader toward it.

**The Word *ʿĀqibah*: The End That Reveals the Truth**

The verse asks the traveler to look at the *ʿāqibah*, the end, the final outcome, of the deniers. The root *ʿ-q-b* relates to what follows, what comes at the heel of something. The Qur'an's concept of *ʿāqibah* teaches that a thing is judged by how it ends, not by how it appears in the middle. The deniers, in their day, were powerful; ʿĀd boasted, *"Who is mightier than us in strength?"* (41:15). Their *ʿāqibah* was the wind that left them like hollow palm trunks (69:7). The Qur'an promises that *"the end belongs to the God-fearing"* (7:128; 11:49; 28:83). The traveler who reads the ruins learns to distrust the appearance of the middle and to attend to the end.

**The Verse's Enduring Charge**

For the believer, the verse establishes three things to hold onto. First, the universality of God's justice: no people was abandoned, and therefore no people can claim to have been unfairly judged. Second, the simplicity of the core message: worship God and avoid *ṭāghūt* — everything else in religion is the unfolding of these two commands. Third, the discipline of learning from history: the believer looks at the fate of past arrogance with the eyes the Prophet ﷺ modeled at al-Ḥijr — not with tourist curiosity but with weeping, because the same pattern applies to every generation, including his own. The ruins are not a museum; they are a mirror.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:37

> **Though thou eagerly desire that they be guided, verily God guides not those who lead astray, and they shall have no helpers.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Addressed to the Prophet's Heart**

Verse 36 stated that among every community some were guided and some deserved error. Verse 37 turns to the Prophet ﷺ personally and addresses something the sūrah has not yet named: his longing. *In taḥriṣ ʿalā hudāhum*, "if you are eager for their guidance" — or, in the sense the grammar carries, "however eagerly you desire their guidance." The verb *ḥaraṣa* denotes intense, anxious desire — the kind of wanting that consumes a person's attention and effort. The Qur'an uses it of the Prophet's concern for his people in a verse of tender description:

> *"There has certainly come to you a Messenger from among yourselves; grievous to him is what you suffer; he is anxious (ḥarīṣ) over you; to the believers he is kind and merciful."* (Qur'an 9:128)

The Prophet's *ḥirṣ* for the guidance of his people was one of his defining qualities. He is described as nearly destroying himself with grief over their refusal: *"Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief over their footsteps, if they do not believe in this message"* (18:6), and *"Perhaps you would kill yourself because they are not believers"* (26:3). Verse 37 addresses this anguish directly and sets a boundary around it.

**The Limit of the Prophet's Power**

The verse's central statement is *fa-inna Allāha lā yahdī man yuḍill*, "then truly God does not guide whoever leads astray" — with a variant reading discussed below. The sense is that the matter of guidance belongs to God, and the Prophet's desire, however intense, cannot override the divine decree regarding those who have chosen error. The Qur'an states this limit in the most direct terms in another verse, revealed — according to the commentators — about the Prophet's uncle Abū Ṭālib, who died without professing Islam despite the Prophet's pleading:

> *"You do not guide whom you love, but God guides whom He wills. And He is most knowing of the rightly guided."* (Qur'an 28:56)

The story of Abū Ṭālib's death, recorded by al-Bukhārī (1360) and Muslim (24), shows the Prophet at his uncle's bedside urging him to say "there is no god but God," while Abū Jahl and others urged him to die on the religion of his fathers. Abū Ṭālib's last words were that he remained on the religion of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib. The Prophet said, "I will continue to seek forgiveness for you unless I am forbidden," and then the verse was revealed forbidding it (9:113) and the verse of 28:56 was revealed as consolation. The scene gives 16:37 its emotional depth. The Prophet's desire could not have been greater; the object of it could not have been closer; and still the outcome was not in his hands.

**Two Readings: "Those Who Lead Astray" and "Those Whom He Leads Astray"**

The Arabic *man yuḍill* admits two vocalizations, and both are transmitted among the recitations, as Ibn Kathīr notes.

On the first reading, *man yuḍillu* with the person who misleads as the subject: "God does not guide those who lead [others] astray." This connects to verse 25, which described those who "lead astray without knowledge" and bear a share of their followers' burdens. The verse then says: those who have made themselves agents of misguidance are not guided — a fitting recompense, since they have chosen to be the opposite of guides.

On the second reading, *man yuḍillu* with God as the subject, or the passive *man yuḍallu*: "God does not guide those whom He leads astray" or "those who are led astray." This connects to verse 36: those upon whom error has been justly established are not thereafter guided. The Qur'an has parallels: *"And whomever God leads astray, for him there is no guide"* (13:33; 7:186; 39:23, 36).

Both readings converge on one teaching: there is a state of misguidance — entered by choice, sealed by persistence — from which the Prophet's longing cannot extract a person, because God has justly withheld the inner guidance that the person has refused. The distinction between the guidance of clarification (which the Prophet gives) and the guidance of enablement (which only God gives), discussed in the commentary on verse 9, is the framework here. The Prophet gave the first to everyone; the second was not his to give.

**Why God Withholds Guidance From Some**

The verse says God does not guide those who lead astray, and it is important to understand that this withholding is not arbitrary. The Qur'an specifies, over and over, the categories of people from whom guidance is withheld: the wrongdoers (2:258; 3:86; 5:51; 6:144; 9:19, 109; 28:50; 46:10; 61:7; 62:5), the disbelievers (2:264; 5:67; 9:37; 16:107), the iniquitous (5:108; 9:24, 80; 61:5; 63:6), the liars and ungrateful (39:3), and the extravagant doubters (40:28, 34). In every case, the withholding follows a prior act by the person. The sequence is stated explicitly:

> *"So when they deviated, God caused their hearts to deviate. And God does not guide the iniquitous people."* (Qur'an 61:5)

They deviated first; the divine deviation of their hearts followed. Ibn Kathīr, commenting on 16:37, emphasizes that God's not guiding is a consequence and not a cause of the person's misguidance. The person who has repeatedly refused the light, mocked the messenger, and led others into darkness has, by his own conduct, rendered himself unfit to receive what he has spent his life rejecting. God's justice consists in giving him what he has chosen.

**"And They Shall Have No Helpers"**

The verse closes: *wa-mā lahum min nāṣirīn*, "and they have no helpers." The word *nāṣir* means one who gives victory, aid, or protection against an enemy. The verse says that on the Day of Judgment — and, in a sense, already in this world — those who have been left in error have no one to rescue them from the consequence. Not their idols (verse 20 established their powerlessness), not their followers (who will disown them), not their fathers whose religion they clung to, and not the Prophet whose intercession does not extend to those who died in *shirk*.

The Qur'an repeats this phrase for the disbelievers in many places (2:270; 3:22, 56, 91; 5:72; 30:29; 45:34). Its function is to remove the last false hope: the hope that someone, somehow, will intervene. There is no intervention for the one who has refused the only Helper. The Prophet ﷺ said to his own tribe, in the earliest days of his mission, that he could not avail them anything against God (al-Bukhārī 2753; Muslim 204) — even his nearest relatives had to save themselves by faith.

**The Consolation Hidden in the Limit**

The verse might seem harsh — a boundary placed on the Prophet's love. But the commentators saw in it a profound mercy toward him. The Prophet was consuming himself with grief over people who had chosen not to be helped. The verse releases him from a burden that was never his to carry. His task was the clear proclamation (v. 35); the outcome was God's. To be told this is to be freed from an impossible responsibility. The Qur'an says in another place: *"Your duty is only to convey; upon Us is the reckoning"* (13:40).

This release has a direct application for every believer engaged in calling others to good — parents whose children have strayed, teachers whose students refuse, friends whose counsel is rejected. The verse teaches that one may desire the guidance of another with all one's heart, and one should; but one cannot produce it, and one is not to be destroyed by the failure to produce it. The believer does his part — with wisdom and beautiful exhortation, as verse 125 will command — and entrusts the rest to the only One who opens hearts. This is not indifference; it is the correct division of labor between the servant and the Lord.

**The Danger of Being a Misleader**

If the first reading of *man yuḍill* is adopted — "those who lead astray" — the verse carries a specific warning. The person who makes himself an instrument of misguidance places himself beyond the reach even of the Prophet's prayer. This is a sobering thought for anyone who influences others. Verse 25 said the misleader bears a share of his followers' sins; verse 37 says he is not guided. The two together describe a spiral: the more one leads others astray, the more one is confirmed in one's own error, and the further one moves from the possibility of return. The remedy is to reverse the direction immediately — to become, by God's grace, a caller to guidance rather than to error, and thereby to enter the category of those whom God does guide and does help.

**A Reflection on Love and Its Limits**

The verse contains a hidden teaching about love itself. The Prophet's love for his people was real, intense, and — in the case of Abū Ṭālib — personal beyond measure. Yet love, however great, cannot make choices for another person. This is one of the hardest truths of human life, and the verse states it without softening: you may desire their guidance with all your being, and they may still refuse. What the verse offers in place of the outcome one cannot control is the peace of having done what one could, and the knowledge that the One who withholds guidance does so justly and knows the hearts better than the lover does. The Prophet accepted this, and continued to call, and continued to grieve, and continued to entrust the result to God. That combination — full effort, real sorrow, and complete trust — is the model the verse sets before every believer who loves someone who will not be helped.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:38

> **And they swear by God their most solemn oaths [that] God will not resurrect those who die. Nay, but it is a promise binding upon Him, though most of mankind know not.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Central Denial**

The sūrah has been circling the Makkans' rejection of the Hereafter since verse 22, which identified "those who believe not in the Hereafter" as the arrogant deniers. Verse 38 now presents that rejection in its most emphatic form: *wa-aqsamū bi'Llāhi jahda aymānihim lā yabʿathu Allāhu man yamūt*, "and they swore by God their strongest oaths: God will not raise the one who dies." This is the belief that underlay everything else — their idolatry, their mockery, their persecution. If there is no resurrection, there is no judgment; if there is no judgment, nothing ultimately matters; and if nothing ultimately matters, one may as well worship what one's fathers worshipped and live as one pleases.

**"Their Most Solemn Oaths": *Jahda Aymānihim***

The phrase *jahda aymānihim* means "the utmost of their oaths" — *jahd* denotes exertion, effort, the maximum one can do. They did not merely deny the resurrection; they swore to its impossibility with every form of solemn emphasis available to them. The Qur'an records the content of their denial elsewhere:

> *"And they say, 'When we are bones and crumbled particles, will we truly be raised as a new creation?'"* (Qur'an 17:49)

> *"Does he promise you that when you have died and become dust and bones, you will be brought forth? Far, far is that which you are promised! There is nothing but our worldly life; we die and we live, and we will not be raised."* (Qur'an 23:35–37)

> *"There is nothing but our worldly life; we die and live, and nothing destroys us except time."* (Qur'an 45:24)

The last verse shows the shape of their worldview: time (*al-dahr*) is the only power; death is the end; there is nothing beyond.

**The Two Observations of the Commentators**

The commentators drew two lessons from the fact that they *swore*.

Al-Rāzī takes the oaths as evidence of the completeness of their conviction. A person swears to what he is certain of. The Makkans had so thoroughly rejected the resurrection that they regarded it as self-evidently absurd — as irrational as a square circle. Their hearts and minds had closed on the matter. This is important for understanding why the Qur'an argues the resurrection so persistently and from so many angles: it was not addressing mild doubt but total denial reinforced by oath.

Al-Qurṭubī notes a paradox in the oaths. They swore *by God*. To swear by God is to invoke Him as the supreme witness and guarantor — to acknowledge His power, His knowledge, and His authority over the outcome. Yet the content of the oath was a denial of His power to raise the dead. They affirmed God's greatness in the form of their speech and denied it in the substance. This inconsistency is the same one the sūrah has exposed repeatedly: the Makkans acknowledged God as Creator (v. 3, v. 17) and yet worshipped idols; they invoked God in oaths and yet denied His power. Their disbelief was never coherent. It was a refusal that used God's name while rejecting God's claim.

Al-Rāzī adds a further observation: to deny the resurrection was, in effect, to deny the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ, since his mission consisted so largely in warning of the accounting to come. The oath against resurrection was an oath against the messenger.

**"Nay, But It Is a Promise Binding Upon Him"**

The Qur'an's reply begins with *balā*, the particle that contradicts a negative — "on the contrary," "yes indeed He will." Then: *waʿdan ʿalayhi ḥaqqan*, "a promise upon Him, true" — that is, a promise that God has made binding upon Himself and that is certainly true.

The phrase deserves careful attention. The resurrection is described as a *waʿd*, a promise. A promise is a commitment freely made by the one who promises. It is described as *ʿalayhi*, "upon Him" — incumbent upon God, an obligation He has taken on. And it is *ḥaqq*, true, real, right, deserved. The grammatical construction, with *waʿdan* and *ḥaqqan* as emphatic accusatives, has the force of "He has promised it as a binding, true promise."

The commentators addressed the theological question this raises: in what sense can anything be "binding upon" God? Al-Ṭabrisī explains that the resurrection is something God has promised and will therefore fulfill, since He does not break His promise: *"Truly God does not fail in His promise"* (3:9; 13:31). The obligation is self-imposed, arising from His own word and His own justice, not imposed from outside. The Qur'an uses this same language of divine self-commitment elsewhere: *"He has prescribed mercy upon Himself"* (6:12, 54), *"It is a promise upon Us; truly We do it"* (21:104).

**Why the Resurrection Is Necessary**

Al-Ṭabrisī goes further and argues that the resurrection is not merely promised but *required* by the divine wisdom and justice. Without resurrection and judgment, moral accountability in this world would be meaningless. The oppressor who dies in his palace and the oppressed who dies in his prison would share the same end; the murderer and his victim would be equal in the grave; the truthful and the liar would meet the same nothingness. If this were so, the whole moral order that every human conscience recognizes — that wrong should be answered and right rewarded — would be a delusion. God, Who is just and wise, does not create a world in which justice is a delusion. Therefore there must be a reckoning, and a reckoning requires resurrection.

The Qur'an makes this argument explicitly:

> *"Did you think that We created you in vain, and that you would not be returned to Us?"* (Qur'an 23:115)

> *"Or should We treat those who believe and do righteous deeds like the corrupters on earth? Or should We treat the God-fearing like the wicked?"* (Qur'an 38:28)

> *"And God created the heavens and the earth in truth, and so that every soul may be recompensed for what it has earned, and they will not be wronged."* (Qur'an 45:22)

The last verse connects the resurrection to the theme of verse 3 of this sūrah — creation "in truth." A purposeful creation requires a purposeful conclusion. The resurrection is that conclusion. It is "binding upon Him" in the sense that a wise and just Creator, having made the world for a purpose, has committed Himself to completing it.

**The Argument From Possibility**

Alongside the argument from justice, the Qur'an repeatedly answers the Makkans' denial with the argument from possibility, which this sūrah has already introduced in verse 4 and will develop in verse 40. The one who created human beings from a drop can certainly reconstitute them from dust; the one who revives dead earth with rain (v. 65) can certainly revive dead bodies. The Qur'an's formula is:

> *"Say: He will give them life Who produced them the first time; and He is Knowing of every creation."* (Qur'an 36:79)

> *"As We began the first creation, We will repeat it. A promise upon Us. Truly We do it."* (Qur'an 21:104)

The second passage uses the same construction as 16:38 — "a promise upon Us" — and adds "truly We do it." The Makkans' oath is answered by God's oath.

**"Though Most of Mankind Know Not"**

The verse ends: *wa-lākinna akthara al-nāsi lā yaʿlamūn*, "but most people do not know." What is it they do not know? Al-Ṭabrisī gives two answers, both valid: they do not know the certainty of the resurrection, and they do not know the wisdom behind it — the purpose it serves in giving meaning to moral responsibility and to earthly life itself.

The phrase is characteristic of the Qur'an's realism about human belief. It does not claim that the truth is universally acknowledged; it states that most people are ignorant of it, and it explains why. The ignorance is not for lack of evidence — the evidence is in every seed that sprouts and every child that is born — but for lack of attention, distracted by *"the life of this world"* (30:7) and the assumption that what is not seen is not real. The verse thus implicitly summons the reader to be among the minority who know.

**The Existential Weight of the Question**

The denial of resurrection is not an abstract philosophical position; it shapes everything about how a person lives. If death is the end, then every injustice unpunished in this world is unpunished forever, every love ended by death is ended forever, and every sacrifice for a good that one will not see is a sacrifice for nothing. The Makkans who swore that God would not raise the dead were not merely making a claim about cosmology; they were declaring that the universe is ultimately indifferent to right and wrong. Their idolatry, their burial of daughters, their persecution of the weak — all of it followed from the belief that nothing would be answered.

The Qur'an's affirmation of resurrection is correspondingly not merely a claim about the future but a claim about the present: everything matters. Every deed is recorded (v. 19, v. 23); every soul will be paid in full (v. 111). This is a heavy truth and a liberating one. It is heavy because it means one cannot escape the consequences of one's actions by dying. It is liberating because it means the oppressed will be vindicated, the patient will be rewarded, and no good is ever wasted. The believer lives in a moral universe; the denier lives in a meaningless one. The verse insists that the believer's universe is the real one — *waʿdan ʿalayhi ḥaqqan*, a true promise, binding on the One who cannot lie.

**A Practical Consequence**

The Prophet ﷺ taught his Companions to live with the resurrection as a daily reality, not a distant doctrine. He said:

> *"The intelligent person is the one who takes account of himself and works for what comes after death; and the incapable one is he who follows his desires and then hopes in God."* (al-Tirmidhī 2459)

To "work for what comes after death" is the practical form of believing in 16:38. The person who truly knows that the resurrection is a binding promise arranges his life around it — as a traveler who knows his destination arranges his journey. The Makkans' oath was, in the end, a way of avoiding this arrangement. The verse takes the avoidance away.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:39

> **[This is so] that He might make clear unto them that wherein they differed, and that those who disbelieved might know that truly they were liars.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Purpose of the Resurrection Stated**

Verse 38 affirmed that the resurrection is a promise binding upon God. Verse 39 gives its purpose, introduced by the particle *li-*, "in order that": *li-yubayyina lahum alladhī yakhtalifūna fīh*, "that He may make clear to them that wherein they differ." The resurrection is not merely a display of power; it has a function. It is the moment when every dispute is settled, every falsehood exposed, and every truth made plain. The verse thus supplies the "why" that verse 38 left implicit: God raises the dead so that the truth may be shown.

**"That Wherein They Differed": The Scope of Human Disagreement**

Human beings have differed about God, about revelation, about right and wrong, about the meaning of life, and about the fate of the dead, throughout their entire history. Within Makkah alone, the Prophet ﷺ and the Quraysh differed about whether God is one, whether the Qur'an is revelation, and whether the dead will rise. Among the People of the Book, Jews and Christians differed about Jesus, about the law, about the coming prophet. The Qur'an repeatedly states that these differences will be resolved on the Day of Judgment:

> *"So God will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection concerning that over which they used to differ."* (Qur'an 2:113)

> *"To God is your return all together, and He will inform you concerning that over which you used to differ."* (Qur'an 5:48)

> *"Truly your Lord will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection concerning that over which they used to differ."* (Qur'an 10:93)

This sūrah returns to the theme in verses 92 and 124. The consistency reveals something about the Qur'an's understanding of truth: it is not that truth is unknowable in this world — the messengers were sent precisely to make it known — but that in this world, truth can be denied, argued against, and obscured by those who do not wish to see it. The Day of Judgment removes that possibility. What was disputed becomes evident. What was claimed becomes verified or refuted. The resurrection is, among other things, the end of all argument.

**The Verb *Yubayyinu*: Making Manifest**

The verb *bayyana*, "to make clear," is central to the Qur'an's vocabulary. Its root, *b-y-n*, denotes separation and distinction — what is *bayyin* is what stands out clearly from its surroundings. The Qur'an calls itself *al-bayān*, the clarification (3:138), and describes the Prophet's task as *li-tubayyina*, "that you may make clear" (16:44). In this world, clarification is by word: God speaks, and people may believe or deny. On the Day of Judgment, clarification is by reality: the thing itself is present. The disbeliever who denied the resurrection will not be told he was wrong; he will be standing, resurrected. The dispute ends not by superior argument but by the arrival of the fact.

**Why Disputes Must Be Settled**

The commentators drew from this verse a reflection on divine wisdom. Al-Ṭabrisī notes that God's justice requires that truth and falsehood not remain permanently confused. If the world simply ended, with the liar's lie and the truthful person's truth equally buried, there would be a kind of injustice in the very structure of existence — an injustice against truth itself. The resurrection is the moment when God, Who is *al-Ḥaqq*, the Truth, vindicates the truth. He does not leave the question open forever.

This has a consoling dimension for the believer. Those who hold to truth in a world that mocks it live with the daily experience of being told they are wrong, foolish, or backward. The verse promises that this experience is temporary. There will be a Day when what they held is shown to be what was real. The martyr who died for the truth and the scholar who defended it against ridicule will see, on that Day, that they were right — not by their own assertion, but by the manifest reality of God's judgment.

**"And That Those Who Disbelieved Might Know That They Were Liars"**

The verse's second purpose is more specific: *wa-li-yaʿlama alladhīna kafarū annahum kānū kādhibīn*, "and that those who disbelieved may know that they were liars." The word *kādhibīn*, "liars," refers back to the oaths of verse 38. They swore by God that God would not raise the dead. On the Day they are raised, the oath is proven false — not merely mistaken, but a lie, because they swore to what they had no knowledge of, as though they knew.

The Qur'an's insistence that the disbelievers will *know* their own falsehood is significant. It is not enough, in the divine justice, that they be punished; they must understand why. The Qur'an repeatedly depicts the moment of this recognition:

> *"And they will say, 'Woe to us! This is the Day of Recompense.' This is the Day of Judgment which you used to deny."* (Qur'an 37:20–21)

> *"Then they will be presented before their Lord. He will say, 'Is this not the truth?' They will say, 'Yes, by our Lord.' He will say, 'Then taste the punishment for what you used to deny.'"* (Qur'an 6:30)

The exchange in 6:30 contains the same "yes, by our Lord" — an oath — that answers the oath of denial in 16:38. They swore it would not happen; they will swear that it has. The symmetry is precise, and it is the verse's purpose: that they should know.

**The Justice of Self-Knowledge**

There is a profound principle here about the nature of punishment in Islam. The punishment of the Hereafter is not inflicted on the bewildered. The disbeliever is shown, before he is punished, exactly what he did and why it was wrong. His own book is placed in his hand (17:13–14; 69:25); his own limbs testify (24:24; 36:65; 41:20–21); his own memory returns (89:23). The justice of God is a justice of full disclosure. Al-Rāzī observes that this is why the resurrection is described as a *bayān*, a clarification: it is the moment when the veil that the disbeliever drew over his own conscience is removed, and he sees himself as God saw him.

This principle has a mirror image for the believer. The believer, too, will see clearly — will see the deeds he had forgotten, the small kindnesses recorded, the tears he shed in private, and the mercy of God that covered his faults. The clarification of the Day is total, and it clarifies good as well as evil.

**A Second Structural Reading**

Al-Ṭabrisī and others note that verse 39 can also be read as continuing verse 36 rather than verse 38: "We sent a messenger to every community... that He might make clear to them that wherein they differed." On this reading, the *sending of messengers* is what clarifies differences — which is also true, and which the sūrah will state explicitly in verse 64: *"We did not send down the Book to you except that you might make clear to them that wherein they differed."* The two readings are complementary. Messengers clarify the truth in this world by word; the resurrection clarifies it in the next by reality. The first clarification makes the second just: because the truth was made clear by messengers, the disbelievers have no excuse when it is made clear by resurrection.

**Living Toward the Day of Clarification**

The verse invites a specific orientation of the heart. Since every dispute will be settled and every claim tested, the believer has no need to win every argument in this world. He states the truth with wisdom and beautiful exhortation (v. 125), and he leaves the vindication to the Day appointed for it. This releases him from two temptations: the temptation to compromise the truth in order to be accepted, and the temptation to defend it with anger and harshness as though everything depended on this world's verdict. It does not. The Qur'an tells the Prophet, regarding those who dispute with him: *"God will judge between you on the Day of Resurrection concerning that over which you used to differ"* (22:69). The believer's calm in controversy comes from knowing that the last word has already been reserved for God.

The verse also invites honesty with oneself now. Since the Day will clarify everything, including one's own self-deceptions, the wise course is to seek that clarification early — to examine one's beliefs and deeds in the light of revelation before they are examined in the light of judgment. The person who does this will find that the Day of Clarification holds no terrors for him, because he has already asked to be shown the truth and has already turned toward it. The Prophet ﷺ prayed: *"O God, show me the truth as truth and grant me to follow it, and show me falsehood as falsehood and grant me to avoid it."* That prayer is the believer's way of asking, in this life, for the clarification that 16:39 promises in the next.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:40

> **And Our Word unto a thing, when We desire it, is only to say to it, "Be!" and it is.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Answer to "How?"**

The Makkans swore that God would not raise the dead (v. 38). Behind their oath lay an unspoken question: how could He? Bones decay, bodies scatter, generations dissolve into dust; by what conceivable process could they be reassembled? Verse 40 answers the question by dissolving it. God does not need a process. *Innamā qawlunā li-shayʾin idhā aradnāhu an naqūla lahu kun fa-yakūn*, "Our Word to a thing, when We will it, is only that We say to it 'Be!' — and it is." The resurrection, which seems impossible to a mind that thinks in terms of mechanisms, is trivial to a will that operates by command.

**The Restrictive Particle *Innamā***

The verse opens with *innamā*, "only," "nothing more than." It restricts God's creative act to a single thing: His word. There is no labor, no material, no assistant, no time elapsed, no effort expended. Al-Rāzī explains that the restriction excludes every conception of divine creation as difficult or gradual: God does not make the way a builder builds, assembling parts over time; He makes the way a king commands — and more perfectly, since even a king's command requires servants to execute it, whereas God's command *is* its own execution.

**"Be!" — *Kun***

The word *kun* is the imperative of *kāna*, "to be." It is the shortest complete sentence in the Arabic language — two letters, *kāf* and *nūn*. The Qur'an chooses the briefest possible utterance to express the totality of creative power. The brevity is the point: the vastest thing — a universe, a resurrection of all who ever lived — requires from God no more than the smallest word.

The formula *kun fa-yakūn* appears eight times in the Qur'an, each in a context where the impossible is at issue:

> *"Originator of the heavens and the earth. When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, 'Be!' and it is."* (Qur'an 2:117)

> *"She said, 'My Lord, how will I have a child when no man has touched me?' He said, 'Thus; God creates what He wills. When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, "Be!" and it is.'"* (Qur'an 3:47)

> *"Truly the likeness of Jesus in the sight of God is as the likeness of Adam. He created him from dust, then said to him, 'Be!' and he was."* (Qur'an 3:59)

> *"His command, when He wills a thing, is only that He says to it, 'Be!' and it is. So glory be to Him in Whose hand is the dominion of all things, and to Him you will be returned."* (Qur'an 36:82–83)

The passage in Yā Sīn is the closest parallel to 16:40, and its context is identical: it follows the objection "Who will give life to bones when they are decayed?" (36:78) and the reply that the One who created them the first time will do so (36:79). The formula *kun fa-yakūn* is the Qur'an's standard answer to the "how" of resurrection.

**Does God Literally Speak the Word?**

The commentators discussed the nature of the "word." Al-Rāzī presents the views. Some understood *kun* literally: God utters a word, in a manner befitting His majesty and unlike human speech, and the thing comes to be. Others understood it as a figure for the immediacy and ease of divine creation: the verse does not describe a literal command addressed to a thing that does not yet exist — which would be paradoxical, since the addressee would have to exist to be addressed — but expresses that creation follows God's will without any delay or difficulty, as instantly as a thing would obey if it could hear "Be!"

Al-Rāzī also raises and answers the paradox of the addressee: if the thing does not yet exist, how can it be commanded? He answers that the thing exists in God's knowledge as a determined object of His will, and the command "Be!" is the transition from His knowledge to its existence. Ibn Kathīr and the mainstream Sunnī tradition affirm the reality of God's speech as an attribute befitting Him, while declining to specify its modality. The practical meaning, on any of these views, is the same: creation is by will, not by process, and therefore nothing is difficult for God.

**"When We Desire It": Will Precedes Word**

The verse specifies *idhā aradnāhu*, "when We will it." Creation begins with the divine will; the word follows; the thing exists. This sequence — will, word, being — excludes randomness. Nothing comes into existence except what God has willed. The Makkans' universe, governed by *al-dahr*, blind time (45:24), is replaced by a universe governed by intention. Every raindrop, every child, every star, and every resurrected body exists because it was willed and commanded.

The verse also excludes the idea of any resistance to God's will. Between "Be!" and "it is" there is no gap in which the thing might refuse or delay. Al-Zamakhsharī notes that the verb *fa-yakūn*, "and it is," follows immediately with the conjunction *fa-*, which indicates direct succession without interval. This is the theology behind verse 1's declaration that God's Command is "coming": what God has willed cannot be prevented, hastened, or delayed by any creature.

**Why the Resurrection Is Easy**

The verse does not argue that the resurrection is possible; it makes the very question of possibility disappear. Human beings judge difficulty by the resources and time required. Rebuilding a decayed body from scattered atoms would require, by human standards, resources and time beyond imagining. But God's creation does not use resources or time. It uses a word. The Qur'an states the consequence directly:

> *"Your creation and your resurrection are only as that of a single soul."* (Qur'an 31:28)

> *"And the matter of the Hour is only as the blinking of an eye, or nearer."* (Qur'an 16:77)

The second of these verses belongs to this very sūrah, and it restates 16:40 in temporal terms. The Hour, which will raise every human being who ever lived, takes no longer than a blink — because it takes only a "Be!"

**The Broader Theology: God's Independence**

The verse teaches a foundational truth about God: He is utterly independent of means. Human beings make things through causes — the farmer needs seed, soil, water, and time; the builder needs stone, tools, and workers. God ordinarily creates *through* causes, as the sūrah has shown at length (rain causes crops, cattle give milk), but He does not *need* them. The causes are His creation too, and He is free to act with them or without them. This is why miracles are possible: the fire did not burn Abraham (21:69), the sea parted for Moses (26:63), and Jesus was born without a father (3:47). Each was a case of "Be!" operating without the usual intermediaries. And the resurrection is the greatest case of all.

**A Reflection on the Word and Human Hope**

There is a personal dimension to this verse that the commentators noted. The believer who faces a situation that seems impossible — a disease that medicine cannot cure, a debt that cannot be paid, a heart that will not soften, a hope that every calculation says is futile — is addressed by this verse. The One to Whom he prays does not operate within the constraints of his calculations. What seems impossible by means is possible by "Be!" This is not an invitation to abandon means; the sūrah has honored means throughout. It is an invitation to remember that means are not the limit. The Qur'an gives the example of Zechariah, who asked for a son in extreme old age and was told, *"Thus; it is easy for Me"* (19:9). Easy — because it required only a word.

The Prophet ﷺ taught the believers to pray with this awareness: *"When one of you supplicates, let him be resolute in his asking, and let him not say 'O God, give me if You will,' for there is none who can compel God"* (al-Bukhārī 6338; Muslim 2679). The believer asks confidently, because he knows that the One asked is not limited by the size of the request. The greatest thing he could ask for and the smallest are equal before "Be!"

**The Verse's Place in the Argument**

Verse 40 completes the sūrah's response to the denial of resurrection. Verse 38 affirmed that the resurrection is a binding promise; verse 39 gave its purpose; verse 40 explains its ease. The Makkans had demanded to know how the dead could rise. The Qur'an's answer is that they were asking the wrong question. The right question is not "how" but "by Whom" — and the One by Whom it is done needs only to say "Be!" Once the reader has grasped this, the resurrection ceases to be a puzzle and becomes what it always was: a certainty awaiting its appointed time.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:41

> **And those who emigrate for the sake of God, after having been wronged, We shall surely settle them in a good place in this world—and the reward of the Hereafter is greater, if they but knew—**

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Turn From Argument to Consolation**

The sūrah has spent forty verses in argument with the Makkan idolaters — refuting their idols, exposing their excuses, warning of their end. Verse 41 turns, for the first time, to the believers directly and speaks of their suffering and their reward. The shift is not arbitrary. Al-Rāzī explains the sequence: once the Makkans had sworn their strongest oaths that there would be no resurrection (v. 38), it was clear that they were beyond persuasion and would persist in persecuting the believers. The logical next step was emigration. Verse 41 therefore addresses those who leave their homes for God's sake and tells them what awaits.

**"Those Who Emigrate for the Sake of God": *Hājarū fī Allāh***

The verb *hājara* comes from the root *h-j-r*, which means to leave, to abandon, to separate from. *Hijrah*, emigration, is the act of leaving one's home for the sake of one's faith. The phrase *fī Allāh*, "in God," "for God," specifies the motive: they did not leave for wealth, safety, or adventure, but for God — to preserve their religion, to worship freely, and to seek His pleasure. Ibn Kathīr and al-Rāzī both stress that the emigration in question is one undertaken "in the way of God and seeking His pleasure"; the same act performed for worldly gain would not earn the promise. The Prophet ﷺ established this principle in the ḥadīth that opens al-Bukhārī's collection:

> *"Actions are but by intentions, and every person shall have only what he intended. So whoever's emigration was to God and His Messenger, his emigration was to God and His Messenger; and whoever's emigration was for some worldly gain or a woman to marry, his emigration was to that for which he emigrated."* (al-Bukhārī 1; Muslim 1907)

The ḥadīth was spoken about *hijrah* specifically, and it shows that the outward act does not by itself earn the reward. The intention is decisive.

**"After Having Been Wronged": *Min Baʿdi Mā Ẓulimū***

The verse specifies that these emigrants left *after having been wronged* — after suffering *ẓulm*, injustice and oppression. The condition is important. Emigration in the Qur'an is not flight from difficulty in general; it is the response of those who have been persecuted for their faith to the point where remaining is no longer possible. The phrase reminds the reader of what the early Muslims endured: the boycott in the valley of Abū Ṭālib, the torture of the weak, the beatings, the confiscations, the murder of Sumayyah, the mother of ʿAmmār — the first martyr of Islam, killed by Abū Jahl.

Which emigration is meant? The commentators identify two possibilities, and both fit.

The first is the emigration to Abyssinia, which took place in the fifth year of the mission, when the Prophet ﷺ advised a group of persecuted believers to seek refuge with the Christian king of Abyssinia, the Negus, "in whose land no one is wronged." Ibn Kathīr notes that this group numbered around eighty and included ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān, his wife Ruqayyah, the Prophet's daughter, and Jaʿfar ibn Abī Ṭālib, whose speech before the Negus is one of the treasures of early Islamic history. Since al-Naḥl is Makkan, this earlier emigration is the most likely immediate reference.

The second is the emigration to Madinah, which the verse may anticipate, since the promise of "a good place in this world" was most fully realized there. Al-Ṭabrisī, al-Wāḥidī, and al-Zamakhsharī mention specific Companions who had been tortured in Makkah and who later emigrated: Bilāl, ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir, Ṣuhayb al-Rūmī, Khabbāb ibn al-Aratt, and Abū Jandal ibn Suhayl. Bilāl was dragged through the streets with a stone on his chest, repeating "One, One." Khabbāb was laid on burning coals until the fat of his back extinguished them. Ṣuhayb gave up his entire wealth to the Quraysh as the price of leaving, and the Prophet said to him, "Ṣuhayb has profited!" These are the people described by "after having been wronged."

**"We Shall Surely Settle Them in a Good Place in This World"**

The first promise is worldly: *la-nubawwiʾannahum fī al-dunyā ḥasanah*, "We will surely settle them in this world in a good [place]." The verb *bawwaʾa* means to give a dwelling, to establish in a place, to settle. The word *ḥasanah*, "good," is left unspecified — a good dwelling, a good situation, a good outcome.

The commentators identify several fulfillments. Ibn Kathīr, al-Jalālayn, al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabarī, and al-Ṭabrisī all name Madinah: the emigrants were given a city that received them with love, where the Anṣār shared their homes and wealth, and which became the capital of the first Islamic state. Others, including Ibn Kathīr and al-Ṭabarī, understand it more broadly as provision and honor in this world. Al-Rāzī and al-Ṭabrisī point to the ultimate victory: within eight years of the emigration to Madinah, the Muslims returned to Makkah as its rulers, and within a generation they governed lands from Egypt to Persia. The emigrants who had left with nothing became the founders of a civilization.

The Qur'an confirms this worldly promise in other verses:

> *"And whoever emigrates in the way of God will find on the earth many a refuge and abundance."* (Qur'an 4:100)

> *"Those who emigrated in the way of God and then were killed or died — God will surely provide for them a good provision."* (Qur'an 22:58)

The Prophet ﷺ himself, in the darkest days of Makkah, promised Khabbāb — who had come to him complaining of the torture — that God would complete this matter until a rider could travel from Ṣanʿāʾ to Ḥaḍramawt fearing none but God (al-Bukhārī 3612). That promise, and 16:41, were fulfilled.

**"And the Reward of the Hereafter Is Greater"**

The second promise is otherworldly: *wa-la-ajru al-ākhirati akbar*, "and the reward of the Hereafter is greater." Whatever the emigrants received in this world — and they received a great deal — the next world holds more. The Qur'an ranks the emigrants at the highest level:

> *"Those who believed and emigrated and strove in the way of God with their wealth and their lives are greater in rank in the sight of God, and it is they who are the triumphant."* (Qur'an 9:20)

> *"So those who emigrated and were driven from their homes and were harmed in My way and fought and were killed — I will surely remove from them their misdeeds and admit them to Gardens beneath which rivers flow."* (Qur'an 3:195)

The Prophet ﷺ told his Companions that the emigrants would enter Paradise before the rest of the community. The worldly "good place" was Madinah; the otherworldly reward is the Garden, and the verse insists on the comparison: *akbar*, greater. The believer who has been compensated in this world for his sacrifice should not think the account is closed.

**"If They But Knew"**

The verse ends with a conditional that has been read in two ways, both preserved by al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabrisī, and al-Zamakhsharī.

On the first reading, "they" refers to the disbelievers: if the Makkans knew what the emigrants would receive in both worlds, they would have accepted the religion themselves rather than persecuting those who did. The verse thus contains a hidden invitation to the persecutors.

On the second reading, "they" refers to the emigrants themselves: if they fully knew the greatness of what awaits them, their joy would be greater, their striving more intense, and their patience easier. This reading is consoling. The emigrant who has lost his home, his wealth, and perhaps his family cannot fully see what he has gained; the verse tells him that if he could see it, his loss would appear as nothing. The Prophet ﷺ said:

> *"The place of a whip in Paradise is better than the world and all that is in it."* (al-Bukhārī 3250)

If a hand's breadth of Paradise outweighs the entire world, then the emigrant who traded his house in Makkah for a place in the Garden made the greatest bargain in history — "if he but knew."

**Emigration as a Permanent Principle**

Although the verse addresses a historical event, the commentators recognized that its principle endures. Ibn ʿAjībah extends it to all who set out on the path to God, leaving behind what hinders them. The Prophet ﷺ himself extended the concept:

> *"The emigrant (muhājir) is the one who abandons what God has forbidden."* (al-Bukhārī 10)

On this understanding, every believer is called to a *hijrah*: from sin to obedience, from heedlessness to remembrance, from the company that corrupts to the company that strengthens. The physical emigration from Makkah ended with the conquest — the Prophet said, "There is no emigration after the conquest, but there is striving and intention" (al-Bukhārī 2783) — but the inner emigration never ends. And the promise attached to it never ends either: a good state in this world — the peace, dignity, and contentment that follow from leaving what harms — and a greater reward in the next.

**The Verse for the Displaced**

Finally, the verse has a specific resonance for those in every age who are driven from their homes for their faith. The refugee who has lost everything for the sake of his religion stands exactly where Bilāl, Khabbāb, and Ṣuhayb stood. The verse is addressed to him: God will settle him in a good place in this world — perhaps not the one he expected, but one that God has prepared — and the reward of the Hereafter is greater. He is not forgotten; he is among those whom the Qur'an names first when it turns from argument to promise. And the believers who receive him inherit the role of the Anṣār, whose welcome of the emigrants earned them a praise in the Qur'an that has never faded: *"They love those who emigrated to them and find in their breasts no need for what they were given, and prefer them over themselves even though they are in need"* (59:9).

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:42

> **those who are patient and trust in their Lord.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Inner Qualities Behind the Outward Act**

Verse 41 described the emigrants by what they did: they left their homes for God after being wronged. Verse 42 describes them by what they were: *alladhīna ṣabarū wa-ʿalā rabbihim yatawakkalūn*, "those who were patient and who rely upon their Lord." The verse is short — five Arabic words — but it names the two virtues that made the emigration possible and that made it acceptable. Without patience, the emigrants could not have endured the persecution that preceded departure or the hardship that followed it. Without trust in God, they could not have stepped into the unknown, leaving security behind. Al-Zamakhsharī identifies the referent as the emigrants who endured suffering and separation from their homeland; the verse tells us what sustained them.

**Patience: *Ṣabr***

The word *ṣabr* comes from a root meaning to restrain, to hold back, to bind. The classical definition is the restraining of the soul from panic, the tongue from complaint, and the limbs from acts of despair. It is not passive resignation; it is active endurance — holding one's ground under pressure without abandoning what one knows to be right. The Arabs called a bitter desert plant *ṣabir* (aloe) because of its bitterness, and there is a sense in which *ṣabr* is the willingness to swallow what is bitter for the sake of what is good.

The scholars distinguished three kinds of *ṣabr*, and the emigrants practiced all three. There is patience in obedience — persisting in prayer, in truthfulness, in the profession of faith when each of these brought punishment. There is patience against disobedience — refusing to recant, refusing to worship the idols even under torture, as Bilāl refused with "One, One." And there is patience under affliction — bearing the loss of home, wealth, family, and safety without turning against God.

The Qur'an places patience at the center of the believer's life:

> *"O you who believe, seek help through patience and prayer. Truly God is with the patient."* (Qur'an 2:153)

> *"And We will surely test you with something of fear and hunger and loss of wealth and lives and fruits — but give glad tidings to the patient, who, when disaster strikes them, say, 'Truly we belong to God, and truly to Him we return.'"* (Qur'an 2:155–156)

> *"Only the patient will be given their reward without measure."* (Qur'an 39:10)

The last verse is remarkable: every reward in the Qur'an is measured — tenfold, seven hundredfold — except the reward of patience, which is "without measure." The emigrants, whose reward verse 41 called "greater," are here identified as the patient, whose reward has no ceiling.

The Prophet ﷺ described patience as the greatest gift a person can be given:

> *"No one has been given a gift better and more comprehensive than patience."* (al-Bukhārī 1469; Muslim 1053)

And he described the believer's condition in terms of it:

> *"Wondrous is the affair of the believer, for all of it is good, and that is for no one but the believer: if something pleasing befalls him, he is grateful, and that is good for him; and if something harmful befalls him, he is patient, and that is good for him."* (Muslim 2999)

**Trust in God: *Tawakkul***

The second quality is *tawakkul*, from the root *w-k-l*, which means to entrust a matter to another, to appoint an agent (*wakīl*) to act on one's behalf. *Tawakkul ʿalā Allāh* is entrusting one's affairs to God — relying on Him for the outcome after doing what is within one's power. The verse's phrasing is emphatic: *ʿalā rabbihim yatawakkalūn*, with "upon their Lord" placed before the verb, which in Arabic gives the sense of exclusivity — upon their Lord *alone* they rely. The emigrants did not rely on the Negus, on their allies, or on their own strength; they relied on God.

The Qur'an makes *tawakkul* the disposition of the believer in every uncertainty:

> *"And whoever relies upon God — He is sufficient for him. Truly God accomplishes His purpose."* (Qur'an 65:3)

> *"And upon God let the believers rely."* (Qur'an 3:122, 160; 5:11; 9:51; 14:11)

> *"So when you have decided, then rely upon God. Truly God loves those who rely upon Him."* (Qur'an 3:159)

The last verse contains a crucial qualification: "when you have decided" — *tawakkul* comes after deliberation and action, not instead of them. The Prophet ﷺ clarified this with a Bedouin who asked whether he should tie his camel or trust in God. He replied:

> *"Tie it, and trust in God."* (al-Tirmidhī 2517)

The emigrants tied their camels: they planned their departure, chose their destination, gathered what provisions they could. And then they trusted God for what planning could not secure. The Prophet's own emigration to Madinah is the model — he arranged a guide, a hiding place, a supply of food, and a decoy in his bed, and then, in the cave with Abū Bakr and the pursuers at its mouth, he said: *"Do not grieve; truly God is with us"* (9:40). Preparation and trust were not in tension; they were two halves of one act.

**Why These Two Virtues Together?**

The pairing of *ṣabr* and *tawakkul* is not accidental, and al-Rāzī offers a profound analysis of their relationship. Patience, he says, is the effort to subdue the ego — to restrain the self from its impulses to complain, to flee, to give up, to strike back. Trust in God is the state reached when the self has severed its attachment to worldly things and devoted itself entirely to God. Patience is therefore the beginning of the spiritual path, and trust is its end. One begins by struggling to endure; one arrives at a state in which endurance is no longer a struggle, because one has handed the matter over to God and rests in that handing-over.

The two also answer to two dimensions of the emigrant's situation. Patience addresses the past and present: what has been suffered and what is being suffered now. Trust addresses the future: what will happen next, where one will live, how one will eat, whether one will ever return. The emigrant needed both — to bear what was behind him and to face what was before him. The believer in any trial needs both as well.

**The Psychological Reality of the Verse**

Modern psychology has rediscovered, under other names, the two qualities the verse names. What the verse calls patience corresponds to what is now studied as resilience — the capacity to endure adversity without breaking. What the verse calls trust corresponds to what is studied as the reduction of anxiety through the acceptance of what one cannot control. The Qur'an's teaching, however, differs from secular versions in one decisive respect: it grounds both qualities in a relationship. The believer is patient not because endurance is admirable in the abstract but because "God is with the patient" (2:153). He trusts not because worry is unproductive but because the One he trusts is his *Rabb*, his Lord and Caretaker, Who "accomplishes His purpose" (65:3). Patience without a Companion is mere stoicism; trust without a Trustee is mere resignation. The verse's *ʿalā rabbihim*, "upon their Lord," is what transforms both into worship.

**The Verse as a Description of the Path**

The commentators saw in this verse a description of the whole journey of the soul. The believer's life is an emigration — from the world toward God — and its two provisions are the ones named here. Every day brings occasions for patience: an insult borne, a temptation resisted, a loss accepted. Every day brings occasions for trust: a decision made without certainty, a need placed before God, an outcome released. The person who cultivates both is, in the Qur'an's terms, an emigrant on the way to "a good place in this world" and a "greater reward" in the next, whether or not he ever leaves his physical home.

**A Practical Word**

The emigrants of Makkah did not choose their trial; it was forced on them by persecution. But they chose their response, and the verse records the response that earned the promise. For the reader who faces a trial he did not choose — illness, loss, injustice, displacement — the verse offers the same two instruments and the same promise. Be patient: hold your ground, restrain complaint, refuse despair. Trust your Lord: do what is in your power and hand the rest to Him. And know that the reward for doing so is the one the Qur'an reserves for the patient alone: *bi-ghayri ḥisāb*, without measure.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:43

> **We sent no messengers before thee, save men unto whom We revealed—ask the people of the Reminder, if you know not—**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Objection Behind the Verse**

The Makkans raised many objections to the Prophet ﷺ, but one of the most persistent was to his humanity. How could a man — one who ate food, walked in the markets, had a wife and children, and grew tired — be God's messenger? If God wished to send a message, surely He would send an angel, or at least a man of visible grandeur. The Qur'an records this objection in many forms:

> *"And they say, 'What is this messenger who eats food and walks in the markets? Why was an angel not sent down to him to be a warner with him?'"* (Qur'an 25:7)

> *"Is it a wonder to people that We revealed to a man from among them?"* (Qur'an 10:2)
