> *"They said, 'You are only a human being like us.'"* (Qur'an 14:10; 26:154, 186; 36:15)

Verse 43 answers with history. *Wa-mā arsalnā min qablika illā rijālan nūḥī ilayhim*, "And We did not send before you except men to whom We revealed." Every messenger God has ever sent was a human being. Noah, Abraham, Moses, Jesus — men, all of them, who ate and slept and died. The Prophet ﷺ was not an anomaly; he was the latest in an unbroken line. The verse's *illā*, "except," excludes every other possibility: not angels, not jinn, not beings of some intermediate nature — only men.

**Why Men and Not Angels?**

The Qur'an gives the reason elsewhere, and it is a reason of mercy and of logic. Human beings cannot receive an angel in his true form; the encounter would overwhelm them. And even if an angel were sent, he would have to take human form to be perceived, which would reintroduce the very objection:

> *"And if We had made him an angel, We would have made him a man, and We would have confused them with that which they confuse themselves."* (Qur'an 6:9)

> *"Say: If there were on earth angels walking securely, We would have sent down to them from heaven an angel as a messenger."* (Qur'an 17:95)

The second verse states the principle: a messenger must be of the same kind as those he is sent to. Angels would be sent to angels; men are sent to men. There is a deeper wisdom as well. A human messenger can be a model. He shows that the commands are livable — that a being with human weaknesses, appetites, and sorrows can nonetheless pray, fast, forgive, endure, and love God. An angel could deliver the law but could not demonstrate it. The Qur'an calls the Prophet *"a beautiful example"* (33:21) precisely because he was a man. His humanity was not a defect in his messengership; it was essential to it.

**"Unto Whom We Revealed": The Mark of the Messenger**

What distinguished these men from other men was not their nature but what happened to them: *nūḥī ilayhim*, "We revealed to them." The verb *awḥā* denotes the communication of revelation — the same word used in verse 2 for the sending of the Spirit and later in verse 68 for God's "revealing" to the bee. The prophets were ordinary in their humanity and extraordinary in their reception of the divine word. Al-Zamakhsharī notes that the revelation came through the medium of angels: the angel was the bearer, the man was the recipient. Al-Rāzī adds that when the angel appeared to the prophet, he appeared in human form — as Gabriel appeared to Mary "as a perfect man" (19:17) and to the Prophet in the form of Diḥyah al-Kalbī. Even the angelic bearer of revelation accommodated himself to human perception.

**"Men": The Word *Rijāl***

The word *rijāl*, "men," raised a question that the commentators addressed. Does it mean "human beings" as opposed to angels, or "males" as opposed to females? Most commentators, including Ibn Kathīr, al-Qurṭubī, and al-Ṭabrisī, understood the primary sense as human as opposed to angelic, since that is the objection the verse answers. Al-Rāzī, however, notes that the word can also carry its gender-specific meaning and that the verse may indicate that God sends men, not women, as prophets. This became the majority position among the scholars regarding *nubuwwah*, prophethood, though some — notably Ibn Ḥazm and al-Qurṭubī in one discussion — held that Mary, the mother of Jesus, and the mother of Moses received a form of divine communication that could be called prophethood, since God "revealed" to the mother of Moses (28:7) and sent an angel to Mary (19:17–19). The question is discussed in the commentaries on Sūrah Maryam. What the verse under discussion establishes without dispute is that messengers were human, and that this humanity is no argument against the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ.

**"Ask the People of the Reminder, If You Know Not"**

The verse then does something characteristic of the Qur'an: it invites verification. *Fa-sʾalū ahla al-dhikri in kuntum lā taʿlamūn*, "so ask the people of the Reminder if you do not know." If the Makkans doubted that earlier messengers were men, they were told to consult those who had knowledge of earlier messengers.

Who are "the people of the Reminder"? The commentators offer several answers, and the breadth of the phrase allows all of them.

The most common identification, held by al-Qurṭubī, al-Ṭabarī, al-Ṭabrisī, and al-Zamakhsharī, is the People of the Book — Jews and Christians — who possessed the scriptures recording the history of the prophets. *Al-Dhikr*, "the Reminder," is used in the Qur'an for the Torah (21:105), and the People of the Book knew that Moses, David, and Jesus were men. Even the Makkan idolaters respected their knowledge of ancient history, and the verse directs them to it. This is a striking move: the Qur'an appeals to the testimony of Jews and Christians against the idolaters, confident that on this point their scriptures agree with it.

A second identification, noted by al-Rāzī and al-Ṭabrisī, is those among the Arabs who were knowledgeable about the histories of earlier peoples, whether believers or not.

A third, held by al-Qurṭubī, al-Ṭabarī, and others, is those knowledgeable in the Qur'an itself, since the Qur'an is also called *al-Dhikr* (15:9; 16:44). On this reading, the verse is telling the doubters to ask those who know the Qur'an about what it says regarding earlier messengers.

A fourth, and the most general, is all people of knowledge — anyone who possesses the relevant learning.

The Shīʿī tradition, as al-Ṭabrisī records, identifies the people of the Reminder as the Imams of the Prophet's household, on the ground that the Prophet is himself called *dhikr* (65:10–11) and his family are therefore "the people of the *dhikr*." Ibn Kathīr, a Sunnī commentator, notes this interpretation and observes that while the family of the Prophet are indeed among the people of knowledge, the verse's primary reference is to the People of the Book in the context of the Makkan debate.

**The Principle Established: Asking the Knowledgeable**

Beyond its immediate context, the verse established a principle that became foundational in Islamic law and life: *fa-sʾalū ahla al-dhikri in kuntum lā taʿlamūn* — when you do not know, ask those who do. The jurists derived from it the obligation of the layperson to consult the scholar, and the legitimacy of following (*taqlīd*) a qualified authority in matters one cannot investigate oneself. Al-Rāzī reports that some who opposed analogical reasoning (*qiyās*) used the verse to argue that a jurist facing a new question should consult a more knowledgeable jurist rather than reason for himself; he rejects this narrow application, since *qiyās* was practiced by the Companions themselves, but affirms the general principle.

The verse thus carries a humility and a discipline. The humility: no one knows everything, and the honest person admits what he does not know. The discipline: ignorance is not a resting place; it is to be remedied by asking. The Prophet ﷺ said, about people who gave a ruling in ignorance and caused a man's death:

> *"They killed him, may God kill them! Why did they not ask when they did not know? Truly the cure for ignorance is asking."* (Abū Dāwūd 336)

"The cure for ignorance is asking" — *innamā shifāʾu al-ʿiyyi al-suʾāl* — is the ḥadīth's summary of this verse.

**The Confidence of the Verse**

There is a remarkable confidence in the Qur'an's invitation to ask others. A message that feared scrutiny would not send its doubters to consult its rivals. The Qur'an sends the Makkans to the Jews and Christians, sure that on the question of the humanity of the prophets, the scriptures will confirm what it says. This confidence appears throughout the Qur'an — in its challenges to produce a chapter like it (2:23), in its invitation to journey and see (16:36), in its command to reflect (16:17). The Qur'an does not ask for belief in the dark; it asks for belief after inquiry, and it points the inquirer toward the evidence.

**The Application for the Reader**

The verse teaches the believer two things about knowledge. First, that revelation came through human beings, and that the Prophet's humanity is a gift, not a difficulty: he showed what a human life devoted to God looks like, in every detail from the way he ate to the way he grieved. Second, that the path to knowledge runs through asking. The believer who does not know a ruling asks a scholar; the believer who does not understand a verse consults the commentaries; the believer who is confused about history reads those who know it. And the believer who is himself among "the people of the Reminder" bears the corresponding duty: to answer honestly when asked, and to make himself available to those who do not know. The verse describes a community in which knowledge flows from those who have it to those who seek it, and in which no one is ashamed to say, "I do not know — let me ask."

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:44

> **clear proofs and scriptures. And We have sent down the Reminder unto thee that thou mightest clarify for mankind that which has been sent down unto them, that haply they may reflect.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Completing the Sentence About the Messengers**

Verse 43 stated that God sent only men as messengers and told the doubters to ask the people of the Reminder. Verse 44 completes the thought by naming what those men were sent with: *bi'l-bayyināti wa'l-zubur*, "with clear proofs and scriptures." The messengers were human, but what they carried was not. Their humanity was matched by the divinity of their message and confirmed by the evidence that accompanied it.

**"Clear Proofs": *Al-Bayyināt***

The word *bayyināt* is the plural of *bayyinah*, from the root *b-y-n* that verse 39 discussed — clarity, distinctness, evidence that makes something manifest. In the Qur'an the word designates the proofs that accompanied each messenger, and the commentators identify two dimensions of it.

The first is the miracles — the *muʿjizāt* — by which God confirmed the truthfulness of His messengers. Al-Rāzī gives this as a primary sense, citing 2:87 and 2:92, where the word refers to the miracles of Jesus and Moses respectively: the staff, the white hand, the parting of the sea; the healing of the blind and the leper, the raising of the dead. Each messenger was given signs suited to his people. The Prophet ﷺ said:

> *"There was no prophet but that he was given signs such that people believed on account of them. What I have been given is a revelation that God revealed to me, so I hope to have the most followers among them on the Day of Resurrection."* (al-Bukhārī 4981; Muslim 152)

The Prophet's greatest *bayyinah* was the Qur'an itself — a miracle of speech that outlasts the moment of its performance and can be examined by every generation.

The second dimension of *bayyināt* is broader: any clear demonstration of the truth of the guidance conveyed — the proofs, arguments, and evidences contained in the message. The Qur'an describes itself as containing *"clear proofs of guidance"* (2:185). On this reading, the messengers brought not only wonders but reasons: arguments from creation, from history, from the moral sense — the very arguments this sūrah has been making since its third verse.

**"Scriptures": *Al-Zubur***

The word *zubur* is the plural of *zabūr*, from a root meaning to write or inscribe. In the Qur'an, *al-Zabūr* in the singular designates the scripture given to David — the Psalms (4:163; 17:55; 21:105) — while the plural *zubur* denotes revealed books in general (3:184; 23:53; 26:196; 35:25; 54:43, 52). Al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī, the great lexicographer of the Qur'an, observed that *zabūr* denotes a scripture containing wisdom and exhortation rather than legal prescription — which fits the Psalms — while *kitāb* denotes a book with laws. The pairing of *bayyināt* and *zubur* in this verse and in 3:184 and 35:25 thus describes the messengers' full equipment: proofs to establish their truth and scriptures to convey their teaching.

**"And We Have Sent Down the Reminder Unto Thee"**

The verse now turns from the earlier messengers to the Prophet ﷺ: *wa-anzalnā ilayka al-dhikr*, "and We have sent down to you the Reminder." *Al-Dhikr*, here, is the Qur'an, as al-Qurṭubī and al-Ṭabrisī specify. The word itself is instructive. The Qur'an is called a Reminder — not a novelty, not a new philosophy, but a *reminder* of what human beings already know in the depths of their nature and have forgotten. Its message is the primordial one: there is one God, worship Him, and avoid what exceeds its bounds (v. 36). The Qur'an reminds; it does not invent.

The word also connects to the sūrah's repeated call to *tadhakkur*, reflection or remembrance (vv. 13, 17). The Reminder is sent to awaken remembrance. The Qur'an states the same purpose elsewhere: *"This is only a reminder to the worlds"* (38:87; 81:27), and God promises to preserve it as such: *"Truly We sent down the Reminder, and truly We are its Guardian"* (15:9).

**The Prophet's Task: *Li-tubayyina li'l-nāsi mā nuzzila ilayhim***

The verse then states why the Reminder was sent to the Prophet: *li-tubayyina li'l-nāsi mā nuzzila ilayhim*, "that you may make clear to the people what has been sent down to them." This clause is one of the most consequential in the Qur'an for understanding the role of the Prophet ﷺ and the status of his Sunnah.

Notice the structure. The Qur'an was "sent down to the Prophet" (*ilayka*) and also "sent down to the people" (*ilayhim*). It is addressed to all. But the Prophet has a distinct function: to *make it clear*, *tubayyina*. The Qur'an is not merely to be recited to the people; it is to be explained, demonstrated, and applied by the one to whom it was first given. Al-Ṭabrisī explains the content of this clarification: the laws, the rulings, and the proofs of God's oneness. The Prophet clarified the Qur'an in three ways, which the scholars of *uṣūl* have detailed.

He clarified it by his words, explaining what a verse meant when its meaning was not evident — as when he was asked about the "wrong" (*ẓulm*) in 6:82 and explained that it meant *shirk*, citing 31:13 (al-Bukhārī 32).

He clarified it by his actions, showing how a general command was to be performed — the Qur'an commands prayer but does not detail its postures and times; the Prophet said, *"Pray as you have seen me pray"* (al-Bukhārī 631). The Qur'an commands pilgrimage; he said, *"Take your rites from me"* (Muslim 1297).

He clarified it by his approval and silence, confirming or correcting the Companions' understanding as they applied the revelation in their lives.

From this verse the scholars derived the principle that the Sunnah is the authoritative explanation of the Qur'an — that the two cannot be separated, and that the person who claims to follow the Qur'an while rejecting the Prophet's clarification of it has rejected the very function the Qur'an assigns him. The Qur'an confirms this elsewhere: *"Whatever the Messenger gives you, take it; and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it"* (59:7), and *"Obey God and obey the Messenger"* (4:59; 5:92; 24:54; 47:33; 64:12). The Prophet himself said:

> *"Truly I have been given the Book and something like it along with it."* (Abū Dāwūd 4604; Aḥmad 17174)

The "something like it" is the Sunnah, which explains the Book.

**Why the Message Needs a Human Explainer**

The verse's assignment of a clarifying role to the Prophet answers, at a deeper level, the objection of verse 43. The Makkans asked why a man was sent. The verse replies: because a man is needed to clarify. A book delivered without a teacher is subject to endless misreading. Every scripture in history that was cut off from its authoritative interpretation fragmented into competing sects. The Qur'an came with its interpreter built in — a living human being who showed, for twenty-three years, what every verse meant in practice. This is why his humanity was essential: an angel could not have modeled how a human father treats his daughter, how a human ruler treats a defeated enemy, how a human being prays when exhausted or forgives when wronged. The clarification the verse describes was not a lecture; it was a life.

**"That Haply They May Reflect"**

The verse ends: *wa-laʿallahum yatafakkarūn*, "and that perhaps they may reflect." The purpose of the clarification is not merely that people receive correct information, but that they *think*. The Prophet's explanation of the Qur'an was meant to provoke reflection, not to replace it. Al-Ṭabrisī and al-Zamakhsharī draw from this phrase a theological conclusion: God's expressed purpose in sending the Reminder and its explainer is that *all* people should reflect and come to know the truth. This indicates a divine desire for the guidance of all, which stands alongside the verses that speak of God's not compelling guidance (16:9, 93). God wills, in the sense of desiring and commanding, that everyone reflect and believe; He does not will, in the sense of compelling, that they do so. The invitation is universal; the response is free.

**The Reader's Share in the Verse**

The verse describes a chain: God sends the Reminder; the Prophet clarifies it; the people reflect. The reader stands at the end of this chain, and the verse asks something of him. He is to receive the Qur'an not as a text to be admired from a distance but as something "sent down to *him*" (*ilayhim* includes every reader). He is to receive it together with its clarification — the Sunnah, and the tradition of understanding built on it — rather than reinventing its meaning from scratch. And he is to *reflect*: to think about what it says, why it says it, and what it asks of him. The three verbs of the passage — *nazzala* (sent down), *bayyana* (made clear), *tafakkara* (reflected) — describe the whole relationship between God, the Prophet, and the believer. The first two have been done. The third is the reader's task.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:45

> **Do those who have plotted evil deeds feel secure that God will not cause the earth to engulf them, or that the punishment will not come upon them whence they are not aware?**

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Question Addressed to the Feeling of Safety**

The sūrah has warned of the Hereafter at length. It now turns, in verses 45 through 47, to the danger that lies nearer: punishment in this world, arriving without warning. The verses are framed as questions, and the questions all target a single psychological state — *amn*, the feeling of security. *A-fa-amina alladhīna makarū al-sayyiʾāti*, "Do those who plot evil deeds feel secure...?" The question exposes an assumption the plotters had not examined: that because nothing had happened to them yet, nothing would.

**"Those Who Have Plotted Evil Deeds": The Target**

The phrase *alladhīna makarū al-sayyiʾāt* recalls verse 26, where "those before them plotted" and their building collapsed upon them. Here the plotters are the Makkans themselves. Al-Rāzī identifies them as the idolaters who schemed against the Prophet ﷺ and the believers by hidden means — the secret councils, the plans to imprison, expel, or kill the Prophet (8:30), the persecution of those too weak to resist. Al-Qurṭubī extends the reference to all who work to undermine the religion by stratagem.

The word *makara*, as discussed at verse 26, denotes hidden scheming — planning harm behind a mask. The plotter's whole method depends on concealment, and his sense of security depends on believing that his concealment succeeds. Verses 19 and 23 already established that God knows what is hidden. Verse 45 draws the consequence: the one whose plots are known to God has no ground for security.

**The First Danger: The Earth Engulfing Them**

*An yakhsifa Allāhu bihimu al-arḍ*, "that God should cause the earth to swallow them." The verb *khasafa* describes the earth's sinking, collapsing, or opening to swallow what is upon it. The Qur'an uses it for the fate of Qārūn (Korah), the wealthy tyrant of the time of Moses who boasted that his riches were the fruit of his own knowledge:

> *"So We caused the earth to swallow him and his home. And there was for him no company to help him apart from God, nor was he of those who could defend themselves."* (Qur'an 28:81)

Al-Qurṭubī and al-Rāzī note that this fate was literal in Qārūn's case and remains a real possibility. The Prophet ﷺ described a future in which such swallowings would recur, and he described a man swallowed by the earth for arrogance:

> *"While a man was walking in a garment, admiring himself, with his hair combed, strutting in his gait, God caused the earth to swallow him, and he will continue sinking into it until the Day of Resurrection."* (al-Bukhārī 5789; Muslim 2088)

Al-Qurṭubī also allows a broader sense: that God might cause them to vanish from the earth — remove them utterly, as though the ground had taken them.

The image is chosen with precision. The plotters trusted the ground beneath them — their city, their position, their established order. The verse asks whether they are sure that the very ground is secure. What seems most solid — the earth itself — is held in place only by God's decree (v. 15, "lest it shake beneath you"), and He can withdraw it.

**The Second Danger: Punishment From an Unexpected Direction**

*Aw yaʾtiyahumu al-ʿadhābu min ḥaythu lā yashʿurūn*, "or that the punishment should come upon them from where they do not perceive." This is the same phrase used in verse 26 of the ancient plotters, and it describes the characteristic mode of divine judgment: it arrives from the side one is not guarding. Al-Qurṭubī and al-Rāzī connect it to the fate of the people of Lot, who were overturned in the night while asleep, and al-Qurṭubī reads it as a foretelling of Badr — where the Makkan chiefs marched out expecting an easy victory over a small band and were destroyed by it.

The phrase exposes the fundamental weakness of every plot. The plotter plans against the dangers he can foresee. He cannot plan against the dangers he cannot foresee, and those are precisely the ones God sends. Abū Jahl, marching to Badr with a thousand men, feared nothing from three hundred; he did not perceive that the punishment would come through them. The verb *yashʿurūn*, "they perceive," is the same used of the idols in verse 21 — those who worshipped the unperceiving were themselves unperceiving of what was coming.

**Parallel Passages: The Series of Questions**

The Qur'an poses this set of questions in several places, and the parallels illuminate the structure:

> *"Do the people of the towns feel secure that Our punishment will not come to them at night while they sleep? Or do the people of the towns feel secure that Our punishment will not come to them in the morning while they play? Do they feel secure from the plan of God? None feels secure from the plan of God except the losing people."* (Qur'an 7:97–99)

> *"Do you feel secure that He Who is in heaven will not cause the earth to swallow you, and then it should shake? Or do you feel secure that He Who is in heaven will not send against you a storm of stones? Then you will know how was My warning."* (Qur'an 67:16–17)

> *"Do you feel secure that He will not cause a side of the land to swallow you or send against you a storm of stones? Then you would not find for yourselves a guardian."* (Qur'an 17:68)

The verse in al-Aʿrāf gives the conclusion the others imply: *"None feels secure from the plan of God except the losing people."* False security is not a neutral state; it is the mark of those who will lose.

**Why False Security Is the Root of Persistence in Sin**

The verse's psychological insight is that people persist in wrongdoing not because they have weighed the consequences and accepted them, but because they have stopped believing the consequences will come. Every day that passes without punishment reinforces the belief. The Qur'an describes this mechanism:

> *"And when a wave covers them like canopies, they call upon God, sincere to Him in religion. But when He delivers them to the land, some of them are moderate."* (Qur'an 31:32)

At sea, in the storm, the feeling of security vanishes and the heart turns to God. On land, with the ground steady underfoot, the security returns and the heart forgets. The verse under discussion is designed to disturb the security of those on land — to make them feel, before the storm, what they would feel in it.

The Prophet ﷺ taught his community to guard against this false security with a specific supplication:

> *"O God, I seek refuge in You from the withdrawal of Your blessing, the change of Your protection, the suddenness of Your punishment, and all Your displeasure."* (Muslim 2739)

"The suddenness of Your punishment" — *fujāʾati niqmatik* — is precisely the danger of 16:45.

**The Balance: Fear Without Despair**

The Islamic tradition insisted that the believer live between two states: *khawf*, fear, and *rajāʾ*, hope. The verse addresses the first. But it must be read with the verses that address the second, and the sūrah itself provides them: verse 47 will end this very passage by describing God as "Kind, Merciful," and verse 61 will describe His reprieve of sinners. The believer does not live in terror of the ground opening; he lives in *awareness* that it could, and that his safety is God's gift rather than his right. This awareness is *taqwā* in its practical form — the alertness of the traveler who knows the road has dangers and walks accordingly, neither paralyzed nor careless.

The scholars said that the believer should be like a bird with two wings, fear and hope, and that when death approaches, hope should predominate. In health and strength, however, the fear of 16:45 should be present enough to prevent the false security that lets sin become habit.

**The Application to the Present**

The verse's questions apply to every person and every society that plots evil while feeling secure. The corrupt official who has never been caught; the oppressor whose victims have no recourse; the individual who sins in private and has never suffered for it — each is asked: do you feel secure? The ground you stand on is not yours. The direction you are not watching is the one from which the reckoning comes. Modern experience confirms the verse's realism: empires that seemed permanent collapsed within years; fortunes built over decades vanished in days; men who controlled nations were, in the end, controlled by nothing. The verse does not predict when the earth will engulf or the punishment will arrive. It asks only whether one is *sure* that it will not — and the honest answer, for anyone, is no.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:46

> **Or that He will not seize them in the midst of their going to and fro, and they will be powerless to thwart [it]?**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Second Question in the Series**

Verse 45 asked whether the plotters felt secure from the earth swallowing them or from punishment arriving from an unforeseen direction. Verse 46 continues the interrogation with a third possibility: *aw yaʾkhudhahum fī taqallubihim*, "or that He should seize them in the midst of their movement." The series is building a picture of comprehensive exposure. There is no place where the plotter is safe — not in the ground beneath him, not from the direction he is not watching, and now, not in the ordinary activity of his daily life.

**"In the Midst of Their Going To and Fro": *Fī Taqallubihim***

The word *taqallub* comes from the root *q-l-b*, which means to turn, to turn over, to move about — the same root that gives *qalb*, the heart, so called because it is constantly turning. *Taqallub* is the restless movement of human activity: coming and going, traveling and returning, buying and selling, working and resting. The Qur'an uses the word for the disbelievers' bustling in the land — *"Let not the movement (taqallub) of those who disbelieve throughout the land deceive you"* (3:196) — and for the turning of people in their affairs.

The commentators unpacked the phrase's range. Al-Qurṭubī and al-Rāzī take it first as travel: the punishment may seize them while they are on the road, on their journeys to Syria and Yemen, far from home and unprepared. Al-Qurṭubī adds broader senses: wherever they may be, in whatever they are doing, by night or by day. The point is that the punishment does not wait for a convenient moment or a fixed location. It may come while the person is in the middle of his business, thinking of nothing but the transaction before him.

**The Suddenness of Judgment in the Midst of Life**

The verse describes the mode of judgment that the Qur'an calls *baghtah*, suddenness — arriving while people are occupied with the ordinary. The Qur'an returns to this theme repeatedly:

> *"It will not come upon you except suddenly."* (Qur'an 7:187)

> *"Until, when they rejoiced in what they were given, We seized them suddenly, and at once they were in despair."* (Qur'an 6:44)

> *"And they will not await except one blast; it will seize them while they are disputing. And they will not be able to make a bequest, nor return to their people."* (Qur'an 36:49–50)

The passage from Yā Sīn is the clearest picture of what 16:46 describes: the blast comes while they are *disputing* — in the middle of an argument, an ordinary quarrel — and there is no time even to make a will. The Prophet ﷺ described the Hour arriving in exactly this manner:

> *"The Hour will come while two men have spread out their cloth between them and they will not have completed the sale or folded it up. And the Hour will come while a man has milked his camel and taken the milk away, and he will not have drunk it. And the Hour will come while a man is repairing his watering trough, and he will not have watered from it. And the Hour will come while a man has raised his morsel to his mouth, and he will not have eaten it."* (al-Bukhārī 6506; Muslim 2954)

Each image is *taqallub*: a sale, a milking, a repair, a meal. The judgment falls not on people engaged in extraordinary wickedness but on people engaged in the ordinary, who assumed the ordinary would continue.

**"And They Will Be Powerless to Thwart It": *Fa-mā hum bi-muʿjizīn***

The verse ends: *fa-mā hum bi-muʿjizīn*, "and they cannot frustrate [it]" — literally, "they are not ones who can render [God] incapable." The verb *aʿjaza* means to make something unable, to escape it, to defeat it. The Qur'an uses this word repeatedly of the impossibility of escaping God: *"You cannot frustrate God on earth or in heaven"* (29:22), *"They will not frustrate [Him]"* (8:59), *"He is not one to be frustrated"* (35:44).

The word answers the plotters' implicit calculation. Plotters plan on the assumption that they can evade consequences — that their cleverness, their resources, or their position will allow them to escape. The verse denies this at the root. When God seizes, there is no evasion, because evasion would require power over God, and no creature has that. Al-Zamakhsharī notes that the negation is emphatic: *mā hum bi-muʿjizīn* uses the strengthening *bi-*, asserting that they have not the slightest capacity to thwart what comes.

**The Logic of the Verse: Preparedness Cannot Be Postponed**

The verse teaches a lesson that human beings resist: there is no "later" that can be relied upon. The plotter thinks, "I will repent when I am old," or "I will set things right after this deal closes," or "I will address my affairs when things settle down." The verse says that the seizure may come *in the midst* — during the deal, before things settle, while one is still young and busy. The postponement itself is the danger, because it rests on an assumption of time that no one has been given.

The Prophet ﷺ pressed this lesson on his Companions. Ibn ʿUmar reported that the Prophet took him by the shoulder and said:

> *"Be in this world as though you were a stranger or a traveler on the road."* And Ibn ʿUmar used to say: *"When you reach the evening, do not expect the morning; and when you reach the morning, do not expect the evening. Take from your health for your sickness, and from your life for your death."* (al-Bukhārī 6416)

"Do not expect the morning" — this is the discipline that 16:46 imposes. The person who lives in *taqallub*, in the constant motion of affairs, must carry within him the awareness that the motion may stop at any moment.

**The Reference to Travel and the Makkan Merchants**

The commentators' primary reading of *taqallub* as travel had a sharp relevance for the first audience. The Quraysh were merchants whose wealth depended on caravans, and their journeys were their pride. The verse tells them that even on those journeys — perhaps especially on those journeys, far from the sanctuary of Makkah — they are exposed. And history supplied the confirmation: the Battle of Badr was fought because a Makkan caravan returning from Syria was threatened; the Makkan army marched out to protect its commerce and was destroyed. The punishment came, quite literally, "in the midst of their going to and fro."

**A Broader Reading: The Heart That Turns**

Some commentators noted the connection between *taqallub* and *qalb*, the heart, and drew a spiritual sense from it. The human heart turns constantly — toward God, then toward the world, then toward God again. The verse may be read as a warning about the state in which one is seized: God may take a person in the midst of his turning, at whatever point the heart happens to be. This is why the Prophet ﷺ prayed constantly:

> *"O Turner of hearts, make my heart firm upon Your religion."* (al-Tirmidhī 2140; Ibn Mājah 3834)

The believer cannot control when he is seized; he can only work to ensure that his heart, whenever seized, is turned toward God.

**The Verse and Its Mercy**

As with verse 45, this verse must be read together with verse 47's ending: "Truly your Lord is Kind, Merciful." The threat is real, but it is issued in mercy — as a warning that precedes the seizure and gives time to prepare. The one who hears the verse and amends his life has been rescued by it. The one who hears it and continues in his *taqallub* unchanged has been warned, and the warning will be counted for him or against him. God does not seize without first sending the verse that says He might. That is the kindness within the threat.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:47

> **Or that He will not seize them with a gradual diminishing? And truly your Lord is Kind, Merciful.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Fourth and Final Possibility**

The interrogation that began in verse 45 reaches its conclusion. The plotters were asked whether they felt secure from the earth swallowing them, from punishment arriving from an unexpected quarter, and from seizure in the midst of their activity. The fourth possibility is different in kind from the first three: *aw yaʾkhudhahum ʿalā takhawwuf*, "or that He should seize them upon *takhawwuf*." The previous three were sudden. This one is slow.

**"Gradual Diminishing": The Meaning of *Takhawwuf***

The word *takhawwuf* has been understood in two ways, both attested among the earliest authorities.

The first reading takes it from the root *kh-w-f*, fear: God seizes them "in a state of fear" — that is, after they have seen others punished, live in dread of the same, and are then taken. Al-Ṭabarī reports this from a group of the early commentators. On this reading the punishment is preceded by terror: the plotters watch the towns around them destroyed, know that they are next, and are seized in that knowledge. The Qur'an describes such fear in the case of Pharaoh's people, struck by plague after plague, each time promising to believe and each time reneging (7:134–135).

The second reading, which the majority of commentators prefer, takes *takhawwuf* to mean *tanaqquṣ*, gradual reduction — seizing them "by diminishing," taking them little by little. Al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī, and al-Rāzī all report this, and al-Qurṭubī records the famous incident that established it. ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb asked the people from the pulpit what they understood by the verse, and a man from the tribe of Hudhayl replied that *takhawwuf* in their dialect meant *tanaqquṣ*, and he recited a verse of their poetry in which a she-camel's hump is described as "diminished" (*takhawwafa*) by the saddle as an adze diminishes a piece of wood. ʿUmar then said:

> *"O people, hold fast to your collection of poetry (dīwānakum) from the Age of Ignorance, for in it is the explanation of your Book."*

The incident is cited in every discussion of how the Qur'an's language relates to the Arabic of its time. The Qur'an was revealed in a living tongue whose full range was preserved in pre-Islamic poetry, and the early scholars regarded that poetry as a legitimate resource for understanding rare words.

On this second reading, the verse means that God may take the plotters gradually: reducing their numbers, their wealth, their strength, their lands, one piece at a time, until they are gone. Al-Ṭabarī explains it as God taking them by diminishing their bodies and their possessions until He destroys them. The Qur'an elsewhere describes exactly this process:

> *"Do they not see that We come to the land, reducing it from its borders?"* (Qur'an 13:41; cf. 21:44)

The reduction "from its borders" is *takhawwuf*: the slow erosion of a people's territory, influence, and life, so gradual that they do not perceive it as punishment until it is complete.

**Why the Gradual Punishment Is the Most Dangerous**

The three earlier possibilities were sudden and dramatic, and their danger is obvious. The fourth is subtle, and its danger lies in its subtlety. A sudden catastrophe at least has the effect of awakening those who witness it. A gradual diminishing awakens no one. Each loss seems explicable on its own terms — a bad harvest, a lost war, a death in the family, a shift in trade — and no single loss is large enough to prompt the question the verse asks: is this the seizure?

The Qur'an describes the process of *istidrāj*, in which God leads a people to destruction step by step:

> *"And those who deny Our signs — We will lead them on gradually from where they do not know. And I will grant them respite. Truly My plan is firm."* (Qur'an 7:182–183)

> *"So when they forgot what they had been reminded of, We opened to them the doors of every [good] thing, until, when they rejoiced in what they were given, We seized them suddenly."* (Qur'an 6:44)

The passage from al-Anʿām describes a diminishing that is, paradoxically, disguised as increase: the doors of prosperity are opened, and the prosperity itself is the trap. Whether the process appears as slow loss or as deceptive gain, it shares the same feature — it is not recognized for what it is until it is finished.

**The Historical Fulfillment**

Al-Rāzī and others note that all four possibilities were realized among the enemies of the Prophet ﷺ. Some were seized suddenly, as at Badr. Some were taken in their travels. And the power of Quraysh as a whole was diminished gradually — through the loss of their chiefs at Badr, the emigration of their best people to the Prophet, the erosion of their trade, the defection of their allies — until, at the conquest of Makkah, there was nothing left to resist. The verse describes a process that unfolded over eight years, and no one who lived through it could have pointed to the single moment when Quraysh's power was destroyed. It diminished, as the hump diminishes under the saddle.

**"And Truly Your Lord Is Kind, Merciful": The Turn**

The verse, and the whole passage of threats, ends in an unexpected place: *fa-inna rabbakum la-raʾūfun raḥīm*, "and truly your Lord is Kind, Merciful." After four descriptions of how God might seize the plotters, the verse affirms His kindness and mercy. The commentators explain the connection in several ways, each of which is true.

Al-Rāzī observes that the mercy lies precisely in the fact that God does *not* hasten the punishment. Every one of the four possibilities described is within His power; He has not exercised it. The plotters continue to live, to eat, to trade, to plot. Their continued existence is itself the proof of His *raʾfah*. The verse warns of what could happen in order to make plain what is not happening — and why. God's delay is not weakness; it is mercy.

Al-Ṭabarī explains that God is kind and merciful in not hastening punishment upon the sinner, giving him time to repent, and in sending warnings — such as this very verse — before He acts. The Qur'an states the principle:

> *"And if God were to seize people for their wrongdoing, He would not leave upon [the earth] any creature. But He defers them until an appointed term."* (Qur'an 16:61)

Verse 61 of this same sūrah will develop the point. The interval between the plot and the punishment is filled with mercy: the mercy of warning, the mercy of respite, the mercy of the open door.

**The Two Names: *Raʾūf* and *Raḥīm***

The verse pairs two names of God. *Al-Raʾūf* is from *raʾfah*, a tenderness and compassion that is often described as the most intense form of mercy — a gentleness that shrinks from causing harm. *Al-Raḥīm* is from *raḥmah*, the mercy that is active in bestowing good. The scholars distinguished the two: *raʾfah* is expressed in *removing* harm and *withholding* punishment; *raḥmah* is expressed in *giving* blessing and benefit. Together they describe the two sides of God's dealing with the sinner in the interval of respite: He withholds the blow (*raʾfah*) and continues to provide (*raḥmah*). The Qur'an pairs the names in the same order elsewhere (2:143; 9:117; 22:65; 24:20; 57:9; 59:10), and uses the first for the Prophet ﷺ in his tenderness toward his community (9:128).

**The Psychology of the Passage**

Verses 45–47 form a carefully constructed sequence. They open with the assumption of security, dismantle it through four possibilities of increasing subtlety, and end by naming the reason the security exists at all: God's kindness. The reader who follows the sequence arrives at a different state from the one in which he began. He started, like the plotters, feeling safe because nothing had happened. He ends knowing that nothing has happened because God is kind — and that kindness, unlike security, is something one must respond to. The proper response to a threat is fear. The proper response to kindness is gratitude and return. The passage produces both, and in the right order.

**The Application: Reading One's Own Diminishing**

The verse asks the reader to consider whether his own life shows signs of *takhawwuf*. Not every loss is punishment; the Qur'an is clear that the righteous are tested with loss (2:155). But a pattern of diminishing — of blessings withdrawn one by one, of relationships eroding, of capacity declining — accompanied by persistence in wrongdoing, should prompt the question the verse poses. And the verse's ending offers the way out: the Lord who diminishes is Kind and Merciful, and the diminishing stops when the person turns. The Prophet ﷺ said:

> *"Whoever repents before the sun rises from the west, God will accept his repentance."* (Muslim 2703)

Until that final sign, the door stands open, and the *raʾfah* of the verse's last clause is available to anyone who walks through it.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:48

> **Have they not considered that whatsoever God has created casts its shadow to the right and to the left, prostrating to God while in a state of abject humility?**

**Expanded Commentary**

**From Threat to Contemplation**

After the four questions of verses 45–47, which threatened the plotters with punishment from every direction, the sūrah changes its register. It returns to the mode of the opening verses — pointing to the created world as evidence — but now with a new object. The earlier signs were the heavens, the animals, the rain, the sea, the mountains. The sign here is more subtle: the shadow. *A-wa-lam yaraw ilā mā khalaqa Allāhu min shayʾin*, "Have they not looked at whatever thing God has created...?" The verse asks the plotters, and every reader, to look at something they see every day and have never considered.

**The Shadow as a Sign**

The verse states that everything God has created *yatafayyaʾu ẓilāluhu ʿani al-yamīni wa'l-shamāʾil*, "its shadows shift from the right and the lefts." The verb *tafayyaʾa* comes from the root *f-y-ʾ*, which means to return or to turn; *fayʾ* is specifically the shadow of the afternoon, which "returns" after the sun has passed its zenith — as opposed to *ẓill*, the shadow of the morning. Al-Qurṭubī and al-Rāzī note the distinction: *ẓill* is what exists before the sun moves past the meridian, *fayʾ* what returns after it. The verse uses the noun *ẓilāl* (shadows) with the verb *tafayyaʾa*, describing the shadows' movement from one side to the other over the course of the day.

The phrase "from the right and the lefts" — *ʿani al-yamīni wa'l-shamāʾil* — uses the singular for right and the plural for left. Al-Zamakhsharī and others explain that the singular *yamīn* is generic, standing for the class, while the plural *shamāʾil* matches the plural *ẓilāl*; the same variation between singular and plural appears in 16:81 ("its heat" and "your wars") and elsewhere, and is a feature of Arabic style that varies the rhythm without changing the sense. Others suggested that the shadow begins in one direction in the morning (the "right") and then spreads and turns through several positions (the "lefts") in the afternoon.

The verse describes a phenomenon known to every observer: the shadow of a tree, a mountain, a building, or a person lengthens toward one side at dawn, shrinks toward noon, and lengthens toward the other side until sunset. This constant, silent, regular movement, repeated by every object on earth every day, is the verse's chosen sign.

**"Prostrating to God": The Shadow's Sujūd**

The verse says the shadows move *sujjadan li'llāh*, "prostrating to God." Al-Qurṭubī and al-Rāzī observe that the shadow, as it lengthens and falls along the ground, has the appearance of prostration — a body stretched out low upon the earth. Every shadow is, in this sense, a prostration performed by the object that casts it, whether that object wills it or not.

But the commentators take the prostration to be more than an appearance. The Qur'an speaks repeatedly of all creation prostrating and glorifying God:

> *"Do you not see that to God prostrates whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth, and the sun, the moon, the stars, the mountains, the trees, the moving creatures, and many of the people? But upon many the punishment has been justified."* (Qur'an 22:18)

> *"And to God prostrates whoever is in the heavens and the earth, willingly or unwillingly, and their shadows, in the mornings and the evenings."* (Qur'an 13:15)

> *"The seven heavens and the earth and whatever is in them exalt Him. And there is not a thing except that it exalts Him by His praise, but you do not understand their exaltation."* (Qur'an 17:44)

The verse in al-Raʿd (13:15) is the closest parallel, and it explicitly includes "their shadows" among what prostrates. The commentators explain this prostration as the total submission of every created thing to the laws God has set for it. The shadow cannot choose where to fall; it falls exactly where the sun's position and the object's form require. This perfect obedience to the divine decree is its prostration. Al-Ṭabarī explains that the prostration of the shadow is its submission to what God has ordained for it, and al-Rāzī elaborates that everything possible in its existence is subject to the divine power and thus, in this sense, "prostrate."

**"In a State of Abject Humility": *Wa-hum Dākhirūn***

The verse ends: *wa-hum dākhirūn*, "and they are humbled" or "abject." The word *dākhir* is from *dakhara*, to be lowly, small, submissive. The Qur'an uses it for those who will enter Hell "in abasement" (40:60) and for all creatures coming to God on the Day of Judgment "humbled" (27:87). Here it describes the state of everything that casts a shadow: it is submissive, small before God, unable to resist His arrangement of it.

The pronoun *hum*, "they," is the pronoun used for rational beings, and its use for shadows and objects drew comment. Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Rāzī note that because the verse ascribes prostration — an act of rational beings — to these things, it treats them grammatically as rational; the same phenomenon occurs in 12:4, where Joseph sees the sun, moon, and stars "prostrating to me," using the plural form for rational beings. The grammar itself is teaching: the created world, in its obedience, is more "rational" than the human being who refuses to obey.

**The Argument Against the Plotters**

Why does this verse follow the threats of verses 45–47? The commentators identify the logic. The plotters imagined themselves secure, independent, capable of resisting God. The verse points to their own shadows. Their shadows prostrate to God whether they will it or not; their bodies, their possessions, the very ground they plot upon all submit to the divine order. The plotter is the one anomaly in creation: everything about him obeys God except his choosing heart. He cannot make his shadow fall in a different direction; he cannot stop it from lengthening at evening. And yet he imagines he can escape the One whom his own shadow obeys. The argument is a form of *a fortiori*: if even the shadow — the most insubstantial thing — is subject to God, how much more the plotter himself?

Al-Rāzī sees the verse as a proof of God's absolute power and ownership: the shadows' regular movement is not self-caused but is arranged by the One who moves the sun, and the submission of the shadow points to the submission of all things.

**The Companion Verse: 25:45–46**

The Qur'an develops the shadow as a sign in one other passage:

> *"Have you not considered your Lord — how He extends the shadow? And if He willed, He could have made it stationary. Then We made the sun for it an indication. Then We hold it in Our hand for a brief grasp."* (Qur'an 25:45–46)

The passage in al-Furqān adds what 16:48 assumes: the shadow's movement is God's doing, and He could have made it fixed. A world without moving shadows — with a sun fixed at one point, or with no sun at all — is conceivable, and would be uninhabitable. The daily movement of shadows is the visible sign of the cycle of night and day on which all life depends, and which verse 12 named among the subjected things.

**The Shadow and the Human Heart**

The scholars of the inner life drew a lesson from the verse about human prostration. Every person's shadow prostrates to God constantly. The question the verse poses to the person is whether he will do voluntarily what his shadow does involuntarily — whether the prostration of his body in prayer will match the prostration of his shadow on the ground. Al-Qurṭubī notes that the sujūd of the shadow is a rebuke to the person who refuses sujūd. The Qur'an makes the same contrast in 22:18, where after listing all that prostrates — sun, moon, stars, mountains, trees, animals — it says, "and *many* of the people." Not all. The shadows are unanimous; the people are divided.

The Prophet ﷺ described the state of a servant in prostration as the nearest he comes to his Lord:

> *"The nearest a servant is to his Lord is when he is in prostration, so make much supplication then."* (Muslim 482)

The shadow, always prostrate, is always in this nearness, though it cannot know it. The human being, who can know it, must choose it.

**The Modern Reader and the Verse**

The verse invites a practice: to watch a shadow. To notice that at every moment of the day, without pause, every object on earth is doing exactly what it was made to do, in perfect regularity, in a way that no one arranges and no one could alter. A person who spends ten minutes watching the shadow of a tree move across the ground has performed the *naẓar* the verse demands — and has been shown, in the simplest possible form, that the world is not his and does not answer to him. That seeing is the beginning of the humility (*dukhūr*) the verse names, and humility is the beginning of worship.

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:49

> **And unto God prostrates whatever crawling creature is in the heavens or on the earth, and the angels [as well], and they do not wax arrogant.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**From Shadows to Living Things**

Verse 48 described the prostration of shadows — the submission of the inanimate world. Verse 49 broadens the picture to the animate: *wa-li'llāhi yasjudu mā fī al-samāwāti wa-mā fī al-arḍi min dābbatin wa'l-malāʾikah*, "and to God prostrates whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth of moving creatures, and the angels." The progression is deliberate. First the shadow, which has no life; then the creatures that move; then the angels, the highest of created beings. Every level of creation, from the least substantial to the most exalted, is shown in prostration. The only exception, implied by contrast, is the arrogant human being.

**The Structure: "To God" Placed First**

The verse begins *wa-li'llāhi*, "and to God," fronting the prepositional phrase before the verb. In Arabic, this placement conveys exclusivity: it is to God, and to none other, that all these prostrate. The same fronting occurs in verse 52, "and to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth," and in verse 53, "whatever blessing you have is from God." In the context of a sūrah addressed to idolaters, the fronting is an argument: the creatures they worship — or the powers they associate with God — are themselves among what prostrates to Him.

**"Whatever Crawling Creature": *Min Dābbah***

The word *dābbah*, from *dabba*, "to move slowly, to creep," designates any creature that moves on the earth — animals of every kind, including, in the Qur'an's usage, human beings (as in 8:22, "the worst of moving creatures before God are the deaf and dumb who do not reason"). Here the commentators take it broadly: every animate being on earth, and — because the verse says "in the heavens" as well — every animate being there too.

The mention of *dābbah* "in the heavens" prompted discussion. What creatures move in the heavens? Al-Qurṭubī notes that the verse may refer to creatures God has placed in the heavens whose nature we do not know, and cites the general principle that God's creation is vaster than human knowledge. The Qur'an itself affirms that there are moving creatures in the heavens and earth:

> *"And among His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth and what He has dispersed in them of moving creatures (dābbah). And He is able to gather them when He wills."* (Qur'an 42:29)

Some also read the angels themselves as included in "what is in the heavens," with the explicit mention of them afterward being a specification of the general by the particular — the honor of being named separately. Al-Rāzī prefers this: the angels are mentioned distinctly after the general statement because of their nobility and to make explicit that even they, the highest, prostrate.

**"And the Angels": Why They Are Named**

The separate mention of the angels is significant in the context of the sūrah's polemic. The Makkans held that the angels were daughters of God (v. 57; 17:40; 37:150; 43:19) and worshipped them as intermediaries. The verse places the angels among those who prostrate — that is, among the servants, not the served. The Qur'an makes this point repeatedly:

> *"And they say: The Most Merciful has taken a son. Glory be to Him! Rather, they are honored servants. They do not precede Him in speech, and they act by His command."* (Qur'an 21:26–27)

> *"Never would the Messiah disdain to be a servant of God, nor would the angels near [to Him]. And whoever disdains His worship and is arrogant — He will gather them to Himself all together."* (Qur'an 4:172)

The verse in al-Nisāʾ pairs the angels' servanthood with the same vice named at the end of 16:49 — arrogance. Those who disdain servanthood and are arrogant will be gathered for judgment; the angels are not among them.

**The Nature of the Angels' Prostration**

The prostration of the angels is real worship, chosen and conscious, and differs from the prostration of the shadow or the beast. Al-Rāzī distinguishes the prostration of *taskhīr*, subjection — the involuntary submission of all things to God's decree — from the prostration of *ʿibādah*, worship — the deliberate act of a being that knows God and humbles itself before Him. The shadows and beasts perform the first; the angels perform the second. The Prophet ﷺ described the extent of the angels' worship:

> *"The heaven has groaned, and it has a right to groan. There is not a space of four fingers in it but that an angel is placing his forehead in prostration to God."* (al-Tirmidhī 2312; Ibn Mājah 4190)

And the Qur'an describes their ceaseless glorification:

> *"They exalt [Him] night and day, and do not slacken."* (Qur'an 21:20)

> *"Those who are near to your Lord are not too proud to worship Him, and they exalt Him, and to Him they prostrate."* (Qur'an 7:206)

The verse in al-Aʿrāf is a near-twin of 16:49 and 16:50: it names the same three elements — the angels near to God, their absence of pride, and their prostration.

**"And They Do Not Wax Arrogant": *Wa-hum lā yastakbirūn***

The verse closes on the point that gives it its edge: *wa-hum lā yastakbirūn*, "and they are not arrogant." The word *istikbār*, discussed at verse 22, is the vice of considering oneself great — too great to submit. It is the vice of Iblīs, who "refused and was arrogant" (2:34) when commanded to prostrate to Adam, and it is the vice the sūrah has repeatedly attributed to the deniers (vv. 22, 23, 29).

The angels are the most powerful, knowledgeable, and exalted of creatures. If any created being had grounds for pride, they would. Yet they do not exalt themselves; they prostrate. The verse contrasts them implicitly with the Makkan chiefs, who had far less — a little wealth, a little authority over a small town — and were too proud to bow. The argument is one the Qur'an makes often: the higher the creature, the more complete its submission. Pride is not the mark of greatness but of smallness that has forgotten its size.

Al-Zamakhsharī notes that the negation of arrogance is stated in a way that emphasizes its permanence: the angels *do not* (ever) become arrogant. It is not that they happen not to be arrogant at the moment; arrogance is not in their nature. And the reason is given in the next verse: they fear their Lord.

**The Verse of Prostration**

According to the consensus of the schools, 16:49–50 is one of the verses of prostration (*sajadāt al-tilāwah*) in the Qur'an — one of the fourteen or fifteen places at which the reciter and the listener perform a prostration. Al-Qurṭubī records this. The reason is evident: a verse that describes all creation prostrating to God, and praises the angels for not being too proud to do so, calls for a response in kind. The reciter who reaches the end of verse 50 places his own forehead on the ground, joining the shadows, the beasts, and the angels in the act the verse describes. The Prophet ﷺ said that when the son of Adam prostrates upon reciting a verse of prostration, Satan withdraws weeping, saying, "The son of Adam was commanded to prostrate and he prostrated, so for him is Paradise; I was commanded to prostrate and I refused, so for me is the Fire" (Muslim 81). The verse of prostration thus reenacts the primordial choice: Iblīs's arrogance or the angels' humility.

**The Meaning for the Human Being**

The verse places the human being at a decision point. Everything else in creation prostrates — the shadow by nature, the beast by instinct, the angel by knowledge and love. The human being alone can refuse. This freedom is his distinction and his danger. If he prostrates, he joins the universal worship consciously, as the angels do, and surpasses them in one respect: he prostrates despite having the capacity not to, and despite the pull of desire and pride that the angels do not feel. If he refuses, he becomes the single dissonance in a universe of harmony — the one creature whose shadow bows while he stands.

The Qur'an's description of the true servants of God is, accordingly, a description of those who have chosen to join the prostration:

> *"Only those believe in Our signs who, when they are reminded of them, fall down in prostration and exalt [God] with praise of their Lord, and they are not arrogant."* (Qur'an 32:15)

The phrase "and they are not arrogant" — *wa-hum lā yastakbirūn* — is identical to the close of 16:49. The believers who prostrate are described in exactly the words used for the angels. That identity of description is the verse's promise: the human being who bows becomes, in that act, what the angels are.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:50

> **They fear their Lord above them, and they do what they are commanded.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Reason Behind the Angels' Humility**

Verse 49 ended by stating that the angels are not arrogant. Verse 50 explains why: *yakhāfūna rabbahum min fawqihim wa-yafʿalūna mā yuʾmarūn*, "they fear their Lord above them, and they do what they are commanded." Two things are named — fear and obedience — and the order matters. Fear comes first because fear is the root of obedience. The angels obey perfectly because they fear perfectly; their freedom from arrogance is the fruit of their awe.

**Fear as the Foundation**

The verse ascribes fear to the angels, and this alone is a striking statement. The angels are sinless. They have never disobeyed and never will (66:6, "they do not disobey God in what He commands them"). What, then, do they fear? Al-Rāzī addresses the question directly. Their fear is not the fear of a sinner dreading punishment for what he has done. It is the fear of *taʿẓīm*, of magnification — the awe that arises from knowing the greatness of God. The more completely a being knows God, the more it fears Him, because it perceives more fully the distance between His majesty and its own smallness. The Qur'an states the principle: *"Only those of His servants who have knowledge fear God"* (35:28). The angels, whose knowledge is greatest, fear most.

Al-Qurṭubī adds that the angels' fear includes awareness that God's power over them is absolute — that He could, if He willed, punish them, and that their safety depends on His grace, not on their merit. This is confirmed by the hadith in which the Prophet ﷺ described Gabriel's state:

> *"When God decrees a matter in heaven, the angels beat their wings in submission to His word, like a chain [dragged] over smooth stone. When their hearts are relieved of fear, they say: What did your Lord say? They reply: The truth, and He is the Most High, the Most Great."* (al-Bukhārī 4701)

The angels who hear God's word are so struck by awe that they fall into a state of fear until it passes. This is the fear of 16:50 — not a fear that paralyzes, but the trembling of those who stand near to overwhelming majesty.

**"Their Lord Above Them": The Question of *Fawqiyyah***

The phrase *min fawqihim*, "from above them," has been a locus of theological discussion, and the commentators approach it carefully. The Qur'an describes God as "above" His servants in several places: *"He is the Subduer over (fawqa) His servants"* (6:18, 61); *"They fear their Lord above them"* here. The question is what "above" means when applied to God.

Al-Ṭūsī, the Shiite commentator, insists that the phrase is not spatial: God is not located in a place, and "above" denotes superiority of rank, power, and authority — as one says a king is "above" his subjects without meaning that he is physically higher. Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Rāzī take the same approach: *fawq* here is the elevation of dominion and might. God is "above" the angels in the sense that He rules them completely.

Other scholars, including Ibn Taymiyyah and the traditionalist school, affirmed the text as it stands — that God is above His creation in a manner befitting Him, without asking how (*bilā kayf*), without likening it to the aboveness of bodies, and without denying it. On this view, the Qur'an's repeated language of God's being above, His ascending the Throne (7:54; 20:5), things ascending *to* Him (35:10) and descending *from* Him, is affirmed without interpretation into mere rank. Ibn Taymiyyah argued that affirming God's aboveness does not entail placing Him in a created space, since space itself is His creation and He is not contained by anything.

Both approaches agree on what matters for the verse: God's aboveness is His absolute transcendence and authority, and it is the object of the angels' fear. The scholar Mālik, asked about how God ascended the Throne, gave the answer that became the traditionalist rule:

> *"The ascending is known; the how is unknown; belief in it is obligatory; and asking about it is an innovation."*

Al-Qurṭubī records that the phrase *min fawqihim* may also be construed with *yakhāfūn*, "they fear [what might come] from above them" — that is, punishment descending from above — though the construction with *rabbahum* is the primary reading.

**"They Do What They Are Commanded"**

The second clause states the angels' obedience: *wa-yafʿalūna mā yuʾmarūn*. This describes their essential function. The angels are, in the Qur'an's picture, the instruments of God's command in the world — carrying revelation, recording deeds, taking souls, managing the rain and the wind, guarding the Fire. Everything they do is by command, and they never deviate from it. The Qur'an states this of the guardians of Hell:

> *"Over it are angels, stern and severe; they do not disobey God in what He commands them, but do what they are commanded."* (Qur'an 66:6)

The identical phrase — *yafʿalūna mā yuʾmarūn* — appears in both verses. The angels' obedience is not partial or reluctant; they do *what* they are commanded, no more and no less, without delay or alteration.

The commentators note the contrast with the human being once more. Human obedience is always incomplete: we obey some commands and neglect others, obey in one moment and lapse in the next, obey outwardly while resisting inwardly. The angels' obedience is total, and this is because their fear is total. The verse links the two clauses in a chain of cause and effect that the human reader can apply to himself: to the degree that one fears God as one ought, one obeys as one ought.

**The Angels as Model, Not Object of Worship**

The verse serves the sūrah's polemical purpose in a precise way. The Makkans worshipped angels as intermediaries and imagined them as daughters of God. The verse shows the angels as the Makkans' fellow servants — fearing, obeying, prostrate before the Lord. To worship them is absurd, because they themselves are worshippers; the proper response to the angels is not to pray to them but to imitate them. Al-Rāzī states that the verse establishes that the angels are servants and thus cannot be gods, and that this refutes the idolaters' attribution of divinity to them.

The Qur'an makes the same point through the words of the angels themselves on the Day of Judgment, when God asks them whether the idolaters worshipped them:

> *"They will say: Glory be to You! You are our protector, not they. Rather, they used to worship the jinn; most of them were believers in them."* (Qur'an 34:41)

**The Human Application: The Two Halves of Servanthood**

The verse gives a definition of servanthood in two clauses, and the definition applies to the human being as much as to the angel. Servanthood is fear of God and obedience to His command. Neither is complete without the other. Fear without obedience is mere emotion, which passes; obedience without fear becomes mechanical, or turns into pride in one's own obedience. The believer aims at both: a heart that trembles before God's majesty and a body that does what He commands.

The Prophet ﷺ described his own community's obligation in terms that echo the angels' obedience:

> *"What I have forbidden you, avoid; and what I have commanded you, do as much of it as you can."* (al-Bukhārī 7288; Muslim 1337)

The phrase "as much as you can" marks the difference between human and angelic obedience. The angels do all they are commanded; the human being does what he can. But the direction is the same, and the standard is the same. The believer who fears God and does what he can of what he is commanded is walking toward the state the verse describes, even if he never fully reaches it in this world.

**The Prostration of Recitation**

As noted at verse 49, this verse ends a passage that the schools of law recognize as a verse of prostration. Al-Qurṭubī records it, and the prostration is performed at the end of verse 50. The placement is exact: the reader has just been told that the angels fear their Lord above them and do what they are commanded. He is now commanded — by the practice of the Prophet ﷺ, who prostrated at this verse — to prostrate. If he does, he has done, in that moment, what the verse describes: he has feared and obeyed. The verse does not merely inform; it enlists. The prostration that follows it is the reader's answer to the question the passage has been posing since verse 48: will the human being join the worship of everything else?

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:51

> **And God has said, "Do not take two gods. He is only One God. So be in awe of Me."**

**Expanded Commentary**

**From the Angels' Fear to the Command to Fear**

Verse 50 described the angels fearing their Lord. Verse 51 turns the description into a command addressed to human beings: after establishing that God is one, it says *fa-iyyāya fa'rhabūn*, "so fear Me." The passage has moved from what the angels do to what humans must do. The angels' fear was presented as a model; the command now requires the reader to adopt it.

**"Do Not Take Two Gods": The Wording**

The verse says *lā tattakhidhū ilāhayni ithnayn*, "do not take two gods, two." The phrase appears redundant: *ilāhayni* is already dual; why add *ithnayn*, "two"? The commentators address this, and their answers illuminate the verse's emphasis.

Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Rāzī explain that the dual noun *ilāhayn* conveys the plurality, but the addition of *ithnayn* stresses the *number itself* as the point of prohibition. The verse is not merely saying "do not take gods" but "do not take *two*" — the number two is the target, because the moment there is a second, the first is no longer God. Divinity does not admit of number. The same structure appears in the second half: *innamā huwa ilāhun wāḥid*, "He is only one God, one" — the emphasis on *wāḥid* mirrors the emphasis on *ithnayn*. The verse sets "two" against "one" and forbids the first as it affirms the second.

Al-Rāzī also notes that "two" is specified, rather than "many," because two is the minimal violation of unity. Whoever forbids two forbids everything beyond two *a fortiori*. And the Makkans, though they had many idols, in practice tended toward dualisms: God and a chief partner; God and the angels as His daughters; the God of the heavens and the deities of the earth. The Zoroastrian dualism of light and darkness was known in Arabia. The verse addresses the root of all these: the idea that divinity can be shared even once.

**Why Two Gods Are Impossible**

The prohibition rests on a rational impossibility that the Qur'an states elsewhere:

> *"Had there been in them gods other than God, they both would have been ruined."* (Qur'an 21:22)

> *"God has not taken any son, nor is there any god with Him. [Had there been], each god would have taken away what it created, and some of them would have sought to overcome others."* (Qur'an 23:91)

The argument, developed by the theologians as the "proof from mutual hindrance" (*dalīl al-tamānuʿ*), runs as follows. Suppose two gods. Either their wills always coincide, or they may differ. If they may differ — one willing that a thing exist, the other that it not exist — then either both wills take effect (impossible, since a thing cannot both exist and not exist), or neither does (in which case neither is omnipotent), or one prevails (in which case the other is not God). If their wills always necessarily coincide, then each is bound by the other, and a bound will is not the will of a god. In every case, the supposition of two gods destroys the concept of God. Verse 51 states the conclusion — "He is only one God" — and the Qur'an's parallel verses supply the reasoning.

**"So Be in Awe of Me": The Shift to the First Person**

The most striking feature of the verse is its grammatical shift. It begins in the third person — "God has said... He is only one God" — and then, without transition, moves to the first person: *fa-iyyāya fa'rhabūn*, "so Me, fear." This is *iltifāt*, the rhetorical "turning" from one person to another, and the commentators explain its effect.

Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Rāzī note that the shift makes the command immediate and personal. The verse has been speaking *about* God; suddenly God speaks *for Himself*, and the hearer finds himself addressed directly by the One he has just been told is alone. The effect is that of a ruler who has been spoken of in his absence and then suddenly appears in the room and speaks. The abstraction of "one God" becomes the presence of "Me."

The word order adds a second emphasis. In Arabic, the normal order would be *irhabūnī*, "fear Me." The verse instead fronts the object pronoun — *iyyāya fa'rhabūn* — placing "Me" before the verb. This fronting conveys exclusivity: "fear *Me* [alone]." The same construction governs the most famous verse of the Qur'an: *iyyāka naʿbudu wa-iyyāka nastaʿīn*, "You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help" (1:5). The verse says not merely "fear Me" but "let your fear be directed at Me and at nothing else." This is the natural consequence of what preceded: if there is only one God, there is only one being to be feared with the fear of a god.

**The Word *Rahbah***

The verse uses *fa'rhabūn* from the root *r-h-b*, a word for fear that carries the sense of awe and dread — a fear that produces caution and reverence. It is distinct from *khawf*, the more general term for fear used of the angels in verse 50, and from *khashyah*, the fear that arises from knowledge. Al-Rāghib defines *rahbah* as a fear accompanied by anxiety and vigilance. The Qur'an uses the root for the state of the monks (*ruhbān*, 5:82; 57:27) — those whose lives are shaped by awe of God — and for the command addressed to the Children of Israel: *"And fear Me alone"* (2:40), *wa-iyyāya fa'rhabūn*, with exactly the same wording as this verse.

The command to fear God alone has a positive corollary: freedom from fear of everything else. The one who fears only God does not fear the idols, the tribe, the powerful, or the future. This is why the Qur'an repeatedly pairs the command to fear God with the command not to fear people: *"So do not fear them, but fear Me"* (2:150; 3:175; 5:3, 44). Fear cannot be eliminated from the human heart; it can only be directed. The verse directs it.

**The Connection to the Preceding Passage**

The verse concludes the argument of verses 48–51 as a whole. The shadows prostrate to God; the beasts and the angels prostrate; the angels fear their Lord above them and obey. All of creation, in other words, testifies to the oneness of God and responds to it with submission and awe. Verse 51 states the doctrine explicitly — one God, not two — and demands from the human being the response that the rest of creation already gives. The angels' fear (v. 50) becomes the human command (v. 51). The reader, who has just watched everything else bow, is told: you also.

**The Verse and *Tawḥīd* as the Center of the Sūrah**

The sūrah opened with the declaration "Exalted is He above what they associate" (v. 1) and stated the message of every prophet as "Worship God and shun false gods" (v. 36). Verse 51 restates the doctrine at the exact center of the sūrah in its most compressed form: *ilāhun wāḥid*, one God. The Qur'an regards this as the foundation of everything else — the first pillar, the first word of the testimony of faith, the point on which salvation turns. The Prophet ﷺ said:

> *"Whoever dies knowing that there is no god but God enters Paradise."* (Muslim 26)

The knowledge referred to is the knowledge that 16:51 conveys: not merely that God exists, but that He is *one*, and that no second can be set beside Him in worship, love, hope, or fear.

**The Practical Dimension: Fear Directed Rightly**

The verse's command has a direct bearing on the shape of a life. Most human misconduct is driven by misdirected fear: fear of poverty drives dishonesty; fear of people drives hypocrisy; fear of loss drives oppression; fear of death drives cowardice. The verse offers a single correction that addresses them all — fear God alone. The person who fears God more than poverty does not steal. The person who fears God more than people speaks truth. The person who fears God more than death stands firm. The verse does not ask the believer to be fearless; it asks him to let a single, rightly-placed fear expel the many misplaced ones. As the Prophet ﷺ taught, the one who fears God finds that all things fear him, while the one who does not fear God is made to fear everything. Verse 51 is the doctrine of God's oneness stated as a rule for the heart: one God, therefore one fear.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:52

> **Unto Him belongs whatsoever is in the heavens and on the earth, and unto Him is religion due forever. Will you then be in awe of anyone other than God?**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Ground of the Command to Fear**

Verse 51 commanded, "So fear Me." Verse 52 gives the reasons why fear is due to God alone and to no other: everything belongs to Him, and obedience is His perpetually. The verse then closes with a question that makes the conclusion inescapable: given all this, "will you then fear other than God?" The structure is that of a proof — premise, premise, rhetorical conclusion.

**"Unto Him Belongs Whatsoever Is in the Heavens and on the Earth"**

The verse begins *wa-lahu mā fī al-samāwāti wa'l-arḍ*, "and to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth." As in verse 49, the prepositional phrase is fronted — *lahu*, "to Him" — conveying exclusivity: to Him *alone* belongs all this. The statement is the Qur'an's most frequent expression of God's absolute ownership (*mulk*), repeated dozens of times (2:116, 255, 284; 3:109, 129; 4:126, 131, 132, 171; 10:55, 66, 68; 14:2; 20:6; 21:19; 22:64; 24:64; 30:26; 31:26; 34:1; 42:4, 53; 53:31).

Ownership is the foundation of the argument for exclusive worship. The idols the Makkans feared and worshipped were themselves "in the heavens or the earth" — the angels in the former, the stones in the latter — and therefore among what God owns. To fear a thing that belongs to God, rather than the Owner Himself, is like fearing a servant rather than the master who commands him. Al-Rāzī draws out the logic: since everything other than God is His possession and creation, and since possessions are subject to their owner's will, no possession can harm or benefit except by the owner's leave. Fear directed at the possession is therefore misplaced; it belongs to the Owner.

**"And Unto Him Is Religion Due Forever": *Wa-lahu al-dīnu wāṣiban***
