The second clause is the verse's most discussed phrase: *wa-lahu al-dīnu wāṣiban*, "and to Him is *al-dīn*, *wāṣiban*." Two words require attention.

The word *dīn* has a range of meanings in the Qur'an, and the commentators canvass them for this verse. It may mean obedience (*ṭāʿah*), the sense Ibn ʿAbbās gave here according to al-Ṭabarī: obedience is owed to God perpetually. It may mean religion in the sense of the whole system of worship and law — as in "the religion with God is Islam" (3:19). It may mean judgment or recompense, as in "Master of the Day of Judgment" (1:4) — on this reading, the verse would mean that final judgment belongs to God forever. Al-Qurṭubī records all of these, and they are not mutually exclusive: obedience is owed to God, the religion He prescribes is His, and the judgment of the obedient and disobedient is His. The word *dīn*, in its root sense, denotes a relationship of debt and submission between a superior and an inferior, and every meaning of the word flows from that.

The word *wāṣiban* is rarer. Its root, *w-ṣ-b*, has two senses: permanence and continuity on one hand, and hardship or fatigue on the other. Al-Ṭabarī, Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, and most commentators take the first: *wāṣib* means *dāʾim*, perpetual, unceasing. The Qur'an uses the same word of the punishment of the devils who eavesdrop on heaven: *"and for them is a perpetual (wāṣib) punishment"* (37:9). On this reading the verse means: obedience and religion belong to God *always* — not at some times and not at others, not in this world and not in the next, but permanently.

Al-Qurṭubī records the second sense as well: *wāṣib* as toilsome, wearying — meaning that obedience to God, though it involves hardship and effort, is owed to Him. Al-Zamakhsharī suggests the combination: religion is owed to God perpetually *and* it requires effort, the effort being part of what is owed. Al-Rāzī draws out the spiritual point on the first reading: the worship of others is temporary and ceases — the idols will be abandoned on the Day of Judgment and their worshippers will disown them (v. 86) — while the worship of God is permanent and continues in Paradise, where the believers' final word is praise of Him (10:10).

**The Implication: Religion Is Not Divisible**

The phrase "to Him is religion perpetually" has an implication that the sūrah's later verses will develop: religion cannot be divided among God and others. The Makkans practiced a divided religion — acknowledging God as Creator while giving portions of worship, fear, and sacrifice to intermediaries. Verse 53–55 will describe this precisely: in distress they call on God alone; in ease they associate partners. Verse 52 forbids the division in principle. If religion belongs to God *wāṣiban*, perpetually, then it belongs to Him in ease as well as distress, in prosperity as well as calamity, in youth as well as age. There is no season in which a portion of religion may be assigned elsewhere.

The Qur'an makes the point through the command to sincerity:

> *"Say: Truly I have been commanded to worship God, making religion sincere to Him alone."* (Qur'an 39:11)

> *"Unquestionably, to God belongs the pure religion."* (Qur'an 39:3)

The "pure religion," *al-dīn al-khāliṣ*, is the religion of 16:52 — belonging to God without partner or interruption.

**"Will You Then Fear Other Than God?": The Conclusion**

The verse ends: *a-fa-ghayra Allāhi tattaqūn*, "is it then other than God that you fear?" The question follows from the two premises. If everything belongs to God, and if obedience is owed to Him perpetually, then fearing anything else is irrational — a fear of possessions rather than the Possessor, of the temporary rather than the Permanent.

The word order again carries the emphasis: *ghayra Allāhi*, "other than God," is placed before the verb, so that the question targets the object precisely: "Is it *other than God* that you fear?" The same construction appears in 6:14 (*a-ghayra Allāhi attakhidhu waliyyan*, "Is it other than God I should take as protector?") and 6:164 (*a-ghayra Allāhi abghī rabban*, "Is it other than God I should seek as Lord?"). In each case, the fronting expresses astonishment that the object could be anything but God.

The verb here is *tattaqūn*, from *taqwā*, rather than the *rahbah* of verse 51. *Taqwā* is the fear that protects — the caution that leads a person to guard himself against what he fears. The verse thus asks: do you take your protective measures against something other than God? Do you guard yourself against the anger of idols, of tribes, of men, while neglecting to guard yourself against the displeasure of the Owner of all things? The question is meant to expose the folly of the ordering.

**The Three Verses as a Unit**

Verses 50, 51, and 52 form a tight progression on the theme of fear. Verse 50: the angels fear their Lord. Verse 51: God commands, "fear Me." Verse 52: God asks, "will you then fear other than Me?" The angels are the model; the command is the norm; the question is the challenge. The reader is placed between the example of the highest creatures and the interrogation of his own conduct.

**The Verse in the Believer's Life**

The verse's doctrine has a practical shape that the Prophet ﷺ articulated in his instruction to Ibn ʿAbbās:

> *"Know that if the whole community were to gather to benefit you with something, they would not benefit you except with what God has written for you; and if they were to gather to harm you with something, they would not harm you except with what God has written against you. The pens have been lifted and the pages have dried."* (al-Tirmidhī 2516)

This is 16:52 applied. Because everything belongs to God, no one can harm or benefit except by His leave. The fear of people, therefore, is a fear of instruments rather than of the Hand that moves them. The person who internalizes the verse is freed from a great deal of anxiety — not because nothing can harm him, but because he knows that whatever harms him does so within a decree issued by the One he already fears and trusts. The fear of God, rightly understood, is not an addition to the fears of life but their replacement. "To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth" means that there is nothing outside His ownership to be feared independently of Him. The question that ends the verse — will you fear other than God? — expects the answer that the whole verse has made inevitable: no.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:53

> **And whatever blessing you have is from God. Then, when affliction befalls you, unto Him do you cry for help.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**From Fear to Gratitude**

Verses 50–52 addressed fear: whom one should fear, and why. Verse 53 turns to blessing: from whom it comes, and how people respond. The two themes are complementary. Fear and gratitude are the two fundamental orientations of the servant toward God — fear of His power, gratitude for His gifts — and the sūrah, whose name and theme is *al-niʿam*, the blessings, now states the principle of gratitude in its most compressed form: *wa-mā bikum min niʿmatin fa-mina Allāh*, "whatever blessing is with you is from God."

**"Whatever Blessing You Have": The Scope**

The construction *mā bikum min niʿmah* is comprehensive. *Mā* here is conditional or relative — "whatever" — and *min niʿmah* extends the reference to every kind of blessing: not this blessing or that, but blessing as such. Al-Zamakhsharī notes that the structure means every single blessing, without exception, whether small or great, worldly or religious, visible or hidden. The list the sūrah has given so far — the animals (vv. 5–8), the rain and crops (vv. 10–11), the night and day, sun and moon (v. 12), the sea and its bounties (v. 14), the mountains and rivers (v. 15), the stars (v. 16) — is now summarized: all of it, and everything not listed, "is from God."

The verse repeats in principle what verse 18 stated: "If you would count the blessings of God, you could not number them." Verse 18 spoke of the impossibility of counting; verse 53 speaks of the unity of source. However many they are, they come from one place.

**"From God": *Fa-mina Allāh***

The predicate is introduced with *fa-*, which in this construction gives the sense of a conclusion or consequence: "whatever blessing you have — then [know that] it is from God." The word *min*, "from," denotes origin. The blessings did not arise from the idols, from the person's own effort, from chance, or from nature; they originated with God. The Qur'an develops the point elsewhere with a series of questions designed to trace every blessing to its source:

> *"Have you considered what you sow? Is it you who make it grow, or are We the grower? ... Have you considered the water that you drink? Is it you who brought it down from the clouds, or is it We who bring it down? ... Have you considered the fire that you kindle? Is it you who produced its tree, or are We the producer?"* (Qur'an 56:63–72)

Each question strips away the intermediary and exposes the source. The farmer sows, but he does not make the seed grow. The person drinks, but he did not bring the water down. The verse in al-Naḥl states the conclusion of all such questions: every blessing is from God.

The commentators distinguish this from a denial of secondary causes. The farmer's sowing is real, and the Qur'an commands work. But the chain of causes terminates in God, and the blessing itself — the growth, the water, the fire — is His gift, mediated through causes He created. The error of the idolaters was not that they used causes but that they attributed the blessing to them, or to the idols, rather than to the One behind them. This is the *kufr al-niʿmah*, ingratitude for blessing, that the sūrah will name explicitly in verse 55 and again in verse 112.

**The Blessing of Faith Included**

Al-Rāzī and others note that "whatever blessing" includes the greatest blessing of all — faith and guidance. The Qur'an states this: *"Rather, God confers favor upon you that He has guided you to faith"* (49:17). The Companions used to say, when they were reminded of their state before Islam, that guidance was the blessing that made all others meaningful. A person who attributes his faith to his own intelligence or effort has committed the same error, in the religious sphere, that the farmer commits when he attributes the harvest to himself. The verse's *mā*, "whatever," leaves no blessing outside its scope, and the blessing of being able to read the verse and understand it is among them.

**"Then, When Affliction Befalls You, Unto Him Do You Cry": The Proof From Distress**

The second half of the verse offers a proof drawn from human behavior itself: *thumma idhā massakumu al-ḍurru fa-ilayhi tajʾarūn*, "then when harm touches you, to Him you cry out." The argument is one of the Qur'an's most frequent, and its force lies in appealing not to doctrine but to what people actually do.

The word *ḍurr* denotes harm, adversity, affliction — sickness, poverty, danger, loss. The verb *tajʾarūn* is from *juʾār*, which originally describes the loud cry of cattle or wild animals in distress; applied to humans, it means to cry out loudly in supplication, to bellow for help. The choice of word is pointed. The idolaters, who in ease affected sophistication and mocked the Prophet, in distress cried out like animals — and cried out to *God*, not to their idols. The fronted *ilayhi*, "to *Him*," conveys the exclusivity: in genuine distress, they turned to Him alone.

The Qur'an documents this behavior repeatedly:

> *"And when adversity touches you at sea, those you call upon besides Him vanish, except for Him. But when He delivers you to the land, you turn away."* (Qur'an 17:67)

> *"And when adversity touches man, he calls upon Us, [lying] on his side or sitting or standing; but when We remove his adversity from him, he passes on as though he had never called upon Us."* (Qur'an 10:12)

> *"And when they board a ship, they call upon God, sincere to Him in religion. But when He delivers them to the land, at once they associate others with Him."* (Qur'an 29:65)

The commentators cite the well-known incident of ʿIkrimah ibn Abī Jahl, who fled Makkah by sea after the conquest; when the ship was caught in a storm, the sailors told the passengers to call on God alone, for nothing else would avail them. ʿIkrimah reflected that if only God could save him at sea, only God could save him on land, and he resolved to return and accept Islam — which he did. The behavior the verse describes became, for him, the argument that converted him.

**The Logic of the Argument**

The argument from distress is a form of *argumentum ad hominem* in the proper sense: it convicts people out of their own conduct. In ease, the idolater claims that his idols benefit him. In distress, he does not call on them — he calls on God. His behavior in extremity reveals what he actually believes beneath his professed belief: that only God can help. The verse invites him to notice this and to bring his professed belief into line with his real one. Al-Rāzī frames it as a demonstration that the knowledge of God's oneness is innate (*fiṭrī*): distress strips away the acquired layers of habit and culture and exposes the primordial recognition of the one Lord.

**The Movement of the Passage: 53 to 55**

Verse 53 begins a three-verse sequence. Verse 53: all blessing is from God, and in distress you cry to Him. Verse 54: when He removes the distress, a party of you associate others with Him. Verse 55: they do so to show ingratitude for what He gave them. The sequence traces the full cycle of *kufr al-niʿmah*: gift, distress, sincere cry, relief, and then — the betrayal — a return to *shirk*. The verse under discussion presents the first two moments, and both are to the idolaters' credit: they receive God's blessing and, when tested, call on Him alone. The following verses show what they do with the relief.

**The Verse as Instruction for the Believer**

For the believer, the verse teaches two disciplines. The first is *attribution*: to trace every blessing consciously to God. The Prophet ﷺ modeled this in his supplications, especially the "master of seeking forgiveness":

> *"O God, You are my Lord; there is no god but You. You created me and I am Your servant... I acknowledge to You Your blessing upon me, and I acknowledge my sin."* (al-Bukhārī 6306)

"I acknowledge to You Your blessing upon me" — *abūʾu laka bi-niʿmatika ʿalayya* — is 16:53 turned into a daily prayer.

The second discipline is *consistency*: to call on God in ease as one calls on Him in distress, so that the relationship does not depend on need. The Prophet ﷺ said:

> *"Know God in ease and He will know you in hardship."* (Aḥmad 2803; cited by al-Tirmidhī)

The idolater knows God only in hardship. The believer knows Him in both, and the verse, by exposing the idolater's inconsistency, warns the believer against a subtler form of the same thing — remembering God fervently in crisis and forgetting Him in comfort. The cry of distress is natural to every human being; the gratitude of ease is the mark of faith.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:54

> **Then, when He removes the affliction from you, behold, a group among you ascribes partners unto their Lord,**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Turn After Relief**

Verse 53 described human beings crying out to God alone when affliction strikes. Verse 54 describes what happens when the affliction is lifted: *thumma idhā kashafa al-ḍurra ʿankum idhā farīqun minkum bi-rabbihim yushrikūn*, "then when He removes the harm from you, behold, a party of you associate partners with their Lord." The verse completes the cycle that the Qur'an documents so often — sincerity under pressure, betrayal after relief — and it does so with grammatical features that make the betrayal's suddenness and ingratitude vivid.

**"When He Removes the Affliction": The Relief Is God's Act**

The verse attributes the removal of harm explicitly to God: *kashafa al-ḍurra*, "He removed the harm." The verb *kashafa* means to uncover, lift off, remove — as one lifts a covering. The affliction is pictured as something laid over a person that God lifts away. The same verb governs the Qur'an's statement that only God can lift affliction:

> *"And if God should touch you with adversity, there is no remover (kāshif) of it except Him; and if He intends good for you, there is no repeller of His bounty."* (Qur'an 10:107)

> *"Say: Have you considered those you call upon besides God? If God intended harm for me, could they remove (kāshifāt) His harm? Or if He intended mercy for me, could they withhold His mercy?"* (Qur'an 39:38)

The verse in al-Zumar states the argument that 16:54 assumes: the idols cannot remove harm. Only God removes it. And the people themselves know this — which is why, in verse 53, they cried to Him and not to the idols. The removal that follows is thus a direct answer to a direct plea. God heard and responded. The ingratitude that follows is therefore not ingratitude for an anonymous benefit but for a specific, requested, and granted rescue.

**"Behold": The Suddenness of the Betrayal**

The verse uses the particle *idhā* twice, in two different functions. The first, *idhā kashafa*, is conditional-temporal: "when He removes." The second, *idhā farīqun*, is *idhā al-fujāʾiyyah*, the "*idhā* of surprise," which introduces something sudden and unexpected: "*behold*, a party of you...!" Al-Zamakhsharī explains that this construction conveys that the association of partners follows the relief *immediately*, with no interval. There is no period of gratitude that gradually fades; the *shirk* returns the moment the danger passes. The Qur'an captures the same immediacy in 29:65: "when He delivers them to land, *at once* they associate."

The psychological observation is exact. Under pressure, the heart is concentrated on the single source of help. When the pressure lifts, the heart does not slowly drift back to its old habits; it snaps back, as a compressed spring releases. The intensity of the crisis-sincerity is matched by the speed of its abandonment. Al-Rāzī observes that this reveals the crisis-sincerity for what it was: not a conviction but a reflex, produced by fear and dissolving with it.

**"A Group Among You": *Farīqun Minkum***

The verse does not say "you associate" but "a *party* of you associate." The commentators note the precision. Not everyone who cries to God in distress betrays Him afterward; some are transformed by the experience and remain faithful. ʿIkrimah, whose story was mentioned at verse 53, is an example: the storm at sea made him a Muslim for life. The verse, by saying *farīq*, "a party," acknowledges the distinction. It condemns those who revert, not all who were rescued.

Al-Zamakhsharī also notes that *farīq* here may be a deliberate understatement or restraint — the Qur'an does not say "most of you," though it might have, but "a party," leaving room for each hearer to decide which party he belongs to. The verse thus functions as a mirror: it does not accuse the hearer directly but describes a group and lets him recognize himself.

**"Ascribes Partners Unto Their Lord": The Weight of *Bi-rabbihim***

The verse says they associate partners *bi-rabbihim*, "with their Lord." The choice of the word *Rabb* — Lord, Sustainer, the One who nurtures and provides — rather than *Allāh* is deliberate and sharpens the reproach. The one with whom they associate partners is not a distant deity but *their Lord*: the One who created them, sustained them, and has just now rescued them from the harm they cried about. Al-Rāzī notes the pointedness: to associate partners with one's *Rabb*, immediately after He has demonstrated His lordship by removing one's affliction, is the height of ingratitude and inconsistency.

The word order — *bi-rabbihim yushrikūn*, with the object fronted before the verb — adds emphasis: "with *their Lord* they associate." It is as if to say: of all beings with whom to associate partners, they choose the very One who has just saved them.

**The Forms of the Return to *Shirk***

The commentators describe how the return to *shirk* manifested among the Makkans. They returned to their idols, offering them thanks for the rescue that God alone had performed. They attributed the relief to the intercession of the idols, or to their own cleverness, or to fortune. Al-Qurṭubī notes that they would say, "Had it not been for such-and-such a god, we would have perished." The Prophet ﷺ was alert to subtler forms of the same thing among the believers, and forbade even the language of it. When a man said to him, "What God wills and you will," he replied:

> *"Have you made me a rival to God? Rather: What God alone wills."* (Aḥmad 1839; al-Nasāʾī in al-Kubrā)

And after a night of rain, he reported God as saying:

> *"Whoever said, 'We were given rain by the grace and mercy of God,' is a believer in Me and a disbeliever in the stars; and whoever said, 'We were given rain by such-and-such a star,' is a disbeliever in Me and a believer in the stars."* (al-Bukhārī 846; Muslim 71)

Attributing relief to a star, a person, or one's own effort, rather than to God, is the "association" of 16:54 in a modern dress. The idols have changed; the mechanism has not.

**The Doctrine: Blessing as a Test**

The verse teaches that relief is a test as much as affliction is. The Qur'an states the principle in general terms:

> *"And We test you with evil and with good as a trial, and to Us you will be returned."* (Qur'an 21:35)

The test of affliction is whether one turns to God; most pass it, as verse 53 shows. The test of relief is whether one remains with God after the need has passed; verse 54 shows that many fail. The second test is harder because it is not felt as a test. In affliction the stakes are obvious; in relief, the person feels that the test is over and relaxes. This is precisely when the return to old habits occurs. Al-Ghazālī and the scholars of the inner life taught that the servant should be more vigilant in ease than in hardship, because hardship guards him by its very nature while ease leaves him unguarded.

**The Contrast With the Believer**

The Prophet ﷺ described the believer as one for whom both states — ease and hardship — become good, precisely because he responds correctly to both:

> *"How wonderful is the affair of the believer, for all of his affairs are good, and that is for no one but the believer. If ease befalls him, he is grateful, and that is good for him; and if hardship befalls him, he is patient, and that is good for him."* (Muslim 2999)

The idolater of 16:53–54 is patient in neither sense and grateful in neither. In hardship he cries out — not patience, but panic — and in ease he associates partners — not gratitude, but betrayal. The believer's response inverts both: patience in hardship, gratitude in ease. The two verses, read together, thus define the believer by negation: he is the one who, when God removes affliction from him, does *not* belong to "the party that associates."

**The Application: What One Does After Being Answered**

The verse asks every reader a concrete question: what did you do after the last time God answered you? Every person has cried out in some extremity — illness, danger, loss, fear — and been relieved. The verse asks whether, after the relief, the person's life changed in the direction of God or snapped back to what it was. The honest answer for most is the second, at least in part. The verse does not condemn without remedy; its purpose is to make the pattern visible so that it can be broken. The next time relief comes, the person who has read 16:54 knows that a second test has begun, and that its passing consists of one thing: remaining, in ease, where one was driven in distress.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:55

> **so as to be ungrateful for that which We have given them. So enjoy yourselves! For soon you will know.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Purpose Clause and the Threat**

Verse 55 completes the sentence begun in verse 54. The party who associate partners with their Lord after He has relieved them do so *li-yakfurū bimā ātaynāhum*, "so as to disbelieve in what We have given them." The verse then breaks off from description into direct address — a command that is in fact a threat: *fa-tamattaʿū fa-sawfa taʿlamūn*, "so enjoy yourselves; soon you will know." The verse thus gives, in a single line, both the inner meaning of the idolaters' behavior and its consequence.

**"So as to Be Ungrateful": The *Lām* of Consequence**

The clause begins with *li-*, which ordinarily introduces purpose ("in order to"). But the idolaters did not consciously intend to be ungrateful; ingratitude was the *result* of their *shirk*, not its aim. The commentators therefore identify this *lām* as *lām al-ʿāqibah*, the *lām* of consequence or outcome — the same construction used in 28:8, where Pharaoh's family took up the infant Moses "so that he might become for them an enemy and a grief," though this was the last thing they intended. Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Rāzī both read the *lām* here in this sense: their association of partners *had the effect* of ingratitude for God's gifts.

Some commentators, however, retain a sense of purpose, sharpened by irony. Al-Zamakhsharī suggests that the verse frames their action *as if* ingratitude were their goal — as if they had said, "Let us associate partners with Him precisely in order to deny His blessing" — in order to expose the absurdity of what they did. No sane person would set out to be ungrateful to his rescuer, yet their conduct amounts to exactly that, and the verse describes it as though it were deliberate to make its ugliness plain.

**"For That Which We Have Given Them": *Kufr al-Niʿmah***

The object of their ingratitude is *mā ātaynāhum*, "what We have given them" — the blessings of verse 53 and, immediately, the rescue of verse 54. The verse thus names the specific sin that the sūrah has been building toward: *kufr al-niʿmah*, disbelief in or ingratitude for blessing.

The Arabic word *kufr* originally means to cover. The farmer who covers seed with earth is a *kāfir* in the root sense (57:20 uses the word *kuffār* for tillers). Applied to belief, *kufr* is covering the truth that one knows; applied to blessing, it is covering the gift — denying its source, hiding it, treating it as though it had not been given or had come from elsewhere. *Shirk* after rescue is *kufr al-niʿmah* in its purest form: the gift is acknowledged (they enjoy the relief) but its Giver is covered over (they thank the idols).

The sūrah returns to this concept at its climax, in the parable of the ungrateful town:

> *"And God presents an example: a town that was secure and at ease, its provision coming to it in abundance from every place; but it was ungrateful for the blessings of God (fa-kafarat bi-anʿumi Allāh), so God made it taste the garment of hunger and fear for what they had been doing."* (Qur'an 16:112)

Verse 55 names the sin; verse 112 shows its punishment. The sūrah's name — al-Naḥl, but also, by its theme, *al-Niʿam* — identifies the axis on which the whole chapter turns: blessing given, blessing acknowledged or denied.

**The Opposite: *Shukr***

The Qur'an sets *shukr*, gratitude, against *kufr* as its exact contrary: *"If you are grateful, I will surely increase you; but if you are ungrateful (kafartum), My punishment is severe"* (14:7). Gratitude, for the scholars, consists of three elements: acknowledging the blessing in the heart as coming from God, praising Him with the tongue, and using the blessing in obedience to Him. The idolaters of 16:54–55 failed at the first step: they did not acknowledge the source. Everything else follows from that failure.

Ibn al-Qayyim summarized the relationship: *shukr* is built on five foundations — the submission of the grateful to the one thanked, love of him, acknowledgment of his blessing, praise of him for it, and not using the blessing in what he dislikes. *Kufr al-niʿmah* is the negation of each.

**"So Enjoy Yourselves!": The Imperative of Threat**

The verse then shifts abruptly to direct address: *fa-tamattaʿū*, "so enjoy yourselves." This is a grammatical imperative, but its meaning is not permission or command; it is *amr al-tahdīd*, the imperative of threat. The commentators — al-Zamakhsharī, al-Rāzī, al-Qurṭubī — all identify it as such. It is the form of speech used by one who has finished arguing and is warning: "Go on, then; do as you like; you will see."

The Qur'an uses this form in several places:

> *"Say: Enjoy yourselves, for your destination is the Fire."* (Qur'an 14:30)

> *"So enjoy yourselves; soon you will know."* (Qur'an 30:34; 39:8)

> *"Do what you will; truly He sees what you do."* (Qur'an 41:40)

Verse 30:34 and 39:8 use the identical phrase to 16:55, and in the same context — the ingratitude of those who associate partners after being relieved. The formula has a fixed meaning: enjoyment now, knowledge later. The word *tamattuʿ*, enjoyment, derives from *matāʿ*, the provision or goods of this world, and always in the Qur'an carries the connotation of the temporary — *"the enjoyment of this world is little"* (4:77). To be told to "enjoy yourselves" is to be told that enjoyment is all one will have.

**"For Soon You Will Know": *Fa-sawfa Taʿlamūn***

The verse ends with the threat proper: *fa-sawfa taʿlamūn*, "soon you will know." The particle *sawfa* marks the future with a sense of certainty and some interval — not "immediately" but "assuredly, in time." What they will know is left unstated, and the ellipsis is more forceful than any specification. Al-Rāzī notes that omitting the object leaves the mind to fill it with the worst: they will know the consequence of their ingratitude, the reality of the resurrection they denied, the worthlessness of the partners they associated, the truth of the Prophet they rejected.

The verb is *taʿlamūn*, "you will know." The choice of "know" rather than "see" or "suffer" connects to the sūrah's recurring theme of knowledge and ignorance. The idolaters acted from ignorance — "most of them do not know" (vv. 38, 75, 101) — and the verse promises that the ignorance will end. They will know. But the knowledge will come when it no longer benefits, as verse 39 implied of the deniers of resurrection. The Qur'an describes this useless knowledge: *"They will say: Alas for us! We were wrongdoers"* (21:14). The threat of 16:55 is not that they will never know but that they will know *too late*.

**The Transition From Third Person to Second Person**

The verse begins in the third person ("so as to be ungrateful for what We have given *them*") and shifts to the second ("so enjoy *yourselves*"). This is *iltifāt* again, as in verse 51, and the effect is similar: the description of a group becomes a direct confrontation with it. Al-Zamakhsharī notes that the shift signals the end of patience — God has been speaking *about* them; now He speaks *to* them, and what He says is a dismissal. The verse thus dramatizes, in its grammar, the movement from divine forbearance to divine warning.

**The Theological Point: Gratitude as the Response to Rescue**

The three verses 53–55 together teach a doctrine about the proper response to divine rescue. God answers the cry of the distressed — this is His mercy, and it is unconditional; He answers even the idolater. But the answer creates an obligation: the one rescued owes acknowledgment to the Rescuer. The Qur'an describes the correct response in the mouth of those who are saved:

> *"And when you have boarded the ship, you and those with you, then say: Praise be to God, Who has saved us from the wrongdoing people."* (Qur'an 23:28)

> *"Praise be to God, Who has removed grief from us."* (Qur'an 35:34)

"Praise be to God who saved us" — that is *shukr*. "Thanks to our gods" — that is *kufr*. The rescue is the same in both cases; the difference lies entirely in what the rescued person does with it.

**The Application: Auditing One's Own Gratitude**

The verse invites a specific self-examination. Every person has been rescued — from illness, from danger, from financial ruin, from despair. The verse asks: after each rescue, did you cover the gift or uncover it? Did you attribute it to the doctor alone, to luck, to your own resilience, to "things working out" — or did you trace it, as verse 53 requires, to God? The verse does not forbid thanking the doctor; the Prophet ﷺ said that whoever does not thank people does not thank God (al-Tirmidhī 1954). It forbids *stopping* at the doctor — treating the means as the source. The remedy is a habit: after every relief, however small, to say what the rescued in 23:28 said. The verse's threat — "enjoy yourselves; soon you will know" — is addressed to those who never acquire this habit, and its mercy lies in being spoken now, while the enjoyment lasts and the knowing can still be chosen rather than imposed.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:56

> **And they dedicate a share of that which We have provided them to what they know not. By God, you shall surely be questioned about that which you used to fabricate.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**From Ingratitude in Principle to Ingratitude in Practice**

Verse 55 named the sin — ingratitude for what God has given. Verse 56 provides the concrete example: the idolaters take a portion of the very provision God gave them and dedicate it to their idols. The ingratitude is no longer abstract. It has a shape, a ritual, a quantity. And the verse closes with an oath and a promise of interrogation: they will be asked about it.

**"They Dedicate a Share of That Which We Have Provided Them"**

The verse says *wa-yajʿalūna li-mā lā yaʿlamūna naṣīban mimmā razaqnāhum*, "and they assign to what they do not know a share of what We have provided them." The word *naṣīb* means a portion, a share, an allotment. The word *razaqnāhum*, "We provided them," names the source: the crops, the cattle, the wealth that verses 5–16 described as God's gifts. The idolaters took from these gifts and set aside a portion for their idols.

The Qur'an describes the practice in detail in Sūrat al-Anʿām:

> *"And they assign to God from what He has created of crops and cattle a share, and they say: This is for God — by their claim — and this is for our partners. But what is for their partners does not reach God, while what is for God — this reaches their partners. Evil is that which they rule."* (Qur'an 6:136)

The commentators, drawing on this verse and on reports about pre-Islamic practice, describe the custom. The Makkans would divide their harvest and their livestock into two portions, one designated for God and one for the idols. When the portion for God was depleted or damaged, they would not replace it from the idols' portion; but when the idols' portion suffered, they would take from God's portion to make it up. Their reasoning, as Ibn ʿAbbās reported, was that God was rich and had no need, while the idols were poor and needed the offering. The result was a systematic cheating of God in favor of stones — which 6:136 ends by calling "evil judgment."

Al-Ṭabarī and al-Qurṭubī connect 16:56 directly to this practice. The share given "to what they do not know" is the share given to the idols from the crops and animals. Al-Rāzī adds the broader category of sacrifices and offerings made to idols — the *baḥīrah*, *sāʾibah*, *waṣīlah*, and *ḥām* animals that the Qur'an condemns in 5:103, set free and dedicated to the gods and forbidden for ordinary use.

**"To What They Know Not": Three Readings**

The phrase *li-mā lā yaʿlamūn*, "to what they do not know," has been read in three ways, each attested among the commentators.

The first, which al-Ṭabarī prefers, takes the subject of "know" as the idolaters and the object as the idols: they dedicate offerings to things they do not know — that is, to things about whose divinity they have no knowledge, whose supposed power to harm or benefit is unproven and in fact false. They give to what they merely *suppose* to be gods (cf. 10:66, "they follow only supposition"). This reading treats "what they know not" as a description of the epistemic groundlessness of idolatry: they give their wealth to beings whose very claim to receive it they cannot establish.

The second reading takes the idols themselves as the subject of "know": they dedicate offerings to things that *do not know* — inanimate objects that have no awareness of being worshipped, cannot perceive the offering, and will disown their worshippers on the Day of Judgment. This connects to verse 21, "they are not aware when they will be raised," and to verse 20, "they create nothing and are themselves created." Al-Zamakhsharī allows this reading: to give to what does not know is the most absurd form of giving, since the recipient cannot even receive.

The third reading, which al-Rāzī mentions, understands the phrase to refer to something the idolaters do not know the *reality* of — they give to what they do not understand, acting from blind custom and inherited habit rather than from knowledge. This connects to the sūrah's polemic against following the fathers (v. 35) and to the accusation of "legends of the ancients" (v. 24).

The readings converge on a single charge: the offering is made in ignorance, to ignorance, from ignorance. There is no knowledge anywhere in the transaction. The verse contrasts implicitly with the "people of knowledge" mentioned in verse 27 and the "people of the Reminder" in verse 43. Knowledge belongs to those who worship the One who knows; the idolaters and their idols are alike in not knowing.

**The Deeper Irony: Giving God's Provision to His Rivals**

Al-Rāzī draws out the moral logic. The provision was given by God. The idolaters take a portion of it and dedicate it to those they set beside God. They are, in effect, using the gift against the Giver — spending God's money to honor His rivals. This is the concrete form of the ingratitude named in verse 55. It is as if a man received a gift from a benefactor and immediately gave part of it to the benefactor's enemy while proclaiming the enemy's generosity. The verse exposes the practice in these terms so that its offensiveness is felt.

The Qur'an makes the same point about a related practice — the Makkans' claim that the idols intercede for them — in 10:18: "They worship besides God what neither harms them nor benefits them, and they say: These are our intercessors with God." The offering to the idols and the belief in their intercession went together, and both rested on "what they do not know."

**"By God, You Shall Surely Be Questioned": The Oath**

The second half of the verse is an oath: *ta'llāhi la-tusʾalunna ʿammā kuntum taftarūn*, "By God, you will surely be asked about what you used to fabricate." The oath particle *ta-* (as in *ta'llāhi*) is one of the three oath particles in Arabic (*wa-*, *bi-*, *ta-*) and is used only with the name of God; it carries a sense of wonder or emphasis. The verb *la-tusʾalunna* is strengthened by both the emphatic *la-* and the heavy *nūn* of emphasis: "you will most certainly be asked."

The shift to the second person — "you will be asked" — is again *iltifāt*, turning from description ("they dedicate") to confrontation. God swears by Himself that He will interrogate them. The questioning referred to is the questioning of the Day of Judgment, which the Qur'an describes as universal:

> *"So by your Lord, We will surely question them all about what they used to do."* (Qur'an 15:92–93)

> *"Stop them; indeed, they are to be questioned."* (Qur'an 37:24)

The questioning is not for God's information; He knows what they did (vv. 19, 23). It is for the establishment of proof against them — the *iqāmat al-ḥujjah* that verse 39 described — and for their own confrontation with what they did. Al-Rāzī notes that the questioning is *tawbīkh*, reproach: the question "Why did you do this?" will be asked, and there will be no answer.

**"That Which You Used to Fabricate": *Iftirāʾ***

The object of the questioning is *mā kuntum taftarūn*, "what you used to fabricate." The verb *iftarā* means to invent a falsehood, to forge a lie, to fabricate. The idolaters' entire system — the divinity of the idols, the legitimacy of the offerings, the claim that God had sanctioned the division — was a fabrication. The Qur'an uses the word most severely of fabrications about God Himself: *"Who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie about God?"* (6:21, 93, 144; 7:37; 10:17; 11:18; 18:15; 29:68; 61:7). The offerings to idols were such a fabrication: a lie about God, claiming He had partners deserving of a share.

The continuous form *kuntum taftarūn*, "you *used to* fabricate," indicates habitual practice. This was not a single act but a way of life, sustained over generations, and every instance of it will be brought forward.

**The Sequence With What Follows**

Verse 56 begins a new subsection of the sūrah (vv. 56–62) that catalogues specific fabrications of the idolaters: offerings to idols (v. 56), daughters ascribed to God (v. 57), the murder of their own daughters (vv. 58–59), and the ascription of evil to God while claiming good for themselves (vv. 60–62). Each is a fabrication, and each will be questioned. The verse's closing oath thus governs the whole passage: everything about to be described is subject to interrogation.

**The Application: Where One's Share Goes**

The verse has a direct modern application, once the idols are recognized in their contemporary forms. Every person receives provision from God and allots it. The question the verse poses is: to what? A portion of wealth spent on what God has forbidden, a portion of time dedicated to what displaces Him, a portion of loyalty given to ideologies or persons treated as ultimate — these are the modern *naṣīb li-mā lā yaʿlamūn*, shares dedicated to what one does not truly know. The Prophet ﷺ said that no servant's feet will move on the Day of Judgment until he is asked about four things, including *"his wealth: from where he acquired it and on what he spent it"* (al-Tirmidhī 2417). The verse's oath — "you will surely be asked" — applies to that spending. The believer, aware of it, allots his share consciously: to God, to what God has commanded, to what he *knows* rather than merely supposes, so that when the question comes, there is an answer.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:57

> **And they assign daughters unto God—glory be to Him!—while they have what they desire.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Second Fabrication**

Verse 56 described the idolaters' first fabrication: dedicating a share of God's provision to idols. Verse 57 describes the second, more offensive one: *wa-yajʿalūna li'llāhi al-banāt*, "and they assign daughters to God." The verb is the same — *yajʿalūna*, "they assign" or "make" — connecting the two verses and marking both as arbitrary human inventions. The first assigned God's property to others; the second assigns to God Himself something He does not have and something they themselves despise.

**The Belief Behind the Verse**

The commentators identify the belief and those who held it. Al-Qurṭubī and al-Ṭabarī report that the tribes of Khuzāʿah and Kinānah, among others, held that the angels were the daughters of God. The Qur'an addresses this belief repeatedly:

> *"Has your Lord chosen you for sons and taken from among the angels daughters? Truly you speak a grave word."* (Qur'an 17:40)

> *"And they have made the angels, who are servants of the Most Merciful, females. Did they witness their creation? Their testimony will be recorded, and they will be questioned."* (Qur'an 43:19)

> *"So ask them: Does your Lord have daughters while they have sons? Or did We create the angels female while they were witnesses?"* (Qur'an 37:149–150)

> *"Is the male for you and the female for Him? That, then, is an unjust division."* (Qur'an 53:21–22)

The passage in al-Najm gives the belief's context: the Makkans worshipped al-Lāt, al-ʿUzzā, and Manāt, three goddesses they regarded as female intermediaries and as daughters of God. Their theology thus assigned to God female offspring, and the angels were assimilated into this scheme as divine daughters. The verse in Sūrat al-Zukhruf (43:19) asks the question that exposes its groundlessness: *"Did they witness their creation?"* They had no knowledge; they fabricated.

**"Glory Be to Him!": The Interjection**

The verse interrupts itself with *subḥānahu*, "Glory be to Him!" — a declaration of God's transcendence inserted between the statement of the fabrication and its completion. Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Rāzī explain the function: it is an immediate rejection, a repudiation that cannot wait until the sentence is finished. As soon as the claim "they assign daughters to God" is uttered, the divine speech recoils from it: *Glory be to Him* — He is far exalted above this.

The word *subḥān* derives from *sabaḥa*, to swim or move swiftly through water or air, and by extension to be distant, removed. *Subḥān Allāh* means "God is far removed from" — from every defect, every attribute of creatures, every imperfection. The commentators note that the interjection here carries two meanings: exaltation of God above having any offspring at all (since offspring implies need, division, and likeness — all impossible for God), and exaltation above the specific insult of being assigned the offspring the idolaters themselves considered inferior.

The Qur'an makes the first point systematically in Sūrat al-Ikhlāṣ: *"He neither begets nor is begotten"* (112:3). Begetting requires a partner, a process, a passage of time, and a resulting being that is of the same kind as the begetter — none of which is possible for the One who is eternal, without partner, and without likeness (42:11). The angels, whom the idolaters called God's daughters, are His creation and His servants (v. 49–50), and to call them His offspring is to place them in a relation to Him that no creature can have.

**"While They Have What They Desire"**

The second clause is the verse's cutting edge: *wa-lahum mā yashtahūn*, "and they have what they desire." The idolaters assigned daughters to God, but for themselves they wanted — and claimed — sons. The word *yashtahūn*, from *shahwah*, desire, describes what they craved: male offspring, which in their culture meant strength, honor, continuation of the line, and protection.

The verse's construction has been noted by the grammarians. The first clause, *yajʿalūna li'llāhi al-banāt*, has the verb, the indirect object, and the direct object. The second clause, *wa-lahum mā yashtahūn*, is a nominal sentence — "and for them is what they desire" — with no verb. Al-Zamakhsharī observes that this asymmetry is deliberate: it would have been improper to say "and they assign to themselves what they desire" as a parallel, because that would make it seem they had the power to assign themselves sons; the Qur'an instead states the fact of their preference without granting them the agency. Others note that the shift from verbal to nominal sentence gives the second clause the tone of an aside — "and they, of course, have what they want" — that heightens the irony.

**The Argument: Their Own Standard Convicts Them**

The verse's argument does not depend on establishing that daughters are inferior to sons; the Qur'an does not hold this, and the following verses (58–59) will condemn the idolaters' contempt for daughters as a crime. The argument is rather *ad hominem* in the proper sense: it convicts the idolaters by their own standard. *They* considered daughters inferior. *They* were ashamed of daughters and buried them. And yet *they* assigned daughters to God while keeping the sons for themselves. By their own valuation, they had given God the lesser and kept the greater — an insult that would enrage any human being, let alone the Lord of all.

The Qur'an states this argument most sharply in Sūrat al-Zukhruf:

> *"Or has He taken, out of what He creates, daughters and chosen you for sons? And when one of them is given tidings of what he attributes to the Most Merciful, his face becomes dark, and he suppresses grief."* (Qur'an 43:16–17)

And in Sūrat al-Najm: *"That, then, is an unjust division"* (53:22) — *qismatun ḍīzā*, a crooked, unfair apportionment. The verse in al-Naḥl relies on the same logic: the inconsistency between what they attribute to God and what they want for themselves reveals both the falsity of the attribution and the baseness of the attitude behind it.

**Two Wrongs in One Verse**

The commentators identify two distinct offenses compressed into the verse. The first is theological: ascribing offspring to God at all, which is *shirk* and a denial of His transcendence. The second is moral: the contempt for daughters implied in the comparison, which is a wrong against half of humanity and against the divine wisdom in creating both sexes. The verse addresses the first through *subḥānahu* and the second through the contrast with "what they desire." Verses 58 and 59 will develop the second offense in full.

**The Qur'an's Valuation of Daughters**

Because the verse's argument uses the idolaters' contempt for daughters, it is necessary to state clearly that the Qur'an itself does not share that contempt. The Qur'an attributes the distribution of sons and daughters to God's will and wisdom alone:

> *"To God belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth; He creates what He wills. He gives to whom He wills females, and He gives to whom He wills males, or He pairs them males and females, and He makes whom He wills barren. Truly He is Knowing, Powerful."* (Qur'an 42:49–50)

Here, notably, the females are mentioned first. The Prophet ﷺ raised daughters and honored them, and he made the raising of daughters a path to Paradise:

> *"Whoever has three daughters and is patient with them, and feeds them and gives them drink and clothes them from his wealth, they will be a shield for him from the Fire on the Day of Resurrection."* (Ibn Mājah 3669; Aḥmad 17403)

> *"Whoever raises two girls until they reach maturity, he and I will come on the Day of Resurrection like this"* — and he joined his fingers. (Muslim 2631)

The verse under discussion, read with these texts, teaches that the idolaters' error was double: they lied about God, and they were wrong about daughters. The Islamic reform corrected both.

**The Modern Form of the Verse's Error**

The specific belief — angels as God's daughters — no longer exists, but the structure of the error persists. Every ideology that assigns to God what it would not accept for itself, or projects onto the divine its own hierarchies of value, repeats the Makkan move. And every society that, while professing equality, still receives the birth of a daughter with less joy than a son, or ranks female life below male, still harbors the attitude the verse exposes. The Qur'an's response is *subḥānahu* — God is above your projections — and the reminder that "He gives to whom He wills females" as a gift, not a burden. The verse asks its readers to examine what they assign to God and what they keep for themselves, and to make sure that the apportionment is not, in the words of Sūrat al-Najm, "a crooked division."

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:58

> **And when one of them receives tidings of a female [child], his face darkens, and he is choked with anguish.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**From the Doctrine to the Man**

Verse 57 stated that the idolaters assign daughters to God while keeping sons for themselves. Verse 58 leaves the level of doctrine and shows an individual man at the moment he learns that a daughter has been born to him. The sūrah's method here is to make the abstract concrete — to expose the contempt behind the theology by portraying it in a single face. *Wa-idhā bushshira aḥaduhum bi'l-unthā ẓalla wajhuhu muswaddan wa-huwa kaẓīm*, "And when one of them is given tidings of a female, his face remains darkened, and he is choked with grief."

**"Receives Tidings": The Irony of *Bushshira***

The verb *bushshira* is from *bushrā*, good news, and *bashshara* means to bring glad tidings. The Qur'an uses it for the announcement of Isaac to Abraham (11:71; 15:53), of John to Zechariah (3:39; 19:7), of Jesus to Mary (3:45). The birth of a child is, in the Qur'an's vocabulary, *bushrā* — good news, a divine gift. Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Rāzī note the irony: the verse uses the word for glad tidings precisely because the birth of a daughter *is* glad tidings in reality, even though the man receives it as calamity. The word judges him. What God sends as good news, he receives as disgrace.

Some commentators observed that the word may also be used in Arabic for any news that changes the face — good or bad — but the dominant sense is glad tidings, and the Qur'an's usage confirms the ironic reading.

**"His Face Darkens": *Ẓalla Wajhuhu Muswaddan***

The verse describes the physical effect: *ẓalla wajhuhu muswaddan*, "his face becomes and remains blackened." The verb *ẓalla* denotes continuance through the day — the darkness does not pass in a moment but settles on his features. *Muswadd* is from *sawād*, blackness, and describes the darkening of the face with grief, shame, or rage — the blood draining, the features contracting. Al-Rāzī explains that the Arabs used "blackening of the face" for extreme grief and humiliation, as they used "whitening of the face" for joy and honor. The Qur'an uses the same imagery for the Day of Judgment, when "faces will be whitened and faces will be blackened" (3:106).

The image thus carries a hidden judgment. The man's face darkens at the birth of his daughter. The Qur'an reserves the darkened face for the disgraced on the Day of Judgment. The man who darkens at God's gift is, in the verse's imagery, already wearing the face of the condemned.

The identical phrase appears in Sūrat al-Zukhruf, in the parallel discussion of the same belief:

> *"And when one of them is given tidings of what he attributes to the Most Merciful, his face becomes darkened, and he is choked with grief."* (Qur'an 43:17)

The wording of 43:17 adds a phrase that makes the argument of 16:57 explicit: he is given tidings "of what he *attributes to the Most Merciful*" — that is, of the very thing he assigns to God. His own face reveals what he thinks of what he has given God.

**"And He Is Choked With Anguish": *Wa-huwa Kaẓīm***

The final word, *kaẓīm*, is from the root *k-ẓ-m*, which describes holding in, suppressing, restraining — as a waterskin is tied shut to hold its contents, or as a person holds his breath. *Kaẓm al-ghayẓ* is the suppression of anger, praised in 3:134 as a quality of the righteous: "those who restrain anger." Here, however, *kaẓīm* describes a man full of grief and rage that he suppresses — swallowing it, holding it in, unable to express it because custom forbids him from showing it openly, yet unable to release it. Al-Zamakhsharī defines *kaẓīm* as one filled with grief who holds it in. The Qur'an uses the word for Jacob's grief over Joseph — *"his eyes whitened from grief, and he was suppressing"* (12:84) — and for Jonah in the belly of the fish, *"choked with distress"* (68:48).

The man of 16:58 is thus portrayed in a state of internal suffocation. He cannot celebrate, because he considers the daughter a disgrace; he cannot openly weep or rage, because that too would be shameful; so he holds it in, and the suppressed emotion darkens his face and chokes his breath. The verse presents this as pathetic, not sympathetic — a man tormented by a falsehood, suffering over a blessing because he has been taught to see it as a curse.

**The Psychology the Verse Exposes**

The verse's portrait is psychologically exact, and the commentators draw out its implications. The man's suffering is entirely self-inflicted, generated by a system of values that was itself a fabrication. Nothing about the daughter is harmful. The harm exists only in his valuation of her, and that valuation was inherited from a society whose beliefs the sūrah has been dismantling since its first verse. The darkened face is the visible cost of a false belief — the way a lie about the world produces real pain when the world fails to conform to it.

Al-Rāzī identifies the roots of the attitude: fear of poverty (a daughter was seen as a mouth to feed who would not earn), fear of shame (a daughter could be captured in raids and dishonored, or could marry beneath the family), and the calculation of tribal strength (sons fought; daughters did not). Each of these fears was a failure of trust in God — the fear of poverty a denial that God provides (17:31: "We provide for them and for you"), the fear of shame a substitution of tribal honor for divine honor, the calculation of strength a reliance on numbers rather than on God.

**The Contrast With the Prophet's Practice**

The Prophet ﷺ transformed this reception of daughters through his own example and his teaching. His own children who survived infancy were daughters — Zaynab, Ruqayyah, Umm Kulthūm, and Fāṭimah — and he loved and honored them publicly. Of Fāṭimah he said, *"Fāṭimah is a part of me; whoever angers her angers me"* (al-Bukhārī 3714). He would stand when she entered and seat her in his place (Abū Dāwūd 5217). He taught that a daughter was not a burden but a shield:

> *"Whoever is tested with anything of daughters and treats them well, they will be a screen for him from the Fire."* (al-Bukhārī 1418; Muslim 2629)

And he condemned the preference for sons in the strongest terms through his treatment of the practice that followed from it, as verse 59 will show.

**The Verse as an Argument in Its Context**

Within the sequence of verses 56–62, verse 58 serves a precise function. Verse 57 made the charge: they assign daughters to God. Verse 58 proves the charge's offensiveness by showing that they themselves cannot bear daughters. The argument is complete when the reader sees the man's darkened face: *this* is what they give God; *this* is how they receive it themselves. The inconsistency is not an intellectual error but a visceral one, written on the face.

**The Verse and the Continuing Reality**

The sūrah's portrait has not lost its relevance. In many societies today, the birth of a daughter is still received with disappointment, and in some, sex-selective practices have produced demographic distortions that the Qur'an's condemnation of female infanticide anticipated. The face that darkens at the news of a daughter is not confined to seventh-century Arabia. The verse's response is the same in every age: the darkening is a judgment on the man, not on the child. What God sends as *bushrā* is *bushrā*. The person who cannot receive it as such has been captured by a falsehood, and the falsehood, not the daughter, is his real misfortune.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:59

> **He hides from the people on account of the evil of the tidings he has been given. Shall he keep it in humiliation, or bury it in the dust? Behold! Evil indeed is the judgment they make.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Man Continues: From Grief to Crime**

Verse 58 showed the man's face darkening at the news of a daughter. Verse 59 follows him out of the room. *Yatawārā mina al-qawmi min sūʾi mā bushshira bih*, "he hides himself from the people because of the evil of what he was given tidings of." His shame drives him into concealment, and in concealment he deliberates between two options — both shameful — before the verse pronounces its judgment on the whole calculus: *alā sāʾa mā yaḥkumūn*, "evil indeed is what they judge."

**"He Hides From the People": *Yatawārā***

The verb *tawārā*, from the root *w-r-y*, means to conceal oneself, to go behind something. The man hides from his people — his tribe, his neighbors, those whose opinion determines his honor. Al-Rāzī notes the significance: the man's shame is entirely social. He is not ashamed before God; he is ashamed before *al-qawm*, the people. The whole system of contempt for daughters was a social construction, sustained by the anticipated judgment of others, and the man's flight into hiding shows that the judgment he feared was theirs.

The Qur'an's diagnosis is precise: the man's suffering comes from fear of what people will say. This is the disease the sūrah has been treating throughout — the substitution of the community's approval for God's approval, the worship of the fathers' ways (v. 35), the preference for the tribe's standards over the truth.

**"The Evil of the Tidings": The Reversal of Value**

The phrase *min sūʾi mā bushshira bih*, "because of the evil of what he was given tidings of," repeats the ironic word *bushshira* from verse 58 and now pairs it with *sūʾ*, evil. The tidings were *bushrā*, good news; he received them as *sūʾ*, evil. The juxtaposition names the man's error exactly: he has inverted the value of what God sent. Al-Zamakhsharī notes that the "evil" belongs to the man's estimation, not to the thing itself — it is evil *in his judgment*, and the verse will end by condemning that judgment.

**The Two Options: Keep in Humiliation or Bury in the Dust**

In his hiding place the man deliberates: *a-yumsikuhu ʿalā hūnin am yadussuhu fī al-turāb*, "shall he keep it in humiliation, or bury it in the dust?" The verse presents his options in his own terms, and both are monstrous.

The first option is to keep the daughter *ʿalā hūn*, "in humiliation" or "in contempt" — that is, to let her live but to treat her as a disgrace, to raise her with the daily reminder that her existence is a shame. The word *hūn* denotes lowness, abasement, degradation. Al-Ṭabarī explains that this means keeping her in a state of contempt and neglect. Some early authorities read *ʿalā hawān*, with the same meaning, and Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to have glossed it as "in disgrace."

The second option is *yadussuhu fī al-turāb*, "to thrust it into the dust" — to bury the infant alive. The verb *dassa* means to push something into something else so as to conceal it, and the choice of word is chilling: the daughter is not "buried" with the dignity of a funeral but *thrust*, shoved into the earth like something to be hidden. This was the practice of *waʾd*, the burying of female infants alive, which the Qur'an condemns in its most memorable form:

> *"And when the girl buried alive is asked, for what sin she was killed."* (Qur'an 81:8–9)

The passage in al-Takwīr places the questioning of the buried girl among the events of the Day of Judgment. She will be asked — not her killer, but she — and the question will be posed in her hearing so that the murderer must listen to it. Al-Qurṭubī notes that this indirect framing is more devastating than a direct accusation.

**The Practice of *Waʾd* in Pre-Islamic Arabia**

The commentators describe the practice from historical reports. Al-Qurṭubī records that a man would leave his pregnant wife near a pit when her time approached; if she gave birth to a son, she kept him, and if to a daughter, the child was thrown into the pit. Others waited until the girl was older — some accounts speak of six years — and then took her into the desert on the pretext of a visit, dug a pit, and pushed her in. The Qur'an mentions the motive of poverty in 17:31 and 6:151 ("do not kill your children for fear of poverty") and the motive of shame here.

Al-Qurṭubī records the report of Qays ibn ʿĀṣim, a chief of Tamīm, who came to the Prophet ﷺ and confessed that he had buried daughters alive in the Age of Ignorance — some accounts say eight, others twelve. He asked what he could do to expiate this. The Prophet told him to free a slave for each of them, and when Qays said he was a man of camels, he told him to sacrifice a camel for each. And al-Qurṭubī records the report that a man told the Prophet that he had taken his daughter, who was old enough to speak, to a pit and pushed her in, and that as he threw the earth on her she was calling, "Father, father!" — and that the Prophet wept until his beard was wet, and said, "I am not able to bear it. Tell me no more."

The Prophet ﷺ made the prohibition of *waʾd* one of the things God forbade absolutely:

> *"Truly God has forbidden you disobedience to mothers, burying daughters alive, withholding [what is due] and demanding [what is not due]."* (al-Bukhārī 2408; Muslim 593)

**"Evil Indeed Is the Judgment They Make": The Verdict**

The verse ends: *alā sāʾa mā yaḥkumūn*, "Behold! Evil is what they judge." The particle *alā* is a call to attention — "Listen! Take note!" — and *sāʾa* is a verb of blame, "how evil is." The object of the blame is *mā yaḥkumūn*, "what they judge" or "how they rule."

The commentators identify what "judgment" the verse condemns, and there are two layers. The first is the judgment of the man in his hiding place — the deliberation between humiliation and burial, in which both options are evil and the possibility of simply loving the child does not occur to him. The second, and larger, is the judgment of verse 57: the assignment of daughters to God while wanting sons for themselves. Al-Rāzī connects the two: their evil judgment is that they assign to God what they themselves find so intolerable that they kill it. The word *yaḥkumūn* thus picks up the whole passage since verse 56 and pronounces a single verdict on it: everything they have judged — about the idols' share, about God's daughters, about their own daughters — is evil.

The phrase echoes 6:136, "evil is what they rule" (*sāʾa mā yaḥkumūn*), where the same words condemned the division of crops between God and the idols. The identical verdict on two different fabrications marks them as products of the same corrupt faculty of judgment.

**The Theological Root of the Crime**

The passage as a whole (vv. 56–59) traces female infanticide to its theological root. A society that had lost the knowledge of God's oneness and of His provision (v. 53) came to fear poverty and shame more than it feared God. Fearing these, it devalued daughters. Devaluing daughters, it killed them. The crime was not, at bottom, an economic or social phenomenon; it was a consequence of a false theology. This is why the Qur'an addresses it in a passage about *shirk* and ingratitude, and why the reform of the practice came through the reform of belief. The verse's *sāʾa mā yaḥkumūn* condemns a *judgment* — an act of the mind — because the crime began in the mind, in a valuation that God had not authorized.

The Qur'an's alternative is stated in the verses on killing children:

> *"And do not kill your children for fear of poverty. We provide for them and for you. Truly, killing them is a great sin."* (Qur'an 17:31)

"We provide for them and for you" — the order is significant: the child's provision is mentioned first. The fear that motivated the crime is dissolved by the doctrine of *rizq* that the sūrah has been teaching since verse 5.

**The Legacy of the Verse**

Islam ended *waʾd* in Arabia within a generation. The verse and its companions accomplished what no tribal custom, no philosophical argument, and no economic change had accomplished: they made the killing of daughters unthinkable to those who believed. This is one of the clearest historical demonstrations of the Qur'an's transforming power, and it was achieved not by legislation alone but by changing the *judgment* — by making people see the daughter as *bushrā* rather than *sūʾ*. The verse's verdict on the old judgment, *sāʾa mā yaḥkumūn*, became the community's verdict, and the girl who was once thrust into the dust became the one whose good upbringing was a shield from the Fire.

**The Contemporary Echo**

The practice the verse condemns has modern forms — sex-selective abortion, the neglect of girls' nutrition and education, the social demotion of families with daughters. Wherever the birth of a girl is received as *sūʾ*, the man of 16:59 is still hiding from his people. The verse's response is unchanged: the judgment is evil, the child is a gift, and the God who provides for her has forbidden her killing and promised Paradise to those who raise her well. The verse ends with a call to attention — *alā* — because the crime it describes has always depended on people not looking. It asks them to look.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:60

> **To those who believe not in the Hereafter belongs the description of evil, and unto God belongs the loftiest description. And He is the Mighty, the Wise.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Summing Up the Passage**

Verses 56–59 catalogued the idolaters' fabrications: the share of provision given to idols, the daughters assigned to God, the murderous contempt for their own daughters. Verse 60 steps back and pronounces a general judgment on the two parties involved — the idolaters and God. *Li'lladhīna lā yuʾminūna bi'l-ākhirati mathalu al-sawʾ*, "to those who do not believe in the Hereafter belongs the attribute of evil"; *wa-li'llāhi al-mathalu al-aʿlā*, "and to God belongs the highest attribute." The verse sets the two descriptions against each other so that the contrast is total.

**"Those Who Believe Not in the Hereafter": Why This Designation**

The idolaters are identified here not as "those who associate partners" but as "those who do not believe in the Hereafter." The choice is deliberate. Al-Rāzī observes that the denial of the Hereafter is the root from which their other evils grew. A man who believed he would be questioned about his daughters (v. 56, "you will surely be asked") would not bury them; a man who believed he would stand before the God he had assigned daughters to would not have made the assignment. The fabrications of verses 56–59 were possible only because their authors did not expect to answer for them. The verse names the root, not the branches.

The connection was made explicit in verse 22: "those who do not believe in the Hereafter, their hearts are denying, and they are arrogant." The denial of the Hereafter and the corruption of the heart go together, and 16:60 names the result: *mathalu al-sawʾ*.

**"The Description of Evil": *Mathalu al-Sawʾ***

The word *mathal* here requires care. Its ordinary meaning is likeness, example, parable; but the commentators explain that in this verse it means *ṣifah*, attribute or description — the qualities by which something is characterized. Al-Ṭabarī, al-Zamakhsharī, and al-Rāzī take *mathalu al-sawʾ* as "the evil attribute" or "the evil description": the idolaters are characterized by evil qualities.

The commentators specify what these are. Al-Zamakhsharī lists them: the need for offspring, the preference for sons, the contempt for daughters, the burying of infants, the fear of poverty — all the qualities that the preceding verses displayed. Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to have glossed the phrase more specifically as the ascription of offspring to God, or the reality of their belief in idols. Al-Rāzī broadens it to the whole complex of ignorance, cruelty, and inconsistency that the passage exposed. The idolaters, in short, are described by evil: their beliefs are evil, their practices are evil, their judgment (v. 59) is evil.

Some commentators read *mathal* in its parabolic sense here as well: the idolaters are themselves an example of evil — a cautionary instance to be held up and learned from. Both senses hold.

**"And Unto God Belongs the Loftiest Description": *Al-Mathalu al-Aʿlā***

Against the evil description of the deniers stands *al-mathalu al-aʿlā*, "the highest description." The word *aʿlā* is the superlative of *ʿalī*, high: not merely "high" or "higher" but "highest," the summit beyond which nothing rises. To God belongs every attribute of perfection in its highest degree.

The commentators fill out the meaning. Al-Ṭabarī and al-Qurṭubī report from Ibn ʿAbbās that *al-mathal al-aʿlā* is the testimony *lā ilāha illā Allāh*, "there is no god but God" — the highest description of God is His absolute oneness. Others read it as the totality of His attributes: His self-sufficiency (*ghinā*), which means He needs no offspring; His transcendence above every likeness; His knowledge, power, and wisdom; His generosity and mercy. Al-Rāzī states the general principle: God possesses every attribute of perfection and is free of every attribute of deficiency, and this is the "highest description."

The verse's logic is thus a direct answer to verse 57. The idolaters assigned daughters to God — an attribute of *deficiency*, since offspring implies need and likeness. The verse replies: the attribute of deficiency is *theirs*; God's attributes are the highest. He does not need offspring because He is self-sufficient (*al-Ghanī*); He does not have a likeness because He is one (*al-Aḥad*); He is not subject to the fears that drove the idolaters to their crimes because He is *al-ʿAzīz*, the Mighty.

**The Same Phrase in Sūrat al-Rūm**

The expression *al-mathalu al-aʿlā* appears in one other place in the Qur'an, and its context illuminates this one:

> *"And it is He Who begins creation and then repeats it, and that is easier for Him. And to Him belongs the highest description in the heavens and the earth, and He is the Mighty, the Wise."* (Qur'an 30:27)

The verse in al-Rūm uses the phrase in an argument for resurrection — God who began creation can repeat it — and ends with the same two names as 16:60, "the Mighty, the Wise." The parallel is not accidental. Both verses are addressed to deniers of the Hereafter; both assert God's highest attributes against their low conceptions; both conclude with *al-ʿAzīz al-Ḥakīm*. The "highest description" includes the power to resurrect, which the deniers of 16:38 rejected.

**The Tension With "Do Not Strike Parables for God"**

Verse 74 of this same sūrah will command: *"So do not strike parables for God"* (*fa-lā taḍribū li'llāhi al-amthāl*), and 42:11 states that "there is nothing like Him." How, then, can verse 60 speak of God's *mathal*, His likeness or description? The commentators resolve the apparent tension through the meaning of *mathal* in each place. In verse 74, *amthāl* means likenesses or comparisons — the idolaters compared God to their idols, or imagined Him as a king who needs intermediaries, and this is forbidden. In verse 60, *mathal* means attribute or description — and God does have attributes, revealed by Himself, which the believer affirms. There is no likeness *of* God (v. 74) but there is a description *belonging to* God (v. 60), and it is the highest.

Al-Rāzī frames the distinction: the *mathal* forbidden is one struck *by* creatures *for* God from their own imagination; the *mathal* affirmed is the one God has revealed of Himself. The first is fabrication (v. 56's *iftirāʾ*); the second is revelation. The believer speaks of God only as God has spoken of Himself — the principle that governs the entire Islamic doctrine of the divine attributes.

**"The Mighty, the Wise": Why These Two Names**

The verse closes with two names: *wa-huwa al-ʿAzīzu al-Ḥakīm*, "and He is the Mighty, the Wise." Al-Rāzī explains their relevance. *Al-ʿAzīz*, the Mighty, the Invincible, answers the whole complex of fears behind the idolaters' crimes. They feared poverty, shame, and weakness, and these fears drove them to attribute offspring to God and to kill their daughters. God has no such fears; He is *ʿAzīz*, unassailable, needing no sons to protect Him and fearing no daughters to shame Him. *Al-Ḥakīm*, the Wise, answers the charge of evil judgment: where their judgment was evil (v. 59, *sāʾa mā yaḥkumūn*), His judgment is wise. Everything He creates and decrees — including the daughters they despised — proceeds from wisdom.

The pairing of the two names is one of the most frequent in the Qur'an (some forty-seven occurrences), and the scholars have noted that it combines what human power and human wisdom rarely combine: might without tyranny, wisdom without weakness. Human might tends toward injustice; human wisdom tends toward impotence. God's might is governed by His wisdom, and His wisdom is executed by His might.

**The Verse as a Principle for Speaking About God**

Verse 60 establishes a rule that governs all Islamic theology: God is to be described by the highest attributes, and every attribute of deficiency is to be denied of Him. The rule has two sides. The negative side is *tanzīh*, declaring God free of imperfection — the *subḥānahu* of verse 57. The positive side is *ithbāt*, affirming the perfections He has revealed — the names and attributes of the Qur'an and Sunnah. The scholars held both together: one does not deny God's attributes for fear of likening Him to creatures, nor affirm them in a way that likens Him. One affirms *al-mathal al-aʿlā* — the highest description — knowing that His attributes are as far above ours as His essence is above ours. The Prophet ﷺ expressed this in his supplication:

> *"I cannot enumerate Your praise; You are as You have praised Yourself."* (Muslim 486)

"You are as You have praised Yourself" — this is 16:60 turned into a prayer. The highest description belongs to God, and only God can give it.

**The Application**

The verse offers a diagnostic and a discipline. The diagnostic: what a person believes about the Hereafter will determine what description he comes to bear. Denial of the reckoning produces, over time, the *mathal al-sawʾ* — the qualities of the man in verses 58–59. Belief in it produces the opposite. The discipline: to think of God only in the highest terms, to purge from one's conception of Him every trace of the human limitations that the idolaters projected onto Him — need, fear, partiality, weakness. The person who has done this finds that his conception of God has become both more true and more sustaining, because a God who is *al-ʿAzīz al-Ḥakīm* can be relied upon absolutely, while a god who needs sons and fears shame cannot be relied upon at all.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:61

> **And were God to take mankind to task for their wrongdoing, He would not leave upon it a single creature; but He grants them reprieve till a term appointed. And when their term comes, they shall not delay it by a single hour, nor shall they advance it.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Why the Fabricators Still Live**

The preceding verses catalogued grave sins: theft from God's share, lies about His nature, the murder of daughters. A natural question follows: why has God not destroyed those who do these things? Verse 45–47 threatened punishment; verse 60 declared the deniers characterized by evil; yet they continue to live and prosper. Verse 61 answers the question with a statement of principle: *wa-law yuʾākhidhu Allāhu al-nāsa bi-ẓulmihim mā taraka ʿalayhā min dābbah*, "and if God were to take people to task for their wrongdoing, He would not leave upon it a single moving creature." The reason the sinners live is not that their sins are small. It is that God defers.

**"Were God to Take Mankind to Task": The Conditional**

The verse opens with *law*, the particle of a hypothetical condition that is contrary to fact: "*if* God *were* to take people to task" — but He does not. The verb *yuʾākhidhu*, from *akhadha*, to seize, in this form means to hold accountable, to punish, to call to account immediately. The Qur'an uses it for the seizing of the ancient nations (29:40; 40:5, 21) and, in the negative, for the divine forbearance toward slips: *"God will not take you to task for what is unintentional in your oaths"* (2:225).

The object is *al-nās*, "people" — humanity in general, not only the idolaters. The verse broadens its scope beyond the immediate targets of the passage. Every human being does wrong; if God punished each wrong as it occurred, no one would survive.
