**"He Would Not Leave Upon It a Single Creature"**

The consequence is stated absolutely: *mā taraka ʿalayhā min dābbah*, "He would not leave upon it any moving creature." The pronoun *ʿalayhā*, "upon it," refers to the earth, though the earth has not been mentioned in the verse. The commentators note that the reference is clear from context — *dābbah*, moving creature, evokes the earth on which creatures move — and that the Qur'an uses the same ellipsis in 35:45, the verse's closest parallel:

> *"And if God were to take people to task for what they have earned, He would not leave upon its surface any moving creature. But He defers them until an appointed term. And when their term comes, then truly God is ever Seeing of His servants."* (Qur'an 35:45)

The two verses share the structure and nearly the wording. The word *dābbah* raised a question the commentators addressed: why would the animals perish for human wrongdoing? Several answers are given. Al-Ṭabarī reports from some early authorities that the punishment of a people typically involves the withholding of rain, and that the animals die of the resulting drought — as Abū Hurayrah is reported to have said when he heard a man say that the wrongdoer harms only himself: "By God, the bustard dies in its nest from the wrongdoing of the wrongdoer." On this reading the animals suffer as collateral, and the verse describes the actual scope of a general punishment.

Others, including Ibn Masʿūd according to al-Qurṭubī, read *dābbah* as referring to human beings themselves — the "moving creatures" who are the wrongdoers — so that the verse means that no human would be left. Al-Zamakhsharī suggests that *dābbah* is used to include every human being, believer and unbeliever alike, because even the righteous have some wrongdoing that would, strictly judged, merit punishment; the verse thus states that immediate divine justice would empty the earth of humanity altogether.

Al-Rāzī addresses the objection that punishing the innocent animals or the righteous humans along with the guilty would be unjust. He answers that the verse is a hypothetical (*law*), describing what the *consequence* of immediate justice would be, not what God does; and that the death of animals or the righteous in a general destruction is not a punishment for them but a transfer to another state — for the righteous, to reward; for the animals, to the end God has decreed for them. The verse's point is not to describe an injustice but to magnify the scale of human sin and the scale of divine forbearance.

**"But He Grants Them Reprieve Till a Term Appointed"**

The verse then states what God actually does: *wa-lākin yuʾakhkhiruhum ilā ajalin musamman*, "but He defers them until a named term." The verb *akhkhara* means to postpone, to delay. God does not cancel the reckoning; He postpones it. And the postponement has a limit: *ajal musammā*, an appointed, specified term.

The commentators identify two levels of this term. For the individual, it is the moment of death, after which the reckoning begins. For humanity as a whole, it is the Day of Resurrection. Al-Ṭabarī takes the first sense primarily: each person is deferred until his death. Al-Rāzī includes both. The Qur'an uses *ajal musammā* for both the individual's lifespan (6:2; 40:67) and the cosmic term (30:8; 46:3).

The deferral is a mercy, as verse 47's ending ("Kind, Merciful") indicated, but it is a mercy with a purpose. The Qur'an states the purpose in the parallel passage 18:58: *"And your Lord is the Forgiving, Full of Mercy. If He were to take them to task for what they have earned, He would hasten the punishment for them. Rather, for them is an appointment from which they will never find an escape."* The deferral gives time — time to repent, to change, to fill the interval with something other than wrongdoing. The Prophet ﷺ described the deferral as a kind of divine patience unlike any other:

> *"No one is more patient with harmful words heard than God. They attribute to Him a son, and yet He grants them health and provides for them."* (al-Bukhārī 6099; Muslim 2804)

The hadith is the verse in narrative form. They attribute a son — or, in this sūrah, daughters — to God; He responds by feeding them.

**"When Their Term Comes, They Shall Not Delay It by a Single Hour"**

The verse closes with the limit of the reprieve: *fa-idhā jāʾa ajaluhum lā yastaʾkhirūna sāʿatan wa-lā yastaqdimūn*, "then when their term comes, they cannot delay it an hour, nor can they advance it." The formula appears in several places (7:34; 10:49; 34:30; 63:11), and it states the fixity of the appointed term. The deferral is real but not indefinite; it has an end that cannot be moved by an hour in either direction.

The word *sāʿah*, "hour," is used here in its general sense of a short span of time, as al-Rāzī notes — not a fixed sixty minutes but "a moment." The point is that no delay of any length is possible. The Qur'an states this of the moment of death:

> *"And God will never delay a soul when its time has come. And God is Acquainted with what you do."* (Qur'an 63:11)

The addition "nor can they advance it" is not redundant. Al-Zamakhsharī explains that it completes the statement of fixity: the term is fixed against both directions, so that neither the wish to delay (felt by the sinner who wants more time) nor the wish to hasten (felt by the desperate, or claimed by the mockers who said "bring on the punishment") has any effect. The decree is what it is.

**The Theology of the Verse: Divine Forbearance (*Ḥilm*)**

The verse is the Qur'an's principal statement of the attribute of *ḥilm*, divine forbearance — the patience of the One who has full power to punish and full knowledge of the offense, and who nonetheless withholds. *Al-Ḥalīm* is among God's names (2:225, 235, 263; 3:155; 4:12; 17:44; 22:59; 33:51; 35:41; 64:17), and the verse describes its operation: the earth continues to be populated only because God is *Ḥalīm*.

The commentators note that *ḥilm* is not weakness or indifference. God is "the Mighty" (v. 60); His forbearance is exercised from a position of total power. And it is not indifference, because it has a term. The scholars distinguished divine *ḥilm* from divine *ʿafw*, pardon: forbearance postpones; pardon cancels. The verse speaks of the first. Whether the postponed reckoning will end in pardon or punishment depends on what the person does in the interval — which is precisely why the interval is given.

**The Verse in the Sequence**

Verse 61 answers a question that verses 45–47 raised and that verses 56–60 sharpened. Verses 45–47 asked whether the plotters felt secure from punishment; verse 47 ended by naming God as Kind and Merciful. Verses 56–60 showed sins that seemed to cry out for punishment. Verse 61 explains the interval between sin and punishment as the exercise of divine mercy in the form of deferral, and marks its limit. The reader thus understands both why the wicked prosper — deferral, not approval — and why they will not prosper forever — the term is fixed.

**The Application: Living in the Reprieve**

For the reader, the verse establishes a fact about his own situation: he is living in a reprieve. Whatever wrongdoing he has committed has not been punished as it occurred; this is not because it was not noticed but because God has deferred. The correct response to a reprieve is to use it. ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb's counsel is often cited in this connection: *"Take account of yourselves before you are taken to account, and weigh your deeds before they are weighed for you."* The person who understands 16:61 does not mistake the deferral for acquittal. He knows that "when their term comes, they cannot delay it an hour," and he does not wait until the hour to begin the accounting that the hour will demand. The verse's mercy is the time it describes; its warning is the term that ends it.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:62

> **And they assign unto God that which they themselves dislike, while their tongues utter the lie that the most beautiful [reward] shall be theirs. Without doubt, theirs shall be the Fire, and they shall be hastened [into it].**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Third Fabrication and the Self-Deception That Accompanies It**

The passage on the idolaters' fabrications resumes with a verse that combines two charges. The first repeats and generalizes the offense of verse 57: *wa-yajʿalūna li'llāhi mā yakrahūn*, "and they assign to God what they themselves dislike." The second is new: *wa-taṣifu alsinatuhumu al-kadhiba anna lahumu al-ḥusnā*, "and their tongues describe the lie that the best is theirs." The idolaters not only insult God; they simultaneously expect the best from Him. The verse then delivers a verdict: *lā jarama anna lahumu al-nāra wa-annahum mufraṭūn*, "without doubt, theirs is the Fire, and they will be hastened into it."

**"They Assign Unto God That Which They Dislike"**

The verb *yajʿalūna*, "they assign," appears now for the third time in the passage (vv. 56, 57, 62), marking the three fabrications as a series. Here the object is *mā yakrahūn*, "what they dislike" — a generalization of the daughters of verse 57. The commentators identify the daughters as the primary reference, since the whole passage has concerned them, but the phrase is broader. Al-Rāzī and al-Zamakhsharī note that it includes everything the idolaters found distasteful for themselves and yet attributed to God: daughters, but also partners in dominion (no chief would accept a partner in his own authority), and the share of provision given to the idols — the worse share, since they cheated God's portion in favor of the idols' (6:136).

The principle at stake is one the Qur'an states directly in Sūrat al-Zukhruf: they attribute to God what, if it were attributed to one of them, would darken his face (43:17). The verse in al-Naḥl names the inconsistency: what they dislike for themselves, they assign to God. Elementary justice requires that one give the superior at least what one gives oneself; the idolaters gave God what they would not accept.

**"Their Tongues Utter the Lie That the Best Shall Be Theirs"**

The second charge is more subtle and, in a way, more revealing. Despite everything — the fabrications, the insults, the murdered daughters — the idolaters expected *al-ḥusnā*, "the best," for themselves. The word *al-ḥusnā* is the feminine superlative of *ḥasan*, good, and denotes the best outcome, the finest reward. The Qur'an uses it for Paradise and for the good end promised to believers (4:95; 10:26; 13:18; 21:101; 41:50; 92:6).

The commentators explain what the idolaters claimed. Al-Ṭabarī and al-Qurṭubī report that they said they would have sons (in the immediate sense of *ḥusnā* as the good of this world), and that if there were a resurrection — which they doubted — they would fare well in it, since they were prosperous in this life and prosperity was, in their reckoning, a sign of divine favor. The Qur'an records this attitude in the mouth of the rich man of Sūrat al-Kahf:

> *"And I do not think the Hour will come; and if I am brought back to my Lord, I will surely find better than this as a return."* (Qur'an 18:36)

And in Sūrat Fuṣṣilat: *"And if I am returned to my Lord, truly for me with Him is the best (al-ḥusnā)"* (41:50). This is the self-deception the verse exposes: the assumption that present prosperity guarantees future favor, that a person who has been given much in this world must be loved by God.

The verse's phrasing is precise: *taṣifu alsinatuhumu al-kadhib*, "their tongues describe the lie." Al-Zamakhsharī notes the unusual construction — the tongue "describes" the lie, as though the lie were the tongue's characteristic product. The claim of *al-ḥusnā* is not an error of judgment but a lie: they say it while their own hearts, as verse 22 stated, are denying. The same phrase appears in verse 116 — *"do not say, concerning what your tongues describe as a lie, 'This is lawful and this is unlawful'"* — where it condemns the fabrication of religious rulings. The tongue that lies about God's law and the tongue that lies about one's own destiny are the same tongue.

Some grammarians read *al-kadhib* as the direct object of *taṣifu* ("their tongues describe the lie"), with *anna lahumu al-ḥusnā* in apposition explaining what the lie is; others read *al-kadhib* as an adverbial ("their tongues falsely describe that the best is theirs"). The sense is identical: the claim of the best is a lie.

**"Without Doubt": *Lā Jarama***

The verdict begins with *lā jarama*, the same phrase that opened verse 23 ("without doubt, God knows what they conceal"). The phrase was discussed there: it means "no doubt," "assuredly," "it is inevitable." Al-Zamakhsharī and others explain it as originating from *jarama*, to earn or to cut, with the sense "there is no denying" or "it has become established." The phrase gives the verdict the tone of a settled fact rather than a threat.

**"Theirs Shall Be the Fire"**

The verdict inverts their claim exactly. They said *lahumu al-ḥusnā*, "theirs is the best"; the verse says *lahumu al-nār*, "theirs is the Fire." The parallel structure makes the reversal visible: same preposition, same pronoun, opposite object. What they claimed for themselves and what is actually theirs stand side by side. Al-Rāzī notes that this is the response to the lie: not an argument but a plain statement of the truth that the lie concealed.

**"And They Shall Be Hastened Into It": *Mufraṭūn***

The verse ends with a word whose reading and meaning the commentators discussed at length: *wa-annahum mufraṭūn*. The word is from the root *f-r-ṭ*, which carries the basic sense of preceding, going ahead, or going to excess. Three readings are recorded.

The majority reading is *mufraṭūn* (with *a* after the *r*), a passive participle meaning "sent ahead," "hastened forward," "left behind and forgotten." Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr are reported by al-Ṭabarī to have understood it as "made to go first" — they will be the first sent into the Fire, hurried ahead of others. Al-Ṭabarī explains the root: the *fāriṭ* is the one who goes ahead of a traveling party to the water; the *mufraṭ* is the one sent ahead. The idolaters will be sent ahead into the Fire. Other early authorities took the passive in the sense of "abandoned," "forgotten" — left in the Fire and neglected (as *afraṭa* can mean to leave behind). Both senses are compatible: they are hurried in and left there.

A second reading, attributed to Nāfiʿ, is *mufriṭūn* (with *i*), an active participle meaning "those who exceed the bounds" — those who go to excess in wrongdoing, who are immoderate. On this reading the verse describes their character rather than their fate: they are transgressors of every limit, and their transgression is the reason the Fire is theirs.

A third reading, attributed to Abū Jaʿfar, is *mufarriṭūn* (with doubled *r*), the active participle of *farraṭa*, to neglect or fall short — those who neglected their duty, who were remiss. This is the sense of *farraṭa* in 39:56, "Alas for what I neglected in regard to God."

Al-Rāzī collects all three and observes that each is true of the idolaters: they exceeded the bounds (*mufriṭūn*), they neglected their duty (*mufarriṭūn*), and therefore they will be hurried into the Fire and left there (*mufraṭūn*). The variant readings, as often in the Qur'an, are not competing but cumulative.

**The Logic of the Passage: Self-Deception as the Core of Sin**

Verse 62 completes the analysis of the idolaters' state that began in verse 56, and it ends on the deepest layer: self-deception. The idolaters' fabrications about God (vv. 56–57) and their crimes against their daughters (vv. 58–59) were sustained by a fabrication about themselves — that they were, despite everything, favored. This belief insulated them from repentance. A person who expects the best does not seek to change. The verse identifies the belief as a lie told by the tongue, and its verdict is designed to shatter it: not the best, but the Fire.

The Qur'an regards this kind of self-deception as one of the gravest spiritual dangers, and it addresses it repeatedly. The People of the Book claimed that the Fire would touch them only for a few days (2:80); the hypocrites claimed to be reformers while they were corrupters (2:11–12); the idolaters claimed that if God had willed they would not have associated (v. 35). In each case, a false belief about one's own standing before God prevents the honest self-examination that repentance requires. The Prophet ﷺ described the opposite attitude:

> *"The intelligent one is he who takes himself to account and works for what comes after death; and the incapable one is he who follows his soul's desires and entertains false hopes about God."* (al-Tirmidhī 2459)

"Entertains false hopes about God" — *tamannā ʿalā Allāh* — is the precise disposition of 16:62's liars.

**The Application: Testing One's Expectation of "the Best"**

The verse asks the reader to examine his own expectation. Most people expect the best for themselves — in this world and, if they believe in the next, there too. The verse does not condemn hope; the Qur'an commands hope in God's mercy (39:53). It condemns hope that is *unfounded* — hope that coexists with persistent wrongdoing and rests on nothing but the tongue's assertion. The test is whether the expectation of *al-ḥusnā* is accompanied by the works that God has attached to it. Verse 30 stated that "for those who do good in this world is good (*ḥasanah*)"; the *ḥusnā* belongs to the *muḥsinīn*. The person who expects it without doing good has joined the idolaters in their lie, and the verse's *lā jarama* applies to him as it applied to them.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:63

> **By God, We have indeed sent [messengers] to communities before thee; but Satan made their deeds seem fair unto them. So he is their protector today, and theirs shall be a painful punishment.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**From the Makkans to the Pattern of History**

Verse 62 ended with the verdict on the idolaters of Makkah. Verse 63 widens the frame: what is happening in Makkah has happened before. *Ta'llāhi laqad arsalnā ilā umamin min qablika*, "By God, We have sent to communities before you." The Prophet ﷺ is told that the resistance he faces is not new, and the mechanism of that resistance is named: Satan made the deeds of those communities seem fair to them, and the result was that he became their guardian and they earned a painful punishment. The verse is both consolation to the Prophet and diagnosis of his opponents.

**The Oath: *Ta'llāhi***

The verse opens with the same oath particle used in verse 56, *ta'llāhi*, "by God." The commentators note that the oath emphasizes the certainty of what follows and, as al-Zamakhsharī observes, is directed at the Prophet as reassurance: God swears to him that the pattern he is witnessing is ancient. The Qur'an offers this consolation repeatedly:

> *"And messengers before you were denied, but they were patient over the denial and the harm until Our help came to them."* (Qur'an 6:34)

> *"Nothing is said to you except what was already said to the messengers before you."* (Qur'an 41:43)

The oath also serves the argument against the Makkans: it confirms, with the strongest emphasis, the historical fact of prior messengers — a fact the Makkans acknowledged in principle (they knew of Abraham, Moses, and others) but whose implication they refused.

**"We Have Sent to Communities Before Thee"**

The clause repeats the doctrine of verse 36 — "We sent to every community a messenger" — but now with a different purpose. Verse 36 established the universality of the message. Verse 63 establishes the universality of the *response*: the communities were sent messengers, and Satan intervened. The word *umam*, communities, is the plural of *ummah*, discussed at verse 36. The verse implies that the messengers' message was rejected, since the following clause describes the mechanism of rejection; the ellipsis is filled by the reader's knowledge of the stories the Qur'an tells elsewhere (ʿĀd, Thamūd, the people of Noah, of Lot, of Shuʿayb).

**"Satan Made Their Deeds Seem Fair to Them": *Tazyīn***

The mechanism of rejection is named: *fa-zayyana lahumu al-shayṭānu aʿmālahum*, "and Satan beautified for them their deeds." The verb *zayyana*, from *zīnah*, ornament or adornment, means to make something appear beautiful, attractive, right. *Tazyīn* is Satan's primary method in the Qur'an. He does not usually persuade people that evil is evil and should be done anyway; he persuades them that evil is good. The Qur'an records his own declaration of the method:

> *"[Iblīs] said: My Lord, because You have put me in error, I will surely make [disobedience] attractive to them on earth, and I will mislead them all, except Your chosen servants among them."* (Qur'an 15:39–40)

And it describes the effect on the ancient nations:

> *"And ʿĀd and Thamūd — and it has become clear to you from their dwellings. And Satan made their deeds pleasing to them and averted them from the path, though they were perceptive."* (Qur'an 29:38)

> *"Then why, when Our punishment came to them, did they not humble themselves? But their hearts became hardened, and Satan made attractive to them what they were doing."* (Qur'an 6:43)

The verse in al-ʿAnkabūt (29:38) adds a detail relevant to 16:63: Satan made their deeds pleasing "though they were perceptive" (*wa-kānū mustabṣirīn*). *Tazyīn* does not work only on fools. It works on the intelligent, by giving them reasons. The Makkans who buried their daughters had reasons — poverty, honor, tribal strength. Those who dedicated shares to idols had reasons — the idols were intercessors, the fathers had done it. *Tazyīn* is the process by which a wrong acquires a rationale, and once it has one, the intelligent defend it more ably than the foolish.

**How *Tazyīn* Operates: The Commentators' Analysis**

The commentators explain how Satan's beautification works. Al-Rāzī describes it as the whispering (*waswasah*) by which Satan presents the immediate pleasure or benefit of a sin while concealing its consequence, and presents the difficulty of obedience while concealing its reward. The sinner sees the ornament and not the price. Ibn al-Qayyim, in his treatment of Satan's methods, describes the gradation: Satan first presents the sin as small, then as excusable, then as normal, then as good, and finally as a duty. The idolaters of Makkah had reached the last stage: they regarded the dedication of shares to idols and the burying of daughters not as sins but as honor and piety.

The verse's ascription of *tazyīn* to Satan does not remove human responsibility. Al-Rāzī notes that Satan can only beautify; he cannot compel. The person who accepts the beautification does so by his own choice, and the Qur'an records Satan's own disclaimer of responsibility on the Day of Judgment:

> *"And Satan will say, when the matter has been concluded: Truly God promised you the promise of truth, and I promised you, but I betrayed you. And I had no authority over you except that I called you, and you responded to me. So do not blame me, but blame yourselves."* (Qur'an 14:22)

The passage from Sūrat Ibrāhīm is the key to 16:63's next clause.

**"So He Is Their Protector Today": *Fa-huwa Waliyyuhumu al-Yawm***

The verse continues: *fa-huwa waliyyuhumu al-yawm*, "so he is their protector today." The word *walī* means guardian, protector, ally, patron — the one to whom one turns for help and under whose authority one stands. The Qur'an sets two *wilāyah*s against each other: God is the *walī* of the believers (2:257; 3:68; 45:19), and Satan and the *ṭāghūt* are the *walī* of the disbelievers (2:257; 4:76; 7:27, 30). To have Satan as *walī* is to have chosen him as guardian in place of God — and to have, therefore, no real guardian at all, since Satan, as 14:22 shows, will disown his clients when they need him most.

The word *al-yawm*, "today," has been read in two ways, both recorded by al-Ṭabarī and al-Rāzī.

The first takes "today" as the present time — the time of the Prophet. On this reading, the verse shifts from the ancient communities to the Makkans: Satan beautified the deeds of the ancients, and he is *today*, in Makkah, the guardian of those who follow the same path. The verse thus connects past and present: the same Satan who ruined the ancient communities is now the patron of the Makkan idolaters. This reading is supported by the shift in the pronoun's reference, which al-Ṭabarī allows.

The second takes "today" as the Day of Judgment, described in the present tense for vividness: on that Day, Satan will be their "guardian" — which is to say, they will have no guardian, since Satan will be as helpless as they. Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Rāzī note the irony: the one they took as protector will be unable to protect, and the verse's naming him as their *walī* on that Day is a statement of their utter abandonment. This reading links directly to the verse's ending: "and theirs is a painful punishment."

Al-Rāzī reconciles the readings: Satan is their guardian today, in this world, in the sense that they follow him; and he will be their only "guardian" on the Day of Judgment, in the sense that they will have no other — and he will be worthless. Both readings describe the same relationship at its two ends.

**"And Theirs Shall Be a Painful Punishment"**

The verse closes with the consequence: *wa-lahum ʿadhābun alīm*. The phrase *ʿadhāb alīm*, painful punishment, is among the Qur'an's most frequent descriptions of the fate of the disbelievers. Its placement here, immediately after Satan is named as their *walī*, states the outcome of that *wilāyah*: the guardian they chose leads them to pain. The Qur'an makes the contrast explicit in 2:257: God brings the believers "out of darknesses into light," while the *ṭāghūt* brings their clients "out of light into darknesses; those are the companions of the Fire."

**The Verse as Consolation and Warning**

The verse works on two audiences. To the Prophet ﷺ it is consolation: the resistance he meets is the work of an ancient enemy using an ancient method; it is not a sign of his failure, and it will end as it always ends. To the Makkans it is warning: they are not innovators but imitators, repeating a pattern whose conclusion is known, and their guardian is the one who has betrayed every client he ever had.

**The Application: Recognizing *Tazyīn***

The verse teaches the reader to recognize the operation of *tazyīn* in his own life. The mark of it is not that a sin appears tempting — that is ordinary desire — but that it appears *justified*: that one has a reason for it, a rationale that makes it seem acceptable or even good. When a person finds himself defending a wrong with arguments, he is in the presence of what 16:63 describes. The remedy is the one the Qur'an prescribes throughout: to measure one's deeds not by how they seem but by what God has revealed, and to seek refuge from the beautifier. The Prophet ﷺ taught that Satan flows in the human being like blood (al-Bukhārī 2039; Muslim 2175) — that is, the whispering is constant and intimate — and that the defense against it is remembrance of God, which verse 98 of this sūrah will command directly: "When you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in God from Satan the accursed." The one whose *walī* is God is not left to the *tazyīn* of the one whose *wilāyah* ends in pain.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:64

> **And We sent down unto thee the Book only that thou mightest make clear unto them that wherein they differed, and as a guidance and a mercy for a people who believe.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Book as the Answer to Satan's Beautification**

Verse 63 described Satan's method: making evil deeds seem fair, so that communities differed from the truth and from one another and followed him to punishment. Verse 64 states God's remedy: the Book. *Wa-mā anzalnā ʿalayka al-kitāba illā li-tubayyina lahumu alladhī ikhtalafū fīh*, "And We have not sent down the Book to you except that you may clarify for them that in which they differed." Against the confusion Satan produces, God sends clarity. The verse thus restates the purpose of revelation given in verse 44 — "that you may make clear to the people what was sent down to them" — but now with a specific object: the differences.

**"We Sent Down the Book Only That...": The Restriction**

The verse uses the structure *mā... illā*, "not... except," which restricts the purpose of revelation to what follows. Al-Rāzī notes that the restriction is not absolute — the Qur'an has many purposes, including those named in the verse's second half — but rhetorical: it emphasizes that *this* purpose, the clarification of differences, is central and sufficient to justify the revelation. Even if the Book had done nothing else, resolving what people differed about would have been reason enough.

The verse says the Book was sent *ʿalayka*, "upon you" — to the Prophet ﷺ — and the clarification is to be performed by him: *li-tubayyina*, "that *you* may make clear." As at verse 44, the Prophet is not a passive conduit but the active explainer. The Book clarifies through him; he is the one who brings its clarification to bear on the actual disputes of actual people.

**"That Wherein They Differed": What Differences?**

The commentators identify the differences the Book was sent to resolve. Al-Ṭabarī takes the pronoun "they" as referring to the idolaters of the preceding verses — those who differed about God, attributing to Him daughters and partners, and who differed about the Hereafter, denying resurrection. The Book clarifies these matters: God is one, has no offspring, and will raise the dead.

Al-Rāzī extends the reference to the whole of humanity, whose differences in religion the Book was sent to adjudicate: the differences between the People of the Book about Jesus, the Sabbath, the laws of food (v. 118, 124); the differences among the Arabs about idols and rites; the differences among all people about God, the soul, and the end. Al-Qurṭubī includes both.

The Qur'an describes its own function in these terms elsewhere:

> *"Truly this Qur'an relates to the Children of Israel most of that over which they differ."* (Qur'an 27:76)

> *"Mankind was one community; then God sent the prophets as bearers of good tidings and warners, and sent down with them the Book in truth to judge between people concerning that in which they differed."* (Qur'an 2:213)

The verse in al-Baqarah gives the general principle: the Book was sent to *judge* — *li-yaḥkuma* — between people in their differences. Verse 64 of al-Naḥl says the same with *li-tubayyina*, to clarify. The Book judges by clarifying: it does not impose an arbitrary settlement but makes the truth manifest, so that the difference dissolves in the light of what is now clear.

**The Connection to Verse 39**

Verse 39 stated that God will raise the dead "to make clear to them that in which they differed" — *li-yubayyina lahumu alladhī yakhtalifūna fīh* — with the clarification occurring on the Day of Judgment. Verse 64 uses almost the identical phrase, but places the clarification in this world, through the Book. The two verses describe two clarifications: the Book clarifies now, for those who will listen; the Resurrection clarifies finally, for those who would not. The person who accepts the first does not need the second as a rebuke, only as a confirmation. The person who rejects the first will receive the second as the exposure of what he refused to see. The sūrah returns to the theme in verses 92 and 124: God will judge between people on the Day of Resurrection concerning what they differed about. The Book is the merciful precursor to that judgment.

**"And as a Guidance and a Mercy": The Second Purpose**

The verse's second half names two further purposes: *wa-hudan wa-raḥmatan li-qawmin yuʾminūn*, "and as a guidance and a mercy for a people who believe." The pairing of *hudā* and *raḥmah* — guidance and mercy — is one of the Qur'an's standard descriptions of scripture (7:52, 154, 203; 10:57; 12:111; 16:89; 27:77; 31:3; 45:20). The two are related as means and end: guidance is the showing of the way; mercy is the good that reaches the one who walks it. Al-Rāzī explains that *hudā* refers to the Book's function in the intellect — it shows the truth — while *raḥmah* refers to its function in the heart and in the person's whole condition — it brings relief, healing, and ultimately salvation.

The verse's structure implies a distinction the commentators note. The first purpose — clarifying differences — is stated for "them," the people generally, including the disbelievers. The second — guidance and mercy — is stated for "a people who believe." The Book clarifies for everyone; it guides and shows mercy only to those who accept the clarification. The same distinction appears in 2:2 (guidance "for the God-fearing") and 41:44 ("Say: It is, for those who believe, a guidance and a healing; and those who do not believe — in their ears is deafness"). Al-Qurṭubī observes that the restriction to believers is not because the Book withholds itself from others but because guidance and mercy, unlike clarification, require acceptance to become effective. A lamp illuminates the room for everyone; only those who open their eyes see by it.

**"For a People Who Believe": The Condition**

The phrase *li-qawmin yuʾminūn* recurs throughout the sūrah, with variations: "for a people who reflect" (v. 11), "who reason" (v. 12), "who remember" (v. 13), "who believe" (vv. 64, 79), "who know" (v. 65 in some readings). Each variation names a faculty or disposition that must be present for the sign or the Book to have its effect. Here, belief is named because the Book's guidance and mercy are the fruit of belief — one who does not believe the Book cannot be guided by it, any more than one who does not trust a map can be led by it.

The present tense *yuʾminūn*, "who believe" (rather than "who have believed"), indicates continuing, active faith. Al-Zamakhsharī notes that the Book is guidance and mercy to those whose belief is a living disposition, renewed in their engagement with it, not a past event.

**The Verse and the Prophet's Explanatory Role**

The verse reinforces what verse 44 established about the Prophet's function. He was given the Book *in order that he might clarify* — which means that the clarification is part of the divine purpose in sending the Book, and that the Prophet's explanations carry the authority of that purpose. The scholars of *uṣūl* cite this verse, with 16:44, as the foundation of the authority of the Sunnah. The Prophet's clarification of the Qur'an — his explanation of its meanings, his application of its rulings, his adjudication of the disputes brought before him — was the fulfillment of *li-tubayyina*. The Qur'an confirms this in 4:65: "By your Lord, they will not believe until they make you judge in what arises among them, and then find in themselves no discomfort with what you have decided, and submit fully." The Prophet's judgment in differences was the Book's clarification in action.

**The Historical Fulfillment**

The Prophet ﷺ did, in fact, resolve the differences of his time. He settled the Arabs' disputes about God and the idols — by the end of his life, the Arabian Peninsula worshipped one God. He adjudicated between the Jews of Madinah in their disputes about the law (5:42–43). He answered the Christians of Najrān concerning Jesus (3:59–61). He corrected the practices of the Age of Ignorance concerning inheritance, marriage, blood-feud, and commerce. The clarification the verse describes was accomplished historically, and its record — the Qur'an with the Sunnah — remains the standard by which the community continues to resolve its differences.

**The Application: Referring Differences to the Book**

The verse gives the Muslim community a method for dealing with disagreement. Differences are inevitable; the Qur'an acknowledges this (11:118–119). What the verse prescribes is not the elimination of difference but its *reference*: differences are to be brought to the Book and the Prophet's clarification, and settled there. The Qur'an commands exactly this:

> *"And if you disagree over anything, refer it to God and the Messenger, if you believe in God and the Last Day. That is best and most suitable for final determination."* (Qur'an 4:59)

The person or community that settles disputes by reference to the Book has understood 16:64. The person or community that settles them by faction, by power, or by the beautified reasoning of verse 63 has not. And the verse adds a promise for those who take the first path: for them, the Book is not only a judge but a guidance and a mercy — it does not merely end the dispute; it leads the disputants, together, toward what is good.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:65

> **And God sends down water from the sky, and thereby revives the earth after its death. Truly in that is a sign for a people who hear.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Return to the Signs of Creation**

After the long passage on the idolaters' fabrications and God's remedy in the Book (vv. 56–64), the sūrah returns to its other great mode of argument: the signs in creation. Verses 65–69 present a new sequence of blessings — rain, cattle and their milk, the fruits of palm and vine, and the bee and its honey. Each is a sign of the one Creator, a blessing demanding gratitude, and — in the first case — a demonstration of resurrection. The sequence opens with the most fundamental: *wa'llāhu anzala mina al-samāʾi māʾan fa-aḥyā bihi al-arḍa baʿda mawtihā*, "And God sends down water from the sky and revives the earth by it after its death."

**The Connection to Verse 64**

The commentators note the link between verse 64 and verse 65, which might otherwise seem an abrupt transition. Verse 64 described the Book as guidance and mercy for a people who believe. Verse 65 describes rain that revives the dead earth. Al-Rāzī and al-Zamakhsharī draw the analogy that the Qur'an makes elsewhere: the revelation is to hearts what rain is to the earth. The Book comes down from above (*anzalnā*, v. 64; *anzala*, v. 65 — the same verb) and gives life to what was dead. The Prophet ﷺ made the comparison explicit:

> *"The likeness of the guidance and knowledge with which God has sent me is that of abundant rain falling on the earth. Some of it was fertile soil that absorbed the water and brought forth vegetation and grass in abundance. Another part was hard and held the water, and God benefited people by it: they drank from it and gave drink and irrigated. And another part was barren land that neither held water nor brought forth vegetation."* (al-Bukhārī 79; Muslim 2282)

The hadith describes what verse 64's "for a people who believe" implied: the same rain falls on all soils, but only the receptive soil is revived. Verse 65 is thus both a physical sign and a parable of the spiritual process the previous verse described.

**"God Sends Down Water From the Sky"**

The verse attributes the sending of rain directly to God, as verse 10 did: "He it is who sends down water from the sky." The repetition is deliberate. The sūrah's method is to return to the same blessings from different angles, each time adding a new dimension. Verse 10 presented rain as the source of drink and pasture; verse 65 presents it as the reviver of the dead earth and, therefore, as evidence of the resurrection.

The word *al-samāʾ*, "the sky," here denotes the region above — the clouds — as al-Qurṭubī notes. The Qur'an elsewhere specifies: "He sends down from the sky, from mountains [of clouds] therein, hail" (24:43). The point is the direction: the water comes from above, from a source no human controls or produces. Verse 56:68–70, cited at verse 53, asks the question directly: "Is it you who brought it down from the clouds, or are We?"

**"And Thereby Revives the Earth After Its Death": The Argument for Resurrection**

The verse's central phrase is *fa-aḥyā bihi al-arḍa baʿda mawtihā*, "and revives the earth by it after its death." The earth is described as dead — dry, barren, lifeless — and then as revived by the water. The commentators recognize this as the Qur'an's most frequent argument for the resurrection of the dead, and they trace the analogy with care.

The dead earth shows no sign of life. Its seeds lie hidden and inert; nothing moves on its surface; it appears finished. Then water falls, and within days it is green, moving, alive with growth. What seemed permanent was not; what seemed dead was capable of life. The Qur'an draws the conclusion explicitly in many places:

> *"And you see the earth barren, but when We send down upon it rain, it quivers and swells and grows something of every beautiful kind. That is because God is the Truth, and because He gives life to the dead, and because He is over all things competent, and because the Hour is coming, no doubt about it."* (Qur'an 22:5–7)

> *"And it is God who sends the winds, and they stir the clouds, and We drive them to a dead land and give life thereby to the earth after its death. Thus is the resurrection."* (Qur'an 35:9)

> *"And among His signs is that you see the earth humbled; but when We send down rain upon it, it quivers and grows. Truly He who gives it life is the Giver of life to the dead. Truly He is over all things competent."* (Qur'an 41:39)

The argument, as al-Rāzī frames it, is from the actual to the possible: the revival of the dead earth is *observed* every year; therefore the revival of dead bodies, which is the same kind of act — bringing life from what appears lifeless — is *possible*, and the One who does the first can do the second. The Makkans, who denied resurrection with their strongest oaths (v. 38), witnessed its analogue every spring and drew no conclusion.

Ibn Kathīr adds a further observation: the resurrection of the body, like the revival of the earth, will be accomplished through rain. He cites the hadith in which the Prophet ﷺ described that before the resurrection God will send down water from the sky, and from it the bodies will grow "as vegetables grow" (Muslim 2955), from the coccyx which does not decay. The earth's revival is thus not merely an analogy for the resurrection but, according to this hadith, its actual mechanism.

**The Forward Connection: Verses 65 to 69**

Verse 65 opens a sequence, and the commentators note its structure. Rain (v. 65) produces pasture; pasture feeds cattle, whose milk is described in verse 66; rain also produces the palms and vines of verse 67; and the flowers that the bee visits in verse 68–69. Al-Rāzī observes that the four blessings — water, milk, the fruit-drinks, and honey — correspond to the four rivers of Paradise:

> *"The description of Paradise which the God-fearing are promised: in it are rivers of water unaltered, rivers of milk whose taste never changes, rivers of wine delicious to those who drink, and rivers of purified honey."* (Qur'an 47:15)

The correspondence was noted at verse 31, where the "rivers flowing beneath" the gardens of Eden were mentioned. The four drinks God gives on earth — water, milk, the juice of fruits, honey — are the earthly foreshadowing of the four rivers of Paradise. What is given here in limited form, tainted and perishable, will be given there in perfection.

**"Truly in That Is a Sign for a People Who Hear"**

The verse ends with the sūrah's characteristic formula, but with a distinctive final word: *inna fī dhālika la-āyatan li-qawmin yasmaʿūn*, "truly in that is a sign for a people who *hear*." The earlier formulas named reflection (v. 11), reason (v. 12), and remembrance (v. 13). Here the faculty named is hearing.

The commentators explain the choice. Al-Rāzī notes that the argument from rain to resurrection is one that must be *heard* — it is conveyed through revelation, which states the conclusion the sign points to, and the person who hears the revelation with an open ear will see the sign confirm it. Al-Zamakhsharī defines "those who hear" as those who hear with the hearing of reflection and acceptance — not the physical hearing that the disbelievers also possess, but the hearing that leads to understanding. The Qur'an distinguishes the two: the disbelievers "have ears with which they do not hear" (7:179), and God says of them, "If God had known any good in them, He would have made them hear" (8:23).

There is also a connection to the verse's context. Verse 64 spoke of the Book sent down to clarify. The Book is heard. The person who hears the Book's account of resurrection and then looks at the earth revived by rain will find the two confirming each other — the heard word and the seen sign. The "people who hear" are those who allow what they hear from revelation to interpret what they see in the world.

**The Physical Reality as Sign**

The phenomenon the verse describes remains one of the most striking in human experience. The transformation of a desert after rain — the appearance, within days, of grass and flowers where there had been only sand and stone — is a sight that has moved observers in every age. The seeds were there, dormant, capable of life but showing none. The water did not create them; it awakened them. This is precisely the model of resurrection the Qur'an presents: the human being does not cease to exist at death but returns to a dormant state from which God, when He wills, awakens him. The Qur'an states that even the bodies' dispersal is no obstacle: "We know what the earth diminishes of them, and with Us is a preserving record" (50:4).

**The Application: Hearing the Sign**

The verse asks the reader to become one of "the people who hear." This involves a discipline: when one sees the earth revive after rain — or a garden after winter, or a field after drought — to hear, in that sight, what revelation has said about it. "Thus is the resurrection" (35:9). The believer who has trained himself in this hearing does not experience spring as a mere season; he experiences it as an annual demonstration of what God has promised to do with him. The Prophet ﷺ modeled this attention to rain, going out to let it touch him and saying, "It has just come from its Lord" (Muslim 898). The rain has just come from its Lord, and it carries His sign. The verse invites the reader to receive it as such.

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:66

> **And truly in the cattle there is a lesson for you: We give you to drink of that which is in their bellies, between refuse and blood—pure milk, palatable to those who drink [it].**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Second Drink**

Verse 65 presented water from the sky. Verse 66 presents the second of the four drinks: milk from the cattle. *Wa-inna lakum fī al-anʿāmi la-ʿibrah*, "And truly for you in the cattle is a lesson." The cattle were the first blessing the sūrah enumerated (vv. 5–8), and the sūrah returns to them, as it returned to rain, from a new angle. In verses 5–8 the cattle provided warmth, food, beauty, and transport. Here they provide milk — and the production of milk is presented as a *lesson*, an *ʿibrah*, that demands a specific kind of attention.

**"A Lesson": The Meaning of *ʿIbrah***

The word *ʿibrah* comes from the root *ʿ-b-r*, which means to cross over — as one crosses a river (*ʿabara al-nahr*) or as a tear crosses the cheek (*ʿabrah*). *ʿIbrah* is a lesson because it is something one crosses *from* — from the visible to the invisible, from the sign to what it signifies. Al-Rāghib defines it as a state by which one passes from the knowledge of what is witnessed to the knowledge of what is not witnessed. The Qur'an uses the word for the lessons in the stories of the prophets (12:111), in the fate of the destroyed nations (3:13; 79:26), and in the alternation of night and day (24:44). Here, the *ʿibrah* is in the cattle's milk: one is to cross from the observed fact of milk to the unobserved fact of the One who produces it.

Al-Zamakhsharī notes that *ʿibrah* is a stronger word than *āyah*, sign, which the sūrah uses elsewhere. An *āyah* is something that points; an *ʿibrah* is something that one must *cross* — it demands the active movement of the mind from the sign to its meaning. The choice of word signals that what follows requires thought.

**"We Give You to Drink of That Which Is in Their Bellies"**

The verse says *nusqīkum mimmā fī buṭūnihi*, "We give you to drink from what is in their bellies." The verb *nusqī* (some readings *nasqī*) means to give drink, and its subject is "We" — God. The milk is not produced by the cattle in any ultimate sense; it is given by God through them.

A grammatical detail prompted discussion. *Al-anʿām* is a plural noun, but the pronoun in *buṭūnihi*, "its bellies," is masculine singular. In the parallel verse 23:21, the pronoun is feminine plural: *buṭūnihā*. The commentators offer several explanations. Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Rāzī note that *anʿām* is a collective, and Arabic permits both singular and plural agreement with collectives; the singular here may refer to the genus or kind (*al-naʿam*), or to the specific category of the milk-giving animals. Some, including al-Farrāʾ, took the singular pronoun as referring to *baʿḍ*, "some" of the cattle — since not all cattle give milk but only the females. The variation illustrates the flexibility of Qur'anic Arabic and its precision: the two verses, using different pronouns, together cover both the genus and the plurality.

**"Between Refuse and Blood": The Wonder of the Process**

The verse then describes the origin of the milk with remarkable specificity: *min bayni farthin wa-damin*, "from between refuse and blood." The word *farth* denotes the contents of the stomach and intestines — the partially digested food, the dung before it is expelled. *Dam* is blood. Milk, the verse says, comes forth from *between* these two.

The commentators, drawing on the medical knowledge of their time and on the plain observation the verse invites, explain the process. Ibn ʿAbbās, as al-Ṭabarī reports, described it: the animal eats fodder, which settles in the stomach and becomes *farth*; from it the body draws what becomes blood, which flows in the veins; and from the blood, in the udder, milk is drawn — so that the milk's source lies between the *farth* below and the blood above. Al-Rāzī elaborates with the physiology available to him: the digested food is processed in the stomach, the finer parts are absorbed and carried by the blood to the liver, and from the blood the mammary glands separate out the milk. What was food, and then blood, becomes — in the udder — a substance entirely unlike either.

Modern physiology confirms the structure of the description. The nutrients from digested food are absorbed through the intestinal wall into the bloodstream; the mammary glands extract from the blood the water, sugars, fats, proteins, and minerals from which milk is synthesized. Milk is, in a literal sense, produced from between the digestive contents and the blood. The Qur'an does not present this as a scientific treatise but as an *ʿibrah* — and the lesson does not depend on the details of physiology but on the plain fact that a clean, sweet, nourishing white liquid emerges from an animal whose interior contains dung and blood.

**"Pure Milk": *Labanan Khāliṣan***

The product is described as *labanan khāliṣan*, "pure milk." The word *khāliṣ* means pure, unmixed, free of any admixture. Al-Rāzī and al-Zamakhsharī emphasize the wonder: the milk comes from between the refuse and the blood, and yet carries no trace of either — no color of blood, no odor or taste of dung. The separation is total. The commentators note that if the milk were to carry even a slight admixture of its neighbors, it would be undrinkable; its purity is what makes it a blessing, and that purity is not a natural inevitability but a divine arrangement.

The adjective connects to a theme the sūrah develops throughout: God's provision is pure and good (*ṭayyib*), and human beings should receive it as such (v. 114). The purity of the milk, extracted from impurity, is a physical instance of a spiritual principle — that God brings forth the clean from the unclean, the living from the dead (v. 65), the believer from the disbeliever (3:27).

**"Palatable to Those Who Drink": *Sāʾighan li'l-shāribīn***

The final description is *sāʾighan li'l-shāribīn*, "easy to swallow for those who drink." The word *sāʾigh* comes from *sāgha*, to pass easily down the throat; it describes something pleasant to drink, that goes down without difficulty. Al-Qurṭubī records that milk is unique in this respect: it is reported that no one chokes on milk, and the Prophet ﷺ described milk as sufficient food and drink together. When he was given milk on the Night Journey, alongside wine, he chose the milk, and Gabriel said:

> *"You have been guided to the fiṭrah [the natural disposition], and so has your community."* (al-Bukhārī 3394; Muslim 168)

The commentators draw a lesson from this choice. Milk is the drink of *fiṭrah* — the first food of every human being, the natural nourishment. Its ease and purity are signs of a Creator who provides for His creatures not merely adequately but gently. The Prophet ﷺ taught a specific supplication upon drinking milk:

> *"O God, bless us in it and increase us of it."* And he explained: *"There is nothing that suffices for both food and drink except milk."* (Abū Dāwūd 3730; al-Tirmidhī 3455)

**The Argument of the Verse**

The *ʿibrah* the verse demands has several dimensions, and the commentators trace them. First, the argument for the Creator: the production of pure milk from between dung and blood is a process no cow designed and no human could replicate; it points to a wise and powerful Arranger. Second, the argument for gratitude: the milk is a gift, extracted for the human being's benefit through a process he did not devise, in an animal he did not make. Third, the argument for resurrection, continuing from verse 65: the God who brings pure milk from between filth and blood — who transforms one substance into a wholly different one — can bring life from death and reconstitute what has decayed. Al-Rāzī notes that the transformation of grass into blood and blood into milk is a sequence of "creations" as remarkable as any resurrection.

**The Verse and the Sūrah's Structure**

Verse 66 is the second in the sequence of four drinks (vv. 65–69) that mirror the rivers of Paradise (47:15). The commentators observe that the earthly milk is described as *khāliṣ*, pure, but the heavenly milk is described as "whose taste never changes" — the earthly blessing is pure but perishable (milk sours), while the heavenly is pure and permanent. The earthly sign points to the heavenly reality it foreshadows.

**The Application: Attention to the Ordinary**

The verse asks the reader to look at something as ordinary as a glass of milk and to *cross over* — to perform the *ʿibrah* — from the glass to the process behind it, and from the process to its Author. The discipline it teaches is attention to the ordinary as extraordinary. Nothing in the world is more familiar than milk; nothing, on reflection, is more remarkable than its production. The person who has trained himself to see the *ʿibrah* in milk will see it everywhere, because everything he consumes has a similar history — a chain of transformations he did not design, ending in a benefit he did not earn. The verse's instruction is to let that history become visible, and to respond to it with the gratitude that the sūrah has been demanding since its fifth verse.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:67

> **And from the fruits of the date palm and the vine, from which you derive strong drink and goodly provision. Truly in that is a sign for a people who understand.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Third Drink**

The sequence of drinks continues. Verse 65 gave water; verse 66 gave milk; verse 67 gives the produce of the palm and the vine: *wa-min thamarāti al-nakhīli wa'l-aʿnābi tattakhidhūna minhu sakaran wa-rizqan ḥasanan*, "and from the fruits of the date palms and the grapevines, from which you take an intoxicant and good provision." The verse is one of the most discussed in the sūrah because of its mention of *sakar*, strong drink, and its place in the history of the prohibition of wine.

**The Grammar of the Opening**

The verse begins *wa-min thamarāt*, "and from the fruits," and the commentators note that the sentence is elliptical. Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Rāzī propose two constructions. Either the verse continues from verse 66 — "We give you to drink from what is in their bellies... and [We give you] from the fruits of the palm and the vine" — or a phrase is understood: "and from the fruits of the palm and the vine [is something] from which you take..." In either case, the verse presents the fruits as another gift from which humans derive drink.

The palm and the vine are named because they were the two principal fruit-bearing plants of Arabia and the two from which drink was made. The Qur'an frequently pairs them (2:266; 17:91; 18:32; 23:19; 36:34). The date palm was the staple of Madinah and the oases; the vine grew in Ṭāʾif and the highlands. Between them they represent the whole range of the region's fruit.

**"Strong Drink": The Meaning of *Sakar***

The word *sakar* is from the root *s-k-r*, which denotes intoxication; *sukr* is drunkenness, and *sakrān* is a drunk person. The word *sakar* itself has been understood in several ways, and the difference matters for the verse's status in Islamic law.

The majority of the early commentators — Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Masʿūd, Mujāhid, Qatādah, and others, as al-Ṭabarī reports — took *sakar* to mean intoxicating drink: wine (*khamr*) or the fermented date-drink (*nabīdh*) that intoxicates. On this reading the verse mentions intoxicants as something people *take* from the fruits — a statement of fact, not of permission.

A minority reading, recorded by al-Ṭabarī from some of the linguists and adopted by some later scholars, took *sakar* to mean any drink or food derived from the fruits — vinegar, date-syrup, juice — or, more specifically, what is *eaten* (from a supposed sense of *sakar* as food, attested in some dialects). Al-Qurṭubī records the view of some Ḥanafī scholars that *sakar* here means the non-intoxicating drink made from dates. The Shāfiʿī and majority view holds the first meaning.

**The Verse and the Prohibition of Wine**

The verse's mention of *sakar*, and its pairing with "good provision" (*rizq ḥasan*), raised a question the commentators addressed directly: does the verse approve of intoxicants? Two positions developed, and al-Qurṭubī and al-Ṭabarī set them out.

The first position holds that the verse was revealed before the prohibition of wine, when wine was still permitted, and that it was subsequently abrogated in its permissive implication by the verses of prohibition. Al-Qurṭubī records this as the view of most commentators. The prohibition of wine was gradual, and the Qur'an's verses trace its stages:

> *"They ask you about wine and gambling. Say: In them is great sin and [some] benefit for people, but their sin is greater than their benefit."* (Qur'an 2:219)

> *"O you who believe, do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated, until you know what you are saying."* (Qur'an 4:43)

> *"O you who believe, wine, gambling, [sacrificing on] stone altars, and divining arrows are but defilement from the work of Satan, so avoid it that you may be successful."* (Qur'an 5:90)

The Makkan verse 16:67 precedes all of these, and on this view it belongs to the period in which wine was neither prohibited nor praised but simply mentioned as a fact of life. Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to have said that *sakar* here was permitted at the time, then prohibited.

The second position holds that the verse was never permissive and needs no abrogation, because it merely *describes* what people do, without approving it. Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Rāzī develop this reading with attention to the verse's wording. The verse says people "take" (*tattakhidhūna*) *sakar* from the fruits; it does not say God gives it. And the verse distinguishes *sakar* from *rizq ḥasan*, "good provision" — a distinction that implies the *sakar* is *not* good provision. Al-Rāzī notes that if intoxicants were included in the "good provision," the verse would not have named them separately. The verse thus presents two things people derive from the same fruit: one intoxicating, one good. The contrast is itself a quiet judgment on the first.

Al-Qurṭubī records a related observation attributed to al-Shaʿbī: the verse mentions the intoxicant *before* the good provision because it was the first thing revealed concerning wine, and its distinction from "good provision" was an early indication of what would later be made explicit.

**"Good Provision": *Rizqan Ḥasanan***

The second product is *rizqan ḥasanan*, "good provision." The commentators identify it as everything wholesome derived from the palm and the vine: dates fresh and dried, raisins, vinegar, date-syrup (*dibs*), and the non-intoxicating juices. Ibn ʿAbbās glossed it as "what God has made lawful of it." The adjective *ḥasan*, good, is the same root as the *ḥasanah* and *ḥusnā* that the sūrah has used for the reward of the righteous (vv. 30, 41, 62) — the "good provision" is what the good receive and what the good use rightly.

The pairing of *sakar* and *rizq ḥasan* teaches a principle that runs through Islamic ethics: the same created thing can be turned to harm or to benefit by human choice. The grape is neutral; what one *takes* from it — wine or raisins — is the human act, and it is the act that God judges. The fruits are His gift; the intoxicant is the human misuse of the gift; the good provision is its proper use. The verse thus places human agency in the foreground: *tattakhidhūna*, "*you* take."

**The Later Legal Discussion**

The verse figured in the later dispute between the Ḥanafīs and the majority about *nabīdh* — the fermented drink made from dates or raisins. The Ḥanafīs, following certain Kūfan authorities, held that only wine from grapes (*khamr* proper) was categorically forbidden, while other fermented drinks were forbidden only in intoxicating quantities. The majority — Mālikīs, Shāfiʿīs, Ḥanbalīs — held that every intoxicant is *khamr* and forbidden in any amount, on the basis of the hadith:

> *"Every intoxicant is khamr, and every khamr is forbidden."* (Muslim 2003)

> *"Whatever intoxicates in large quantities, a small quantity of it is forbidden."* (Abū Dāwūd 3681; al-Tirmidhī 1865)

Al-Qurṭubī, discussing 16:67, sides with the majority and notes that the verse's *sakar* includes every intoxicant from dates and grapes alike; the verse's descriptive mention of it cannot establish a permission that the later explicit texts removed.

**"A Sign for a People Who Understand"**

The verse ends: *inna fī dhālika la-āyatan li-qawmin yaʿqilūn*, "truly in that is a sign for a people who use reason." Verse 65 named "a people who hear"; verse 66 called the milk a "lesson"; verse 67 names reason. The commentators explain the fit. The transformation of the fruit — the same fruit — into either an intoxicant that destroys the reason or a good provision that sustains it, is a sign for those who *have* reason and use it. Al-Rāzī notes the pointed irony: the verse mentions the thing that removes the intellect and then addresses those who possess the intellect, as if to say that only the one who has not drunk can grasp the sign. The intoxicant is the enemy of the very faculty by which the sign is understood.

The sign itself is the same as in the preceding verses: a Creator who brings, from a palm tree rooted in the earth and fed by water, sweet fruit in abundance, and from a vine, clusters of grapes — nourishment from wood, sugar from soil. The Qur'an points to the palm's fruit as a special sign elsewhere: "tall palm trees with layered fruit, as provision for the servants" (50:10–11), and Mary was fed by it in her extremity (19:25).

**The Symbolic Reading**

The mystical commentators, whom al-Qurṭubī and al-Ālūsī mention, read the verse's two products as symbols of two spiritual states: the intoxicant as the ecstasy that overwhelms the seeker and the good provision as the sober knowledge that sustains him. In their usage, *sukr* (spiritual intoxication) and *ṣaḥw* (sobriety) became technical terms, and the "wine" of the Sufi poets was the love of God. This reading is allegorical and does not affect the verse's plain sense or its legal status; the commentators who mention it are careful to note that the literal intoxicant remains forbidden.

**The Application: Choosing What One Takes**

The verse's most direct lesson is stated in its own verb: *tattakhidhūna*, "you take." From every blessing, one takes something — either a misuse or a good use. The palm and the vine do not decide; the person does. The verse asks the reader to be conscious of what he takes from what God gives — from wealth, from time, from talent, from relationship — and to ensure that it falls on the side of *rizq ḥasan* rather than *sakar*. And the verse's closing appeal to reason is its safeguard: the good use of a blessing is the one that preserves and strengthens the intellect by which one recognizes the Giver, while the misuse is the one that clouds it. A people who understand can tell the difference; that is what the verse asks them to be.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:68

> **And thy Lord revealed unto the bee, "Take up dwellings among the mountains and the trees and among that which they build.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Verse That Names the Sūrah**

The sūrah takes its name from this verse and the next. Among all the blessings enumerated — cattle, rain, crops, sea, mountains, stars, milk, fruit — the bee is the one chosen to title the chapter, and the commentators asked why. The answer lies in what the bee exemplifies: a small creature, without reason as humans understand it, that performs a work of astonishing precision and produces a substance of healing sweetness, entirely by following what its Lord has *revealed* to it. The bee is the perfect emblem of the sūrah's argument. Everything in creation works by God's guidance and produces blessing; only the human being, given a higher form of the same guidance, resists.

**"Thy Lord Revealed Unto the Bee": The Meaning of *Awḥā***

The verse's first word after the conjunction is startling: *wa-awḥā rabbuka ilā al-naḥl*, "and your Lord *revealed* to the bee." The verb *awḥā* is the verb of revelation — the word used for God's communication to the prophets (4:163; 42:51). Its application to an insect demanded explanation, and the commentators provided it.

The root *w-ḥ-y* has a basic meaning of swift, hidden communication — a signal, an inspiration, a message conveyed subtly. Al-Rāghib defines it as "a swift indication." The Qur'an uses the verb in a range of applications: God's revelation to prophets (the technical sense); God's inspiration to the mother of Moses (28:7); Zechariah's signaling to his people (19:11); the devils' whispering to their allies (6:121); God's command to the earth on the Day of Judgment (99:5); and here, God's guidance to the bee. In every case, something is communicated secretly and directly.

Al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī, and al-Rāzī agree that the *waḥy* to the bee is not prophetic revelation but *ilhām*, inspiration — the implanting in the creature of an instinctive knowledge that guides it to what it must do. Al-Rāzī defines it as God's creating in the bee the knowledge of how to build its dwelling and produce its honey, without teaching, without deliberation, and without error. The bee does not learn its craft; it is born knowing it, and the knowing is God's *waḥy*.

The commentators note that the choice of the word *awḥā*, rather than *alhama* (inspired) or *ʿallama* (taught), is deliberate. It places the bee's guidance in continuity with the revelation given to the Prophet ﷺ. The same Lord who reveals the Qur'an reveals to the bee; the same *waḥy*, in different degrees and modes, orders both the hive and the community. Al-Rāzī observes that the bee, receiving *waḥy*, obeys it perfectly; the human being, receiving a higher *waḥy*, often disobeys. The word thus contains a reproach.

**"Thy Lord": The Address to the Prophet**

The verse says *rabbuka*, "your Lord" — addressing the Prophet ﷺ. Al-Rāzī notes the gentleness: the Lord who cares for the bee, guiding it to its dwelling and its food, is *your* Lord. The Prophet, facing the rejection of Makkah, is reminded that the One who sent him is the One whose providence extends to the smallest creature and does not fail. If God does not neglect the bee, He will not neglect His messenger.

**The Bee: *Al-Naḥl***

The word *naḥl* is a collective noun for bees, from a root that some connect to *naḥala*, to give freely, to grant as a gift (*niḥlah*, 4:4) — an etymology the commentators found apt, since the bee gives its honey freely to humans. The grammatical treatment of the noun varies: the verse uses feminine verbs for it (*ittakhidhī*, *kulī*, *fa'slukī*), which the grammarians explain by the collective's feminine gender or by the fact that the worker bees are female. The latter observation, made by some classical commentators on linguistic grounds, corresponds to the biological fact that the bees that build, forage, and produce honey are all female.

**"Take Up Dwellings": The First Command**

The content of the revelation is given in the imperative: *an ittakhidhī mina al-jibāli buyūtan wa-mina al-shajari wa-mimmā yaʿrishūn*, "that: take for yourself, among the mountains, dwellings, and among the trees, and among what they construct." The word *buyūt*, dwellings or houses, is the ordinary word for human homes, and its use for the bee's hive is significant. The bee's cells are *buyūt*, houses, built with an architectural precision that the commentators marked. Al-Rāzī, drawing on the observations available to him, notes that the bee builds its cells as regular hexagons — a shape it produces without instrument or measure, and which is the most efficient possible: hexagons tile a plane without gaps, use the least wax for the greatest storage, and share walls between cells. A human geometer, he says, could not produce such regularity without compass and ruler; the bee produces it by *waḥy*.

The verse names three sites for the dwellings. *Al-jibāl*, the mountains: wild bees nest in rock crevices and caves. *Al-shajar*, the trees: hollows in trunks and branches. *Mimmā yaʿrishūn*, "what they construct" — the hives and trellises that human beings build, from *ʿarasha*, to construct a trellis or roof (the same root as *ʿarsh*, throne, and *maʿrūshāt*, trellised vines, 6:141). Al-Qurṭubī notes that the third category refers to the structures people build for bees — the domesticated hives — while the first two are the bee's natural habitats. The verse thus covers the bee's whole range: wild in the rocks, wild in the woods, and domesticated among humans. In each setting, the *waḥy* guides it to build.

**The Significance of the Command Form**

The verse renders the bee's instinct as a series of commands: take dwellings, eat, follow the paths. The commentators discussed why the Qur'an frames instinct as command. Al-Zamakhsharī notes that it expresses the reality that the bee's behavior is not random or self-originated but is a *response* — the bee does what it was told, though the telling was inscribed in its nature rather than spoken. The framing also serves the argument to the human reader: the bee is *commanded* and *obeys*; the reader is commanded and — the verse leaves the question open. The Qur'an elsewhere describes all creation as responding to command: "He said to it and to the earth: Come, willingly or unwillingly. They said: We come willingly" (41:11). The bee's construction of its hive is its "we come willingly."

**The Bee as Argument for Design**

The commentators recognized in the bee a proof of the Creator that requires no scripture. Al-Rāzī sets out the argument. The bee is a small creature with a minute brain and no capacity for reasoning as humans practice it. Yet it builds a structure of perfect geometry, organizes a society of thousands with a division of labor, navigates over long distances and returns unerringly to its hive, communicates the location of food to its fellows, and transforms nectar into a substance that human chemistry cannot synthesize. None of this can be attributed to the bee's own intelligence, because the bee has not the intelligence to have devised it. It must be attributed to the intelligence of the One who made the bee and "revealed" to it. The verse states the conclusion the argument reaches: *awḥā rabbuka* — your Lord revealed.

Modern knowledge of the bee has deepened the argument rather than weakened it. The waggle dance by which foragers communicate direction and distance; the temperature regulation of the hive; the chemical composition of honey with its antimicrobial properties; the bee's role in pollinating the plants on which human agriculture depends — each is a further instance of the *waḥy* the verse names.

**The Connection to the Sequence of Verses 65–69**

The bee is the fourth and last in the sūrah's sequence of drinks and their sources: water from the sky (v. 65), milk from cattle (v. 66), juice from fruit (v. 67), and now honey from the bee (v. 68–69). The commentators note that the sequence ascends in wonder: water falls; milk is extracted; juice is pressed; but honey is *made*, by a creature that gathers from a thousand flowers what no single flower contains and transforms it into something new. The bee's production is the most "creative" of the four, and it is therefore the one in which God's *waḥy* is named explicitly. And the sequence's correspondence to the four rivers of Paradise (47:15), noted at verse 65, culminates in "rivers of purified honey" — the earthly honey of verse 69 being the foretaste of the heavenly.

**The Lesson for the Human Reader**

The verse addresses the human being through the bee. The bee has a dwelling given by God, a work given by God, and a method given by God, and it does not depart from any of them. The human being has all three in a higher form — the earth as dwelling, worship and building as work, the revealed law as method — and departs from them constantly. The bee, in the verse's framing, is the model of what the sūrah has been asking for since its first verse: a creature that receives what its Lord reveals and simply *does* it. The Prophet ﷺ compared the believer to the bee:

> *"By the One in whose hand is my soul, the likeness of the believer is that of the bee: it eats what is good, produces what is good, and when it alights on something it neither breaks nor spoils it."* (Aḥmad 6872; al-Ḥākim; graded authentic)

The comparison holds at every point. The bee takes only what is pure; the believer consumes only the lawful. The bee produces healing; the believer produces benefit. The bee harms nothing it touches; the believer is one from whose hand and tongue people are safe. And the bee does all this by following what was revealed to it — which is exactly what the believer is asked to do with the Reminder that verse 44 says was sent down for his sake.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:69

> **Then eat of every kind of fruit, and follow the ways of thy Lord made easy." A drink of diverse hues comes forth from their bellies wherein there is healing for mankind. Truly in that is a sign for a people who reflect.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Revelation to the Bee Continues**

Verse 68 gave the bee its first command: take dwellings in the mountains, the trees, and human constructions. Verse 69 continues the revelation with two further commands — eat and follow the paths — and then describes the result: a drink of varied colors that heals. The verse moves from what God tells the bee to what God brings forth from it, and ends with the sūrah's characteristic formula, this time addressed to "a people who reflect."

**"Then Eat of Every Kind of Fruit": *Kulī min kulli al-thamarāt***

The second command is *thumma kulī min kulli al-thamarāt*, "then eat of every kind of fruit." The word *thamarāt*, fruits, is used here in its broad sense of what plants produce — the commentators understand it as the flowers, blossoms, and nectar from which bees gather, not only fruit in the narrow sense. Al-Qurṭubī notes that the bee is given license over "every" kind: it is not restricted to one plant but ranges over all that flowers, sweet and bitter alike. And from this diversity of sources it produces a single product.

The commentators drew a lesson from the bee's diet. The bee eats what is pure — nectar and pollen — and takes from each plant without harming it; the flower is left intact, and indeed benefited, since the bee pollinates it. Al-Rāzī sees in this an image of the ideal relationship between a creature and its provision: taking what one needs, leaving the source unharmed, and producing benefit in return. The hadith cited at verse 68 — the believer as bee, who "neither breaks nor spoils" what it alights upon — draws exactly this lesson.

**"And Follow the Ways of Thy Lord Made Easy": *Fa'slukī subula rabbiki dhululan***

The third command is *fa'slukī subula rabbiki dhululan*, "then travel the paths of your Lord, made smooth." The verb *salaka* means to enter upon or travel a path; *subul* is the plural of *sabīl*, way. The bee is told to follow "the paths of your Lord" — the routes from hive to flower and back, which God has laid out for it.

The word *dhululan* has two readings, both recorded by al-Ṭabarī and al-Qurṭubī. It may be an adjective describing the paths — "the paths of your Lord, made easy" — meaning that God has made the routes smooth and passable for the bee, so that it does not lose its way even over great distances. Or it may describe the bee itself — "travel the paths of your Lord *in submission*" — from *dhalūl*, submissive, tractable, as a trained animal is *dhalūl*. On the second reading the bee travels obediently, following God's paths as a docile mount follows its rider. Mujāhid held the first reading; Qatādah the second. Al-Zamakhsharī notes that both are true and that the ambiguity may be intentional: the paths are made easy, and the bee follows them submissively.

Al-Rāzī observes the wonder the phrase points to: the bee travels far from its hive — over fields, across obstacles, through changing winds — and returns unerringly to the same small entrance. It does not lose its way. The commentators knew this from observation; modern study has detailed the bee's navigation by the sun's position, by polarized light, and by landmark memory, and its communication of routes to other bees by dance. All of this is *subul rabbik*, the Lord's paths, made *dhulul*, easy, for a creature that could not have devised them.

The phrase "the paths of your Lord" was also read by the commentators as an image of the human situation. God has laid out paths for the human being too — the *sabīl* of verse 9, "unto God leads the straight path" — and made them easy; the person who follows them arrives, as the bee arrives, at his dwelling. The Sufi commentators extended this: the seeker who follows the paths of his Lord in submission, taking from every source what is pure, produces from within himself something that heals others.

**"A Drink of Diverse Hues Comes Forth From Their Bellies"**
