The verse then turns from command to description: *yakhruju min buṭūnihā sharābun mukhtalifun alwānuhu*, "there comes forth from their bellies a drink whose colors vary." The verb is in the present tense, describing a continuing reality. The word *sharāb*, drink, is used for honey — a substance that is both food and drink, as milk was described in verse 66. The word "bellies" connects the verse to verse 66, where milk came "from what is in their bellies": the same divine operation — a pure product emerging from an animal's interior — is repeated in the bee.

The phrase *mukhtalifun alwānuhu*, "of varied colors," describes honey precisely. Honey ranges from nearly white through gold and amber to dark brown, depending on the flowers from which the nectar was gathered. The commentators noted the variety: al-Qurṭubī records white, yellow, red, and black honey, each from different sources. The verse's phrase is the same used in verse 13 for what God has "multiplied for you in the earth of varied colors" — the diversity of color is, throughout the sūrah, a sign of the Creator's deliberate artistry, since a mechanical process would produce uniformity while a purposeful Maker produces variety.

The commentators also addressed the question of how honey is produced. The classical view, following observation, was that the bee gathers nectar, carries it in its body, and produces honey from it — which is accurate: the bee stores nectar in a special stomach (the honey stomach or crop), where enzymes begin to transform its sugars, and then deposits it in the comb, where evaporation and further enzymatic action complete the conversion. The verse's "from their bellies" describes this. Some commentators, aware that the process involved the bee's body, hesitated over whether honey was then an "excretion" and therefore impure; al-Qurṭubī resolves the question by noting that the Qur'an calls it a drink with healing, and that the Prophet ﷺ drank it and praised it — its purity is thus established by revelation and practice regardless of the mechanism.

**"Wherein There Is Healing for Mankind": *Fīhi Shifāʾun li'l-nās***

The verse's central claim about honey is medical: *fīhi shifāʾun li'l-nās*, "in it is healing for people." The word *shifāʾ* means cure, healing, recovery from illness. The Qur'an uses it for the Qur'an itself — "a healing for what is in the breasts" (10:57), "a healing and a mercy for the believers" (17:82) — and for honey. The commentators drew the connection: Ibn Masʿūd is reported to have said:

> *"Take hold of the two cures: honey and the Qur'an."* (Ibn Mājah 3452; al-Ḥākim)

The Qur'an heals the heart; honey heals the body. The pairing is not accidental — the same sūrah that describes the Qur'an as clarification, guidance, and mercy describes honey as healing, and Ibn Masʿūd's saying joins them.

The Prophet ﷺ used honey as medicine and prescribed it. The most famous report concerns a man whose brother suffered from a stomach ailment:

> *A man came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: "My brother has a complaint of the stomach." He said: "Give him honey to drink." The man gave it and returned, saying: "I gave him honey and it only increased his looseness." The Prophet said: "Give him honey." He did so, and returned, saying: "It only increased." The Prophet said: "God has spoken the truth, and your brother's stomach has lied. Give him honey." He gave it, and the brother was cured.* (al-Bukhārī 5684; Muslim 2217)

"God has spoken the truth, and your brother's stomach has lied" — the Prophet's confidence rested on this verse. The verse said there is healing in honey; the man's report contradicted it; the Prophet trusted the verse over the report and was vindicated. The hadith illustrates a principle the commentators drew from it: the verse's statement is true, though its application may require persistence and though honey is not a cure for every ailment in every case.

The Prophet also said:

> *"Healing is in three things: a drink of honey, the incision of a cupper, and cauterization with fire — and I forbid my community from cauterization."* (al-Bukhārī 5680)

And he himself loved honey (al-Bukhārī 5431), and would drink it with water in the morning.

**The Scope of "Healing": The Commentators' Discussion**

The verse says *shifāʾ*, "a healing," not *al-shifāʾ*, "the healing." Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Rāzī note the indefinite form: honey contains *a* healing — it is a cure for some ailments, not a universal cure for all. This is the correct reading of the verse's claim, and it is confirmed by the hadith's "healing is in three things." Al-Rāzī, drawing on the medicine of his time, lists honey's uses: as a remedy for digestive complaints, for wounds, for coughs and chest ailments, and as a base for many compound medicines; he notes that physicians used it as a preservative and a vehicle for other drugs. Modern medicine has confirmed honey's antibacterial properties, its effectiveness in wound healing, its use for cough, and its nutritional value. The verse does not claim more than this, and it claims no less.

Some commentators read the pronoun *fīhi*, "in it," as referring not to honey but to the Qur'an — "in it [the Qur'an] is healing for people" — but the majority, following the plain flow of the verse, refer it to the honey. Al-Qurṭubī notes that the mystical commentators combined both: the honey's healing is a sign of the Qur'an's.

**"A Sign for a People Who Reflect": *Li-qawmin yatafakkarūn***

The verse ends with the sūrah's formula and names the faculty of *tafakkur*, reflection. The verse 65 named hearing; 67 named reason; 69 names reflection. The commentators explain the fit: the bee and its honey require sustained thought to be understood as a sign. One must consider the smallness of the creature, the perfection of its work, the diversity of its sources, the unity of its product, the variety of the product's colors, and the healing in it — and then ask how any of this could be. The one who reflects arrives at *awḥā rabbuka*: the Lord revealed. The one who does not reflect sees only an insect and a sweet.

**The Sign Within the Sign**

The commentators saw in the bee a compressed image of the whole sūrah's teaching. The bee receives revelation and obeys; the human is asked to do the same. The bee takes from every flower and produces one pure thing; the human is asked to take from every experience the good and to produce, from his life, benefit. The bee's product heals others; the believer's life should heal the community. And the bee does all this by *following the paths of its Lord, made easy* — which is the definition of the straight path that verse 9 said leads to God. The sūrah named itself after this creature because the creature is the argument: if the bee can do what its Lord reveals, so can the one for whom the Reminder was sent.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:70

> **And God created you; then He takes you [unto Himself]. And among you are those who are brought back to the most abject age, so that after having known, they know nothing. Truly God is Knowing, Powerful.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**From the Creatures Outside to the Human Being Himself**

Verses 65–69 pointed to the signs in rain, cattle, fruit, and bees — realities outside the human being. Verse 70 turns the gaze inward: *wa'llāhu khalaqakum thumma yatawaffākum*, "And God created you; then He takes you." The human being is himself a sign, and the verse presents the arc of his existence — creation, death, and, for some, the decline of extreme age — as evidence of the same power that governs the bee and the rain. The sūrah's method is to move from the world to the self, so that the reader cannot treat the argument as being about something else.

**"God Created You; Then He Takes You"**

The verse's opening asserts God's authorship of both ends of human life. *Khalaqakum*, "He created you," names the origin; *yatawaffākum*, "He takes you in full," names the end. The verb *tawaffā*, discussed at verse 28, means to take something completely, to receive it in full — and its use for death expresses that the soul is not annihilated but *taken*, received back by the One who gave it. The Qur'an describes the same arc elsewhere: "God is the One who created you, then provided for you, then causes you to die, then gives you life. Is there among your partners one who does any of that?" (30:40).

The word *thumma*, "then," between creation and death marks the interval — the whole of a human life, compressed to a single conjunction. Al-Rāzī notes the effect: from God's perspective, and from the perspective of eternity, the lifespan that seems so long to the one living it is a "then" between two divine acts. The sūrah has already used this compression in verse 1 ("the command of God is coming") and will use it again in verse 77 ("the Hour is but as the blink of an eye").

The verse's first clause is an argument in itself. The Makkans acknowledged that God created them (v. 31:25; 43:87). If He created them, He controls their end. And if He controls both origin and end, He controls what lies between and what lies after. The denial of resurrection (v. 38) is inconsistent with the admission of creation; verse 70 sets the two side by side so that the inconsistency is felt.

**"Among You Are Those Brought Back to the Most Abject Age"**

The verse's second clause introduces a specific phenomenon: *wa-minkum man yuraddu ilā ardhali al-ʿumur*, "and among you is one who is returned to the most abject of life." The word *ardhal* is the superlative of *radhīl*, base, contemptible, worthless; *ardhal al-ʿumur* is the most abject, most degraded stage of life — extreme old age, when the faculties fail. The verb *yuraddu*, "is returned" or "sent back," is precise: the very old person is returned to a state resembling infancy — dependent, weak, unable to reason or remember.

The Qur'an describes the same phenomenon in Sūrat al-Ḥajj, in a passage that parallels this one in its argument from the human life-cycle to resurrection:

> *"O mankind, if you are in doubt about the Resurrection, then [consider that] We created you from dust, then from a drop, then from a clinging clot, then from a lump of flesh, formed and unformed, that We may make clear to you. And We settle in the wombs whom We will for a specified term, then We bring you out as infants, then [We develop you] that you may reach your maturity. And among you is he who is taken in death, and among you is he who is returned to the most abject age so that he knows, after knowledge, nothing."* (Qur'an 22:5)

And in Sūrat Yā Sīn: *"And he to whom We grant long life, We reverse him in creation. Do they not understand?"* (36:68). The word "reverse" (*nunakkis-hu*) is the image: the arc of growth bends back, and the old man declines through the stages he once ascended.

**The Commentators on the Age Meant**

The commentators discussed what age constitutes *ardhal al-ʿumur*. ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib is reported to have said seventy-five; others said eighty, or ninety; Qatādah said ninety. Al-Qurṭubī records these and notes that the verse does not specify a number, because the onset of decline varies from person to person; the phrase describes a *state* — the state of losing what one had — rather than a fixed year. Some noted that the Prophet ﷺ sought refuge from this state:

> *"O God, I seek refuge in You from incapacity and laziness, from cowardice and miserliness, from decrepitude (al-haram) and the punishment of the grave."* (al-Bukhārī 6367; Muslim 2706)

> *"O God, I seek refuge in You from... being returned to the most abject age."* (al-Bukhārī 6374, using the verse's own phrase)

The Prophet's use of the verse's exact wording in his supplication shows that *ardhal al-ʿumur* was understood as a real affliction from which one may rightly ask to be spared. The commentators add that the believer is not returned to this state in the same way as the disbeliever: some reports hold that the Qur'an-reciter is protected from its worst effects, and al-Qurṭubī cites the report that the one who has memorized the Qur'an is not returned to *ardhal al-ʿumur* — though he acknowledges the report is not strong and that the observation is not universal.

**"So That After Having Known, They Know Nothing": *Li-kaylā yaʿlama baʿda ʿilmin shayʾan***

The verse describes the effect of extreme age precisely: *li-kaylā yaʿlama baʿda ʿilmin shayʾan*, "so that he knows, after knowledge, nothing." The person who had accumulated a lifetime of knowledge — of people, of skills, of memories, of the world — loses it. He does not recognize his children; he forgets what he was told a moment ago; he cannot perform what he once did with ease. The phrase *baʿda ʿilmin*, "after knowledge," is the hinge: the loss is not the absence of knowledge that the infant has, but the *loss* of knowledge once possessed, which is worse.

The commentators note the *lām* in *li-kaylā*. It is not the *lām* of purpose in the sense that God's aim in prolonging life is to strip the person of knowledge; it is the *lām* of consequence, as in verse 55 — the result of extreme age is that knowledge departs. Al-Rāzī adds that the verse describes the general pattern, not an absolute rule; some very old people retain their faculties, and the verse's "among you" marks the phenomenon as common rather than universal.

The description has a modern resonance that the classical commentators could not have anticipated in its clinical detail: the dementias of old age, in which memory and recognition are progressively lost, are among the most feared conditions of contemporary life. The verse describes their outcome exactly — knowing nothing after knowing — and presents it as a sign.

**The Argument of the Verse**

What is the sign? The commentators identify it. First, the decline of old age demonstrates that the human being does not own his faculties. He did not give himself knowledge, and he cannot keep it; both the acquisition and the loss are God's doing. Al-Rāzī notes that the person who imagines his intelligence to be his own possession has only to look at the very old to see that it is a loan. Second, the reversal of the human being — from strength to weakness, from knowledge to ignorance — demonstrates that the One who can reverse the process can also repeat it: the God who returns the old man to the state of infancy can return the dead man to life. The verse belongs to the sūrah's cumulative argument for resurrection, and its contribution is the observation that God visibly *undoes* human development within a single lifetime. Undoing and redoing are the same power. Third, the verse is an argument for humility: no one, however strong or learned, is exempt from the arc it describes. The chief of Quraysh who mocked the Prophet would, if he lived, become a dependent old man who could not remember his own arguments.

**"Truly God Is Knowing, Powerful": The Two Names**

The verse ends: *inna Allāha ʿalīmun qadīr*, "truly God is Knowing, Powerful." Al-Rāzī explains the pairing. The verse has described human knowledge failing; against it stands God, whose knowledge does not fail — *ʿAlīm*. The verse has described human strength collapsing; against it stands God, whose power does not collapse — *Qadīr*. The two names are the answer to the two losses. What the human being holds only for a time, God holds eternally. And the names complete the argument for resurrection: the One who knows every particle of every decayed body and has the power to reassemble it can raise the dead. The Qur'an makes the point directly: "He is over all things Powerful" (v. 77) and "He knows what the earth diminishes of them" (50:4).

**The Human Application**

The verse asks the reader to see his own life in its full arc and to draw the consequences. He was created; he will be taken; and between these two, he may be returned to weakness before he goes. The correct responses, which the tradition drew from this verse, are several. Gratitude for present faculties, which are loans: the Prophet ﷺ said, *"Take advantage of five before five: your youth before your old age, your health before your sickness..."* (al-Ḥākim 7846). Compassion for the old, who are living the verse's second clause: the Qur'an commands kindness to aged parents in terms that anticipate their dependence (17:23–24), and the Prophet said, *"He is not of us who does not have mercy on our young and respect our old"* (al-Tirmidhī 1919). And the use of knowledge while one has it — since "after knowledge, nothing" is a possibility for everyone, the knowledge one has now is the only knowledge one can be sure of acting upon. The verse's closing names remind the reader that his own knowledge and power are borrowed from the One whose knowledge and power are His own, and that the loan will be called in.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:71

> **And God has favored some of you above others in provision. But those who have been favored do not hand over their provision to those whom their right hands possess, such that they would be equal in respect thereto. Do they then deny the blessing of God?**

**Expanded Commentary**

**A New Kind of Argument: From Human Practice**

The preceding verses drew signs from creation — rain, milk, fruit, bees, the human life-cycle. Verse 71 draws its argument from human social behavior. It observes a fact about how people treat their own property, and it uses that fact to expose the absurdity of *shirk*. The reasoning is a parable drawn from the idolaters' own conduct: you do not share your wealth equally with your slaves so as to make them your equals; how, then, do you assign God's servants as equals to Him? The verse is thus both an observation about economic inequality and a *reductio* of idolatry.

**"God Has Favored Some of You Above Others in Provision"**

The verse begins with a plain statement: *wa'llāhu faḍḍala baʿḍakum ʿalā baʿḍin fī al-rizq*, "and God has preferred some of you over others in provision." The verb *faḍḍala* means to give preference, to grant more to one than another. The statement is descriptive, not prescriptive: it observes that human beings differ in wealth, and it attributes the difference ultimately to God's apportionment.

The Qur'an makes this observation repeatedly and treats it as a fact of the created order:

> *"Is it they who apportion the mercy of your Lord? It is We who have apportioned among them their livelihood in the life of this world, and We have raised some of them above others in degrees, that some may employ others in service. And the mercy of your Lord is better than what they accumulate."* (Qur'an 43:32)

> *"And God has favored some of you over others in provision."* (Qur'an 16:71; cf. 17:21, 30; 30:37; 34:36, 39; 42:12)

The commentators address the apparent difficulty: does the verse endorse inequality? Al-Rāzī's answer is that the verse states a fact and attributes it to divine wisdom — the wisdom named in 43:32, "that some may employ others in service," that is, so that human society may function through mutual need and exchange. If all were equal in every respect, no one would work for another and no cooperation would arise. The differentiation is functional. But the verse does not thereby endorse the *abuse* of difference; the same Qur'an that observes inequality commands *zakāt*, charity, and justice, and condemns the hoarding of wealth (9:34; 104:2–3). The verse's purpose here is not to legislate about wealth but to draw an argument from the fact of its distribution.

The passage also contains a corrective to envy. Since the differences are God's apportionment, the Qur'an forbids coveting what others have been given: *"Do not wish for that by which God has favored some of you over others"* (4:32). The person who understands that his provision is God's allotment neither resents the one who has more nor despises the one who has less.

**"Those Who Have Been Favored Do Not Hand Over Their Provision to Those Whom Their Right Hands Possess"**

The verse then makes its observation: *fa-mā alladhīna fuḍḍilū bi-rāddī rizqihim ʿalā mā malakat aymānuhum fa-hum fīhi sawāʾ*, "but those who were favored are not going to hand over their provision to what their right hands possess so that they become equal in it." The phrase *mā malakat aymānuhum*, "what their right hands possess," is the Qur'an's expression for slaves — those held in bondage under the system that existed in seventh-century Arabia and that Islam regulated and progressively dismantled.

The observation is this: the wealthy master does not distribute his property to his slaves in such a way that master and slave become equal partners in it. He may feed and clothe them — Islam commanded that — but he does not make them co-owners. Masters and slaves are not "equal in it" (*sawāʾ*). Al-Ṭabarī and al-Qurṭubī explain the verse as describing what the Arabs actually did: no man made his slave his equal in wealth.

The commentators read this as the premise of an argument, and its conclusion is drawn in the form of a parable in Sūrat al-Rūm, which states explicitly what 16:71 leaves implicit:

> *"He presents to you an example from yourselves: Do you have, among those whom your right hands possess, partners in what We have provided for you, so that you are equal therein, fearing them as you fear one another? Thus do We detail the signs for a people who use reason. But those who do wrong follow their desires without knowledge."* (Qur'an 30:28)

The verse in al-Rūm gives the full form: you would not accept your slaves as partners in your property; yet you make God's slaves — the angels, the idols, the creatures — partners in His divinity. If you, in your smallness, refuse to be equated with your possessions, how do you equate God with His? The argument is *a fortiori* from the lesser to the greater. Al-Rāzī states it: since it is regarded as absurd that a master should make his slave his equal in what he owns, it is more absurd that God should have partners from among what He owns — and everything is what He owns (v. 52).

**The Second Reading: Ingratitude for Provision**

Some commentators, including al-Ṭabarī in one of his reports and al-Zamakhsharī, read the verse's middle clause not only as the premise of the argument against *shirk* but as a reproach in its own right. On this reading, the verse observes that the wealthy do not share their provision with their dependents to the point of equality — and finds fault with it. The wealth, after all, is *God's* provision (*rizqihim* — "their provision," but given by God); the wealthy hold it as stewards; and their refusal to share it is a form of the ingratitude the verse names at its end. Al-Zamakhsharī develops this: the masters and the slaves are equally God's creatures and equally dependent on His provision; that the masters withhold what they were given, treating it as their own, is *kufr al-niʿmah*.

The Prophet's teaching about slaves supports this reading as an ethical complement to the argumentative one. He commanded:

> *"Your slaves are your brothers whom God has placed under your authority. So whoever has his brother under his authority, let him feed him from what he eats and clothe him from what he wears, and do not burden them with what overwhelms them; and if you do so, help them."* (al-Bukhārī 30; Muslim 1661)

The command to feed the slave "from what you eat" and clothe him "from what you wear" moves toward the equality the verse observes that people do not practice. Islam did not immediately abolish slavery, but it demanded that masters treat slaves as brothers and made manumission an act of the highest merit (90:13; 2:177) and an expiation for many sins (4:92; 5:89; 58:3). Both readings of the verse — the argument against *shirk* and the reproach of hoarding — are thus sustained by the tradition, and the commentators generally allowed both.

**"Do They Then Deny the Blessing of God?"**

The verse ends: *a-fa-bi-niʿmati Allāhi yajḥadūn*, "is it then the blessing of God that they deny?" The verb *jaḥada* means to deny what one knows to be true — to reject with the tongue what the heart acknowledges (cf. 27:14, "they denied them while their souls were convinced of them"). The word is stronger than mere disbelief; it connotes willful rejection.

The commentators connect the question to both readings. On the first, the idolaters deny God's blessing by attributing His gifts — the provision He apportioned — to partners; by making the idols equal to God, they deny that the blessings came from Him alone. On the second, the wealthy deny God's blessing by treating it as their own achievement rather than His gift, and by withholding it from those He placed in their care. In both cases the denial is *jaḥd*: they know, at some level, that the provision is God's, and they act as though it were not.

The fronting of *bi-niʿmati Allāh*, "the blessing of God," before the verb gives the question its edge: "is it *the blessing of God* — of all things — that they deny?" Al-Zamakhsharī notes that the question expresses astonishment: having received the blessing, and having it demonstrated to them through the very arrangement of their own society, they still deny it.

**The Sūrah's Recurring Theme**

The verse returns to the sūrah's central axis — blessing acknowledged or denied. Verse 18 said the blessings cannot be counted; verse 53 said every blessing is from God; verse 55 named the ingratitude that follows relief; verse 71 asks whether the blessing itself is denied; verse 83 will say they "recognize the blessing of God and then deny it"; verse 112 will show the town that "was ungrateful for the blessings of God." The verse's closing question is a link in this chain, and its distinctive contribution is to locate the denial in *social* conduct — in how people treat God's gifts in relation to other people.

**The Application: Two Lessons From One Verse**

The verse teaches two things that the modern reader can take directly. The first is the argument against every form of *shirk*: if one would not accept a subordinate as an equal partner in what one owns, one should not assign God partners from what He owns — whether those partners are idols, saints, ideologies, or one's own desires. The second is the ethic of provision: what one has was apportioned by God, and the person who has more is not thereby better but is more responsible. The refusal to share to the point of equality is a fact of human nature that the verse observes; but the verse's closing question — do they deny God's blessing? — implies that the fact should trouble the one who holds the wealth. The believer who has been favored in provision is asked to remember that the favor was God's, that the one beneath him is his brother, and that the denial of blessing takes the form not only of false worship but of a closed hand.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:72

> **And God has made for you spouses from among yourselves, and has made for you, from your spouses, children and grandchildren, and has provided you with good things. Do they then believe in falsehood, and deny the blessing of God?**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Blessing Closest to Home**

The sūrah has enumerated the blessings of the external world — rain, animals, fruits, the bee — and of the human body and lifespan (v. 70) and of provision (v. 71). Verse 72 turns to the blessing that touches human life most intimately: the family. *Wa'llāhu jaʿala lakum min anfusikum azwājan*, "And God has made for you, from yourselves, spouses." The verse names the spouse, the children, and the grandchildren as gifts, and then asks the same question that closed verse 71, now sharpened: after all this, do they believe in falsehood and deny God's blessing?

**"Spouses From Among Yourselves": *Min Anfusikum***

The verse says God made spouses for human beings *min anfusikum*, "from yourselves" — of the same kind, the same nature, the same species. The commentators note two dimensions of the phrase. The first is the creation of Eve from Adam, which the Qur'an describes: "He created you from one soul and created from it its mate" (4:1; 7:189; 39:6). The first spouse was literally "from" the first human. The second is the ongoing reality: every spouse is a human being like oneself, not an angel or a jinn or a creature of another kind. Al-Rāzī observes the wisdom in this: intimacy, companionship, and understanding are possible only between beings of the same nature. A human being could not find rest with a spouse of a different kind. The Qur'an names this rest as the purpose of marriage:

> *"And among His signs is that He created for you, from yourselves, spouses that you may find tranquility in them, and He placed between you affection and mercy. Truly in that are signs for a people who reflect."* (Qur'an 30:21)

The verse in al-Rūm expands on 16:72: the spouse is "from yourselves" so that *sakan*, tranquility, may be found, and God places between the spouses *mawaddah* and *raḥmah*, affection and mercy. The commentators note that these are not produced by the spouses themselves — two strangers cannot manufacture love by decision — but are *placed* by God. The bond of marriage is thus a blessing in its very existence, not merely in its benefits.

The word *azwāj*, spouses, is the plural of *zawj*, which means one of a pair — either member. The Qur'an uses it for both husband and wife, and the verse's address is to all human beings, male and female: God has made spouses for each from the other.

**"From Your Spouses, Children and Grandchildren": *Banīn wa-Ḥafadah***

The verse then names the second blessing: *wa-jaʿala lakum min azwājikum banīna wa-ḥafadah*, "and has made for you from your spouses children and *ḥafadah*." The word *banīn* is children — sons, or children generally. The word *ḥafadah* is rarer and prompted extensive discussion.

The root *ḥ-f-d* means to be quick and eager in service — *ḥafada* is to hasten in serving someone. From this root, the commentators derived several meanings for *ḥafadah*, and al-Ṭabarī records them at length. The most common reading, held by Ibn ʿAbbās in one report and adopted by many, is *grandchildren* — the children of one's children, who are named separately from *banīn* as a further gift. A second reading, held by Ibn Masʿūd and others, is *servants* or *helpers* — those who serve one eagerly, which may include one's children in their capacity as helpers, or servants generally. A third reading, attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās in another report, is *sons-in-law* — the husbands of one's daughters, who come "from your spouses" in the sense that they enter the family through the marriages of one's children. A fourth reading takes *ḥafadah* as the children who serve their parents — so that *banīn* names them as offspring and *ḥafadah* names them as helpers.

Al-Ṭabarī, after surveying the readings, concludes that the word denotes all who serve and assist one eagerly, whether children, grandchildren, or others, since this is the root meaning; and he notes that the verse's "from your spouses" restricts it to those who come through marriage — thus children, grandchildren, and in-laws. Al-Qurṭubī and al-Rāzī survey the same range. The verse's meaning, on any reading, is that marriage produces not only offspring but a network of relationship and mutual help — the extended family, which was, in the Arab context and remains in most human societies, the primary structure of support, protection, and continuity.

**"And Has Provided You With Good Things": *Al-Ṭayyibāt***

The third blessing is *wa-razaqakum mina al-ṭayyibāt*, "and has provided you from the good things." The word *ṭayyibāt* denotes what is good, wholesome, pure, pleasant — lawful food, drink, and the pleasant things of life. The commentators note that after naming the family, the verse names the provision that sustains it: God gives the spouse, the children, and the means to feed them. Al-Rāzī observes the order: the verse follows the natural sequence of a human life — one marries, one has children, one provides for them from the good things God gives.

The phrase also anticipates verse 114, "so eat of what God has provided you, lawful and good," and stands against the arbitrary prohibitions of verses 116–117, in which the idolaters forbade themselves some of the *ṭayyibāt* God had permitted.

**"Do They Then Believe in Falsehood?"**

The verse's closing question has two parts. The first is *a-fa-bi'l-bāṭili yuʾminūn*, "is it then in falsehood that they believe?" The word *bāṭil* denotes what is false, vain, void — the opposite of *ḥaqq*, truth. The commentators identify the falsehood as the idols and the whole system of belief around them: the claim that the idols benefit or harm, that they intercede, that they deserve a share of God's provision (v. 56), that God has daughters (v. 57). Al-Rāzī notes the irony the verse constructs: God has given them spouses, children, grandchildren, and good provision — real, tangible, daily blessings — and they respond by believing in things that are *bāṭil*, void, that never gave them anything. They trust the empty and distrust the Giver.

**"And Deny the Blessing of God?"**

The second part is *wa-bi-niʿmati Allāhi hum yakfurūn*, "and in the blessing of God they disbelieve?" The verse ends where verse 71 ended, but with a different verb: verse 71 used *yajḥadūn*, "they deny [what they know]"; verse 72 uses *yakfurūn*, "they disbelieve" or "are ungrateful." The two verbs together give the full picture: they know the blessings are God's and deny it (*jaḥd*), and they cover the blessings with ingratitude (*kufr*). The pronoun *hum*, "they," is added for emphasis — "and *they*, of all people, are ungrateful for God's blessing" — they who have been given so much.

Al-Zamakhsharī notes the structure of the two clauses: belief is placed with falsehood, disbelief with God's blessing. The idolaters have inverted the proper objects of belief and disbelief. They believe in what deserves rejection and reject what deserves gratitude. The verse asks, in astonishment, how such an inversion is possible — and the sūrah's answer, given in verse 63, is Satan's beautification of their deeds.

**The Family as Sign and Blessing**

The verse treats the family as a *sign* — evidence of God's design and care — and a *blessing* — a gift that demands gratitude. The commentators drew out both. As sign: the pairing of human beings into spouses, the emergence of children from the union, the extension into generations, and the bonds of love and service that hold the structure together, none of which the human being designed, all point to a Designer. The Qur'an says of the spouse "that you may find rest" and of the bonds "He placed between you affection" — the verbs are God's. As blessing: the spouse is companionship against loneliness, the children are continuity against extinction, the grandchildren are joy in old age, and the family is support in weakness. The Prophet ﷺ described the righteous wife as the best of this world's goods:

> *"This world is provision, and the best provision of this world is a righteous wife."* (Muslim 1467)

And he described children as an ongoing source of good after death:

> *"When the son of Adam dies, his deeds are cut off except from three: a continuing charity, knowledge that benefits, or a righteous child who prays for him."* (Muslim 1631)

The family, in this light, is not merely a social arrangement but a channel of divine blessing that extends beyond the grave.

**The Gratitude the Verse Demands**

The verse's question implies its answer: the proper response to spouse, children, grandchildren, and provision is not belief in falsehood but gratitude to God. The tradition specified the forms this gratitude takes. Toward the spouse: kindness, as the Prophet ﷺ said, *"The best of you are the best to their wives"* (al-Tirmidhī 3895). Toward children: upbringing in faith and justice between them, as he commanded (al-Bukhārī 2587). Toward provision: lawful use and sharing. And toward God: acknowledgment that the whole structure is His gift — expressed in the supplication the Qur'an teaches: *"Our Lord, grant us from our spouses and offspring comfort to our eyes, and make us leaders of the God-fearing"* (25:74). The one who prays this prayer has answered the verse's question correctly: he believes not in falsehood but in the Giver, and he does not deny the blessing but asks for its increase.

**The Verse and the Modern Reader**

The verse describes what most people would name, if asked, as the most important things in their lives — spouse, children, family, sustenance. It asks them to see these as gifts and to trace them to their source. The modern tendency is to regard the family as a private achievement or a biological accident; the verse regards it as a divine act, *jaʿala lakum*, "He made for you." The difference determines how one holds the gift: as owner, anxious and entitled, or as recipient, grateful and responsible. The verse's question — do they believe in falsehood and deny God's blessing? — applies to anyone who enjoys the family and credits it to anything but the One who "placed affection and mercy" between strangers and made them one.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:73

> **And they worship, apart from God, that which has no power over any provision that may come to them from the heavens and the earth, nor are they capable [of anything].**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Turn From Blessings to the Objects of False Worship**

Verses 70–72 enumerated the blessings God gives the human being — life, provision, spouse, children, good things — and ended by asking whether people deny these blessings. Verse 73 identifies what they do instead: *wa-yaʿbudūna min dūni Allāhi mā lā yamliku lahum rizqan*, "and they worship, besides God, what has no control over any provision for them." The verse contrasts the Giver of the blessings just listed with the idols that give nothing, and it frames the contrast in terms of the sūrah's dominant concern: *rizq*, provision.

**"They Worship, Apart From God": The Root of the Error**

The phrase *min dūni Allāh*, "apart from God" or "besides God," recurs throughout the Qur'an as the marker of *shirk*. It denotes worship directed at anything other than God, whether alongside Him or instead of Him. The commentators note that the idolaters did not deny God; they worshipped others *besides* Him, claiming these others as intermediaries (39:3) and intercessors (10:18). The verse does not dispute their acknowledgment of God; it targets what they added to it.

The verb *yaʿbudūna*, "they worship," is from the root *ʿ-b-d*, whose basic sense is servitude and submission. Worship in the Qur'anic sense is not confined to ritual; it is the whole orientation of dependence, hope, fear, and obedience. To "worship" the idols was to look to them for benefit and protection — which is precisely what the verse says they cannot provide.

**"That Which Has No Power Over Any Provision": *Mā Lā Yamliku***

The verse describes the idols as *mā lā yamliku lahum rizqan*, "what possesses no provision for them." The verb *malaka* means to own, to have control over. The idols own nothing and control nothing; they cannot give provision because provision is not theirs to give. The pronoun *mā*, "what," is the pronoun used for non-rational things, and its use here — as in verse 20, "those they call upon besides God create nothing" — emphasizes that the objects of worship are things, not persons: stones and images that do not perceive.

The word *rizq*, provision, connects the verse to the sūrah's entire argument. Every blessing enumerated since verse 5 has been *rizq* in the broad sense: what God gives for the sustenance and benefit of His creatures. Verse 71 spoke of God favoring some over others "in provision"; verse 72 spoke of God providing "good things." Verse 73 asks: who among the idols has provided any of this? The answer is none, and the worship of that which provides nothing, in place of the One who provides everything, is the absurdity the verse exposes.

**"From the Heavens and the Earth"**

The verse specifies the sources of provision: *mina al-samāwāti wa'l-arḍi*, "from the heavens and the earth." The commentators explain the reference. From the heavens comes rain (v. 10, 65) — the source of all vegetation and therefore of all food; from the earth come the crops, the fruits, the minerals, the animals that graze upon it. Al-Rāzī notes that this pair encompasses every source of sustenance a human being has: nothing he eats or uses comes from anywhere else. And the idols control neither. They cannot send rain from the sky nor bring forth a single plant from the ground. The Qur'an makes the same point through a series of questions:

> *"Say: Who provides for you from the heaven and the earth? Or who controls hearing and sight? And who brings the living out of the dead and the dead out of the living? And who arranges every matter? They will say: God. So say: Then will you not fear Him?"* (Qur'an 10:31)

> *"Say: Have you considered your partners whom you call upon besides God? Show me what they have created of the earth, or do they have a share in the heavens?"* (Qur'an 35:40)

The Makkans, when asked who provides from heaven and earth, answered "God" (10:31). Verse 73 draws the consequence they refused to draw: if God alone provides, God alone deserves worship.

**"Nor Are They Capable of Anything": *Wa-lā Yastaṭīʿūn***

The verse ends: *shayʾan wa-lā yastaṭīʿūn*, "[no provision] at all, nor are they able." The word *shayʾan*, "anything," has been construed in two ways. It may be the object of *rizqan* — "no provision *at all*" — emphasizing the absolute negation: not the least particle of provision. Or it may be a separate object — "they possess nothing" — reinforcing the first clause. The final phrase, *wa-lā yastaṭīʿūn*, "and they are not able," extends the negation beyond provision: the idols cannot do *anything*. They cannot provide; they cannot help; they cannot even, as the next verses will show, defend themselves.

The commentators note the two levels of the negation. The first denies *possession*: the idols do not own provision. The second denies *capacity*: even if provision were somehow entrusted to them, they would lack the power to deliver it. Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Rāzī observe that the verse thus closes every avenue: the idols neither have nor can. A human patron, at least, may have wealth and the ability to give it; the idols have neither the wealth nor the ability. To worship them is to serve what is doubly empty.

The verb *yastaṭīʿūn* is the plural form used for rational beings, though the subject *mā* is non-rational. Al-Zamakhsharī explains that the verse uses the rational plural because the idolaters *treated* the idols as rational agents — as beings who could hear, respond, and act — and the verse addresses them in the idolaters' own terms in order to negate the claim: these "agents" you worship are not able. The grammar mirrors the idolaters' delusion and then dissolves it.

**The Argument in the Context of the Sūrah**

Verse 73 is the negative counterpart of verses 70–72. Those verses said: God created you, provides for you, gave you spouses and children and good things. Verse 73 says: the idols do none of this. The two halves form a single argument: worship belongs to the one who provides, and the one who provides is God alone. The commentators note that this is the argument of *rubūbiyyah* (lordship) leading to *ulūhiyyah* (worship), which was discussed at verse 17: since the Makkans admitted God's lordship — His creating and providing — they were bound by consistency to admit His sole right to worship.

Al-Rāzī frames the logic in terms of self-interest, which the idolaters would understand. People worship in hope of benefit and fear of harm. Benefit and harm come through provision and its withholding. The idols control neither. Therefore worshipping them serves no purpose even on the idolaters' own terms. The only rational object of worship is the One who controls what the worshipper needs. The argument does not yet appeal to God's intrinsic worthiness of worship — the sūrah has made that argument elsewhere (vv. 3, 17, 60) — but meets the idolaters where they stand, at the level of need.

**The Idols of Every Age**

The commentators, and later the reformers of the tradition, applied the verse beyond the stone idols of Makkah. Ibn Taymiyyah and Ibn al-Qayyim noted that anything a person looks to for provision and protection *independently of God* — a patron, a ruler, a saint at a tomb, wealth itself, one's own cleverness — falls under the verse's description: it does not control provision from heaven and earth and is not able. The Prophet ﷺ warned specifically against the worship of wealth: *"Wretched is the slave of the dinar, the slave of the dirham"* (al-Bukhārī 2887). The slave of the dirham worships what "has no power over any provision" — the dirham does not provide; God provides through it, and the one who forgets this has taken a coin as his idol.

The verse also addresses the modern confidence in systems and structures as the ultimate sources of security — the economy, the state, technology, the market. Each of these is a means; none controls the rain or the earth's yield; and each has failed, at one time or another, those who trusted it absolutely. The verse's question is whether one's ultimate reliance rests on what can fail or on what cannot.

**The Practical Discipline: Directing Dependence**

The verse's teaching resolves into a discipline that the tradition called *tawakkul*, reliance on God, discussed at verse 42. The believer uses means — he works, plants, trades, plans — but he does not *worship* the means; his dependence, hope, and fear are directed at the One who controls provision from the heavens and the earth. The Prophet ﷺ taught the balance in his instruction to the man who asked whether he should tie his camel or trust in God: *"Tie it, and trust in God"* (al-Tirmidhī 2517). The camel is tied; the trust is in God. The idolater's error was to trust the camel — or the stone — rather than the One who made both. The verse corrects the error by naming, with total clarity, what the idol lacks: control over any provision, and the ability to do anything at all.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:74

> **So do not set forth parables for God. Truly God knows and you know not.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Prohibition That Guards the Doctrine of God**

After exposing the idols as powerless over provision (v. 73), the sūrah issues a command that addresses the root of the idolaters' error: *fa-lā taḍribū li'llāhi al-amthāl*, "so do not strike parables for God." The idolaters had reached their theology by analogy — by likening God to what they knew. The verse forbids this method, and gives the reason: God knows, and they do not. The verse is short but foundational; it governs how Muslims think and speak about God.

**"Do Not Set Forth Parables": The Meaning of *Ḍarb al-Amthāl***

The idiom *ḍaraba mathalan* means to strike a likeness, to set forth a comparison or parable. The Qur'an uses it for its own parables (2:26; 14:24; 16:75, 76, 112) and for the false analogies of the disbelievers (17:48; 25:9; 36:78). Here it is forbidden with respect to God: do not make comparisons *for* Him, do not liken Him to created things.

The commentators identify the specific likenesses the verse forbids. Al-Ṭabarī explains that the idolaters had said, in effect, that God was like a great king whom one could not approach directly and who required intermediaries — courtiers, ministers — through whom petitions were carried; and they made the idols these intermediaries. Their *shirk* rested on this analogy. Al-Qurṭubī and al-Rāzī add the further likenesses the sūrah has been refuting: they likened God to a father who has children (vv. 57, 62); they likened Him to a master who might share his property with partners (v. 71, from the opposite side — they refused for themselves what they assigned to Him); they treated Him as a being who might need offerings (v. 56). Each was an *amthāl*, a comparison drawn from their own experience and projected onto God.

Al-Zamakhsharī states the principle the verse enforces: comparisons proceed from the known to the unknown, and they are valid only when the two share the relevant nature. God shares no nature with any created thing. Therefore every comparison applied to Him fails at the root, and the theology built on it is false.

**The Foundation: "There Is Nothing Like Him"**

The verse's prohibition rests on the doctrine the Qur'an states most directly in Sūrat al-Shūrā:

> *"There is nothing like unto Him, and He is the Hearing, the Seeing."* (Qur'an 42:11)

And in Sūrat al-Ikhlāṣ: *"And there is none comparable to Him"* (112:4). The Arabic of 42:11, *laysa ka-mithlihi shayʾun*, is emphatic: not merely "nothing is like Him" but "nothing is like His likeness" — a doubling of negation that excludes even the possibility of a likeness. The commentators note that 16:74 is the practical corollary of 42:11: because nothing is like Him, one must not make likenesses for Him.

The verse in al-Shūrā also shows the balance the tradition maintained. It denies likeness — *laysa ka-mithlihi shayʾ* — and in the same breath affirms attributes: *wa-huwa al-samīʿ al-baṣīr*, "and He is the Hearing, the Seeing." The prohibition of likeness does not mean the denial of attributes. God hears and sees; but His hearing and seeing are not like ours. This is the *via media* between two errors: *tashbīh*, likening God to creatures (the error 16:74 forbids), and *taʿṭīl*, stripping God of the attributes He has affirmed for Himself (which would contradict the affirmation of 42:11 and the "highest description" of 16:60).

**The Relationship to Verse 60**

Verse 60 said, "To God belongs the highest description" — *al-mathal al-aʿlā*. Verse 74 says, "Do not strike parables for God" — *lā taḍribū li'llāhi al-amthāl*. The same word, *mathal*, is affirmed in one and forbidden in the other, and the commentators reconcile them, as was noted at verse 60. The *mathal* God has for Himself — the description He has given of Himself in revelation — is affirmed; the *amthāl* human beings strike for Him from their imagination are forbidden. Al-Rāzī states the rule: one describes God only as He has described Himself, and one does not go beyond revelation in either direction. The believer's theology is *received*, not *constructed*.

This distinction underlies the classical approach to the divine attributes. The scholars of the *salaf*, the early generations, affirmed what the texts affirmed — God's hand, face, ascending the Throne, descending in the last third of the night, and so on — *bilā kayf*, without asking how, and *bilā tashbīh*, without likening. The rule of Mālik, cited at verse 50 — "the ascending is known; the how is unknown" — is 16:74 applied: to ask "how" is to seek a likeness, and likeness is forbidden. Ibn Taymiyyah formulated the same principle: "Whoever likens God to His creation has disbelieved; whoever denies what God has described Himself with has disbelieved; and there is no likening in what God has described Himself with or what His Messenger has described Him with."

**"Truly God Knows and You Know Not": The Reason**

The verse gives the reason for the prohibition: *inna Allāha yaʿlamu wa-antum lā taʿlamūn*, "truly God knows, and you do not know." The commentators identify two objects of knowledge.

The first is knowledge of God Himself. Only God knows what He is; human beings, confined to the created order, cannot reach His essence by their own faculties. Every likeness they strike is therefore ignorant — an attempt to describe what they have not seen by means of what they have. Al-Rāzī notes that the verse's phrase "you do not know" is an absolute negation in this domain: human reason can establish *that* God is and *that* He has certain perfections, but it cannot establish *what* He is like, because it has nothing to compare Him to.

The second is knowledge of the consequences. God knows the harm that follows from false analogies about Him — the *shirk*, the daughters, the murdered infants, the offerings to stones — and human beings, caught in the analogies, do not see where they lead. Al-Ṭabarī reads the clause in this direction: God knows the error of what you do, and you do not know it because Satan has made it seem fair to you (v. 63).

Both readings are operative, and both point to the same conclusion: in the matter of God's nature, the human being must be taught rather than teach himself. This is why revelation exists (v. 44, 64) and why verse 43 said to ask those who know.

**The Legitimate Use of Analogy**

The verse does not forbid all analogical thinking about God; it forbids the striking of likenesses *for* Him. The Qur'an itself uses analogies to convey truths about God's actions — the very next verses (75–76) are parables, and 24:35 gives the famous parable of light. The difference, as the commentators note, is between analogies *God* strikes to convey a meaning to human understanding, and analogies human beings strike to define God's nature. The first are pedagogical instruments of revelation; the second are presumptions. When God says His light is "like a niche in which is a lamp," He does not claim to be a lamp; He gives the human mind a handhold. When the idolaters say God is like a king who needs intermediaries, they define His nature and derive a practice (idol-worship) from the definition. The verse forbids the second.

The scholars also permitted the argument called *qiyās al-awlā*, the analogy of the greater: reasoning that whatever perfection is found in creatures must belong to the Creator in a higher way, and whatever imperfection is found in creatures must be denied of Him. This is not likening God to creatures; it is the opposite — it uses creatures to establish God's *superiority* to them. Verse 60's "highest description" authorizes this.

**The Psychological Root of Forbidden Analogy**

The commentators, especially al-Rāzī, observed why human beings are prone to the error the verse forbids. The mind seeks to understand the unknown by means of the known, and this is a legitimate method in the created world. But applied to God, it produces a God made in the image of the human being — a projection of human needs, hierarchies, and limitations onto the Unlimited. The idolaters' God had daughters because they had daughters; He needed courtiers because their kings needed courtiers; He accepted offerings because their chiefs accepted tribute. The verse breaks this projection at the root. God is not a magnified human being; He is *other*, and the only way to know Him is to receive His self-description.

**The Application: Discipline in Speaking of God**

The verse establishes a discipline that every believer should practice. When speaking or thinking about God, one restricts oneself to what He has revealed and does not invent. When one encounters a text about God's attributes that one does not understand, one affirms it as God intended and does not force it into a human likeness. When one is tempted to reason "God must be like this because..." — drawing on human experience — one recalls the verse: you do not know. And when one encounters, in oneself or in others, conceptions of God that are clearly human projections — a God who shares human prejudices, who favors one's own tribe, who is indifferent to injustice or delighted by cruelty — one recognizes them as the *amthāl* the verse forbids. The verse's closing clause is not a rebuke only; it is a relief. The believer is not required to construct God from his own resources, which are inadequate. He is required only to receive what the One who knows has said about Himself.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:75

> **God sets forth a parable: a slave who is owned, who has no power over anything, and one whom We have provided with a goodly provision, from which he spends secretly and openly. Are they equal? Praise be to God! Nay, but most of them know not.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**God Strikes the Parable He Forbade to Others**

Verse 74 forbade human beings from striking parables for God. Verse 75 begins with God striking a parable: *ḍaraba Allāhu mathalan*, "God sets forth a parable." The juxtaposition is deliberate. As the commentators observe, the verse illustrates by contrast what the previous verse meant: human beings may not liken God to creatures, but God may use created likenesses to teach human beings, because He knows — and they do not — what likeness is apt. The parable that follows is God's own analogy, and its purpose is to make the difference between God and the idols palpable in terms the idolaters used every day.

**The First Figure: The Owned Slave Who Has No Power**

The parable's first figure is *ʿabdan mamlūkan lā yaqdiru ʿalā shayʾ*, "a slave, owned, who has no power over anything." Three descriptors accumulate. He is a *ʿabd*, a slave; he is *mamlūk*, owned — the word emphasizes his status as property; and he *lā yaqdiru ʿalā shayʾ*, has no power over anything — he cannot dispose of property, cannot act on his own authority, has nothing to give.

The commentators note the redundancy of *ʿabd* and *mamlūk*. Al-Zamakhsharī explains that *ʿabd* alone might be ambiguous — the Qur'an calls all human beings *ʿibād*, servants of God — so *mamlūk* specifies that this is a slave in the legal sense, owned by a human master. And "who has no power over anything" specifies further: not every slave is powerless (some were entrusted with their masters' affairs), but this one is the pure case — a slave who controls nothing whatsoever.

**The Second Figure: The Free Man With Goodly Provision**

The second figure is *wa-man razaqnāhu minnā rizqan ḥasanan fa-huwa yunfiqu minhu sirran wa-jahran*, "and one whom We have provided from Ourselves with a goodly provision, and he spends from it secretly and openly." The contrast is complete. Where the first has nothing, the second has "goodly provision"; where the first can do nothing, the second *spends* — freely, at his discretion, in both private and public. The phrase "from Ourselves" (*minnā*) attributes his wealth to God, in keeping with the sūrah's insistence that all provision is God's (v. 53, 71). The phrase "secretly and openly" describes the fullness of his freedom: he gives when no one sees and when everyone sees; he is not constrained in either.

Al-Rāzī notes that the second figure is not merely wealthy but *generous* — he spends. The parable does not contrast a poor man with a rich miser, which would complicate the point; it contrasts one who has nothing and can give nothing with one who has much and gives freely. The relevant difference is the capacity to benefit others.

**"Are They Equal?": *Hal Yastawūn***

The parable's question is *hal yastawūn*, "are they equal?" The verb is plural rather than dual, though only two figures have been named; al-Zamakhsharī explains that the two figures stand for two *classes* — all who are like the slave and all who are like the free giver — and the plural addresses the classes. The question is rhetorical, and its answer is obvious to anyone: no, they are not equal. No Arab of Makkah would have regarded a powerless slave as the equal of a wealthy, generous free man.

**The Application of the Parable**

The commentators are unanimous that the parable's application is to God and the idols, and they explain it. The powerless slave stands for the idols — who own nothing, control nothing, and can give nothing (v. 73). The generous free man stands for God — who owns all, controls all, and gives without limit, "secretly and openly," in blessings seen and unseen. The question "are they equal?" is thus the question: is the idol equal to God? And the answer the idolaters must give about the slave and the free man — no — is the answer they must give about the idol and God. Al-Ṭabarī states the argument: if you would not equate a slave who has nothing with a free man who gives freely, how do you equate the idols, which have nothing, with God, who provides everything?

Al-Rāzī draws out the force. The idolaters were being asked to apply to theology the same judgment they applied to social life. In their daily dealings, they knew the difference between one who could benefit them and one who could not, and they honored the first and not the second. Their worship of the idols violated this elementary discrimination: they honored what could not benefit them as though it were equal to — or a means to — the One who could. The parable exposes the inconsistency between their practical wisdom and their religious folly.

Some commentators offered a second application: the slave stands for the disbeliever, who has nothing of real value and can do nothing of lasting good, while the free giver stands for the believer, whom God has provided with faith and good works and who spends them in charity and obedience. Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to have applied the parable to specific individuals — a disbelieving Qurayshī and a believing Companion. Al-Ṭabarī records this reading alongside the primary one and notes that the primary application to God and the idols fits the context (v. 73–74) more closely, while the secondary application is a legitimate extension.

**"Praise Be to God!": *Al-Ḥamdu li'llāh***

After the question, the verse says *al-ḥamdu li'llāh*, "praise be to God." The placement puzzled some readers — why praise here? — and the commentators give several answers. Al-Zamakhsharī explains that once the question has been posed and its answer is evident — that God alone is worthy, and the idols are as nothing — praise is the immediate response: praise to God, who alone deserves it, in contrast to the idols, who deserve nothing. Al-Rāzī adds that the phrase expresses gratitude for the clarity of the proof: the parable has established the truth so plainly that praise follows. Others read it as an instruction: the Prophet ﷺ is to say "Praise be to God" as the conclusion of the argument, declaring that all praise belongs to the One who has been shown to be beyond comparison.

A further sense: *al-ḥamd*, praise, is due to the one who benefits. The parable has just shown that God is the one who provides and gives; therefore praise is His. The idols, who give nothing, receive no praise. The phrase is thus the parable's verdict in the form of an act of worship.

**"Nay, but Most of Them Know Not"**

The verse ends: *bal aktharuhum lā yaʿlamūn*, "rather, most of them do not know." The particle *bal* is one of correction or transition — "rather," "but" — and here it corrects an implicit assumption: one might expect that so clear a parable would be accepted; *rather*, most do not know. The commentators identify what they do not know: that all praise belongs to God alone (al-Ṭabarī); that the idols are as the powerless slave (al-Rāzī); the truth that the parable makes plain (al-Qurṭubī). The phrase recurs throughout the sūrah (vv. 38, 101) and describes the condition that the sūrah's arguments are meant to remedy: an ignorance that is not lack of information — the parable has supplied the information — but a failure to apply what one knows.

**Why a Parable About Slavery?**

The parable's use of the slave-master relationship reflects the world of its first hearers, in which slavery was a universal institution, and it uses that world to make a theological point. The point does not endorse slavery; it uses a known reality — the powerlessness of the owned slave — as an image of the powerlessness of the idols. The Qur'an elsewhere uses the same institution to argue in the opposite direction: 30:28, discussed at verse 71, asks whether masters would accept their slaves as partners, in order to show that God has no partners. The institution is a source of images, not of norms; the norms — kindness to slaves, manumission as merit, the eventual dissolution of the practice — the Qur'an supplies elsewhere.

**The Application: Judging by the Same Standard**

The verse asks the reader to apply to his ultimate loyalties the same judgment he applies to his ordinary dealings. In practical life, one does not rely on what cannot help; one does not honor what cannot benefit; one does not equate the empty-handed with the generous. The verse asks: do you apply this standard to what you worship, trust, and fear? Whatever a person relies on that "has no power over anything" — whether an idol, an ideology, or a human patron treated as ultimate — is the slave of the parable, and the One who "provides goodly provision and spends secretly and openly" is the alternative. "Are they equal?" The verse's *al-ḥamdu li'llāh* is the response of the one who has answered honestly.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:76

> **And God sets forth a parable: two men, one of them dumb, with power over nothing, a burden to his master—wherever he directs him, he brings no good. Is he equal to one who enjoins justice and is himself on a straight path?**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Second Parable**

Verse 75 contrasted a powerless slave with a generous free man. Verse 76 offers a second parable, more developed, contrasting two men of whom one is not merely powerless but positively useless — a burden — and the other is not merely capable but a commander of justice on a straight path. The two parables work together: the first established that the idols cannot benefit; the second establishes that they are a liability. And the second parable's positive figure introduces a new element — not merely provision but *justice* and *guidance*, the moral dimension that the idols entirely lack.

**The First Man: Four Descriptions of Uselessness**

The parable's first figure is described by four accumulating traits.

*Abkam*, "dumb" — unable to speak. The root *b-k-m* denotes muteness, and the commentators note that in the Qur'an's usage it often implies muteness from birth combined with the inability to understand (as in 2:18, "deaf, dumb, blind"). This man cannot communicate; he can neither receive instruction nor give it.

*Lā yaqdiru ʿalā shayʾ*, "with power over nothing" — the same phrase used of the slave in verse 75. He can accomplish nothing.

*Wa-huwa kallun ʿalā mawlāhu*, "and he is a burden on his master." The word *kall* denotes a weight, a burden, a dependent who must be carried — from *kalla*, to be weary or dull. He does not merely fail to contribute; he consumes. His master (*mawlā*, here the guardian or owner responsible for him) must feed and care for him and receives nothing in return.

*Aynamā yuwajjihhu lā yaʾti bi-khayr*, "wherever he directs him, he brings no good." Whatever task the master sets him, he fails at it. The phrase completes the picture: the man is not only passive but actively unproductive; every attempt to use him ends in nothing.

Al-Zamakhsharī notes the cumulative force: the parable does not stop at "powerless" but adds "burdensome" and "useless in every direction," so that the first man represents the lowest possible degree of value — less than zero, since he costs his master without benefit.

**The Second Man: Justice and the Straight Path**

The second figure is described by two traits: *man yaʾmuru bi'l-ʿadl*, "one who commands justice," and *wa-huwa ʿalā ṣirāṭin mustaqīm*, "and he is on a straight path."

The first trait, commanding justice, implies several things. He can speak — unlike the dumb man. He has authority — he *commands*. And what he commands is *ʿadl*, justice, equity, the giving of each thing its due. He is thus a moral agent of the highest kind: one who not only acts rightly but directs others to act rightly. The Qur'an regards commanding justice as the mark of the best community (3:104, 110) and the function of the prophets (57:25).

The second trait, being on a straight path, describes his own conduct: he not only commands justice but practices it; his way is straight, without deviation. Al-Rāzī notes the pairing: the second man is right in word (he commands justice) and in deed (he walks the straight path). He is the complete opposite of the first man in every respect — where the first is mute, he speaks; where the first is powerless, he commands; where the first is a burden, he benefits others; where the first brings no good, he brings the greatest good, which is justice.

**"Is He Equal?": The Question**

The verse asks *hal yastawī huwa wa-man yaʾmuru bi'l-ʿadl*, "is he [the first man] equal to one who commands justice...?" As in verse 75, the answer is self-evident. No one would regard a mute, powerless, burdensome, useless man as the equal of one who commands justice and walks straight.

**The Application: God and the Idols**

The commentators apply the parable as they applied the previous one. The first man represents the idols: they are dumb — they cannot speak or answer prayers (cf. 7:194–195, "do they have feet with which they walk... or ears with which they hear?"); they are powerless; they are a burden — their worshippers must carry them, guard them, feed them offerings, and receive nothing; and wherever they are turned, they bring no good. Al-Ṭabarī reports this as the primary application: the idol is the *abkam* who cannot speak and must be carried.

The second man represents God: He commands justice — His entire revelation is a command to justice (v. 90, "God commands justice and excellence"); and He is on the straight path — His way is truth, without deviation (11:56, "My Lord is on a straight path"). Al-Rāzī notes the fittingness of the description: God does not merely possess power (as the free man of v. 75 possessed provision) but exercises it in the direction of justice and guides others to it. The parable thus adds to the argument of verse 75 the dimension of *moral* superiority: God is not merely more powerful than the idols but is the source of justice, while the idols are the source of nothing.

**The Secondary Application: Believer and Disbeliever**

As with verse 75, a second application was offered by the early commentators. Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to have identified the two men with specific persons: the mute burden with a Qurayshī disbeliever — some reports name Abū Jahl, others a slave of ʿUthmān who refused Islam — and the commander of justice with a believer — ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān, or Ḥamzah, or ʿUmar. On this reading the parable contrasts the disbeliever, who brings no good to anyone and is a burden on his community, with the believer, who commands justice and walks straight. Al-Qurṭubī and al-Ṭabarī record this application; al-Ṭabarī regards the application to God and the idols as primary because of the context, while acknowledging the secondary reading as valid.

The two applications are compatible: the believer *resembles* the second man because he follows the One the second man primarily represents, and the disbeliever resembles the first because he follows idols that are like it.

**"He Brings No Good": The Emptiness of the Idols**

The phrase *lā yaʾti bi-khayr*, "he brings no good," has a particular sharpness in the sūrah's context. The sūrah is about blessings — *khayr* in its most concrete form. Every verse from 5 to 18, and again from 65 to 72, listed the good God brings. The idols, in the parable's words, bring *no good* — none. Al-Zamakhsharī notes the total negation: not little good, but none. The contrast with the One who brings all good is thus absolute.

**The Parable and the Doctrine of Guidance**

The second man's description — "commanding justice" and "on a straight path" — connects the parable to the sūrah's doctrine of guidance. Verse 9 said, "Unto God leads the straight path"; verse 76 describes God as the One who is *on* the straight path and commands justice. The straight path is His, and He guides to it. The idols cannot guide because they cannot speak; the God who commands justice guides by His command. The parable thus implies that the choice between God and the idols is not only a choice between power and powerlessness but between guidance and its absence.

**The Verse and the Human Reader**

The parable holds up two human types and asks the reader which he resembles — because the reader, though not the parable's primary referent, cannot avoid measuring himself against its figures. The first man is a burden who brings no good wherever he is sent. The second commands justice and walks straight. The Prophet ﷺ described the best of people in terms that echo the second figure:

> *"The best of people are those most beneficial to people."* (al-Ṭabarānī; graded ḥasan by al-Albānī)

And he described the believer's presence as a source of good: *"Blessed is the one whom God has made a key to good and a lock against evil"* (Ibn Mājah 237). The one who is a key to good is the second man of the parable; the one who is a lock against good is the first. The verse asks the reader to be the former — to speak truth, to command justice, to walk straight, and to bring good wherever he is directed — and thereby to become, in his own measure, a sign of the One he worships rather than of the idols he rejects.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:77

> **Unto God belongs the Unseen of the heavens and the earth. And the matter of the Hour is as the blinking of an eye, or nearer still. Truly God is Powerful over all things.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**From the Parables to the Unseen**

Verses 75–76 used parables drawn from the visible world to establish that God, not the idols, is worthy of worship. Verse 77 moves to what the visible world cannot show: *wa-li'llāhi ghaybu al-samāwāti wa'l-arḍ*, "and to God belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth." Having reasoned from what can be seen, the sūrah now states what only God knows — and identifies the greatest of the unseen matters, the Hour, whose arrival will be instantaneous. The verse thus closes one argument (the idols are nothing) and reopens another (the resurrection is certain and sudden) that has run through the sūrah since verse 1.

**"Unto God Belongs the Unseen": *Al-Ghayb***

The word *ghayb* denotes what is absent from perception — hidden, unseen, beyond the reach of the senses and, in its fullest sense, beyond the reach of created knowledge altogether. The Qur'an makes belief in the *ghayb* the first characteristic of the God-fearing (2:3), and it reserves knowledge of the *ghayb* to God alone:

> *"And with Him are the keys of the unseen; none knows them except Him. And He knows what is on the land and in the sea. Not a leaf falls but that He knows it, nor a grain in the darknesses of the earth, nor anything moist or dry, but that it is in a clear record."* (Qur'an 6:59)

> *"Say: None in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen except God, and they do not perceive when they will be resurrected."* (Qur'an 27:65)

The verse in al-Naml (27:65) is especially relevant: it pairs God's exclusive knowledge of the *ghayb* with the creatures' ignorance of the time of resurrection — the same pairing 16:77 makes. The commentators identify the *ghayb* of the heavens and the earth as everything hidden in either: the future, the secrets of hearts, the location of every hidden thing, the moment of every death, and — as the verse's next clause specifies — the time of the Hour.

The fronted *li'llāhi*, "to God," conveys exclusivity, as in verses 49 and 52: the *ghayb* belongs to Him *alone*. The relevance to the polemic is immediate. The idols, who could not speak or provide (vv. 73–76), certainly do not know the unseen; and the soothsayers and diviners whom the Makkans consulted did not know it either. The Prophet ﷺ himself, though he received revelation, did not know the unseen except what God revealed to him: *"Say: I do not tell you that I possess the treasuries of God, nor do I know the unseen"* (6:50). Knowledge of the *ghayb* is a divine prerogative, and any claim to it by a creature is false.

**"The Matter of the Hour Is as the Blinking of an Eye"**

The verse then singles out the Hour: *wa-mā amru al-sāʿati illā ka-lamḥi al-baṣari aw huwa aqrab*, "and the matter of the Hour is only like the glance of the eye, or it is nearer." The word *amr*, "matter" or "command," was discussed at verse 1, where "the command of God" (*amr Allāh*) was identified with the Hour. Here *amr al-sāʿah* is the coming of the Hour — its occurrence, the divine command that brings it about.

The comparison is to *lamḥ al-baṣar*, the glance or blink of the eye — the swiftest motion a human being performs and the standard image of instantaneity in Arabic. The Hour will come as fast as that. And then the verse adds *aw huwa aqrab*, "or it is nearer" — faster still. The commentators addressed the meaning of this addition, since nothing in human experience is faster than the blink.

Al-Zamakhsharī explains that *aw* here does not express doubt (God does not doubt) but functions as it does in human speech to indicate that the first comparison is insufficient and the reality exceeds it: "like the blink of an eye — or, rather, faster." The same construction appears in 37:147 ("a hundred thousand or more") and 53:9 ("two bows' lengths or nearer"). The point is that the Hour's arrival is *faster than the fastest thing you can imagine*. Al-Rāzī gives the theological ground: the Hour comes by God's command, and God's command is instantaneous — "His command, when He wills a thing, is only that He says to it, Be, and it is" (36:82; cf. 16:40). The blink of an eye takes time, however little; the divine "Be" takes none. The Hour is therefore "nearer" than the blink because it is not a motion in time at all but the effect of a timeless command.

Al-Qurṭubī adds a further sense: the Hour is "near" not only in the speed of its occurrence but in its proximity — it is closer than people think, as the Prophet ﷺ said, holding up two fingers:

> *"I and the Hour have been sent like these two"* — and he joined his index and middle fingers. (al-Bukhārī 6504; Muslim 2951)

**The Two Dimensions of the Hour's Suddenness**

The commentators distinguish two things the verse asserts. The first is the instantaneity of the Hour's *occurrence*: when it comes, it will not unfold gradually, allowing preparation; it will be complete in an instant. The Qur'an describes the single blast that ends the world and the single blast that raises the dead (39:68; 79:13–14, "it will be but one shout, and behold, they will be awake"). The second is the suddenness of its *arrival*: it will come when people are not expecting it, in the midst of their affairs (v. 46), as the hadith about the two men spreading their cloth described (al-Bukhārī 6506). Both dimensions are contained in *ka-lamḥ al-baṣar*: the Hour is fast in coming and fast in happening.

**The Connection to Verse 1**

The sūrah opened with *atā amru Allāh*, "the command of God has come," using the past tense for a future event to convey its certainty and nearness. Verse 77 explains why the past tense was justified: the Hour is as near as a blink, or nearer. What is that near can be spoken of as already present. The two verses frame the sūrah's first half — from the announcement of the Hour's nearness to the statement of its instantaneity — and both are addressed to those who mocked the Prophet's warnings by demanding that the Hour be hastened (v. 1, "so do not seek to hasten it"). The verse answers: it will come faster than you can blink; you do not need to hasten it, and you will not be able to slow it.

**"Truly God Is Powerful Over All Things"**

The verse ends: *inna Allāha ʿalā kulli shayʾin qadīr*, "truly God is Powerful over all things." The commentators explain the connection to what preceded.
