The deniers of resurrection found it incredible that the dead could be raised, and more incredible that all the dead — every human being who ever lived — could be raised at once, in an instant. The verse answers with God's omnipotence. Al-Rāzī states the principle: for the One whose power extends to all things, there is no difference between raising one and raising all, between doing it slowly and doing it instantly. Human power is limited and works through time; divine power is unlimited and does not need time. The Qur'an states this exactly:

> *"Your creation and your resurrection are but as a single soul. Truly God is Hearing, Seeing."* (Qur'an 31:28)

To create or raise all humanity is, for God, no more than to create or raise one — because His act is not a labor that scales with its object but a command that is obeyed.

**The Theological Weight of the Verse**

The verse combines three doctrines that the sūrah has been establishing: God's exclusive knowledge (the *ghayb* is His), God's absolute power (over all things), and the certainty and suddenness of the Hour. Together they constitute the answer to the deniers of verse 38, who swore that God would not raise the dead. God knows when; God can; and it will be sudden. The verse leaves the denier nowhere to stand: he cannot claim to know it will not happen (the *ghayb* is not his), he cannot claim it is impossible (God is powerful over all things), and he cannot count on time to prepare (it comes in a blink).

**The Application: Living in Readiness**

The verse's teaching resolves into the disposition the Prophet ﷺ described when asked when the Hour would come. He replied with a question: *"What have you prepared for it?"* (al-Bukhārī 6167; Muslim 2639). The time is *ghayb* and belongs to God; the preparation is the human being's. Because the Hour comes as a blink, the only readiness that counts is a readiness that is *always* present — not a plan to prepare later, which the blink will preempt, but a state in which one lives. The verse's final clause is the ground of both fear and hope: the God who can raise all humanity in an instant can also, in an instant, forgive the one who turns to Him. Both the reckoning and the mercy are "nearer than the blink of an eye" for the One who is Powerful over all things.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:78

> **And God brought you forth from the bellies of your mothers, knowing naught; and He endowed you with hearing, sight, and hearts, that haply you may give thanks.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Blessing of the Faculties**

Verse 77 spoke of God's power over all things and the suddenness of the Hour. Verse 78 returns to the human being and names a blessing so fundamental that it is rarely noticed: the faculties of perception and understanding. *Wa'llāhu akhrajakum min buṭūni ummahātikum lā taʿlamūna shayʾan*, "And God brought you out of the bellies of your mothers knowing nothing." Everything a human being knows, he acquired through faculties he did not make. The verse names them — hearing, sight, hearts — and states their purpose: gratitude.

**"He Brought You Forth From the Bellies of Your Mothers"**

The verse begins with birth. The verb *akhraja*, "He brought out," attributes the act to God; the human being did not bring himself into the world. The phrase *buṭūn ummahātikum*, "the bellies of your mothers," recalls verse 66 ("what is in their bellies") and verse 69 ("from their bellies") — the sūrah's repeated image of God bringing forth something valuable from a hidden interior. Milk from the cattle's belly, honey from the bee's, and the human being from the mother's: each is a divine extraction, and the human being is the most remarkable of the three.

The word *ummahāt*, mothers, is the plural of *umm*, and the commentators note that its use here — rather than a more general "wombs" — evokes the relationship and the debt. The Qur'an elsewhere commands gratitude to the mother precisely for the labor the verse alludes to: "His mother carried him in weakness upon weakness" (31:14); "his mother carried him with hardship and gave birth to him with hardship" (46:15). The verse's first clause thus contains an implicit second blessing: the mother through whom God brought one forth.

**"Knowing Naught": *Lā Taʿlamūna Shayʾan***

The verse's central assertion about the newborn is *lā taʿlamūna shayʾan*, "you knew nothing." The human being enters the world without knowledge — no language, no concepts, no memory, no understanding of the world or of himself. Al-Rāzī takes this as a plain statement of fact: the infant has no acquired knowledge whatsoever. Whatever a person later knows, he learned; and he learned through the faculties the verse next names.

The commentators drew a theological conclusion. The human being's knowledge is not his own; it is acquired, and the instruments of acquisition were given. This connects to verse 70, where extreme old age returns the person to "knowing nothing after knowledge" — the arc of human knowledge begins and may end in the same ignorance, and the middle is a loan. Al-Rāzī also connects the clause to verse 74, "God knows and you do not know": the human being's native state is ignorance, and everything he comes to know is God's gift, so that the presumption of striking likenesses for God from one's own knowledge is doubly unfounded.

The scholars of *ʿaqīdah* used the verse in discussing the human soul's initial state. The verse is compatible with the doctrine of *fiṭrah*, the innate disposition toward God (30:30; and the hadith, "every child is born upon the *fiṭrah*," al-Bukhārī 1358), because *fiṭrah* is a disposition, not an item of acquired knowledge. The infant knows nothing in the sense of articulate, conceptual knowledge; but he is oriented toward the truth, and when the faculties develop and are used rightly, they lead him to what the *fiṭrah* was inclined toward. The verse's "knowing nothing" is the starting point from which, with the faculties, knowledge of God is reached.

**"He Endowed You With Hearing, Sight, and Hearts"**

The verse then names the faculties: *wa-jaʿala lakumu al-samʿa wa'l-abṣāra wa'l-afʾidah*, "and He made for you hearing, sights, and hearts." The three are the instruments of knowledge, and the Qur'an names them together repeatedly (17:36; 23:78; 32:9; 46:26; 67:23), always in this order.

The commentators observed the grammatical detail: *al-samʿ*, hearing, is singular, while *al-abṣār*, sights, and *al-afʾidah*, hearts, are plural. Several explanations are given. Al-Zamakhsharī notes that *samʿ* is a verbal noun (*maṣdar*) and such nouns are used in the singular for the plural. Al-Rāzī and others suggest a deeper reason: hearing receives a single kind of object (sound) through a single channel, and all hearers hear the same sound, whereas sight receives many kinds of objects (colors, shapes, distances) and each seer sees differently, and hearts differ most of all in what they understand. The singularity of hearing and the plurality of sights and hearts thus mirror the nature of the faculties.

The order of the three has also been discussed. Hearing is named first, and the commentators offered reasons. Hearing is the first faculty to function — the infant responds to sound before sight develops fully, and the fetus hears in the womb. Hearing is the channel of revelation: the Qur'an is heard before it is read, and the "people who hear" of verse 65 are those for whom the sign functions. And hearing is the faculty through which most knowledge is transmitted — one learns language, and through language everything else, by hearing. Sight follows as the faculty of direct observation of the signs in creation, which the sūrah has been pointing to. And the heart — *fuʾād*, plural *afʾidah* — comes last as the faculty in which what is heard and seen is understood, judged, and either accepted or rejected.

**The Heart: *Al-Fuʾād***

The word *fuʾād*, translated "heart," is distinct from *qalb*, the more common word. The root *f-ʾ-d* is connected with burning or kindling, and the commentators explain that *fuʾād* denotes the heart in its capacity as the seat of understanding and feeling — the "kindled" heart, the heart in activity. Al-Rāghib distinguishes it from *qalb* as the heart when it is set ablaze with emotion or thought. In this verse it denotes the faculty of understanding — the intellect as seated in the heart, according to Qur'anic anthropology, which locates reason and comprehension in the heart rather than in the brain alone: "they have hearts with which they do not understand" (7:179); "it is not the eyes that are blind but the hearts within the breasts" (22:46).

The three faculties thus form a hierarchy: hearing and sight gather; the heart understands. The verse names them together because knowledge requires all three, and the person who has the first two but does not use the third — who hears and sees the signs but does not understand them — is, in the Qur'an's judgment, like cattle or worse (7:179).

**"That Haply You May Give Thanks": The Purpose**

The verse ends: *laʿallakum tashkurūn*, "that perhaps you may be grateful." The purpose of the faculties is gratitude. The commentators explain the logic. The faculties were given to acquire knowledge; the highest knowledge is knowledge of God; and knowledge of God produces gratitude to Him for the faculties and for everything else. The verse thus describes a circle: God gives the faculties; the faculties, rightly used, lead to knowledge of the Giver; knowledge of the Giver produces gratitude; and gratitude is the use of the faculties in obedience — hearing what should be heard, seeing what should be seen, understanding what should be understood. Al-Rāzī states it: the faculties are the means, gratitude is the end, and the person who uses the means for anything else has misused them.

The Qur'an makes the point through its condemnation of those who misuse the faculties:

> *"And We have certainly created for Hell many of the jinn and mankind. They have hearts with which they do not understand, they have eyes with which they do not see, and they have ears with which they do not hear. Those are like livestock; rather, they are more astray. It is they who are the heedless."* (Qur'an 7:179)

And it holds the faculties accountable: *"Truly the hearing, the sight, and the heart — about all of those one will be questioned"* (17:36). The gift entails a reckoning: each faculty will be asked what it was used for.

**Gratitude for the Faculties in Practice**

The Prophet ﷺ taught a specific expression of the gratitude the verse commands. Every morning he would say:

> *"O God, grant me health in my body; O God, grant me health in my hearing; O God, grant me health in my sight. There is no god but You."* (Abū Dāwūd 5090)

Naming hearing and sight in the morning supplication is an enactment of the verse's *tashkurūn*: an acknowledgment that these faculties are gifts renewed each day. The tradition also taught that gratitude for a faculty is its use in obedience — that the gratitude of the ear is to listen to the Qur'an and to truth, the gratitude of the eye is to look at the signs and to lower it from the forbidden, and the gratitude of the heart is to understand and to believe. Al-Ghazālī, in his treatment of *shukr*, describes the ungrateful use of each faculty as a form of *kufr al-niʿmah*: to use the eye God gave to look at what God forbade is to turn the gift against the Giver.

**The Verse in the Sūrah's Argument**

Verse 78 occupies a precise place. The sūrah has been presenting signs — in creation, in the human being, in parables — and demanding reflection. Verse 78 names the instruments by which the signs are perceived and understood, and points out that these instruments are themselves signs and blessings. The person who uses his hearing, sight, and heart to consider the sūrah's argument is using God's gifts for their intended purpose; the one who refuses to consider it has closed the faculties given for that purpose. The verse thus turns the sūrah's argument back on the reader: the very act of reading and understanding is possible only through what the verse describes, and understanding this is the beginning of the gratitude the verse names as the goal.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:79

> **Have they not considered the birds, made subservient, in the air of the sky? None holds them but God. Truly in that are signs for a people who believe.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Lifting the Eyes**

Verse 78 named the faculties — hearing, sight, hearts — and their purpose. Verse 79 immediately puts sight to use: *a-lam yaraw ilā al-ṭayri*, "have they not looked at the birds?" The verse directs the eye upward, to a sign that every human being has seen and few have considered. The birds fly. They are held up in the air by nothing visible. The verse asks the reader to see this as what it is: a demonstration of God's power that hangs, literally, in the sky above him.

**"Have They Not Considered": The Verb of Attention**

The verse uses the same construction as verse 48 (*a-wa-lam yaraw*): a question that implies rebuke. The birds are visible to everyone; the question is whether anyone has *looked*. The verb *raʾā* with the preposition *ilā* means to look attentively, to direct one's gaze toward something with consideration — not merely to see, which the eye does passively, but to *regard*. The commentators note that the question addresses the idolaters who deny the resurrection and worship idols: the sign that refutes them is above their heads, and they have not looked.

**"The Birds, Made Subservient, in the Air of the Sky"**

The birds are described as *musakhkharāt fī jawwi al-samāʾ*, "subjected in the air of the sky." The word *musakhkharāt*, from the root *s-kh-r* discussed at verse 12, means made subservient, subjected to a purpose — the same word used for the sun, moon, and stars (v. 12) and the sea (v. 14). The birds are *subjected*: their flight is not their own achievement but a capacity God has imposed on them, a law they follow. Al-Rāzī explains that *taskhīr* here denotes that God has made the birds able to fly by giving them the form, the wings, the lightness, and the instinct — and that He sustains this capacity at every moment.

The phrase *jaww al-samāʾ*, "the air of the sky," denotes the space between the earth and the visible sky — the atmosphere. Al-Qurṭubī defines *jaww* as the air distant from the earth, and the phrase locates the birds in the open expanse where nothing supports them.

**"None Holds Them but God": *Mā Yumsikuhunna illā Allāh***

The verse's central assertion is *mā yumsikuhunna illā Allāh*, "none holds them except God." The verb *amsaka* means to hold, to grasp, to keep from falling. The birds are held up; the question is by what. The verse answers: by God alone.

The commentators address the obvious objection: do the birds not hold themselves up by their wings? Al-Rāzī gives the fullest answer. The bird is a heavy body, and heavy bodies fall. The bird's wings beat against the air, and this — together with the bird's form — enables flight. But every element of this arrangement is God's: the air with its density, the wing with its structure, the bird's strength and instinct, the laws by which a beating wing produces lift. None of these was made by the bird, and none is sustained by the bird. Remove any one — thin the air, weaken the wing, alter the law — and the bird falls. The wings are the *means* of flight; God is its *cause*. The verse does not deny the means; it identifies the One behind them. The Qur'an makes the same point in its parallel verse, which mentions the wings explicitly:

> *"Do they not see the birds above them, spreading their wings and folding them? None holds them except the Most Merciful. Truly He is, of all things, Seeing."* (Qur'an 67:19)

The verse in al-Mulk describes what the bird does — spreads and folds its wings — and still says that only the Most Merciful holds it. The action of the wings and the holding of God are not alternatives; the first is the instrument of the second.

Al-Zamakhsharī draws out a further sense of *yumsiku*: God holds the birds not only in the sense of sustaining their flight but in the sense of preventing them from falling — the Qur'an uses the same verb for God's holding the heavens and the earth from collapsing (35:41). The birds in the air are like the sky itself: they remain where they are because God holds them, and if He let go, they would fall.

**The Sign in the Bird**

The commentators identify what the bird demonstrates. First, it demonstrates a Maker: the bird's form — hollow bones, feathers, the shape of the wing, the arrangement of muscles — is designed for flight with a precision that no bird designed. Al-Rāzī notes that the bird combines lightness and strength in a balance that would be difficult for a human engineer to achieve; and the balance is *exact*, since a slightly heavier bird could not fly and a slightly weaker one could not sustain flight.

Second, it demonstrates continual sustenance: the bird does not fly once and then remain aloft; it must be held at every moment. The sign is not a past act of creation but a present act of maintenance. The believer who watches a bird is watching God's power *now*.

Third, and in the sūrah's context most importantly, it demonstrates the possibility of resurrection. The idolaters said that the dead could not be raised because bodies cannot rise from the earth. The verse points to bodies that rise from the earth every day — heavy bodies, held in the air by God's power. If God holds birds aloft against the pull that draws all things down, He can raise the dead against the decay that dissolves all things. Al-Rāzī frames the argument: the one who can suspend a heavy body in the air, in defiance of its nature to fall, can restore a decayed body to life, in defiance of its nature to remain dead. Both are acts of the same power over the same kind of obstacle.

**The Bird in Other Verses**

The Qur'an returns to birds as signs in several places, and the parallels enrich the reading of 16:79. Birds glorify God: "Do you not see that God is glorified by whoever is in the heavens and the earth, and the birds with wings outspread? Each knows its prayer and its glorification" (24:41). Birds form communities: "there is no creature on the earth or bird that flies with its wings but that they are communities like you" (6:38). Birds were subjected to David and praised God with him (21:79; 34:10) and served Solomon (27:16–20). Birds were sent by God against the army of the Elephant (105:3). And Abraham's proof of resurrection was performed with birds (2:260). The bird, across the Qur'an, is a creature especially associated with God's power, His praise, and the demonstration of resurrection.

The Prophet ﷺ also used the bird as an image of trust in God's provision:

> *"If you were to rely upon God with true reliance, He would provide for you as He provides for the birds: they go out in the morning hungry and return in the evening full."* (al-Tirmidhī 2344; Ibn Mājah 4164)

The bird that is held in the air by God is also fed by Him, and the hadith makes the bird the model of the *tawakkul* that verse 42 commended.

**"Signs for a People Who Believe"**

The verse ends: *inna fī dhālika la-āyātin li-qawmin yuʾminūn*, "truly in that are signs for a people who believe." The plural *āyāt*, signs, is used, where earlier verses used the singular — because the bird presents several signs at once, as the commentators enumerated. And the faculty named is belief. The formula in verse 65 named hearing, 67 reason, 69 reflection, and here belief. Al-Rāzī explains that the sign of the birds is available to everyone, but it functions as a sign — as evidence pointing to God — only for those who are disposed to believe. The disbeliever sees a bird and thinks of nothing; the believer sees a bird and thinks of the One who holds it. The verse does not say the sign creates belief; it says the sign is *for* believers — it feeds and confirms the belief that receives it.

There is also a connection to verse 78: the faculties were given "that you may be grateful," and verse 79 shows the faculties at work — the eye looking at the bird, the heart understanding its meaning, and the result being belief and gratitude. The one who has looked at the bird as the verse asks has used his sight as it was meant to be used.

**The Application: Learning to Look**

The verse teaches a practice: to look at the ordinary sky with attention. Birds cross it constantly, and the person who has internalized the verse cannot see one without the thought *mā yumsikuhunna illā Allāh*. This is what the tradition called *tafakkur*, reflection on creation, which the Prophet ﷺ performed in the last portion of the night, reciting the verses of Āl ʿImrān about the heavens and the earth (al-Bukhārī 4569). The verse offers the bird as an object for this reflection precisely because it requires no instrument, no journey, and no expertise — only the lifting of the eyes. The person who lifts them and sees, in the suspended bird, the hand that holds it, has moved from the ignorance of verse 78 ("knowing nothing") to the knowledge the faculties were given for. And the argument the verse makes is completed in the believer's own experience: the God who holds the bird will hold him.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:80

> **And God has made for you, from your houses, places of rest, and He has made for you, from the skins of cattle, dwellings you find light on the day you travel and the day you halt; and from their wool and their fur and their hair, furnishings and enjoyment for a while.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**From the Sky to the Tent**

Verse 79 lifted the eyes to the birds. Verse 80 lowers them to the home. The sūrah's method, throughout, is to alternate between the vast and the near, the cosmic and the domestic, so that the reader sees God's provision in every register. After the bird held in the air, the verse names the house, the tent, and the woolen furnishings — blessings so close and ordinary that they are almost invisible, and precisely for that reason in need of being named.

**"God Has Made for You, From Your Houses, Places of Rest": *Sakanan***

The verse begins *wa'llāhu jaʿala lakum min buyūtikum sakanan*, "and God made for you, from your houses, a place of rest." The word *sakan* comes from the root *s-k-n*, which means to be still, to settle, to be at rest — the same root as *sakīnah*, tranquility, and the "rest" that the spouse provides in 30:21 (*li-taskunū ilayhā*). A house is a *sakan*: the place where motion ceases, where one is sheltered from heat and cold, from view and from danger, where one rests.

The commentators note the wording. God did not simply make houses; He made *from* houses a *sakan* — that is, He gave the house its function of rest. The stones and timber are one thing; the tranquility one finds within them is another, and the verse attributes the second to God. Al-Rāzī observes that a house is a rest for the body from exertion, for the eye from the gaze of strangers, and for the heart from anxiety; and that this threefold rest is a blessing that human beings take for granted until they lose it. The traveler, the refugee, and the homeless know what the verse names.

The verse also attributes the making of houses themselves to God, though human beings build them. Al-Zamakhsharī explains the attribution in the manner of the whole sūrah: God created the materials, gave human beings the knowledge and strength to build, and made the built house serve its purpose. The builder is the means; God is the Maker. The same principle governed the milk (v. 66), the honey (v. 69), and every other blessing the sūrah has named.

**"From the Skins of Cattle, Dwellings You Find Light"**

The verse then names a second kind of dwelling: *wa-jaʿala lakum min julūdi al-anʿāmi buyūtan tastakhiffūnahā yawma ẓaʿnikum wa-yawma iqāmatikum*, "and He made for you, from the skins of cattle, dwellings that you find light on the day of your traveling and the day of your staying." These are tents — the dwellings of leather and hide used by the nomadic Arabs, which could be struck and carried on the move and pitched again at the halt.

The phrase *tastakhiffūnahā*, "you find them light," names the tent's distinctive virtue: portability. A house of stone is a rest, but it cannot move; a tent is a rest that travels. The verse names the two occasions — *yawma ẓaʿnikum*, "the day you journey," and *yawma iqāmatikum*, "the day you stay" — and says the tents are light on *both*: light to carry when traveling, light to pitch and manage when halted. Al-Qurṭubī notes the fittingness of the blessing for the Arab context, in which much of the population moved with its herds and required dwellings that moved with them.

The commentators observe that the verse names two kinds of human life — the settled and the nomadic — and provides for both. The houses of verse 80's first clause are for those who stay; the tents of the second are for those who move. God's provision is not designed for one way of life only.

**"From Their Wool and Their Fur and Their Hair": The Three Fibers**

The verse's third blessing is *wa-min aṣwāfihā wa-awbārihā wa-ashʿārihā*, "and from their wool, their fur, and their hair." The three words correspond to the three kinds of cattle named in the sūrah's opening (v. 5, *al-anʿām*): *ṣūf*, wool, is from sheep; *wabar*, fur or soft hair, is from camels; *shaʿr*, hair, is from goats. The verse thus names the specific fiber of each animal, and the commentators note the precision: it does not say generally "their coats" but distinguishes the three, each of which has different properties and uses. Wool is spun into warm clothing and blankets; camel hair into cloaks and tent-cloth; goat hair into coarser tents, sacks, and ropes.

This connects to verse 5, which said that in the cattle "is warmth" (*difʾ*). The warmth named in verse 5 is specified in verse 80: it comes from the wool, the fur, and the hair, worked into the furnishings the verse next names.

**"Furnishings and Enjoyment for a While": *Athāthan wa-matāʿan ilā ḥīn***

From the three fibers come *athāthan wa-matāʿan*, "furnishings and enjoyment." The word *athāth* denotes household goods — furnishings, bedding, carpets, cushions, garments — the material comfort of a home. Al-Ṭabarī explains it as the goods and wealth of a household. The word *matāʿ* denotes enjoyment, provision, the goods one benefits from; in the Qur'an it is often qualified as temporary (*matāʿ al-ḥayāt al-dunyā*, the enjoyment of this world's life).

And the verse adds *ilā ḥīn*, "for a while," "until a time." The commentators pause on this phrase, which introduces a note of limitation into a list of blessings. Al-Rāzī gives two readings. The first: the furnishings themselves wear out — wool frays, hides crack, the goods perish — and the phrase notes their finite durability. The second: the human being enjoys them only for a time — until his death, when he leaves them all. Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Qurṭubī take the second as primary: the phrase reminds the reader that all the comfort of the house, the tent, and the furnishings lasts *ilā ḥīn*, until the appointed term, and no longer.

The phrase functions as a corrective within the enumeration of blessings. The sūrah names the blessings so that they may be recognized and God thanked for them; but it does not want them mistaken for permanent possessions or ultimate goods. They are *matāʿ ilā ḥīn* — enjoyment for a while. The Qur'an states the principle in general: "Whatever you have been given is the enjoyment of this world's life and its adornment, and what is with God is better and more lasting" (28:60). The furnishings are real blessings; they are also temporary; and both facts are to be held together.

**The Verse's Realism About the Ordinary**

The commentators noted the remarkable ordinariness of what the verse lists. Houses, tents, wool, carpets — these are not wonders like the birds or the bee; they are the stuff of daily life. The verse's inclusion of them teaches that God's blessing is not confined to the extraordinary but fills the ordinary, and that the person who thanks God only for miracles has missed most of what he has been given. Al-Rāzī observes that the verse trains the reader to see the divine hand in a blanket. The one who can do this has understood the sūrah; the one who cannot is like the idolaters, who acknowledged God in the storm (v. 53) and forgot Him at home.

The Prophet ﷺ modeled this attention. He gave thanks upon entering a house, upon lying down to sleep, upon wearing a garment:

> *"Praise be to God who has clothed me with this and provided it for me without any power or strength on my part."* (Abū Dāwūd 4023; al-Tirmidhī 3458)

The supplication upon wearing a garment — "without any power or strength on my part" — is the verse's teaching in a sentence: the wool was the sheep's, the spinning was another's, the wearing is mine, and the whole is God's.

**The Verse and Verses 5–8**

Verse 80 completes what verses 5–8 began. There, the cattle were named for warmth, food, beauty, and transport. Here, the cattle's skins become tents and their fibers become furnishings. The sūrah returns to its first blessing and shows that it had more in it than was first stated — that a single created thing, the animal, yields a whole range of goods, each of which is a distinct mercy. This is the sūrah's method with all its blessings: each is revisited, and each time something new is drawn from it, so that the reader learns to see the inexhaustibility of what verse 18 said could not be counted.

**The Application: The Home as Blessing and Trust**

The verse asks the reader to see his home — whatever form it takes — as *sakan*, a rest given by God, and its contents as *athāth* and *matāʿ*, furnishings and enjoyment granted for a time. Two responses follow. The first is gratitude, expressed in the Prophet's supplications and in the use of the home for what God loves — prayer, family, hospitality, refuge for the guest. The second is detachment, expressed in the awareness that the home is *ilā ḥīn*, for a while, and that the true and lasting home is elsewhere. The Prophet ﷺ combined both in his own house — a room of mud brick, furnished with a mat and a waterskin, in which he was content and grateful, and of which he said, when ʿUmar wept at its poverty: *"Are you not pleased that they have this world and we have the Hereafter?"* (al-Bukhārī 4913; Muslim 1479). The home is a blessing; it is not the destination.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:81

> **And God has made for you, from that which He created, shade; and He has made for you places of refuge in the mountains; and He has made for you coats that protect you from the heat, and coats that protect you from your own might. Thus does He complete His blessing upon you, that haply you may submit.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Completion of the Blessings**

Verse 81 is the last verse in the sūrah's long enumeration of physical blessings, which began at verse 5 and has proceeded, with interruptions for argument and warning, through the whole chapter. It names four more — shade, mountain refuges, garments against heat, and armor against violence — and then states, with a phrase that marks the closing of the list, that "thus does He complete His blessing upon you." The verse's final clause names the purpose of all of it: *laʿallakum tuslimūn*, "that haply you may submit."

**"From That Which He Created, Shade": *Ẓilālan***

The verse begins *wa'llāhu jaʿala lakum mimmā khalaqa ẓilālan*, "and God made for you, from what He created, shades." The word *ẓilāl* is the plural of *ẓill*, shade or shadow — the same word used in verse 48 for the shadows that prostrate. There the shadow was a sign of submission; here it is a blessing. The commentators identify the sources of shade the verse intends: trees, buildings, mountains, clouds — everything God has created that casts a shadow in which a person may shelter from the sun. Al-Qurṭubī notes the phrase *mimmā khalaqa*, "from what He created": shade is not a thing in itself but a property of created things, and God made those things such that they give shade.

In the Arabian climate, shade was not a comfort but a necessity; the traveler without it could die. The verse names it first among the four protections because it is the most elemental. And the Qur'an makes shade an image of Paradise — "its shade is perpetual" (13:35), "extended shade" (56:30) — and of God's protection on the Day of Judgment, when there will be no shade but His (al-Bukhārī 660, the seven whom God shades). The earthly shade of verse 81 is the foretaste of both.

**"Places of Refuge in the Mountains": *Aknānan***

The second blessing is *wa-jaʿala lakum mina al-jibāli aknānan*, "and He made for you, from the mountains, places of concealment." The word *aknān* is the plural of *kinn*, a place that covers and conceals — a cave, a grotto, a hollow in the rock where one may shelter from weather and enemies. Al-Ṭabarī explains it as the caves and shelters of the mountains. The mountains were named in verse 15 as stabilizers of the earth; here they are named as shelters for those who live on it. The same created thing serves two purposes, and the sūrah names both.

The Prophet ﷺ himself used such a refuge: the cave of Ḥirāʾ, where he received the first revelation, and the cave of Thawr, where he and Abū Bakr hid from the Makkans during the Emigration (9:40). The mountain refuge was, in the Prophet's own life, the place of revelation and the place of rescue.

**"Coats That Protect You From the Heat": *Sarābīl***

The third blessing is *wa-jaʿala lakum sarābīla taqīkumu al-ḥarr*, "and He made for you garments that protect you from the heat." The word *sarābīl* is the plural of *sirbāl*, a garment, shirt, or coat — any covering worn on the body. The verse says these garments protect from *al-ḥarr*, heat.

The commentators addressed a question the verse raises: why does it mention protection from heat and not from cold, which garments equally provide? Several answers are recorded. Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Qurṭubī note that the Arabs, living in a hot land, felt the need for protection from heat more acutely, and the verse addresses them in terms of their experience; the protection from cold is understood by implication, since a garment that shields from one extreme shields from the other. Al-Rāzī adds that the mention of heat, in the context of a list that has just named shade, continues the theme of protection from the sun. And some noted that verse 5 already mentioned the cattle's provision of *difʾ*, warmth against cold, so that the sūrah covers both extremes across its verses.

Al-Ṭabarī records a rhetorical explanation: Arabic often mentions one of a pair and intends both, as in 12:97 where "the burning sun" implies also the cold, or as in the Qur'an's naming of "the heat" when both are meant. The verse's protection from heat stands for protection from all extremes of weather.

**"And Coats That Protect You From Your Own Might": Armor**

The fourth blessing is *wa-sarābīla taqīkum baʾsakum*, "and garments that protect you from your violence." The word *baʾs* means might, force, and specifically the violence of war. These *sarābīl* are coats of mail, armor — the garments worn in battle to protect against weapons. The commentators are unanimous: this refers to armor, which the Qur'an elsewhere attributes to David's craft, taught by God (21:80; 34:10–11).

The phrase *baʾsakum*, "your might" or "your violence," is precise and somewhat pointed. The armor protects human beings from *their own* violence — from the harm they inflict on one another. Al-Rāzī draws out the observation: the other protections in the verse — shade, refuge, garments against heat — shield from natural dangers; this one shields from a danger human beings create themselves. The verse names it as a blessing without commenting on the sadness of its necessity, but the phrasing registers it: the thing you need protection from is *yourselves*.

The commentators note that the verse presents armor as God's blessing even though human beings make it. The iron was created by God (57:25, "We sent down iron, in which is great might and benefits for people"); the knowledge of working it was taught by God (21:80); and the protection it affords is God's mercy operating through human craft. The principle is the same as with the houses of verse 80.

**"Thus Does He Complete His Blessing Upon You"**

The verse then states: *kadhālika yutimmu niʿmatahu ʿalaykum*, "thus does He complete His blessing upon you." The verb *atamma* means to complete, to perfect, to bring to fullness. The commentators read the phrase as both a summary and a promise. As summary: the blessings just named, added to all the others in the sūrah, constitute a completeness of provision — God has provided for every need, from food to shelter to protection. As promise: the completion is ongoing — God continues to complete His blessing, and the fullness of it is not yet reached. Al-Ṭabarī reads it as pointing forward to the completion of religion and the conquest of Makkah; al-Rāzī reads it as the completion of worldly blessings preparatory to the greater blessing of guidance.

The Qur'an uses the same phrase for the completion of the religion: "This day I have perfected for you your religion and completed My blessing upon you" (5:3). Al-Rāzī connects the two: the blessings of the body (verse 81) and the blessings of faith (5:3) are both God's completion, and the first prepares for the second.

**"That Haply You May Submit": *Laʿallakum Tuslimūn***

The verse's closing clause names the purpose: *laʿallakum tuslimūn*, "that perhaps you may submit." The verb *aslama*, from which *Islām* derives, means to surrender, to submit, to make oneself over to God. The commentators note the fittingness: the enumeration of blessings — which began with "that you may be grateful" (v. 14, 78) and "that you may reflect" (v. 11, 69) — ends with "that you may submit." Gratitude and reflection lead to their proper conclusion, which is *islām*: the acknowledgment of the Giver in the total orientation of one's life.

Al-Rāzī states the logic: the blessings are proofs of the Benefactor; the recognition of the Benefactor obliges gratitude; and complete gratitude is submission — giving oneself to the One who gave everything. The verse's *laʿalla*, "perhaps," is the usual Qur'anic softening: God's purpose in the blessings is that human beings submit; whether they do is their choice.

A variant reading, recorded by al-Ṭabarī and al-Qurṭubī, has *tuslamūn* (with *a*) instead of *tuslimūn* — "that you may be kept safe" — a reading attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās. On this reading, the verse means that the protections just named (shade, refuge, garments, armor) are given so that you may be *safe* from heat and violence. The majority reading, *tuslimūn*, "that you may submit," is preferred by the commentators as the conclusion the whole sūrah has been building toward; al-Rāzī notes that the two readings are complementary: the one who submits to God is the one who is truly safe.

**The Connection to Verse 48**

The verse opens with *ẓilāl*, shades, and verse 48 spoke of the shadows (*ẓilāl*) of all things prostrating to God. The commentators saw a design in the repetition. In verse 48, the shadow was the sign of creation's submission; in verse 81, the shadow is a blessing for the human being, and the verse ends by asking him to submit. The shadow that already prostrates is given to the one who is asked to prostrate. The blessing carries within it the model of the response it calls for.

**The Application: The Completed Blessing and the Expected Response**

The verse asks the reader to survey the whole list of blessings the sūrah has given — food, warmth, transport, rain, crops, sea, mountains, stars, milk, fruit, honey, spouse, children, faculties, houses, tents, furnishings, shade, refuge, clothing, armor — and to recognize that it is *complete*: nothing needed has been withheld. And it names the only adequate response: *islām*. Not a partial gratitude that thanks God for some things and credits oneself or others with the rest, but a total surrender that acknowledges Him as the source of all and orients the whole self toward Him. The Prophet ﷺ described the state of one who has done this:

> *"He has tasted the sweetness of faith who is pleased with God as Lord, with Islam as religion, and with Muḥammad as Messenger."* (Muslim 34)

To be *pleased with God as Lord* is the submission verse 81 calls for — the contentment of one who has counted the blessings, found them complete, and given himself to the One who gave them.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:82

> **But if they turn away, then thine is only to convey the clear message.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**After the Complete Blessing, the Possible Refusal**

Verse 81 ended the enumeration of blessings with the purpose "that haply you may submit." Verse 82 addresses what happens if they do not: *fa-in tawallaw fa-innamā ʿalayka al-balāghu al-mubīn*, "but if they turn away, then upon you is only the clear conveyance." The verse is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ, and it defines the limit of his responsibility. He has been given signs to present and blessings to point to; he has presented and pointed; if the response is refusal, the failure is not his.

**"If They Turn Away": *Tawallaw***

The verb *tawallā* means to turn one's back, to turn away from something — to reject it by turning aside. It is the Qur'an's standard word for the refusal of guidance: "Whoever turns away — God is Rich, Praiseworthy" (60:6); "So if they turn away, then We have not sent you as a guardian over them" (42:48). The image is physical: the one addressed turns his back on the speaker. The commentators note that the verse anticipates this response from the idolaters, whom the sūrah has been addressing for eighty-one verses, and that the anticipation is realistic — many did turn away.

The conditional *in*, "if," leaves the outcome open. The verse does not say "when they turn away" but "if." Some will and some will not; the verse addresses the case of those who do.

**"Thine Is Only to Convey": The Restriction**

The verse's core is *innamā ʿalayka al-balāgh*, "upon you is only the conveyance." The particle *innamā* restricts: the Prophet's duty is *only* this and not more. The word *ʿalayka*, "upon you," denotes obligation — what is incumbent on him. And *al-balāgh* is the delivery of a message — from *balagha*, to reach; *ballagha*, to cause to reach, to convey. The Prophet's obligation is to cause the message to reach its audience. Whether it enters their hearts is not within his obligation, because it is not within his power.

The Qur'an states this limit repeatedly, and the parallels show that it is a settled principle of prophethood:

> *"The Messenger has no duty but to convey. And God knows what you reveal and what you conceal."* (Qur'an 5:99)

> *"So remind; you are only a reminder. You are not over them a controller."* (Qur'an 88:21–22)

> *"Truly you do not guide whom you love, but God guides whom He wills."* (Qur'an 28:56)

> *"And if your Lord had willed, all who are on the earth would have believed together. Would you then compel the people until they become believers?"* (Qur'an 10:99)

The commentators read 16:82 as a consolation to the Prophet and a definition of his task. As consolation: the Prophet grieved intensely over the refusal of his people — "perhaps you would kill yourself with grief over them" (18:6; 26:3) — and the verse relieves him of a burden that was never his. He is responsible for conveying, not for converting. As definition: the verse establishes what the Prophet does and does not do. He does not compel; he does not guarantee outcomes; he does not carry the guilt of those who refuse. He delivers, and delivery is complete when the message has been made clear.

**"The Clear Message": *Al-Balāgh al-Mubīn***

The conveyance is qualified as *mubīn*, "clear," "making clear." The adjective, from the root *b-y-n* that verses 39, 44, and 64 employed, denotes a delivery that leaves no ambiguity — the message is conveyed in such a way that its meaning is plain and its proofs are evident. Al-Rāzī notes the importance of the adjective: the obligation is not merely to say the words but to make them *clear* — to explain, to demonstrate, to remove obstacles to understanding. This is the *bayān* that verse 44 assigned to the Prophet: "that you may make clear to the people what was sent down to them." Verse 82 says that when this clarity has been achieved, the Prophet's duty is done.

The phrase *al-balāgh al-mubīn* appears in the same form in several places (5:92; 24:54; 29:18; 36:17; 64:12), always in the context of the messenger's limited responsibility, and it was discussed at verse 35 of this sūrah, where the idolaters' deterministic excuse was answered: "Is there upon the messengers anything but the clear conveyance?" The sūrah thus returns to a principle it stated earlier, now applying it directly to the Prophet after the full presentation of the signs.

**The Balance: Responsibility Without Guarantee**

The commentators were careful to note what the verse does not say. It does not say the Prophet should cease to convey when people turn away; the Prophet continued to preach to those who rejected him, returning again and again. It does not say he should be indifferent to their refusal; his grief was real and was not condemned, only limited. It does not say the message is unimportant; the message is *mubīn*, clear, and its rejection carries consequences for the rejecter. What the verse says is that the *outcome* is not the messenger's burden. Al-Zamakhsharī summarizes: the Prophet's duty is the means — clear conveyance — and God's prerogative is the end — guidance or its withholding.

This balance protected the Prophet from two errors that afflict those who carry a message: despair, which sets in when one feels responsible for results one cannot produce, and coercion, which tempts one to force the results one cannot persuade. The verse forecloses both. The result is not his to produce; therefore he need not despair. The result is not his to force; therefore he may not coerce. The Qur'an's "there is no compulsion in religion" (2:256) rests on the same foundation as 16:82: the message is delivered; the response is free.

**The Verse Is Not Abrogated**

Some early commentators suggested that verses of this kind — limiting the Prophet's duty to conveyance — were abrogated by the later verses commanding fighting. The majority rejected this, and al-Qurṭubī and al-Rāzī explain why. The verses commanding fighting addressed specific circumstances of hostility and aggression; they did not alter the principle that belief cannot be compelled and that the messenger is not responsible for the hearts of his hearers. Even in the Madinan period, after fighting was permitted, the Qur'an continued to state the principle: "Your duty is only to convey" (3:20; 42:48, both Madinan or late Makkan). The principle is permanent; it defines the nature of prophetic mission and, by extension, of all religious invitation.

**The Application to Those Who Carry the Message After the Prophet**

The commentators extended the verse to everyone who invites to God after the Prophet — the scholar, the teacher, the parent, the friend. Each is bound by the same limit. One's duty is to convey clearly; one is not responsible for the response. The Prophet ﷺ described the reward of one who conveys:

> *"Whoever calls to guidance has a reward like the rewards of those who follow him, without that diminishing their rewards in the least."* (Muslim 2674)

The reward is for *calling*, not for the number who answer. And he described the case of the prophet who will come on the Day of Judgment with no followers at all (al-Bukhārī 5705; Muslim 220) — a prophet who conveyed and was refused entirely, and whose mission was nonetheless complete.

This teaching has a liberating effect on anyone who has tried to guide another and failed. The parent whose child left the religion; the teacher whose student did not learn; the friend whose counsel was ignored — each is told by 16:82 that if the message was clearly conveyed, the duty was discharged. The grief may remain, as the Prophet's did; but the guilt is lifted. And the teaching has a restraining effect on anyone tempted to force belief: the verse says *balāgh*, conveyance, not *ikrāh*, compulsion.

**The Placement of the Verse**

The verse comes at a hinge in the sūrah. Before it lie the great enumerations of blessing and the arguments from creation. After it lies the description of the ungrateful — those who "recognize the blessing of God and then deny it" (v. 83) — and the scene of the Day of Judgment (vv. 84–89). The verse stands between the presentation and the refusal, and it marks the transfer of responsibility: the Prophet has presented; what follows is on those who heard. The commentators read this placement as deliberate. God completed His blessing (v. 81); the Prophet completed his conveyance (v. 82); if there is refusal (v. 83), the account is now theirs.

**The Application: Peace in the Discharge of Duty**

The verse teaches a peace that comes from knowing the limits of one's task. The believer who invites others to good does what he can — clearly, patiently, repeatedly — and then rests in the knowledge that guidance is God's. He is not the guarantor of outcomes. His account with God concerns the clarity and sincerity of his conveyance, and he can render that account whatever the response. The Prophet ﷺ, at ʿArafah in his final sermon, asked the assembled thousands: "Have I conveyed?" They said yes. He said: "O God, bear witness" (Muslim 1218). That question and that witness are the discharge of 16:82. The messenger who can ask it, and call God to witness the answer, has done his whole duty.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:83

> **They recognize the blessing of God, and then deny it; and most of them are disbelievers.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Diagnosis**

After the Prophet's duty has been defined (v. 82), the sūrah describes the state of those who turn away, and the description is precise: *yaʿrifūna niʿmata Allāhi thumma yunkirūnahā*, "they recognize the blessing of God, then they deny it." The verse does not say they are ignorant of the blessing. It says they *recognize* it — and deny it anyway. The whole enumeration of the sūrah, from verse 5 to verse 81, has presented blessings that no one could fail to recognize; the problem was never recognition. The problem is what happens after.

**"They Recognize the Blessing": *Yaʿrifūna***

The verb *ʿarafa* means to know, to recognize, to be acquainted with — knowledge of a thing as familiar, as identified. The idolaters *recognized* the blessing of God: they knew that the rain came from the sky, that the cattle gave milk, that the earth produced crops, and they acknowledged, when asked, that God created these things (v. 31:25; 39:38). Al-Ṭabarī explains that they knew the blessings to be from God in the sense that they admitted He was the Creator. Al-Rāzī adds that the recognition was of the *fact* of blessing and of its ultimate source — the knowledge the *fiṭrah* gives and that verse 53's argument from distress confirmed: in extremity, they called on Him alone.

**"And Then Deny It": *Thumma Yunkirūnahā***

The verb *ankara* means to deny, to disavow, to treat as strange or unrecognized — the opposite of *ʿarafa*. The pairing is exact: they *ʿarafa*, recognized, and then *ankara*, denied. The word *thumma*, "then," marks the sequence: the denial follows the recognition. It is not that they never knew; it is that they knew and then, in their conduct and speech, treated the blessing as though it were not God's.

The commentators identify the forms the denial took. Al-Ṭabarī reports from Mujāhid that they said, "This is our wealth; we inherited it from our fathers" — attributing the blessing to inheritance rather than to God. Al-Suddī reports that they said, "Were it not for so-and-so, we would not have this" — attributing it to human patrons. Others report that they attributed the blessings to the intercession of the idols, thanking the idols for what God had given (cf. v. 56). ʿAwn ibn ʿAbd Allāh is reported to have said that the denial is in their saying "the wind blew and the rain came" — attributing the blessing to natural causes alone. And al-Qurṭubī records the view that the denial was of the greatest blessing, the Prophet himself: they recognized him as truthful (they called him *al-Amīn*, the trustworthy, before his mission) and then denied his message.

Each of these is a form of *kufr al-niʿmah*, the ingratitude for blessing that verse 55 named and that the sūrah's climax (v. 112) will punish. The common structure is the *attribution* of a recognized blessing to something other than its Giver. The blessing is not denied as a fact; its source is denied. And this, the commentators note, is the essence of *shirk*: not the denial of God's existence but the assignment of His gifts and His rights to others.

**The Psychology of Recognizing and Denying**

The verse describes a state that the commentators found significant and that requires explanation: how can a person know a thing and deny it? Al-Rāzī addresses this. The recognition is in the intellect; the denial is in the will and the tongue. The intellect sees that the rain is from God; but pride, habit, social pressure, and the beautification of Satan (v. 63) prevent the will from acting on what the intellect sees, and the tongue says what the will prefers. The Qur'an describes the same condition in Pharaoh's people: "They denied them, though their souls were convinced of them, out of injustice and arrogance" (27:14). Conviction and denial coexist, the denial overriding the conviction.

This is the condition the Qur'an calls *juḥūd* (v. 71) — denial of the known — and it is the most culpable form of disbelief, because it cannot plead ignorance. The one who does not know may be excused until he learns; the one who knows and denies has no excuse. The verse's *thumma*, "then," is an indictment: they had the recognition and threw it away.

The condition is also, the commentators note, a form of self-contradiction that the person must actively maintain. To recognize and deny at once requires continual effort — the suppression of what one knows, the construction of alternative explanations, the avoidance of situations (like the storm at sea, v. 53) that expose the truth. This effort is the "plotting" of verses 26 and 45; and it is unsustainable, because the recognition returns in every crisis and will return absolutely on the Day of Judgment, when "they will know" (v. 39, 55).

**The Broader Reference: The Blessing of the Prophet**

Some commentators, including al-Qurṭubī and al-Zamakhsharī, give particular weight to the reading that the "blessing" denied is the Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ himself. The Qur'an calls the Prophet a mercy (21:107) and a blessing, and the Makkans recognized him — they knew his character, his truthfulness, his lineage; they knew, as Abū Jahl admitted in private, that he did not lie. And they denied him. The verse's structure — recognizing then denying — fits this case exactly, and the same charge is made of the People of the Book: "they recognize him as they recognize their own sons" (2:146; 6:20), and yet they conceal and deny. On this reading, verse 83 names the greatest instance of *kufr al-niʿmah*: the rejection of the guidance that was the culmination of all the blessings, the completion promised in verse 81.

The readings are not exclusive. The blessing recognized and denied includes the physical gifts, their divine source, and the Prophet sent to explain them; the idolaters denied all three in the same act.

**"And Most of Them Are Disbelievers": *Wa-aktharuhumu al-kāfirūn***

The verse ends: *wa-aktharuhumu al-kāfirūn*, "and most of them are the disbelievers." The word *kāfir*, from the root *k-f-r* discussed at verse 55, denotes one who covers — covers the truth, covers the blessing. The verse's final clause names the condition as *kufr*, and applies it to "most" of them.

The commentators address the "most." Why not "all"? Al-Ṭabarī and al-Rāzī give complementary answers. Some among the idolaters would come to believe — the verse leaves room for them, as verse 54's "a party of you" did. Some were excused by youth or incapacity. And some had not yet received the message in its fullness. The Qur'an's precision here, as elsewhere, refuses the sweeping generalization: it says *most*, because most is the truth. Al-Zamakhsharī notes that the definite article in *al-kāfirūn* — "*the* disbelievers" — marks them as the full instance of the type: the ones who recognized and denied are disbelievers in the complete sense, because their disbelief is not ignorance but refusal.

Al-Rāzī also distinguishes the two clauses: the first ("they recognize and deny") describes the *act* of ingratitude, which many commit in degrees; the second ("most of them are disbelievers") describes the *state* of those in whom the act has become settled. Not everyone who denies a blessing once is a *kāfir*; the one who lives in denial is.

**The Verse in the Sūrah's Structure**

Verse 83 is the pivot of the sūrah's argument about blessing. Verse 18 said the blessings cannot be counted; verses 5–81 listed them; verse 81 said God completed them "that you may submit"; verse 82 said the Prophet's duty was only to convey; and verse 83 now states what the idolaters did: recognized and denied. The verse thus names the failure the whole sūrah has been building to expose. And it prepares for what follows: verses 84–89 describe the Day of Judgment, when a witness from every community will testify, and the deniers will be confronted with what they recognized and denied.

**The Application: The Subtle Forms of Recognizing and Denying**

The verse applies beyond the idolaters, and the tradition applied it. The believer, too, may recognize a blessing and deny it — not by attributing it to idols, but by attributing it to himself ("I earned this"), to luck ("things worked out"), to other people alone ("I owe it all to so-and-so"), or to nothing ("that's just how it is"). Each attribution recognizes the blessing and denies its source. The Prophet ﷺ warned against exactly this in the hadith of the three men — the leper, the bald man, and the blind man — whom God healed and enriched, and who, when asked by an angel where their wealth came from, said, "I inherited it from my forefathers," and were stripped of it; while the blind man said, "God restored my sight and gave me this," and kept it (al-Bukhārī 3464; Muslim 2964). The two who recognized and denied were punished; the one who recognized and acknowledged was rewarded. The hadith is 16:83 in narrative, and its application is to every reader who has ever received something and forgotten to say from Whom.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:84

> **And on the Day when We raise up a witness from every community, then those who disbelieved will not be given leave, nor will they be allowed to make amends.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**From the Denial in This World to the Testimony in the Next**

Verse 83 described those who recognize God's blessing and then deny it. Verse 84 moves to the Day on which the denial will be exposed: *wa-yawma nabʿathu min kulli ummatin shahīdan*, "and the Day We raise up from every community a witness." The sūrah's method is to follow every description of wrongdoing with a description of its reckoning, so that the reader never sees the sin without seeing its end. Here the reckoning takes the form of a court: witnesses are called, and the accused are denied the two things they would most want — the right to speak and the chance to make amends.

**"A Witness From Every Community": The Prophets as Witnesses**

The verse says God will raise *min kulli ummatin shahīdan*, "from every community a witness." The commentators identify the witness as the prophet sent to that community. Verse 36 established that every community received a messenger; verse 84 says that messenger will testify. The Qur'an states this in several places:

> *"So how will it be when We bring from every community a witness, and We bring you [O Muḥammad] against these as a witness?"* (Qur'an 4:41)

> *"And the Day We raise from every community a witness, then those who disbelieved will not be given leave..."* (Qur'an 16:84)

> *"And We will extract from every community a witness and say: Produce your proof. Then they will know that the truth belongs to God, and lost from them is what they used to invent."* (Qur'an 28:75)

The prophet's testimony has a content the commentators specify: he will testify that he conveyed the message (the *balāgh* of v. 82) and that his people either accepted or rejected it. The Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ will testify concerning his community, and — according to 4:41 and 2:143 — his community will testify concerning the earlier communities, confirming that their prophets conveyed. The Prophet ﷺ explained 2:143 thus:

> *"Noah will be called on the Day of Resurrection and asked: Did you convey? He will say: Yes, my Lord. Then his community will be asked: Did he convey to you? They will say: No warner came to us. He will be asked: Who will testify for you? He will say: Muḥammad and his community. So they will testify that he conveyed, and the Messenger will be a witness over you."* (al-Bukhārī 3339)

The verse in al-Nisāʾ (4:41) moved the Prophet ﷺ to tears when Ibn Masʿūd recited it to him (al-Bukhārī 4582) — the thought of standing as witness over his own community was heavy to him.

**Why Witnesses Are Needed**

God does not need witnesses; He knows what every soul did (vv. 19, 23). The commentators explain the function of the witness as the establishment of proof against the accused in a manner they cannot dispute — the *iqāmat al-ḥujjah*, establishment of the argument, that verse 39 described. The prophet who lived among his people, spoke their language, and conveyed to them in person testifies that they received the message; this testimony removes the excuse of ignorance. Al-Rāzī notes that the form of a trial, with witnesses and testimony, is adopted because it is the form human beings recognize as just; the justice of God's judgment is displayed in terms they understand. The Qur'an also names other witnesses: the angels who recorded (50:21), the limbs of the accused themselves (24:24; 36:65; 41:20–21), and the earth (99:4–5). The prophet's testimony is one strand in a case that cannot be answered.

**"Those Who Disbelieved Will Not Be Given Leave": *Lā Yuʾdhanu***

After the witness is raised, *thumma lā yuʾdhanu li'lladhīna kafarū*, "then those who disbelieved will not be given permission." Permission for what? The commentators identify two objects, both attested in other verses.

The first is permission to speak — to offer excuses, to argue, to defend themselves:

> *"This is a Day on which they will not speak, nor will they be permitted to offer excuses."* (Qur'an 77:35–36)

The disbelievers will not be allowed to plead their case because there is no case to plead; the witness has testified, the record is complete, and speech would serve only to delay. Al-Rāzī notes that the denial of permission to speak comes at a particular stage of the Judgment — the Qur'an elsewhere records the disbelievers speaking (6:23; 16:86), and the commentators reconcile this by distinguishing stages: they will speak at first, offering denials and excuses, and then, when their limbs testify against them and the case is closed, they will be silenced.

The second is permission to return to the world — to go back and do better:

> *"And if you could see when they are made to stand before the Fire and will say: Oh, would that we could be returned and not deny the signs of our Lord and be among the believers!"* (Qur'an 6:27)

The request to return is made and refused (23:99–100; 32:12; 35:37). Verse 84's "not given leave" includes this refusal.

**"Nor Will They Be Allowed to Make Amends": *Wa-lā hum yustaʿtabūn***

The verse's final clause is *wa-lā hum yustaʿtabūn*, "nor will they be asked to make amends." The verb is from the root *ʿ-t-b*, which concerns blame and its removal: *ʿitāb* is reproach, *iʿtāb* is the removal of the cause of reproach — making amends, giving satisfaction, so that the offended party is appeased. *Istaʿtaba* is to seek or request such satisfaction. The passive *yustaʿtabūn* means "they will [not] be asked to give satisfaction" — that is, God will not seek from them the reconciliation that would remove His displeasure, because the time for it has passed.

The commentators explain the phrase's force. In this world, the sinner can make amends: he repents, God accepts, and the reproach is lifted (v. 119). On the Day of Judgment, this door is closed. The disbelievers will not be *asked* to make amends — the very request will not be made to them — because amends are made in the world of action, and they are now in the world of recompense. Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Rāzī note that the phrase is more devastating than a refusal of their plea: it is not that they ask to make amends and are refused, but that no one even asks them to. The offer is not on the table. The Qur'an states the finality elsewhere: "So today they will not be taken out of it, nor will they be asked to make amends" (45:35; cf. 30:57; 41:24).

**The Contrast With This World**

The verse's two negations — no permission, no amends — define the difference between this world and the next. Here, one may speak: one may argue, excuse, plead, and one's plea may be heard. Here, one may make amends: one may repent and be forgiven, restore what was taken, reconcile with those wronged. The verse says that on the Day of the witnesses, both possibilities are gone. The commentators draw the practical conclusion the verse intends: the time for speaking and for amends is *now*. Verse 61 described God's deferral "until an appointed term"; verse 84 describes the term's arrival, when what was deferred is demanded and what was possible is no longer.

**The Connection to Verse 27 and Verse 89**

Verse 27 mentioned the "people of knowledge" who will speak on the Day of Judgment, saying that disgrace is upon the disbelievers; verse 84 names the witnesses from every community; verse 89 will return to the theme with the fullest statement: "the Day We raise in every community a witness against them from among themselves, and We bring you as a witness against these." The three verses form a thread. The witnesses are the prophets and the knowledgeable; their testimony is that the message was conveyed; and its effect is that the disbelievers are silenced and their case is closed. The thread ties the sūrah's warnings to the specific scene in which they are fulfilled.

**The Application: Speaking and Making Amends While It Is Possible**

The verse's teaching is straightforward and urgent. Two things will be denied on that Day — speech and amends — and both are available now. The believer uses his speech now to acknowledge what he will not be permitted to argue then: to confess, to ask forgiveness, to declare faith. And he makes amends now that will not be sought from him then: he repents of sins, restores rights, reconciles with those he has wronged. The Prophet ﷺ urged exactly this:

> *"Whoever has wronged his brother in his honor or in anything, let him seek his pardon today, before there is no dinar and no dirham — when, if he has good deeds, they will be taken from him in proportion to his wrong, and if he has no good deeds, the other's sins will be taken and cast upon him."* (al-Bukhārī 2449)

"Let him seek his pardon *today*" — this is *istiʿtāb*, the seeking of amends, performed while it is still possible. The verse describes the Day on which it will not be; the hadith describes the day on which it must be. That day is the present one.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:85

> **And when those who did wrong see the punishment, it will not be lightened for them, nor will they be granted respite.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Moment of Seeing**

Verse 84 described the Day of witnesses, on which the disbelievers will be denied speech and amends. Verse 85 moves to the next moment: the sight of the punishment. *Wa-idhā raʾā alladhīna ẓalamū al-ʿadhāba*, "and when those who did wrong see the punishment." The sūrah returns to the theme of seeing that it has used before — the deniers "await nothing but the angels or the command of the Lord" (v. 33), the idolaters will "see" their partners disown them (v. 86) — and here the object of sight is the punishment itself. Two things follow from the sight, both negative: no lightening and no respite.

**"Those Who Did Wrong": *Alladhīna Ẓalamū***

The verse names its subjects not as "disbelievers" (as v. 84) but as *alladhīna ẓalamū*, "those who did wrong." The word *ẓulm*, discussed at verse 33 and elsewhere, denotes injustice in its broadest sense — placing a thing where it does not belong — and its gravest form is *shirk*, "a tremendous wrong" (31:13). The commentators take the term here as referring to the same people as verse 84's disbelievers, described now by their act rather than their state: they wronged God by denying His blessing (v. 83), wronged the Prophet by rejecting him, and wronged themselves by earning the punishment. Al-Rāzī notes that the shift in terminology reminds the reader that disbelief *is* a wrong — not merely an error of opinion but an injustice, for which the punishment is a just recompense.

**"See the Punishment": The Finality of Sight**

The verb *raʾā*, "see," marks a transition from hearing about the punishment to beholding it. In this world, the punishment is described — in the Qur'an, by the Prophet, by the reflection on signs — and the wrongdoers denied what they heard. On that Day, description gives way to sight, and denial becomes impossible. The Qur'an repeatedly marks this transition:

> *"And if you could see when they are made to stand before their Lord..."* (Qur'an 6:30)

> *"And the criminals will see the Fire and will be certain that they are to fall therein, and they will not find from it a way elsewhere."* (Qur'an 18:53)

> *"And those who did wrong will know to what return they will be returned."* (Qur'an 26:227)

The commentators note that seeing produces the certainty that hearing did not — but too late for the certainty to benefit. This is the tragedy the sūrah has been warning of since verse 39: the knowledge will come, but after the time in which knowledge could be acted upon.

**"It Will Not Be Lightened for Them": *Fa-lā yukhaffafu ʿanhum***

The first consequence is *fa-lā yukhaffafu ʿanhum*, "it will not be lightened for them." The verb *khaffafa* means to make light, to reduce, to ease. The punishment will not be reduced in intensity or duration. The Qur'an states this repeatedly, and it records the request for lightening and its refusal:

> *"And those in the Fire will say to the keepers of Hell: Call upon your Lord to lighten for us a day of the punishment. They will say: Did your messengers not come to you with clear proofs? They will say: Yes. They will say: Then call — but the call of the disbelievers is in vain."* (Qur'an 40:49–50)

> *"Their punishment will not be lightened, nor will they be granted respite."* (Qur'an 2:162; 3:88)

The passage from Ghāfir (40:49–50) is the fullest picture of what 16:85 states. The wrongdoers ask the keepers of Hell to intercede for a lightening of *one day*. The keepers' response is a question — did your messengers not come with clear proofs? — that recalls verse 84's witnesses. The answer is yes. And the keepers decline: the call is in vain. The lightening is refused because the proof was established and rejected.

The commentators observe that the denial of lightening is a consequence of the wrongdoers' own conduct. They were offered, in this world, every lightening — the deferral of verse 61, the clarity of the message (v. 82), the open door of repentance. They refused them all. What they refused as mercy in the world will not be granted as relief in the Fire. Al-Rāzī frames the justice: the punishment fits the wrong, and to lighten it would be to disturb the fit.

**"Nor Will They Be Granted Respite": *Wa-lā hum yunẓarūn***

The second consequence is *wa-lā hum yunẓarūn*, "nor will they be given respite." The verb *anẓara* means to grant a delay, to give time — the respite that Iblīs asked for and received in this world (7:14–15, "Give me respite until the Day they are raised. He said: You are of those given respite"). The wrongdoers will not receive this. There will be no postponement of the punishment, no interval between the sentence and its execution, no reprieve.

The word connects to verse 61, where God was said to defer people "until an appointed term." That deferral is the *inẓār*, respite, of this world. Verse 85 states that when the term arrives, the respite ends and is not renewed. The two verses frame the whole logic of divine forbearance: respite is given here, in abundance; it is not given there, at all. Al-Zamakhsharī notes the pairing of the two negations — no lightening of the punishment's *intensity* and no respite from its *onset* — as covering both dimensions in which relief could be sought. There is no relief in degree and no relief in time.

**The Repeated Formula**

The phrase "it will not be lightened for them, nor will they be granted respite" appears in the Qur'an as a set formula (2:162; 3:88; 16:85; cf. 35:36; 43:75), and the commentators note that its repetition serves the Qur'an's method of warning: the same consequence is stated in the same words in different contexts, so that the hearer meets it again and again and cannot claim not to have understood. The formula is a legal one — a sentence, pronounced in fixed terms — and its recurrence conveys that the sentence is settled.

**The Question of Eternity**

The two negations bear on the question, discussed at verse 29, of whether the punishment of the disbelievers is eternal. The majority of the scholars held that it is, on the basis of verses like this one, which deny any lightening or respite, and of the explicit statements of abiding forever (2:162, "abiding therein; the punishment will not be lightened, nor will they be respited"; 4:168–169; 33:64–65). The verse's absolute negations — no lightening, no respite — leave no interval in which the punishment could cease. A minority position, associated with some later scholars, held that the Fire itself might eventually end for those in it; the majority rejected this on the basis of texts such as the present verse, and the commentators of 16:85 read it as affirming the permanence of the disbelievers' punishment.

**The Verse as Warning, Not Description Only**

The commentators emphasize that verses like this one are revealed *now*, to people who can still act, and that their purpose is preventive. The Qur'an describes the Day in order that the description may keep people from arriving at it. Al-Rāzī notes that the verse, read as a warning, is a mercy: it tells the wrongdoer, while he is still in the world of lightening and respite, that neither will exist in the next. The person who hears this and changes has been spared what the verse describes; the verse has done its work. The person who hears it and does not change has been warned, and the warning will be counted among the proofs the witnesses of verse 84 testify to.

**The Application: Using the Respite**

The verse's teaching, as with verse 84, resolves into urgency. The respite that will not be granted then is granted now. The lightening that will not be given then is given now — every act of repentance lightens; every good deed erases a bad one (11:114; and the hadith, "follow a bad deed with a good one and it will wipe it out," al-Tirmidhī 1987). The believer who understands 16:85 does not wait for the sight of the punishment to seek relief from it. He seeks it now, when it is available, from the One who described the Day precisely so that no one would have to see it unprepared. The Prophet ﷺ said:

> *"Protect yourselves from the Fire, even with half a date; and if you cannot find that, then with a good word."* (al-Bukhārī 1417; Muslim 1016)

Half a date and a good word — these are the lightenings available now, and the verse's severity is the measure of their value.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:86

> **And when those who ascribed partners see the partners they ascribed, they will say, "Our Lord! These are our partners whom we used to call upon apart from Thee." But they will fling back the word to them, "Truly you are liars."**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Confrontation With the Partners**

Verse 85 showed the wrongdoers seeing the punishment. Verse 86 shows them seeing something else: the partners they had associated with God. *Wa-idhā raʾā alladhīna ashrakū shurakāʾahum*, "and when those who associated see their partners." The scene is one of the most dramatic in the sūrah, and it completes the argument against *shirk* that the sūrah has been building through parables and proofs. The idols, the angels, and the false objects of worship are brought face to face with those who worshipped them, and the result is mutual disavowal.

**"Those Who Ascribed Partners See Their Partners"**

The verse's subjects are *alladhīna ashrakū*, those who committed *shirk*, and its objects are *shurakāʾahum*, "their partners" — the beings they set beside God. The commentators note the possessive: the partners are called "*their* partners," not God's, because God has no partners; the partnership existed only in the idolaters' invention. Al-Zamakhsharī observes that the phrase carries a quiet irony: they are called partners in relation to the ones who made them so, and that relation is about to be repudiated.

The partners are identified variously by the commentators: the idols themselves, which God will cause to speak on that Day; the angels and the righteous whom some worshipped without their consent; and the devils who whispered the worship. Al-Rāzī notes that all three categories are attested in the Qur'an's descriptions of the Day, and that the scene applies to whichever partners a given idolater worshipped.

**"Our Lord! These Are Our Partners Whom We Used to Call Upon"**

Seeing the partners, the idolaters speak: *rabbanā hāʾulāʾi shurakāʾunā alladhīna kunnā nadʿū min dūnik*, "Our Lord, these are our partners whom we used to call upon apart from You." The commentators analyze the motive behind this speech, and several are proposed.

The first is the desire to shift blame. The idolaters identify the partners in the hope that responsibility for the *shirk* will be transferred to them — "these are the ones who led us astray; let them bear our punishment." Al-Ṭabarī and al-Rāzī read the speech in this way: it is an attempt to make the partners share or absorb the guilt. The Qur'an elsewhere records the followers asking that their leaders be given double punishment (7:38; 33:67–68; 38:61).

The second is the desire for intercession — a last, desperate hope that the partners might, after all, help them, as they had believed in the world. Al-Qurṭubī allows this reading but notes that the idolaters, at this stage, have already seen the punishment (v. 85) and the hope is faint.
