The third is simple acknowledgment — a confession, wrung from them by the sight, that they had worshipped these beings. The address *rabbanā*, "our Lord," is significant here: the idolaters now address God as Lord, acknowledging what they denied, and identify the partners as those they called upon *min dūnik*, "apart from You" — admitting the *shirk* in its own terms.

Whatever the motive, the speech accomplishes nothing, because of what follows.

**"They Will Fling Back the Word to Them": *Fa-alqaw ilayhimu al-qawl***

The partners respond: *fa-alqaw ilayhimu al-qawla innakum la-kādhibūn*, "so they will cast the word to them: Truly you are liars." The verb *alqā* means to throw, to cast, to fling. The commentators note the violence of the image: the partners do not merely reply; they *throw* the word at the idolaters, as one throws back something rejected. Al-Zamakhsharī explains that *alqā al-qawl* conveys a forceful, dismissive rejoinder — the partners hurl the accusation back.

The word cast is *innakum la-kādhibūn*, "truly you are liars," with the double emphasis of *inna* and *la-*. The partners call the idolaters liars.

**In What Were They Liars?**

The commentators discuss what the lie was, since the idolaters had, in fact, worshipped the partners, and the partners' denial seems to contradict this. Several resolutions are given, and they are compatible.

Al-Ṭabarī explains that the partners deny having *commanded* or *desired* the worship. The angels and the righteous never called anyone to worship them; the idols, being inanimate, neither called nor consented. The idolaters' implicit claim — "these are our partners; they led us to this" — is false, because the partners did no such thing. The Qur'an records the angels' words: "Glory be to You! You are our Protector, not they. Rather, they worshipped the jinn" (34:41). And Jesus' words: "I said to them only what You commanded me: Worship God, my Lord and your Lord" (5:117).

Al-Rāzī adds that the partners deny being *partners* at all. The idolaters said "these are our partners," and the partners reply, "You lie — we are not partners of God; we never were; the partnership was your invention." On this reading, the "lie" is the fundamental claim of *shirk* itself.

Al-Zamakhsharī notes a third dimension: the partners deny that the idolaters truly worshipped *them*. What the idolaters worshipped was their own desires, their own fabrications, the devils who whispered to them (34:41) — not the beings they named. The stone was an object; the true object of their worship was the falsehood in their own hearts. The partners say "you are liars" because the idolaters' whole account of their religion — what they worshipped, why, and on whose authority — was false from beginning to end.

**How Do the Idols Speak?**

The verse describes the partners speaking, and the commentators address how idols of stone could do so. Al-Qurṭubī and al-Rāzī answer that God will give them speech on that Day, as He will give speech to the limbs of the accused (24:24; 36:65; 41:21) and to the earth (99:4–5). The Qur'an states that on the Day of Judgment God will "give speech to all things" (41:21). The speech of the idols is thus not a difficulty; it is one instance of the general reality that on that Day, everything testifies.

**The Parallel Scenes in the Qur'an**

The Qur'an presents this confrontation in several places, and the parallels fill out the picture of 16:86:

> *"And the Day We gather them all together, then We will say to those who associated: Where are your partners whom you used to claim? Then there will be no [excuse for] them except that they will say: By God, our Lord, we were not associators! See how they will lie about themselves, and lost from them will be what they used to invent."* (Qur'an 6:22–24)

> *"And when they see the punishment, they will conceal regret... And the Day He will call them and say: Where are My partners whom you used to claim? ... And they will call their partners, but they will not respond to them."* (Qur'an 28:62–64)

> *"And it will be said: Call your partners. And they will call them, but they will not respond to them, and they will see the punishment. If only they had followed guidance!"* (Qur'an 28:64)

> *"And your partners will say: It was not us that you worshipped."* (Qur'an 10:28)

The scene from Yūnus (10:28–29) is the closest parallel: God separates the idolaters from their partners, and the partners say, "It was not us you worshipped; God suffices as witness between us and you; we were unaware of your worship." The disavowal in 16:86 — "you are liars" — is the same disavowal in sharper words.

**The Argument the Scene Completes**

Verse 86 completes an argument that began in verse 20 ("those they call upon besides God create nothing") and ran through verses 73–76 (the idols control no provision, are like a powerless slave, like a mute burden). Those verses established that the partners *could* not help. Verse 86 establishes that they *will* not — that at the moment of need, they will turn against their worshippers. The idolaters had invested their hope in beings who will call them liars. Al-Rāzī draws out the lesson: every relationship not founded on God ends in mutual repudiation on the Day of Judgment, as the Qur'an states of friendships generally: "Friends on that Day will be enemies to one another, except the God-fearing" (43:67).

**The Application: Testing One's Partners Now**

The verse invites the reader to ask, of everything he relies upon, trusts in, and orients his life around: will this stand with me on that Day, or will it cast the word back at me? The idols of Makkah are gone, but the structure of *shirk* persists in every ultimate loyalty given to what is not God — wealth, status, ideology, persons treated as infallible, one's own desires. Each of these, on the Day described, will disown the one who served it. Wealth will say, "I did not ask to be hoarded"; status will say, "I did not ask to be worshipped"; the desires will say, "You followed us, and we were nothing." The only relationship that does not end in "you are liars" is the relationship with the One who is Truth. The verse's scene is offered now so that the reader may choose his partners before they are called to testify.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:87

> **And on that Day they will offer submission to God, and that which they used to fabricate will forsake them.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Surrender That Comes Too Late**

Verse 86 showed the idolaters' partners disowning them. Verse 87 shows what remains when the partners are gone: *wa-alqaw ilā Allāhi yawmaʾidhin al-salam*, "and they will offer submission to God on that Day." Stripped of every false support, the idolaters surrender — to the One they had refused to surrender to in the world. The surrender is real, but it is worthless, because it is compelled by sight rather than chosen by faith. And the verse ends by naming the final loss: everything they fabricated abandons them.

**"They Will Offer Submission": *Alqaw al-Salam***

The phrase *alqaw ilā Allāhi al-salam* uses the same idiom that verse 28 used of the dying disbelievers: *fa-alqaw al-salam*, "they offer submission." There, at the moment of death, the wrongdoers said, "We were not doing any evil," and the angels rejected the claim. Here, at the Judgment, the same idiom recurs. The commentators explained it at verse 28: *alqā al-salam* means to throw down one's surrender, to give up resistance, to submit — as a defeated enemy throws down his arms. The word *salam* is from the root *s-l-m*, the root of *islām*, and the idolaters' act is a kind of *islām* — but a coerced one, the *islām* of the vanquished, not of the believer.

Al-Zamakhsharī notes the verb's force: *alqā*, "they cast," is the same verb the partners used when they "cast the word" at the idolaters in verse 86. The partners cast rejection at the idolaters; the idolaters cast submission at God. The two castings frame the scene: rejected by what they worshipped, they throw themselves upon the One they rejected.

**Why the Submission Is Void**

The commentators are unanimous that this submission avails nothing, and they explain why. Faith is accepted when it is chosen in the domain of the unseen (*ghayb*), when the truth is believed on the basis of proof rather than sight. Once the unseen becomes seen, belief is no longer faith but perception, and perception carries no merit. The Qur'an states the principle in the case of Pharaoh, who submitted as he drowned:

> *"Until, when drowning overtook him, he said: I believe that there is no god but the One in whom the Children of Israel believe, and I am of the Muslims. Now? And you had disobeyed before and were of the corrupters."* (Qur'an 10:90–91)

And in general terms:

> *"But their faith did not benefit them when they saw Our punishment. [This is] the way of God which has preceded among His servants, and there the disbelievers lost."* (Qur'an 40:85)

> *"The Day some of the signs of your Lord come, no soul will benefit from its faith if it had not believed before, or earned good through its faith."* (Qur'an 6:158)

The submission of 16:87 is the submission of 10:90 and 40:85 — made after the sight, when the way of God does not accept it. Al-Rāzī explains that the very purpose of the test of this world is that faith be chosen freely; a submission compelled by the sight of punishment does not fulfill the test, because it would be given by anyone, believer or not, and therefore distinguishes nothing.

**The Contrast With Voluntary *Islām***

The verse's use of *salam* — the root of *islām* — creates a contrast that the sūrah has been preparing. Verse 81 ended the enumeration of blessings with *laʿallakum tuslimūn*, "that haply you may submit." The submission asked for there was voluntary: the response of a grateful heart to a complete blessing. The submission described in verse 87 is involuntary: the collapse of a defeated will before an inescapable power. The word is the same; the act is opposite. Al-Rāzī draws out the lesson: everyone will submit to God eventually — the only question is whether one submits now, as an act of faith that is accepted, or then, as an act of defeat that is not. The Qur'an states that all creation submits, "willingly or unwillingly" (3:83; 13:15); the human being chooses which.

**"That Which They Used to Fabricate Will Forsake Them": *Ḍalla ʿanhum***

The verse's second clause is *wa-ḍalla ʿanhum mā kānū yaftarūn*, "and what they used to fabricate will stray from them." The verb *ḍalla* means to go astray, to be lost, to vanish — the same root as *ḍalāl*, misguidance. What "strays from" the idolaters is *mā kānū yaftarūn*, "what they used to fabricate" — the same phrase used in verse 56 ("you will be asked about what you used to fabricate") and throughout the Qur'an for the inventions of the idolaters: the divinity of the idols, their intercession, the daughters of God, the lawful and unlawful they devised.

The commentators explain the image. The fabrications were the idolaters' constructions — the beliefs and hopes they had built and leaned upon. On the Day of Judgment these constructions *go astray*, vanish, are lost, as though they had wandered off and left their makers standing alone. Al-Zamakhsharī notes the irony in the verb: the fabrications, which led the idolaters astray in the world, are themselves lost on that Day; the misguiders are mis-guided away. Al-Ṭabarī explains simply: what they had hoped for from the idols — intercession, benefit — disappears, and they find nothing.

The formula *ḍalla ʿanhum mā kānū yaftarūn* (or *yadʿūn*, "call upon") is one of the Qur'an's repeated descriptions of the Day (6:24; 7:53; 10:30; 11:21; 28:75; 40:74; 41:48), and its recurrence marks a settled reality: on that Day, every false thing vanishes, and only the true remains.

**The Sequence of Verses 84–87**

The four verses form a single scene, and the commentators read them as stages. Verse 84: the witnesses are raised, and the disbelievers are denied speech and amends. Verse 85: they see the punishment; no lightening, no respite. Verse 86: they see their partners and appeal to them; the partners call them liars. Verse 87: abandoned by the partners, they surrender to God; and everything they had invented vanishes. The scene moves from the establishment of proof, to the sight of consequence, to the collapse of false hope, to the empty surrender that follows. Each stage removes one more thing the idolaters had relied upon — their speech, their time, their partners, their inventions — until nothing is left but themselves and the truth.

**The Theological Point: The End of Fabrication**

The verse teaches that fabrication (*iftirāʾ*) has a term. In this world, a lie about God can be sustained — by social agreement, by inherited habit, by the beautification of Satan (v. 63). It can seem solid, even permanent. The verse says it is not. On the Day when things are seen as they are, the fabricated has no existence, because it never had one; it was always only a story told by human tongues (v. 62, "their tongues describe the lie"). The commentators connect this to the sūrah's insistence on *ḥaqq*, truth: God created the heavens and the earth "in truth" (v. 3); the Book was sent "in truth" (v. 102); and on the Day of Truth, only the true survives.

**The Application: Submitting Before the Day**

The verse's lesson is the one the sūrah has been pressing from its first verse: submit now. The *islām* that verse 81 asked for and the *salam* that verse 87 describes are two ends of a single choice, and the difference between them is everything. The one who submits now does so in faith, and the submission is accepted, rewarded, and made the ground of a relationship with God that lasts. The one who submits then does so in defeat, and the submission is void. The Prophet ﷺ described the acceptance of repentance as available "so long as the soul has not reached the throat" (al-Tirmidhī 3537) — that is, until the moment of sight begins. Verse 87 describes what lies beyond that moment. The reader who takes it seriously does not wait to be abandoned by his fabrications; he abandons them himself, while abandoning them still counts.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:88

> **Those who disbelieve and turn [others] from the way of God—We shall add punishment upon punishment for them, for the corruption they used to work.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Two Crimes, Two Punishments**

The scene of the Judgment continues, and the verse singles out a class among the disbelievers for a heavier sentence: *alladhīna kafarū wa-ṣaddū ʿan sabīli Allāh*, "those who disbelieved and turned [others] away from the way of God." Two acts are named — disbelief and obstruction — and two punishments correspond: *zidnāhum ʿadhāban fawqa al-ʿadhāb*, "We will increase them in punishment upon punishment." The verse thus establishes a principle of proportion: the one who not only rejects the truth but prevents others from reaching it bears a double burden.

**"Those Who Disbelieve and Turn Others From the Way of God"**

The verse's first act is *kafarū*, disbelief — the covering of truth and blessing that verse 83 described. The second is *ṣaddū ʿan sabīli Allāh*. The verb *ṣadda* has two senses in Arabic, both attested in the Qur'an: intransitively, to turn away oneself (as in 4:61, "you see the hypocrites turning away from you"); transitively, to turn others away, to bar, to obstruct. The commentators take it here in the transitive sense — they turned *others* away — because the verse distinguishes it from *kafarū*, which already covers the person's own rejection. Al-Ṭabarī explains: they disbelieved themselves and prevented others from believing.

*Sabīl Allāh*, "the way of God," is the Qur'an's term for the path of faith and obedience — the "straight path" of verse 9, the religion He prescribes. To turn others from it is to stand between them and God. The commentators describe how the Makkan leaders did this: they mocked the Prophet publicly so that others would be ashamed to follow him; they intercepted travelers coming to Makkah and warned them against him (as al-Ṭufayl ibn ʿAmr reported being warned, and as the pilgrims were warned at the fairs); they persecuted those who believed, to deter others; they spread the charge that the Qur'an was "legends of the ancients" (v. 24); and they made noise during its recitation so that it could not be heard (41:26). Each of these was *ṣadd* — active obstruction of the way.

**"Punishment Upon Punishment": The Doubling**

The sentence is *zidnāhum ʿadhāban fawqa al-ʿadhāb*, "We will add for them a punishment above the punishment." The commentators explain the structure. The first punishment (*al-ʿadhāb*, with the definite article) is the punishment for their own disbelief — the punishment every disbeliever receives. The second (*ʿadhāban*, indefinite) is an additional punishment for the obstruction — a punishment on top of the first. The one who disbelieved *and* obstructed receives both.

The principle behind the doubling is stated in the Qur'an's rule about leading others astray, which was discussed at verse 25:

> *"That they may bear their own burdens in full on the Day of Resurrection, and some of the burdens of those whom they misguide without knowledge."* (Qur'an 16:25)

The obstructer bears his own burden (the first punishment) and a share of the burdens of those he obstructed (the second). The Prophet ﷺ stated the same rule:

> *"Whoever calls to misguidance has upon him sin like the sins of those who follow him, without that diminishing their sins in the least."* (Muslim 2674)

The verse's "punishment upon punishment" is the enactment of this rule at the Judgment.

**The Nature of the Added Punishment**

The commentators transmitted reports describing the additional punishment, and al-Ṭabarī and al-Qurṭubī record them. Ibn Masʿūd is reported to have said that it is scorpions with fangs like tall palm trees, and serpents like the necks of camels, that will be set upon them in the Fire. Others described it as springs of molten copper, or as an intensification of the Fire's heat. Al-Rāzī treats these reports as illustrations of the *degree* of the additional punishment rather than as fixed specifications, and notes that the verse itself does not detail the added punishment; it states only that it is *fawqa*, above, the ordinary — more severe than what the mere disbeliever receives. The Qur'an confirms that the Fire has degrees: "For each are degrees according to what they did" (6:132; 46:19), and that the hypocrites are in its lowest depth (4:145).

**"For the Corruption They Used to Work": *Bimā kānū yufsidūn***

The verse gives the reason for the added punishment: *bimā kānū yufsidūn*, "for what they used to corrupt." The word *fasād*, corruption, is the Qur'an's term for the disruption of the order God established — in the earth, in society, in religion. Its opposite is *iṣlāḥ*, setting right. The commentators identify the corruption here as the obstruction itself: to turn people from the way of God is to corrupt the earth, because the earth's order depends on human beings' relationship with their Creator, and the one who severs that relationship for others has damaged the foundation of everything else.

The verse's framing of *ṣadd* as *fasād* is significant. The Makkan leaders regarded themselves as guardians of order — of the tribe, the sanctuary, the ancestral religion. The verse names their guardianship as corruption. Al-Rāzī draws out the point: what appears as preservation of a false order is, in truth, the corruption of the true one; and the leaders who "protected" their people from the Prophet were in fact destroying them.

**The Principle of Aggravated Responsibility**

The verse establishes a principle that the tradition developed at length: responsibility is aggravated by influence. The one whose disbelief affects only himself is punished for himself; the one whose disbelief affects others is punished for the effect as well. This is why the Qur'an reserves its severest language for leaders, chiefs, and those who command a following — Pharaoh and his council (28:41, "We made them leaders inviting to the Fire"), the *malaʾ* (chiefs) of every destroyed nation, the "arrogant" who are addressed by their followers on the Day (34:31–33). The Makkan chiefs — Abū Jahl, Abū Lahab, al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah, and the others — belonged to this class; their disbelief was multiplied by their obstruction.

The principle has a positive counterpart, stated in the same hadith of Muslim 2674: "Whoever calls to guidance has a reward like the rewards of those who follow him." Influence doubles the reward as it doubles the punishment. The one who opens the way of God to others receives a share of everything they do; the one who closes it bears a share of everything they fail to do.

**The Two Kinds of Obstruction**

The commentators distinguished two forms of *ṣadd*, both covered by the verse. The first is direct: forbidding, persecuting, preventing by force — as the Makkans prevented the believers from praying at the Kaʿbah and, later, from performing the pilgrimage (48:25). The second is indirect: making the way of God repellent by mockery, misrepresentation, or bad example, so that people turn from it without being forced. The second is subtler and, in some ways, more effective. Al-Rāzī notes that both are *ṣadd*, and both incur the added punishment, because in both the result is the same: a person who might have reached God was prevented.

**The Application: Neither Obstructing Nor Being Obstructed**

The verse teaches two lessons. To those with influence — parents, teachers, leaders, anyone whose words and conduct affect others' relationship with God — it teaches that their influence is weighed. To obstruct the way of God, whether by forbidding it, mocking it, or misrepresenting it, is to incur a punishment beyond one's own disbelief; and conversely, to open the way — by teaching, by example, by removing obstacles — is to earn beyond one's own faith. The Prophet ﷺ said that the one who guides another to good is like its doer (Muslim 1893).

To those who are the objects of obstruction, the verse offers reassurance: the one who bars the way will answer for it. The believer who was mocked, discouraged, or prevented is not forgotten; the account is kept, and the obstructer's "punishment upon punishment" is, in part, the vindication of those he obstructed. The Qur'an promises the obstructed that God knows what was done to them (v. 41, "We shall surely settle them in a good place in this world"), and verse 88 shows the other side of that settlement.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:89

> **And on the Day when We raise up in every community a witness against them from among themselves, and We bring thee as a witness against these. And We have sent down unto thee the Book as a clarification of all things, and as a guidance and a mercy and glad tidings for those who submit.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Scene Returns to the Witnesses, and the Book Is Named**

Verse 84 opened the scene of the Judgment with the raising of a witness from every community. Verse 89 returns to that moment and completes it, adding two elements: the witness is "from among themselves," and the Prophet ﷺ is brought as witness against "these" — his own people. The verse then turns, in its second half, from the Judgment to the present, naming the Book that was sent down as the basis of the Prophet's testimony and describing it in four terms: clarification of all things, guidance, mercy, and glad tidings for the Muslims. The verse thus binds together the Judgment and the revelation: the witness will testify to what the Book made clear.

**"A Witness Against Them From Among Themselves"**

The verse says *shahīdan ʿalayhim min anfusihim*, "a witness against them from among themselves." The phrase *min anfusihim* was absent from verse 84 and adds a precision the commentators noted. The witness is not a stranger. He is one of them — of their language, their lineage, their city — who lived among them and spoke to them in terms they understood. Al-Rāzī explains the significance: a witness from among the people cannot be dismissed as ignorant of their circumstances or as an outsider whose testimony is suspect. He knew them, and they knew him; his testimony that he conveyed and they refused is unanswerable. The Qur'an emphasizes the same point about the Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ: "There has come to you a Messenger from among yourselves" (9:128); "God has favored the believers by sending among them a Messenger from among themselves" (3:164).

The preposition *ʿalā*, "against," in *shahīdan ʿalayhim* has been read in two ways. The primary sense is testimony *against* — the prophet testifies to his people's rejection. But the commentators note that *shahīd ʿalā* can also mean a witness *over* or *concerning* — testifying to what the people did, whether acceptance or rejection. The prophet testifies for the believers among his people and against the disbelievers; the preposition covers both.

**"And We Bring Thee as a Witness Against These"**

The verse then addresses the Prophet: *wa-jiʾnā bika shahīdan ʿalā hāʾulāʾ*, "and We bring you as a witness against these." The demonstrative *hāʾulāʾ*, "these," refers to the Prophet's own community — the Arabs to whom he was sent, and by extension all who received his message. Al-Ṭabarī reads it as the Prophet's community generally; al-Rāzī includes the Makkans specifically. The Prophet ﷺ will testify concerning them as every prophet testifies concerning his people.

This is the verse — with its parallel in 4:41 — that moved the Prophet ﷺ to tears. Ibn Masʿūd reported:

> *The Prophet ﷺ said to me: "Recite to me." I said: "Shall I recite to you when it was revealed to you?" He said: "I love to hear it from another." So I recited Sūrat al-Nisāʾ until I reached: "And We bring you against these as a witness." He said: "Enough for now." I turned to him, and his eyes were flowing with tears.* (al-Bukhārī 4582; Muslim 800)

The commentators explain the tears. The Prophet wept at the weight of the testimony — at the thought of standing before God to give account of his community, and of what he would have to say of those who refused. His witness was not a formality; it was a responsibility he felt for every person to whom he had been sent.

**The Transition: "And We Have Sent Down Unto Thee the Book"**

The verse's second half turns from the Day of Judgment to the present: *wa-nazzalnā ʿalayka al-kitāb*, "and We have sent down to you the Book." The commentators explain the connection. The Prophet's testimony on that Day will be *based on* the Book: he will testify that he conveyed what was sent down, and the Book is the record of what was conveyed. Al-Rāzī states it: the mention of the Book after the mention of the witness establishes the content of the testimony. The Prophet does not testify to his own opinions but to what God revealed; and the Book, being preserved, is itself a witness that what he conveyed was God's word.

The verb is *nazzalnā*, the intensive form, which the commentators associate with gradual, repeated sending down — the Qur'an revealed over twenty-three years, piece by piece, as circumstances required. The form fits a Book that was sent down *as a clarification*: clarification is given as questions arise, and the Qur'an's gradual revelation matched the community's need.

**"A Clarification of All Things": *Tibyānan li-kulli shayʾ***

The Book is described first as *tibyānan li-kulli shayʾ*, "a clarification of all things." The word *tibyān* is an intensive verbal noun from *bayyana*, to make clear — the root that has run through the sūrah (vv. 39, 44, 64, 82). The Book makes clear; and the scope is *kullu shayʾ*, "everything."

The phrase raised a question the commentators addressed: how can a book of finite length clarify *everything*? The answers are complementary. Al-Ṭabarī and al-Qurṭubī explain that "everything" means everything of religion — everything human beings need to know for their guidance: the doctrines of faith, the rulings of law, the ethics of conduct, the accounts of the past that instruct, and the descriptions of the future that warn. Mujāhid is reported to have said: "everything of the lawful and the unlawful." The Book clarifies all that is necessary for salvation; it does not claim to be a manual of every craft and science.

Al-Rāzī and al-Shāfiʿī (whom al-Qurṭubī cites) develop a second sense: the Book clarifies everything either *directly*, by explicit statement; or *indirectly*, by referring to the Sunnah ("obey the Messenger," 4:59; "whatever the Messenger gives you, take it," 59:7) and to consensus and analogy ("refer it to God and the Messenger," 4:59; "ask the people of the Reminder," 16:43). Whatever is not stated in the Qur'an is clarified by a principle the Qur'an establishes. On this view, the phrase "clarification of all things" is the foundation of Islamic jurisprudence, which derives every ruling, ultimately, from the Book — directly or through the sources the Book authorizes. Al-Shāfiʿī's *Risālah* opens with this principle.

Ibn Masʿūd stated the same in his own terms: "God has clarified for us in this Qur'an all knowledge and everything" — meaning that the Qur'an contains the roots of all beneficial knowledge, and that its "clarification" extends, through its principles, to matters it does not name.

**"Guidance, Mercy, and Glad Tidings for Those Who Submit"**

The Book is then described by three further terms: *wa-hudan wa-raḥmatan wa-bushrā li'l-muslimīn*, "and a guidance and a mercy and glad tidings for the Muslims." The first two repeat the description of verse 64 ("a guidance and a mercy for a people who believe"), and the commentators explain them as before: guidance shows the way; mercy is the good that comes to those who walk it. The third, *bushrā*, glad tidings, is new: the Book brings good news — of forgiveness, of Paradise, of God's pleasure — to those who accept it.

The recipients are named as *al-muslimīn*, "those who submit." The choice of word closes a thread that verses 81 and 87 opened. Verse 81 asked for submission (*tuslimūn*); verse 87 described the worthless submission of the defeated (*alqaw al-salam*); verse 89 names the Book's glad tidings as belonging to *al-muslimīn* — those who submitted voluntarily, in the world, while submission counted. Al-Rāzī notes the fittingness: the Book clarifies for all, but it is guidance, mercy, and good news only for those who receive it in submission. For the others it is proof against them — the content of the witness's testimony.

**The Verse as a Summary of the Book's Function**

The four descriptions together give a complete account of what the Qur'an is. It is *tibyān*: it makes clear what would otherwise be obscure — about God, the world, the self, and the end. It is *hudā*: it directs toward the destination. It is *raḥmah*: its effect on those who follow it is healing and salvation. And it is *bushrā*: it promises good to those who submit. The commentators note that the four correspond to four human needs — for knowledge, for direction, for relief, and for hope — and that the Book meets all four.

**The Application: The Book as Witness and as Gift**

The verse presents the Book under two aspects, and the reader is asked to hold both. It is the basis of the testimony that will be given against those who rejected it: on that Day, the Prophet will testify that this Book was conveyed, and the record will confirm it. And it is the gift that makes the testimony unnecessary for those who accepted it: a clarification, a guidance, a mercy, and glad tidings. The same Book is proof against one reader and good news for another, and the difference is not in the Book but in the reader's response. The verse invites the reader to be among the *muslimīn* for whom it is *bushrā* — to receive the clarification as clarification, to follow the guidance, to accept the mercy, and to hear the good news as addressed to himself. The Prophet ﷺ described the Qur'an as "an argument for you or against you" (Muslim 223). Verse 89 shows both possibilities and asks the reader which he will make it.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:90

> **Truly God commands justice, virtue, and giving to kinsfolk, and He forbids indecency, wrong, and rebelliousness. He admonishes you, that haply you may remember.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Most Comprehensive Verse in the Qur'an**

Verse 89 described the Book as "a clarification of all things." Verse 90 immediately demonstrates the claim. In a single sentence it names three things God commands and three He forbids, and the tradition has regarded this sentence as the most complete summary of the whole ethical content of the revelation. ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd said:

> *"The most comprehensive verse in the Qur'an for good and evil is the verse in Sūrat al-Naḥl: 'Truly God commands justice, virtue, and giving to kinsfolk...'"* (al-Bukhārī in al-Adab al-Mufrad; al-Ḥākim; al-Ṭabarī)

Al-Qurṭubī records that the verse was recited by ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz as the conclusion of the Friday sermon in place of the cursing of ʿAlī that the Umayyads had instituted, and that the practice continued in the Muslim world thereafter — so that this verse has been heard by more Muslims, more regularly, than almost any other. The commentators also record the response of the pagan al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah, who, on hearing the Prophet ﷺ recite it, said: "By God, it has a sweetness, and a grace upon it; its lowest part is fruitful and its highest is abundant; and this is not the speech of a human being." And ʿUthmān ibn Maẓʿūn reported that this verse, recited to him by the Prophet, was the moment his faith settled in his heart, because he saw that the religion commanded only what every sound mind honors.

**"Truly God Commands": The Authority of the Ethic**

The verse begins *inna Allāha yaʾmuru*, "truly God commands." The ethical content that follows is not offered as advice, philosophy, or custom, but as *command* from God. The commentators note the significance. Justice and virtue are not merely good; they are *commanded*, and their neglect is disobedience. The verse grounds ethics in divine authority — which gives it a force that no human ethic possesses, since the one who commands is the One who will judge (v. 84–89). Al-Rāzī observes that the verse follows immediately upon the description of the Book as clarification, guidance, mercy, and glad tidings (v. 89), and shows what the Book guides to: these three things and the avoidance of those three.

**The First Command: Justice — *Al-ʿAdl***

The first thing commanded is *al-ʿadl*, justice. The root *ʿ-d-l* denotes balance, equality, straightness — giving each thing its due, neither more nor less. The commentators offered several definitions, each capturing an aspect.

Ibn ʿAbbās is reported by al-Ṭabarī to have explained *al-ʿadl* here as *lā ilāha illā Allāh* — the testimony that there is no god but God. This is justice at its root: to give worship to the One who deserves it and to no other. *Shirk*, by contrast, is "a tremendous wrong" (*ẓulm*, 31:13), the placing of worship where it does not belong. Justice toward God is the foundation of all other justice.

Al-Rāzī, drawing on the philosophical tradition, defines justice as the mean between excess and deficiency in every matter — in belief (between denying God's attributes and likening Him to creatures, cf. v. 74), in action (between miserliness and prodigality), in treatment of others (between cruelty and weakness). Justice is the *middle*, and the Qur'an calls the community a "middle nation" (2:143).

The jurists define justice as giving every right-holder his right: the right of God (worship), the rights of people (honesty, fairness, fulfillment of trust), and the right of oneself (not to be destroyed by excess). Al-Qurṭubī cites the definition: justice is *al-inṣāf*, equity — treating others as one would be treated, judging between people without favor.

The Qur'an's other commands of justice fill out the meaning:

> *"O you who believe, be persistently standing firm in justice, witnesses for God, even if it be against yourselves or parents and relatives."* (Qur'an 4:135)

> *"And do not let the hatred of a people prevent you from being just. Be just; that is nearer to piety."* (Qur'an 5:8)

> *"Truly God commands you to render trusts to whom they are due, and when you judge between people, to judge with justice."* (Qur'an 4:58)

The verse in al-Māʾidah (5:8) states the hardest form of justice: toward those one hates. Justice that extends only to friends is not justice; the verse commands it toward enemies.

**The Second Command: Virtue — *Al-Iḥsān***

The second thing commanded is *al-iḥsān*, which the translation renders "virtue" and which means, more precisely, excellence — doing what is good, and doing it beautifully and well. The root *ḥ-s-n* denotes beauty and goodness; *aḥsana* is to do well, to do good, to perfect.

The commentators distinguish *iḥsān* from *ʿadl* in a way that gives the verse its structure. Justice is giving what is due; *iḥsān* is giving *more* than is due. Justice is the minimum; *iḥsān* is the excellence above it. Al-Rāzī illustrates: justice is to repay a kindness with an equal kindness; *iḥsān* is to repay it with a greater one. Justice is to take one's right; *iḥsān* is to forgo it. Justice is the obligatory; *iḥsān* is the supererogatory. A society founded on justice alone is fair but cold; a society in which *iḥsān* is practiced is warm. The Qur'an commands both, in this order, because justice is the foundation and *iḥsān* is the building.

Ibn ʿAbbās, according to al-Ṭabarī, explained *al-iḥsān* here as the performance of what God has made obligatory — that is, doing one's duties *well*. And the Prophet ﷺ gave the definitive definition of *iḥsān* in its religious sense, in the hadith of Gabriel:

> *"Iḥsān is that you worship God as though you see Him; for if you do not see Him, He sees you."* (al-Bukhārī 50; Muslim 8)

This is *iḥsān* toward God: worship performed with the awareness of His presence, so that it is done with the care one would take if one saw Him. The commentators join the two dimensions: *iḥsān* toward God is worship as though seeing Him; *iḥsān* toward creatures is doing them good beyond what justice requires. The Prophet ﷺ extended *iḥsān* to every act, even the slaughter of an animal:

> *"Truly God has prescribed iḥsān in all things. So when you kill, kill well; and when you slaughter, slaughter well; let each of you sharpen his blade and spare suffering to the animal he slaughters."* (Muslim 1955)

**The Third Command: Giving to Kinsfolk — *Ītāʾ dhī al-qurbā***

The third thing commanded is *ītāʾi dhī al-qurbā*, "giving to the possessor of nearness" — to relatives. The commentators note that this is a specific instance of *iḥsān*, singled out because of its importance and because it was the foundation of Arab social order. Al-Rāzī explains why it is named separately after *iḥsān* had already been commanded: to emphasize it, because the rights of kin are the most binding after the rights of God and parents, and because the neglect of kin is among the most common failures.

The "giving" is broad: it includes financial support, visiting, kindness, forgiveness of their faults, and the maintenance of the bond called *ṣilat al-raḥim*, joining the womb-relation. The Prophet ﷺ made this bond a condition of faith and a cause of long life:

> *"Whoever believes in God and the Last Day, let him maintain the ties of kinship."* (al-Bukhārī 6138; Muslim 47)

> *"Whoever would like his provision to be expanded and his life to be extended, let him maintain his ties of kinship."* (al-Bukhārī 5986; Muslim 2557)

And he described the severing of kinship as among the gravest sins, and its victim as one who is barred from Paradise: *"The severer of kinship will not enter Paradise"* (al-Bukhārī 5984; Muslim 2556). The verse's third command thus carries the weight of a whole institution — the family as the first community, in which justice and *iḥsān* are first learned and first tested.

**The First Prohibition: Indecency — *Al-Faḥshāʾ***

The verse then turns to what God forbids: *wa-yanhā ʿani al-faḥshāʾi*. The word *faḥshāʾ*, from the root *f-ḥ-sh*, denotes what is excessive, gross, shameful — whatever exceeds the bounds of decency. In the Qur'an it most often refers to sexual immorality: adultery is called "a *fāḥishah*" (17:32), and the acts of Lot's people are *al-fāḥishah* (7:80). But the term is broader. Ibn ʿAbbās explained it as adultery; others as every sin whose ugliness is evident; al-Rāzī as every act that exceeds the proper limit and is recognized as shameful by sound nature. The commentators generally take it as the sins of desire — the indulgence of appetite beyond what God permitted.

**The Second Prohibition: Wrong — *Al-Munkar***

The second prohibition is *al-munkar*, "the rejected," "the wrong" — from the root *n-k-r*, to not recognize, to reject. *Munkar* is what sound reason and revealed law reject: everything that is recognized as wrong. The Qur'an pairs it with *maʿrūf*, "the recognized," the good, in its command that the community "enjoin the *maʿrūf* and forbid the *munkar*" (3:104, 110). Ibn ʿAbbās explained it here as *shirk*; others as every disobedience. Al-Rāzī reads it as the sins of the tongue and the limbs generally — as *faḥshāʾ* covers the sins of desire, *munkar* covers the sins of action.

**The Third Prohibition: Rebelliousness — *Al-Baghy***

The third prohibition is *al-baghy*, from the root *b-gh-y*, which means to seek, to desire, and, in this form, to seek beyond one's right — to transgress, to oppress, to rebel, to exceed bounds against others. *Baghy* is aggression: the wrong done to others through arrogance and the desire for what is not one's own. Ibn ʿAbbās explained it as *al-ẓulm*, oppression. Al-Rāzī classifies it as the sins of anger and pride — the third category after desire (*faḥshāʾ*) and general wrongdoing (*munkar*).

The Prophet ﷺ singled out *baghy* as the sin most swiftly punished:

> *"There is no sin more deserving of God's hastening its punishment in this world, along with what He stores up for its doer in the Hereafter, than baghy and the severing of kinship."* (Abū Dāwūd 4902; al-Tirmidhī 2511; Ibn Mājah 4211)

The pairing in this hadith — *baghy* and severing kinship — mirrors the verse: the third command (giving to kin) and the third prohibition (*baghy*) are the two things whose neglect God punishes soonest.

**The Structure: Al-Rāzī's Analysis of Three Faculties**

Al-Rāzī offers a structural reading of the verse that has been widely accepted. The human soul, in the classical psychology, has three faculties: the rational (*nāṭiqah*), the appetitive (*shahwāniyyah*), and the irascible (*ghaḍabiyyah*). Each has its virtue and its vice. The verse's three commands correspond to the three virtues and its three prohibitions to the three vices — or, on another arrangement, the three commands are ascending degrees of good and the three prohibitions are the three sources of evil: *faḥshāʾ* is the excess of the appetitive faculty, *munkar* is the corruption of the rational faculty (since *munkar* is what reason rejects), and *baghy* is the excess of the irascible faculty. The verse thus addresses the whole human being — every faculty, in its right use and its wrong use — and this comprehensiveness is why Ibn Masʿūd called it the most comprehensive verse.

Another reading of the structure, also given by al-Rāzī, sees the three commands as three degrees: justice (the obligatory minimum), *iḥsān* (the excellent maximum), and giving to kin (the most important specific instance). And the three prohibitions as three degrees of wrong: *faḥshāʾ* (the wrong against oneself and one's own dignity), *munkar* (the wrong against the law), and *baghy* (the wrong against others). Whichever structure one prefers, the verse covers the field.

**"He Admonishes You, That Haply You May Remember"**

The verse ends: *yaʿiẓukum laʿallakum tadhakkarūn*, "He admonishes you that perhaps you may remember." The verb *waʿaẓa*, to admonish, exhort, counsel, denotes speech that softens the heart and moves it toward good. The commentators note the word's gentleness: God does not merely legislate; He *admonishes* — He speaks to the heart as a counselor, not only to the will as a lawgiver.

And the purpose is *tadhakkur*, remembering. The verse's commands and prohibitions are not new information; they are what every sound nature already knows. Justice, kindness, care for family, and the avoidance of shamelessness, wrong, and aggression are recognized by every human conscience. The verse *reminds*. This is the meaning of the Qur'an's name *al-Dhikr*, the Reminder (v. 44): it calls the human being back to what he knew and forgot. Al-Rāzī notes that the appeal to memory is an appeal to the *fiṭrah* — the disposition toward good that verse 78 said the human being was born with, in potential, before knowledge covered or uncovered it.

**The Verse as a Constitution**

The tradition treated the verse as a summary of the whole law, and its use in the Friday sermon made it a kind of weekly constitution recited before the entire community. Its genius, as the commentators recognized, is its combination of generality and specificity: general enough to cover every act, specific enough to be applied. A person can measure any deed against it: does this deed give what is due (justice)? Does it go beyond duty in doing good (*iḥsān*)? Does it honor the bonds of family? Does it involve shamelessness, wrong, or aggression? The verse is a complete moral examination in one sentence.

**The Application**

The verse asks the believer to make its six terms the frame of his conduct. Positively: to be just in every dealing, especially with those he dislikes; to do good beyond what is owed, especially where no one requires it; to maintain his family bonds, especially the difficult ones. Negatively: to guard his appetites from *faḥshāʾ*, his actions from *munkar*, and his temper and ambition from *baghy*. And the verse's close reminds him that these are not foreign demands but his own nature recalled to itself. The person who lives by this verse has, in the judgment of Ibn Masʿūd and the community that recited it every Friday for fourteen centuries, lived by the whole Qur'an.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:91

> **And fulfill the pact of God when you have made a pact, and do not break oaths after having affirmed them, when you have made God a witness over you. Truly God knows whatsoever you do.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**From the General Ethic to a Specific Obligation**

Verse 90 gave the comprehensive ethic: justice, excellence, care for kin; no indecency, wrong, or aggression. Verse 91 begins a series of specific applications, and the first is the fulfillment of covenants. The commentators note the fittingness: the covenant is where justice is tested most directly, since breaking a pledge is a wrong against the one to whom it was made, and the bond of oath is the most explicit form of the trust on which all social order rests.

**"Fulfill the Pact of God": *ʿAhd Allāh***

The command is *wa-awfū bi-ʿahdi Allāhi idhā ʿāhadtum*, "and fulfill the covenant of God when you have covenanted." The word *ʿahd* denotes a pact, covenant, pledge, promise — a binding undertaking. It is called "the pact *of God*" (*ʿahd Allāh*), and the commentators explain the genitive in two ways, both true.

First, the pact of God is any pact made in His name, sworn by Him, or made with Him as witness — as the verse's next clause specifies. When a person swears by God to do something, the oath makes God a party to the pledge; to break it is to break faith with God. Al-Ṭabarī takes this as the primary sense.

Second, the pact of God is the covenant of faith itself — the pledge every believer makes to God to obey Him, and specifically the pledge the Companions made to the Prophet ﷺ at their conversion and at the oaths of allegiance (*bayʿah*). The commentators, including al-Qurṭubī and al-Rāzī, identify this verse with the *bayʿah* the believers gave the Prophet — the pledge to hear and obey, to defend him, to fight if called — and especially with the Pledge of Riḍwān at al-Ḥudaybiyah (48:10, 18), where the Companions swore under the tree. Some, including Mujāhid and Qatādah as reported by al-Ṭabarī, read the verse as revealed with reference to that pledge; others note that the sūrah is Makkan and the pledge is Madinan, and read the reference as general — every pledge of loyalty to God and His Messenger. Al-Ṭabarī's own view, after surveying the reports, is that the verse is general and includes every covenant a person makes with God's name upon it.

The Qur'an makes the covenant with God the mark of the believer:

> *"Those who fulfill the covenant of God and do not break the pact."* (Qur'an 13:20)

> *"And fulfill the covenant; truly the covenant will be questioned about."* (Qur'an 17:34)

> *"O you who believe, fulfill your contracts."* (Qur'an 5:1)

**"When You Have Made a Pact": The Condition**

The phrase *idhā ʿāhadtum*, "when you have covenanted," makes clear that the obligation arises from the act of covenanting. No one is compelled to make a pact; but once made, it binds. Al-Rāzī draws out the ethical principle: the freedom to make or not make a promise is the ground of the obligation to keep it. The one who promised did so freely and therefore owes what he promised. This is why the Qur'an treats promise-breaking so gravely: it is a betrayal of a bond one created oneself.

**"Do Not Break Oaths After Having Affirmed Them"**

The second command is *wa-lā tanquḍū al-aymāna baʿda tawkīdihā*, "and do not break oaths after their confirmation." The verb *naqaḍa* means to undo, to untie, to break — as one unravels a rope or demolishes a building; it is the verb the next verse will use for the woman who unravels her yarn. *Aymān* is the plural of *yamīn*, oath — literally "right hand," from the custom of clasping right hands when swearing. And *tawkīd* is confirmation, emphasis, binding: the oath made deliberately and solemnly, not the casual expression that slips from the tongue.

The commentators distinguish this from the *laghw*, the idle oath, which the Qur'an says God does not hold against a person (2:225; 5:89). The oath *baʿda tawkīdihā*, after its confirmation, is the deliberate oath — sworn with intention, perhaps repeated, perhaps witnessed. Breaking such an oath is *naqḍ*, a demolition of what one deliberately built. Al-Zamakhsharī notes the accumulation of terms: *ʿahd* (pact), *aymān* (oaths), *tawkīd* (confirmation) — the verse names every degree of solemnity to make clear that the more solemn the bond, the graver its breach.

The scholars addressed an apparent tension with the Prophet's teaching that one who swears to do something and then sees a better course should do the better thing and expiate the oath (al-Bukhārī 6622; Muslim 1652). They resolved it by distinguishing oaths concerning matters of choice — where breaking and expiating is permitted when the alternative is better — from oaths of covenant with others, which create rights in another party and may not be broken unilaterally. The verse addresses the second: pacts made with others and confirmed, in which God is made witness. Al-Qurṭubī notes that the verse's context — the following verses on breaking pacts for gain — confirms this reading.

**"When You Have Made God a Witness Over You": *Kafīlan***

The verse gives the reason the oath binds: *wa-qad jaʿaltumu Allāha ʿalaykum kafīlan*, "and you have made God a guarantor over you." The word *kafīl* means a surety, guarantor, one who stands behind an undertaking and answers for it. When a person swears by God, he makes God the guarantor of his oath — he invokes God as the one who will hold him to it. Al-Rāzī explains the logic: to break such an oath is to treat God's guarantee as worthless, to insult the One invoked. The oath-breaker has said, in effect, "God stands behind this," and then acted as though He did not.

The commentators note that this clause makes the offense theological, not merely social. Breaking a promise to a person wrongs the person; breaking an oath in which God was named as *kafīl* wrongs God. The Qur'an says of such people that they "have no share in the Hereafter":

> *"Truly those who exchange the covenant of God and their oaths for a small price — for them there is no share in the Hereafter, and God will not speak to them or look at them on the Day of Resurrection, nor will He purify them; and for them is a painful punishment."* (Qur'an 3:77)

The Prophet ﷺ listed the breaking of covenants among the marks of the hypocrite:

> *"The signs of the hypocrite are three: when he speaks he lies; when he promises he breaks it; and when he is entrusted he betrays."* (al-Bukhārī 33; Muslim 59)

And he taught that on the Day of Judgment, a banner would be raised for every betrayer, announcing his treachery (al-Bukhārī 3188; Muslim 1735).

**"Truly God Knows Whatsoever You Do"**

The verse ends: *inna Allāha yaʿlamu mā tafʿalūn*, "truly God knows what you do." The commentators note the function of the reminder. Oaths are often broken in secret — the promise made publicly and abandoned quietly, or kept in letter and broken in spirit. The verse forecloses the concealment. God, who was made *kafīl* over the oath, knows whether it was kept. The clause is both warning and consolation: warning to the one tempted to break faith unseen, and consolation to the one betrayed, whose betrayer is known.

**The Covenant and the Sūrah's Structure**

The verse begins a passage (vv. 91–96) on covenants and their breaking that the commentators connect to the Makkan context. The Makkans had made pacts with the Prophet — including the pact of the boycott's lifting, and the earlier tribal alliances — and there was pressure on the new Muslims, who had pledged themselves to Islam, to break their pledge under persecution or for gain. The verses address both: the believers are commanded to keep their covenant with God against every inducement, and the general principle of fidelity is established for all human dealings. The verse's placement after the "most comprehensive verse" (v. 90) signals that fidelity to covenant is among the first applications of justice.

**The Application: The Culture of the Kept Word**

The verse establishes fidelity to one's word as a religious obligation of the first rank. The believer's promise is a pact of God; his oath makes God his guarantor; and his breaking of either is a matter God knows and will judge. The practical discipline is twofold. First, caution in making pacts: the Prophet ﷺ warned against swearing lightly, and the Qur'an says, "Do not make God, by your oaths, an obstacle" (2:224). One should promise only what one intends to fulfill. Second, fidelity in keeping them: once given, the word binds, even when circumstances change and keeping it becomes costly. The Qur'an praises those who "fulfill their promise when they promise" (2:177), and it names the fulfillment of covenant among the marks of the righteous in the same verse that names prayer and charity. A society of kept promises is the social form of justice; the verse commands it, and the next verse will show, in a single vivid image, what its opposite looks like.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:92

> **And be not like her who unravels her yarn after it was firmly spun, [by] taking your oaths as a means of deceit between you, lest one community be more numerous than another. God only tries you thereby, and on the Day of Resurrection He will make clear to you that wherein you differed.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Image of the Unraveled Yarn**

Verse 91 commanded fidelity to oaths. Verse 92 gives a picture of infidelity: *wa-lā takūnū ka'llatī naqaḍat ghazlahā min baʿdi quwwatin ankāthan*, "and do not be like her who unraveled her yarn, after strength, into fragments." The verse's image is domestic and vivid — a woman who spins thread and then pulls it apart — and it has entered the moral vocabulary of the Muslim world as the emblem of futile self-destruction. The verse then names the specific vice the image warns against, gives its motive, and reveals its purpose in the divine plan.

**"Her Who Unravels Her Yarn"**

The verb is *naqaḍat*, the same root as verse 91's "do not break (*tanquḍū*) oaths." The verse thus picks up the previous verse's verb and gives it a body. *Ghazl* is spun yarn or thread; *quwwah*, "strength," here denotes the firmness of the spinning — the thread twisted tight; and *ankāth* is the plural of *nikth*, a strand undone, a fragment of unraveled thread. The picture is of a woman who has spent effort spinning wool into strong yarn and then undoes her work, pulling the thread apart into loose fibers again. The effort is wasted; the result is worse than if she had never begun, since the fibers, once spun and unspun, are tangled and weakened.

The commentators record a specific referent. Al-Kalbī, Muqātil, and others, as reported by al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Rāzī, and the Jalālayn, identify the woman as a Makkan known for foolishness — some name her Rayṭah bint Saʿd of the Banū Taym, others give different names — who would spin with her slave-girls all day and then, in the evening, command them to unravel everything they had spun. Whether the woman was a historical individual or a proverbial type, her behavior was known in Makkah as the image of futile labor. Al-Rāzī and al-Zamakhsharī note that the verse may refer to such a woman or may be a general parable; in either case the meaning is the same.

**The Point of the Comparison**

The one who makes a solemn oath and then breaks it is like this woman. He has built something — a bond of trust, confirmed by oath, with God as guarantor (v. 91) — and then he demolishes it. The commentators draw out the aptness. First, the breaking undoes real work: the oath-maker invested effort and solemnity in the pledge, and breaking it wastes that investment. Second, the result is worse than never having pledged: the broken oath leaves distrust where there was none, as the unspun yarn leaves tangle where there was clean wool. Third, the act is irrational: the woman gains nothing by unraveling, and the oath-breaker gains, at most, a fleeting advantage at the cost of his credibility and his standing with God. Al-Rāzī emphasizes the element of *foolishness*: the comparison is not to a wicked woman but to a foolish one, because breaking a confirmed oath is above all stupid — it destroys what one needs.

**"Taking Your Oaths as a Means of Deceit Between You": *Dakhalan***

The verse then names the specific vice: *tattakhidhūna aymānakum dakhalan baynakum*, "taking your oaths as *dakhal* among yourselves." The word *dakhal* denotes deceit, corruption, fraud — literally, something that enters (*dakhala*) where it does not belong, like a hidden flaw in a fabric or a secret motive in a transaction. Oaths used as *dakhal* are oaths sworn to deceive: the swearer takes the oath as a device to gain trust, intending to break it when convenient. The oath is a tool of fraud rather than a bond of truth.

Al-Ṭabarī explains: they swear to a treaty or alliance to reassure the other party, while inwardly planning treachery. The oath thus becomes the instrument of the very thing it was meant to prevent.

**"Lest One Community Be More Numerous Than Another": The Motive**

The verse gives the motive: *an takūna ummatun hiya arbā min ummah*, "that one community be more numerous than another." The word *arbā* is from the root *r-b-w*, to increase — the root of *ribā*, usury — and means more numerous, more abundant, greater. The commentators explain the reference. The Arabs made alliances by oath. When a tribe found that another tribe was stronger, more numerous, or more advantageous as an ally, it would break its existing oath and swear a new one to the stronger party. The oath was kept only as long as the ally was the more powerful; the moment a more numerous community appeared, the oath was unraveled. Al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī, and Mujāhid (as reported) describe this as the practice the verse condemns.

The commentators also apply this to the Muslim community. The believers had pledged themselves to Islam when it was small and weak; the Quraysh were "more numerous." The temptation was to break the pledge and return to the stronger side. The verse forbids this: the oath to God is not to be measured against the numbers of one's opponents. Al-Rāzī states the principle: the fidelity of an oath cannot depend on the strength of the party to whom it was made, because then it is not fidelity but calculation, and calculation is the *dakhal* the verse condemns.

**"God Only Tries You Thereby"**

The verse then discloses the divine purpose: *innamā yablūkumu Allāhu bihi*, "God only tests you by it." The pronoun "it" refers, according to the commentators, to the command to keep oaths — or to the situation of disparity between communities that makes breaking them tempting. Al-Zamakhsharī reads it: God tests you by the command to fulfill your covenants, to see who keeps faith when it is costly. Al-Rāzī reads it: God tests you by making one community more numerous than another, so that the temptation to defect exists and fidelity has meaning.

The concept of *ibtilāʾ*, testing, was discussed at verse 54. The verse here applies it to covenant: the covenant is a test, and the test is precisely whether one keeps it when breaking it would be advantageous. A covenant that costs nothing to keep tests nothing. The believers' pledge to God, made when Islam was weak and its enemies strong, was the sharpest form of the test, and the verse names it as such so that the believers would understand their situation: the disparity was not a reason to defect but the very condition of the trial.

**"On the Day of Resurrection He Will Make Clear to You That Wherein You Differed"**

The verse ends: *wa-la-yubayyinanna lakum yawma al-qiyāmati mā kuntum fīhi takhtalifūn*, "and He will surely make clear to you on the Day of Resurrection what you used to differ about." The phrase echoes verse 39 ("that He may make clear to them that in which they differ") and verse 64 ("that you may make clear to them that in which they differed"). The commentators note the thread: the Book clarifies differences now (v. 64); the Resurrection clarifies them finally (vv. 39, 92). The differences here are the differences between the faithful and the treacherous, the Muslims and their opponents, the community that kept its oath and the community that broke it. On that Day, it will be clear who was right.

Al-Rāzī draws out the consolation: the believer who kept his covenant at cost, and saw the oath-breakers prosper, is told that the account is not closed. The apparent success of the treacherous is not the verdict; the verdict comes on the Day of Resurrection, when what was hidden — the *dakhal*, the concealed treachery — is made plain and its consequences delivered.

**The Verse's Wider Application**

The verse's image has been applied in the tradition to every kind of self-undoing. The scholars applied it to the one who performs a good deed and then destroys it by boasting or by following it with sin (cf. 2:264, "do not nullify your charity by reminders of generosity and injury"); to the one who acquires knowledge and then abandons it; to the one who builds a relationship and then betrays it; to the one who fasts all day and breaks it with backbiting. In each case, the work is unraveled after strength. The image is a diagnosis of a specific human folly: the destruction of one's own achievement, not by an enemy, but by oneself.

**The Application: The Kept Covenant in an Age of Calculation**

The verse addresses a temptation that is permanent: to keep one's word only as long as it pays, and to defect when the other side appears stronger or the alternative more profitable. The verse names this as *dakhal*, fraud, and as the unraveling of one's own yarn. The believer is asked to keep faith irrespective of the numbers — to remain with the truth when it is the minority, to honor the pledge when the party pledged to is weak, to keep the promise when keeping it costs. The Prophet ﷺ modeled this at al-Ḥudaybiyah, where he honored the treaty even when its terms seemed to favor the Quraysh, and when a Muslim who had fled to him had to be returned under its provisions (al-Bukhārī 2731). His fidelity in weakness was the seed of the conquest that followed. The verse's promise is that the one who keeps the covenant will have it made clear on the Day of Resurrection that he was right; its warning is that the one who unravels it will stand among the fibers of his own undoing.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:93

> **Had God willed, He would have made you one community. But He leads astray whomsoever He will, and guides whomsoever He will. And you will surely be questioned about that which you used to do.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Question Behind the Difference**

Verse 92 ended by saying that God will clarify on the Day of Resurrection what people differed about. Verse 93 addresses the question that this raises: why is there difference at all? If God wanted people united in truth, why did He not make them so? The verse answers in three movements: God could have made all one community; He guides and misguides according to His will; and every person will be questioned for what he did. The verse thus holds together divine power, divine will, and human responsibility, and the commentators of every school have labored over how the three cohere.

**"Had God Willed, He Would Have Made You One Community"**

The verse begins *wa-law shāʾa Allāhu la-jaʿalakum ummatan wāḥidah*, "and if God had willed, He would have made you one community." The conditional *law* introduces a counterfactual: God did not so will. The statement affirms God's *power* — He could have made all humanity one in religion — and denies that He *chose* to do so by compulsion.

The Qur'an makes this statement repeatedly:

> *"And if your Lord had willed, He would have made mankind one community; but they will not cease to differ, except whom your Lord has given mercy. And for that He created them."* (Qur'an 11:118–119)

> *"And if God had willed, He would have made you one community, but [He intended] to test you in what He has given you. So race to good deeds."* (Qur'an 5:48)

> *"And if your Lord had willed, all who are on the earth would have believed together. Would you then compel the people until they become believers?"* (Qur'an 10:99)

The parallels supply what 16:93 leaves implicit. The "one community" would have been one *by compulsion* — all believing because forced to. God did not will this because it would have defeated the purpose of creation, which is *test* (5:48) — the free choice of belief or disbelief, for which reward and punishment are just. Al-Rāzī states the reasoning: if God had compelled faith, faith would have no merit, and the whole structure of moral responsibility would collapse. The difference among people is the condition of their freedom, and their freedom is the condition of their accountability.

The verse in Hūd (11:119) adds the striking phrase "and for that He created them" — *wa-li-dhālika khalaqahum*. The commentators debated whether "that" refers to the differing or to the mercy; the majority read it as the mercy, or as the test that includes both. In any case, the difference among human beings is not an accident God failed to prevent but a feature of the design.

**"But He Leads Astray Whomsoever He Will, and Guides Whomsoever He Will"**

The verse continues: *wa-lākin yuḍillu man yashāʾu wa-yahdī man yashāʾ*, "but He misguides whom He wills and guides whom He wills." This is one of the Qur'an's recurring formulas about guidance (14:4; 35:8; 74:31), and it was the center of the classical debate on free will and predestination. The commentators of al-Naḥl take positions along the spectrum, and their positions were sketched at verses 9, 36, and 37.

The Ashʿarī reading, represented by al-Rāzī, takes the verse at its plain sense: guidance and misguidance are God's acts, decreed by His will, and the human being's choice is *created* by God even as it is genuinely the human's own (the doctrine of *kasb*, acquisition). God guides whom He wills to guide and misguides whom He wills to misguide; and He wills according to His wisdom, which is not subject to human evaluation.

The Muʿtazilī reading, represented by al-Zamakhsharī, interprets "misguides" as God's *naming* or *judging* a person misguided, or *abandoning* him to his choice, or *withholding* the additional grace He gives the believer; and "guides" as God's giving success (*tawfīq*) to the one who chooses faith. On this reading, God's will does not determine the initial choice; it responds to it.

The Shiite reading, represented by al-Ṭūsī and al-Ṭabrisī, is close to the Muʿtazilī: God guides all in the sense of showing the way (v. 9); He "misguides" only those who have already chosen misguidance, by leaving them in it; the verse's "whom He wills" refers to those whom His wisdom determines deserve each outcome.

The Salafī reading, represented by Ibn Taymiyyah and Ibn Kathīr, affirms both truths without resolving them into a single system: God's will is universal and nothing occurs outside it; the human being genuinely chooses and is justly held responsible; God's guidance and misguidance follow His knowledge of what each person deserves, so that He guides those who seek guidance and abandons those who turn away (61:5, "when they deviated, God caused their hearts to deviate"). The two truths are held together, and the "how" is left to God.

What all the readings share is the verse's final clause, which none can evade.

**"And You Will Surely Be Questioned About That Which You Used to Do"**

The verse ends: *wa-la-tusʾalunna ʿammā kuntum taʿmalūn*, "and you will most certainly be questioned about what you used to do." The emphatic *la-* and the heavy *nūn* give the statement the force of an oath. Whatever the relationship between God's will and human action, the human being *will be questioned* — and the object of the questioning is *what you used to do*: your actions, your choices, your conduct.

The commentators of all schools read this clause as the decisive limit on any fatalistic reading of the verse's middle. Al-Rāzī, despite his Ashʿarī commitments, insists that the clause establishes responsibility: the questioning would be unjust if the actions were not genuinely the person's own, and God is just. Al-Zamakhsharī reads it as confirming his interpretation: the questioning proves that the actions were free. Ibn Kathīr reads it as the practical conclusion: whatever the metaphysics, act as one who will be questioned. The verse's structure — God's will in the middle, human accountability at the end — teaches the believer how to hold the two: acknowledge God's absolute will *and* live as one who will answer for his deeds. The Prophet ﷺ gave the same instruction when asked whether, since everything is decreed, people should not simply rely on the decree:

> *"Work, for everyone is eased toward that for which he was created."* Then he recited: *"As for one who gives and fears God and believes in the best, We will ease him toward ease..."* (al-Bukhārī 4949; Muslim 2647)

"Work" — the answer to the question of decree is action. The decree is God's business; the work is the servant's.

**The Verse's Function in Its Context**

The commentators connect verse 93 to the preceding verses on covenants. Verse 92 warned against breaking oaths "lest one community be more numerous than another." Verse 93 explains why communities differ in number and belief at all: God did not will a single compelled community; the differences are the field of the test. The believer who is tempted to defect to the more numerous community is told that numbers are not the measure — God's will has distributed people among communities for a purpose, and the questioning will be about what each person *did* within that distribution, not about which community was larger.

The verse also answers, in advance, the deterministic excuse the sūrah refuted in verse 35: "If God had willed, we would not have worshipped anything besides Him." The idolaters used God's will as an excuse for inaction. Verse 93 affirms God's will *and* attaches the questioning to human deeds — which is exactly the combination that removes the excuse. Yes, God willed; and yes, you will be questioned. The first does not cancel the second.

**The Wisdom of Difference**

The commentators, especially al-Rāzī, reflected on why God willed a world of difference rather than uniformity. Several reasons emerge from the Qur'an's own statements. Difference is the condition of test (5:48). Difference makes possible the virtues that uniformity would make unnecessary — patience under opposition, steadfastness in minority, the invitation to others, the practice of justice toward those who differ (5:8). Difference displays the full range of God's names — His mercy to those who turn to Him, His justice to those who refuse. And difference reveals the truth by contrast: the light is known by the darkness beside it. None of this makes misguidance good; it makes the *possibility* of misguidance the necessary background of freely chosen guidance.

**The Application: Acting Under the Decree**

The verse asks the believer to hold two things in his mind without letting either cancel the other. The first: God's will governs all, including who is guided and who is not, and the believer's own faith is a gift for which he should be grateful, not proud (49:17). The second: he will be questioned about his deeds, and the questioning presupposes that the deeds were his. The practical result is a disposition the tradition called the union of *tawakkul* and *ʿamal* — reliance and action. The believer relies on God's will for the outcome and works as though the outcome depended on him. He does not use the decree as an excuse for sin (as the idolaters did in v. 35), nor does he imagine that his guidance is his own achievement. He asks God for guidance every day in the Fātiḥah ("guide us to the straight path"), knowing that guidance is God's to give — and he walks the path, knowing that the walking is his to do and will be asked about.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:94

> **And take not your oaths as a means of deceit among you, lest a foot slip after it was firmly planted, and you taste evil for having turned [others] from the way of God, and there be a great punishment for you.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Warning Repeated, With Its Consequences Named**

Verse 92 forbade taking oaths as a means of deceit (*dakhal*) and gave the image of the unraveled yarn. Verse 94 repeats the prohibition in the same words — *wa-lā tattakhidhū aymānakum dakhalan baynakum* — and then names three consequences that verse 92 did not: the slipping of a foot, the tasting of evil, and a great punishment. The commentators explain the repetition. Verse 92 addressed the folly of oath-breaking (it is like unraveling one's own work); verse 94 addresses its harm — to oneself, to others, and in the Hereafter. The first verse appealed to reason; the second appeals to fear.

**"Lest a Foot Slip After It Was Firmly Planted"**

The first consequence is *fa-tazilla qadamun baʿda thubūtihā*, "lest a foot slip after its firmness." The image is of a person standing securely — on a path, a ledge, a foothold — whose foot suddenly slides from under him. *Zalla* is to slip, to slide; *thubūt* is firmness, stability, being planted. The foot was firm; then it slipped.

The commentators explain the image's application. The foot that was firm is the person established in faith, in the covenant, in Islam. Al-Ṭabarī explains: the one who breaks his oath after being firm in it slips from the path of guidance as a foot slips from a firm place. Al-Rāzī elaborates: the breaking of one covenant is rarely isolated; it is the first slip that leads to a fall. The person who breaks faith once has loosened the ground beneath him, and the next breach comes more easily, until he has slid entirely from where he stood. The Arabic idiom "his foot slipped" (*zallat qadamuhu*) denotes a fall from a position of security into error or disgrace.

The verse's use of the singular *qadam*, "a foot," rather than the plural has been noted. Al-Zamakhsharī explains the indefinite singular as conveying the gravity of even a single slip — "lest even one foot slip" — and as intensifying the warning: the slipping of a single foot is enough to bring the whole person down. Others read the singular as generic, standing for any foot, any person.

The image had a specific application in the Makkan context that the commentators draw out. The new Muslims had planted their feet in Islam. If they broke their pledge — returning to idolatry under pressure or for advantage — their feet would slip from the firmness they had attained, and they would fall back into what they had escaped. The verse warns them that the ground they stand on is secure only as long as they keep the covenant that placed them on it.

**"And You Taste Evil for Having Turned Others From the Way of God"**

The second consequence is *wa-tadhūqū al-sūʾa bimā ṣadadtum ʿan sabīli Allāh*, "and you taste evil because you turned [others] away from the way of God." The verse introduces a dimension that verse 92 did not mention: the effect of oath-breaking on *others*.

The commentators explain the connection between breaking oaths and turning others from God's way. When a Muslim breaks his covenant — especially a covenant with God or a pledge made in His name — the disbelievers observe it and conclude that Islam does not produce fidelity. They say: "These people swear and then break their word; their religion is worthless." The oath-breaker thus becomes a cause of others' turning away from Islam. Al-Rāzī states it: the one who breaks his oath after entering Islam becomes a proof, in the eyes of the disbelievers, against the religion, and turns them from it by his example. Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Qurṭubī give the same reading: the *ṣadd*, obstruction, of verse 94 is the obstruction caused by bad example.

This reading connects the verse to verse 88, which prescribed "punishment upon punishment" for those who "disbelieve and turn others from the way of God." Verse 94 shows that a believer, too, can be guilty of *ṣadd* — not by forbidding Islam but by discrediting it through his conduct. The commentators regarded this as one of the gravest dangers of the Muslim's public behavior: his infidelity, dishonesty, or injustice is charged not only to him but to the religion he represents, and the obstruction that results is on his account.

The word "taste" (*tadhūqū*) is the Qur'an's standard verb for experiencing punishment, and *al-sūʾ*, "the evil," is what they will taste. The commentators identify it as the evil consequences in this world — loss of trust, the collapse of the community's credibility, the punishment God may send — and, together with the next clause, in the Hereafter.

**"And There Be a Great Punishment for You"**

The third consequence is *wa-lakum ʿadhābun ʿaẓīm*, "and for you is a great punishment."
