This is the punishment of the Hereafter, and it is called *ʿaẓīm*, great, because the sin is compound: the breaking of a covenant with God as guarantor (v. 91), the folly of self-destruction (v. 92), the slipping from faith, and the obstruction of others. Each element adds to the weight. Al-Rāzī notes that the verse escalates through its three consequences — the slip (personal), the taste of evil (social), the great punishment (eternal) — so that the oath-breaker sees the full range of what he has done.

**The Three Consequences as a Sequence**

The commentators read the three consequences as stages of a single decline. First, the personal: the foot slips; the oath-breaker's own faith and standing are damaged. Second, the social: others are turned from God's way; the damage spreads to the community and to those outside it who might have entered. Third, the eternal: the great punishment; the damage is finalized in the Hereafter. The sequence teaches that no breach of faith is private. It begins in the individual, spreads to the community, and ends before God.

**The Verse and the Believer's Representative Role**

The verse introduces, in the phrase "turned others from the way of God," a theme that the tradition developed at length: the Muslim as representative of Islam before those who do not know it. The Qur'an says the community was made "a middle nation, that you may be witnesses over mankind" (2:143); the believer's conduct is the witness. The Prophet ﷺ was acutely aware of this. He refused to execute known hypocrites lest people say, "Muḥammad kills his companions" (al-Bukhārī 4905; Muslim 2584); he honored the treaty of al-Ḥudaybiyah at cost so that the Arabs would see that Muslims keep their word; he told his emissaries to make things easy and not to repel people (al-Bukhārī 69; Muslim 1734). The verse's warning is the negative form of this awareness: the Muslim who breaks faith turns people from God, and is answerable for it.

The Qur'an makes the same point about the People of the Book, whose bad conduct led others to blaspheme the name of God (as the Prophet cited in the context of the Jews' treatment of the covenant), and it warns the Muslims not to repeat their example. The believer's oath is not his private affair; it is the religion's reputation in his hands.

**The Application: Fidelity as Witness**

The verse asks the believer to see his promises as public testimony to his faith. When he keeps his word, especially at cost, he confirms the religion to those who watch; when he breaks it, he discredits it, and the discrediting is on his account. The practical disciplines follow: to make no oath one does not intend to keep; to keep every oath made, even when circumstances change; and to remember, when tempted to break faith for advantage, that the advantage is purchased with three currencies — one's own footing, others' access to God, and one's standing in the Hereafter. The Prophet ﷺ said:

> *"Every betrayer will have a banner on the Day of Resurrection, by which he will be known."* (al-Bukhārī 3188; Muslim 1735)

The banner is the public form of the private betrayal. The verse's warning is that the betrayal was never private — it turned feet from the path while the betrayer's own foot was slipping — and the banner on that Day will only announce what the betrayal already was.

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:95

> **And sell not the pact of God for a paltry price. Truly that which is with God is better for you, if you but knew.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Motive Behind the Broken Oath**

Verses 91–94 commanded fidelity to covenant and warned against breaking oaths. Verse 95 goes to the motive that most often drives the breach: gain. *Wa-lā tashtarū bi-ʿahdi Allāhi thamanan qalīlan*, "and do not purchase with the covenant of God a small price." The oath-breaker breaks faith because something is offered — money, position, safety, advantage — and he takes it. The verse names the transaction for what it is: a sale, in which the covenant of God is the thing given up and a paltry price is what is received.

**"Sell Not the Pact of God": The Language of Commerce**

The verb *ishtarā* means to buy, and in this idiom — *ishtarā bi-kadhā thamanan* — it means to exchange one thing for another, to give up the first for the second. The Qur'an uses this commercial language repeatedly for spiritual transactions: the hypocrites "purchased error with guidance" (2:16); the People of the Book "sell the signs of God for a small price" (3:199; 5:44); those who "exchange the covenant of God and their oaths for a small price" have no share in the Hereafter (3:77). The idiom treats the covenant as a possession of value and its breaking as a sale.

The commentators explain the aptness of the metaphor. The oath-breaker imagines he is *gaining* — he receives the bribe, the advantage, the escape. The verse corrects the accounting: he is *selling*. He gave up the covenant of God, and what he received in exchange is the price. The question the verse then poses is whether the price was worth it. Al-Rāzī notes that the metaphor exposes the breach as a *choice* with two sides: the oath-breaker did not merely fail to keep his word; he actively traded it for something else, and he is accountable for the trade.

**"A Paltry Price": *Thamanan Qalīlan***

The price is *qalīl*, small, paltry, little. The commentators note that the adjective is not relative but absolute: *whatever* is received for the covenant of God is a small price, because nothing in this world is commensurate with the covenant. Al-Zamakhsharī states it: even if the oath-breaker received the whole world, it would be a small price, because the world is small beside what he gave up. The Qur'an makes the same point about the world in general: "Say: The enjoyment of this world is little" (4:77); "The life of this world is nothing but the enjoyment of delusion" (3:185).

The commentators record the circumstance that gave the verse its first application. Al-Qurṭubī and al-Ṭabarī report that the verse addressed the Muslims of Makkah who were offered inducements by the Quraysh to abandon Islam — wealth, protection, restoration to their tribes — and were tempted. The verse told them that whatever the Quraysh offered was a paltry price for the covenant with God. The same situation recurs in every age: the believer is offered something to compromise his faith, and the verse names the offer as *qalīl*.

Ibn Kathīr and others also note the verse's application to those who sell false oaths in commerce — swearing falsely to sell goods — which the Prophet ﷺ condemned:

> *"Three God will not speak to on the Day of Resurrection, nor look at, nor purify, and theirs is a painful punishment: ... a man who swears a false oath after the afternoon prayer in order to take a Muslim's property."* (al-Bukhārī 2369; Muslim 108)

> *"Swearing sells the goods but erases the blessing."* (al-Bukhārī 2087; Muslim 1606)

The merchant who swears falsely to make a sale has sold the covenant of God for the price of the goods — a paltry price indeed.

**"Truly That Which Is With God Is Better for You"**

The verse's second half gives the reason: *innamā ʿinda Allāhi huwa khayrun lakum*, "truly what is with God — that is better for you." The construction is emphatic: *innamā* restricts, *huwa* points, and the sentence asserts that what God has in store for the faithful is better than any price offered for infidelity. The commentators identify "what is with God" as the reward of the Hereafter — Paradise, His pleasure, the permanence of what He gives — and also as His provision in this world for those who trust Him.

The comparison is the heart of the verse. The oath-breaker sold the covenant because he thought the price was better than keeping it. The verse says: what is with God is better. The next verse (96) will explain why — because what is with you perishes and what is with God remains. Verse 95 states the conclusion; verse 96 gives the proof.

The phrase *khayrun lakum*, "better for you," addresses the oath-breaker's self-interest directly. The verse does not say only that keeping the covenant is *right*; it says it is *better for you* — more advantageous, on any honest calculation. The commentators note that the Qur'an frequently argues in this way, appealing not only to duty but to true self-interest, because the person who breaks faith for gain believes he is serving himself, and the most direct refutation is to show that he is not. Al-Rāzī: the verse meets the oath-breaker on his own ground, the ground of profit, and shows him that he has made a bad bargain.

**"If You But Knew": *In Kuntum Taʿlamūn***

The verse ends with the conditional *in kuntum taʿlamūn*, "if you knew." The condition implies that those who sell the covenant do *not* know — do not know the value of what they sell, the smallness of what they receive, or the greatness of what is with God. Their transaction is a product of ignorance. Al-Zamakhsharī notes that the phrase is not a doubt about their knowledge but a rebuke: if you had knowledge, you would not do this; the fact that you do shows that you lack it.

The clause connects to the sūrah's pervasive theme of knowledge and its absence (vv. 38, 41, 55, 74, 75, 101). The idolaters "do not know"; the believers who are tempted to break faith are told "if you knew." The knowledge in question is not information — everyone knows that God promises reward — but the *realized* knowledge that makes the promise weigh more than the bribe. The commentators call this *yaqīn*, certainty, and distinguish it from mere belief: the one who is certain that what is with God is better cannot be bought, because no price competes with what he sees.

**The Verse in the Sequence on Covenant**

Verses 91–96 form a unit on covenant, and verse 95 is its motivational core. Verse 91 commanded fidelity. Verse 92 showed the folly of breach. Verse 93 explained the difference among communities as test. Verse 94 named the consequences of breach. Verse 95 addresses the reason people breach — gain — and undercuts it. Verse 96 will complete the argument with the contrast between the perishing and the abiding. The sequence moves from command to persuasion to proof, and the commentators note that this is the Qur'an's usual method: it does not merely legislate but brings the hearer to see why the legislation is wise.

**The Application: The Price of One's Word**

The verse asks the believer to consider what he would accept in exchange for his covenant with God — and to recognize that any answer other than "nothing" is a bad bargain. In practice, the verse addresses every situation in which faith, honesty, or fidelity is exchanged for advantage: the lie that secures a promotion; the compromise of principle that avoids conflict; the false oath that wins a case; the abandonment of religious duty that brings social acceptance. In each case, something is received and the covenant of God is given up, and the verse names the receipt *qalīl*. The believer's defense is the knowledge the verse names: the realized certainty that what is with God is better. The Prophet ﷺ described the believer's ideal state:

> *"He who has tasted the sweetness of faith is pleased with God as Lord, Islam as religion, and Muḥammad as Messenger."* (Muslim 34)

The one who has tasted this sweetness has no interest in selling it. He knows its value, and he knows, as the next verse says, that what is with God remains.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:96

> **That which is with you comes to an end, but that which is with God remains. And We shall surely render unto those who were patient their reward according to the best of that which they used to do.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Proof of the Better Bargain**

Verse 95 asserted that "what is with God is better for you." Verse 96 gives the reason, and it is a reason of the simplest kind: *mā ʿindakum yanfadu wa-mā ʿinda Allāhi bāq*, "what is with you runs out, and what is with God remains." The paltry price for which the covenant might be sold is perishable; the reward for keeping it is permanent. No further argument is needed. A perishable thing cannot be worth more than a permanent one, and the person who trades the permanent for the perishable has, by definition, lost.

**"That Which Is With You Comes to an End": *Yanfadu***

The verb *nafida* means to run out, to be exhausted, to be depleted — as provisions run out on a journey or water in a well. Everything "with you" — wealth, position, pleasure, the enjoyments of this life — *yanfadu*: it is consumed, spent, exhausted. The commentators note the precision of the verb: it does not say what is with you is *destroyed* (which might suggest a sudden loss) but that it *runs out* — it is finite, and finitude means it will be used up. Even if nothing takes it from you, it will end, because it was always limited.

The Qur'an develops the point in several images:

> *"Wealth and children are the adornment of the life of this world; but the enduring good deeds are better with your Lord for reward and better for hope."* (Qur'an 18:46)

> *"The likeness of this worldly life is like rain We sent down from the sky, and the plants of the earth mingled with it... until the earth had taken on its adornment and was beautified, and its people supposed they had power over it — Our command came upon it by night or by day, and We made it as a harvest, as if it had not flourished yesterday."* (Qur'an 10:24)

The word *bāqiyāt*, "enduring," in 18:46 is the same root as *bāq*, "remains," in 16:96. The Qur'an sets the two categories against each other consistently: the perishable adornment and the enduring deeds.

**"But That Which Is With God Remains": *Bāq***

The word *bāq* is the active participle of *baqiya*, to remain, to endure, to last. What is with God — His reward, His pleasure, Paradise — does not run out. It is *bāq*, remaining. The Qur'an describes Paradise's provision in exactly these terms: "its fruit is lasting and its shade" (13:35); "a gift never cut off" (11:108); "provision that has no end" (38:54).

The commentators draw out the asymmetry. What is with you is *yanfadu*, a verb — in process of running out, even now. What is with God is *bāq*, a participle — a settled state, permanence as a fixed quality. The grammar mirrors the reality: the worldly is always slipping; the divine is always there.

Al-Rāzī states the resulting argument in full. Any rational person, offered a choice between a good that will end and a good that will not, chooses the second, provided the two are otherwise comparable. And the two are not merely comparable: what is with God is greater in kind as well as duration. The oath-breaker who sells the covenant for a worldly price has therefore made the worst possible bargain: he has given the greater and permanent for the lesser and perishable. Verse 95 called the price "paltry"; verse 96 shows that even that undervalues it, since the paltry thing will also vanish.

**"We Shall Surely Render Unto Those Who Were Patient Their Reward"**

The verse then turns to the reward: *wa-la-najziyanna alladhīna ṣabarū ajrahum*, "and We will surely recompense those who were patient with their reward." The emphatic *la-najziyanna* — "We will *most certainly* recompense" — gives the promise the force of an oath.

The recipients are *alladhīna ṣabarū*, "those who were patient." The commentators explain why patience is named here. Keeping the covenant of God against the inducements of the world requires *ṣabr* — the patience to forgo the paltry price, to endure the hardship that fidelity may bring, to wait for the reward that is with God rather than seize the one that is with you. Al-Rāzī: the one who refrains from selling the covenant must be patient in two respects — patient in bearing the loss of what he could have gained, and patient in the persecution or difficulty that fidelity may cost. The Makkan Muslims who refused the Quraysh's offers were patient in both senses; the verse promises them their reward.

Patience was discussed at verse 42 as the first quality of the emigrants. Here it is the quality of those who keep faith under temptation. The two contexts are related: the emigrants were patient in leaving; the covenant-keepers are patient in staying faithful. Both trade the perishable for the permanent, and both are promised what is with God.

**"According to the Best of That Which They Used to Do": *Bi-aḥsani mā kānū yaʿmalūn***

The verse's final phrase has been the subject of careful discussion: the reward is given *bi-aḥsani mā kānū yaʿmalūn*, "according to the best of what they used to do." Two readings are recorded, and the commentators generally accept both.

The first reading: God rewards them for their deeds as though all their deeds were of the quality of their *best* deed. The believer's deeds vary — some excellent, some adequate, some flawed. God, in His generosity, takes the best as the standard and rewards all at that rate. Al-Rāzī and al-Zamakhsharī develop this reading: it is an expression of divine bounty (*faḍl*), by which God elevates the reward of the lesser deeds to the level of the greater. The Qur'an confirms this generosity elsewhere: "Whoever brings a good deed will have ten times its like" (6:160); "God will remove from them the worst of what they did and reward them according to the best of what they used to do" (39:35).

The second reading: the reward is given for their *good* deeds — *aḥsan* here meaning "the good," in the sense that only good deeds are rewarded, while permitted acts that are neither good nor bad (the *mubāḥ*) receive no reward and evil deeds receive punishment. On this reading the verse says: the patient will be rewarded for the good they did. Al-Ṭabarī allows this reading.

The verse in al-Zumar (39:35), which uses the identical phrase and pairs it with "remove from them the worst of what they did," supports the first reading and adds a further dimension: not only are the deeds rewarded at the rate of the best, but the worst are removed. The full picture of divine generosity toward the patient is that their failures are erased and their successes are magnified.

**The Verse as the Climax of the Passage on Covenant**

Verses 91–96 move from command to consequence to persuasion to proof, and verse 96 is the proof's conclusion. It gives the believer the two-sided calculation the whole passage has been building: on one side, the price of breaking faith — paltry (v. 95) and perishable (v. 96a); on the other, the reward of keeping it — with God (v. 95), permanent (v. 96b), and calculated at the best rate (v. 96c). No honest accounting could prefer the first. The commentators note that the Qur'an's method here is to make fidelity not merely a duty but the obvious choice of a rational person, so that the oath-breaker cannot claim even self-interest as his excuse.

**The Broader Application: The Perishable and the Permanent**

The verse's first sentence — "what is with you runs out; what is with God remains" — has been treated in the tradition as a principle governing far more than oaths. It is the principle by which the believer evaluates every choice between the world and the Hereafter. The scholars of the inner life made it the foundation of *zuhd*, detachment: not the rejection of the world, but the refusal to prefer the perishable to the permanent. The Prophet ﷺ taught the principle in a single exchange:

> *ʿĀʾishah reported that they slaughtered a sheep and gave most of it away. The Prophet ﷺ asked what remained, and she said: "Nothing remains of it but its shoulder." He said: "All of it remains except its shoulder."* (al-Tirmidhī 2470)

What was given away "remains" — it is with God; what was kept "runs out" — it is with them. The hadith is verse 96 in a household scene, and it shows how the verse reorders ordinary perception: the kept portion, which seems to remain, is what will run out; the given portion, which seems gone, is what remains.

**The Application: Choosing the Remaining**

The verse asks the believer to make his choices by the measure of duration. When faced with a trade between what is with him and what is with God — between keeping faith and gaining advantage, between spending on the permanent and hoarding the perishable, between patience now and reward later — he asks which side *remains*. The answer is always the same, and the verse states it as a fact, not a hope: what is with God remains. The patient who act on this fact are promised their reward at the best rate. The verse is the Qur'an's final word to the tempted oath-breaker, and to everyone tempted to sell the permanent: look at what you would receive, and watch it run out.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:97

> **Whosoever works righteousness, whether male or female, and is a believer, We shall give them new life, a good life, and We shall surely render unto them their reward according to the best of that which they used to do.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Promise That Covers Both Worlds**

Verse 96 promised the patient their reward "according to the best of what they used to do." Verse 97 widens the promise to every believer who does good, states explicitly that it includes women as well as men, and adds a promise that concerns this world, not only the next: *fa-la-nuḥyiyannahu ḥayātan ṭayyibah*, "We shall surely give him a good life." The verse is among the most cited in the Qur'an, because it states in a single sentence the conditions of divine reward, the equality of the sexes before that reward, and the assurance that faith bears fruit here as well as hereafter.

**"Whosoever Works Righteousness": The First Condition**

The verse begins *man ʿamila ṣāliḥan*, "whoever does a righteous deed." The word *ṣāliḥ*, from the root *ṣ-l-ḥ*, denotes what is sound, right, fitting, good — the opposite of *fāsid*, corrupt. A righteous deed is one that is good in itself and performed in accordance with what God has prescribed. The commentators note the indefinite *ṣāliḥan*, "a righteous deed" — any good deed, however small; the verse does not require a lifetime of great works but the doing of good as such. The Qur'an's phrase for the righteous is *alladhīna āmanū wa-ʿamilū al-ṣāliḥāt*, "those who believe and do righteous deeds," which occurs more than fifty times; verse 97 states the same pairing in conditional form.

**"Whether Male or Female": The Explicit Inclusion of Women**

The verse then adds *min dhakarin aw unthā*, "whether male or female." The commentators explain why this is stated. The Arabic *man*, "whoever," is grammatically masculine but semantically general, and in ordinary usage it includes women. The verse nonetheless makes the inclusion explicit, and the explicitness is the point. Al-Rāzī states it: the verse removes any possibility of supposing that the promise is for men alone. In a society that had, a few verses earlier, been condemned for burying its daughters (vv. 58–59), the explicit statement that women's righteous deeds earn the same reward as men's was a declaration of a new order.

The Qur'an makes this declaration in several places, and the parallels show that it is a settled principle:

> *"And their Lord responded to them: Never will I allow to be lost the work of any worker among you, whether male or female; you are of one another."* (Qur'an 3:195)

> *"And whoever does righteous deeds, whether male or female, while being a believer — those will enter Paradise and will not be wronged even as much as the speck on a date seed."* (Qur'an 4:124)

> *"Truly the Muslim men and Muslim women, the believing men and believing women, the obedient men and obedient women, the truthful men and truthful women, the patient men and patient women, the humble men and humble women, the charitable men and charitable women, the fasting men and fasting women, the men who guard their private parts and the women who do so, and the men who remember God often and the women who do so — for them God has prepared forgiveness and a great reward."* (Qur'an 33:35)

The verse in al-Aḥzāb (33:35) was revealed, according to the reports, when Umm Salamah asked the Prophet ﷺ why the Qur'an addressed men and not women — and the answer was a verse that names women ten times alongside men. Verse 97 of al-Naḥl belongs to this body of teaching. Al-Qurṭubī notes that in the matter of reward, there is no distinction whatsoever between the sexes: the woman's prayer, fasting, charity, patience, and every good deed weigh exactly as the man's do.

**"And Is a Believer": The Second Condition**

The verse then states the second condition: *wa-huwa muʾmin*, "while he is a believer." Righteous deeds earn the promised reward only when joined to faith. The commentators explain why. Faith is the root, and deeds are the fruit; a deed without faith is a fruit without a tree — it may look like the real thing but it has no source and no life. The Qur'an states that the deeds of those without faith are "like ashes on which the wind blows hard on a stormy day" (14:18) and "like a mirage in a desert" (24:39). The good that a disbeliever does may be rewarded in this world — the Prophet ﷺ said that God does not wrong the believer of a good deed, rewarding him for it in this world and the next, while the disbeliever is fed for his good deeds in this world so that when he reaches the Hereafter he has no good deed left for which to be rewarded (Muslim 2808) — but the "good life" and the reward "according to the best" that this verse promises are for the believer.

The commentators also note that faith is what makes the deed *ṣāliḥ* in the full sense. A deed is righteous not only by its outward form but by its intention, and the intention that makes a deed acceptable to God is the intention to please Him — which presupposes faith in Him. Al-Rāzī: the condition of faith is not an arbitrary addition but the specification of what makes a deed righteous at all.

**"We Shall Give Them a Good Life": *Ḥayātan Ṭayyibah***

The verse's central promise is *fa-la-nuḥyiyannahu ḥayātan ṭayyibah*, "We will surely cause him to live a good life." The verb *nuḥyiyannahu* is emphatic — "We will *most certainly* give him life" — and the life is qualified as *ṭayyibah*, good, pure, pleasant, wholesome.

The commentators discussed what this good life is and when it is lived, and the discussion is one of the richest in the exegesis of the sūrah.

The majority hold that the good life is in *this world*, since the verse goes on to promise the reward of the Hereafter separately ("and We shall surely render unto them their reward"). If the good life were the Hereafter, the second promise would be redundant. So the verse promises two things: a good life here and a reward there. On this reading, the commentators identified the content of the good life:

Ibn ʿAbbās, according to al-Ṭabarī, said it is *lawful provision* (*rizq ḥalāl*) — the believer is given sustenance that is pure in its source. Others among the early authorities said it is *contentment* (*qanāʿah*) — the believer is given a heart that is satisfied with what it has, which is the true wealth. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said it is lawful provision and worship in this life. ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib is reported to have said it is contentment. Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and others said the good life is not possible in its fullness except in Paradise, and read the verse as referring to the Hereafter.

Al-Rāzī gathers these into a single account. The good life of the believer in this world consists in the inner states that faith produces: contentment, which frees him from the anxiety of want; trust in God, which frees him from the anxiety of the future; the knowledge that his affairs are in the hands of a wise and merciful Lord, which frees him from despair; the joy of worship and remembrance; and the certainty of the reward to come, which makes every hardship bearable. The disbeliever, however rich, lacks these; his life, however comfortable outwardly, is troubled by fear of loss, by the emptiness of pleasure, and by the absence of meaning. The believer's life is *ṭayyibah* not because it is free of hardship but because hardship itself is transformed for him — as the Prophet ﷺ said, "All of the believer's affairs are good" (Muslim 2999). Al-Rāzī notes that this reading fits the verse's placement after verse 96: the perishable goods of this world "run out," but the good life of the believer, being an inner state grounded in what "remains," does not.

The Shiite commentators record a saying from Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq that the good life is *contentment* (*al-qunūʿ*), and al-Ṭabrisī favors this reading — a life that is good because the heart is at rest.

The Prophet ﷺ described this life:

> *"He has succeeded who has embraced Islam, been provided with sufficiency, and been made content by God with what He has given him."* (Muslim 1054)

> *"Richness is not the abundance of goods; richness is the richness of the soul."* (al-Bukhārī 6446; Muslim 1051)

The "richness of the soul" is the *ḥayāt ṭayyibah*. It is available to the poor believer and unavailable to the rich disbeliever, because it depends on faith and not on possessions.

The minority reading — that the good life is the life of the grave or the life of Paradise — is recorded by al-Qurṭubī and others and is not excluded: the believer's good life begins in this world and continues, in intensified form, in the *barzakh* and in Paradise. The verse's promise covers the whole span.

**The Renewal of Life: *Nuḥyiyannahu***

The commentators noticed that the verse says God will *give life* (*nuḥyī*), not merely "grant a good life." The verb suggests that faith and righteous action produce a kind of new life — a life different in quality from the biological life the believer already had. Al-Rāzī connects this to the Qur'an's description of the disbeliever as dead and the believer as alive: "Is one who was dead and We gave him life and made for him a light by which to walk among the people like one who is in darkness, never to emerge from it?" (6:122). The believer is *made alive* by faith; his righteous action is the activity of that new life; and the *ḥayāt ṭayyibah* is what that life feels like from within.

**"According to the Best of That Which They Used to Do"**

The verse ends with the same phrase as verse 96 — reward "according to the best of what they used to do" — and the commentators read it as before: God rewards the believers' deeds at the rate of their best deed, out of generosity, and removes from them the worst (39:35). The repetition of the phrase in consecutive verses is deliberate: verse 96 promised it to the patient covenant-keepers; verse 97 extends it to every believing doer of good, male or female.

**The Structure of the Verse: Conditions and Promises**

The verse has a clear logical structure that the commentators drew out. Two conditions: righteous action and faith. Two clarifications: the conditions apply equally to male and female. Two promises: a good life (here) and the best reward (hereafter). The structure teaches that the divine reward is conditional but not arbitrary — it depends on faith and deeds, not on sex, tribe, wealth, or status — and that it is comprehensive — it covers both worlds. Ibn Kathīr calls the verse a promise from God to whoever does good, and notes that God's promises are true.

**The Application: The Life Worth Living**

The verse offers the believer a criterion for evaluating his own life that differs from the world's. The world measures a life by what it has; the verse measures it by what it is — by whether it is *ṭayyibah*, good in its inner quality. The believer who does righteous deeds in faith is promised that his life will be good in this sense, whatever its outward circumstances. This promise has been the consolation of believers in poverty, in persecution, in illness, and in obscurity, who have found — as the verse says — that faith and good works produce a life that the wealthy and powerful, lacking those things, cannot obtain. And the promise is stated for women as explicitly as for men, so that no one who reads the verse can doubt that the good life and the best reward are hers on the same terms as his. The verse's two conditions are within every person's reach; its two promises are within God's power; and the verse's emphatic verbs — *la-nuḥyiyannahu*, *la-najziyannahum* — declare that He will fulfill them.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:98

> **So when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in God from Satan the outcast.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Instruction Before Reading**

After the promise of the good life and the best reward (v. 97), the sūrah gives a practical instruction concerning the Book that conveys these promises: *fa-idhā qaraʾta al-Qurʾāna fa-staʿidh bi'llāhi mina al-shayṭāni al-rajīm*, "so when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in God from Satan the outcast." The verse is the source of the practice, universal among Muslims, of saying *aʿūdhu bi'llāhi min al-shayṭān al-rajīm* before reading the Qur'an. It is brief, but the commentators drew from it a whole theology of the encounter between the reader and the Book.

**The Connection to the Preceding Verses**

The commentators explain the verse's placement. Verses 89–97 have described the Book as clarification, guidance, mercy, and good news, and have set out its central commands. The reader who now turns to the Book to receive these things must approach it rightly. Al-Rāzī notes that the Qur'an is the source of the "good life" and the reward just promised, and that Satan's chief aim is to prevent human beings from benefiting from it — by distraction, by doubt, by misinterpretation, by making them forget what they read. The instruction to seek refuge before reciting is a defense of the Book's benefit against the one who would nullify it.

There is also a connection to verse 63, which said that Satan "made their deeds seem fair" to the ancient communities and is the guardian of those who follow him. The Qur'an is the antidote to Satan's beautification; and Satan therefore attacks the reading of it. The verse arms the reader before he opens the Book.

**"When You Recite the Qur'an": The Timing of the *Istiʿādhah***

The verse says *idhā qaraʾta*, "when you recite" — literally, "when you have recited." The past tense in Arabic conditional constructions often has a future or general sense ("whenever you recite"), and the commentators are unanimous that the *istiʿādhah* (seeking refuge) is to be said *before* the recitation, not after. Al-Qurṭubī records this as the consensus of the community, based on the Prophet's practice; the verse's meaning is "when you *intend* to recite." The same construction appears in 5:6, "when you rise to pray, wash your faces" — that is, when you intend to pray, wash first.

A minority view, attributed to Abū Hurayrah and a few early authorities, held that the *istiʿādhah* should be said after the recitation, following the verse's literal tense. Al-Qurṭubī and al-Rāzī record this view and reject it on the basis of the Prophet's practice, which is to seek refuge before beginning. Some scholars held that one may say it both before and after — before, to protect the recitation, and after, to protect against the pride or forgetfulness that might follow it.

**The Wording of the *Istiʿādhah***

The verse's wording — *aʿūdhu bi'llāhi min al-shayṭān al-rajīm* — became the standard formula, and the commentators discuss its parts.

*Aʿūdhu* is from the root *ʿ-w-dh*, to seek refuge, to take shelter, to flee to something for protection. The verb expresses the movement of one who is threatened toward one who can protect. Al-Rāghib defines it as fleeing from what one fears to what will shield one. The one who says *aʿūdhu* acknowledges two things: that there is a danger, and that he cannot face it alone.

*Bi'llāh*, "in God," names the refuge. The commentators note that refuge is sought in God alone, because only God can protect from Satan; no human, no angel, no amulet, no ritual has power over him except by God's leave. The Qur'an gives the *istiʿādhah* its fullest form in the last two sūrahs, al-Falaq and al-Nās, which seek refuge in "the Lord of the daybreak" and "the Lord of mankind."

*Min al-shayṭān*, "from Satan." The word *shayṭān*, from a root meaning to be distant or to burn, denotes the rebellious one, distant from God's mercy — Iblīs and his followers among the jinn, and by extension every devil, human or jinn, who whispers evil (6:112; 114:6).

*Al-rajīm*, "the outcast," "the stoned," "the accursed." The word is from *rajama*, to stone, to cast out, to curse. Satan is *rajīm* in several senses the commentators enumerate: he is expelled from the divine presence (15:34, "get out of it, for you are *rajīm*"); he is pelted with shooting stars when he tries to eavesdrop on heaven (67:5; 37:6–10); and he is cursed. The epithet reminds the one seeking refuge that the enemy he fears is himself a defeated, expelled creature, and that God's protection against him is not in doubt.

The Prophet ﷺ sometimes expanded the formula. Before prayer he would say: "I seek refuge in God, the Hearing, the Knowing, from Satan the outcast, from his goading, his puffing, and his spitting" (Abū Dāwūd 775; al-Tirmidhī 242) — the three terms glossed by the narrators as madness, pride, and poetry, the three channels of Satan's influence on the human being.

**Why Refuge Is Needed Precisely at Recitation**

The commentators asked why the Qur'an commands seeking refuge at the moment of reciting the Qur'an rather than, for example, at the moment of temptation. Several answers are given, and they illuminate the nature of the Book.

Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Rāzī explain that recitation is the moment when Satan is most active against the believer, because the Qur'an is the source of the guidance he most wants to prevent. He attacks the reciter by distraction (turning his thoughts elsewhere), by doubt (raising objections to what he reads), by misunderstanding (suggesting false interpretations), by pride (making him admire his own recitation), and by making him forget. The *istiʿādhah* at the outset places the recitation under God's protection against all of these.

Ibn al-Qayyim adds that the Qur'an is a healing (v. 69; 17:82) and that Satan, like a disease, resists the medicine; seeking refuge is the clearing of the vessel before the medicine enters. He also notes that the tongue that recites should be purified of the devil's whispering before it pronounces God's word, as the mouth is rinsed before eating.

Al-Qurṭubī records the view that the *istiʿādhah* is a preparation of the heart — an act of humility in which the reciter acknowledges his vulnerability and asks God to open the Book's meaning to him. The one who approaches the Qur'an confident in his own understanding is exposed; the one who approaches it seeking refuge is protected.

**The Legal Status of the *Istiʿādhah***

The jurists discussed whether the *istiʿādhah* is obligatory or recommended. The majority — including the Ḥanafīs, Shāfiʿīs, Mālikīs, and Ḥanbalīs in their dominant positions — hold that it is *mustaḥabb*, recommended, not obligatory: the Prophet ﷺ did not always audibly say it, and its omission does not invalidate the recitation or the prayer. Al-Qurṭubī records this majority view. A minority, including ʿAṭāʾ and, in one report, Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal, held that it is obligatory, following the plain imperative of the verse. The Ẓāhirīs also held it obligatory. Al-Qurṭubī and al-Rāzī note that the imperative can bear a recommendatory sense in context, and that the practice of the community confirms its recommendation.

Within prayer, the *istiʿādhah* is said silently before the Fātiḥah in the first unit, according to most schools; the Shāfiʿīs recommend it in every unit. It is not part of the Qur'an itself and is not written in the codex; the *basmalah* is a separate question.

**The Dog and the Refuge: An Analogy**

The commentators offered an analogy that the tradition preserved. Satan is like a dog that bites and harries; one cannot fight it off by one's own strength, but if one calls on its owner, the owner restrains it. To seek refuge in God from Satan is to call on the One who has power over him. The analogy conveys a truth the commentators emphasize: the believer is not asked to defeat Satan by his own effort — Satan's whispering is constant, "flowing in the son of Adam like blood" (al-Bukhārī 2039) — but to place himself under the protection of the One from whom Satan flees. The Qur'an says of Satan's whispering: "If an evil suggestion comes to you from Satan, then seek refuge in God; truly He is Hearing, Knowing" (7:200; 41:36). Refuge, not combat, is the prescribed response.

**The Broader Teaching: Approaching the Sacred With Awareness**

The verse establishes a principle beyond the specific formula: the sacred is approached with preparation, and the preparation is an acknowledgment of one's need for God. The reciter does not open the Book as he opens a newspaper. He pauses, names the danger, and asks for protection. This pause changes the reading. It makes the reader aware that he is entering into the word of God, that there is an enemy who wishes to spoil the encounter, and that God has promised to protect those who ask. The commentators note that the Qur'an's benefit to a reader depends on the state in which he reads it — "a healing for the believers, and it increases the wrongdoers only in loss" (17:82) — and that the *istiʿādhah* is the first step in placing oneself among the former.

**The Application: The Habit of the Threshold**

The verse asks the believer to make the *istiʿādhah* a habit — a threshold ritual that precedes every reading of the Qur'an. The habit has effects beyond the moment. It trains the believer to recognize that his encounters with God's word are contested; that distraction, doubt, and forgetfulness are not merely psychological accidents but the work of an enemy; and that the remedy is not greater willpower but refuge. It also trains humility: the one who says *aʿūdhu bi'llāh* before reading has confessed that he cannot understand the Book rightly without God's help, and this confession is the disposition in which the Book opens itself. The verses that follow (99–100) will explain why the refuge works: Satan has no authority over those who believe and trust in their Lord.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:99

> **Truly he has no authority over those who believe and trust in their Lord.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Ground of the Refuge**

Verse 98 commanded seeking refuge in God from Satan. Verse 99 explains why the refuge is effective: *innahu laysa lahu sulṭānun ʿalā alladhīna āmanū wa-ʿalā rabbihim yatawakkalūn*, "truly he has no authority over those who believe and rely upon their Lord." The one who seeks refuge is not asking for something uncertain. He is claiming a promise: Satan has no *sulṭān* — no power, no authority, no dominion — over the believer who trusts in God. The verse thus turns the *istiʿādhah* from a plea into an affirmation of a settled fact.

**"He Has No Authority": The Meaning of *Sulṭān***

The word *sulṭān* denotes authority, power, dominion, or a warrant that confers them — the root *s-l-ṭ* conveys the sense of mastery and control. In the Qur'an, *sulṭān* is used for political power (as in the derived title *sulṭān*), for a proof or warrant that authorizes (as in 7:71, "names for which God has sent down no *sulṭān*"), and for the power one being has over another. The verse denies that Satan has any of this over the believer.

The commentators discuss what kind of authority is denied, since Satan clearly *does* whisper to believers and sometimes leads them into sin. The resolution is stated in the Qur'an itself, in Satan's own words on the Day of Judgment:

> *"And Satan will say, when the matter has been concluded: Truly God promised you the promise of truth, and I promised you, but I betrayed you. And I had no authority (sulṭān) over you except that I called you, and you responded to me. So do not blame me, but blame yourselves."* (Qur'an 14:22)

Satan's authority is limited to *calling* — to suggestion, whispering, invitation. He cannot compel. He has no power to force a person to sin; he can only propose, and the person responds or refuses. This is the *sulṭān* the verse denies: the power of compulsion. Al-Rāzī states it: Satan's influence is a *daʿwah*, an invitation, not a *qahr*, a coercion; and against the believer who trusts in God, even the invitation loses its force.

The Qur'an confirms this in the account of Iblīs's original threat and God's response:

> *"[Iblīs] said: My Lord, because You have put me in error, I will surely make [disobedience] attractive to them on earth, and I will mislead them all — except, among them, Your chosen servants. [God] said: This is a path [that leads] straight to Me. Truly, My servants — no authority will you have over them, except those who follow you of the deviators."* (Qur'an 15:39–42)

"My servants — no authority will you have over them" — this is the promise 16:99 restates. And 15:42 adds the exception that 16:100 will develop: Satan has authority only over "those who follow you."

**The Two Readings of the Denial**

The commentators distinguish two levels at which the denial holds.

The first is the denial of *compulsion*: Satan cannot force any human being to sin, believer or not. This is universal, and it is the basis of human responsibility. If Satan could compel, no one could be blamed for what he compelled. The verse in Sūrat Ibrāhīm (14:22) states this universal denial.

The second is the denial of *effective influence* over the believer who trusts in God: not only can Satan not compel such a person, but his whispering does not take hold. The believer hears the suggestion and rejects it; the whisper finds nothing in him to grip. This is the specific sense of 16:99, which limits the denial to "those who believe and trust in their Lord." Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Rāzī read the verse in this second sense: the believer who truly relies on God is protected not merely from being forced but from being *moved*. The Prophet ﷺ described this state when he said that his own devil (*qarīn*) had submitted and commanded him only to good (Muslim 2814) — the extreme case of the influence being neutralized.

**"Those Who Believe": The First Condition**

The verse names two conditions for immunity. The first is *āmanū*, "they believe." Faith is the ground of protection because faith is the recognition of God's sovereignty, and Satan's whisper is, at root, a proposal to act as though God were not sovereign — to prefer the immediate to the eternal, the self to the Lord. The believer who holds God's sovereignty firmly in view has already rejected the premise of every whisper. Al-Rāzī: faith is the light in which Satan's suggestions are seen for what they are, and what is seen clearly as evil is not chosen.

**"And Trust in Their Lord": The Second Condition**

The second condition is *ʿalā rabbihim yatawakkalūn*, "upon their Lord they rely." The fronting of *ʿalā rabbihim*, "upon their Lord," conveys exclusivity: they rely on *Him alone*. *Tawakkul*, discussed at verse 42, is the entrusting of one's affairs to God with confidence in His care. The commentators explain its relevance to protection from Satan. Satan's chief instruments are fear and desire — fear of loss, desire for gain — and both depend on the person's believing that his welfare is in his own hands or in the hands of worldly forces. The one who relies on God has removed both handles: he does not fear loss, because his provision is with God; he does not crave gain, because his portion is decreed. Satan's whisper, which works by inflaming fear and desire, finds nothing to inflame. Al-Zamakhsharī: *tawakkul* closes the doors through which Satan enters.

The Qur'an pairs faith and *tawakkul* elsewhere as the qualities of those whom God protects: "God suffices for whoever relies upon Him" (65:3); "the believers rely upon God alone" (3:122, 160; 5:11; 9:51). The one for whom God suffices needs no other protector, and no other can overpower the One who suffices him.

**The Believer's Experience of the Verse**

The commentators are careful to note that the verse does not promise that the believer will never hear a whisper or never stumble. The Prophet ﷺ said that Satan flows in the human being like blood, and the Companions complained of intrusive thoughts — to which the Prophet replied, "That is pure faith" (Muslim 132), meaning that the very distress at the thought is a sign that faith has rejected it. The verse promises that Satan has no *sulṭān* — no authority, no dominion, no capacity to rule the believer. He may knock; he cannot enter by force. He may propose; he cannot impose. And the believer who relies on God finds, over time, that the knocking grows fainter, because the one who is repeatedly refused eventually turns to easier prey. Verse 100 will name that prey.

**The Relationship to the *Istiʿādhah***

Verse 99 gives the *istiʿādhah* of verse 98 its confidence. The believer who says "I seek refuge in God from Satan" is not uncertain whether refuge will be granted; the verse tells him it has been granted in principle, by God's decree that Satan has no authority over those who believe and rely. The *istiʿādhah* is the believer's active taking-up of a protection that already exists. Al-Rāzī frames it: the refuge is available; the *istiʿādhah* is the reaching for it; and faith and *tawakkul* are the hands with which one reaches. The three verses (98–100) form a single teaching: seek refuge (98), because you are protected (99), and the unprotected are those who take Satan as ally (100).

**The Application: Removing the Handles**

The verse gives the believer a practical diagnosis of his own vulnerability. When Satan's whispers take hold — when the believer finds himself moved by fear or desire toward what he knows to be wrong — the verse names the two remedies: faith, renewed and strengthened; and *tawakkul*, the deliberate placing of one's affairs in God's hands. The believer who strengthens these two finds that the whispers lose their grip, not because he has fought them harder but because they have less to hold. The verse's promise is absolute in its terms — *laysa lahu sulṭān*, "he has no authority" — and its conditions are within the believer's reach. The Prophet ﷺ taught that the one who says, on leaving his house, "In the name of God; I rely upon God; there is no power and no strength except with God," is told: "You have been guided, sufficed, and protected," and Satan turns away from him (Abū Dāwūd 5095; al-Tirmidhī 3426). The supplication is faith and *tawakkul* in a sentence; and the result — Satan turning away — is 16:99 in effect.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:100

> **His authority is only over those who take him as a protector, and those who ascribe partners unto God.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Other Side of the Promise**

Verse 99 said that Satan has no authority over those who believe and trust in God. Verse 100 states the converse: *innamā sulṭānuhu ʿalā alladhīna yatawallawnahu wa'lladhīna hum bihi mushrikūn*, "his authority is only over those who take him as protector and those who are, through him, associators." The two verses together map the whole field. Satan's authority is real but bounded; verse 99 marks the boundary from the inside, verse 100 from the outside. Those over whom he has power are named, and the naming is itself instructive: his power is over those who *give* it to him.

**"His Authority Is Only Over": The Restriction**

The particle *innamā*, "only," restricts Satan's *sulṭān* to the two classes that follow and excludes all others. The commentators note the parallel with 15:42, where God tells Iblīs, "My servants — no authority will you have over them, *except those who follow you* of the deviators." The exception in 15:42 is the restriction in 16:100: Satan's authority is only over those who follow him.

The word *sulṭān* was discussed at verse 99: authority, dominion, the power to rule. The verse says Satan has this — over some. The commentators are careful to state that even here, the authority is not compulsion. Satan does not force even his followers; he leads them, and they follow. His authority over them is like the authority of a leader over willing followers — real, effective, and yet dependent at every moment on their continued consent. Al-Rāzī states the principle: Satan's *sulṭān* over the disbeliever is a *sulṭān* the disbeliever has granted him by taking him as protector; it is not an authority Satan seized but one he was given.

**"Those Who Take Him as a Protector": *Yatawallawnahu***

The first class is *alladhīna yatawallawnahu*, "those who take him as *walī*." The verb *tawallā* with an object means to take someone as one's guardian, protector, ally, patron — to turn to him for support and follow his direction. The noun *walī* was discussed at verse 63, where Satan was called "their *walī* today." The relationship of *wilāyah* is one of loyalty and dependence: the *walī* leads, protects, and is obeyed; the one under his *wilāyah* follows and relies.

To take Satan as *walī* is to obey his suggestions habitually — to make his whispers the guide of one's conduct, to follow him where he leads, to prefer his counsel to God's. The commentators note that no one does this consciously, saying "I take Satan as my protector." The taking is enacted, not declared. Whoever consistently follows the suggestions that come from Satan — to sin, to disbelieve, to prefer the world — has taken him as *walī* in fact, whatever he says in words. The Qur'an describes the outcome:

> *"God is the protector (walī) of those who believe; He brings them out of darknesses into the light. And those who disbelieve — their protectors are the ṭāghūt; they bring them out of the light into darknesses."* (Qur'an 2:257)

The Qur'an also notes that Satan's followers may believe themselves guided: "Truly they had taken the devils as protectors instead of God, and they think that they are guided" (7:30). The *wilāyah* of Satan is often invisible to the one under it, because Satan's method is beautification (v. 63) — he makes his path look like the right one.

**"And Those Who Ascribe Partners Unto God": *Bihi Mushrikūn***

The second class is *alladhīna hum bihi mushrikūn*. The phrase has been read in two ways, depending on the referent of *bihi*, "through/with him/it."

The first reading takes *bihi* as referring to God: "those who associate partners *with Him*" — the *mushrikūn* in the ordinary sense, who set up partners alongside God. On this reading, the verse names two classes: those who take Satan as protector, and those who commit *shirk*. Al-Ṭabarī allows this reading.

The second reading takes *bihi* as referring to Satan: "those who are, *through him* or *because of him*, associators" — that is, those whose *shirk* is the result of following Satan. Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Rāzī prefer this: Satan's authority is over those who take him as protector and who, by obeying him, become *mushrikūn*, since he is the one who calls to *shirk*. The two classes are then one class described from two angles: they took Satan as *walī* (the cause) and became *mushrikūn* (the effect).

A third reading, also recorded, takes *bihi* as referring to God and *mushrikūn* as "associating [Satan] with God" — that is, those who make Satan a partner with God by obeying him as they should obey God. Obedience is a form of worship, and the one who obeys Satan against God has, in effect, made him a partner. The Qur'an uses this sense when it says that those who follow their scholars in forbidding the lawful "have taken them as lords besides God" (9:31) — not by prostrating to them, but by obeying them in place of God. Al-Rāzī notes this reading as consistent with the sūrah's broad conception of *shirk*.

All three readings converge on a single truth: the *shirk* the sūrah has been condemning throughout is the fruit of Satan's *wilāyah*, and Satan's authority extends exactly as far as that *wilāyah* does. The idolaters of Makkah — with their offerings to idols (v. 56), their daughters assigned to God (v. 57), their prohibitions of the lawful (v. 116) — were under Satan's authority because they had taken him as protector by following the beautified path he laid for them.

**The Logic of the Two Verses Together**

Verses 99 and 100 form a complete statement about Satan's power that the commentators regarded as central to Islamic anthropology. Satan cannot compel anyone; his only instrument is suggestion. Over those who believe and rely on God, even suggestion fails, because faith and *tawakkul* leave it nothing to hold. Over those who take him as protector, suggestion succeeds, because they have handed him the reins. The authority is thus a *function* of the human response. This places responsibility squarely on the human being: Satan is a real enemy, but he is an enemy who can be refused, and whose power over a person is precisely the measure of that person's consent.

Al-Rāzī draws the theological consequence: the verse refutes the excuse "Satan made me do it." Satan's authority is only over those who took him as protector; the one who blames Satan for his sin is confessing that he took Satan as protector, which is itself the fault. Satan himself will say on the Day of Judgment: "Do not blame me, but blame yourselves" (14:22).

**The Boundary and the Choice**

The verses draw a boundary and place the human being on one side or the other according to his choice. On one side are those who believe and rely on God; Satan has no authority over them. On the other are those who take Satan as protector and associate partners with God; Satan's authority is over them. There is no third territory. The commentators note that the boundary is not fixed for any individual: a person may cross it in either direction, by turning from Satan's *wilāyah* to God's or the reverse. The *istiʿādhah* of verse 98 is one of the acts by which the boundary is crossed toward safety; every act of obedience to a whisper is a step toward the other side.

**The Application: Checking One's Allegiance**

The verse gives the believer a diagnostic question: *whom do I follow when the whisper comes?* Not in theory — every believer would say he follows God — but in practice, in the moment of decision. The one who habitually follows the suggestion to sin, to neglect duty, to prefer the world, has, in that habit, taken Satan as *walī*, and the verse says Satan's authority is over such a person. The remedy is the reversal of the habit: to make God the *walī* in practice, by following His command when the whisper opposes it. Each such act weakens Satan's *sulṭān* and strengthens the protection of verse 99. The Prophet ﷺ described the believer's devil as growing thin from the believer's refusals, as a camel grows thin from hard use; the disbeliever's devil grows fat from his compliance. The verse's "authority" is fed or starved by the human being over whom it is claimed, and the verse's message is that the feeding is a choice.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:101

> **And when We replace one sign with another—and God knows best what He sends down—they say, "You are only a fabricator." Nay, but most of them know not.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Objection of Abrogation**

After the instruction on reciting the Qur'an and the protection from Satan (vv. 98–100), the sūrah turns to a specific objection the Makkans raised against the Qur'an itself: that its verses changed. *Wa-idhā baddalnā āyatan makāna āyah*, "and when We substitute a sign in place of a sign" — when one ruling or verse is replaced by another — *qālū innamā anta muftar*, "they say: You are only a fabricator." The objection was that a book from God would not need revision; the fact that some verses replaced others proved, they said, that the Prophet was composing as he went. The verse records the objection, inserts God's answer in the middle of it, and dismisses the objectors as ignorant.

**"When We Replace One Sign With Another": *Tabdīl***

The verb *baddala* means to substitute, to exchange one thing for another. The verse describes God substituting one *āyah* — sign, verse — for another. The commentators identify this with *naskh*, abrogation: the replacement of an earlier ruling by a later one within the period of revelation. The Qur'an states the principle directly:

> *"We do not abrogate a verse or cause it to be forgotten except that We bring one better than it or similar to it. Do you not know that God is over all things competent?"* (Qur'an 2:106)

The commentators give the classic examples. The direction of prayer (*qiblah*) was changed from Jerusalem to Makkah (2:142–144). Wine was progressively restricted and then forbidden (2:219; 4:43; 5:90 — discussed at verse 67). The waiting period of the widow was changed from a year to four months and ten days (2:240 → 2:234). The obligation of night prayer was lightened (73:1–4 → 73:20). The requirement that one believer stand against ten enemies was reduced to one against two (8:65–66). In each case, a later revelation modified an earlier one, and the Makkans — and later the Jews of Madinah — pointed to this as evidence of human authorship.

Some commentators, including al-Rāzī, note that the sūrah is Makkan and that most of the legal abrogations occurred in Madinah; they suggest that the Makkan objection concerned changes in the Qur'an's *style*, *emphasis*, or the substitution of one *argument* or *narrative* for another, or that the verse anticipates the later objections. Others hold that some changes did occur in the Makkan period (the modification of the night prayer, for instance), and that the objection had a basis then. Al-Ṭabarī takes the verse as referring to abrogation in general.

**"And God Knows Best What He Sends Down": The Parenthesis**

Between the description of the substitution and the report of the objection, the verse inserts a clause: *wa'llāhu aʿlamu bimā yunazzil*, "and God knows best what He sends down." The commentators explain the placement. Before the objection is even stated, its answer is given: the substitution is God's, and God knows what He is doing. He knows what is appropriate for each time, each circumstance, each stage of the community's development. Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Rāzī explain the wisdom of abrogation. A community cannot be brought from ignorance to perfection in a single step; the law is revealed gradually, and earlier rulings, suited to earlier stages, are replaced by later ones suited to later stages, as a physician changes the prescription as the patient recovers. The change is not in God's knowledge but in the patient's condition. God knew from eternity that the earlier ruling would be replaced; the sequence was designed.

The parenthesis also answers the deeper implication of the objection — that change implies error. Al-Rāzī: change in a human author's work implies that he did not foresee; change in God's revelation implies only that He addressed different circumstances in the manner each required. The wisdom of a ruling is relative to its time; a ruling perfect for one time may be replaced by one perfect for the next, and the replacement is itself an expression of perfect knowledge.

**"They Say: You Are Only a Fabricator": *Muftar***

The objection is stated: *innamā anta muftar*, "you are only a fabricator." The word *muftar* is the active participle of *iftarā*, to fabricate, to invent a lie — the verb used in verse 56 for the idolaters' own fabrications. The charge is that the Prophet invents the Qur'an himself, and the evidence is its revisions. The commentators note the irony: the fabricators (v. 56, 62, 87) accuse the truthful of fabrication, and the accusation exposes their own method — they assumed that the Qur'an was produced as they would have produced it, by human contrivance, and read its features accordingly.

The charge of fabrication was the Makkans' standard accusation (10:38; 11:13, 35; 21:5; 25:4; 32:3; 34:8, 43; 42:24; 46:8), and the Qur'an answered it repeatedly, most directly by the challenge to produce a sūrah like it (2:23; 10:38; 11:13). Verse 101 answers it here by attributing the substitution to God ("*We* replace") and by pointing out that the objectors do not know what they are talking about.

**"Nay, but Most of Them Know Not"**

The verse ends: *bal aktharuhum lā yaʿlamūn*, "rather, most of them do not know." The commentators identify the object of their ignorance: they do not know the wisdom of abrogation; they do not know that God's law is revealed in stages according to His knowledge of what each stage requires; they do not know the difference between the change of a human author who did not foresee and the change of a divine Lawgiver who did. Al-Rāzī notes that the phrase is not merely dismissive but diagnostic: the objection arises from ignorance of the nature of revelation, and the cure is knowledge — which the next verse begins to supply, by identifying the true source of the Qur'an.

The phrase "most of them" repeats the sūrah's refrain (vv. 38, 75, 83) and preserves its precision: not all — some among the Makkans would come to understand — but most.

**The Doctrine of Abrogation in the Tradition**

The verse became one of the principal texts for the doctrine of *naskh*, and the commentators outline its parameters. Abrogation occurs only within the period of revelation; after the Prophet's death, no ruling can be abrogated. It applies to rulings (*aḥkām*), not to reports of fact or to fundamental doctrines — God's oneness, the resurrection, the moral principles of verse 90 are not subject to abrogation. It is established by clear evidence of chronology and of contradiction that cannot be reconciled; where reconciliation is possible, abrogation is not assumed. The scholars differed considerably on how many verses were actually abrogated — the early generations used the term broadly for any qualification of one verse by another, while later scholars narrowed it, and some, like al-Suyūṭī, reduced the list to about twenty cases, and modern scholars have reduced it further. Al-Rāzī notes that the *existence* of abrogation is established by 2:106 and 16:101; the *extent* is a matter of investigation.

The commentators also record the position of some Jewish scholars in Madinah who denied abrogation in principle — holding that God's law could not change — and to whom the Qur'an's response was the same as to the Makkans: God knows best what He sends down, and He sent down to Moses a law that itself modified earlier practices (3:50, where Jesus says he came to "make lawful for you some of what was forbidden to you"). Change within revelation is not unique to the Qur'an; it is the pattern of all revelation, which meets each community at its stage.

**The Verse as a Test**

Al-Rāzī offers a further reading of the verse's function. Abrogation is a *test*: it distinguishes those who obey God because He commands from those who obey a rule because they are attached to the rule. When the *qiblah* changed, those who were attached to Jerusalem as such stumbled; those who were attached to God's command turned with it (2:143, "We made the qiblah you were on only to know who follows the Messenger from who turns on his heels"). The one who says "you are a fabricator" when a ruling changes has revealed that his allegiance was to the ruling, not to the Ruler. The believer's allegiance is to God; whatever He sends down, and whatever He replaces, the believer follows, because he knows that "God knows best what He sends down."

**The Application: Obedience to the Lawgiver, Not the Law**

The verse teaches a disposition that extends beyond the historical question of abrogation. The believer's obedience is to God, and his attachment to any specific practice is conditional on its being what God commands *now*. This protects against two errors: the rigidity that clings to a form after its purpose has passed, and the skepticism that concludes, from the fact of change, that nothing is fixed. The verse holds both in check: God *does* replace one sign with another — so rigidity is misplaced — and God *knows best* what He sends down — so skepticism is misplaced. The believer trusts the Lawgiver through every change in the law, and the verse's closing phrase tells him that the alternative is not sophistication but ignorance.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:102

> **Say, "The Holy Spirit has brought it down from thy Lord in truth, to make firm those who believe, and as a guidance and glad tidings for those who submit."**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Answer to the Charge of Fabrication**

Verse 101 recorded the Makkans' accusation: "You are only a fabricator." Verse 102 gives the Prophet ﷺ the answer: *qul nazzalahu rūḥu al-qudusi min rabbika bi'l-ḥaqq*, "Say: The Holy Spirit has brought it down from your Lord in truth." The Qur'an is not the Prophet's composition; it is brought down by a named agent, from a named source, in a named manner. And the verse states three purposes of the revelation — including its substitutions — that turn the objection on its head: what the Makkans called evidence of fabrication is, in fact, a means of strengthening the believers.

**"Say": The Command to Respond**

The verse opens with *qul*, "say" — the Prophet is instructed to give this answer. The commentators note that the response is not left to the Prophet's improvisation; God tells him what to say, which is itself a demonstration of the point: the Prophet speaks what is revealed to him, not what he devises.

**"The Holy Spirit": *Rūḥ al-Qudus***

The agent of revelation is *rūḥ al-qudus*, "the Spirit of Holiness" or "the Holy Spirit." The commentators are unanimous that this is Gabriel (*Jibrīl*), the angel of revelation. The Qur'an identifies him by name elsewhere as the one who brought the Qur'an down:

> *"Say: Whoever is an enemy to Gabriel — it is he who has brought it down upon your heart by permission of God, confirming what was before it, and as a guidance and glad tidings for the believers."* (Qur'an 2:97)

> *"The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down upon your heart, that you may be of the warners, in a clear Arabic tongue."* (Qur'an 26:193–195)

The title *rūḥ al-qudus* appears in the Qur'an also in connection with Jesus, whom God "strengthened with the Holy Spirit" (2:87, 253; 5:110) — again understood as Gabriel. The word *rūḥ*, spirit, was discussed at verse 2, where God sends down the angels "with the Spirit of His command" — the revelation that gives life to hearts. *Al-qudus* means holiness, purity — Gabriel is called the Spirit of Holiness because he is pure of every fault and because what he brings purifies. Al-Rāzī explains the title: the revelation is *rūḥ* because it is the life of the soul, as breath is the life of the body; and it is *qudus* because it is free of error and impurity.

The naming of the agent answers the charge of fabrication directly. The Qur'an did not arise in the Prophet's mind; it was *brought down* (*nazzala*, the intensive form denoting repeated, gradual descent) by a messenger from God. The Prophet was the recipient, not the author.

**"From Thy Lord": The Source**

The source is *min rabbika*, "from your Lord." The commentators note the address *rabbika*, "your Lord" — the Lord who sustains and cares for the Prophet, and who sends him what he needs. The phrase is one of intimacy and reassurance in the face of the accusation: the Prophet is told that his Lord is the source of what he conveys, and that the Makkans' charge is a charge against God.

**"In Truth": *Bi'l-Ḥaqq***

The manner is *bi'l-ḥaqq*, "in truth" or "with the truth." The phrase was discussed at verse 3, where God created the heavens and the earth "in truth." Applied to revelation, it means several things the commentators enumerate: the Qur'an was sent down *containing* truth — its content is true; it was sent down *for* a true purpose — to guide; and it was sent down *by right* — the sending was just and wise. Al-Zamakhsharī reads *bi'l-ḥaqq* as an answer to the objection about abrogation: the substitution of one verse for another is done *in truth* — for a true reason, with wisdom — not arbitrarily as the Makkans imagined.

**"To Make Firm Those Who Believe": *Li-yuthabbita***

The first purpose is *li-yuthabbita alladhīna āmanū*, "to make firm those who believe." The verb *thabbata* means to make firm, to stabilize, to establish — the root of *thubūt*, "firmness," used in verse 94 for the firmly planted foot. The revelation strengthens the believers.

The commentators explain how this purpose relates to the objection of verse 101. The Makkans said that the substitution of verses proved fabrication and should shake the believers' confidence. The verse says the opposite: the gradual revelation, with its substitutions, *strengthens* the believers. Al-Rāzī gives the reasons. The gradual revelation meets the believers' needs as they arise, so that each new verse comes as an answer, a comfort, or a guidance at the moment it is needed — which strengthens their sense of God's care. The substitution of an easier ruling for a harder one strengthens them by relieving them. And the very fact that they accept the substitution — trusting the Lawgiver through the change — is itself an exercise of faith that makes it firmer, as a muscle is strengthened by use. The Qur'an states this purpose of gradual revelation explicitly:

> *"And those who disbelieve say: Why was the Qur'an not revealed to him all at once? Thus [it is] that We may strengthen your heart thereby, and We have recited it in stages."* (Qur'an 25:32)

The same objection — why not all at once? — receives the same answer: to strengthen. What the objector reads as weakness is the method of strengthening.

The commentators also read *tathbīt* as the steadying of the believers under persecution. The Makkan Muslims were being pressured to abandon Islam (vv. 41–42, 94–96); the revelation, arriving verse by verse, held them firm. Al-Ṭabarī: the Qur'an came down to make firm the hearts of the believers so that they would not slip.

**"And as a Guidance and Glad Tidings for Those Who Submit"**

The second and third purposes are *wa-hudan wa-bushrā li'l-muslimīn*, "and a guidance and glad tidings for those who submit." The phrase repeats the description of verse 89 (which had "guidance, mercy, and glad tidings for the Muslims") and of 2:97 (which describes Gabriel's revelation as "guidance and glad tidings for the believers"). The Qur'an guides the submitters to the right path and gives them good news of what awaits them on it.

The commentators note the structure of the three purposes. The first, *tathbīt*, is for "those who believe" — the strengthening of faith already present. The second and third, guidance and good news, are for "those who submit" — the direction and encouragement of those who have surrendered to God. The three together describe the Qur'an's action on the believer: it steadies him, directs him, and cheers him. And none of these purposes is served by a fabrication; all are served by a revelation from the Lord, brought down by the Holy Spirit, in truth.

**The Verse as the Positive Statement of the Qur'an's Origin**

Verses 101–105 form a passage on the origin of the Qur'an, and verse 102 is its positive core. Verse 101 recorded the charge of fabrication; verse 102 states the true origin; verse 103 will address a specific version of the charge (that a foreigner taught the Prophet); verses 104–105 will identify who actually fabricates. Al-Rāzī notes that the passage places the Prophet's answer between two statements of the Makkans' error, so that the truth stands framed by the falsehoods it refutes.

**The Application: The Steadying Power of the Book**

The verse names a function of the Qur'an that every believer has experienced: it *makes firm*. The believer who is shaken — by doubt, by hardship, by the arguments of opponents, by the pressure of a hostile environment — and who turns to the Qur'an finds his footing restored. This is not accidental; it is the purpose for which the Book was sent down. The verse teaches the believer where to go when he is unsteady, and it tells him that the Book's structure — its gradualness, its responsiveness, even its substitutions — was designed for this. The one who reads the Qur'an in times of trial is using it as it was meant to be used, and the verse's promise is that he will find in it what the Holy Spirit brought it down to provide: firmness, guidance, and good news.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:103

> **And We know well that they say, "It is only a human being who teaches him." The tongue of him whom they falsely allude to is foreign, while this is a clear Arabic tongue.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Specific Version of the Charge**

Verse 101 recorded the general accusation of fabrication. Verse 103 records a specific theory the Makkans proposed to explain where the Qur'an came from: *innamā yuʿallimuhu bashar*, "it is only a human being who teaches him." Unable to deny the Qur'an's power, and unwilling to admit its divine origin, they sought a human source — a teacher from whom the Prophet ﷺ was supposedly learning the stories and doctrines he recited. The verse names the theory and refutes it with a single observation about language.

**"We Know Well That They Say": The Divine Awareness**

The verse opens *wa-laqad naʿlamu annahum yaqūlūn*, "and We certainly know that they say." The emphatic *laqad* and the verb of knowledge establish that the accusation is not hidden from God; He knows what they whisper. The commentators read this as both reassurance to the Prophet — God is aware of the slander and will answer it — and warning to the slanderers — their words are recorded. The phrase recurs in the Qur'an for the Prophet's comfort: "We know that your breast is straitened by what they say" (15:97).

**"It Is Only a Human Being Who Teaches Him": The Theory**

The theory is that a *bashar*, a human being, taught the Prophet. The commentators record the candidates the Makkans proposed, and the reports vary.

Several reports name a Christian slave or freedman in Makkah. Ibn ʿAbbās, according to some, named a blacksmith called Balʿām (or Abū Fukayhah Yasār), a Byzantine Christian slave who worked at al-Marwah; the Prophet used to stop at his forge and speak with him, and the Makkans said the man was teaching him. Others name two slaves, Jabr and Yasār, of the Banū al-Ḥaḍramī, who were Christians and used to read their scriptures, and whom the Prophet would sometimes visit. Others name ʿĀʾish or Yaʿīsh, a slave of the Banū al-Mughīrah who had read books. Al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Rāzī, and al-Wāḥidī collect these reports. Some later writers suggested Salmān al-Fārisī, but the commentators reject this: Salmān embraced Islam in Madinah, years after this Makkan verse, and could not have been the referent.

What the candidates have in common is that they were foreigners — non-Arabs — who knew something of the earlier scriptures. The Makkans, hearing the Qur'an tell the stories of Abraham, Moses, Joseph, and Jesus, and unable to account for how an unlettered Arab knew them, concluded that he was being fed by someone who did.

**The Refutation: The Argument From Language**

The verse's refutation is compressed into a single observation: *lisānu alladhī yulḥidūna ilayhi aʿjamiyyun wa-hādhā lisānun ʿarabiyyun mubīn*, "the tongue of the one they allude to is foreign, while this is a clear Arabic tongue."
