The word *aʿjamī* denotes a non-Arab, or one who does not speak Arabic clearly — a foreigner whose Arabic, if he has any, is halting and accented. The word *ʿarabī mubīn*, "clear Arabic," denotes Arabic of the highest purity and eloquence.

The argument is this. The men the Makkans pointed to spoke broken Arabic at best. The Qur'an is Arabic of a perfection that the Makkans themselves — the masters of Arabic eloquence — could not match, as the challenge to produce a sūrah like it demonstrated (2:23; 10:38; 11:13; 17:88). How could a foreigner who could barely speak the language have taught a text whose language defeated the best Arab poets? The proposed cause is inadequate to the effect. Al-Rāzī states the argument formally: the Qur'an's miracle is in its eloquence as much as in its content; a foreign teacher could at most have supplied content; he could not have supplied the eloquence; therefore the theory fails to explain what most needs explaining.

Al-Zamakhsharī adds that the theory is self-defeating in a second way: if the Makkans thought a foreign slave could produce this Qur'an, why did they not go to him — or to any of the many learned foreigners available to them — and have another produced? Their failure to meet the challenge, while pointing to a supposed human source, exposes the pointing as bad faith.

**"Falsely Allude To": *Yulḥidūna***

The verb *yulḥidūna* is from the root *l-ḥ-d*, which means to deviate, to incline away from the straight — the root of *ilḥād*, heresy, and *laḥd*, the side-niche of a grave (which deviates from the vertical shaft). Here it means to allude to, to incline toward, to point at — with a connotation of deviation from truth. The Makkans "deviated toward" the foreign slave — they turned their accusation in his direction, and the turning was itself a deviation. Al-Ṭabarī reads it as "they incline to," "they point to," and notes the root's implication of crookedness: the accusation was not merely false but perverse, a deliberate turning-away from the evident explanation to a contrived one.

A variant reading, *yalḥadūna* (with *a*), is recorded and carries the same meaning.

**The Content Argument, Implicit**

The commentators also drew out an argument the verse implies but does not state. Even granting that a foreigner supplied the content, the content itself refutes the theory. The Qur'an's accounts of the earlier prophets differ from the Jewish and Christian scriptures in significant ways — it corrects them, denies the crucifixion as commonly narrated, rejects the divinity of Jesus, and presents Abraham as neither Jew nor Christian (3:67). A student who had learned from a Christian slave would have reproduced Christian doctrine; the Qur'an contradicts it. Moreover, the Qur'an contains predictions that were fulfilled (30:2–4, the Byzantine victory), legislation that no slave could have devised, and a critique of the Makkans' own society in detail — none of which a foreign blacksmith could have supplied. Al-Rāzī notes that the theory of a human teacher was never seriously believed by the Makkans themselves; it was a talking point, and the verse treats it as such — refuting it in a single clause and moving on.

**The Illiteracy of the Prophet**

The verse's argument is strengthened by a fact the Qur'an states elsewhere: the Prophet ﷺ was *ummī*, unlettered (7:157–158), and had never read a book or written one:

> *"And you did not recite before it any scripture, nor did you inscribe one with your right hand; then the falsifiers would have doubted."* (Qur'an 29:48)

The Makkans knew this; it was the reason they needed a "teacher" theory at all. A man who could not read could not have studied the scriptures himself, so he must have been taught orally — and the only oral teachers available were foreigners with broken Arabic. The verse closes the last gap in the explanation.

**The Broader Principle: The Qur'an's Self-Attestation**

Verse 103 belongs to a group of verses in which the Qur'an argues for its own divine origin from its own properties. Its eloquence exceeds human capacity (17:88); its consistency across twenty-three years is beyond human composition (4:82, "had it been from other than God, they would have found in it much contradiction"); its knowledge exceeds what its bearer could have had (11:49, "this is from the news of the unseen which We reveal to you; you did not know it, nor did your people, before this"). Verse 103's argument from language is one instance of this self-attestation. The commentators note that the Qur'an's insistence on its Arabic — *lisān ʿarabī mubīn* (16:103; 26:195; cf. 12:2; 13:37; 20:113; 39:28; 41:3; 42:7; 43:3; 46:12) — is not linguistic pride but an argument: the Book's perfection in the language of its first hearers was the proof they were best equipped to evaluate, and their inability to match it was the proof's confirmation.

**The Application: The Inadequacy of Reductive Explanations**

The verse teaches a pattern of reasoning that applies beyond its occasion. When confronted with something that exceeds ordinary explanation, the skeptic proposes a reductive cause — a human teacher, a psychological state, a borrowing from elsewhere — and the verse's method is to test the cause against the effect. Is the proposed cause adequate? A foreigner with broken Arabic cannot produce clear Arabic. The theory collapses on inspection. Modern reductive accounts of the Qur'an — as compilation, as borrowing, as the product of a milieu — face the same test, and the tradition has answered them with the same argument: the effect exceeds the cause. The verse asks the reader to examine the explanations offered for the Book he holds, and to notice, as the Makkans should have noticed, when the explanation cannot account for what is in his hands.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:104

> **Truly those who believe not in the signs of God, God guides them not, and theirs shall be a painful punishment.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Verdict on the Accusers**

Verses 101–103 recorded the Makkans' accusations against the Qur'an — that it was fabricated, that a human being taught it — and refuted them. Verse 104 turns from refutation to verdict: *inna alladhīna lā yuʾminūna bi-āyāti Allāhi lā yahdīhimu Allāh*, "truly those who do not believe in the signs of God, God does not guide them." The verse names the condition of those who make such accusations, states its consequence in this world (they are not guided), and states its consequence in the next (a painful punishment).

**"Those Who Believe Not in the Signs of God"**

The subjects are *alladhīna lā yuʾminūna bi-āyāti Allāh*, "those who do not believe in the signs of God." The word *āyāt* has, throughout the sūrah, carried two senses: the signs in creation (the rain, the cattle, the bee, the birds) and the verses of the Qur'an. Here, following the discussion of the Qur'an's origin, the primary sense is the verses — those who reject the Qur'an, calling it fabrication (v. 101) or human teaching (v. 103). But the commentators note that the two senses converge: the one who rejects the Qur'an's verses has also failed to read the signs in creation, since both point to the same truth.

The present tense *lā yuʾminūna*, "they do not believe," describes a settled state, not a momentary doubt. These are people whose disbelief is their condition — who have heard the signs, seen the refutations, and persisted in rejection.

**"God Guides Them Not": The Consequence in This World**

The first consequence is *lā yahdīhimu Allāh*, "God does not guide them." The statement must be read in the light of the sūrah's earlier treatment of guidance (vv. 9, 36, 37, 93). The commentators explain it in two complementary ways.

The first, following the Salafī and Ashʿarī reading: God's withholding of guidance is a *consequence* of their disbelief, not its cause. They chose not to believe in the signs; God, in response, does not grant them the further guidance — the *tawfīq*, the success and inner light — that He grants those who accept. The Qur'an states the sequence in 61:5: "When they deviated, God caused their hearts to deviate." And in the present sūrah's verse 107–108: they preferred this world, "so God has set a seal upon their hearts." The seal follows the preference. Ibn Kathīr reads verse 104 in this way: God does not guide those who have rejected His signs, because guidance is given to those who seek it.

The second, following the Muʿtazilī and Shiite reading: "God does not guide them" means that God does not *judge* them guided, or does not guide them *to Paradise*, or does not give them the additional grace He gives believers — in each case, because they have rejected the guidance already offered. Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Ṭabrisī read it thus.

On either reading, the verse describes a closed circuit: rejection of the signs leads to the withholding of guidance, which confirms the rejection. The commentators note that the verse is a warning against entering this circuit: the first rejection is the most consequential, because it sets in motion a process that becomes progressively harder to reverse. Al-Rāzī: the one who rejects a sign once finds the next sign less compelling, and the one who rejects it a hundred times can no longer see it at all.

**"And Theirs Shall Be a Painful Punishment": The Consequence in the Next**

The second consequence is *wa-lahum ʿadhābun alīm*, "and for them is a painful punishment." The phrase was discussed at verse 63. The commentators note its placement: after the withholding of guidance in this world comes the punishment in the next, and the two are related as cause and effect. The unguided, remaining in disbelief, arrive at the reckoning in that state and receive its consequence.

**The Connection to the Accusations**

The commentators draw out the verse's specific application to the accusers of verses 101–103. Those who called the Qur'an fabrication or the teaching of a foreign slave did not do so from honest inquiry; they did so because they did not believe in God's signs and were looking for reasons to justify their disbelief. The theory of the human teacher was not the cause of their rejection but its rationalization. Al-Rāzī: the verse identifies the root of the accusations — not a genuine doubt about the Qur'an's origin, which the refutations would have resolved, but a prior refusal to believe, which no refutation can reach. This is why the verse pronounces a verdict rather than offering another argument: arguments have been offered; what remains is the state of those who reject them.

**The Verse's Diagnosis of Unbelief**

The verse implies a diagnosis that the commentators made explicit. Unbelief is not primarily an intellectual condition — a lack of evidence — but a volitional one — a refusal to accept evidence. The signs of God are abundant; the sūrah has spent a hundred verses displaying them. The one who does not believe in them has not failed to see them; he has refused to accept what he saw. And this refusal has a consequence in the faculty of seeing itself: God does not guide him, and the refusal becomes blindness. The Qur'an describes the process in the case of the disbelievers generally: "They have hearts with which they do not understand, eyes with which they do not see, ears with which they do not hear" (7:179) — the faculties named in verse 78 as gifts have been rendered useless by their misuse.

**The Verse and Verse 105: A Pair**

Verse 104 and verse 105 form a pair that the commentators read together. Verse 104 describes those who do not believe in God's signs; verse 105 identifies them as the true fabricators. The two verses thus complete the response to verse 101's accusation: the accusers charged the Prophet with fabrication; verse 104 names their condition (disbelief in the signs, withheld guidance, punishment); verse 105 turns the charge back on them (it is they who fabricate). The pair moves from diagnosis to counter-accusation.

**The Application: The Cost of the First Refusal**

The verse teaches the reader to take seriously the first act of rejection. The signs of God come constantly — in creation, in scripture, in the events of one's life — and each presents a choice: to accept what it shows or to explain it away. The one who habitually explains away finds that the signs stop speaking; "God does not guide" him, not by arbitrary decree but by the operation of the law the verse describes. The believer's discipline is the opposite habit: to receive each sign as a sign, to let it point where it points, and to follow. The Qur'an promises the reverse of verse 104 to those who do this: "Those who strive for Us — We will surely guide them to Our ways" (29:69). Between the two verses lies the whole difference between the accuser and the believer, and it begins in a single response to a single sign.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:105

> **Only they fabricate lies who believe not in the signs of God, and it is they who are the liars.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Charge Returned**

Verse 101 recorded the Makkans saying to the Prophet ﷺ, "You are only a fabricator." Verse 105 returns the charge to its authors: *innamā yaftarī al-kadhiba alladhīna lā yuʾminūna bi-āyāti Allāh*, "only those who do not believe in the signs of God fabricate lies." The verse uses the same restrictive particle the Makkans used — *innamā*, "only" — and the same verb — *iftarā*, to fabricate — and applies them to the accusers. The rhetorical move is exact: the accusation is not merely denied but reversed, and the reversal is grounded in a principle about who lies and why.

**"Only They Fabricate Lies Who Believe Not in the Signs of God"**

The verse states a general truth: fabrication of lies is the characteristic act of those who do not believe in God's signs. The commentators explain the logic. The one who believes in God's signs — who knows that God sees, hears, and will judge (vv. 19, 23, 56) — is restrained from lying by that belief. Lying is possible for him, but it is against the grain of his faith, and when he lies he knows he has betrayed something. The one who does not believe in God's signs has no such restraint. He does not fear the reckoning; he does not believe his words are recorded; he lies as freely as advantage dictates. Fabrication is thus the *natural* act of the disbeliever, and the *unnatural* act of the believer.

Al-Rāzī states the argument as it applies to the Prophet. The Makkans knew the Prophet to be truthful; they had called him *al-Amīn*, the trustworthy, for forty years before his mission. A man who never lied about small worldly matters would not suddenly lie about God — the gravest lie possible. The Prophet believed in God's signs more firmly than anyone; therefore, by the verse's principle, he was the last person who would fabricate. The Makkans, on the other hand, did not believe in God's signs; therefore, by the same principle, they were the ones prone to fabrication — and their fabrications were on record: the idols' divinity (v. 56), God's daughters (v. 57), the "legends of the ancients" (v. 24), the theory of the foreign teacher (v. 103).

The Prophet ﷺ articulated the same principle when asked whether a believer could be a coward or a miser; he said yes to both. Asked whether a believer could be a liar, he said no (Mālik, *al-Muwaṭṭaʾ*, 2:990). Lying is incompatible with faith in a way that other faults are not, because it is a direct assault on truth, and faith is the acceptance of truth. The verse states this incompatibility as a rule.

**Heraclius's Question**

The commentators connect the verse's principle to a famous historical episode. When Abū Sufyān — then still an enemy of the Prophet — was questioned by the Byzantine emperor Heraclius about the Prophet's claims, one of Heraclius's questions was whether they had ever accused him of lying before he made his claim. Abū Sufyān said no. Heraclius replied:

> *"I asked you whether you had ever accused him of lying before he said what he said, and you said no. So I knew that he would not refrain from lying about people and then lie about God."* (al-Bukhārī 7; Muslim 1773)

Heraclius reasoned exactly as verse 105 reasons: a man of established truthfulness does not fabricate about God. The emperor, a stranger to Islam, reached the verse's conclusion by ordinary inference, and the Makkans, who knew the Prophet far better, refused to.

**"And It Is They Who Are the Liars": The Emphatic Close**

The verse ends: *wa-ulāʾika humu al-kādhibūn*, "and those — they are the liars." The construction is maximally emphatic: the demonstrative *ulāʾika*, the pronoun of separation *hum*, and the definite article *al-kādhibūn* together assert that these people are the liars *par excellence*, the ones who deserve the name. Al-Zamakhsharī notes the force: it is not merely that they lie sometimes but that they are *the* liars — lying is their identity, and the accusation of lying, which they leveled at the Prophet, belongs properly to them.

The word *kādhibūn* has been used before in the sūrah: verse 39 said God will show the disbelievers "that they were liars," and verse 86 showed the partners casting the word back at the idolaters: "you are liars." Verse 105 completes the thread: the liars are identified, in this world, as those who do not believe in God's signs, and their identification as such will be confirmed on the Day when their fabrications vanish (v. 87).

**The Distinction Between Fabricating and Being Mistaken**

The commentators note that the verse speaks of *fabricating lies* — *iftirāʾ al-kadhib* — not of being mistaken. Fabrication is deliberate: the fabricator knows what he says is false and says it anyway, to deceive. The Makkans who said "a human teaches him" knew it was not true; they had no evidence and had seen the refutation; they said it to discredit. This is *iftirāʾ*. The verse does not condemn honest error, which the Qur'an treats differently (33:5, "there is no blame upon you for that in which you have erred"); it condemns deliberate falsehood, which is the act of those who do not believe they will be called to account for it.

**The Verse as the Conclusion of the Passage**

Verses 101–105 form a passage on the origin of the Qur'an and the accusations against it. Verse 101 recorded the charge of fabrication. Verse 102 stated the true origin — the Holy Spirit from the Lord in truth. Verse 103 refuted the specific theory of a foreign teacher. Verse 104 pronounced the accusers unguided and doomed. Verse 105 returned the charge: the fabricators are the accusers. The passage thus moves from charge to answer to counter-charge, and ends with the accusers' own word — *muftar*, fabricator — hung around their necks. Al-Rāzī observes that the passage is a model of how the Qur'an handles slander: it does not merely deny but identifies the source of the slander in the slanderer's own condition, so that the slander becomes evidence against him.

**The Broader Principle: Faith and Truthfulness**

The verse establishes a connection that the tradition made central to Islamic ethics: faith and truthfulness are inseparable. The Qur'an calls the believers *al-ṣādiqūn*, the truthful (9:119; 49:15; 59:8), and commands them to "be with the truthful" (9:119). The Prophet ﷺ said:

> *"Truthfulness leads to righteousness, and righteousness leads to Paradise; a man keeps telling the truth until he is recorded with God as truthful. And lying leads to wickedness, and wickedness leads to the Fire; a man keeps lying until he is recorded with God as a liar."* (al-Bukhārī 6094; Muslim 2607)

"Recorded with God as a liar" — this is the *al-kādhibūn* of verse 105. The verse describes the destination of a path; the hadith describes the path. Both teach that lying is not a minor fault but a sign of the absence of faith, and that the liar and the believer are, in the end, two different kinds of person.

**The Application: Truthfulness as the Mark of Faith**

The verse asks the believer to see his own truthfulness as an expression of his faith and his lies as a betrayal of it. The one who believes in God's signs — who knows that God hears every word and will bring every word to account — has, in that belief, the strongest possible motive for truthfulness, and the verse says that fabrication belongs to those who lack it. In practice, the verse addresses every temptation to lie for advantage, to slander an opponent, to invent an accusation, or to distort the truth for a cause: each is *iftirāʾ*, and each is, in the verse's judgment, the act of one who does not truly believe he will be questioned. The believer who wishes to be counted among those who believe in God's signs has, in the verse, a simple test: does he fabricate? If not, he has passed; and if so, the verse tells him where the habit leads and whose company it places him in.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:106

> **Whosoever disbelieves in God after having believed—save one who is coerced, while his heart is at peace in faith—but whosoever opens his breast unto disbelief, upon them shall be the Wrath of God, and theirs shall be a great punishment.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Verse of Coercion**

Verses 101–105 addressed those who accused the Qur'an of fabrication. Verse 106 turns to a matter that pressed on the Makkan Muslims with terrible urgency: what happens to the believer who, under torture, utters words of disbelief? The verse answers with a distinction that has governed Islamic law and ethics ever since — between the one who is coerced while his heart remains at peace in faith, and the one who opens his breast to disbelief. The verse is among the most consequential in the sūrah for the lives of persecuted believers, and its occasion of revelation is one of the most moving in the *sīrah*.

**The Occasion: ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir**

The commentators are nearly unanimous that the verse was revealed concerning ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir. His family were among the earliest Muslims and among the most defenseless — clients of the Banū Makhzūm with no tribal protection. The Makkans tortured them in the sun. ʿAmmār's father Yāsir died under torture; his mother Sumayyah was killed by Abū Jahl with a spear — the first martyr of Islam. ʿAmmār himself was tortured until, according to the reports, he said what they demanded: he spoke well of their gods and spoke ill of the Prophet ﷺ.

Al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Wāḥidī, and others record what followed. ʿAmmār came to the Prophet weeping. The Prophet asked what had happened, and ʿAmmār told him. The Prophet asked:

> *"How do you find your heart?"* ʿAmmār said: *"At peace in faith."* The Prophet said: *"Then if they return, you return."* (al-Ḥākim, al-Mustadrak 3362; al-Bayhaqī; the report is graded ṣaḥīḥ by al-Ḥākim and accepted by the commentators)

And the verse was revealed: "save one who is coerced, while his heart is at peace in faith." The Prophet's question — "how do you find your heart?" — and ʿAmmār's answer — "at peace in faith" — are the verse's exception in dialogue. The Prophet's permission — "if they return, you return" — is the legal ruling that the verse establishes.

Some commentators add that the people said, "ʿAmmār has disbelieved," and the Prophet replied: "No; ʿAmmār is filled with faith from his crown to his feet; faith has mingled with his flesh and blood" (Ibn Mājah 147; Ibn Saʿd). The community's judgment was corrected by the Prophet's, and the verse confirmed the Prophet's.

**The Structure of the Verse**

The verse's grammar is complex and has been much discussed. It begins *man kafara bi'llāhi min baʿdi īmānihi*, "whoever disbelieves in God after his faith" — a conditional whose apodosis (the "then" clause) is delayed. It then inserts the exception: *illā man ukriha wa-qalbuhu muṭmaʾinnun bi'l-īmān*, "except one who is coerced while his heart is at peace in faith." Then it resumes with a second subject: *wa-lākin man sharaḥa bi'l-kufri ṣadran*, "but whoever opens his breast to disbelief." And only then comes the apodosis: *fa-ʿalayhim ghaḍabun mina Allāhi wa-lahum ʿadhābun ʿaẓīm*, "upon them is wrath from God, and theirs is a great punishment."

The commentators explain that the apodosis governs both the first subject (whoever disbelieves after faith) and the second (whoever opens his breast to disbelief), and that the exception (the coerced) is removed from both. The effect is to define three cases: the apostate who freely disbelieves after faith — wrath and punishment; the coerced whose heart remains firm — excepted, no wrath; and the one who opens his breast to disbelief — wrath and punishment. The second case is the verse's focus; the first and third frame it. Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Rāzī trace this structure and note that the delay of the apodosis creates suspense that heightens the exception's prominence: the reader hears "whoever disbelieves after faith" and braces for the sentence, and then hears "except one who is coerced" before the sentence falls.

An alternative construction, recorded by al-Ṭabarī, takes the first clause as connected to the preceding verse: "only those fabricate lies who do not believe... [and] whoever disbelieves after faith" — making the apostate a further instance of the fabricator. The majority read the verse as self-contained.

**"Whosoever Disbelieves in God After Having Believed": Apostasy**

The first case is *man kafara bi'llāhi min baʿdi īmānihi*, the one who disbelieves after having believed — the apostate. The commentators note the gravity implied by "after his faith": this is not the disbelief of one who never knew, but the abandonment of a faith once held. The Qur'an treats it as the gravest turning-away (2:217; 3:86–91; 4:137; 47:25–28). The verse's structure places this case under the sentence of wrath, but immediately qualifies it: not every utterance of disbelief after faith is apostasy.

**"Save One Who Is Coerced": *Ukriha***

The exception is *illā man ukriha*, "except one who is coerced." The verb *akraha* means to force, to compel against one's will. *Ikrāh*, coercion, is the state of one whose choice has been removed by threat of grave harm. The jurists defined the coercion that excuses: a credible threat of death, severe injury, or comparable harm, from one who has the power to carry it out, with no reasonable means of escape. Al-Qurṭubī discusses the definitions at length. The torture of ʿAmmār — under which his parents had already died — was the paradigm case.

The exception establishes a principle that the commentators regarded as fundamental: God does not hold a person responsible for what he is forced to do. The Prophet ﷺ stated it generally:

> *"God has pardoned my community for error, forgetfulness, and what they are coerced into."* (Ibn Mājah 2045; al-Bayhaqī; graded ḥasan)

Words uttered under coercion are not the person's own; they are the coercer's, extracted through the victim's mouth. God, who looks at hearts (v. 19, 23), does not judge by the extracted word.

**"While His Heart Is at Peace in Faith": *Muṭmaʾinn bi'l-īmān***

The exception has a condition: *wa-qalbuhu muṭmaʾinnun bi'l-īmān*, "while his heart is at peace in faith." The word *muṭmaʾinn*, from *iṭmaʾanna*, to be tranquil, at rest, settled, describes a heart that is not disturbed — that has not moved from its faith even as the tongue moved. The coerced person's tongue says what the torturer demands; his heart remains where it was.

This condition is what makes the exception coherent. Faith, in the Qur'an's anthropology, is located in the heart (49:14, "faith has not yet entered your hearts"; 58:22, "He has written faith in their hearts"). The tongue expresses faith but does not constitute it. If the heart's faith is intact, the tongue's words under coercion do not touch it. Al-Rāzī: the verse establishes that faith is the heart's assent, and that the tongue's confession is its outward sign, which may be suspended under duress without the reality being affected. This is why the Prophet's question to ʿAmmār was about his *heart*: "How do you find your heart?" The state of the heart was the whole matter.

**The Debate: Is It Better to Speak or to Refuse?**

The verse permits the coerced person to utter words of disbelief. The jurists asked whether it is better to use the permission or to refuse and die. Al-Qurṭubī records the discussion. The majority held that using the permission is *permitted* (*rukhṣah*), and that refusing and dying is *better* (*ʿazīmah*) — the higher path of one who will not let his tongue say what his heart denies, even at the cost of his life. The example cited is Bilāl, who under the same torture refused to say anything but *Aḥad, Aḥad* — "One, One" — and whose refusal the Prophet praised. Others cited Khubayb ibn ʿAdī, who was crucified by the Makkans and, offered his life in exchange for wishing that the Prophet were in his place, replied that he would not wish the Prophet pricked by a thorn to save himself. Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī is reported to have said that the concession applies to speech but not to acts of idolatry, since the heart's peace cannot be maintained through prostration to an idol.

The commentators agree that both paths are honorable. ʿAmmār took the concession and was declared full of faith; Bilāl took the higher path and was praised. The verse establishes the concession as valid so that no believer is condemned for taking it; the tradition establishes the higher path as praiseworthy so that no believer is discouraged from choosing it. Al-Rāzī notes that the choice depends on the person and the circumstances: the concession protects the weak and the many; the higher path is for those God strengthens for it.

**The Extension to Other Coercion**

The jurists extended the principle of the verse to coercion in other matters — the coerced divorce, the coerced sale, the coerced confession — holding, by analogy, that acts extracted by valid coercion are not binding. Al-Qurṭubī discusses these applications. The verse thus became the foundation of an entire chapter of Islamic law on *ikrāh*, all of it flowing from the recognition that God excused ʿAmmār.

**"But Whosoever Opens His Breast Unto Disbelief": *Sharaḥa bi'l-kufri ṣadran***

The third case is *man sharaḥa bi'l-kufri ṣadran*, "whoever opens his breast to disbelief." The verb *sharaḥa* means to open, to expand, to lay open — the Qur'an uses it for God's opening the breast to Islam (6:125; 39:22; 94:1, "Did We not expand for you your breast?"). Here it is used in the opposite direction: the one who opens his breast to *kufr* — who welcomes it, is content with it, makes room for it. This is the true apostate: not the one whose tongue was forced but the one whose heart consented. Al-Ṭabarī: the one who opens his breast to disbelief is the one who chose it, whose heart embraced it, whether under pressure or not.

The contrast with the exception is exact. The coerced believer's *heart* is at peace in faith; the apostate's *breast* is open to disbelief. The verse thus locates the whole difference in the interior. Two people may say the same words under the same torture; one has a heart at rest in faith and is excused; the other has opened his breast to disbelief and is condemned. Only God sees which is which — and the verse's structure tells the community not to judge the coerced by his words, as the Prophet told those who said "ʿAmmār has disbelieved."

**"Upon Them Shall Be the Wrath of God, and Theirs Shall Be a Great Punishment"**

The sentence on the apostate and the one who opens his breast to disbelief is *ʿalayhim ghaḍabun mina Allāhi wa-lahum ʿadhābun ʿaẓīm*, "upon them is wrath from God, and theirs is a great punishment." Divine wrath (*ghaḍab*) is named — the strongest term for God's displeasure, used in the Fātiḥah for "those who have incurred wrath" (1:7) — and the punishment is *ʿaẓīm*, great. The commentators note that the severity corresponds to the offense: to have known the truth and freely abandoned it is worse than never to have known it, and the punishment reflects this.

**The Verse's Mercy and Its Severity Together**

The verse holds mercy and severity in a single sentence, and the commentators regard this combination as its genius. Its mercy: the persecuted believer, broken by torture, is not lost; God looks at his heart, and if his heart is at peace in faith, the words extracted from him do not count. This mercy sustained the Makkan Muslims under persecution and has sustained persecuted believers in every age since. Its severity: the one who freely abandons faith — who opens his breast to disbelief — faces God's wrath. This severity protects the faith from being treated as a garment to be put on and off at convenience. The verse's structure places the mercy *inside* the severity — as an exception within a sentence of wrath — so that the reader understands both: the sentence is real, and the exception is real, and the difference between them is the state of the heart.

**The Application: The Heart as the Seat of Faith**

The verse teaches every believer what faith is and where it lives. It lives in the heart. The tongue confesses it, the limbs enact it, but the heart holds it, and the heart's hold is what God judges. This has consequences beyond the case of coercion. It means that the believer's first care must be the state of his heart — that his outward practice, however correct, is not the whole of his religion, and that a heart "at peace in faith" is the treasure the verse protects. And it means that the believer should extend to others the judgment the Prophet extended to ʿAmmār: not to condemn on the basis of words extracted under pressure, and to remember that only God sees whether a breast is open to disbelief or a heart is at rest in faith. The verse was revealed to comfort a young man weeping at what he had been made to say. Its comfort has not expired.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:107

> **That is because they preferred the life of this world over the Hereafter, and because God guides not the disbelieving people.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Reason Behind the Wrath**

Verse 106 pronounced God's wrath and a great punishment upon those who open their breasts to disbelief. Verse 107 explains why they did so: *dhālika bi-annahumu istaḥabbū al-ḥayāta al-dunyā ʿalā al-ākhirah*, "that is because they preferred the life of this world over the Hereafter." The verse names the motive behind apostasy — and behind the disbelief of those who never believed — as a preference: a choice of this world over the next. And it names the consequence of that preference: God does not guide such people.

**"That Is Because": The Explanatory *Dhālika***

The verse begins *dhālika*, "that," referring to the wrath and punishment of the previous verse, followed by *bi-anna*, "because." The construction gives the reason for the sentence. The commentators note that the Qur'an frequently follows a judgment with its cause in this form (2:61; 3:112; 8:13, 51; 22:6), so that the reader understands the judgment as just — not arbitrary but the consequence of something the person did. Here the cause is a preference, and the preference is the root of the whole condition.

**"They Preferred the Life of This World Over the Hereafter": *Istaḥabbū***

The verb *istaḥabba* is the tenth form of *ḥabba*, to love; it means to prefer, to choose out of love, to love one thing more than another. The apostates and disbelievers *preferred* — loved more — *al-ḥayāt al-dunyā*, the life of this world, over *al-ākhirah*, the Hereafter. The word *dunyā* means "the nearer," "the lower" — this life is called *dunyā* because it is near at hand and because it is low in comparison with what follows.

The commentators draw out the relevance to the case of apostasy. The one who opens his breast to disbelief under pressure — as distinct from the coerced whose heart remains firm — does so because he values his life, his property, his position, his comfort in this world more than he values the Hereafter. When faced with a choice between the two, he chooses this world. Al-Rāzī: the apostate's act reveals his valuation; he has weighed the two lives and found this one heavier. The verse names this weighing as the root sin.

The Qur'an uses the same verb for the same preference elsewhere:

> *"O you who believe, do not take your fathers and your brothers as allies if they prefer (istaḥabbū) disbelief over faith."* (Qur'an 9:23)

> *"Those who prefer (yastaḥibbūna) the life of this world over the Hereafter and avert [people] from the way of God, seeking to make it crooked — those are in extreme error."* (Qur'an 14:3)

> *"As for he who transgressed and preferred (āthara) the life of this world, then truly Hell will be his refuge."* (Qur'an 79:37–39)

The verse in Ibrāhīm (14:3) is closest: the preference for this world is coupled with turning others from God's way — as verse 88 of this sūrah named — and is called "extreme error." The preference is not a minor disposition; it is the root of the disbeliever's whole orientation.

**The Preference as the Root of All Disbelief**

The commentators generalized the verse's diagnosis beyond apostasy. Al-Rāzī observes that every form of rejecting the truth can be traced to this preference. The Makkan chiefs rejected the Prophet because his message threatened their position in this world. The idolaters clung to their gods because the gods were tied to their trade, their prestige, and their inherited order. The one who fabricates lies (v. 105) does so for worldly gain. The one who breaks his oath (v. 92–95) does so for a "paltry price." In every case, the choice of this world over the next is the operative motive, and disbelief is its rationalization. The verse names the motive because the motive, not the argument, is what must be addressed. A person who prefers this world will not be moved by proofs of the next, however strong, because his preference has already decided the matter.

**"And Because God Guides Not the Disbelieving People"**

The verse's second clause gives a second reason: *wa-anna Allāha lā yahdī al-qawma al-kāfirīn*, "and because God does not guide the disbelieving people." The clause repeats verse 104's principle and applies it to the case at hand. The commentators read the two clauses as a sequence. First, the person prefers this world over the Hereafter — this is his act. Then, God does not guide him — this is the consequence. The preference for this world, once settled, closes the heart to guidance, and God, who guides those who seek Him, leaves the one who has chosen otherwise in what he chose. Ibn Kathīr and al-Ṭabarī read the clause in this way.

The phrase *al-qawm al-kāfirīn*, "the disbelieving people," describes them by their settled state. As at verse 104, "God does not guide" the disbelievers means that guidance is withheld from those who have rejected it — not that God prevents anyone from believing who wishes to. The commentators note that the phrase is a description, not a decree: those who *are* disbelievers are not guided *as long as* they remain so; the door is not shut to one who turns. The following verses (108–110) will describe the sealing of hearts and then, immediately, the forgiveness of those who repent — the two possibilities side by side.

**The Two Loves and the Human Heart**

The commentators reflected on why the preference for this world is so powerful and so dangerous. This world is present; the Hereafter is promised. This world is seen; the Hereafter is unseen. This world's rewards are immediate; the Hereafter's are deferred. Every natural inclination favors the near over the far, and the Qur'an acknowledges this: "You love the fleeting and leave the Hereafter" (75:20–21); "Rather, you prefer the life of this world, while the Hereafter is better and more lasting" (87:16–17). The human being is not condemned for feeling the pull of the world; he is condemned for *settling* the matter in the world's favor — for making the preference his fixed orientation, so that when faith and the world conflict, faith loses.

The remedy the Qur'an prescribes is the correction of the valuation: to see this world as it is — small, fleeting, "the enjoyment of delusion" (3:185) — and the Hereafter as it is — "better and more lasting" (87:17; cf. 16:96, "what is with you runs out, and what is with God remains"). The Prophet ﷺ taught the correction in his own life and in his sayings:

> *"What have I to do with this world? I and this world are but as a rider who takes shade under a tree, then departs and leaves it."* (al-Tirmidhī 2377; Ibn Mājah 4109)

> *"If this world were worth the wing of a gnat to God, He would not have given a disbeliever a drink of water from it."* (al-Tirmidhī 2320)

The one who has absorbed this valuation cannot be made to apostatize, because the world the persecutor threatens to take from him is not, in his estimation, worth keeping at the price of the Hereafter. This is what the martyrs knew, and what the verse says the apostate did not.

**The Verse and the Context of Persecution**

In the immediate context, the verse addresses the Makkan Muslims who were being pressured to abandon Islam. It tells them what the choice before them really is: not "faith or death" but "this world or the Hereafter." Framed this way, the choice becomes clear. The one who is coerced and whose heart remains firm (v. 106) has not preferred this world; he has only used a concession God gave him, and his heart's preference is for the Hereafter. The one who opens his breast to disbelief has preferred this world, and the verse names the preference as the reason for his sentence. The distinction between the two lies entirely in which life the heart loves more.

**The Application: Auditing the Preference**

The verse asks the reader to examine his own valuation. When faith and worldly interest conflict — in small matters as well as large — which does he choose? The pattern of small choices reveals the settled preference, and the settled preference is what the verse says God judges. The remedy, if the audit reveals a preference for the world, is not despair but correction: the deliberate cultivation of the opposite valuation, through remembrance of death, reflection on the world's fleetingness, and the study of what God has promised. The Prophet ﷺ prescribed: "Remember often the destroyer of pleasures — death" (al-Tirmidhī 2307). The remembrance of death is the practical means by which the preference for this world is loosened, and the verse's warning is the reason it must be.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:108

> **It is they upon whose hearts, hearing, and sight God has set a seal; and it is they who are the heedless.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Faculties Sealed**

Verse 107 explained the apostates' condition by their preference for this world and God's withholding of guidance. Verse 108 describes what the withholding looks like: *ulāʾika alladhīna ṭabaʿa Allāhu ʿalā qulūbihim wa-samʿihim wa-abṣārihim*, "those are the ones upon whose hearts, hearing, and sight God has set a seal." The three faculties named are exactly the three that verse 78 named as God's gifts to the newborn — hearing, sight, and hearts — given "that you may be grateful." Verse 108 shows what becomes of the faculties when they are used for the opposite of gratitude: they are sealed.

**"God Has Set a Seal": *Ṭabaʿa***

The verb *ṭabaʿa* means to stamp, to impress a seal upon, to close with a seal. The image is of a vessel or a letter sealed shut so that nothing enters or leaves. Applied to the heart, it describes a heart closed to guidance — one into which no light penetrates and from which no response emerges. The Qur'an uses this verb and its synonym *khatama* (2:7, "God has set a seal upon their hearts") for the same condition.

The theological question the verse raises was discussed at verses 22, 37, 93, and 104: if God seals the heart, how is the person responsible? The commentators of all schools answer with the sequence the sūrah itself establishes. Verse 107 gave the cause: they preferred this world. Verse 108 gives the effect: God sealed. The seal follows the preference; it does not precede it. Al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Kathīr read the verse thus: because they chose this world and turned from guidance, God sealed the faculties they had refused to use. Al-Zamakhsharī, from the Muʿtazilī side, reads the seal as God's *abandoning* them to their choice, or as a description of the hardened state they produced in themselves, attributed to God as the one who created the law by which such hardening occurs. Al-Rāzī, from the Ashʿarī side, affirms that God is the creator of the seal as He is of all things, while insisting that the sealed are justly punished because the seal is the consequence of what they earned.

The Qur'an states the sequence explicitly elsewhere: "So when they deviated, God caused their hearts to deviate" (61:5); "They said: Our hearts are wrapped. Rather, God has cursed them for their disbelief" (2:88); "Rather, God has sealed them because of their disbelief" (4:155). In each case, the seal is *because of* (*bi-*) something the person did. Verse 108's seal is because of verse 107's preference.

**The Three Faculties**

The verse names three faculties, and the commentators trace each.

*Qulūbihim*, "their hearts" — the seat of understanding and assent, discussed at verse 78. A sealed heart does not understand what it hears and does not assent to what it understands. The Qur'an describes such hearts as "hardened like stones, or harder" (2:74).

*Samʿihim*, "their hearing" — the channel through which revelation reaches the heart. A sealed hearing hears sounds but not meaning; the Qur'an is recited and the person hears words without receiving them. The Qur'an says of the disbelievers that God "placed over their ears a deafness" (6:25; 17:46; 18:57).

*Abṣārihim*, "their sight" — the channel through which the signs of creation reach the heart. A sealed sight sees the rain, the cattle, the bee, the birds — everything the sūrah has displayed — and sees nothing in them. The Qur'an says "over their sight is a covering" (2:7; 45:23).

The commentators note the order. The heart is named first, though in verse 78 hearing came first. Al-Rāzī explains: in verse 78 the order was that of acquisition — hearing develops first, then sight, then understanding. In verse 108 the order is that of corruption — the heart is corrupted first, by its preference for this world, and then the hearing and sight, which serve the heart, are sealed as a consequence. The disorder of the faculties begins in the heart and spreads outward. This is why the Prophet ﷺ said that the heart is the organ on which the whole body depends: "If it is sound, the whole body is sound; if it is corrupt, the whole body is corrupt" (al-Bukhārī 52; Muslim 1599).

**The Reversal of Verse 78**

The commentators observed the deliberate symmetry between verses 78 and 108. Verse 78: God brought you forth knowing nothing and gave you hearing, sight, and hearts, that you may be grateful. Verse 108: those who preferred this world — God sealed their hearts, hearing, and sight, and they are the heedless. The gift and its forfeiture are stated in the same terms. The faculties were given for gratitude; used for ingratitude, they are sealed. The one who was born knowing nothing (v. 78) and given the means to know, and who used the means to reject knowledge, ends in a state worse than the ignorance he began in — not the innocent ignorance of the infant but the culpable ignorance of the sealed. Al-Rāzī reads the pairing as a warning about the faculties: they are not permanent possessions; they are instruments that God gave and can render useless.

**"And It Is They Who Are the Heedless": *Al-Ghāfilūn***

The verse ends: *wa-ulāʾika humu al-ghāfilūn*, "and those — they are the heedless." The word *ghāfil*, from *ghaflah*, heedlessness, negligence, denotes one who is unaware — whose attention is elsewhere, who does not notice what is before him. The sealed are *the* heedless: their inattention is total and settled. The emphatic construction (*ulāʾika humu*) marks them as the heedless *par excellence*, as verse 105 marked the fabricators as *the* liars.

The commentators explain the connection between the seal and heedlessness. The sealed heart is not aware that it is sealed. The one whose faculties have been closed does not experience himself as blind and deaf; he experiences himself as seeing and hearing normally, and the truth as simply absent. This is *ghaflah*: not the consciousness of missing something but the unconsciousness that anything is missed. Al-Rāzī: the heedless person is heedless of his own heedlessness, and this is what makes the condition so grave — there is no internal alarm to prompt a search for what is lost.

The Qur'an describes the heedless as those whom the signs pass by unnoticed: "How many a sign in the heavens and the earth do they pass by, while they turn away from it" (12:105). And it warns the believers against sliding into the same state: "Do not be among the heedless" (7:205). Heedlessness is presented as the ordinary condition of the disbeliever and the constant danger of the believer.

**The Verse in Its Immediate Context**

Verse 108 describes the apostate of verse 106 — the one who opened his breast to disbelief — in his final condition: sealed and heedless. The commentators note that this is not the description of the coerced believer whose heart remained at peace. His heart was not sealed; his heart was the very thing that saved him. The contrast between the two cases in verse 106 is now drawn to its conclusion: one heart at peace in faith, the other sealed in heedlessness; one excused, the other condemned; and the whole difference in what each preferred.

**The Verse Is Not the Last Word**

The commentators are careful to note that verse 108 is followed immediately by verse 109 ("without doubt, in the Hereafter they are the losers") and then, in verse 110, by the promise of forgiveness to those who emigrated after persecution and struggled and were patient. The seal is described, but so is the way out. Al-Qurṭubī observes that the Qur'an never describes the sealed heart without, somewhere nearby, describing the open door — because the seal is a consequence of the preference for this world, and the preference can be reversed by anyone still alive. The seal is total for those who remain in it; it is not irreversible for those who turn. The Qur'an says of hearts that God "turns them" (6:110), and the Prophet ﷺ prayed constantly, "O Turner of hearts, make my heart firm upon Your religion" (al-Tirmidhī 2140) — a prayer that presupposes that hearts can be turned in either direction.

**The Application: Guarding the Faculties**

The verse asks the believer to see his hearing, sight, and heart as instruments held in trust — given for gratitude (v. 78), liable to be sealed if used for its opposite (v. 108). The practical discipline is the maintenance of the faculties in their intended use: to hear the Qur'an and the truth attentively; to look at the signs of creation with the attention verse 79 demanded; to keep the heart soft by remembrance, so that it does not harden. The Qur'an warns that hearts harden over time if left untended: "Has the time not come for those who have believed that their hearts should become humbly submissive at the remembrance of God... and not be like those who were given the Scripture before, and a long period passed over them, so their hearts hardened?" (57:16). The verse's *ghāfilūn*, the heedless, are those for whom the long period passed and the hardening was complete. The believer's task is to prevent the passage of that period in his own heart — to remain, in the Qur'an's phrase, among those "whose hearts tremble when God is mentioned" (8:2) rather than among those whose hearts have been sealed shut.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:109

> **Without doubt, in the Hereafter they are the losers.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Verdict Stated in Full Certainty**

Verse 108 described the apostates as sealed and heedless. Verse 109 states their end: *lā jarama annahum fī al-ākhirati humu al-khāsirūn*, "without doubt, in the Hereafter they are the losers." The verse is short — five words in Arabic — and its brevity is its force. After the description of the preference (v. 107) and the seal (v. 108), nothing remains to be argued. The verdict is delivered as a settled fact, introduced by the phrase of certainty and closed by the emphatic identification of the losers.

**"Without Doubt": *Lā Jarama***

The phrase *lā jarama* opens the verse for the third time in the sūrah (vv. 23, 62, 109). Its sense was discussed at verse 23: "no doubt," "assuredly," "it is inevitable," with a background sense of something *earned* — the root *j-r-m* concerns earning and cutting off, so that *lā jarama* carries the connotation "it has been earned; there is no escaping it." Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Rāzī note that the phrase functions like an oath: what follows is as certain as if sworn.

The three occurrences of *lā jarama* in the sūrah mark three verdicts, and the commentators note their progression. Verse 23: without doubt, God knows what they conceal and what they reveal — the verdict of *knowledge*. Verse 62: without doubt, theirs is the Fire, and they will be hastened into it — the verdict of *punishment*. Verse 109: without doubt, in the Hereafter they are the losers — the verdict of *loss*. God knows; God punishes; and the result is total loss. The three phrases trace the whole arc from divine awareness to final consequence.

**"In the Hereafter": *Fī al-Ākhirah***

The verdict is located *fī al-ākhirah*, "in the Hereafter." The commentators explain the specification. Verse 107 said the apostates preferred this world over the Hereafter. Verse 109 says that in the Hereafter — the very thing they traded away — they are the losers. The specification makes the loss correspond exactly to the choice. They chose this world; whatever they gained in it is theirs for a time (v. 55, "enjoy yourselves"); but in the Hereafter, which they sold, they have nothing. Al-Rāzī: the verse names the location of the loss to show that the transaction was a loss *precisely where it mattered* — the apostate may have kept his life and property in this world, but he lost the world that lasts.

The commentators also note that the verse does not say they are losers in *this* world. The apostate under pressure may have gained — his life spared, his property kept, his position restored. The Qur'an does not deny this; verse 107 acknowledges that they *preferred* this world, which implies they got something of it. The verse's point is that the gain was in the wrong currency. What is with you runs out (v. 96); the Hereafter remains; and the one who is a loser there has lost everything that does not run out.

**"They Are the Losers": *Humu al-Khāsirūn***

The verse closes with *humu al-khāsirūn*, "they are *the* losers" — the emphatic construction, with the pronoun of separation and the definite article, that marks them as the losers *par excellence*, as verse 105 marked the liars and verse 108 the heedless. The three emphatic identifications in successive verses — the liars, the heedless, the losers — build a portrait of the apostate's condition from three angles: his speech is false, his faculties are closed, and his end is loss.

The word *khāsir*, loser, is from the root *kh-s-r*, which denotes loss in a transaction — the merchant who invests and comes away with less than he put in. The Qur'an uses the commercial metaphor for the whole of human life: the human being is given a capital (life, faculties, time) and trades with it, and the result is profit or loss. "By time, truly the human being is in loss (*khusr*), except those who believe and do righteous deeds and enjoin one another to truth and to patience" (103:1–3). The apostate is the trader who lost the capital itself — not merely failing to profit but losing what he was given.

The commentators explain the magnitude of the loss. The apostate had faith — the most valuable thing a human being can possess — and traded it for this world. He lost the faith; he lost the Hereafter that faith would have earned; and the world he gained will run out. His loss is therefore *total*: he has nothing left in either currency. Al-Zamakhsharī: the loss of the apostate exceeds the loss of the one who never believed, because the apostate had the capital in hand and threw it away. The Qur'an describes this specific loss: "Whoever disbelieves after his faith — his deeds have become worthless, and in the Hereafter he is among the losers" (5:5; cf. 2:217, "their deeds have become worthless in this world and the Hereafter"). The apostate's *previous* good deeds are also lost — the capital of years of worship, erased by the final transaction.

**The Loss and the Coerced Believer**

The commentators once more contrast the apostate with the coerced believer of verse 106. The coerced believer, whose heart remained at peace in faith, lost nothing — not his faith, not his deeds, not the Hereafter. He may have lost, for a moment, the ability to speak his faith aloud; but he kept everything that counts, and the Prophet declared him "filled with faith from crown to foot." The apostate, whose breast opened to disbelief, lost everything. The two stood under the same torture; one came out a loser and the other did not; and the difference was in what the heart held. Verse 109 is the final word on the first; verse 110 will be the final word on the second.

**Why the Verdict Is Brief**

The commentators reflected on the verse's brevity. After the extended description of verses 106–108, the verdict is delivered in a single short sentence. Al-Rāzī suggests that the brevity conveys finality: there is nothing more to say. The preference has been named, the seal described, the heedlessness identified; the consequence follows automatically and is stated without elaboration, as a judge pronounces sentence after the evidence has been heard. The verse's economy is the economy of a closed case.

There is also a rhetorical effect: the short verse, standing between the long verse 108 and the long verse 110, is a hinge. It closes the account of the apostate and opens the way to the account of the faithful emigrants. The reader who has followed the descent — preference, seal, heedlessness, loss — is now turned toward the ascent that the next verse describes.

**The Application: Counting the Cost**

The verse asks the reader to reckon as the apostate failed to reckon. Every choice between faith and the world is a transaction, and the verse names the outcome of choosing the world: loss in the Hereafter, without doubt. The believer who is tempted — not necessarily to formal apostasy, but to any of the smaller apostasies by which faith is compromised for gain — is asked to look at the ledger: what is gained (something that runs out) and what is lost (something that remains). The Qur'an's commercial language is meant to be taken literally: the believer is a trader, his faith is his capital, and the verse describes the bankruptcy of the one who spends it on the world. The Prophet ﷺ described the alternative trader: "Everyone goes out in the morning and sells his soul — either freeing it or destroying it" (Muslim 223). The apostate destroyed his; the verse records the loss; and the reader, who goes out every morning to the same market, is told the price of the wrong sale.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:110

> **Then truly thy Lord—for those who emigrated after having been persecuted, then struggled and were patient—truly thy Lord, after that, is Forgiving, Merciful.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Other Side of the Persecution**

Verses 106–109 described those who, under pressure, opened their breasts to disbelief and were sealed and lost. Verse 110 turns to those who, under the same pressure, held fast: *thumma inna rabbaka li'lladhīna hājarū min baʿdi mā futinū thumma jāhadū wa-ṣabarū*, "then truly your Lord — for those who emigrated after they were persecuted, then struggled and were patient." The verse names three acts — emigration, struggle, patience — and promises, with a repeated and emphatic *inna rabbaka*, that God is Forgiving and Merciful toward those who performed them. The passage on persecution thus ends not with the losers but with the forgiven.

**The Structure: The Repeated *Inna Rabbaka***

The verse's grammar has a notable feature: the phrase *inna rabbaka*, "truly your Lord," appears twice — at the beginning and again before the predicate — with the description of the emigrants between. Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Rāzī explain the repetition as emphasis: the intervening description is long, and the second *inna rabbaka* resumes the sentence and restores its force, so that the predicate — "Forgiving, Merciful" — lands with full weight. The effect is to frame the emigrants' deeds between two assertions of God's lordship, so that their emigration, struggle, and patience are seen as enclosed in His care.

The word *thumma*, "then," at the verse's beginning marks a transition from the preceding case. The commentators read it as a *thumma* of sequence in discourse rather than time: "having said that about the apostates, now [hear this] about the emigrants."

**"Those Who Emigrated After Having Been Persecuted": *Hājarū min baʿdi mā futinū***

The first act is *hājarū*, "they emigrated." The word was discussed at verse 41, where the emigrants were promised "a good place in this world" and a greater reward in the Hereafter. Verse 110 returns to them with a specific qualification: *min baʿdi mā futinū*, "after they had been persecuted." The verb *futina* is from *fitnah*, trial, temptation, persecution — originally the testing of gold by fire, and by extension any severe trial that tests what a person is made of. To be *maftūn* is to be subjected to such a trial — here, the torture and pressure by which the Makkans tried to force the believers back to idolatry.

The commentators discussed who these emigrants were, and the discussion illuminates the verse. Some identified them as the Companions who emigrated to Abyssinia after persecution. Others identified them with those who emigrated to Madinah. But al-Ṭabarī, al-Wāḥidī, and al-Qurṭubī record a more specific occasion that fits the verse's placement after verse 106: the verse concerns those Muslims who had been *forced to utter disbelief* under torture — like ʿAmmār — and who then emigrated. The verse tells them that their coerced words are forgiven: God is Forgiving and Merciful "after that."

Al-Ṭabarī and others record a further group: Muslims who had remained in Makkah, been captured by the Quraysh, and been forced to renounce Islam, and concerning whom the Muslims in Madinah were uncertain — some said they had apostatized. These men then escaped and emigrated to Madinah, or were among those who set out and were recaptured. The verse was revealed to establish that God forgives them, and letters were sent to those still in Makkah to tell them that God had made a way out for them. Some reports name specific individuals, including ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Sarḥ — who later apostatized in earnest and then, after the conquest, returned to Islam — but the commentators note that the verse's primary reference is to those who were coerced and then emigrated and struggled.

Whatever the specific persons, the verse's structure is clear: it addresses believers who passed through *fitnah* — including, perhaps, the *fitnah* of being made to speak disbelief — and who then did three things.

**"Then Struggled": *Jāhadū***

The second act is *jāhadū*, "they struggled." The word *jihād*, from *jahada*, to exert effort, denotes striving with all one's capacity — in the path of God, against one's own soul, against the enemies of the faith. The commentators take it here in its full range: the emigrants struggled against their own weakness (which had, perhaps, yielded under torture), against the hardship of exile, and, later, in the battles of Badr and after. Al-Rāzī notes that the struggle named after emigration is what distinguishes the emigrant from the mere refugee: he did not only flee persecution; he then exerted himself for the faith he had fled to preserve.

**"And Were Patient": *Ṣabarū***

The third act is *ṣabarū*, "they were patient." Patience, discussed at verses 42 and 96, is named here as the completion of the sequence. The emigrants were patient under the persecution that preceded emigration, patient in the hardship of emigration, and patient in the struggle that followed. Al-Zamakhsharī notes the order of the three verbs: emigration is the initial break; struggle is the ongoing exertion; patience is the sustaining virtue that makes both possible. Verse 42 named patience and trust as the emigrants' two qualities; verse 110 names emigration, struggle, and patience as their three acts, with patience the common thread.

**"Truly Thy Lord, After That, Is Forgiving, Merciful"**

The predicate, delivered after the second *inna rabbaka*, is *la-ghafūrun raḥīm*, "is surely Forgiving, Merciful." And between the subject and the predicate stands the phrase *min baʿdihā*, "after that" or "after it."

The commentators discuss what "after that" refers to. The feminine pronoun *-hā* may refer to the *fitnah* — God is forgiving and merciful *after the persecution* they suffered and whatever it drew from them. Or it may refer to the emigration, struggle, and patience — God is forgiving and merciful *after they did these things*. Al-Ṭabarī and al-Rāzī allow both, and the two readings converge: after the persecution, and after their response to it, God forgives whatever weakness the persecution exposed and shows mercy to those who then emigrated, struggled, and endured.

The two names, *Ghafūr* and *Raḥīm*, are the Qur'an's most frequent pairing (over seventy occurrences), and their relevance here is specific. *Ghafūr*, the Forgiving, addresses what the persecution may have extracted — coerced words, moments of weakness, whatever the believer regrets from the time of his trial. All of it is covered. *Raḥīm*, the Merciful, addresses what follows — God's active goodness toward those who emigrated and struggled, His provision for them, His reward. The verse thus tells the persecuted believer two things: your past under persecution is forgiven, and your future under God's care is merciful.

**The Contrast With Verses 106–109**

The commentators read verse 110 as the deliberate counterpart to verses 106–109, and the parallel is precise. Both groups faced the same *fitnah*. One group opened their breasts to disbelief, preferred this world, were sealed, and became the losers. The other group — even if their tongues had been forced — kept their hearts at peace in faith, emigrated rather than stay under pressure, struggled, and were patient; and for them God is Forgiving and Merciful. The verse's placement immediately after the verdict of loss (v. 109) is a mercy in itself: the reader who has just heard the fate of the apostate is told, in the next breath, that the same trial produces, in those who respond rightly, forgiveness and mercy. The trial does not determine the outcome; the response does.

**The Mercy Toward the Coerced Who Emigrated**

The commentators draw particular attention to the verse's mercy toward those who had been *coerced into words of disbelief* and then emigrated. Such a person might have feared that his coerced words had cost him everything — that he was, despite his heart's faith, an apostate. Verse 106 had already excused him. Verse 110 goes further: it does not merely excuse but promises forgiveness and mercy, and it names the path by which the promise is claimed — emigration, struggle, patience. The one who was broken under torture is told that the breaking is forgiven and that God's mercy awaits his continued effort. Al-Rāzī notes that this is the Qur'an's consistent treatment of the weak: it does not demand that they have been strong; it demands that they continue, and it forgives what they could not bear.

**The Application: The Trial and the Response**

The verse teaches that persecution and trial are not, in themselves, the measure of a person; the response is. The believer who has passed through *fitnah* — of whatever kind — and emerged with a sense of failure is told that God is Forgiving and Merciful *after that*, provided he does what the emigrants did: leaves the situation that was destroying his faith, exerts himself for the faith thereafter, and endures. The three verbs are a program for recovery from any trial that has shaken one's religion: *hijrah* — a break with what harmed; *jihād* — effort toward what heals; *ṣabr* — persistence through the difficulty of both. The verse's repeated *inna rabbaka*, "truly your Lord," encloses the whole program in the assurance that the Lord who permitted the trial is the Lord who forgives its wounds. The Prophet ﷺ said: "God is more merciful to His servants than a mother to her child" (al-Bukhārī 5999; Muslim 2754). Verse 110 is that mercy addressed to those who have been through the fire.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:111

> **On the Day when every soul will come pleading for itself, and every soul will be paid in full for that which it did; and they shall not be wronged.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Day of Each Soul Alone**

Verse 110 promised forgiveness and mercy to the emigrants who struggled and were patient. Verse 111 places that promise — and the verdict of loss in verse 109 — on the Day when both will be executed: *yawma taʾtī kullu nafsin tujādilu ʿan nafsihā*, "the Day every soul will come disputing on behalf of itself." The verse describes the Day of Judgment from a specific angle: the isolation of each soul, the fullness of its recompense, and the absence of injustice. It is the sūrah's final major statement of the Judgment before its closing sections.

**"On the Day": The Grammatical Link**

The verse begins with *yawma*, "on the Day," and the commentators discuss what it connects to. It may be governed by an implied verb — "remember the Day" or "[God is Forgiving, Merciful] on the Day" — or it may attach to verse 110's predicate: God's forgiveness and mercy toward the emigrants will be manifest on the Day when every soul pleads for itself. Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Rāzī take the latter: the verse specifies the Day on which the promise of verse 110 is fulfilled — and, by contrast, the Day on which the losers of verse 109 discover their loss. Al-Ṭabarī reads it as governed by "remember" or "mention." The sense on any reading is the same: the verse opens onto the Day of reckoning.

**"Every Soul Will Come Pleading for Itself": *Tujādilu ʿan nafsihā***

The verse's central image is *kullu nafsin tujādilu ʿan nafsihā*, "every soul disputing on behalf of itself." The verb *jādala* means to argue, to dispute, to contend — the root of *jidāl*, debate, which verse 125 will mention. On the Day of Judgment, every soul will argue *for itself* — pleading its own case, offering its own excuses, defending its own conduct.

The commentators draw out the implications. First, the image conveys *isolation*. Every soul pleads for *itself* — not for its parents, its children, its tribe, its friends. The bonds that in this world made people defend one another are dissolved. The Qur'an describes this dissolution repeatedly:

> *"On the Day a man will flee from his brother, and his mother and his father, and his wife and his children — every man among them, that Day, will have a matter sufficient for him."* (Qur'an 80:34–37)

> *"And fear a Day when no soul will suffice for another soul at all, nor will intercession be accepted from it, nor will compensation be taken from it, nor will they be aided."* (Qur'an 2:48)

Al-Rāzī notes the contrast with this world, where a person's family, tribe, and allies rush to his defense. On that Day, each is too occupied with his own case to plead another's. Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to have said that on that Day, no one will speak except of himself, saying "myself, myself" (*nafsī, nafsī*) — the cry that the hadith of intercession attributes to every prophet except Muḥammad ﷺ, who alone will say "my community, my community" (al-Bukhārī 4712; Muslim 194).

Second, the image conveys the *futility* of the pleading. The soul disputes for itself, but the record is complete (v. 84, the witnesses) and the limbs testify (24:24; 36:65). Al-Zamakhsharī: the disputing is the soul's last effort at self-defense, and it fails because there is no defense against a complete record. The Qur'an gives examples of the pleading: the idolaters saying, "By God, our Lord, we were not idolaters" (6:23); the followers blaming the leaders and the leaders disowning the followers (34:31–33); the sinner saying, "Had God guided me, I would have been among the God-fearing" (39:57). Each plea is heard and answered, and none avails.

Third, the commentators note that the disputing is not forbidden — God permits every soul to speak for itself, and this permission is part of the Day's justice. The soul is not condemned unheard. It pleads; its plea is weighed; and the verdict follows. Al-Rāzī: the Day is a trial in the full sense, with the accused given a hearing, so that no one can say he was not allowed to speak. (The denial of speech in verse 84 and 77:35–36 refers, as was noted there, to a later stage, after the pleas have been heard and refuted.)

**"And Every Soul Will Be Paid in Full for That Which It Did": *Tuwaffā***

The verse's second clause is *wa-tuwaffā kullu nafsin mā ʿamilat*, "and every soul will be paid in full for what it did." The verb *waffā* means to give in full, to pay completely, to render the whole of what is due — the same root as *tawaffā*, "to take in full," used for death (vv. 28, 32, 70). Every soul receives the *full* recompense of its deeds: nothing is omitted, nothing is reduced, nothing is added that was not earned.

The commentators emphasize the *fullness*. The good deeds of the righteous are rewarded in full — and, by God's bounty, at the rate of the best (vv. 96–97). The evil deeds of the wicked are recompensed in full — the whole record, including what was hidden (v. 19). The Qur'an states the principle in many forms: "Whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, and whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it" (99:7–8); "And the record will be placed, and you will see the criminals fearful of what is in it, and they will say: Woe to us! What is this record that leaves nothing small or great except that it has enumerated it? And they will find what they did present" (18:49).

The phrase *mā ʿamilat*, "what it did," locates the recompense in the soul's own deeds. The soul is not paid for what others did, nor for what it intended without doing (except that intentions are themselves deeds of the heart), nor for its lineage, wealth, or status. It is paid for *what it did*. Al-Rāzī: the verse is the foundation of individual responsibility — each soul's account is its own, and its recompense is exactly its deeds.

**"And They Shall Not Be Wronged": *Wa-hum lā yuẓlamūn***

The verse ends: *wa-hum lā yuẓlamūn*, "and they will not be wronged." The formula was discussed at verse 33 ("God wronged them not, but they wronged themselves") and appears throughout the Qur'an as the seal of the Judgment's justice (2:281; 3:25, 161; 4:49, 77, 124; 10:47, 54; 11:109; 17:71; 39:69; 40:17; 45:22; 46:19). No soul will be given less than its good deeds earned, and no soul will be given more punishment than its evil deeds deserved. The commentators note that the negation covers both directions: the righteous will not be shortchanged, and the wicked will not be over-punished. God's justice is exact.

The phrase is particularly significant after the image of the soul pleading for itself. The soul pleads because it fears injustice — fears that it will be condemned unfairly, that its excuses will not be heard, that its good will be forgotten. The verse answers the fear: they will not be wronged. The pleading is unnecessary for the righteous, whose good is recorded in full, and unavailing for the wicked, whose evil is recorded in full — but in neither case is there injustice. Al-Zamakhsharī: the verse's last clause is the guarantee that makes the whole Judgment bearable. The one who has done good may face it without fear; the one who has done evil cannot complain of the outcome.

**The Verse in the Sūrah's Structure**

Verse 111 closes the passage that began at verse 106 and, more broadly, the sūrah's long treatment of the Judgment (vv. 84–89, 106–111). It gathers the threads: the witnesses (v. 84), the sight of punishment (v. 85), the disavowal by the partners (v. 86), the empty submission (v. 87), the sealing and loss (vv. 108–109), the forgiveness of the faithful (v. 110) — all converge on the Day when every soul stands alone, pleads for itself, is paid in full, and is not wronged. The verse is the sūrah's most compressed statement of the doctrine of individual recompense, and it functions as the hinge to the sūrah's final movement, which returns to the parable of blessing and ingratitude (v. 112) and then to the Prophet's method and the community's conduct (vv. 114–128).

**The Application: Preparing the Case**

The verse teaches the believer to prepare, in this world, the case he will plead in the next. Since every soul will dispute for itself, the wise soul assembles its defense now — not in the form of excuses, which will not avail, but in the form of deeds, which will be paid in full. The Prophet ﷺ described the believer's preparation:

> *"A servant's feet will not move on the Day of Resurrection until he is asked about his life — how he spent it; his knowledge — what he did with it; his wealth — from where he acquired it and on what he spent it; and his body — how he wore it out."* (al-Tirmidhī 2417)

These four questions are the substance of the soul's plea. The believer who can answer them has prepared his case; the one who cannot will plead in vain. And the verse's final assurance — "they will not be wronged" — is the believer's comfort: whatever good he has done will be counted, in full, on the Day when he stands alone and speaks for himself.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:112

> **And God sets forth a parable: a town that was secure and at peace, its provision coming to it in abundance from every place. Then it was ungrateful for the blessings of God, so God made it taste the garment of hunger and fear for that which they had wrought.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Parable That Names the Sūrah's Theme**

After the great scene of the Judgment (vv. 84–111), the sūrah returns to its central theme — blessing and its denial — and states it in a parable. *Wa-ḍaraba Allāhu mathalan qaryatan kānat āminatan muṭmaʾinnah*, "And God sets forth a parable: a town that was secure and tranquil." The parable is the sūrah's most concentrated statement of the law that has governed it from the beginning: blessing given, blessing denied, blessing withdrawn. It is also, the commentators hold, a description of Makkah itself — the city that had every blessing, denied the greatest of them, and tasted hunger and fear as the consequence.

**"A Town That Was Secure and at Peace": *Āminatan Muṭmaʾinnah***

The town is described first by its security: *āminah*, secure, safe from attack; and *muṭmaʾinnah*, tranquil, settled, at rest — the same word used in verse 106 for the heart "at peace" in faith. The two words together describe a town in which people live without fear: no raids, no war, no displacement.
