In the Arabia of the seventh century, where tribes raided one another constantly and no traveler was safe, such security was rare and precious.

The commentators identify the town. Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Qatādah, and the majority hold that it is Makkah, and the description fits precisely. Makkah was *āminah* because of the sanctuary (*ḥaram*) that God had established around the Kaʿbah — a zone in which fighting was forbidden and in which, by ancient custom, even a man who met his father's killer would not touch him. The Qur'an names this security as God's gift to Quraysh:

> *"Have they not seen that We have made a secure sanctuary, while people are being snatched away from all around them?"* (Qur'an 29:67)

> *"For the accustomed security of Quraysh — their security in the journey of winter and summer — let them worship the Lord of this House, Who has fed them against hunger and made them secure against fear."* (Qur'an 106:1–4)

The verse in Sūrat Quraysh (106:4) names the two blessings of Makkah in exactly the terms that 16:112 will name their removal: fed against *hunger*, secured against *fear*. The parable describes the town's blessings in the words of Sūrat Quraysh and its punishment in the reversal of those words.

A minority of commentators, recorded by al-Ṭabarī, held that the town is a general parable — any town that fits the description — or that it refers to a different historical city. Al-Ṭabarī himself inclines to Makkah, noting that the parable's details and the sūrah's context point to it. Al-Rāzī allows that the parable is general in its lesson and specific in its primary reference.

**"Its Provision Coming to It in Abundance From Every Place": *Raghadan min kulli makān***

The town's second blessing is provision: *yaʾtīhā rizquhā raghadan min kulli makān*, "its provision coming to it abundantly from every place." The word *raghad* means abundant, ample, easy — provision that comes without hardship. And it comes *min kulli makān*, "from every place" — from every direction.

The commentators note that this, too, fits Makkah exactly. Makkah lay in a barren valley — "a valley without cultivation," as Abraham called it in his prayer (14:37) — and produced nothing of its own. Yet it was supplied from every direction: by the trade caravans that came to it as a religious and commercial center, by the pilgrims who brought goods, by the fruits that were carried to it from Ṭāʾif and elsewhere. Abraham's prayer had asked for exactly this:

> *"Our Lord, I have settled some of my descendants in a valley without cultivation, near Your Sacred House... so make hearts among the people incline toward them and provide for them from the fruits that they might be grateful."* (Qur'an 14:37)

> *"My Lord, make this a secure city and provide its people with fruits."* (Qur'an 2:126)

The commentators observe that Abraham's two prayers named the two blessings — security and provision — and named the purpose: "that they might be grateful" (14:37). Verse 112 describes the prayers answered (security and abundant provision) and the purpose defeated (ingratitude).

**"Then It Was Ungrateful for the Blessings of God": *Fa-kafarat bi-anʿumi Allāh***

The turn of the parable is *fa-kafarat bi-anʿumi Allāh*, "then it disbelieved in / was ungrateful for the blessings of God." The verb *kafarat* is the verb of *kufr*, discussed at verse 55 as covering — covering the blessing, denying its source, using it against its Giver. The object is *anʿum Allāh*, "the blessings of God" — the plural *anʿum* (a plural of paucity, as the grammarians note, used here perhaps to suggest that even the few blessings they were conscious of, they denied).

The commentators identify the ingratitude. Makkah denied the source of its security and provision, attributing them to the idols or to its own standing. And it denied the greatest blessing of all — the Prophet ﷺ, sent from among them, whom they rejected, persecuted, and drove out. Al-Rāzī: the ingratitude for the blessings of God culminated in the rejection of the blessing that made all others meaningful — the guidance that would have taught them Whom to thank. Verse 83 said they "recognize the blessing of God and then deny it"; verse 112 shows the denial in the case of a whole city.

**"So God Made It Taste the Garment of Hunger and Fear": *Libāsa al-jūʿi wa'l-khawf***

The consequence is *fa-adhāqahā Allāhu libāsa al-jūʿi wa'l-khawf*, "so God made it taste the garment of hunger and fear." The phrase combines two metaphors — tasting and clothing — and the commentators discuss the combination at length.

*Libās*, garment, clothing: hunger and fear are called a garment because they envelop the person completely, as a garment covers the body; because they cling and cannot be shaken off; and because they are visible on the person, as clothing is — the hungry and the fearful show their condition in their faces and bodies. Al-Zamakhsharī: the effects of hunger and fear appeared on them as a garment appears on the wearer.

*Adhāqa*, made to taste: the verb of tasting is used for the experience of punishment throughout the Qur'an, because tasting is the most intimate form of perception — the thing tasted is inside the mouth, unavoidable. The combination "made them taste the garment" was criticized by some rhetoricians as mixed, but the majority of commentators defend it: the "garment" of hunger and fear is not literally clothing but the enveloping condition, and one "tastes" a condition by experiencing it. Al-Rāzī notes that the Qur'an's imagery here is deliberately layered: the punishment is both enveloping (garment) and intimate (tasted), both outer and inner.

The two punishments correspond exactly to the two blessings. The town was *secure* (v. 112a); it tasted *fear*. Its *provision* came abundantly; it tasted *hunger*. The reversal is complete, and the commentators identify its historical fulfillment. The *hunger* was the famine that struck Makkah after the Prophet ﷺ prayed against them — "O God, help me against them with seven years like the seven of Joseph" — so that they ate carrion, hides, and bones, and a man would look at the sky and see something like smoke from hunger (al-Bukhārī 1007, 4821; Muslim 2798); the Qur'an refers to this in 44:10, "the Day the sky brings a visible smoke." The *fear* was the fear that gripped Makkah after the Hijrah, when the Prophet's raiding parties threatened its caravans, when Badr destroyed its chiefs, and when the city lived in dread of the growing power of Madinah until the conquest.

**"For That Which They Had Wrought": *Bimā kānū yaṣnaʿūn***

The verse ends: *bimā kānū yaṣnaʿūn*, "because of what they used to do." The verb *ṣanaʿa* means to make, to craft, to do deliberately — a stronger word than *ʿamila*. The punishment was for what they *crafted* — their persistent, deliberate ingratitude and rejection. Al-Rāzī notes the verb's implication: their ingratitude was not a lapse but a construction, built over years of denying the Prophet and clinging to the idols.

**The Parable and the Sūrah's Argument**

The commentators regard verse 112 as the summation of the sūrah's argument about blessing. Verse 18 said the blessings cannot be counted. Verses 5–81 enumerated them. Verse 53 said every blessing is from God. Verse 55 named the ingratitude that follows relief. Verse 83 said they recognize the blessing and deny it. Verse 112 shows what happens to a town that does this: the blessings are reversed. The parable thus states the *law* that the sūrah has been illustrating — that blessing denied is blessing withdrawn — and states it in the case of the city where the sūrah was revealed, so that its first hearers could not mistake the reference.

The Qur'an states the law in general terms elsewhere: "Truly God does not change what is in a people until they change what is in themselves" (13:11); "That is because God would never change a blessing He bestowed upon a people until they change what is in themselves" (8:53). Verse 112 is the law in narrative form.

**The Parable and the Believer**

The commentators applied the parable beyond Makkah. Every person, and every community, that is secure and provided for is the town of the parable, and faces the same test. Al-Qurṭubī notes that the parable is a warning to the Muslims as much as to the Quraysh: a community that receives God's blessings and denies them — by attributing them to its own strength, by using them in disobedience, by forgetting their Giver — invites the garment of hunger and fear. The history of Muslim societies, as of all societies, confirms the pattern. And the individual who is secure and provided for is asked to remember, in his security, the town that was secure and forgot Whom to thank.

**The Application: Gratitude as Preservation of Blessing**

The verse teaches that gratitude is not merely the proper response to blessing but the condition of its continuance. The Qur'an makes this explicit: "If you are grateful, I will surely increase you; but if you are ungrateful, My punishment is severe" (14:7). The town of the parable was ungrateful and tasted hunger and fear; the one who is grateful is promised increase. The practical discipline is the constant tracing of one's security and provision to their source — the acknowledgment, in word and act, that the safety one enjoys and the food one eats are *anʿum Allāh*, the blessings of God. The Prophet ﷺ taught the morning and evening supplication: "O God, whatever blessing I or any of Your creation has this morning is from You alone, without partner; so to You is praise and to You is thanks" (Abū Dāwūd 5073). The one who says this has done what the town of the parable did not, and has, in the verse's terms, kept his garment of security and provision by refusing the garment of denial.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:113

> **And there had certainly come to them a Messenger from among themselves, but they denied him. So the punishment seized them while they were wrongdoers.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Greatest Blessing, and Its Denial**

Verse 112 described a town that was ungrateful for God's blessings and tasted hunger and fear. Verse 113 names the specific act that constituted the ingratitude: *wa-laqad jāʾahum rasūlun minhum fa-kadhdhabūh*, "and there had certainly come to them a Messenger from among themselves, but they denied him." The town's greatest blessing was not its security or its provision but the Messenger sent to it; its greatest ingratitude was denying him; and its punishment followed from that denial. The verse thus completes the parable and confirms that the town is Makkah.

**"There Had Certainly Come to Them a Messenger": *Laqad Jāʾahum***

The verse opens with the emphatic *laqad*, "certainly," "indeed," which affirms the fact beyond dispute. The commentators note the emphasis: the town cannot claim that it was not warned. The Messenger *came* — this is a historical fact, and the town's inhabitants were its witnesses. The verse thus removes the excuse that verse 36 established as the ground of all accountability: every community was sent a messenger, and this community's messenger came to it in person.

**"From Among Themselves": *Minhum***

The Messenger was *minhum*, "from among them" — one of their own people, tribe, and city. The phrase was discussed at verse 89, where the witness against each community is "from among themselves." Here it identifies the Messenger to Makkah as a Makkan: Muḥammad ﷺ, of the Quraysh, born and raised among them, known to them for forty years as *al-Amīn* before he brought them the message.

The commentators draw out the aggravation this adds to the denial. The Makkans could not say the Messenger was a stranger whose character they could not assess, a foreigner whose motives were suspect (v. 103), or a man whose lineage was unknown. He was theirs. They knew his honesty, his trustworthiness, his freedom from any prior claim to authority or eloquence. And they denied him. Al-Rāzī: the denial of a messenger from among oneself is worse than the denial of a stranger, because the knowledge that should have compelled acceptance was present and was overridden. The Qur'an notes the same aggravation of the People of the Book: "they recognize him as they recognize their own sons" (2:146) — and deny him.

The phrase also names the blessing. A messenger from among themselves was a gift: he spoke their language, understood their condition, and could be approached and questioned. The Qur'an counts this among God's favors:

> *"Certainly God conferred favor upon the believers when He sent among them a Messenger from among themselves, reciting to them His verses and purifying them and teaching them the Book and wisdom, although they had been before in manifest error."* (Qur'an 3:164)

> *"There has certainly come to you a Messenger from among yourselves. Grievous to him is what you suffer; he is concerned over you; to the believers he is kind and merciful."* (Qur'an 9:128)

The town's ingratitude "for the blessings of God" (v. 112) reached its climax in the rejection of this blessing.

**"But They Denied Him": *Fa-kadhdhabūh***

The town's response is *fa-kadhdhabūh*, "they called him a liar." The verb *kadhdhaba* is the intensive form of *kadhaba*, to lie; it means to accuse of lying, to reject as false, to deny. The Makkans did not merely fail to follow the Messenger; they *denied* him — called him a fabricator (v. 101), a poet, a soothsayer, a madman, a man taught by a foreigner (v. 103). The verse names the denial in a single word and lets the preceding verses (101–105) supply its content.

The commentators note the irony that verse 105 established: the ones who called the Messenger a liar were themselves *the* liars. The verb *kadhdhabūh* in verse 113 is the town's act; *al-kādhibūn* in verse 105 is the town's identity. They accused him of what they were.

**"So the Punishment Seized Them": *Fa-akhadhahumu al-ʿadhāb***

The consequence is *fa-akhadhahumu al-ʿadhāb*, "so the punishment seized them." The verb *akhadha*, to take, to seize, is the Qur'an's verb for divine punishment overtaking a people (7:94–95; 29:40; 40:5). The punishment is the "garment of hunger and fear" of verse 112 — the famine and the dread that followed the Hijrah.

The commentators observe the *fa-*, "so," which links the punishment directly to the denial. The town did not taste hunger and fear for its idolatry alone, which had continued for generations, but for its denial of the Messenger — the act that closed the door on the guidance that could have saved it. Al-Ṭabarī: the punishment followed the denial because the denial was the final ingratitude, after which nothing remained but the consequence.

**"While They Were Wrongdoers": *Wa-hum ẓālimūn***

The verse ends: *wa-hum ẓālimūn*, "while they were wrongdoers." The circumstantial clause describes the state in which the punishment found them: in *ẓulm*, wrongdoing, injustice — the placing of things where they do not belong. The commentators identify the wrong: the *shirk* that gave worship to idols; the denial of the Messenger, which gave the name of liar to the truthful; the persecution of the believers, which gave torture to the innocent; and the ingratitude, which gave credit to the wrong source. Each is a *ẓulm*, and the punishment came while they were in it.

The clause also functions as a justification. As at verse 33 ("God wronged them not, but they wronged themselves") and verse 111 ("they will not be wronged"), the verse insists that the punishment was just: it seized *wrongdoers*. God did not punish a righteous town; He punished a town in the act of wrong. Al-Rāzī: the clause forecloses any objection to the punishment's justice by naming the condition that earned it.

**The Parable Completed**

Verses 112–113 together form a complete parable with a complete application. Verse 112: a town, secure and provided for, ungrateful, punished with hunger and fear. Verse 113: the specific ingratitude — denying the Messenger from among themselves — and the specific punishment — seizure while in wrongdoing. The commentators note that the parable's movement from general (blessings of God) to specific (the Messenger) mirrors the sūrah's own movement: the sūrah began with the blessings of creation and moved to the blessing of revelation (vv. 44, 64, 89, 102); the parable does the same in two verses. The lesson is that the blessings of creation point to the blessing of revelation, and the denial of the second is the ingratitude that forfeits the first.

**The Historical Fulfillment and Its Limit**

The commentators record that the punishment of Makkah was real but bounded. The famine came and was severe; the fear came and was prolonged. But Makkah was not destroyed as the ancient towns were destroyed (vv. 26, 36, 45–47). The Prophet ﷺ, when the Makkans came to him in the famine asking him to pray for its lifting, prayed, and it was lifted (al-Bukhārī 1020). And at the conquest, he forgave them: "Go, for you are free." The commentators explain the difference. The ancient towns were destroyed because their messengers were rejected to the end; Makkah's punishment was a warning that preceded a mercy, because its Messenger was "a mercy to the worlds" (21:107) and because God had promised not to punish them while he was among them or while they sought forgiveness (8:33). The garment of hunger and fear was removed when the town, at last, submitted. The parable thus has a sequel that the verse does not state but the *sīrah* supplies: the town that denied its Messenger was, in the end, the town that received him back — and the verse's warning became, for those who heeded it, the prelude to the greatest mercy.

**The Application: The Messenger as the Test of Gratitude**

The verse teaches that the ultimate test of gratitude for God's blessings is the response to His Messenger. A person or a society may acknowledge God as Creator and Provider and still fail the test, if it denies the guidance He sent. The Makkans acknowledged God (v. 31:25; 39:38) and were punished for denying His Messenger. The lesson for the believer is that gratitude is completed in obedience to what God revealed — that thanking God for rain and cattle and children while ignoring His Book is the town of the parable in a milder form. And the lesson for anyone who has not yet accepted the Messenger is the verse's *laqad jāʾahum*: he has come; the message has reached; and the response is now the responder's account. The Prophet ﷺ said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, no one of this community, Jew or Christian, hears of me and then dies without believing in what I was sent with, except that he will be among the people of the Fire" (Muslim 153). The verse describes the town that heard and denied. The reader has heard.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:114

> **So eat of that which God has provided you, lawful and good, and give thanks for the blessing of God, if it is He whom you worship.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**From the Parable to the Command**

Verses 112–113 showed a town that was ungrateful for God's blessings and was punished with hunger. Verse 114 turns to the believers with the opposite instruction: *fa-kulū mimmā razaqakumu Allāhu ḥalālan ṭayyiban wa-shkurū niʿmata Allāh*, "so eat of what God has provided you, lawful and good, and be grateful for the blessing of God." The town denied the blessing and tasted hunger; the believers are told to eat the blessing and give thanks. The *fa-*, "so," at the verse's opening draws the conclusion: having seen what ingratitude brings, do the opposite.

**"So Eat": The Command to Enjoy**

The verse begins with an imperative: *kulū*, "eat." The commentators note that this is a command — not merely a permission — and they draw out its significance. God commands the believers to eat what He has provided. Eating is not a concession to weakness or a distraction from religion; it is an act God orders, and, when performed with gratitude, an act of worship. The Qur'an addresses the same command to the messengers: "O messengers, eat of the good things and do righteous deeds" (23:51) — placing eating alongside righteous action.

The command also has a polemical edge in context. The following verses (115–118) will address the arbitrary prohibitions the idolaters invented — forbidding themselves certain animals and crops in the name of religion (5:103; 6:136–140). Verse 114's "eat" is a rejection of these self-imposed prohibitions: what God has provided is to be eaten, not forbidden by human invention. Al-Rāzī: the command to eat is a command not to forbid what God has permitted.

**"Of That Which God Has Provided You": *Mimmā Razaqakumu Allāh***

The food is *mimmā razaqakumu Allāh*, "from what God has provided you." The verb *razaqa* and the noun *rizq*, provision, have run through the sūrah (vv. 56, 67, 71, 72, 73, 75, 112). Here they name the source of what is eaten: God. The commentators note the phrase's function. Eating is to be done with the awareness that the food is *God's provision* — not the product of one's own effort alone, not the gift of an idol, not a matter of chance. This awareness is the difference between the believer's meal and the idolater's, and it is what makes the meal an occasion of gratitude rather than heedlessness.

The preposition *min*, "of," "from," is partitive: eat *of* what God has provided — some of it, not necessarily all; and only that part which the next two words specify.

**"Lawful and Good": *Ḥalālan Ṭayyiban***

The provision to be eaten is qualified by two adjectives: *ḥalāl*, lawful, and *ṭayyib*, good. The pairing appears in the Qur'an several times (2:168; 5:88; 8:69), and the commentators distinguish the two terms.

*Ḥalāl* is what God has permitted — the opposite of *ḥarām*, the forbidden. The lawfulness is defined by revelation: God has forbidden certain things (the next verse names them), and everything else is permitted. To eat the *ḥalāl* is to eat within the bounds God set.

*Ṭayyib* is what is good, pure, wholesome, pleasant — the opposite of *khabīth*, foul, harmful, impure. The commentators discuss its meaning. Some take it as a description of *ḥalāl* — the lawful is *by definition* good, and the two words are near-synonyms emphasizing each other. Others distinguish them: *ḥalāl* concerns the legal status, and *ṭayyib* concerns the intrinsic quality — a thing may be lawful in itself but acquired by unlawful means (stolen, or bought with usury), in which case it is *ḥalāl* in its nature but not *ṭayyib* in its acquisition. Al-Rāzī and al-Qurṭubī record both readings. The Shāfiʿī jurists used *ṭayyib* as a criterion in its own right: what sound Arab taste finds wholesome is *ṭayyib* and permitted; what it finds foul is *khabīth* and forbidden (cf. 7:157, "He makes lawful for them the good things and forbids them the foul things").

The two adjectives together describe the believer's food completely: it must be lawful in its kind, and good in its source, acquisition, and nature. The Prophet ﷺ connected this to the acceptance of prayer:

> *"O people, God is good (ṭayyib) and accepts only what is good. And God commanded the believers with what He commanded the messengers, saying: 'O messengers, eat of the good things and do righteous deeds.'... Then he mentioned a man who travels long, disheveled and dusty, raising his hands to the sky: 'O Lord, O Lord!' — while his food is unlawful, his drink is unlawful, his clothing is unlawful, and he is nourished by the unlawful. How can he be answered?"* (Muslim 1015)

The hadith is the commentary on *ḥalālan ṭayyiban*: the food one eats affects the prayer one prays, and the one who eats the unlawful has cut himself off from the answer.

**"And Give Thanks for the Blessing of God": *Wa-shkurū niʿmata Allāh***

The verse's second command is *wa-shkurū niʿmata Allāh*, "and be grateful for the blessing of God." Eating is paired with gratitude; the two commands are joined by *wa-*, and the commentators read them as inseparable. To eat God's provision without thanking Him is the ingratitude of the town in verse 112; to eat it *and* thank Him is the fulfillment of the sūrah's whole demand.

The word *shukr*, gratitude, was discussed at verses 14, 55, 78, and 81. It has three components in the classical analysis: acknowledgment in the heart that the blessing is from God; praise on the tongue; and use of the blessing in obedience. Applied to eating: the believer acknowledges that the food is God's gift, says *bismillāh* before and *al-ḥamdu li'llāh* after, and uses the strength the food gives in what God loves. The Prophet ﷺ taught the specific expression:

> *"Truly God is pleased with the servant who eats a meal and praises Him for it, or drinks a drink and praises Him for it."* (Muslim 2734)

> *"Whoever eats food and says: Praise be to God who fed me this and provided it for me without any power or strength on my part — his past sins are forgiven."* (Abū Dāwūd 4023; al-Tirmidhī 3458)

The supplication's phrase "without any power or strength on my part" is the heart of the gratitude: it attributes the food entirely to God and disclaims the eater's own agency in a way that reverses the town's *kufr*.

**"If It Is He Whom You Worship": *In kuntum iyyāhu taʿbudūn***

The verse ends with a condition: *in kuntum iyyāhu taʿbudūn*, "if you worship Him [alone]." The construction fronts the object — *iyyāhu*, "Him" — for exclusivity, as in verse 51 (*iyyāya fa'rhabūn*) and in the Fātiḥah (*iyyāka naʿbudu*). The condition thus reads: if it is *Him alone* you worship.

The commentators explain the logic. Gratitude for a blessing is owed to its source. If the believers worship God alone — acknowledging Him alone as Lord, Provider, and object of devotion — then their gratitude for food is owed to Him alone, and the command to thank Him follows from their profession. The condition is not a doubt about their worship but an appeal to its consistency: you say you worship Him alone; then thank Him alone. Al-Zamakhsharī: the condition makes gratitude the test of the sincerity of worship. The one who eats and thanks God has shown that his worship is real; the one who eats and thanks the idols, or himself, or no one, has shown that his professed worship of God is incomplete.

The condition also connects the verse to the idolaters' inconsistency, exposed in verses 53–55 and 83: they acknowledged God as Provider and thanked the idols. Verse 114 tells the believers not to repeat this: worship of God alone entails gratitude to God alone, and the meal is where the entailment is tested.

**The Verse in the Sūrah's Final Movement**

Verse 114 opens the sūrah's concluding section (vv. 114–128), which turns from argument and warning to instruction: how the believers are to eat (v. 114–115), how they are to speak about the lawful and forbidden (v. 116–117), how they are to relate to the earlier laws (v. 118, 124), how they are to follow Abraham (v. 120–123), how they are to call others to God (v. 125), and how they are to respond to wrong (v. 126–128). The section begins with the most basic act — eating — because the sūrah's theme is blessing, and eating is the daily encounter with blessing. The commentators note the fittingness: after a hundred verses on God's provision, the sūrah's practical instruction begins with what to do with it.

**The Application: The Meal as Worship**

The verse transforms the ordinary meal into an act of religion. Three things are required: that the food be lawful and good; that it be eaten with the awareness of its source; and that it be followed by gratitude. The believer who does these three has, at every meal, enacted the sūrah's central teaching — that blessing is from God and is to be received with *shukr* — and has distinguished himself from the town of verse 112, which ate the same kind of food and denied its Giver. The verse's condition, "if it is He whom you worship," is the reminder that this daily enactment is not optional for the one who claims to worship God alone; it is the form that claim takes at the table.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:115

> **He has only forbidden you carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and that which has been offered to other than God. But whosoever is compelled—neither desiring nor transgressing—then truly God is Forgiving, Merciful.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Boundaries of the Lawful**

Verse 114 commanded the believers to eat what God has provided, lawful and good. Verse 115 specifies the boundary: *innamā ḥarrama ʿalaykumu al-maytata wa'l-dama wa-laḥma al-khinzīri wa-mā uhilla li-ghayri Allāhi bih*, "He has only forbidden you carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and what has been dedicated to other than God." The restrictive particle *innamā*, "only," is the verse's key: the forbidden foods are *these* — a short, definite list — and everything else is permitted. The verse thus establishes the principle that governs Islamic dietary law: permission is the default, and prohibition is the exception, defined by revelation.

**"He Has Only Forbidden You": The Force of *Innamā***

The commentators dwell on *innamā*. The idolaters had forbidden themselves many things — certain camels, certain crops, certain animals dedicated to idols (5:103; 6:138–139) — and attributed these prohibitions to God. Verse 115 says God has forbidden *only* these four. Everything the idolaters added is a fabrication, which verse 116 will name as such. Al-Rāzī: the restriction is a refutation of the invented prohibitions as much as it is a statement of the real ones. The verse limits the forbidden so that the lawful may be recognized as vast.

The principle is stated in the tradition as the rule of original permissibility (*al-aṣl fī al-ashyāʾ al-ibāḥah*): whatever God has not forbidden is permitted. The Prophet ﷺ expressed it:

> *"The lawful is what God has made lawful in His Book, and the forbidden is what God has forbidden in His Book, and what He was silent about is of what He has pardoned."* (al-Tirmidhī 1726; Ibn Mājah 3367)

Verse 115 is the Qur'anic statement of this rule for food.

**The Four Prohibitions**

The verse names four categories, and the commentators explain each.

*Al-maytah*, carrion: the animal that died without being slaughtered — of disease, of age, of a fall, of another animal's attack — in short, any animal not killed by the proper method. The prohibition's wisdom, as al-Rāzī and others explain, includes the harm of eating an animal whose cause of death is unknown and whose blood remains in its flesh. The Qur'an gives the fuller list in 5:3, which specifies the strangled, the beaten, the fallen, the gored, and the partly eaten — all forms of *maytah* — and excepts what one slaughters before it dies. Two exceptions to the prohibition of carrion are established by the Sunnah: fish and locusts, of which the Prophet ﷺ said, "Two dead things have been made lawful for us: fish and locusts" (Ibn Mājah 3314; Aḥmad 5723), and, for the sea generally, "Its water is pure and its dead are lawful" (Abū Dāwūd 83; al-Tirmidhī 69).

*Al-dam*, blood: the blood that flows from the animal. The Qur'an specifies in 6:145 *daman masfūḥan*, "poured-forth blood" — the flowing blood, not the traces that remain in the flesh after slaughter, which are permitted. The pre-Islamic Arabs would draw blood from a living camel and cook it; the prohibition ended this. The Sunnah excepts two forms of blood: the liver and the spleen (Ibn Mājah 3314).

*Laḥm al-khinzīr*, the flesh of swine: the pig, in all its parts. The commentators note that "flesh" is named but the prohibition extends by consensus to the fat, skin, and all parts. The Qur'an calls the pig *rijs*, filth (6:145), and the commentators discuss the reasons — its diet, its nature, the harm of its flesh — while affirming that the prohibition rests on God's command regardless of the wisdom one discerns in it.

*Mā uhilla li-ghayri Allāhi bih*, "what has been dedicated to other than God": the animal over which a name other than God's was invoked at slaughter, or which was slaughtered as an offering to an idol, a saint, or any being other than God. The verb *uhilla* comes from *ihlāl*, raising the voice — the slaughterer would raise his voice with the name of the deity to whom the animal was dedicated. The commentators note that this prohibition is the one most directly connected to the sūrah's theme: verse 56 condemned the idolaters for assigning God's provision to their idols, and verse 115 forbids eating what was so assigned. To eat the idol's offering is to participate in the dedication; the believer, who eats "what God has provided" (v. 114), does not eat what was given to another.

**The Same List Elsewhere**

The four prohibitions appear in identical or near-identical form in three other places (2:173; 5:3; 6:145), and the commentators note the consistency. Sūrat al-Anʿām (6:145), which is Makkan, states the list with the same *innamā* structure: "Say: I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to one who would eat it except that it be carrion, or poured-forth blood, or the flesh of swine — for it is filth — or a transgression dedicated to other than God." Sūrat al-Māʾidah (5:3), which is Madinan and among the last revealed, expands the list with specifications and adds the prohibition of what is slaughtered on stone altars and divided by arrows. The Sunnah adds further prohibitions — every predator with fangs, every bird with talons, the domestic donkey (al-Bukhārī 5530; Muslim 1932–1934) — and the scholars reconciled these with the verse's *innamā* by explaining that the verse restricts what was forbidden *at the time of its revelation* and that later revelation, including the Sunnah, added to it; or that the verse's *innamā* addresses the idolaters' inventions specifically, denying *those* while not excluding other prohibitions God might establish.

**"But Whosoever Is Compelled": The Exception of Necessity**

The verse then states the exception: *fa-mani uḍṭurra ghayra bāghin wa-lā ʿādin fa-inna Allāha ghafūrun raḥīm*, "but whoever is compelled, neither desiring nor transgressing, then truly God is Forgiving, Merciful." The verb *uḍṭurra* is the passive of *iḍṭarra*, to compel by necessity; *ḍarūrah* is necessity — the situation in which one will die or suffer grave harm without the forbidden thing. The starving person who finds nothing but carrion may eat it.

The exception is qualified by two conditions, and the commentators explain them.

*Ghayra bāghin*, "not desiring": the compelled person may not eat the forbidden out of *baghy* — desire for it, seeking it out, or (in another reading) rebellion against the ruler, since the rebel in his rebellion is not granted the concessions of the traveler. The majority read *bāghin* as "seeking the forbidden out of appetite" — the exception is for the one who eats from need, not from wanting.

*Wa-lā ʿādin*, "nor transgressing": the compelled person may not exceed the limit of necessity — eating more than what preserves life, or continuing after the necessity has passed. The concession is measured by the need.

The two conditions together establish the legal maxim that necessity permits the forbidden, and that what is permitted by necessity is measured by the necessity (*al-ḍarūrāt tubīḥu al-maḥẓūrāt*; *al-ḍarūrah tuqaddaru bi-qadrihā*). The jurists debated whether the compelled person is *permitted* or *obligated* to eat — the majority held that one who refuses to eat carrion and dies of starvation has sinned, since God commanded the preservation of life (2:195; 4:29) — and how much he may eat (enough to sustain life, or to satiety — the schools differ).

**"Then Truly God Is Forgiving, Merciful"**

The verse ends with the two names that closed verse 110: *ghafūrun raḥīm*, Forgiving, Merciful. The commentators note their fittingness. The compelled person who eats the forbidden has done something that, in ordinary circumstances, is a sin; the names assure him that in his circumstance it is forgiven — indeed, not even counted, since God's mercy provided the exception before the act. *Ghafūr* covers the act; *Raḥīm* names the disposition from which the exception flows. The law is severe in its prohibitions and merciful in its exceptions, and the verse states both in a single sentence.

**The Verse and the Sūrah's Theme**

The commentators connect verse 115 to the sūrah's argument about blessing. The idolaters forbade themselves God's blessings by their own invention (v. 116); God forbids only four things, and even these He excepts in necessity. The contrast is between a religion of arbitrary restriction and a religion of generous permission with defined limits. The sūrah has enumerated the vast provision God gives; verse 115 shows how little of it He withholds, and how readily He forgives the taking of even that when need compels. Al-Rāzī: the verse is a display of the divine generosity that the whole sūrah has celebrated, now applied to the law.

**The Application: Eating Within the Limits**

The verse gives the believer a clear and short list of what is forbidden and a broad permission for everything else. The practical result is a disposition of confidence rather than anxiety at the table: the believer knows what to avoid, avoids it, and eats the rest with gratitude (v. 114). The verse also gives him a rule for extremity: if he is compelled by real necessity, the forbidden becomes permitted, within the measure of the need, and God is Forgiving and Merciful. This balance — clear prohibition, generous permission, merciful exception — is the character of the whole law, and the verse teaches it in the domain where every human being encounters the law daily.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:116

> **And say not, concerning the falsehood your tongues describe, "This is lawful and this is forbidden," so as to fabricate a lie against God. Truly those who fabricate lies against God will not prosper.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Prohibition of Inventing Law**

Verse 115 stated the four things God has forbidden. Verse 116 forbids adding to them: *wa-lā taqūlū limā taṣifu alsinatukumu al-kadhiba hādhā ḥalālun wa-hādhā ḥarām*, "and do not say, concerning what your tongues falsely describe, 'This is lawful and this is forbidden.'" The verse addresses the idolaters' practice of inventing prohibitions and permissions and attributing them to God, and it names the practice for what it is: fabricating a lie against God. The verse is the Qur'an's most direct statement of the principle that the authority to declare lawful and forbidden belongs to God alone.

**"The Falsehood Your Tongues Describe": *Limā taṣifu alsinatukumu al-kadhib***

The verse's opening phrase is grammatically dense and has been construed in several ways, but its sense is clear. *Taṣifu alsinatukum*, "your tongues describe," was used in verse 62 for the idolaters' claim that "the best" was theirs: *taṣifu alsinatuhumu al-kadhib*, "their tongues describe the lie." The phrase recurs here for a different lie. Al-Zamakhsharī notes the striking construction: the tongue *describes* the lie — as though the lie were a quality the tongue attributes, or as though the tongue's description *is* the lie. The idolaters' rulings about lawful and forbidden had no source but their own tongues; the tongue spoke, and the speaking was the whole authority.

The commentators identify the specific rulings. The idolaters had declared certain animals forbidden — the *baḥīrah*, the *sāʾibah*, the *waṣīlah*, the *ḥām* (5:103) — camels and sheep set aside for the idols and not to be ridden, milked, or eaten. They had declared certain crops and cattle forbidden to women and permitted to men (6:139). They had declared the flesh of animals dedicated to idols lawful (v. 115's fourth prohibition) and, by implication, had declared lawful the practices the Qur'an forbade. And they had declared certain things lawful — carrion, for instance, which some ate, arguing that what God kills should be more lawful than what men kill (6:121). Each of these was a ruling *described by the tongue* and attributed to God.

**"This Is Lawful and This Is Forbidden": The Usurpation**

The verse quotes the idolaters' formula: *hādhā ḥalālun wa-hādhā ḥarām*, "this is lawful, and this is forbidden." The commentators note the formula's presumption. To say "this is lawful and this is forbidden" is to legislate. And legislation — the determination of what God permits and prohibits — is God's prerogative. The Qur'an states this in the strongest terms:

> *"Say: Have you seen what God has sent down to you of provision, of which you have made some forbidden and some lawful? Say: Has God permitted you, or do you fabricate against God?"* (Qur'an 10:59)

> *"They have taken their scholars and monks as lords besides God."* (Qur'an 9:31)

The verse in Sūrat al-Tawbah (9:31) was explained by the Prophet ﷺ to ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim, a former Christian, who objected that they had not worshipped their scholars. The Prophet replied: "Did they not forbid what God permitted, and you forbade it; and permit what God forbade, and you permitted it?" ʿAdī said yes. The Prophet said: "That is your worship of them" (al-Tirmidhī 3095). To accept a human being's declaration of lawful and forbidden, against God's, is to make that human being a lord. And to *make* the declaration is to claim lordship. Verse 116 forbids the second; 9:31 condemns the first.

**"So as to Fabricate a Lie Against God": *Li-taftarū ʿalā Allāhi al-kadhib***

The verse names the act: *li-taftarū ʿalā Allāhi al-kadhib*, "so as to fabricate a lie against God." The *lām* has been read as the *lām* of consequence (as in vv. 55, 70): the result of saying "this is lawful and this is forbidden" without authority is that one has fabricated a lie against God. The commentators explain why. Every declaration of lawful and forbidden is, implicitly, a claim about God's will — that He permits this, that He forbids that. When the declaration has no basis in revelation, the claim is false, and the one who makes it has attributed to God what God did not say. This is *iftirāʾ ʿalā Allāh*, fabrication against God, which the Qur'an names as the gravest wrong: "Who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against God?" (6:21, 93, 144; 7:37; 10:17; 11:18; 18:15; 29:68; 61:7).

Al-Rāzī draws out the gravity. The idolaters' invented prohibitions might seem like minor matters — a few camels set aside, a few crops restricted. But each was a claim about what God commands, and a false claim about God's command is a lie about God Himself. The verse treats the invention of a single unauthorized prohibition as *iftirāʾ ʿalā Allāh* — placing it in the same category as the ascription of daughters to God (v. 57) and the claim that the idols intercede.

**"Truly Those Who Fabricate Lies Against God Will Not Prosper"**

The verse ends: *inna alladhīna yaftarūna ʿalā Allāhi al-kadhiba lā yufliḥūn*, "truly those who fabricate lies against God will not prosper." The verb *aflaḥa* means to succeed, to attain what one seeks, to prosper — the root of *falāḥ*, the success called to in the *adhān* (*ḥayya ʿalā al-falāḥ*). The fabricators will not attain it — in this world or the next, as verse 117 will specify.

The commentators note the exact wording: "will not prosper" — not "will be punished," which verse 117 will add, but "will not *prosper*." The fabricator seeks something by his fabrication — authority, prestige, the maintenance of a social order, advantage. The verse says he will not attain it. Al-Zamakhsharī: the fabrication is not only sinful but futile; the fabricator loses what he sought as well as what he risked.

**The Verse's Principle: God Alone Legislates**

The commentators derived from the verse a principle that governs Islamic jurisprudence: the declaration of *ḥalāl* and *ḥarām* is God's right, exercised through His revelation and His Messenger, and no one else — no scholar, no ruler, no community — may declare a thing forbidden or lawful except by deriving the ruling from these sources. Al-Qurṭubī records the extreme caution this produced among the early scholars. Mālik ibn Anas, asked about forty-eight questions, answered "I do not know" to thirty-two. Ibn Kathīr cites this verse as the reason the jurists avoided the words "this is *ḥarām*" and "this is *ḥalāl*" in matters of *ijtihād* (independent reasoning), saying instead "I dislike this" or "I do not see it as permitted." Al-Shāfiʿī and Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal were reported to say "I dislike" rather than "forbidden" for anything not explicitly forbidden in the texts. The verse instilled the fear of fabricating against God so deeply that the greatest jurists hesitated to pronounce categorical rulings without clear textual warrant.

Ibn al-Qayyim summarized the principle: the *aṣl* in matters of worship is that nothing is prescribed except what God prescribed; and the *aṣl* in matters of ordinary life is that nothing is forbidden except what God forbade. Both halves are applications of verse 116: the one who adds a ritual God did not command, and the one who forbids a food God did not forbid, have each said "this is lawful and this is forbidden" by their own tongue.

**The Verse and Religious Authority in Every Age**

The commentators applied the verse beyond the idolaters' food taboos. The Jews and Christians who altered God's law were fabricators against God (as 9:31 states). The Muslims who invented prohibitions in the name of piety — forbidding what God permitted out of excess of scruple — fall under the same warning; the Qur'an addressed this in 5:87, "O you who believe, do not forbid the good things God has made lawful to you." And those who *permit* what God forbade — declaring usury, wine, or unlawful intimacy acceptable by their own reasoning — fall under it equally. The verse is symmetrical: "this is lawful *and* this is forbidden" — both directions of invention are condemned.

The verse thus stands as a permanent check on the human tendency to make religion in one's own image — to forbid what one dislikes and permit what one desires, and to call the result God's will. Al-Rāzī: the verse establishes that religion is *received*, not *constructed*; and that the construction of religion, however pious its motive, is fabrication against God.

**The Application: Humility Before the Law**

The verse asks the believer to hold two dispositions together. The first is *confidence* in what God has clearly declared: the four prohibitions of verse 115 are forbidden, the commands of verse 90 are commanded, and about these there is no hesitation. The second is *humility* about everything else: where God has not spoken clearly, the believer does not put words in His mouth. He does not forbid what God permitted, whether from excessive scruple or from cultural habit; he does not permit what God forbade, whether from desire or from the pressure of the age; and when he is uncertain, he says "I do not know" rather than "this is lawful" or "this is forbidden." The fear the verse instilled in Mālik — who said "I do not know" thirty-two times out of forty-eight — is the fear the verse intends every believer to feel before the words *ḥalāl* and *ḥarām*. The one who feels it has understood that these words are God's, and that borrowing them without His authority is the fabrication the verse condemns.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:117

> **A brief enjoyment—and theirs shall be a painful punishment.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Fabricator's Account Settled**

Verse 116 forbade inventing rulings of lawful and forbidden and ended with the declaration that those who fabricate lies against God "will not prosper." Verse 117 states, in the tersest form, what they have instead: *matāʿun qalīlun wa-lahum ʿadhābun alīm*, "a little enjoyment — and theirs is a painful punishment." The verse is three words and a conjunction in Arabic, and its brevity enacts its content: the enjoyment is brief, and the sentence describing it is brief.

**"A Brief Enjoyment": *Matāʿun Qalīl***

The verse begins with *matāʿ*, enjoyment, provision, the goods of this world — the word used in verse 80 for the furnishings "for a while" (*matāʿan ilā ḥīn*). Here it is qualified by *qalīl*, little, brief, paltry — the same adjective used in verse 95 for the "paltry price" for which the covenant might be sold.

The grammatical status of *matāʿun qalīl* has been discussed. It is nominative and indefinite, with no explicit verb or predicate. The commentators supply the ellipsis: "[Their share is] a little enjoyment," or "[What they have is] a little enjoyment," or "[They have] a little enjoyment [in this world]." Al-Zamakhsharī reads it as the predicate of an omitted subject: *dhālika matāʿun qalīl*, "that is a little enjoyment" — where "that" is whatever the fabricators gained by their fabrication. Al-Rāzī reads it similarly: what they obtain from their invented rulings — the authority, the social standing, the maintenance of their order — is a little enjoyment.

The commentators explain what the enjoyment was. The idolaters' invented prohibitions served their interests: they maintained the authority of the priests and chiefs who pronounced them; they channeled wealth to the idols and their keepers; they preserved a social hierarchy (as in the rule that certain foods were for men and not women, 6:139). The fabrication paid. Verse 117 acknowledges the payment and names its size: *qalīl*, little. Whatever the fabricators gained, it was small — small in itself, as all worldly goods are (4:77, "the enjoyment of this world is little"), and small in duration, as verse 96 established ("what is with you runs out").

**The Enjoyment as a Limited Grant**

The commentators note that the verse does not deny that the fabricators enjoy. It concedes the enjoyment and limits it. This is the Qur'an's consistent approach to the prosperity of the wicked: it does not pretend they do not prosper, but it names the prosperity's nature. Verse 55 said "enjoy yourselves, and soon you will know." Verse 61 said God defers them to an appointed term. Verse 117 says their enjoyment is little. The pattern is the same: the enjoyment is real, granted, and bounded. Al-Rāzī: the verse's concession is itself a warning — the fabricators are told that what they have is all they will have, and that it is little.

The Qur'an makes the same point about the disbelievers' movement through the world: "Let not the free movement of the disbelievers in the lands deceive you. A little enjoyment; then their refuge is Hell — and wretched is the resting place" (3:196–197). The phrase "a little enjoyment" (*matāʿun qalīl*) is identical, and the structure — enjoyment, then punishment — is the structure of 16:117.

**"And Theirs Shall Be a Painful Punishment": *Wa-lahum ʿadhābun alīm***

The verse's second half is the counterweight: *wa-lahum ʿadhābun alīm*, "and for them is a painful punishment." The conjunction *wa-*, "and," joins the two halves as a single account: a little enjoyment *and* a painful punishment — the debit and the credit of the fabricator's ledger. The phrase *ʿadhāb alīm* was discussed at verses 63 and 104.

The commentators observe the asymmetry the verse constructs. The enjoyment is *qalīl*, little; the punishment is *alīm*, painful — and, by implication, not little. The verse does not say "a little punishment" to balance "a little enjoyment"; it sets a small pleasure against a great pain. The fabricator's bargain, like the oath-breaker's in verses 95–96, is exposed as a bad one: he received little and owes much. Al-Zamakhsharī: the verse's brevity conceals a full accounting, in which what was gained is dwarfed by what is owed.

**The Verse as Conclusion of the Passage**

Verses 114–117 form a unit on food and law. Verse 114 commanded eating the lawful with gratitude. Verse 115 defined the forbidden and its exception. Verse 116 forbade inventing further rulings and named the invention as fabrication against God. Verse 117 states the fabricators' end. The commentators read the unit as the sūrah's practical application of its theme: God's blessing is to be received (v. 114), within the limits He set (v. 115), without human addition (v. 116), because human addition brings a little gain and a great loss (v. 117). The sūrah's final movement thus begins by establishing the believers' relationship to God's provision and God's law together.

**The Connection to Verse 116's "Will Not Prosper"**

Verse 116 ended: "those who fabricate lies against God will not prosper." Verse 117 explains what "will not prosper" means. It does not mean they gain nothing — they gain "a little enjoyment." It means that what they gain is not *falāḥ*, prosperity in the Qur'anic sense — the lasting success of the Hereafter — but its opposite: a little now and pain later. The commentators note that the Qur'an's word *falāḥ* is reserved for the success that lasts; the fabricators' brief enjoyment is not *falāḥ* but its counterfeit, and verse 117 exposes the counterfeit by naming the punishment that follows.

**The Application: Reckoning the Fabricator's Gain**

The verse asks the reader to see the gains of religious fabrication — and of every compromise with truth for advantage — at their true size. Whoever declares lawful what God forbade, or forbidden what God permitted, to gain something — authority, approval, ease, wealth — gains what verse 117 calls *matāʿun qalīl*, a little enjoyment. The word *qalīl* is the verse's corrective to the fabricator's own perception: to him the gain seems significant, worth the fabrication; the verse tells him it is little, and that the account includes a painful punishment he did not price in. The believer who is tempted to bend God's law for gain is asked to read the ledger as the verse writes it: a little enjoyment, and a painful punishment. The Prophet ﷺ described the same accounting for one who takes what is not his by a false claim: "he has taken a portion of the Fire" (al-Bukhārī 2458; Muslim 1713). The portion of the world he gained was little; the portion of the Fire was what it cost.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:118

> **And unto those who are Jews, We forbade what We recounted to thee before. We wronged them not, but they wronged themselves.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Different Case: Prohibitions That God Did Impose**

Verses 115–117 established that God forbade only four things and condemned those who invent further prohibitions. Verse 118 addresses an apparent objection: the Jews had many more dietary prohibitions than four, and these were, by the Qur'an's own account, imposed by God. Does this contradict the principle? The verse answers: *wa-ʿalā alladhīna hādū ḥarramnā mā qaṣaṣnā ʿalayka min qabl*, "and upon those who are Jews We forbade what We related to you before." The Jewish prohibitions were real, and they were God's — but they were a special case, imposed as a consequence of the Jews' own wrongdoing, and they do not extend to others. The verse thus distinguishes God's legitimate prohibition from human fabrication and, at the same time, explains why the Jewish law was stricter.

**"Unto Those Who Are Jews": *ʿAlā alladhīna hādū***

The phrase *alladhīna hādū*, "those who are Jews" or "those who became Jews," is the Qur'an's usual designation (2:62; 4:46, 160; 5:41, 44, 69; 6:146; 22:17; 62:6). The verb *hāda* has been connected to the root meaning "to return, to repent" (7:156, where Moses says *innā hudnā ilayk*, "we have turned to You"), or to the name Judah (*Yahūdhā*), or to the noun *Yahūd*. The verse addresses the prohibitions specific to them.

**"We Forbade What We Recounted to Thee Before"**

The verse says the prohibitions were *mā qaṣaṣnā ʿalayka min qabl*, "what We related to you before." The commentators identify the reference: the passage in Sūrat al-Anʿām, which is Makkan and was revealed before al-Naḥl, that lists the Jewish prohibitions:

> *"And to those who are Jews We forbade every animal with claws, and of the cattle and sheep We forbade to them their fat, except what adheres to their backs or the entrails or what is joined with bone. That is how We recompensed them for their transgression, and truly We are truthful."* (Qur'an 6:146)

The prohibitions named there — animals with undivided hooves (every "possessor of claws," understood as camels, ostriches, and similar), and the fat of cattle and sheep except certain portions — correspond to prohibitions in the Torah (Leviticus 11; 7:23–25). The Qur'an thus affirms that God did impose these on the Jews, and verse 118 refers back to the earlier statement rather than repeating it.

**The Reason: "That Is How We Recompensed Them for Their Transgression"**

The key to verse 118 is the reason the Qur'an gives, in 6:146 and elsewhere, for the Jewish prohibitions. They were not part of the original, universal law; they were a *punishment* imposed on a specific people for specific wrongdoing:

> *"For wrongdoing on the part of the Jews, We forbade them good things which had been lawful to them, and for their averting many from the way of God, and their taking usury while they had been forbidden it, and their consuming the wealth of people unjustly."* (Qur'an 4:160–161)

> *"All food was lawful to the Children of Israel except what Israel [Jacob] had forbidden to himself before the Torah was revealed."* (Qur'an 3:93)

The verse in Āl ʿImrān (3:93) establishes the original state: all food was lawful to the Children of Israel. The verse in al-Nisāʾ (4:160) explains the change: because of their wrongdoing, God forbade them good things that had been lawful. The Jewish prohibitions were thus a *tightening* of the law as a consequence of sin — a burden added, not a standard set. Jesus was sent, in part, to lift it: "to make lawful for you some of what was forbidden to you" (3:50). And the Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ was described in the Torah and the Gospel as one who "relieves them of their burden and the shackles that were upon them" (7:157).

The commentators draw the consequence for verse 118. The Jewish prohibitions do not contradict the principle of verses 115–116, because they were not a general law but a specific punishment; and the idolaters' prohibitions cannot be justified by appeal to them, because the idolaters were not under that punishment and had no revelation authorizing their inventions. Al-Rāzī: the verse distinguishes three things — the four universal prohibitions (v. 115), the additional prohibitions imposed on the Jews as punishment (v. 118), and the prohibitions invented by the idolaters (v. 116). The first are God's law for all; the second are God's law for a specific people in a specific condition; the third are no law at all.

**"We Wronged Them Not, but They Wronged Themselves"**

The verse ends: *wa-mā ẓalamnāhum wa-lākin kānū anfusahum yaẓlimūn*, "and We did not wrong them, but they used to wrong themselves." The formula was used in verse 33 for the destroyed nations, and it recurs here for the Jews under their added prohibitions. The commentators explain its application. The prohibitions were a hardship — the deprivation of good things once lawful. One might ask whether it was just to impose them. The verse answers: it was not a wrong done *to* them; it was a consequence of the wrong they did *to themselves*. Their transgression, their obstruction of others, their usury, their consumption of wealth unjustly (4:160–161) — these earned the tightening. God's imposition of it was justice, not injustice; and the injustice, such as it was, was their own, against their own souls.

The verse's phrasing is precise in a way the commentators note: *kānū anfusahum yaẓlimūn*, "they *used to* wrong themselves" — the continuous past, indicating persistent, habitual wrongdoing. The prohibitions were not imposed for a single lapse but for a pattern.

**The Theological Principle: Law as Response**

The verse establishes a principle the commentators developed: God's law responds to the condition of those who receive it. A people in a state of obedience receives a law suited to that state; a people in persistent transgression may receive a stricter law as discipline. The Jewish prohibitions were an instance of the second. Al-Rāzī connects this to the doctrine of abrogation discussed at verse 101: God "knows best what He sends down," and He sends down what each people needs — sometimes relief, sometimes restriction. The Qur'an's law for the Muslims — with its four prohibitions and its exceptions in necessity — is described as a relief and a mercy (7:157; 22:78, "He has not placed upon you in religion any hardship"), and the verse's reference to the Jewish prohibitions makes the contrast felt.

The principle also explains something the commentators regarded as important: the Muslims are not to imitate the Jewish prohibitions out of scruple. Some early Muslims, seeing the Jews avoid certain foods, wondered whether they should do the same. The verse tells them that those prohibitions were a specific discipline for a specific wrong, not a standard of piety; to adopt them would be to take on a punishment God did not impose — and, indeed, to fall under verse 116, forbidding what God did not forbid.

**The Verse and the Sūrah's Treatment of the People of the Book**

Verse 118 is the sūrah's first explicit mention of the Jews, and it will be followed by verse 124 (on the Sabbath) and the Abrahamic verses (120–123) that place the Prophet's religion in the line of Abraham, prior to both Judaism and Christianity. The commentators read these verses together as the sūrah's positioning of Islam in relation to the earlier revelations: it affirms them as God's; it explains their specific features as responses to their communities' conditions; and it presents the Qur'an's law as the restoration of the original, Abrahamic, universal way, freed from the additions — divine (as discipline) or human (as fabrication) — that had accumulated.

**The Application: Neither Inventing Nor Borrowing Burdens**

The verse teaches the believer two restraints. The first, from verse 116, is not to invent prohibitions. The second, from verse 118, is not to borrow them — not to adopt restrictions that God imposed on others for reasons that do not apply, or that God never imposed at all, in the belief that more restriction means more piety. The Qur'an's law is described as the "middle" (2:143) and as free of hardship (22:78); its prohibitions are few and its permissions vast (v. 115). The believer who honors this — who eats the lawful with gratitude and refuses to add to God's law from any source — has understood verse 118's lesson: that God did not wrong the Jews with their prohibitions, and that He does not burden the Muslims with them either. The Prophet ﷺ, when asked about matters the questioner feared might be forbidden, sometimes replied by warning against asking too much, lest the asking bring a prohibition that would not otherwise have existed (al-Bukhārī 7288; Muslim 1337). The verse's account of the Jewish prohibitions is the historical illustration of that warning.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:119

> **Then truly thy Lord—for those who do evil in ignorance, then repent after that and make amends—truly thy Lord, after that, is Forgiving, Merciful.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Door of Repentance, Opened Again**

Verses 116–118 described fabrication against God, its punishment, and the disciplinary prohibitions imposed on the Jews for their wrongdoing. Verse 119 follows with mercy: *thumma inna rabbaka li'lladhīna ʿamilū al-sūʾa bi-jahālatin thumma tābū min baʿdi dhālika wa-aṣlaḥū*, "then truly your Lord — for those who do evil in ignorance, then repent after that and make amends." The verse's structure exactly mirrors verse 110 — the same repeated *inna rabbaka*, the same *min baʿdihā*, the same closing names — and the commentators read the two verses as a pair: verse 110 promised forgiveness to those who emigrated after persecution; verse 119 promises it to those who repent after sin. Together they show that the sūrah's severity is always accompanied by an open door.

**The Repeated Structure**

The verse begins *thumma inna rabbaka*, "then truly your Lord," and after describing its subjects, resumes with *inna rabbaka min baʿdihā la-ghafūrun raḥīm*, "truly your Lord, after that, is Forgiving, Merciful." The repetition of *inna rabbaka* was explained at verse 110: the intervening clause is long, and the resumption restores the sentence's force so that the predicate lands with full weight. Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Rāzī note that the repetition also enacts the emphasis: God's forgiveness is affirmed twice over, framing the sinner's repentance on both sides.

The *thumma*, "then," connects the verse to what precedes. The commentators read it as a *thumma* of discourse: having described the fabricators and the disciplined, the sūrah turns to those who sinned and repented. The turn is deliberate. After verses on punishment, the sūrah does not leave the reader in fear; it names the way out.

**"Those Who Do Evil in Ignorance": *Bi-jahālah***

The subjects are *alladhīna ʿamilū al-sūʾa bi-jahālah*, "those who did evil in ignorance." The word *jahālah*, ignorance, is the key term, and the commentators discuss it at length, because the verse's mercy is attached to it.

The narrow reading takes *jahālah* as not knowing that the act is a sin. On this reading, the verse addresses those who sinned without knowing it was forbidden — and then, learning, repented.

The broad reading, held by the majority of the early commentators and recorded by al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī, and al-Rāzī, takes *jahālah* as the state of anyone who sins, regardless of his knowledge. Abū al-ʿĀliyah and Qatādah reported that the Companions agreed that every sin is committed *bi-jahālah* — in ignorance — whether deliberately or not, because the one who sins has, in the moment of sinning, acted as though he did not know God's watching, God's judgment, and the sin's consequence. Mujāhid said: "Whoever disobeys his Lord is ignorant until he desists from his disobedience." Al-Rāzī explains the logic: knowledge, in the full sense, would prevent the sin; the one who sins has therefore acted against his knowledge, which is a kind of ignorance — the ignorance of the one who knows in principle and forgets in practice. The word *jahl* in Arabic also denotes rashness, impetuosity, the overpowering of reason by passion — the sense in which the pre-Islamic era was the *Jāhiliyyah* — and this sense applies to every sin committed under the sway of desire or anger.

The Qur'an uses the same phrase in the same context elsewhere:

> *"Repentance is only for those who do evil in ignorance and then repent soon after. Those — God will accept their repentance, and God is Knowing, Wise."* (Qur'an 4:17)

> *"And when those who believe in Our signs come to you, say: Peace be upon you. Your Lord has prescribed mercy upon Himself: that whoever among you does evil in ignorance and then repents after that and makes amends — then truly He is Forgiving, Merciful."* (Qur'an 6:54)

The verse in Sūrat al-Anʿām (6:54) is nearly identical to 16:119 and adds that God "has prescribed mercy upon Himself" — the forgiveness is not a concession God might withhold but a commitment He has made. On the broad reading, which the parallels support, verse 119 covers every sinner who repents: all sin is "in ignorance," and the door is open to all.

**"Then Repent After That": *Thumma tābū min baʿdi dhālika***

The first condition of forgiveness is *tābū*, "they repented." The verb *tāba*, from the root *t-w-b*, means to turn — to turn back from the sin, to return to God. *Tawbah*, repentance, is the human turning; and God's *tawbah* (as in *al-Tawwāb*, one of His names) is His turning toward the sinner in acceptance. The scholars defined the conditions of valid repentance: ceasing the sin; regretting it; resolving not to return to it; and, where the sin involved another's right, restoring that right. Al-Qurṭubī records these conditions in his commentary on this verse.

The phrase *min baʿdi dhālika*, "after that" — after the evil done in ignorance — marks the sequence: the sin came first, the turning second. The commentators note that the verse does not require that the repentance be immediate (as 4:17's "soon after" might suggest), but that it occur *after* the sin and before death — the limit stated by the Prophet ﷺ: "God accepts the repentance of the servant so long as the death-rattle has not reached his throat" (al-Tirmidhī 3537).

**"And Make Amends": *Wa-aṣlaḥū***

The second condition is *aṣlaḥū*, "they made amends," "they set right." The verb *aṣlaḥa*, from the root *ṣ-l-ḥ* (the root of *ṣāliḥ*, righteous, in verse 97), means to reform, to rectify, to make good. The commentators explain that repentance is not complete with the inner turning alone; it must issue in outward reform — the correction of one's conduct, the repair of what the sin damaged, the doing of good in place of the evil. Al-Rāzī: *tawbah* is the turning of the heart; *iṣlāḥ* is the turning of the life. The Qur'an pairs the two consistently (2:160; 3:89; 4:146; 5:39; 6:54; 24:5), and the pairing establishes that a repentance that does not change conduct is not the repentance the verse describes.

The Prophet ﷺ taught the principle of *iṣlāḥ* after sin in practical form: "Follow a bad deed with a good one, and it will erase it" (al-Tirmidhī 1987). The good deed that follows is the *iṣlāḥ*.

**"Truly Thy Lord, After That, Is Forgiving, Merciful"**

The predicate is *la-ghafūrun raḥīm*, "surely Forgiving, Merciful," preceded by *min baʿdihā*, "after that" — after the sin, the repentance, and the amends. The two names were discussed at verses 110 and 115. Here, *Ghafūr* covers the sin — it is forgiven, covered, erased; and *Raḥīm* covers what follows — the repentant sinner is not merely pardoned but received into mercy, restored to God's favor. The commentators note that the verse promises more than acquittal: the repentant is not treated as a criminal released on a technicality but as a servant welcomed back.

The Qur'an describes the fullness of this restoration elsewhere: "Except for those who repent, believe, and do righteous work; for them God will replace their evil deeds with good. And God is ever Forgiving and Merciful" (25:70). The evil deeds are not only erased but *replaced* with good — the repentant sinner ends with more than he would have had without the sin, because the repentance itself is a good deed and the mercy that follows it is a gift.

**The Verse in Its Context**

The commentators connect verse 119 to what precedes and follows. It follows the account of the fabricators (vv. 116–117) and the Jews (v. 118), and it tells both — and everyone — that whatever wrong was done, repentance and reform open the door to forgiveness. The fabricator who repents of his fabrication, the Jew who repents of the wrongdoing that earned the discipline, the idolater who repents of his idolatry — each is covered by the verse's *alladhīna ʿamilū al-sūʾa bi-jahālah*. And the verse precedes the account of Abraham (vv. 120–123), the model of the one who turned to God with his whole being. The sequence moves from the sinner's turning to the exemplar of turning.

**The Pairing With Verse 110**

The commentators observed the deliberate parallel with verse 110. Verse 110: those who *emigrated* after persecution, then *struggled* and were *patient* — for them, after that, God is Forgiving and Merciful. Verse 119: those who *did evil* in ignorance, then *repented* and *made amends* — for them, after that, God is Forgiving and Merciful. The two verses share their opening (*thumma inna rabbaka*), their structure (subject, then the actions, then the resumed *inna rabbaka min baʿdihā*), and their predicate (*la-ghafūrun raḥīm*). The parallel teaches that the two situations — the believer who was broken by persecution and the believer who was broken by his own sin — are treated with the same mercy. Both require a turning (emigration / repentance), an effort (struggle / amends), and an endurance (patience, implied in both); and both receive the same promise. The sūrah's God is the same God toward the persecuted and the sinner: Forgiving, Merciful, after that.

**The Application: The Sinner's Path**

The verse gives every believer who has sinned a three-step path and a promise at its end. The path: recognize the sin as *jahālah* — an act against one's own knowledge, a lapse of the reason that faith should govern; turn from it, with the regret, cessation, and resolve that constitute *tawbah*; and reform — repair the damage, replace the evil with good, change the conduct. The promise: God, after that, is Forgiving and Merciful — not grudgingly but as He has "prescribed upon Himself" (6:54). The verse's repetition of *inna rabbaka*, "truly your Lord," is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ but overheard by every sinner, and its message is that the Lord of the Prophet is also the Lord of the one who did evil in ignorance, and that His mercy after repentance is as certain as His wrath before it. The Prophet ﷺ said: "The one who repents from sin is like one who has no sin" (Ibn Mājah 4250). That is the state verse 119 describes, and it is available to everyone the verse addresses — which is everyone.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:120

> **Truly Abraham was a community, devoutly obedient to God, a ḥanīf, and he was not of the idolaters.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Exemplar Introduced**

After the passage on law, fabrication, and repentance (vv. 114–119), the sūrah presents the figure who embodies everything it has been teaching: *inna Ibrāhīma kāna ummatan qānitan li'llāhi ḥanīfan wa-lam yaku mina al-mushrikīn*, "Truly Abraham was a community, obedient to God, a *ḥanīf*, and he was not of the idolaters." Abraham is named here for the first time in the sūrah, and the commentators explain the placement. The idolaters of Makkah claimed descent from Abraham and custody of the House he built; they invoked his name for their religion. The sūrah now describes Abraham as he was — the pure monotheist, the model of gratitude, the one who was not an idolater — and thereby exposes the distance between him and those who claimed him.

**"Abraham Was a Community": *Ummah***

The verse's most striking phrase is *kāna ummatan*, "he was a community" — a single man described by a word that denotes a people. The commentators offered several explanations, and they are complementary.

The first, held by Ibn Masʿūd and many of the early authorities as al-Ṭabarī reports, is that *ummah* here means *imām*, leader — one who is followed, a teacher of good. Abraham was an *ummah* because he was the leader whom communities follow, the one God made "a leader for mankind" (2:124). Ibn Masʿūd is also reported to have said, of Muʿādh ibn Jabal, "Muʿādh was an *ummah*, obedient to God" — using the verse's phrase for a man who taught good and was followed in it.

The second, developed by al-Zamakhsharī and al-Rāzī, is that Abraham was equivalent to a whole community in himself. He possessed, alone, the virtues that are normally distributed across a people: the faith of the believer, the knowledge of the scholar, the courage of the warrior, the generosity of the host, the patience of the tried. A community is complete when it contains all these; Abraham contained them all. Al-Rāzī cites the saying that when Abraham stood alone in faith — the only monotheist on earth — he was, by himself, the community of believers, and the *ummah* of God consisted of one man.

The third, related to the second, is that Abraham was the *origin* of the community — the root from which the community of monotheists grew, as a single seed is called by the name of the field it produces. Mujāhid is reported to have said that Abraham was "a community" because he was alone in faith when all the people were disbelievers, and the believers descended from him.

The word *ummah* itself, from the root *ʾ-m-m*, denotes a group united by a common direction (*amma*, to aim at), and also, in Qur'anic usage, a religion or way (43:22), a period of time (11:8; 12:45), and a leader — the range the commentators drew upon. All the readings converge: Abraham was a leader, a complete man, and the root of the faithful; a community in one person.

**"Devoutly Obedient to God": *Qānitan li'llāh***

The second description is *qānitan li'llāh*, "obedient to God." The word *qānit*, from *qunūt*, denotes constant, humble, devoted obedience — the standing in prayer with submission, the persistent worship of one whose whole orientation is toward God. The Qur'an uses it for the angels (2:116), for Mary (66:12), for the righteous women (4:34; 33:35), and for the one who stands in prayer through the night (39:9). Al-Rāzī defines it as continuous obedience joined with humility. Abraham's *qunūt* was displayed in his life: he obeyed when commanded to leave his people, when commanded to settle his family in a barren valley, when commanded to sacrifice his son, when commanded to build the House. "When his Lord said to him: Submit — he said: I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds" (2:131).

**"A Ḥanīf": The Key Term**

The third description is *ḥanīfan*, "a *ḥanīf*." The word is among the most significant in the Qur'an's account of Abraham, and the commentators explain it carefully. The root *ḥ-n-f* denotes inclining, turning away — specifically, turning away from error toward truth. A *ḥanīf* is one who has turned from all false religion to the pure worship of God alone. Al-Ṭabarī defines it as one who follows the religion of Abraham, upright in Islam; al-Zamakhsharī as one who inclines away from every false religion to the true one; al-Rāzī as one whose inclination is straight — toward God and away from everything else.

The Qur'an uses *ḥanīf* almost exclusively for Abraham and for the religion he exemplified (2:135; 3:67, 95; 4:125; 6:79, 161; 10:105; 16:120, 123; 22:31; 30:30; 98:5). Its most important context is the denial that Abraham belonged to either of the later communities:

> *"Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian, but he was a ḥanīf, a Muslim, and he was not of the idolaters."* (Qur'an 3:67)

The *ḥanīf* is thus the monotheist who precedes and transcends the sectarian divisions — the one who worships God alone, without the accretions of later communities. Before Islam, some Arabs who rejected idolatry and sought the religion of Abraham were called *ḥunafāʾ* — Zayd ibn ʿAmr ibn Nufayl, Waraqah ibn Nawfal, and others — and the Prophet ﷺ described the religion he was sent with as *al-ḥanīfiyyah al-samḥah*, "the tolerant *ḥanīf* way" (Aḥmad 2107; al-Bukhārī, *al-Adab al-Mufrad* 287).

The commentators connect *ḥanīf* to the *fiṭrah*, the natural disposition toward God (30:30, "So set your face toward the religion as a *ḥanīf* — the *fiṭrah* of God upon which He created mankind"). The *ḥanīf* is the one who has returned to what he was created upon, turning away from everything that covered it.

**"And He Was Not of the Idolaters": The Decisive Negation**

The verse ends: *wa-lam yaku mina al-mushrikīn*, "and he was not of the idolaters." The commentators explain why this negation is stated after the positive descriptions have already implied it. The Makkans claimed Abraham. They said they followed his religion; they maintained his House; they preserved rites he had instituted — the pilgrimage, the sacrifice. And they worshipped idols around his House. The verse tells them, in the plainest terms, that Abraham was not of them. Whatever they preserved of his rites, they had abandoned his essential characteristic: he was not a *mushrik*, and they were.
