Al-Rāzī: the negation strips the idolaters of their claim to Abraham in a single clause.

The same negation appears in 3:67 and 3:95, and in Abraham's own words in 6:79: "I have turned my face toward Him who created the heavens and the earth, as a *ḥanīf*, and I am not of the idolaters." The Qur'an repeats it because the claim to Abraham was made by every community — Jews, Christians, and Arab idolaters — and each had to be told that Abraham's religion was defined by what they lacked.

**Abraham as the Sūrah's Model**

The commentators explain why Abraham is presented at this point in the sūrah. The sūrah's theme is gratitude for blessing and the pure worship of the Giver; its enemy is *shirk* and *kufr al-niʿmah*. Abraham is the paradigm of gratitude — the next verse will call him "grateful for His blessings" — and the paradigm of pure worship — a *ḥanīf* who was not an idolater. He faced what the Prophet ﷺ faced: a people devoted to idols, including his own father; and he responded with the argument from creation (6:75–79; 21:52–67) that the sūrah has been making, with the rejection of inherited religion (v. 35's "our fathers") that the sūrah has demanded, and with the migration for God's sake (v. 41) that the sūrah has praised. He is, in one person, the sūrah's argument lived out.

The Prophet ﷺ was repeatedly directed to Abraham as his model: "Then We revealed to you to follow the religion of Abraham, a *ḥanīf*" (16:123, three verses hence); "There has been for you an excellent example in Abraham" (60:4). The sūrah's presentation of Abraham is thus not only a rebuke to the idolaters but an instruction to the Prophet and his community: this is whom you follow.

**The Application: Being an *Ummah***

The verse offers the believer a striking possibility: that a single person may be a community. Abraham stood alone in faith and was, by himself, the *ummah* of God. The commentators drew the lesson that faith does not depend on numbers — that the believer who stands alone in truth is not diminished by his solitude but is, in the verse's terms, a community — and that the qualities of a whole people may be gathered in one person who devotes himself wholly to God. The verse also gives the believer a standard: *qānit*, constantly obedient; *ḥanīf*, turned wholly from falsehood to truth; and *not of the idolaters* — free of every form of *shirk*, including the subtle forms the sūrah has exposed. The one who meets this standard is, in his measure, what Abraham was in his fullness, and has taken his place in the *ummah* that Abraham, alone, first constituted.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:121

> **Grateful for His blessings, He chose him and guided him to a straight path.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Quality That Names the Sūrah's Purpose**

Verse 120 described Abraham as a community, obedient, a *ḥanīf*, not an idolater. Verse 121 adds the description that, more than any other, connects him to this sūrah: *shākiran li-anʿumih*, "grateful for His blessings." The sūrah has been called *Sūrat al-Niʿam*, the Chapter of Blessings, and its demand from beginning to end has been *shukr*, gratitude. Abraham is now named as the one who gave it. The verse then states what followed from his gratitude: God chose him and guided him.

**"Grateful for His Blessings": *Shākiran li-anʿumih***

The word *shākir*, grateful, is the active participle of *shakara*, and it describes Abraham's settled disposition: he was *a grateful one*, one whose gratitude was his character rather than an occasional act. The object is *anʿumih*, "His blessings" — the plural *anʿum*, used also in verse 112 for the blessings the ungrateful town denied. The parallel is deliberate: the town was ungrateful for God's *anʿum* and tasted hunger and fear; Abraham was grateful for God's *anʿum* and was chosen and guided.

The commentators explain what Abraham's gratitude consisted of. It was, first, the recognition that every blessing came from God alone — the recognition Abraham expressed in his argument with his people: "Who created me, and He guides me; and who feeds me and gives me drink; and when I am ill, it is He who cures me; and who will cause me to die and then bring me to life" (26:78–81). Every blessing in that catalogue — creation, guidance, food, drink, health, life — is attributed to God with the emphatic pronoun *huwa*, "He." This is the gratitude of the heart: the acknowledgment of the Giver.

It was, second, the praise of the tongue. Abraham's prayers are among the Qur'an's most extended acts of praise: "Praise be to God who has given me, in old age, Ishmael and Isaac; truly my Lord is the Hearer of supplication" (14:39).

It was, third, the use of every blessing in obedience — the gratitude of action. Abraham used his son in obedience (offering him at God's command), his wealth in hospitality (the guests of 11:69; 51:24–27), his body in building the House (2:127), his life in migration and mission. Al-Rāzī: Abraham's gratitude was complete because it engaged all three — heart, tongue, and limbs — and because it was proportioned to the blessings, which he counted (as far as they could be counted, v. 18) and returned, each one, to its Source.

The commentators also note a specific sense of *shākir* in the case of Abraham: he was grateful even in trial. Thrown into the fire, he said, "God is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs" (as the Prophet ﷺ reported he said, al-Bukhārī 4563). Commanded to sacrifice his son, he submitted (37:103). His gratitude was not contingent on ease; it was the gratitude of one who saw God's blessing in the trial itself — the blessing of being tested by the One who chose him.

**Gratitude as the Cause of Election**

The verse's structure has been read as causal: *shākiran li-anʿumih ijtabāh*, "grateful for His blessings — He chose him." The commentators note that the gratitude is named before the choosing, and they draw the connection. Abraham's gratitude was the disposition that made him fit for election; God chose him *because* he was grateful, or *as* one who was grateful. Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Rāzī take the participle as a *ḥāl*, a circumstantial description: God chose him *in the state of* being grateful. The Qur'an establishes the general principle: "If you are grateful, I will surely increase you" (14:7). Abraham's increase was election and guidance.

This connection is the sūrah's central teaching stated in the life of one man. The sūrah has argued that gratitude preserves and increases blessing (v. 114, 112 by contrast) and that ingratitude forfeits it (vv. 55, 83, 112). Abraham is the proof: the grateful one was chosen. And the Makkans, who claimed him, are the counter-proof: the ungrateful town tasted hunger and fear.

**"He Chose Him": *Ijtabāh***

The verb *ijtabā*, from the root *j-b-y*, means to select, to choose out, to gather to oneself — as one collects the best of a harvest. God *chose* Abraham — selected him from among all people for prophethood, for friendship, for leadership. The Qur'an uses the verb for the election of the prophets generally (6:87; 19:58; 22:78; 42:13) and for Abraham specifically here. Al-Rāzī explains that *ijtibāʾ* is the divine act of drawing a servant near — selecting him for a rank and a mission that others do not receive.

The commentators enumerate what Abraham was chosen for. He was chosen as prophet and messenger. He was chosen as *khalīl*, the intimate friend of God — "and God took Abraham as a friend" (4:125) — a rank shared, according to the hadith, only by Muḥammad ﷺ (Muslim 532). He was chosen as *imām*, the leader of mankind (2:124). He was chosen as the father of prophets — from his line came Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and all the prophets of Israel, and finally Muḥammad ﷺ. He was chosen as the builder of the House toward which all Muslims pray. The word *ijtabāh* compresses all these elections into one.

**"And Guided Him to a Straight Path": *Wa-hadāhu ilā ṣirāṭin mustaqīm***

The verse ends: *wa-hadāhu ilā ṣirāṭin mustaqīm*, "and He guided him to a straight path." The straight path was named in verse 9 ("unto God leads the straight path") and in verse 76 (the one who commands justice "is on a straight path"). Abraham was guided to it — and the commentators note the sequence: God *chose* him, and then *guided* him. Election precedes guidance; guidance is what the chosen one receives. Al-Rāzī: the choosing is the divine initiative; the guiding is its content.

The commentators identify the straight path as the religion of *tawḥīd* — the pure worship of God alone, which Abraham reached by God's guidance and then taught. The Qur'an describes the process in 6:75–79, where Abraham considers the star, the moon, and the sun, rejects each as it sets, and turns to "Him who created the heavens and the earth" — and the passage is introduced with "thus We showed Abraham the dominion of the heavens and the earth, that he might be among the certain" (6:75). The guidance was God's; the seeing was Abraham's; and the path he arrived at was straight.

The phrase *ilā ṣirāṭin mustaqīm*, "to a straight path," with the indefinite noun, has been noted. Al-Zamakhsharī reads the indefinite as magnifying: "a path — and what a straight path!" Others note that the definite form, *al-ṣirāṭ al-mustaqīm*, is used in the Fātiḥah and elsewhere for the same path; the indefinite here emphasizes its quality rather than its identity.

**The Verse's Three Movements**

The commentators trace the verse's structure as a sequence of three: Abraham's gratitude (his act), God's election (God's response), and God's guidance (the content of the response). The sequence is the sūrah's law of blessing in miniature. The servant receives blessings and is grateful; God, in return, increases him — here, with the greatest increase possible, election and guidance. The reverse sequence is the sūrah's law of loss: the servant receives blessings and is ungrateful; God withdraws them (v. 112). Abraham and the ungrateful town are the two poles, and the sūrah has placed them within nine verses of each other so that the contrast is unmistakable.

**Abraham's Gratitude and the Prophet's**

The commentators connect Abraham's gratitude to the Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ, who was told to follow Abraham's religion (v. 123) and who embodied the same disposition. When ʿĀʾishah asked the Prophet why he stood in prayer until his feet swelled, when God had forgiven him his past and future sins, he replied: "Should I not be a grateful servant?" (al-Bukhārī 4837; Muslim 2820). The phrase *ʿabdan shakūran*, "a grateful servant," is the disposition verse 121 names in Abraham — *shākiran li-anʿumih* — and the Prophet's answer shows that gratitude, for the prophets, was not a response to reward but the very form of their relationship with God.

**The Application: Gratitude as the Path to Being Chosen**

The verse teaches that gratitude is not merely a duty but a door. Abraham was grateful and was chosen; the connection is not arbitrary. The believer who cultivates the disposition of *shukr* — recognizing every blessing as God's, praising Him for it, using it in His obedience — places himself in the line of Abraham and makes himself, in his measure, fit for the increase God promises the grateful. The verse does not promise prophethood; that door is closed. But it promises what prophethood exemplified: election to God's nearness and guidance on His straight path. And it names the condition in a single word, *shākir*, which the sūrah has been explaining for a hundred and twenty verses. The reader who has followed the sūrah this far knows what the word means; the verse tells him what it earns.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:122

> **And We gave him good in this world, and truly in the Hereafter he shall be among the righteous.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Reward in Both Worlds**

Verse 121 said God chose Abraham and guided him. Verse 122 states what else God gave him: *wa-ātaynāhu fī al-dunyā ḥasanah wa-innahu fī al-ākhirati la-mina al-ṣāliḥīn*, "and We gave him good in this world, and truly in the Hereafter he is among the righteous." The verse completes the account of Abraham's reward by naming its two dimensions — this world and the next — and in doing so it echoes the promises the sūrah made earlier to the emigrants (v. 41, "We shall surely settle them in a good place in this world, and the reward of the Hereafter is greater") and to the righteous (v. 30, "for those who do good in this world is good, and the abode of the Hereafter is better"). Abraham is the fulfillment of those promises.

**"We Gave Him Good in This World": *Ḥasanah***

The word *ḥasanah*, good, is the same word used in verse 30 and verse 41. The commentators identify what constituted Abraham's *ḥasanah* in this world, and their enumerations are rich.

He was given a *good name* — praise on every tongue. Every subsequent religious community honors Abraham: the Jews as their patriarch, the Christians as the father of faith, the Muslims as the *ḥanīf* and *khalīl*, and even the pagan Arabs as the builder of the House. This universal honor was the answer to his prayer: "And grant me a reputation of honor among later generations" (26:84). Al-Rāzī, al-Zamakhsharī, and al-Qurṭubī all cite this as the primary sense of *ḥasanah*: God made him beloved to all peoples, so that no community rejects him. The Muslim's prayer in every ritual prayer — "O God, send blessings upon Muḥammad and the family of Muḥammad, as You sent blessings upon Abraham and the family of Abraham" — is the daily enactment of this honor.

He was given *righteous offspring* — Ishmael and Isaac in his old age (14:39), and from them the line of prophets. Prophethood remained in his descendants until the end of revelation: "And We placed in his descendants prophethood and scripture" (29:27; 57:26). This was the *ḥasanah* of continuity.

He was given *wealth and provision* — the flocks and lands that made his hospitality possible. Al-Qurṭubī records that Abraham was wealthy and generous, and the tradition names him *Abū al-Ḍīfān*, "father of guests," for his hospitality.

He was given *the love of God* — the rank of *khalīl*, intimate friend (4:125) — which is the highest good possible in this world.

He was given *deliverance* — from the fire of Nimrod (21:69), from his people's plot (37:97–98), from the trial of the sacrifice (37:107).

And he was given *the House* — the Kaʿbah, which he built, and which became the center of worship for the community that would follow his religion.

Ibn ʿAbbās, according to some reports, glossed *ḥasanah* here as "the truthful tongue" (*lisān ṣidq*) — the good reputation of 26:84 — and al-Ṭabarī inclines to a comprehensive reading: every good that God gave him in this world.

**The Verse and the Sūrah's Earlier Promises**

The commentators note the correspondence between verse 122 and verses 30 and 41. Verse 30 promised "good in this world" (*ḥasanah*) to those who do good, and "the abode of the Hereafter is better." Verse 41 promised the emigrants "a good place in this world" (*ḥasanah*) and "the reward of the Hereafter is greater, if they but knew." Verse 122 shows both promises fulfilled in Abraham — who did good and who emigrated (29:26, "I am emigrating to my Lord"). The sūrah's promises are thus not abstract; they have a historical exemplar, and the exemplar is the man the Makkans claimed as their ancestor.

The verse also refutes a misconception the commentators addressed: that faith and its reward belong only to the Hereafter, while this world belongs to the disbelievers. Abraham was given *ḥasanah* in this world — honor, offspring, provision, love, deliverance. The Qur'an does not promise the believer worldly ease in every case, but it promises the "good life" (v. 97) and it shows in Abraham that faith and worldly good are not opposed. Al-Rāzī: the verse establishes that God's servants may be given good in both worlds, and that the good of this world, when it comes to them, is a reward and not a distraction.

**"And Truly in the Hereafter He Shall Be Among the Righteous"**

The verse's second half is *wa-innahu fī al-ākhirati la-mina al-ṣāliḥīn*, "and truly in the Hereafter he is surely among the righteous." The emphasis is double — *inna* and *la-* — and the commentators note it: the Hereafter's reward is stated with more emphasis than this world's, because it is greater (v. 41) and because it is the true object of hope.

The phrase *mina al-ṣāliḥīn*, "among the righteous," puzzled some readers: Abraham was a prophet and *khalīl*; was he not far above the rank of "the righteous"? The commentators give several answers.

First, "the righteous" (*al-ṣāliḥūn*) is not a low rank but the highest: the Qur'an describes it as the company of "the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs, and the righteous" (4:69) — the rank of those with whom God is pleased, and to which the prophets themselves belong. To be "among the righteous" is to be in the highest company, and Abraham's prayer was to be placed there: "My Lord, grant me wisdom and join me with the righteous" (26:83). Verse 122 is the answer to that prayer. The commentators note the correspondence: Abraham asked to be joined with the righteous; God says he is among them.

Second, the phrase describes the *company*, not the *rank within* it. Abraham is among the righteous — in their company, in the place where they are — and his rank within that company is the highest. Al-Zamakhsharī: the verse names the group, and Abraham's position in the group is known from other texts.

Third, al-Rāzī observes that the verse teaches humility even about the highest: Abraham, the *khalīl*, is described not by his singular rank but by his membership in the community of the righteous, as though to say that the greatest of the servants does not stand apart from the rest but among them. The Prophet Joseph prayed the same prayer at the height of his power: "Cause me to die as a Muslim and join me with the righteous" (12:101). The prophets asked to be among the righteous; God granted it; and the granting was the fulfillment of their highest hope.

**The Sequence of Abraham's Description (vv. 120–122)**

The commentators read the three verses as a complete portrait with a clear structure. Verse 120: Abraham's *character* — a community, obedient, a *ḥanīf*, not an idolater. Verse 121: Abraham's *disposition* — grateful — and God's *response* — election and guidance. Verse 122: Abraham's *reward* — good in this world and the company of the righteous in the next. The portrait moves from what Abraham was, to what he did, to what God did for him, to what he received. It is the sūrah's argument as biography: character issues in gratitude, gratitude is met with election, and election is rewarded in both worlds.

**The Verse and the Believer**

The verse presents Abraham as the exemplar of a reward that the sūrah has promised to every believer who does what he did. Verse 30 promised *ḥasanah* to those who do good; verse 41 to those who emigrate; verse 97 the good life to whoever does righteousness in faith. Verse 122 shows the promise kept in the case of the one who did all three in the fullest measure. The believer is thus given, in Abraham, both a model and a guarantee: the model of gratitude, obedience, and pure worship; and the guarantee that God rewards these in this world and the next, as He rewarded Abraham. The Prophet ﷺ taught his community to ask, in every prayer, for what Abraham received — "as You blessed Abraham and the family of Abraham" — and verse 122 tells them what they are asking for.

**The Application: Asking to Be Among the Righteous**

The verse teaches a prayer and a hope. The prayer is Abraham's own: "join me with the righteous" (26:83) — the prayer that verse 122 answers. The believer who prays it aligns his hope with Abraham's, and the verse tells him that God grants it. The hope is that faith and gratitude yield *ḥasanah* — good — in this world, and the company of the righteous in the next; and that the two are not in competition. The believer who lives as Abraham lived — obedient, grateful, turned from every falsehood — may expect what Abraham received, in the measure God apportions: a good name, good offspring, provision, deliverance, and the love of God here; and there, the highest company. The verse's emphatic *innahu... la-mina al-ṣāliḥīn* is the assurance that the second, at least, is certain for the one who follows the *ḥanīf* to whom the next verse will direct the Prophet himself.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:123

> **Then We revealed unto thee, "Follow the creed of Abraham, a ḥanīf, and he was not of the idolaters."**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Command That Links the Two Prophets**

Verses 120–122 described Abraham — his character, his gratitude, his election, his reward. Verse 123 turns to the Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ and gives him a command: *thumma awḥaynā ilayka ani ittabiʿ millata Ibrāhīma ḥanīfan*, "then We revealed to you: follow the creed of Abraham, a *ḥanīf*." The verse establishes the continuity of the two missions: the last Prophet is commanded to follow the way of the first great monotheist, and the religion he brings is not an innovation but a restoration. The verse's closing phrase — "and he was not of the idolaters" — repeats verse 120's negation, so that the command to follow Abraham is inseparable from the rejection of *shirk*.

**"Then We Revealed Unto Thee": *Thumma Awḥaynā***

The verse begins *thumma*, "then." The commentators discuss the force of this word, since Abraham lived some two and a half millennia before Muḥammad ﷺ. Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Rāzī explain that *thumma* here conveys not merely temporal sequence but *elevation* — it introduces something greater than what preceded, as in "then We gave Moses the Book" (6:154) after the mention of earlier favors. The revelation to Muḥammad, commanding him to follow Abraham, is presented as the culmination of Abraham's honor: the greatest of God's blessings on Abraham was that the final Prophet would be commanded to follow his way. Al-Rāzī: Abraham was given good in this world (v. 122), and among the greatest of that good was that his religion would be revived by the Seal of the Prophets.

The verb *awḥaynā*, "We revealed," is the verb of revelation — the same root used in verse 68 for the bee (*awḥā rabbuka*), where the commentators explained it as inspiration; here it is revelation in the full prophetic sense. The command to follow Abraham came to Muḥammad by *waḥy*, and its status is therefore that of a divine directive, not a personal preference.

**"Follow the Creed of Abraham": *Ittabiʿ millata Ibrāhīm***

The command is *ittabiʿ millata Ibrāhīm*, "follow the *millah* of Abraham." The word *millah* denotes a religion, a creed, a way of life as a whole — the complete system of belief and practice that defines a community. The commentators distinguish it from *dīn*: *dīn* is religion as the relationship of obedience between the servant and God; *millah* is religion as the path or way that a prophet establishes and a community follows. The Qur'an uses *millah* for the way of Abraham repeatedly (2:130, 135; 3:95; 4:125; 6:161; 12:38; 22:78) and always as the standard to which the later communities are called back.

What is the *millah* of Abraham that the Prophet is commanded to follow? The commentators give a layered answer. At its core, it is *tawḥīd* — the pure worship of God alone, with the rejection of every partner — which is why the verse immediately adds "a *ḥanīf*, and he was not of the idolaters." This core is unchanging across all the prophets: "He has ordained for you of religion what He enjoined upon Noah, and what We revealed to you, and what We enjoined upon Abraham, Moses, and Jesus: establish the religion and do not be divided in it" (42:13). Beyond the core, the *millah* of Abraham includes the principles of worship and conduct he exemplified — submission (2:131), gratitude (16:121), the argument from creation (6:75–79), migration for God (29:26), hospitality, and the rites of the House and the pilgrimage (22:26–29), which the Prophet's law confirmed and purified.

The commentators address a question the command raises: the Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ had his own law, which differed in details from Abraham's; how, then, is he commanded to *follow* Abraham? Al-Rāzī answers that the command concerns the *uṣūl*, the foundations — *tawḥīd*, submission, the rejection of *shirk* — in which all the prophets agreed and which Abraham exemplified most purely; the *furūʿ*, the branches of law, differ from prophet to prophet by God's wisdom (5:48, "to each of you We prescribed a law and a method"). The Prophet follows Abraham in the foundations and receives his own law in the branches. Al-Qurṭubī adds that "following" here also means confirming and reviving: the Prophet is to bring back the *millah* of Abraham that had been corrupted by those who claimed it.

**Why Abraham, and Why Now**

The commentators explain why the command to follow Abraham is given at this point in the sūrah. The Makkan idolaters claimed Abraham as their ancestor and the founder of their religion. They maintained his House and some of his rites, and they used his name to legitimize their idolatry. The sūrah has just described Abraham as one who "was not of the idolaters" (v. 120). Verse 123 now commands the Prophet to follow him — and thereby claims Abraham for Islam. The Prophet, not the Quraysh, is the heir of Abraham; the Prophet's religion, not theirs, is Abraham's *millah*. The Qur'an makes this claim explicit elsewhere:

> *"Truly the people most worthy of Abraham are those who followed him, and this Prophet, and those who believe. And God is the ally of the believers."* (Qur'an 3:68)

> *"And who is better in religion than one who submits his face to God, and is a doer of good, and follows the creed of Abraham, a ḥanīf? And God took Abraham as an intimate friend."* (Qur'an 4:125)

The claim also addressed the Jews and Christians, each of whom claimed Abraham. The Qur'an denies that he was either (3:67) and presents the Prophet's *millah* as the restoration of Abraham's pure monotheism before the sectarian divisions. Verse 123 is thus a positioning of Islam in relation to every community that invoked Abraham: it is not a new religion but the return to his.

**"A Ḥanīf, and He Was Not of the Idolaters"**

The verse repeats verse 120's description: *ḥanīfan wa-mā kāna mina al-mushrikīn*. The word *ḥanīf* was explained at verse 120: one who turns from all falsehood to the pure worship of God. The commentators discuss its grammatical role here — it may describe Abraham ("the creed of Abraham, [who was] a *ḥanīf*") or the Prophet's manner of following ("follow the creed of Abraham, [being yourself] a *ḥanīf*"). Both readings hold: Abraham was a *ḥanīf*, and the Prophet is to follow him *as* a *ḥanīf* — turning wholly from the falsehoods of his own people as Abraham turned from those of his.

The negation — "and he was not of the idolaters" — is repeated for emphasis and for its polemical force. The commentators note that the repetition within four verses (120 and 123) is deliberate: it is the point the Makkans most needed to hear. Whatever else they claimed about Abraham, this they could not claim: that he was one of them. The command to follow Abraham is therefore a command to *not be of the idolaters* — to break, as Abraham broke, with the religion of one's people and one's fathers (v. 35) when that religion is *shirk*.

**The Prophet's Fulfillment of the Command**

The commentators note how the Prophet ﷺ fulfilled the command. He restored the House to the worship of God alone, destroying the three hundred and sixty idols around it at the conquest while reciting, "The truth has come and falsehood has vanished" (17:81; al-Bukhārī 4287). He restored the pilgrimage to its Abrahamic form, purging it of the idolatrous additions. He taught his community to invoke blessings on Abraham in every prayer. He named the religion he brought "the *ḥanīfiyyah*" and described himself as the answer to Abraham's prayer for a messenger from among his descendants (2:129; Aḥmad 17150, "I am the prayer of my father Abraham"). And he exemplified Abraham's qualities — submission, gratitude, migration, the argument from creation, the pure worship of God — in his own life. The command of verse 123 was the program of his mission.

**The Verse and the Community**

The command addressed to the Prophet extends to his community, which follows him as he follows Abraham. The Qur'an says: "Strive for God as He deserves. He has chosen you and has not placed upon you in religion any hardship — the creed of your father Abraham. He named you Muslims before" (22:78). The community is Abraham's heir, and its religion is his *millah*. This gives the community its identity — not as an Arab tribal religion or a seventh-century innovation but as the continuation of the oldest monotheism — and its standard: every practice is measured by whether it is Abrahamic, that is, whether it is pure worship of God alone, free of *shirk* and of human addition (vv. 116–118).

**The Application: Following the Ḥanīf**

The verse asks the believer to see his religion as the *millah* of Abraham and to follow it as the Prophet did. In practice, this means several things the commentators drew out. It means *tawḥīd* without compromise — the rejection of every partner, open or subtle. It means the disposition of the *ḥanīf* — the readiness to turn from falsehood even when falsehood is one's inheritance, one's culture, or one's family's way, as Abraham turned from his father's idols. It means gratitude (v. 121), submission (2:131), and the willingness to migrate for God (29:26). And it means confidence in the antiquity and universality of one's faith: the Muslim who follows Abraham is not a follower of a new sect but of the oldest way, to which the last Prophet was commanded, by revelation, to return. The verse's *thumma awḥaynā ilayka* — "then We revealed to you" — tells the believer that this return was God's own directive, and that in following the *ḥanīf* he follows the command given to the Seal of the Prophets.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:124

> **The Sabbath was only appointed for those who differed concerning it. And truly thy Lord will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection concerning that wherein they differed.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**An Objection Anticipated and Answered**

Verse 123 commanded the Prophet ﷺ to follow the creed of Abraham. An objection arises, and the commentators identify it: if the Prophet follows Abraham, and the Jews claim to follow Abraham, why does the Prophet not observe the Sabbath, which the Jews regard as central? Verse 124 answers: *innamā juʿila al-sabtu ʿalā alladhīna ikhtalafū fīh*, "the Sabbath was only appointed for those who differed concerning it." The Sabbath was not part of Abraham's *millah*; it was imposed later, on a specific people, in specific circumstances; and the Prophet's non-observance of it is no departure from Abraham but a fidelity to him.

**"The Sabbath": *Al-Sabt***

The word *sabt* denotes the seventh day, Saturday, and derives from a root meaning to cut off, to cease, to rest. The Jewish Sabbath is the day of rest commanded in the Torah (Exodus 20:8–11; 31:12–17), on which work is forbidden. The Qur'an mentions it several times: the prohibition on the Sabbath and its violation by the people of the town by the sea, who were turned into apes (2:65; 4:47, 154; 7:163).

**"Was Only Appointed for Those Who Differed Concerning It"**

The verse says the Sabbath *juʿila*, "was made," "was appointed," *ʿalā alladhīna ikhtalafū fīh*, "upon those who differed concerning it." The restrictive *innamā* limits the Sabbath to this group. The commentators explain who "differed" and about what.

The most widely reported explanation, from Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Qatādah, and others as recorded by al-Ṭabarī and al-Qurṭubī, is that the Jews were originally commanded to devote one day of the week to worship, and the day appointed was Friday — the day on which, according to Islamic tradition, Adam was created and which God chose for His community. The Jews differed with their prophet, preferring Saturday because God had completed creation and "rested" on it (a notion the Qur'an rejects, 50:38). God then imposed the Sabbath upon them as they had chosen — and made it a burden, with strict prohibitions and severe punishment for violation. The Christians, in turn, chose Sunday. The Muslim community, guided by God, was given Friday — the day that had been intended. The Prophet ﷺ said:

> *"We are the last, but the first on the Day of Resurrection, though they were given the Book before us. Then this day which God prescribed for them — they differed concerning it, and God guided us to it. So the people follow us in it: the Jews tomorrow, and the Christians the day after tomorrow."* (al-Bukhārī 876; Muslim 855)

> *"God turned away from the Friday those who were before us. The Jews had the Sabbath, and the Christians had Sunday. Then God brought us and guided us to Friday, and He made Friday, Saturday, and Sunday. And thus they follow us on the Day of Resurrection."* (Muslim 856)

On this reading, "those who differed concerning it" are the Jews (and Christians) who differed about which day to observe — and the Sabbath was appointed *upon* them (*ʿalā*, with a sense of imposition) as a consequence of their differing.

A second explanation, also recorded, is that "those who differed" are the Jews who differed *among themselves* about the Sabbath's observance — some keeping it and some violating it, as the story of the town by the sea shows (7:163–166). The Sabbath was appointed upon a people who then disputed and divided over it. Al-Rāzī allows this reading and notes that it, too, places the Sabbath as a specific imposition on a specific people, not a universal law.

A third explanation, from al-Zamakhsharī, connects the verse more directly to Abraham: the Jews claimed the Sabbath was part of Abraham's religion; the verse says it was not — it was appointed for those who differed, that is, for the Jews after Abraham, and Abraham himself never observed it. The Prophet, following Abraham, is therefore not bound by it.

All three readings agree on the verse's function: the Sabbath is not Abrahamic; it is a later and particular institution; and its absence from Islam is fidelity to Abraham, not deviation.

**The Sabbath as Discipline**

The commentators connect verse 124 to verse 118, which said that the Jewish dietary prohibitions were imposed as a consequence of their wrongdoing. The Sabbath, on the first reading above, is a parallel case: an institution imposed as a consequence of their differing from their prophet. Al-Rāzī draws the connection: both the dietary restrictions and the Sabbath were burdens placed on the Jews for their conduct — "We forbade them good things which had been lawful to them, for wrongdoing on their part" (4:160) — and both are lifted in the *ḥanīf* religion, which is "the tolerant way" without hardship (22:78). The Muslim community's Friday is not a day of prohibition but a day of gathering for prayer, after which "disperse in the land and seek the bounty of God" (62:10) — work is permitted before and after. The contrast between the Sabbath and Friday is the contrast between discipline and ease.

**"And Truly Thy Lord Will Judge Between Them on the Day of Resurrection"**

The verse's second half is *wa-inna rabbaka la-yaḥkumu baynahum yawma al-qiyāmati fīmā kānū fīhi yakhtalifūn*, "and truly your Lord will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection concerning what they used to differ about." The phrase echoes verses 39, 64, and 92, and the commentators note that this is the sūrah's fourth statement of the theme: the Book clarifies differences now (v. 64); the Resurrection will judge them finally (vv. 39, 92, 124). Here the differences are those of the People of the Book — about the Sabbath, about Abraham, about the law — and God's judgment will settle them.

The commentators read the clause as both a promise and a deflection. As promise: the disputes that the Prophet could not resolve by argument — the Jews would not concede that the Sabbath was a later imposition — will be resolved by God on the Day when the truth is manifest. As deflection: the Prophet is not to be drawn into endless debate over the Sabbath and similar matters; he states the truth (the Sabbath was appointed for those who differed) and leaves the judgment to God. Al-Rāzī: the clause instructs the Prophet not to concern himself with the disputes of the People of the Book beyond stating the truth; the final word is God's.

The phrase also carries a warning. Those who "differed concerning it" — who disputed God's command and chose their own day — will be judged for the differing. The Sabbath's story in the Qur'an ends with the violators turned into apes (7:166); the verse's promise of judgment recalls that the differing had consequences and will have more.

**The Verse in the Sequence on Abraham**

Verse 124 completes the passage on Abraham (vv. 120–124) by removing the last objection to the Prophet's claim to follow him. The passage's argument, as the commentators trace it: Abraham was a pure monotheist, not an idolater (v. 120); grateful, chosen, guided (v. 121); rewarded in both worlds (v. 122); and the Prophet is commanded to follow him (v. 123). The Jews object: then observe the Sabbath. Verse 124 replies: the Sabbath was not Abraham's; it was yours, appointed upon you for your differing; and God will judge you for it. The Prophet's religion is Abraham's without the additions — divine (as discipline) or human (as fabrication) — that later communities accumulated.

**The Application: The Religion Without Burdens**

The verse teaches the believer to understand his religion's relationship to those before it. Islam is not a rejection of the earlier revelations but the restoration of their Abrahamic core, freed from the burdens that were imposed on specific communities for specific reasons. The believer does not observe the Sabbath, not because he disregards God's commands to the Jews, but because that command was theirs and not his — appointed "for those who differed concerning it." His day is Friday, "to which God guided us," a day of gathering and ease, not of prohibition. The verse also teaches him a discipline in disputation: to state the truth about such matters clearly and then to leave the judgment to God, who "will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection." The Prophet ﷺ was not commanded to win every argument with the People of the Book; he was commanded to follow Abraham and convey. The final settlement of who was right about the Sabbath — and about everything else the communities differed over — belongs to the Day when, as the sūrah has said four times, God will make it clear.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:125

> **Call unto the way of thy Lord with wisdom and goodly exhortation, and dispute with them in the most virtuous manner. Truly thy Lord is He who knows best who strays from His way, and He knows best the rightly guided.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Method of the Mission**

The sūrah has spent a hundred and twenty-four verses making its case — through the signs of creation, the parables, the warnings, the promises, and the example of Abraham. Verse 125 now tells the Prophet ﷺ *how* to convey that case to others: *udʿu ilā sabīli rabbika bi'l-ḥikmati wa'l-mawʿiẓati al-ḥasanati wa-jādilhum bi'llatī hiya aḥsan*, "call to the way of your Lord with wisdom and goodly exhortation, and dispute with them in the manner that is best." The verse is the Qur'an's fundamental statement of the method of *daʿwah*, the invitation to God, and it has governed Muslim preaching, teaching, and dialogue since it was revealed. Verse 25 of this sūrah looked forward to it, and the commentators regard it as the sūrah's practical culmination: after the message, the manner.

**"Call Unto the Way of Thy Lord": *Udʿu ilā sabīli rabbik***

The command is *udʿu*, "call," "invite" — from *daʿā*, to call, to summon, to invite. The object is *sabīl rabbik*, "the way of your Lord" — the straight path of verse 9, the way from which the disbelievers turned others (v. 88), the religion of Abraham (v. 123). The commentators note the phrase's precision: the Prophet calls to *God's* way, not to himself, his tribe, or his own opinions. The invitation is to a path that belongs to the Lord, and the caller is a servant pointing the way, not the destination.

The commentators also note the possessive *rabbik*, "your Lord" — the Lord who has cared for the Prophet, sent him, and will judge his hearers. The intimacy of the address (as in vv. 68, 110, 119) reminds the Prophet that the mission is his Lord's affair, and its outcome in His hands.

**"With Wisdom": *Bi'l-Ḥikmah***

The first instrument of the call is *al-ḥikmah*, wisdom. The word, from the root *ḥ-k-m* (to judge, to restrain, to be firm), denotes sound knowledge joined to sound action — knowing the truth and knowing how to apply it. The commentators define it variously. Ibn ʿAbbās, according to al-Ṭabarī, glossed it as the Qur'an itself — the revelation, which is the wisest speech. Others glossed it as the Sunnah, or as prophethood, or as the knowledge of the religion. Al-Rāzī defines it as demonstrative proof (*al-burhān*) — the argument that produces certainty, addressed to those capable of receiving it. Al-Qurṭubī defines it as speech that is correct, sound, and placed where it belongs.

The commentators converge on a practical sense: wisdom in *daʿwah* is speaking the right truth, in the right way, to the right person, at the right time. It includes knowing what to say and what to withhold; knowing the hearer's condition and addressing it; using proof where proof is needed and gentleness where gentleness is needed. Ibn al-Qayyim summarizes: wisdom is placing each thing in its proper place. The caller with wisdom does not deliver the same speech to everyone; he reads the situation and speaks to it.

**"And Goodly Exhortation": *Al-Mawʿiẓah al-Ḥasanah***

The second instrument is *al-mawʿiẓah al-ḥasanah*, "goodly exhortation." The word *mawʿiẓah*, from *waʿaẓa* (v. 90, "He admonishes you"), denotes admonition — speech that moves the heart, that reminds, warns, encourages, softens. Where *ḥikmah* addresses the intellect, *mawʿiẓah* addresses the heart. And the exhortation is qualified as *ḥasanah*, good, beautiful — the commentators explain that admonition can be harsh or gentle, humiliating or uplifting, and the verse commands the good kind: the exhortation that draws rather than repels, that makes the hearer want the good rather than resent the one who urges it.

Al-Rāzī assigns the three instruments of the verse to three kinds of hearers, following the classical division of persuasion. Wisdom (demonstrative proof) is for the elite who can follow argument. Goodly exhortation (persuasive speech that moves the emotions toward truth) is for the generality who are moved by appeals to the heart. And disputation in the best manner is for the opponent who resists and must be answered. This reading, developed also by al-Ghazālī and Ibn Rushd, sees in the verse a complete theory of religious communication: proof, persuasion, and debate, each for its audience.

**"And Dispute With Them in the Most Virtuous Manner": *Jādilhum bi'llatī hiya aḥsan***

The third instrument is *jidāl*, disputation — argument with one who opposes. The verse commands it — *jādilhum*, "dispute with them" — and qualifies it: *bi'llatī hiya aḥsan*, "with that which is best." The commentators note the escalation of the qualifiers: the exhortation is *ḥasanah*, good; the disputation must be *aḥsan*, *best* — the superlative. Al-Zamakhsharī explains: disputation is the most dangerous of the three, because it can descend into quarreling, pride, and the desire to win rather than to convince; therefore its manner must be not merely good but the best possible.

What is disputation "in the best manner"? The commentators enumerate its features. Gentleness of speech, without harshness or insult. Attention to the strongest form of the opponent's position, not its weakest. The use of premises the opponent accepts, so that he is led from what he grants to what he denies. Acknowledgment of what is true in the opponent's view. The avoidance of provocation — the Qur'an forbids insulting the idolaters' gods lest they insult God in return (6:108). And the aim of guiding the opponent, not defeating him. The Qur'an states the same rule for disputation with the People of the Book:

> *"And do not dispute with the People of the Book except in the way that is best, except for those who do wrong among them; and say: We believe in what was revealed to us and revealed to you; and our God and your God is one, and we are Muslims to Him."* (Qur'an 29:46)

The verse in al-ʿAnkabūt (29:46) gives an example of the best manner: beginning with common ground ("we believe in what was revealed to you; our God and your God is one"). Al-Zamakhsharī uses an image: the caller who disputes harshly is like one striking cold iron — he exhausts himself and shapes nothing. The best disputation heats the iron first.

The commentators also record the model of Abraham's disputation with his people (6:76–79; 21:52–67) and with the king (2:258), and Moses' with Pharaoh, in which God commanded "speak to him with gentle speech, that perhaps he may be reminded or fear" (20:44) — gentleness even to Pharaoh. If Pharaoh was to be addressed gently, the commentators observe, no opponent is beneath the verse's *aḥsan*.

**The Three Instruments as a Whole**

The commentators read the three as a graded method rather than three separate options. The caller begins with wisdom — the clear statement of truth with its proof. If the hearer needs more, he adds exhortation — the appeal to the heart. If the hearer resists and argues, he disputes — in the best manner. Al-Rāzī: the three are the complete toolkit of the one who invites to God, and the verse's order is the order of their use. What the three have in common is that none is coercion, none is insult, and none is aimed at anything but the hearer's guidance. The verse rules out, by omission, every method that does not serve that aim: force, mockery, humiliation, and the desire to win.

**"Truly Thy Lord Is He Who Knows Best Who Strays From His Way"**

The verse's second half turns from the method to its limit: *inna rabbaka huwa aʿlamu bi-man ḍalla ʿan sabīlihi wa-huwa aʿlamu bi'l-muhtadīn*, "truly your Lord is He who knows best who has strayed from His way, and He knows best the guided." The commentators explain the connection. The caller uses wisdom, exhortation, and the best disputation; but the outcome — who accepts and who refuses — is not his to determine or even to know. God knows who has strayed and who is guided. The caller's task is the method; the result is God's.

This clause protects the caller from two errors that the commentators identify. The first is despair: if the caller thinks the outcome depends on him, he will be crushed by refusals. The verse tells him that the outcome is God's, and that his duty was discharged in the calling (v. 82, "upon you is only the clear conveyance"). The second is judgment: if the caller thinks he can identify the strayed and the guided, he will condemn those he should still invite and neglect those he wrongly counts as lost. The verse tells him that God knows best — the person who seems most lost may be nearest to guidance, and the caller does not know. Al-Rāzī: the clause keeps the caller calling, without despair and without presumption.

The pairing of *man ḍalla*, "who strays," and *al-muhtadīn*, "the guided," is the sūrah's recurring pairing (vv. 9, 36, 37, 93), and its appearance at the verse's close ties the method of *daʿwah* to the doctrine of guidance: the caller calls; God guides whom He wills; and the caller trusts Him with what he cannot see.

**The Verse as the Charter of Islamic Invitation**

The commentators regard verse 125 as the foundational text on how the religion is to be conveyed, and its influence on the tradition has been profound. It established that *daʿwah* is a duty of the community (3:104, 110). It established that its means are intellectual and moral, not coercive — the Qur'an's "no compulsion in religion" (2:256) is the negative form of this verse's positive method. It established the etiquette of debate that the scholars of *kalām* and the practitioners of interfaith dialogue drew upon. And it established the disposition of the caller: patient, gentle, learned, and humble about outcomes. The Prophet ﷺ embodied every element. His call was wise — he answered each questioner according to his need. His exhortation was beautiful — his sermons moved hearts to tears. His disputation was the best — he met the delegation of Najrān with courtesy, hosted them in his mosque, and argued from common ground. And he left the outcome to God, grieving over the refusals but not despairing, and never presuming to know who among his enemies would become his Companions.

**The Application: The Caller's Discipline**

The verse gives everyone who speaks of God to others — parent, teacher, friend, preacher — a discipline in three parts and a consolation. The discipline: speak with wisdom (know what you say, and fit it to the hearer); exhort beautifully (move the heart without wounding it); and if you must dispute, dispute in the best manner (gently, fairly, aiming at guidance and not victory). The consolation: the result is not yours. God knows who strays and who is guided, and He will judge; your account is the manner of your calling, not the number who answered. The one who has internalized this verse calls without anxiety and without arrogance — he does his part beautifully, and he leaves the rest to the Lord whose way he is calling to. The sūrah has argued its case for a hundred and twenty-five verses; this verse tells the reader how to carry the case forward, and it tells him that carrying it forward, in the best manner, is the whole of what he is asked.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:126

> **And if you punish, then punish with the like of that with which you were afflicted. But if you are patient, it is truly better for the patient.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Principle of Proportion, and the Better Path Beyond It**

Verse 125 gave the method of inviting to God. Verse 126 addresses what happens when the invitation is met not with argument but with injury: *wa-in ʿāqabtum fa-ʿāqibū bi-mithli mā ʿūqibtum bih*, "and if you punish, then punish with the like of what you were afflicted with." The verse establishes two things: a limit — retaliation may not exceed the injury — and a preference — patience is better than retaliation. The two together define the Islamic ethic of response to wrong: justice is permitted, excess is forbidden, and forgiveness is preferred.

**The Occasion: Uḥud and Ḥamzah**

The commentators are nearly unanimous about the verse's occasion, though its placement in a Makkan sūrah requires explanation. After the Battle of Uḥud, the Prophet ﷺ found the body of his uncle Ḥamzah ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib mutilated — his ears and nose cut off, his belly opened, his liver taken out by Hind bint ʿUtbah, who had hired the Abyssinian slave Waḥshī to kill him in revenge for her father. The Prophet, seeing this, said:

> *"If God gives me victory over Quraysh, I will mutilate thirty of their men."* And the Companions said: *"By God, if God gives us victory over them, we will mutilate them as no Arab has ever mutilated anyone."* Then God revealed: *"And if you punish, then punish with the like of that with which you were afflicted. But if you are patient, it is truly better for the patient."* And the Prophet said: *"Rather, we shall be patient."* And he expiated his oath and forbade mutilation. (al-Tirmidhī 3129; Aḥmad 21229; al-Ḥākim; graded ḥasan)

Al-Qurṭubī, al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabarī, al-Ṭūsī, and others record this. The verse's Madinan occasion within a Makkan sūrah is explained in several ways. Some hold that verses 126–128 were revealed at Uḥud and placed here by the Prophet's instruction, as the Qur'an's arrangement was determined by revelation and not by chronology. Others hold that the verses were revealed in Makkah, when the believers were being tortured and desired revenge, and were then *recited* by the Prophet at Uḥud as the applicable ruling — so that the reports describe an application, not a first revelation. Al-Qurṭubī records both views; al-Rāzī inclines to the second, noting that the sūrah's Makkan themes continue through verse 128 without break. On either view, the verse's meaning is the same.

**"If You Punish, Then Punish With the Like"**

The verse's first clause permits retaliation and limits it. The verb *ʿāqaba* means to punish, to requite, to retaliate — and the commentators note that its use for the *initial* injury (*mā ʿūqibtum bih*, "what you were punished with") is a case of *mushākalah*, the rhetorical matching of terms: the original wrong is called "punishment" so that the response can be called by the same name, though the wrong was aggression and the response is justice. The Qur'an uses the same device in 2:194 ("whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him in the like") and 42:40 ("the recompense of an evil is an evil like it").

The limit is *bi-mithli*, "with the like." Retaliation may equal the injury; it may not exceed it. The commentators identify this as the principle of *qiṣāṣ*, just retaliation, stated generally in 2:178–179 and 5:45 ("a life for a life, an eye for an eye..."), and here applied to the case of wartime injury. The Companions' vow to mutilate "as no Arab has ever mutilated" was a vow to exceed; the verse forbade it. The Prophet's own vow to mutilate thirty for one was a vow to exceed; the verse forbade it, and he expiated the oath.

Al-Rāzī draws out the principle's moral significance. Human beings, when wronged, desire not equivalence but excess — to make the wrongdoer suffer more than they suffered, to deter by disproportion, to satisfy anger that equivalence does not satisfy. The verse forbids this. It permits *justice* — the like for the like — and forbids *vengeance* — the more for the less. The Qur'an states the same limit in 17:33: "whoever is killed unjustly, We have given his heir authority, but let him not exceed in killing." And the Prophet forbade mutilation absolutely after this verse: "Do not mutilate" (Muslim 1731).

**"But If You Are Patient, It Is Truly Better for the Patient"**

The verse's second clause names the higher path: *wa-la-in ṣabartum la-huwa khayrun li'l-ṣābirīn*, "and if you are patient, it is surely better for the patient." The emphatic *la-in... la-huwa* gives the statement the force of an oath. Patience — here meaning the forgoing of retaliation, the endurance of the wrong without requiting it — is *better*.

The commentators explain the relationship between the two clauses. The first permits; the second recommends. Retaliation within the limit is *lawful* — the wronged party has the right to it, and the Qur'an does not deny it. Patience is *better* — it is what God prefers and rewards more richly. The believer may choose either; the verse tells him which is higher. The Qur'an states the same structure in 42:40–43: "the recompense of an evil is an evil like it; but whoever pardons and makes reconciliation, his reward is with God... and whoever is patient and forgives — that is of the matters requiring resolve."

Why is patience better? The commentators give several reasons. It breaks the cycle: retaliation, even proportionate, invites counter-retaliation, and the cycle continues; patience ends it. It is more difficult, and therefore more meritorious: to forgo a right one holds is harder than to exercise it. It is more effective in the mission: the caller of verse 125 who responds to injury with patience is more likely to win the injurer than one who responds with equivalent force; the Qur'an says, "Repel with that which is better, and behold, the one between whom and you was enmity will be as though he were a devoted friend" (41:34). And it is the practice of the prophets: Joseph forgave his brothers (12:92); the Prophet forgave Makkah.

The word "for the patient" (*li'l-ṣābirīn*) rather than "for you" has been noted. Al-Zamakhsharī explains the shift from address to description as a compliment: those who choose patience are named by the virtue they chose, and the goodness is affirmed for the class of the patient — of whom the addressees, if they choose it, become members.

**The Prophet's Choice**

The occasion of revelation records the Prophet's response: "Rather, we shall be patient." He was offered by the verse the lawful path of proportionate retaliation for the mutilation of his uncle, and he chose the better path. The commentators note the completion of this choice at the conquest of Makkah, six years later. Hind, who had mutilated Ḥamzah, came to accept Islam; the Prophet accepted her. Waḥshī, who had killed him, came; the Prophet accepted his Islam, asking only that he not show his face to him, because the memory was too painful (al-Bukhārī 4072). The murderers of his uncle were forgiven. The verse's "better for the patient" was demonstrated in the most extreme case a human being could face.

**Is the Verse Abrogated?**

Some early commentators suggested that verses 126–127, with their counsel of patience, were abrogated by the later commands to fight (9:5, the "verse of the sword"). The majority rejected this, and al-Qurṭubī, al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabarī, and al-Ṭūsī explain why. The verse does not forbid fighting; it regulates the *response to injury* — permitting the equivalent and preferring patience — and this regulation remained in force through the period of fighting and after. The Prophet applied it at Uḥud, before the verse of the sword, and at the conquest, after it. The principles of proportion (2:194; 17:33; 42:40) and of the superiority of forgiveness (42:43; 3:134) are stated in Madinan verses that were not abrogated. The verse is a permanent rule of the believer's conduct, in war and in peace: retaliate at most in kind, and prefer to forgive.

**The Verse and Verse 125**

The commentators connect verse 126 to the method of verse 125. The caller invites with wisdom, exhortation, and the best disputation. What if the invited respond with injury — as the Makkans responded to the Prophet, and the Quraysh at Uḥud? Verse 126 answers: you may requite in kind; but patience is better. The connection teaches that the caller's method extends beyond speech to conduct under provocation. The one who disputes "in the best manner" (v. 125) and then retaliates disproportionately has undone his disputation; the one who is patient has confirmed it. The best manner of speech and the better path of patience are one ethic.

**The Application: The Two Paths Before the Wronged**

The verse gives every believer who has been wronged a clear map. He has a right: to requite in kind, no more. He has a better option: to be patient and forgo the right. The verse forbids the third option — excess — absolutely, and it does not compel the second; but it tells him, with an oath, which is better. In practice, this governs every response to injury, from the smallest slight to the gravest crime: the believer measures his response against the injury and does not exceed it; and then he asks whether he can rise above it, knowing that if he can, "it is better for the patient." The Prophet ﷺ, standing over his uncle's mutilated body, was given this choice and said, "Rather, we shall be patient." The verse asks the believer, in his smaller trials, to say the same.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:127

> **And be patient, and your patience is only through God. And grieve not over them, nor be in distress on account of what they plot.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Command, and Its Source of Strength**

Verse 126 said that patience is better than retaliation. Verse 127 commands it — *wa-ṣbir*, "and be patient" — and then, in the same breath, names where the patience comes from: *wa-mā ṣabruka illā bi'llāh*, "and your patience is only through God." The verse is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ in the singular, and the commentators read it as God's direct counsel to him at the moment of his greatest grief and provocation: be patient; you cannot be patient by yourself; do not grieve over those who refuse; do not be distressed by what they plot. Each clause is a mercy, and together they constitute the sūrah's final instruction to its bearer before its closing assurance.

**"And Be Patient": *Wa-ṣbir***

The command is absolute and unqualified: *iṣbir*, "be patient." Verse 126 had presented patience as the better of two options; verse 127 commands it as the Prophet's course. The commentators note that the Prophet's rank required the higher path: what is permitted to the community as an option is enjoined on the Prophet as a duty, because he is the model, and the model must show the best. The Prophet's response at Uḥud — "Rather, we shall be patient" — was his obedience to this command.

*Ṣabr*, patience, was discussed at verses 42, 96, and 110. Its three classical kinds — patience in obedience, patience against sin, and patience under affliction — are all relevant here, but the third is primary: the Prophet is commanded to endure the injury, the mockery, the plotting, and the refusal of his people without being broken by them and without abandoning the better path.

**"And Your Patience Is Only Through God": *Wa-mā ṣabruka illā bi'llāh***

The verse's central clause is its most theologically rich: *wa-mā ṣabruka illā bi'llāh*, "and your patience is not except by God." The restrictive structure — *mā... illā* — denies that patience has any source but God. The Prophet is commanded to be patient; and immediately told that the patience he is commanded to have is not his own achievement but God's gift.

The commentators draw out the meaning. Al-Ṭabarī: your patience is by God's help (*tawfīq*) and strengthening; without Him you would not be able. Al-Zamakhsharī: the verse guards against the pride that might follow patience — the one who endures a great trial may think the endurance was his own strength; the verse tells him it was God's. Al-Rāzī: the clause is both consolation and instruction. Consolation, because the Prophet, commanded to a patience that seems beyond human capacity (he had just seen his uncle mutilated), is told that the capacity will be supplied — he does not have to produce it from himself. Instruction, because the way to obtain the patience is to seek it from its source: to turn to God for the strength one lacks.

The clause applies a principle the Qur'an states generally: "There is no power and no strength except by God" (*lā ḥawla wa-lā quwwata illā bi'llāh*, the formula the Prophet called "a treasure from the treasures of Paradise," al-Bukhārī 4205; Muslim 2704). Every human capacity — including the capacity to endure — is a divine loan. The one who knows this seeks the capacity from God rather than straining to produce it alone, and is spared both the despair of failure and the pride of success.

The Prophet's own supplications show the clause in practice. In the hardest moment of his mission, after his rejection at Ṭāʾif, he prayed: "O God, to You I complain of my weakness, my lack of resources, and my lowliness before people... If You are not angry with me, I do not care; but Your protection is more encompassing for me" (al-Ṭabarānī; Ibn Isḥāq). The prayer does not claim strength; it confesses weakness and asks for what verse 127 says patience requires — God.

**"And Grieve Not Over Them": *Wa-lā taḥzan ʿalayhim***

The third clause is *wa-lā taḥzan ʿalayhim*, "and do not grieve over them." The pronoun "them" refers to the disbelievers who refuse the call — the Makkans, and by extension all who reject. The Prophet grieved over them intensely; the Qur'an records his grief in the strongest terms: "Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief over them if they do not believe in this message" (18:6); "Perhaps you would kill yourself because they are not believers" (26:3); "Let not your soul waste away in grief over them" (35:8). The grief was that of a man who saw his people walking toward destruction and could not turn them.

The verse does not forbid the feeling — the Prophet's compassion was praised (9:128, "concerned over you") — but its excess: the grief that consumes, that undermines the mission, that treats the refusal as the Prophet's failure. The commentators connect the prohibition to verse 82 ("upon you is only the clear conveyance") and verse 125 ("your Lord knows best who strays"): the outcome is not the Prophet's; therefore the grief over the outcome should not destroy him. Al-Rāzī: the Prophet is told not to grieve because grief presupposes that something within his power was lost, and the guidance of the disbelievers was never within his power.

**"Nor Be in Distress on Account of What They Plot": *Wa-lā taku fī ḍayqin mimmā yamkurūn***

The fourth clause is *wa-lā taku fī ḍayqin mimmā yamkurūn*, "and do not be in distress from what they plot." The word *ḍayq* (read *ḍīq* by some) denotes constriction, narrowness, tightness — the tightening of the chest under anxiety. The Qur'an uses the image for the Prophet's distress: "We know that your breast is constricted by what they say" (15:97). And *yamkurūn*, "they plot," is the verb of *makr*, scheming, used in verses 26 and 45 for the plotting of the disbelievers against the prophets.

The Makkans plotted against the Prophet continuously — to discredit him, to isolate him, to bribe him, and finally to kill him (8:30). The verse tells him not to be constricted by their plotting. The commentators give the reason from the sūrah's own earlier verses: God is aware of the plots (v. 45) and will bring them to nothing, as He brought the plots of the ancients to nothing (v. 26, "God came upon their building from the foundations"). The plotter's plot returns upon him (35:43). The Prophet's chest need not tighten over schemes whose outcome God has already determined.

**The Four Clauses as a Whole**

The commentators read the verse's four clauses as a complete counsel for one who bears a message under persecution. Be patient — the duty. Your patience is through God — the source. Do not grieve over them — the release from responsibility for outcomes. Do not be distressed by their plots — the release from fear of enemies. The first two concern the Prophet's inner state under injury; the last two concern his inner state toward those who injure. Together they describe a man who endures, draws his endurance from God, does not blame himself for others' refusal, and does not fear others' schemes. This is the state the sūrah has been preparing him for since verse 1, and the verse names it as his final instruction.

**The Parallel Verses**

The verse's language is echoed in several other places addressed to the Prophet, and the parallels show that this counsel was repeated to him throughout his mission. In al-Ḥijr: "We know that your breast is constricted by what they say; so glorify your Lord with praise and be among those who prostrate" (15:97–98) — the remedy for constriction is worship. In al-Naml: "And do not grieve over them, and do not be in distress from what they plot" (27:70) — the identical words. In Yā Sīn: "So let not their speech grieve you; truly We know what they conceal and what they declare" (36:76). In Luqmān: "And whoever disbelieves — let not his disbelief grieve you; to Us is their return" (31:23). The repetition marks the counsel as one the Prophet needed to hear often, because the grief and the constriction returned often.

**The Application: Patience That Is Not One's Own**

The verse gives every believer who endures hardship — in the mission of calling to God or in any trial — a counsel and a correction. The counsel: be patient, do not be consumed by grief over what you cannot change, and do not be constricted by fear of what others scheme. The correction: your patience is not yours. The believer who tries to be patient by his own strength will fail, or will succeed and become proud; the one who seeks patience from God will receive it and remain humble. The practical form of this is supplication — asking God for the *ṣabr* one lacks, as the Qur'an teaches: "Our Lord, pour patience upon us" (2:250; 7:126). The verb *afrigh*, "pour," in that prayer is exact: patience is poured from above, not generated from within. Verse 127 tells the Prophet, and everyone who follows him, that this is the only place it comes from — and that the One who commands the patience is the One who supplies it.

---

## Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:128

> **Truly God is with those who are reverent and those who are virtuous.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Sūrah's Last Word**

The sūrah began with the announcement that the command of God has come and with the declaration of His transcendence above all that is associated with Him (v. 1). It ends with a promise of nearness: *inna Allāha maʿa alladhīna ittaqaw wa'lladhīna hum muḥsinūn*, "truly God is with those who are God-fearing and those who do good." Between the first verse and the last lies the whole argument — the signs, the blessings, the warnings, the parables, the law, the example of Abraham, the method of the call, the counsel of patience — and the argument closes on the simplest and most sustaining assurance the Qur'an gives: God is *with* those who fear Him and do good. The verse is the answer to verse 127's command of patience: be patient, do not grieve, do not be distressed — *because God is with you*.

**"Truly God Is With": *Inna Allāha maʿa***

The verse asserts God's *maʿiyyah*, His "being with." The preposition *maʿa*, "with," denotes accompaniment, companionship, presence. The commentators distinguish two senses in which the Qur'an speaks of God being "with" people.

The first is the general *maʿiyyah* of knowledge and power: God is with all creatures in the sense that He knows them, sees them, and encompasses them — "He is with you wherever you are" (57:4); "there is no secret conversation of three but He is the fourth" (58:7). This *maʿiyyah* applies to believer and disbeliever alike; nothing escapes it.

The second is the special *maʿiyyah* of support, help, protection, and love: God is with His servants in the sense that He aids them, guides them, defends them, and brings them through. This is the sense of verse 128, as the commentators agree, because the verse restricts it to two classes — the God-fearing and the doers of good — and the restriction would be meaningless if the general sense were intended. The Qur'an uses this special sense repeatedly: "God is with the patient" (2:153, 249; 8:46, 66); "Do not grieve; truly God is with us" (9:40, the Prophet to Abū Bakr in the cave); "Truly I am with you both; I hear and I see" (20:46, to Moses and Aaron before Pharaoh).

Al-Rāzī explains the special *maʿiyyah* as the sum of God's care: His help against enemies, His guidance in confusion, His provision in need, His protection in danger, His forgiveness in failure, and His companionship in loneliness. To have God "with" one in this sense is to have everything, because the One who is with one is the One who controls all. Ibn Taymiyyah, discussing the two senses, notes that the special *maʿiyyah* does not imply that God is physically located with the servant — He is above His Throne, and "there is nothing like Him" (42:11; cf. v. 74 of this sūrah) — but that His support and care are present with the servant in every place and moment.

**The Verse in Its Immediate Context**

The commentators connect verse 128 to verse 127. The Prophet was commanded to be patient, told that his patience was through God, and told not to grieve or be distressed. Verse 128 gives the ground: God is with the God-fearing and the doers of good — and the Prophet is the foremost of both. The patience is possible because God is with him; the grief is unnecessary because God is with him; the distress at plotting is groundless because God is with him. The Prophet said exactly this to Abū Bakr in the cave, when the Makkans stood at its mouth: "What do you think of two, of whom God is the third?" (al-Bukhārī 3653; Muslim 2381). The verse's *maʿiyyah* was the Prophet's actual experience in the moment of greatest danger.

**"Those Who Are Reverent": *Alladhīna ittaqaw***

The first class is *alladhīna ittaqaw*, "those who have *taqwā*" — the God-fearing, the God-conscious, those who guard themselves against His displeasure. The word *taqwā*, from *waqā*, to protect, denotes the disposition of one who places a shield between himself and what God has forbidden — out of awe of God, awareness of His watching, and fear of His punishment. It was discussed at verse 2 ("fear Me"), verse 30 ("those who feared God"), verse 31 ("thus does God reward the God-fearing"), and verse 52 ("will you then fear other than God?"). The sūrah's repeated command of fear — of God alone (vv. 51–52) — finds its reward in the final verse: those who feared Him have Him with them.

The commentators explain the content of *taqwā* here as the avoidance of what God forbade — the *shirk* the sūrah condemned, the ingratitude, the fabrication, the oath-breaking, the injustice, the excess in retaliation. The God-fearing are those who kept themselves from these. Their fear was not terror but the reverent caution of one who knows Whom he stands before.

**"And Those Who Are Virtuous": *Wa'lladhīna hum muḥsinūn***

The second class is *alladhīna hum muḥsinūn*, "those who are doers of good" — those characterized by *iḥsān*. The word was discussed at verse 90, where God commanded *al-iḥsān* alongside justice, and its definition from the hadith of Gabriel was given: "to worship God as though you see Him; for if you do not see Him, He sees you" (al-Bukhārī 50; Muslim 8). The *muḥsinūn* are those who do good — and do it well, beautifully, with the consciousness of God's presence — beyond what mere duty requires.

The commentators note the pairing of the two classes, and its logic. *Taqwā* is the negative side of righteousness: avoiding what God forbade. *Iḥsān* is the positive side: doing what God loves, and doing it with excellence. Al-Rāzī: the God-fearing one refrains; the *muḥsin* acts; and the complete servant is both — he avoids the forbidden and excels in the good. God is with those who combine the two. The Qur'an pairs them elsewhere in the same sense: "Truly God loves the *muḥsinīn*" (2:195; 3:134, 148; 5:13, 93) and "God loves the *muttaqīn*" (3:76; 9:4, 7).

The construction *alladhīna hum muḥsinūn*, with the pronoun *hum*, "they," inserted, has been noted. Al-Zamakhsharī reads the pronoun as emphasizing that *iḥsān* is their settled character — they *are* doers of good, not merely people who have done good — matching the perfect tense *ittaqaw*, "they have feared," which describes a completed disposition. God is with those whose fear and excellence are who they are.

**The Verse as the Sūrah's Conclusion**

The commentators regard verse 128 as the perfect ending to the sūrah, and they trace the reasons. The sūrah is about God's blessings and the response they demand. The response has been named in many forms — gratitude, submission, worship of God alone, justice, patience — and the final verse names the two dispositions that sum them all: *taqwā* and *iḥsān*. And it names the reward that sums all rewards: God's being *with* one. The "good life" of verse 97, the "good in this world" of verses 30, 41, and 122, the "reward according to the best" of verses 96–97, the forgiveness and mercy of verses 110 and 119 — all are contained in *maʿiyyah*. The one with whom God is has the good life, the good in this world, the best reward, the forgiveness, and the mercy, because he has the Giver of all of them.

The verse also closes the sūrah's structural arc. Verse 1 declared God transcendent — "exalted is He above what they associate." Verse 128 declares Him near — "God is with those who fear Him." The two are not in tension; they are the two poles of the Islamic doctrine of God. He is beyond all likeness (v. 74) and He is with His servants (v. 128). The sūrah that demonstrated His transcendence through creation ends by promising His nearness through righteousness. Al-Rāzī: the servant who has understood the sūrah knows that the God above the heavens is the God at his side.

**The Prophet's Application of the Verse**

The Prophet ﷺ is reported to have recited this verse in the context of its occasion. After Uḥud, having chosen patience over retaliation (v. 126), having been commanded to patience and told not to grieve (v. 127), he was given this verse as the seal: God is with the God-fearing and the doers of good. And his subsequent conduct — the forbidding of mutilation, the treaty of al-Ḥudaybiyah, the forgiveness at the conquest — was the conduct of a man who knew God was with him and therefore needed neither vengeance nor fear. The verse was, for him, not an abstract promise but the fact that governed his response to every injury.

**The Application: Living With God**

The verse gives the believer the sūrah's final and most practical gift: a promise that reorders everything. If God is with him — helping, guiding, protecting, loving — then no enemy's plot is decisive (v. 127), no refusal by others is his failure (v. 125), no hardship is unbearable (v. 42), no loss is final (v. 96), and no loneliness is complete (v. 9:40). The condition is stated in two words: *taqwā* and *iḥsān* — guard yourself from what God forbade, and do good as though you see Him. The one who meets this condition may say, in whatever cave he finds himself, what the Prophet said to his companion: "Do not grieve; truly God is with us." The sūrah's hundred and twenty-eight verses of argument, warning, and promise resolve into this. The blessings were countless (v. 18); the greatest of them is named last; and it is not a thing given but a Presence — the Giver Himself, with those who feared Him and did good.
